Why C: A loan repaid in monthly parts is an installment loan. A CD is a deposit that earns interest for you.
Why D: A checking account allows frequent withdrawals. A CD locks money for a set term, which is why it pays a higher rate.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does FDIC insurance protect?
A: Cash that is kept in a drawer at home for safety
B: Bank deposits up to the legal limit if a bank fails
C: Stocks that you own through a broker or an app
D: Your credit score at the credit bureaus on your report
Why A: Cash kept at home is not in a bank, so FDIC insurance does not cover it if it is lost or stolen.
Why B: FDIC insurance protects bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category if the bank fails.
Why C: Stocks held through a broker are not covered by FDIC insurance and can lose value. Brokerage accounts may have SIPC coverage for broker failure only.
Why D: Credit scores are tracked by credit bureaus, and FDIC insurance has nothing to do with them. It covers bank deposits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person has $300,000 in one account at a single FDIC-insured bank. How much is insured, in the standard individual case?
Why A: $300,000 is the whole balance, but FDIC insurance has a limit per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so the entire amount is not insured.
Why B: $50,000 is an old, lower figure that does not match today's limit. The standard limit is $250,000.
Why C: The standard FDIC limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so $250,000 of the $300,000 is insured and $50,000 is not.
Why D: $100,000 was the limit before 2008 and no longer applies. Today's standard limit is $250,000.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a savings goal?
A: A specific amount you plan to save by a date
B: A required bill that comes in every month
C: A plan for repaying a loan over time in parts
D: A fee that is charged by a bank for an account
Why A: A savings goal is a specific amount you plan to save by a certain date, such as $600 in six months, which gives you something to aim for.
Why B: A required monthly bill is a fixed expense. A savings goal is something you choose to work toward.
Why C: A plan for repaying a loan is a repayment schedule. A savings goal is about building money, not paying off debt.
Why D: A bank fee is a charge for services. A savings goal is a target amount you set for yourself.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Leo wants $600 in 6 months. How much must he save each month?
Why A: $3,600 is $600 times 6, which multiplies instead of dividing. The monthly amount must be $600 split over 6 months.
Why B: $36 is far too small; it would only reach $216 after 6 months. Dividing $600 by 6 gives the right monthly amount.
Why C: $60 a month for 6 months totals only $360, which falls short of $600. The goal requires $600 / 6 = $100 a month.
Why D: Monthly savings equal the goal divided by months: $600 / 6 = $100. Saving that amount each month for 6 months reaches the $600 goal.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
A: Skipping saving so you can spend a lot more money now
B: Spending on wants before you pay the bills so you enjoy it
C: Borrowing money to give yourself a reward each month
D: Moving money to savings before spending on other things
Why A: Skipping saving to spend more is the opposite of paying yourself first, which puts saving ahead of spending.
Why B: Spending on wants before bills is risky and not what pay yourself first means; it is about saving, not wants.
Why C: Borrowing for a reward adds debt. Paying yourself first uses your own income, moved to savings before other spending.
Why D: Pay yourself first means moving money into savings as soon as you are paid, before spending on other things, so saving becomes a habit.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is automatic saving?
A: Regular automatic transfers into savings
B: Withdrawing money from savings every week
C: Closing the savings account once a year
D: Spending money automatically on small items
Why A: Automatic saving sets up regular transfers into savings, often each payday, so saving happens without relying on willpower.
Why B: Withdrawing money from savings every week would drain the account. Automatic saving adds money, it does not take it out.
Why C: Closing the account once a year does not build savings. Automatic saving keeps the account open and growing.
Why D: Automatic spending on small items is the opposite of saving. Automatic saving moves money into savings, not out for purchases.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the Rule of 72 used for?
A: Setting the age at which a person must retire
B: Estimating how long money takes to double
C: Finding the monthly payment on a loan
D: Calculating the taxes owed on income
Why A: The Rule of 72 does not set a retirement age. It estimates how long it takes for money to double.
Why B: Dividing 72 by the annual interest rate estimates the years it takes money to double. At 8 percent, money doubles in about 9 years.
Why C: Loan payments are found with payment formulas or calculators. The Rule of 72 only estimates doubling time for growth.
Why D: Taxes owed are found using tax tables and rates. The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years will it take money earning 4% to double?
A: 72 years
B: 30 years
C: 18 years
D: 4 years
Why A: 72 years is the number 72 itself, not divided by the rate. The Rule of 72 divides 72 by the interest rate.
Why B: 30 years does not match the rule. Dividing 72 by 4 gives 18, so money doubles in about 18 years at 4 percent.
Why C: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate: 72 / 4 = 18 years. A higher rate would shorten that time.
Why D: 4 years is just the rate itself. The rule divides 72 by 4, which gives 18 years, not 4.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a high-yield savings account?
A: A stock account used to trade shares
B: A checking account that pays no interest
C: A loan that charges a high interest rate
D: A savings account paying a higher rate
Why A: A stock account is a brokerage account used to trade shares, not a savings account, and it is not FDIC insured.
Why B: A checking account that pays no interest is not a high yield account. High yield means a higher interest rate on savings.
Why C: A loan that charges high interest is a borrowing product. A high yield savings account pays you interest.
Why D: A high yield savings account pays a higher interest rate than a regular savings account, often at online banks, and is typically FDIC insured.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is inflation's effect on savings kept in cash?
A: Purchasing power declines over time
B: The cash earns interest automatically
C: The cash doubles each year on its own
D: Purchasing power increases over time
Why A: Inflation raises prices, so cash buys less over time. Cash that is not growing loses purchasing power.
Why B: Cash kept as cash earns no interest. Only money in an interest paying account earns interest.
Why C: Cash does not grow on its own. It stays the same amount while prices rise, so it loses value in real terms.
Why D: Inflation reduces purchasing power rather than increasing it, because the same amount buys fewer goods as prices go up.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A savings account pays 1% interest while inflation is 3%. What is happening to the real value of the savings?
A: It is doubling every year on its own with no help at all
B: It is staying exactly the same, as nothing has changed
C: It is decreasing because inflation outpaces interest
D: It is increasing because interest earned is positive
Why A: Savings do not double every year on their own. At 1 percent interest, the balance grows very slowly.
Why B: The balance grows by 1 percent, but prices rise 3 percent, so the real value is not staying the same.
Why C: Real value falls because inflation (3 percent) is higher than interest (1 percent). The real return is about 1 - 3 = negative 2 percent a year.
Why D: Interest is positive, but real value depends on inflation too. With prices up 3 percent and interest only 1 percent, buying power declines.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main purpose of a college savings plan such as a 529?
A: To save for a first home with tax advantages
B: To save for education expenses with tax advantages
C: To build a general emergency fund with tax advantages
D: To pay off credit card bills each month for the family
Why A: A 529 plan is built for education costs. Using it for a home purchase is not a qualified expense and can bring taxes and penalties.
Why B: A 529 plan is a tax advantaged account for education costs, with tax free growth and withdrawals when used for qualified expenses.
Why C: A 529 plan is meant for qualified education costs. Emergency savings belong in a flexible account, since non education withdrawals from a 529 can bring taxes and penalties.
Why D: A 529 plan is for education costs, not paying off credit cards. Credit card payments are not qualified expenses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which of these is a good reason to keep money in a savings account instead of a checking account?
A: Savings accounts allow unlimited checks
B: Savings accounts require no deposits
C: Savings accounts have no safety at all
D: Savings accounts usually pay interest
Why A: Savings accounts do not allow unlimited checks. Checking accounts are the ones made for frequent payments and check writing.
Why B: Deposits are needed to build savings. A savings account is not defined by requiring no deposits.
Why C: Savings accounts are usually FDIC insured, so claiming they have no safety at all is false.
Why D: Savings accounts usually pay interest, while many checking accounts pay little or none, which is the main reason to keep savings there.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main reason to read a contract before signing?
A: To avoid having to talk with the seller in person
B: To make the document last longer on a shelf for years
C: To understand your rights, fees and obligations
D: To make sure the font is easy to read on screen
Why A: Contracts are about legal terms, not conversation; avoiding the seller does not protect you, and reading the document is what actually prevents costly surprises later.
Why B: Reading has no effect on how long paper lasts; the purpose of reviewing a contract is to learn the terms you are legally agreeing to follow.
Why C: Reading shows your rights, any fees or penalties, and your obligations before you sign. A signed contract is legally binding, so surprises found afterward are usually your responsibility.
Why D: Font readability is a minor formatting detail; the real reason to read is to learn the binding terms, costs and duties the contract places on you.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A buyer is told 'sign now or lose the deal' on a big purchase. What is the smartest reaction?
A: Slow down, compare options and read the terms
B: Share financial details with the seller right away
C: Sign immediately to avoid missing out on the deal
D: Sign without reading to save time and effort today
Why A: High-pressure deadlines are a classic sales tactic. Slowing down lets you compare competing offers, read every term, ask questions, and walk away if the deal is not truly good.
Why B: Sharing financial details such as account or Social Security numbers with a pushy seller increases fraud risk and does nothing to help you evaluate the deal.
Why C: Signing immediately because of pressure is exactly what high-pressure sellers want; you could miss hidden fees or poor terms and have little chance to reconsider.
Why D: Signing without reading means agreeing to unknown fees, penalties and obligations; a contract is binding whether or not you read it, so skipping it is risky.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which payment method gives the strongest protection against unauthorized charges in many cases?
A: A gift card
B: A credit card
C: Cash on delivery
D: A wire transfer
Why A: Gift cards work like cash, so if one is lost, stolen or used by a scammer, there is generally little or no way to recover the money.
Why B: Federal law caps cardholder liability for unauthorized charges at $50 and lets you dispute charges while the bank investigates, so you are not out your own money.
Why C: Cash on delivery means paying before you can verify the goods, and there is no automatic dispute process, so recovering money from a bad seller is difficult.
Why D: Wire transfers are nearly instant and very hard to reverse, which is why scammers prefer them; they offer little consumer protection against unauthorized or fraudulent payments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a consumer right?
A: The right to ignore store policies if the price is cheap
B: The right to be informed and protected from deception
C: The right to avoid paying sales tax on purchases
D: The right to buy anything you want for free at all
Why A: Store policies such as return rules apply regardless of price, and consumer rights do not let buyers ignore them; rights concern fair treatment, not exemption from rules.
Why B: Core consumer rights, such as those in the Consumer Bill of Rights, include safety, being informed, choice and being heard, which protect buyers from fraud and misleading claims.
Why C: Sales tax is a legal obligation set by state and local governments; consumer rights do not exempt buyers from it on their purchases.
Why D: No law gives people free goods; consumer rights protect fair treatment and honest information in the marketplace, not a right to get products without paying.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which agency helps protect consumers from deceptive advertising?
A: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
B: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
C: The Social Security Administration
D: The Federal Reserve Board system
Why A: The FTC enforces laws against unfair or deceptive practices, including false advertising, and also takes consumer complaints and shuts down scams, making it the main consumer protection agency.
Why B: The IRS collects federal taxes and enforces the tax code; it has no primary role in policing deceptive advertising claims made to consumers.
Why C: The Social Security Administration runs retirement, disability and survivor benefit programs, not consumer protection or advertising regulation of businesses.
Why D: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and supervises banks to keep the financial system stable; it does not regulate advertising claims aimed at consumers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is credit?
A: Money that you receive as a gift from your relatives each year
B: Money that you earn from a regular paycheck at work
C: Money that you deposit into a savings account each month
D: Borrowing money or buying now with a promise to pay later
Why A: A gift is money given freely with no repayment expected, so it is not credit, which always involves an obligation to repay the lender later.
Why B: Paycheck earnings are income you have already worked for, not borrowed funds; credit is a different concept because it creates a debt that must be repaid.
Why C: Deposits into savings are your own money being set aside; credit is the opposite, since you use someone else's money and owe it back.
Why D: Credit lets you obtain money, goods or services now and repay later, usually with interest, based on the lender's trust that you will pay as promised.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a credit score?
A: A number that shows how much money you have saved up in total
B: A number that shows how many credit cards you currently own or carry
C: A number that shows how likely you are to repay borrowed money
D: A number that shows how much you earn each year at work
Why A: Savings are shown on bank statements and are not part of a credit score, which is calculated from your borrowing and repayment behavior instead.
Why B: The number of cards is only a small part of the picture; a credit score measures repayment reliability, not simply how many cards you hold.
Why C: A credit score, often 300 to 850 in the FICO model, summarizes your credit report to predict how likely you are to repay debts, which lenders use to decide approvals and rates.
Why D: Income is not part of a credit score calculation; lenders may ask for income separately, but the score reflects your credit history only.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which factor has the largest impact on a typical credit score?
A: Payment history
B: Your age in years
C: Your favorite store
D: Your zip code
Why A: Payment history is the largest FICO factor, about 35 percent of the score, because lenders care most about whether you pay bills on time.
Why B: Age in years is not a factor in credit scores, and the law prohibits using age to discriminate in credit; length of credit history is different.
Why C: Your favorite store has no effect on your score; only reported credit behavior such as payments and balances is used in scoring models.
Why D: Zip code is not used in credit scoring, and using location to discriminate could violate fair lending laws; the score uses credit account data.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is credit utilization?
A: The number of credit cards in your wallet
B: The age of your oldest credit card account now
C: The share of available credit you are using
D: The interest rate on your credit card balance
Why A: Counting cards in your wallet is not utilization; utilization compares balances to credit limits, whereas the number of accounts is a separate smaller factor.
Why B: The age of your oldest account relates to length of credit history, a different scoring factor from utilization, which looks at how much of your limit you use.
Why C: Utilization is your balances divided by your credit limits, shown as a percent. Keeping it under about 30 percent helps your score, and lower is generally better.
Why D: Interest rate (APR) is the cost of borrowing and is not what utilization measures; utilization compares the balance you carry to your available limit.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A card has a $2,000 limit and a $500 balance. What is the credit utilization?
Why A: 50 percent would require a $1,000 balance on a $2,000 limit; here $500 divided by $2,000 is only 0.25, so this is too high.
Why B: Utilization equals balance divided by limit: $500 / $2,000 = 0.25, or 25 percent. This is under the commonly recommended 30 percent mark for healthy credit scores.
Why C: 75 percent would mean a $1,500 balance on a $2,000 limit; with a $500 balance the ratio is $500 / $2,000, which equals 25 percent, not 75.
Why D: 400 percent comes from dividing limit by balance ($2,000 / $500 = 4) which inverts the formula; utilization is balance divided by limit, giving 25 percent.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: On a loan or credit card, what is APR?
A: The total balance that you owe on the card this month
B: The credit limit that is set on your card by the bank
C: The amount of your required monthly payment on the account
D: The yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage
Why A: The balance is the amount owed right now; APR is a rate that describes the yearly cost of borrowing, not a dollar balance.
Why B: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow on the card, set by the issuer; APR is the interest rate and is unrelated to the limit.
Why C: The monthly payment is a dollar amount due each billing cycle; APR is a percentage rate and does not by itself tell you the payment.
Why D: APR, annual percentage rate, expresses the yearly cost of credit including interest and certain fees, letting you compare loans and cards on equal terms.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What happens if you pay only the minimum on a credit card balance?
A: Interest stops being charged on the balance
B: Your credit limit doubles right away with no review
C: The balance is erased from the account immediately
D: Interest keeps building and the debt lasts longer
Why A: Interest continues on any unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum does not stop it; most of a minimum payment can go toward interest.
Why B: Paying the minimum does not raise your limit; limit increases require issuer approval and are unrelated to how little you pay each month.
Why C: The minimum payment covers only a small part of the balance, so most of the debt remains and is not erased after one payment.
Why D: Minimum payments are mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly, interest compounds on what remains, and repayment can stretch for years and cost far more overall.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a grace period on a credit card?
A: Time when the debt is forgiven by the lender for good
B: Time during which the card cannot be used for purchases
C: Time after the billing cycle to pay in full without interest
D: Time when you owe double the normal interest rate to the bank
Why A: A grace period does not forgive debt; the lender still expects full repayment, and it only gives you time before interest starts on new purchases.
Why B: Cards remain usable during a grace period; it refers to interest-free time on purchases, not any suspension of the card's use.
Why C: If you pay your statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 or more days after the cycle ends, you pay no interest on purchases.
Why D: A grace period never doubles interest; penalty rates are a separate consequence of late payments, while a grace period is a benefit that avoids interest.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a secured credit card?
A: A card backed by a cash deposit as collateral
B: A card that comes with no spending limit
C: A card that earns cash back on grocery purchases
D: A card that comes with a lower rate for a year
Why A: A secured card requires a refundable cash deposit that usually becomes your credit limit, so the issuer is protected, and it helps people build or rebuild credit.
Why B: Every card has a limit; a secured card's limit is typically tied to the deposit, and no card gives truly unlimited spending.
Why C: Cash back is a rewards feature on many cards. A secured card is defined by the cash deposit that backs its credit limit.
Why D: A temporary low rate describes an introductory offer. A secured card is defined by the cash deposit that backs the credit limit.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a secured loan?
A: A loan approved by the lender based on your credit score
B: A loan backed by collateral the lender can take if you default
C: A loan from a friend that has no written terms or papers
D: A loan with a fixed rate and equal monthly payments
Why A: A loan approved on credit score alone is unsecured. A secured loan is tied to pledged property the lender can take if you default.
Why B: Collateral, such as a car or home, secures the lender, who can repossess or foreclose if you default. That lower risk usually means lower interest rates.
Why C: A secured loan involves property pledged as collateral; informal loans with no paperwork have no collateral or legal protections and are not the definition.
Why D: A fixed rate and equal payments describe how a loan is repaid. A secured loan is defined by collateral the lender can claim if you default.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an unsecured loan?
A: A loan with no collateral, based on credit
B: A loan that is backed by a car or a truck
C: A loan from a pawn shop that holds an item
D: A loan that is backed by a house or a flat
Why A: An unsecured loan, such as a personal loan or credit card, has no collateral, so approval and rates depend on your credit score and income.
Why B: A loan backed by a car or truck is a secured loan, since the vehicle is collateral the lender can repossess if you default.
Why C: Pawn loans are secured by the item you leave, so the pawn shop holds collateral; that makes them secured rather than unsecured.
Why D: A loan backed by a house or flat is a mortgage, a secured loan where the property is collateral the lender can foreclose on.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a cosigner?
A: A person who gives the borrower extra money to spend
B: A person who approves the loan paperwork for the bank staff
C: A person who agrees to repay a loan if the borrower fails
D: A person who inspects collateral for the lender's bank
Why A: A cosigner does not give the borrower spending money; they pledge their own credit and take legal responsibility for the debt if the borrower does not pay.
Why B: Approving paperwork is the lender's job; a cosigner is a third party who guarantees repayment, not an employee of the bank.
Why C: A cosigner signs the loan alongside the borrower and becomes legally liable for repayment if the borrower defaults. This can help a borrower with thin credit qualify.
Why D: Inspecting or appraising collateral is done by an appraiser or lender; a cosigner's role is to guarantee repayment with their own credit.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a loan term?
A: The interest rate that is charged on the loan
B: The amount of money that was first borrowed
C: The fee that is charged for a late payment
D: The length of time you have to repay a loan
Why A: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing as a percentage; the term is a separate feature that states how long you have to repay.
Why B: The amount first borrowed is the principal; the term describes the repayment period, not the loan size.
Why C: A late fee is a penalty charged for missing a due date; the term is simply the length of the repayment period.
Why D: The loan term, such as 36 months or 30 years, is the repayment period. Longer terms lower monthly payments but usually raise total interest paid.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which has the lower monthly payment: a $10,000 loan over 5 years or the same loan over 3 years (same rate)?
A: The 3-year loan, with lower total interest paid
B: The 5-year loan, though total interest is higher
C: Both have exactly the same monthly payment
D: Neither one has any payment due at all each month
Why A: The 3-year loan has the higher monthly payment because the same principal is paid off in fewer payments; it saves total interest but costs more each month.
Why B: Spreading $10,000 over 60 payments rather than 36 makes each payment smaller, but interest accrues longer, so total interest is higher on the 5-year loan.
Why C: Payments depend on the term: 36 payments are larger than 60 payments for the same principal and rate, so they cannot be exactly equal.
Why D: Any loan with a balance requires regular payments until it is repaid; neither term avoids payments, so this option makes no sense.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is principal?
A: The extra amount charged for it
B: The original amount borrowed
C: The monthly payment amount
D: The fee for paying very late
Why A: The extra amount charged for borrowing is interest, not principal; principal is the original sum before interest is added.
Why B: Principal is the original amount borrowed or invested, which interest is calculated on. Payments reduce the principal balance over time, lowering future interest.
Why C: The monthly payment typically combines principal and interest; it is not the same thing as principal, which is only the amount borrowed.
Why D: A fee for paying late is a penalty charge; it is separate from the principal, which is the original amount borrowed.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A loan of $2,000 at 6% simple interest for 2 years accrues how much interest?
Why A: $24 would be interest on only a small base; simple interest is principal times rate times time, which is $2,000 x 0.06 x 2, not $24.
Why B: $120 is just one year of interest ($2,000 x 0.06); the loan runs two years, so the interest must be doubled to $240.
Why C: Simple interest = P x r x t = $2,000 x 0.06 x 2 = $240. Interest is figured only on the original principal, so it does not compound.
Why D: $2,240 is the total owed at the end (principal $2,000 plus $240 interest), not the interest itself, which is $240.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does a credit report contain?
A: Your borrowing and repayment history
B: Your shopping lists and receipts
C: Your bank passwords and card numbers
D: Your medical history and records
Why A: A credit report lists your accounts, balances, payment history, inquiries and public records, which lenders use to judge how reliably you borrow and repay.
Why B: Shopping lists and receipts are not tracked by credit bureaus; the report records credit accounts and payment behavior only.
Why C: Credit reports do not show your passwords, and card numbers are truncated; keeping them off the report protects your private information.
Why D: Medical history is private and not part of a credit report, though unpaid medical debts sent to collections can sometimes appear as accounts.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: How often can you get a free credit report from each major bureau?
A: Once in two years
B: Once per five years
C: Once per decade
D: At least once a year
Why A: Federal law allows a free report from each bureau at least once a year, so a two year wait is longer than needed. Yearly checks help catch errors early.
Why B: Free reports are available at least yearly, so a five year gap would leave errors or identity theft unnoticed for far too long.
Why C: A ten year gap is much longer than the yearly access federal law provides, and it would let errors or fraud go unnoticed.
Why D: Under federal law you may get a free report from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion at least once every 12 months at AnnualCreditReport.com, helping you catch errors early.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What should you do if you find an error on your credit report?
A: Close all your accounts right away to be safe
B: Ignore it because errors fix themselves over time
C: Pay the debt even if it is not yours to pay
D: Dispute it with the credit bureau in writing
Why A: Closing accounts does not remove an error and can lower your score by cutting available credit and shortening your history; the mistake still needs fixing.
Why B: Errors do not fix themselves, and they may hurt loan approvals or rates meanwhile, so waiting leaves the problem unresolved.
Why C: Paying a debt that is not yours could be mistaken for accepting responsibility; the correct step is disputing the error, not paying it.
Why D: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets you dispute inaccurate items; the bureau must investigate, normally within 30 days, and correct or delete wrong information. Include documents as proof.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is identity theft?
A: Using someone's personal data to commit fraud
B: Sharing a photo online with a close friend
C: Forgetting your password to an online account
D: Changing your own name through a court process
Why A: Identity theft is the unauthorized use of someone's personal data, such as a Social Security number, to open accounts or commit fraud. Monitoring reports and freezing credit help prevent it.
Why B: Sharing a photo with a friend is normal sharing with consent, not stealing someone's identity or using it for fraud.
Why C: Forgetting your own password is an access problem and not a crime; identity theft requires another person misusing your identifying information.
Why D: Legally changing your own name through a court is a lawful personal choice, unlike identity theft, which is the misuse of another person's data.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does a credit freeze do?
A: Raises your credit score by a set number of points
B: Blocks access so new accounts are harder to open
C: Lowers the interest rates on your current cards
D: Removes late payments from your credit report
Why A: A freeze does not change your score; it only restricts access to your report, so it cannot add points to your credit score.
Why B: A credit freeze restricts access to your report so lenders cannot check it, making it hard for thieves to open new accounts in your name. It is free to place and lift.
Why C: A freeze restricts access to your credit report and does not change card rates. Rates are set by the issuer under your account terms.
Why D: A freeze does not edit your history, so late payments stay on the report. It blocks lenders from viewing the report for new credit.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a payday loan?
A: A long-term low-cost loan from a credit union
B: A grant that never needs any repayment at all
C: A short, costly loan due on the next payday
D: A loan with no fees and no interest charged
Why A: Credit unions offer low-cost loans such as payday alternative loans, but a payday loan is the opposite: short-term, high cost, and typically due within weeks.
Why B: Payday loans always must be repaid, usually with a large fee; grants and scholarships are the money that does not require repayment.
Why C: A payday loan is a small, short-term loan, usually due on the borrower's next payday, with very high fees equivalent to APRs of 400 percent or more.
Why D: Payday loans carry high fees and effective interest rates, often $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks, so claiming no cost is false.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why are payday loans considered risky?
A: High fees can trap borrowers in a cycle of repeat borrowing
B: They offer some of the lowest rates for people who need cash
C: They are insured by the federal government in all cases
D: They are slowly repaid over thirty years at low rates
Why A: Fees equivalent to triple-digit APRs, plus short due dates, push borrowers to roll over or borrow again, making debt grow instead of shrinking.
Why B: Payday loans have some of the highest rates, often 400 percent APR or more, not the lowest, which is why they are considered risky.
Why C: Payday lenders are not government-insured, and borrowers have no guarantee of protection; their high costs are the main danger.
Why D: Payday loans are due in weeks, not decades, and carry high rates; a thirty-year low-rate loan describes something like a mortgage.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is debt consolidation?
A: Ignoring the debts until they somehow vanish
B: Splitting one large debt into many small fixed ones
C: Borrowing more money so you can spend freely
D: Combining several debts into one loan or payment
Why A: Ignoring debts does not make them vanish; interest, late fees and collections can grow, and missed payments harm your credit score.
Why B: Consolidation combines debts rather than splitting them; splitting one debt into many pieces would make them harder to manage, not simpler.
Why C: Taking on more borrowing for spending increases debt; consolidation is about organizing and paying off existing debts, ideally at a lower rate.
Why D: Debt consolidation merges several debts into one loan or payment, often at a lower rate, which simplifies repayment and may cut interest costs if the terms are better.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which debt-repayment method targets the highest-interest debt first to save the most money?
A: The snowball method
B: The avalanche method
C: The random method
D: The minimum-only method
Why A: The snowball method pays off the smallest balance first for motivation, so it does not focus on the highest interest rate and may cost more.
Why B: The avalanche method pays minimums on all debts and puts extra money toward the highest interest rate first, minimizing total interest paid over time.
Why C: Paying in a random order has no strategy behind it and does not target high rates, so it is not a recognized money-saving method.
Why D: Paying only the minimums keeps debts alive longest and builds the most interest; it is not a method for targeting high-rate debt.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is bankruptcy?
A: A program that pays out tax refunds each spring
B: A type of savings plan for families and children
C: A legal process for those who cannot repay debts
D: A way to make sure you never owe any lender again
Why A: Tax refunds are paid by the government after you file a return; bankruptcy is a court process dealing with debts, not an income payment program.
Why B: Savings plans such as 529s help families save for college; bankruptcy is a legal debt relief process, not a saving option.
Why C: Bankruptcy, such as Chapter 7 or Chapter 13, is a federal court process that can discharge or restructure debts but stays on credit reports for 7 to 10 years.
Why D: Bankruptcy does not guarantee you will never borrow again; it damages credit for years, and you can still take on new debt afterward.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a mortgage?
A: A loan that has no collateral behind it
B: A loan that is taken out to pay for school
C: A loan that is taken out to buy a car
D: A loan to buy real estate, secured by it
Why A: A loan with no collateral is unsecured; a mortgage is the opposite, because the real estate itself serves as collateral for the loan.
Why B: A loan for education is a student loan; a mortgage specifically finances the purchase of property.
Why C: Auto loans finance vehicles; a mortgage is a loan used to buy real estate, with the property as collateral.
Why D: A mortgage is a loan used to buy property where the home is the collateral, so the lender can foreclose if payments stop. Terms often last 15 or 30 years.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does a down payment do?
A: Reduces the amount you must borrow for a large purchase
B: Increases the interest rate on the whole loan for five years
C: Adds fees to the loan for the whole term of years
D: Eliminates the need for a loan always and forever
Why A: A down payment is cash paid upfront, which lowers the loan amount, reduces interest costs and may help avoid private mortgage insurance on home loans.
Why B: A bigger down payment generally lowers, not raises, the interest paid, since you borrow less; it does not increase the rate on the whole loan.
Why C: A down payment does not add fees to the loan; it reduces the amount financed, so total interest and monthly payments usually fall.
Why D: A down payment cuts what you borrow but rarely removes the loan entirely, since it is only part of the price of a large purchase.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A buyer puts $4,000 down on a $20,000 car. How much needs to be financed, ignoring fees?
Why A: $24,000 adds the down payment to the price instead of subtracting it; a down payment reduces the amount financed.
Why B: $4,000 is the down payment itself, not the amount financed; the loan covers the remaining price after the down payment.
Why C: Amount financed equals price minus down payment: $20,000 - $4,000 = $16,000. A larger down payment means a smaller loan and less interest.
Why D: $20,000 is the full price, which would be financed only if nothing were paid down; with $4,000 down, less is borrowed.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a student loan?
A: A grant that never needs to be repaid by the student
B: Money borrowed for education, repaid with interest
C: A scholarship that a school awards to a student
D: A free gift of money from the federal government
Why A: Student loans must be repaid, usually with interest; money that does not need repayment is a grant, so this option describes a different thing.
Why B: A student loan is borrowed money for education costs that must be repaid with interest. Federal loans often have lower rates and more protections than private loans.
Why C: Scholarships are awards that need no repayment; a student loan is borrowed money with repayment and interest.
Why D: Student loans are borrowed and must be repaid; a free gift from the government would be a grant, such as the Pell Grant.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is generally better to apply for first when paying for college?
A: Private loans from big banks first of all
B: Grants, scholarships and federal aid first
C: Credit cards with high interest from a bank
D: Payday loans from short-term lenders first
Why A: Private bank loans usually have fewer protections and often higher rates, so they should come after free aid and federal loans.
Why B: Grants and scholarships never need repayment, and federal aid usually has lower rates and flexible repayment, so they should come before private borrowing. Start by filing the FAFSA.
Why C: High-interest credit cards are an expensive way to pay tuition because balances grow quickly with interest, so they are a poor first choice.
Why D: Payday loans have extremely high fees and short terms, making them a costly and risky way to pay for college.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a late fee?
A: A tax that is charged on interest earned
B: A reward that is given for paying early on
C: A service that the bank gives to every customer
D: A charge for paying a bill after the due date
Why A: Taxes on interest earned are a tax matter; a late fee is a penalty for paying a bill late.
Why B: A reward for paying early is a discount or incentive; a late fee is the opposite, a penalty for paying after the due date.
Why C: A late fee is a penalty rather than a bank service, and customers can avoid it by paying on time.
Why D: A late fee is a penalty charged when a payment arrives after its due date. Late payments can also hurt your credit score if they are over 30 days past due.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best way to build a good credit history?
A: Pay bills on time and keep balances low
B: Miss payments now and then to save cash
C: Open many new cards in a short time
D: Carry a balance to show lenders you use credit
Why A: On-time payments and low balances are the biggest drivers of a score, since payment history and utilization together make up well over half of it.
Why B: Missed payments are reported to the bureaus and can drop your score significantly, so skipping them harms your credit history rather than helping it.
Why C: Many new applications create hard inquiries and lower your average account age, which can hurt a score. Steady on-time payments and low balances build credit.
Why D: Carrying a balance adds interest cost without raising a score. Paying on time and keeping balances low builds a good history.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a hard inquiry?
A: A question from a cashier at the till
B: A bank statement mailed to your home
C: A credit check made when you apply
D: A check you make on your own report
Why A: A cashier's question has no connection to credit; a hard inquiry is a lender looking at your credit report after you apply.
Why B: A mailed bank statement is a regular account summary and does not count as an inquiry on your credit report.
Why C: A hard inquiry occurs when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit. It can lower your score slightly for about a year and stays on your report for two years.
Why D: Checking your own report is a soft inquiry, which does not affect your score, unlike a hard inquiry from a lender.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is predatory lending?
A: Lending only to people who have great credit and high pay
B: Lending money with clear and fair terms to all
C: Unfair or deceptive lending that exploits borrowers
D: Lending money at the lowest market rate available
Why A: Lending only to people with strong credit is standard prime lending, not predatory; predatory lending targets vulnerable borrowers with unfair terms.
Why B: Clear and fair terms for everyone describes responsible lending; predatory lending uses hidden or deceptive terms instead.
Why C: Predatory lending uses deception, hidden fees, or excessive rates to exploit borrowers, often targeting people with low incomes or little financial knowledge. Warning signs include pressure and unclear terms.
Why D: Lending at the lowest market rate is fair pricing, not predatory; predatory lenders charge high or hidden costs to exploit borrowers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a premium?
A: The amount you pay for an insurance policy
B: The amount you pay before the coverage starts
C: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
D: The maximum coverage that you can claim
Why A: A premium is the regular payment, often monthly or yearly, that you make to keep insurance coverage active, and it is the price of the policy.
Why B: What you pay before coverage begins is the deductible, not the premium; the premium is what you pay to hold the policy.
Why C: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payout, not the premium, which is what you pay in.
Why D: The maximum coverage is the policy limit, the most the insurer will pay; the premium is the price of the policy.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a deductible?
A: The profit that the insurer makes each year
B: The premium that you pay each year in full
C: The coverage limit that is set in the policy
D: What you pay before insurance begins to pay
Why A: Insurer profit is its own business result; a deductible is the portion of a covered loss you pay yourself first.
Why B: The premium is the regular price of the policy; the deductible is a separate out-of-pocket amount paid when you file a claim.
Why C: The coverage limit is the maximum the insurer pays; the deductible is the amount you pay first, so they are different parts of a policy.
Why D: A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket on a covered loss before insurance pays the rest. Higher deductibles usually mean lower premiums.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Alex has a $500 deductible and a covered repair bill of $1,800. How much does the insurer pay, ignoring other terms?
Why A: $1,800 is the full bill and ignores the deductible; the insurer only pays what remains after Alex covers the first $500.
Why B: Insurer pays the bill minus the deductible: $1,800 - $500 = $1,300. Alex pays the first $500 and the insurer covers the remaining covered amount.
Why C: $500 is the deductible, which is what Alex pays, not the insurer; the insurer pays the remaining $1,300.
Why D: $2,300 adds the deductible to the bill instead of subtracting it; the insurer cannot pay more than the covered bill, which is $1,800 minus $500.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does liability insurance cover?
A: Your own medical bills and nothing else besides those
B: Damage to your own property and nothing else besides it
C: Harm or damage you cause to other people or their property
D: Routine maintenance and repairs on your property and vehicles
Why A: Your own medical bills are covered by health or medical payments coverage; liability insurance pays for harm you cause to others.
Why B: Damage to your own property is covered by collision, comprehensive or property coverage; liability pays for others' losses.
Why C: Liability insurance pays for injuries or property damage you cause to others and covers legal defense costs, up to your policy limits, protecting your assets from lawsuits.
Why D: Routine maintenance is not insurable because it is a predictable expense, and liability coverage pays for harm to others, not upkeep.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does collision coverage on a car policy pay for?
A: Oil changes and other routine upkeep for a car
B: Theft of the car and nothing else besides
C: Damage to other people's cars only, not yours
D: Damage to your car in an accident, any fault
Why A: Oil changes are routine maintenance costs, which are predictable and not covered by any car insurance; collision pays for accident damage.
Why B: Theft is covered by comprehensive coverage rather than collision, which pays for damage from hitting something or being hit.
Why C: Damage to other people's cars is covered by liability coverage; collision pays to repair your own car.
Why D: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault, minus your deductible.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does comprehensive car coverage pay for?
A: Tire wear from normal driving on public roads
B: Non-collision damage such as theft, fire or hail
C: Injuries to other drivers in a crash that you cause
D: Damage from a crash that you cause yourself
Why A: Normal tire wear is routine maintenance and not an insured event; comprehensive covers sudden, non-collision losses.
Why B: Comprehensive covers damage not caused by a collision, such as theft, fire, vandalism, falling objects, floods and hail, usually minus your deductible.
Why C: Injuries to other drivers that you cause are covered by liability coverage, not comprehensive, which covers your own vehicle.
Why D: Crash damage you cause is covered by collision coverage on your own car, whereas comprehensive covers non-collision events.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does renters insurance cover?
A: A renter's belongings and liability, not the building
B: Unpaid rent owed to the landlord by the renter now
C: The building structure that the landlord owns and insures
D: The income that the landlord earns from tenants' rent
Why A: Renters insurance covers your belongings and your liability if you cause harm, but the building belongs to the landlord, who insures it separately.
Why B: Renters insurance does not pay unpaid rent; rent is a contractual obligation between tenant and landlord that insurance does not cover.
Why C: The landlord insures the building structure with their own property policy; renters insurance covers the tenant's contents and liability.
Why D: A landlord's rental income is protected by the landlord's own policy, not by a tenant's renters insurance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why does a young driver often pay higher car insurance premiums?
A: Young drivers always own pricier cars than older adults do
B: Young drivers are exempt from needing any insurance cover
C: Insurers simply dislike young people as their paying customers
D: Statistics show higher accident risk for inexperienced drivers
Why A: Premiums are based on risk, not on vehicle price alone, and many young drivers drive older, cheaper cars.
Why B: Young drivers are not exempt from insurance; state laws require liability coverage for almost every driver.
Why C: Insurers price using data on risk, not personal dislike; age is a measurable factor tied to accident rates.
Why D: Insurers price using claims statistics, and drivers under about 25 have more accidents per mile because of inexperience, so they pay higher premiums.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which action can lower car insurance premiums?
A: Lowering the deductible all the way down to zero
B: A clean driving record and a higher deductible
C: Driving around without any insurance cover
D: Getting several speeding tickets each year
Why A: Lowering the deductible raises the premium because the insurer takes on more cost per claim, so this raises, not lowers, premiums.
Why B: Insurers reward low-risk drivers with discounts, and choosing a higher deductible means you carry more risk yourself, which lowers your premium.
Why C: Driving uninsured is illegal in nearly every state and brings fines, and it does not lower premiums; it risks big personal costs.
Why D: Speeding tickets signal risk and raise premiums, so collecting them would increase your costs, not lower them.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is health insurance?
A: A loan that is used to pay hospital bills later
B: A discount on memberships at local gyms and clubs
C: Coverage that pays part of the cost of medical care
D: A savings plan employers set up to help with retirement
Why A: Health insurance is not a loan; it is a contract where you pay premiums and the insurer pays covered medical costs, with no repayment of claims.
Why B: Gym discounts are a perk, not health insurance, which covers medical care such as doctor visits and hospital stays.
Why C: Health insurance pays a share of medical costs for covered services such as doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions, protecting you from large bills. You still pay premiums and cost sharing.
Why D: Employer retirement savings plans like a 401(k) are about retirement, not medical care; health insurance covers medical expenses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a copay?
A: A fixed amount you pay for a covered service
B: The yearly premium you pay to the insurer
C: The total claim amount for the whole year
D: A fine for missing a doctor visit without notice
Why A: A copay is a set dollar amount, such as $25 for a doctor visit, that you pay when you receive a covered service, separate from the premium.
Why B: The yearly cost of the policy is the premium; a copay is a small fixed fee paid at the time of care.
Why C: A claim total for the year is not a copay; a copay is a fixed payment made per service.
Why D: A fine for a missed appointment is a no-show fee, and a copay is paid for covered care you actually receive.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is coinsurance?
A: A percentage of costs you share after the deductible
B: A flat fee that you pay at every single doctor visit
C: A penalty for using out-of-network care at a hospital
D: The monthly premium that you pay to the insurer
Why A: After you meet your deductible, coinsurance splits remaining costs, such as the plan paying 80 percent and you paying 20 percent, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum.
Why B: A flat fee per visit is a copay; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost rather than a fixed amount.
Why C: Out-of-network penalties or higher costs are a separate matter; coinsurance is the percentage split of covered costs after the deductible.
Why D: The monthly premium is a fixed charge to keep the policy; coinsurance is a share of covered costs that applies when you use care.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is life insurance?
A: Coverage that pays you money when you retire from work
B: Coverage that pays for car damage and repairs
C: Coverage that pays for medical costs and drugs
D: Coverage paying beneficiaries when the insured dies
Why A: Retirement income comes from pensions, annuities or savings; life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured dies.
Why B: Car damage and repairs are covered by auto insurance, not by life insurance, which pays out upon the insured person's death.
Why C: Medical costs and drugs are covered by health insurance, whereas life insurance pays a benefit after the insured dies.
Why D: Life insurance pays a death benefit to named beneficiaries when the insured person dies, replacing lost income and covering debts, funeral costs and other expenses. Term and whole life are two common types.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Who should consider buying life insurance?
A: Everyone with no dependents or debts to pay
B: People who rent and own few possessions
C: People whose income dependents rely on
D: People who want protection for their car
Why A: People with no dependents or debts generally have little need for it, since there is no one financially relying on their income.
Why B: Renting or owning few things is not a reason for life insurance. It protects dependents who would lose income, not property.
Why C: Life insurance is most useful for people with dependents such as a spouse or children who would suffer financially if that income were lost.
Why D: Protection for a car comes from auto insurance. Life insurance replaces income for dependents who would struggle financially after a death.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is disability insurance?
A: Coverage that pays for damage to a car's body
B: Coverage replacing income if you cannot work
C: Coverage that pays for a vacation trip abroad
D: Coverage that pays the taxes you owe each year
Why A: Car body damage is covered by auto collision coverage, whereas disability insurance replaces income lost when injury or illness prevents work.
Why B: Disability insurance replaces a portion of your income, often 60 percent, if illness or injury keeps you from working. It protects your paycheck, which is usually your largest asset.
Why C: Vacations are not covered by disability insurance; travel insurance may cover trip problems, but disability pays income when you cannot work.
Why D: Taxes are not paid by disability insurance; it replaces lost wages when you cannot work.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is homeowners insurance?
A: Coverage for a home, belongings and liability
B: Coverage for car accidents and medical bills
C: Coverage for tenants' belongings in a rented apartment
D: Coverage that pays your mortgage if jobless
Why A: Homeowners insurance usually covers the dwelling, personal belongings, liability for injuries on your property, and additional living expenses after a covered loss.
Why B: Car accidents are covered by auto insurance, a separate policy. Homeowners insurance protects the house, belongings and liability on the property.
Why C: That describes renters insurance for tenants. Homeowners insurance covers owners' houses, belongings and liability, and mortgage lenders often require it.
Why D: Homeowners insurance does not pay your mortgage if you lose your job; that would require special payment protection, whereas homeowners covers property damage and liability.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk avoidance?
A: Taking safety steps to lower the chance of a loss
B: Saving money to cover a loss that may occur later on
C: Buying insurance for a loss that may occur later on
D: Choosing not to do something that could cause a loss
Why A: Safety steps that lower the chance of loss are risk reduction, which accepts the activity while making it safer, not avoidance.
Why B: Saving money to cover a possible loss is risk retention, because you plan to absorb the cost yourself rather than avoid it.
Why C: Buying insurance is risk transfer, shifting the cost of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.
Why D: Risk avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all, such as not driving, which removes the chance of loss completely but also gives up the benefits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk transfer?
A: Accepting a risk and paying for a loss yourself
B: Shifting the financial burden to an insurer
C: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part
D: Reducing the chance that a loss will happen
Why A: Accepting a risk and paying for losses yourself is risk retention, the opposite of transferring the risk to someone else.
Why B: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, most commonly by buying insurance and paying premiums.
Why C: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part is risk avoidance, not transfer, because no one else takes on the loss.
Why D: Lowering the chance a loss happens is risk reduction, such as installing alarms; transfer moves the cost to someone else.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk retention?
A: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss of money or property
B: Installing safety devices to lower the chance of loss
C: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for a loss yourself
D: Avoiding the risky activity altogether and for good
Why A: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss is risk transfer, because the insurer takes on the cost rather than you.
Why B: Installing safety devices is risk reduction because it lowers the chance of loss, but you still bear any loss that occurs.
Why C: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for any loss yourself, often through savings or a high deductible, and works best for small, affordable losses.
Why D: Avoiding the risky activity altogether is risk avoidance, which eliminates the exposure rather than accepting and paying for it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A family installs smoke detectors and keeps a fire extinguisher. Which risk strategy is this?
A: Risk reduction
B: Risk transfer
C: Risk retention
D: Risk avoidance
Why A: Smoke detectors and extinguishers lower the chance and size of a fire loss, which is risk reduction, also called loss control or prevention.
Why B: Risk transfer would be buying insurance or otherwise shifting the cost to another party; safety equipment does not do that.
Why C: Risk retention means accepting the possible loss and paying yourself, whereas installing safety equipment actively tries to prevent the loss.
Why D: Risk avoidance would mean not having the exposure at all, such as not owning a home; the family keeps the exposure but reduces it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an insurance claim?
A: A type of savings that earns monthly interest
B: A fee that you pay for a policy each month
C: A refund of the premium you paid earlier
D: A request for payment after a covered loss
Why A: A savings type that earns interest is an account; an insurance claim is a request to the insurer for payment of a covered loss.
Why B: The regular fee you pay for a policy is the premium, whereas a claim is something you file after a loss.
Why C: A refund of premiums is not a claim; a claim asks the insurer to pay for a covered loss.
Why D: A claim is a formal request to your insurer for payment after a covered loss, such as an accident or theft. The insurer investigates and pays according to policy terms, minus your deductible.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an insurance exclusion?
A: A discount for very good driving habits
B: The monthly cost of the whole policy
C: Something the policy does not cover
D: The coverage limit in the policy
Why A: A discount for good driving is a credit that lowers cost; an exclusion limits what the policy pays.
Why B: The monthly cost of the policy is the premium; an exclusion is a specific loss or situation the policy does not cover.
Why C: An exclusion lists causes, property or situations the policy will not pay for, such as floods or earthquakes under standard homeowners policies. Reading exclusions helps you spot gaps in coverage.
Why D: The coverage limit is the most the insurer will pay; an exclusion is something not covered at all.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: After a flood damages a home, the owner learns the standard homeowners policy does not pay. What is the likely reason?
A: The home was too old to qualify for coverage
B: Floods are usually excluded; separate coverage is needed
C: The insurer simply made a mistake in the policy terms
D: Floods are covered once the deductible is doubled
Why A: Standard policies exclude flood damage regardless of the home's age. Flood coverage must be bought separately, often through the National Flood Insurance Program.
Why B: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage, so owners must buy separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program. Check exclusions before disasters strike.
Why C: The insurer did not err; the policy terms exclude floods, and the written exclusion is the reason the claim is denied.
Why D: Standard policies exclude flood damage, and a higher deductible does not change that. Separate flood insurance is needed to cover it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an emergency fund's role in managing risk?
A: It is meant only for paying for vacations
B: It replaces the need for all your insurance
C: It covers unexpected costs without borrowing
D: It increases the amount of risk a family faces
Why A: An emergency fund is meant for unexpected needs such as job loss or repairs, not planned expenses like vacations.
Why B: An emergency fund handles smaller shocks, but it cannot replace insurance, because large losses like a house fire or major illness can far exceed savings.
Why C: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs such as car repairs or lost income, so you avoid high-interest debt. Experts recommend three to six months of expenses.
Why D: An emergency fund reduces a family's exposure to financial risk by providing a cushion, so it does not increase risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why compare insurance quotes from several companies?
A: It removes the need for coverage
B: Prices and coverage can vary
C: It guarantees the lowest rate
D: All companies charge the same
Why A: Comparing quotes does not remove the need for coverage; it helps you choose among policies, not skip insurance.
Why B: Insurers set prices differently using their own formulas, so the same coverage can cost very different amounts, and shopping around can save significant money.
Why C: Comparing quotes can find a lower price, but it cannot guarantee that you get the lowest rate available anywhere, as rates change.
Why D: Companies price risk differently, which is exactly why comparing quotes is worth doing; rates are not identical across insurers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is investing?
A: Borrowing money just to have fun
B: Hiding cash in a drawer at home daily
C: Spending money on daily needs each month
D: Putting money into assets to grow it
Why A: Borrowing for fun is spending financed by debt, not investing, which aims to build value over time through assets.
Why B: Hiding cash in a drawer earns nothing and loses value to inflation; investing puts money to work in assets.
Why C: Spending on daily needs is consumption, not investing, because it does not aim to grow your money.
Why D: Investing means buying assets such as stocks, bonds or real estate expecting them to grow in value or earn income over time, though returns are not guaranteed.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a stock?
A: A share of ownership in a company
B: A deposit held at a local bank
C: A type of insurance policy for cars
D: A loan made to a company and repaid
Why A: A stock represents a share of ownership in a corporation, so shareholders may gain from price growth and dividends and often can vote on company matters.
Why B: A deposit at a bank is a savings or checking account, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company.
Why C: Car insurance is a protection product; a stock is an ownership share in a company, so they are different things.
Why D: A loan to a company repaid with interest describes a bond; a stock gives ownership rather than lending.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a mutual fund?
A: A savings account at a local bank branch
B: A loan that a bank makes to a single borrower
C: A single stock owned by one person alone
D: A pool of money buying a mix of securities
Why A: A bank savings account is an insured deposit; a mutual fund pools many investors' money into securities and is not a bank deposit.
Why B: A bank loan to one borrower is lending; a mutual fund pools money from many investors rather than lending to a single borrower.
Why C: A mutual fund spreads money across many holdings, so it is not a single stock owned by one person alone.
Why D: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a diversified mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, managed by professionals, giving small investors instant diversification.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an index fund?
A: A fund that pays a fixed rate of interest on deposits
B: A fund that tries to beat the market through trading each year
C: A fund that aims to match the performance of a market index
D: A fund that employers set up to pay employee pensions
Why A: A fund that pays fixed interest describes a bond or savings product. An index fund holds the securities in a market index and its value rises and falls.
Why B: Trying to beat the market describes an actively managed fund; an index fund simply tracks an index with low trading.
Why C: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500, so it holds the same stocks. It typically has low fees and broad diversification.
Why D: A pension fund is set up by an employer to pay retirement benefits. An index fund is an investment fund that tracks a market index.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is diversification?
A: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk
B: Borrowing money in order to invest it in a business firm today
C: Putting all your money in one single stock that you like
D: Holding only cash and nothing else at all for many years
Why A: Diversification spreads money across different assets, industries or regions so a loss in one has less effect on the whole, lowering risk without necessarily lowering returns.
Why B: Borrowing to invest is leverage, which increases risk, whereas diversification reduces risk by spreading investments.
Why C: Putting everything in one stock is the opposite of diversifying and leaves you fully exposed to that company's performance.
Why D: Holding only cash is a single asset type and gives up growth; diversification means owning a range of different investments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the relationship between risk and return?
A: Risk and return are unrelated, so one tells you nothing
B: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
C: Higher potential returns usually come with lower risk
D: Risk affects an investment's fees but not its returns
Why A: Risk and return are linked, because investors demand higher potential returns for taking on greater uncertainty; saying they are unrelated is wrong.
Why B: Higher expected returns generally come with higher risk, as seen with stocks versus savings accounts. Investors need to be paid for accepting the chance of loss.
Why C: It reverses the relationship. Investors accept more risk in exchange for the chance of higher returns, as with stocks compared with savings accounts.
Why D: Risk is linked to expected returns because investors demand more reward for taking more uncertainty. Fees are a separate cost.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment is generally expected to be riskiest?
A: A broad index fund of many stocks
B: A federally insured savings account
C: A U.S. Treasury bill held to the end
D: A single start-up company's stock
Why A: A broad index fund holds many stocks and is diversified, so it is far less risky than one company's shares.
Why B: Federally insured savings accounts are protected up to $250,000 by the FDIC, making them one of the safest options.
Why C: Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government and, held to maturity, return the principal, making them very low risk.
Why D: A single start-up stock can lose all its value, and its price is volatile, so it carries high risk, though it also has potential for large gains.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a dividend?
A: A share of company profit paid to owners
B: A fee that is paid to a broker each time
C: Interest that is charged to each borrower
D: A tax that is charged on stock trades
Why A: A dividend is a payment to shareholders from company profits, often quarterly, which gives investors income in addition to any price growth.
Why B: Broker fees are commissions or charges for trades, not dividends, which are money received by owners.
Why C: Interest charged to borrowers is a cost of loans; a dividend is a payment to stock owners, not a charge.
Why D: Taxes on trades are a government charge, while a dividend is money that a company pays to its shareholders.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a capital gain?
A: Wages that are earned from a job each month of work
B: Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid
C: A gift of money from a relative in the family each year
D: Interest that is paid on a savings account balance daily
Why A: Wages earned from a job are ordinary income, not capital gains, which come from selling assets for more than their cost.
Why B: A capital gain is the profit when you sell an asset, such as a stock, for more than you paid. Assets held over a year get lower long-term tax rates.
Why C: Gifts from relatives are not capital gains; a gain arises only from the sale of an asset at a profit.
Why D: Interest on savings is interest income and is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains, which arise from selling assets.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a 401(k)?
A: A car loan from a local bank for a new car
B: A type of health insurance plan for workers
C: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan
D: A savings plan that is meant for college costs
Why A: A car loan is borrowing to buy a vehicle; a 401(k) is a retirement account, named after a section of the tax code.
Why B: Health insurance plans cover medical costs; a 401(k) is a retirement savings plan, so these are different products.
Why C: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan where employees contribute from their paychecks, often pre-tax, and employers may match contributions. Investments grow tax-deferred until retirement.
Why D: Savings for college costs is described by a 529 plan, whereas a 401(k) is for retirement.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An employer matches 100% of contributions up to 3% of pay. If you earn $30,000 and contribute 3%, how much does the employer add?
Why A: Employer matches 100 percent of contributions up to 3 percent of pay: 3% x $30,000 = $900 from you, so the employer adds an equal $900.
Why B: $90 comes from misplacing the decimal; 3 percent of $30,000 is $900, so the match equals $900 rather than $90.
Why C: $300 is only 1 percent of $30,000; the match is 100 percent of your 3 percent, which is $900.
Why D: $9,000 would be 30 percent of pay; 3 percent of $30,000 equals $900, so the match is $900.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an IRA?
A: A loan used to buy a home
B: A retirement account with tax perks
C: A pension paid by an employer
D: A federal program that pays monthly benefits
Why A: A home loan is a mortgage. An IRA is an individual retirement account for saving, not a loan.
Why B: An IRA, or individual retirement arrangement, is a personal account for retirement savings that offers tax advantages, such as deductions or tax-free growth. Annual limits apply.
Why C: A pension is an employer-funded retirement benefit. An IRA is a personal account the individual opens and funds, with tax advantages.
Why D: Social Security pays monthly benefits funded through payroll taxes. An IRA is a personal retirement savings account with its own tax advantages.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main feature of a Roth IRA?
A: Withdrawals must start at age 59 and a half
B: Contributions are tax-deductible and withdrawals are taxed
C: Money goes in after tax; qualified withdrawals are tax-free
D: The government matches the contributions you make
