Why B: Records follow a set accounting method, not the owner's feelings; the periodic system updates inventory after a count at period end.
Why C: Periodic inventory is updated after a count at the end of the period, not at the start before sales happen.
Why D: Under the periodic system, inventory is updated only at the end of the period after a physical count, which is then used to find cost of goods sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the perpetual inventory system?
A: A system that updates inventory records with each purchase and sale
B: A system that estimates inventory from sales totals
C: A system that updates inventory records at the end of each period
D: A system that values inventory at its expected selling price
Why A: The perpetual system updates inventory records continuously with each purchase and sale, so the balance is always current, usually through scanners and software.
Why B: Estimating from sales is not the perpetual system, which tracks each purchase and sale directly in the records.
Why C: Updating at period end after a count describes the periodic system, which is the opposite of perpetual.
Why D: Perpetual systems track units and costs as they move; valuing at expected selling price is a different valuation idea.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store scans every sale and its stock records adjust instantly. Which system is this?
A: Cash basis accounting
B: Perpetual inventory
C: Double taxation
D: Periodic inventory
Why A: Cash basis accounting records items when cash moves and has no relation to how inventory is tracked.
Why B: Scanning each sale and updating stock records instantly is perpetual inventory, because the records are adjusted continuously with each transaction.
Why C: Double taxation refers to corporate profits taxed twice, which has no relation to tracking inventory.
Why D: The periodic system updates inventory only after a physical count at period end, so it does not adjust instantly with each sale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does FIFO stand for?
A: First income of owners
B: First-in, first-out
C: Fixed inventory, output
D: Final stock for owners
Why A: First income of owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO is an inventory costing method and has nothing to do with owner income.
Why B: FIFO stands for first-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the oldest goods bought are the first ones sold.
Why C: Fixed inventory, output is not a real phrase, and FIFO refers to the order in which inventory costs flow.
Why D: Final stock for owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO describes the assumed flow of inventory costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does LIFO stand for?
A: Long-term stock order
B: Lowest stock output
C: Last-in, first-out
D: Latest owner income
Why A: Long-term stock order is not what LIFO means, which is an inventory costing assumption about which units are sold.
Why B: Lowest stock output is not an accounting term, because LIFO is about the order in which costs leave inventory.
Why C: LIFO stands for last-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the newest goods purchased are the first ones sold.
Why D: Latest owner income is not an accounting term, since LIFO is an inventory costing method, not a measure of income.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Purchases were 10 units at $5 then 10 units at $7. Ten units are sold. Under FIFO, what is cost of goods sold?
Why A: Under FIFO the oldest units are sold first, so the 10 units sold cost 10 x $5 = $50 as cost of goods sold.
Why B: $70 is 10 x $7, the cost of the newest units, which would be the LIFO cost of goods sold and not the FIFO cost.
Why C: $60 would be an average of $5 and $7 across 10 units, but FIFO uses the actual oldest cost of $5 per unit.
Why D: $120 is the total cost of all 20 units (10 x $5 + 10 x $7), but only 10 units were sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a period of rising prices, which method usually reports the higher net income?
A: Equal
B: Neither
C: LIFO
D: FIFO
Why A: Methods do not produce equal income when prices rise, because they assign different costs to goods sold and so give different profits.
Why B: The methods differ in net income when prices rise, so one of them reports higher income, and saying neither does is not accurate.
Why C: With rising prices LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to cost of goods sold, so it reports lower net income than FIFO.
Why D: FIFO charges the oldest, lower costs to cost of goods sold when prices rise, which leaves higher gross profit and net income than LIFO.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of the adjusted trial balance?
A: To record daily sales in the general journal book
B: To list customers and their contact details too
C: To close temporary accounts at the end of the year overall
D: To check that debits equal credits after adjustments
Why A: Daily sales are recorded in the journal, whereas the adjusted trial balance is prepared after the adjusting entries to test equality.
Why B: Customer contact details are kept in a customer list or subsidiary records, not in a trial balance, which lists ledger accounts and balances.
Why C: Closing temporary accounts is done by closing entries after the adjusted trial balance, so it is not the purpose of the trial balance itself.
Why D: The adjusted trial balance lists all account balances after adjusting entries and confirms total debits equal total credits before financial statements are prepared.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Supplies on hand at year end are $300 and the supplies account shows $900. What adjustment amount is needed?
A: $1,200 to Supplies Expense
B: $300 to Supplies Expense
C: $600 to Supplies Expense
D: $900 to Supplies Expense
Why A: $1,200 is the total of $300 plus $900, but the adjustment is only the supplies used, so adding the two figures is wrong.
Why B: $300 is the supplies still on hand, which stays as an asset, so it is not the amount to expense.
Why C: The supplies account shows $900 and $300 remains, so $900 - $300 = $600 of supplies were used and is debited to Supplies Expense.
Why D: Expensing $900 would write off all supplies, but $300 is still on hand, so only the used portion is expensed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accrued interest receivable?
A: Interest earned but not yet received
B: Interest paid in advance by a firm
C: Interest that is never earned at all
D: Interest owed to a lender by a firm
Why A: Accrued interest receivable is interest that has been earned but not yet received in cash, and it is recorded as an asset at period end.
Why B: Interest paid in advance by a firm is a prepaid expense, which is the opposite of interest earned and not yet collected.
Why C: Interest that is never earned would not be recorded, whereas accrued interest receivable has been earned and is expected to be collected.
Why D: Interest owed to a lender is interest payable, a liability, while receivable refers to interest the firm is owed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A $6,000 note at 8% was held for 3 months by year end with no interest received. What interest should be accrued?
Why A: $12 is far too small, because interest = $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, and $12 mislocates a decimal point.
Why B: Interest is $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, which is recorded as accrued interest receivable and interest revenue.
Why C: $1,440 would use 3 months as 3 years or similar, which is wrong because the period is only a quarter of a year.
Why D: $480 is a full year of interest ($6,000 x 8%), but the note was held for only 3 months, so only one fourth applies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a post-closing trial balance?
A: To prepare reversing entries for the next period before closing
B: To show net income for the full year of trading and sales
C: To prove debits equal credits after closing entries are posted
D: To record new sales made after the year end in the books
Why A: Reversing entries are optional and prepared after closing, at the start of the next period, so a post-closing trial balance is not a tool for preparing them.
Why B: Net income is shown on the income statement, and the post-closing trial balance has only permanent accounts with no income figures.
Why C: The post-closing trial balance proves debits equal credits after closing entries, and it lists only permanent accounts with balances carried to the next period.
Why D: New sales after year end belong in the next period's journal, and the trial balance does not record transactions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bad debt expense adjustment?
A: An entry that records a cash sale at the counter
B: An entry that pays a supplier in cash on time
C: An entry that closes revenue at the year end
D: An entry that estimates uncollectible receivables
Why A: Recording a cash sale is a normal revenue entry and has nothing to do with estimating losses on uncollectible accounts.
Why B: Paying a supplier in cash reduces payables and cash, which is unrelated to adjusting for customers who will not pay.
Why C: Closing revenue is a closing entry made at period end, and a bad debt adjustment is a different type of entry.
Why D: A bad debt adjustment estimates the receivables that will not be collected, recording bad debts expense and an allowance so receivables and income are not overstated.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which accounts are closed at the end of the period?
A: Accounts payable and the equipment
B: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts
C: Owner's capital and supplies accounts
D: Cash and accounts receivable balances
Why A: Accounts payable and equipment are permanent accounts, so they are kept open and carry their balances forward.
Why B: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts are temporary accounts closed at period end so each new period starts at zero and the balances move into owner's equity.
Why C: Owner's capital and supplies are permanent accounts carried forward; capital is updated by closing but is not itself closed.
Why D: Cash and accounts receivable are asset accounts that continue into the next period, so they are not closed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a trade discount?
A: A reduction from a list price given to a buyer
B: A tax on trade between two countries each year
C: A fee for shipping goods to a buyer by truck
D: A discount for paying early, taken off the invoice
Why A: A trade discount is a reduction from a list price given to a buyer, such as for volume or dealers, and is deducted before the invoice price is set.
Why B: A tax on trade between countries is a tariff, which is a government charge and not a seller's price reduction.
Why C: Shipping fees are freight charges, which are separate from discounts that reduce the price.
Why D: A discount for early payment is a cash or sales discount, which differs from a trade discount applied to the list price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An item lists at $400 with a 25% trade discount. What is the invoice price?
Why A: $100 is the amount of the discount (25% of $400), not the price the buyer pays after the discount.
Why B: $425 would add 25% to the price, but a discount reduces the price, so the invoice is lower than $400.
Why C: $375 subtracts only $25, which is not a 25% discount; 25% of $400 is $100, not $25.
Why D: The discount is $400 x 25% = $100, so the invoice price is $400 - $100 = $300.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a purchases return?
A: Goods sent back to a supplier for credit
B: Goods sent back by a customer to the seller
C: Goods sold at a discount to loyal buyers
D: Goods ordered from a supplier by a firm
Why A: A purchases return is goods sent back to a supplier for credit or refund, which reduces what the buyer owes.
Why B: Goods sent back by a customer are a sales return from the seller's viewpoint, not a purchases return.
Why C: Selling goods at a discount is a sales transaction, which is not a return of purchased goods.
Why D: Ordering goods from a supplier is a purchase order, not a return, which sends goods back.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a debit memorandum?
A: A tax form that a firm files with the government every year
B: A notice from a buyer to a seller that a payable is being reduced
C: A receipt for payment that a seller gives to a buyer in a shop
D: A bill sent by a seller to a buyer for goods that were delivered overall
Why A: A tax form filed with the government is unrelated to a debit memorandum, which is a notice between buyer and seller.
Why B: A debit memorandum is a notice from a buyer telling a seller that the buyer is reducing the payable, for example because of returned goods.
Why C: A receipt confirms payment received, and a debit memo is instead a notice reducing an amount owed.
Why D: A bill sent by a seller for goods delivered is an invoice, and a debit memorandum is a notice from the buyer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A credit memorandum issued by a seller to a customer does what to the customer's balance?
A: It has no effect at all
B: It cancels the account
C: It reduces the amount owed
D: It increases the amount owed
Why A: A credit memorandum does have an effect, because it lowers the customer's balance for returns or allowances.
Why B: A credit memo reduces the balance but does not cancel the whole account, unless the credit equals the full amount owed.
Why C: A credit memorandum from a seller reduces the amount the customer owes, such as for returned or damaged goods, and it reduces accounts receivable.
Why D: A credit memo lowers the balance, so saying it increases the amount owed is the opposite of its effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is days sales outstanding (DSO)?
A: The average number of days to collect receivables
B: The number of days in a fiscal year of trade
C: The number of days a supplier waits to be paid overall
D: The number of days goods stay in stock there
Why A: Days sales outstanding measures the average number of days it takes to collect receivables after a credit sale, and a lower number shows faster collection.
Why B: The number of days in a fiscal year is a calendar length, and DSO is a collection measure, not a count of days in a year.
Why C: The days a supplier waits to be paid describes payables, but DSO is about how long customers take to pay the firm.
Why D: Days goods remain in stock is days sales in inventory, which differs from DSO, a measure for receivables.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Receivables turnover is 12. About how many days does collection take using 360 days?
A: 60 days
B: 4,320 days
C: 30 days
D: 12 days
Why A: 60 days would result from a turnover of 6 (360 / 6), not 12, so this uses the wrong number of turns.
Why B: 4,320 is 12 x 360, which multiplies instead of dividing, while the collection period is 360 divided by turnover.
Why C: Average collection days = 360 / 12 = 30 days, so receivables are collected about every 30 days.
Why D: 12 is the turnover number itself (times per year), not days, so it does not convert to a number of days.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the allowance method's balance sheet effect?
A: Receivables are shown at double their value
B: Receivables are shown net of expected losses
C: Receivables are shown at the full invoiced amount
D: Receivables are shown with expected gains added
Why A: The allowance method does not double receivables, since it subtracts expected losses to give a lower value.
Why B: The allowance method shows receivables net of expected uncollectible amounts, so the balance sheet reports the amount the firm expects to collect.
Why C: The allowance method reduces receivables for expected losses, so they are not shown at the full invoiced amount.
Why D: The allowance method subtracts expected losses from receivables; it does not add gains to them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is retained earnings?
A: Cash held in a bank account by the business owner for use
B: Money owed to creditors by the firm after the year end
C: Total sales for the year, shown at the top of the statement overall
D: Accumulated profits kept in the business instead of paid out
Why A: Cash in a bank is an asset, whereas retained earnings is an equity account showing profits kept, and it may not exist as cash.
Why B: Money owed to creditors is a liability, so it is not retained earnings, which belongs to owners' equity.
Why C: Total sales are revenue on the income statement, not retained earnings, which accumulate net income after dividends over time.
Why D: Retained earnings are accumulated profits kept in the business rather than paid out as dividends, and they increase owners' equity over time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A corporation starts with $50,000 retained earnings, earns $20,000 and pays $5,000 in dividends. What is the ending balance?
Why A: $35,000 incorrectly subtracts the earnings and adds nothing; the correct calculation adds net income, then subtracts dividends.
Why B: Ending retained earnings = $50,000 + $20,000 - $5,000 = $65,000, because net income increases it and dividends decrease it.
Why C: $75,000 ignores the dividends, since $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000, and it still does not subtract $5,000.
Why D: $25,000 results from subtracting earnings and dividends from the starting balance, but earnings add to retained earnings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a classified balance sheet?
A: A balance sheet printed in a special font, so that it is easy to read by the board
B: A balance sheet with only assets and nothing about debts or owner equity
C: A balance sheet that is kept secret from the owners and banks of the firm
D: A balance sheet that groups items into categories such as current and long-term
Why A: A classified balance sheet is about grouping accounts into categories, not font style or appearance.
Why B: A balance sheet must show assets, liabilities and equity, so leaving out debts and owner equity does not describe a classified balance sheet.
Why C: Balance sheets are shared with owners, lenders and others, so keeping it secret is not what classified means.
Why D: A classified balance sheet groups items into categories such as current assets, long-term assets, current liabilities and equity, which makes analysis easier.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are intangible assets?
A: Money owed by customers for goods that were sold on credit
B: Assets you can touch, such as machinery and delivery vehicles
C: Assets without physical form, such as patents and trademarks
D: Cash in the bank, which is a current asset held by the firm
Why A: Money owed by customers is accounts receivable, a current asset, which is not an intangible asset.
Why B: Assets you can touch, such as machinery and vehicles, are tangible, so they are the opposite of intangible assets.
Why C: Intangible assets have no physical form but have value, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights and goodwill, and are usually amortized.
Why D: Cash is a current asset and a tangible financial asset, not an intangible one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an intangible asset?
A: A patent
B: Furniture
C: Inventory
D: The truck
Why A: A patent is an intangible asset, because it is a legal right to an invention and has no physical form.
Why B: Furniture is a physical item and a long-term tangible asset, which makes it not intangible.
Why C: Inventory is physical merchandise held for sale and is a current asset, not an intangible.
Why D: A truck is a physical long-term asset, so it is a tangible asset.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is goodwill?
A: A fee paid to a bank for keeping the accounts of the whole firm in order
B: The extra amount paid for a business above the value of its identifiable assets
C: The cash left after paying all the bills and debts of the firm at year end in the end
D: A discount from a supplier for paying early on an invoice, off the price
Why A: A fee paid to a bank for keeping accounts is a bank service charge, which is an expense and not goodwill.
Why B: Goodwill is the amount paid for a business above the fair value of its identifiable net assets, reflecting reputation, customer base and other intangible advantages.
Why C: Cash left after paying bills is simply a cash balance, and it has no connection to the premium paid for a business.
Why D: A discount from a supplier for early payment is a purchase discount, which differs from goodwill, an asset.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is earnings per share?
A: Total assets divided by liabilities, to show debt cover
B: Sales divided by the costs for the whole year of trading
C: Dividends divided by the price paid by the investors
D: Net income divided by the number of shares outstanding
Why A: Total assets divided by liabilities is a solvency ratio, but earnings per share concerns profit per share.
Why B: Sales divided by costs is a ratio of revenue to cost, not earnings per share, which is based on net income and share count.
Why C: Dividends divided by price is the dividend yield, which differs from earnings per share.
Why D: Earnings per share is net income divided by shares outstanding, showing how much profit is attributed to each share of common stock.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company earns $600,000 and has 200,000 shares outstanding. What is its EPS?
Why A: $120,000 is not found by any valid calculation, and EPS is net income divided by shares, not a total.
Why B: $400,000 results from subtracting 200,000 from 600,000, but EPS divides net income by the number of shares.
Why C: EPS = $600,000 / 200,000 shares = $3.00 per share, which shows the profit that belongs to each share outstanding.
Why D: $0.33 is shares divided by income (200,000 / 600,000), which inverts the formula; EPS divides income by shares.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does return on assets (ROA) measure?
A: How efficiently a company uses its assets to earn profit
B: How much debt a company owes compared with owner capital
C: How much cash a company has in the bank on each day
D: How many shares exist in the market for the company
Why A: ROA measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to produce profit, calculated as net income divided by total assets.
Why B: Debt compared with owner capital is the debt to equity ratio, which differs from ROA, a profitability measure.
Why C: Cash on hand is measured by the cash balance or current ratio, and ROA is a profitability measure of assets.
Why D: The number of shares in the market is a share count, and has no connection to return on assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net income is $90,000 and total assets are $900,000. What is ROA?
Why A: 90% would use $90,000 over $100,000 or similar; the correct figure is $90,000 divided by $900,000, which is far smaller.
Why B: 1,000% inverts the ratio ($900,000 / $90,000 = 10 times), but ROA is net income divided by assets.
Why C: 1% comes from misplacing the decimal point, as $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, not 1%.
Why D: ROA = net income / total assets = $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, meaning each asset dollar earned ten cents.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is revenue recognition's five-step idea based on?
A: Recording revenue when the check is printed by the accounting staff
B: Recording revenue when the customer's payment clears the bank
C: Recording revenue when control of goods or services passes to the customer
D: Recording revenue when the sales team signs a price quote
Why A: Printing a check is an internal action and does not shift control of goods or services to the customer, so it does not trigger revenue.
Why B: Waiting for payment describes cash-basis timing; the five-step model recognizes revenue when control of goods or services transfers.
Why C: The five-step model recognizes revenue when control of promised goods or services passes to the customer, in the amount the company expects to receive.
Why D: A price quote is just a proposal and transfers nothing to the customer, so no revenue has yet been earned.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a material misstatement?
A: A tiny typo with no effect on any reader's decision
B: An error large enough to change a reader's decisions
C: A late filing fee charged by the tax authority only
D: A correct entry made on the right date and amount
Why A: A trivial typo that would not sway any reader is the definition of an immaterial item, which auditors and preparers can safely leave uncorrected.
Why B: A misstatement is material when it is large enough that it could change the economic decisions of investors, lenders, or other users relying on the statements.
Why C: A late filing fee is a penalty assessed by a tax authority, not an error in the financial statements, so it says nothing about materiality.
Why D: A correct entry with the right date and amount is simply accurate bookkeeping, not a misstatement of any kind, material or otherwise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A $5 rounding error in a $10 million statement is most likely:
A: Immaterial
B: Material
C: Fraud case
D: A restatement
Why A: A $5 error is only 0.00005% of $10 million, far too small to change any reader's decision, so it is immaterial and needs no correction.
Why B: Material errors are large enough to influence decisions, often judged against a percentage of income or assets, and $5 against $10 million is nowhere near that.
Why C: Fraud requires intentional deception by someone, and a tiny rounding difference is a normal arithmetic artifact, not evidence of any deliberate wrongdoing.
Why D: A restatement reissues prior statements to fix material errors, and a $5 rounding difference would never justify redoing a $10 million set of statements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an internal audit?
A: A review by company staff of controls and records
B: A review of competitors by the company staff
C: A review by the tax agency only, done every few years
D: A review by customers of the products they bought
Why A: An internal audit is performed by the company's own staff or department to evaluate internal controls, accuracy of records, and compliance, then report to management.
Why B: Studying competitors is market or competitive analysis done by marketing or strategy teams, and it has nothing to do with testing controls or records.
Why C: A tax agency review is an external IRS or state audit; internal audits are performed by the company itself and are ongoing rather than occasional.
Why D: Customers reviewing products they bought is a satisfaction survey or product review, not an audit of the company's controls, records, or financial reporting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does separation of duties help prevent?
A: Interest costs
B: Fraud and errors
C: Sales growth
D: Tax bills owed
Why A: Interest costs come from borrowing money and the terms of debt, and splitting tasks among employees does nothing to lower or prevent them.
Why B: Dividing authorization, custody, and recordkeeping among different people means no single employee can hide theft or mistakes, so fraud and errors are prevented or caught.
Why C: Sales growth depends on marketing, pricing, and demand; separating duties is an internal control and does not directly influence how fast sales increase.
Why D: Tax bills depend on income and tax law, and assigning duties to different employees has no effect on how much tax the firm owes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which situation violates separation of duties?
A: One person orders and another pays, both checked
B: Two people count the cash together each day at close
C: A manager reviews all payments made each month
D: One person orders, receives and pays for supplies
Why A: Having one person order and a different person pay, with both checked, is actually separation of duties working as intended, so it is not a violation.
Why B: Two people counting cash together is dual control, a strong safeguard where each person checks the other, so it supports separation of duties rather than violating it.
Why C: A manager reviewing all payments each month is an independent review, which strengthens controls and does not break separation of duties.
Why D: When one person orders, receives, and pays for supplies, nobody checks that work, so they could order fake items and pay themselves, which is the core violation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Fair Credit Reporting Act's concern?
A: Stock prices on the exchange for all listed firms
B: Business tax rates set by the state for all firms
C: Accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
D: Interest rates on savings offered by banks to depositors
Why A: Stock prices on the exchange are overseen by the SEC under securities laws, not by the FCRA, which concerns consumer credit reporting agencies.
Why B: Business tax rates are set by state and federal tax law, while the Fair Credit Reporting Act regulates how consumer credit information is handled.
Why C: The FCRA governs credit bureaus and users of credit reports, requiring accuracy, privacy, and giving consumers the right to dispute errors and see their reports.
Why D: Savings interest rates are set by banks and influenced by the Federal Reserve; the FCRA deals with consumer credit reports rather than deposit rates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an EIN?
A: A tax refund code that the IRS gives to each filer who asks
B: A customer ID number that a store gives to its regular buyers
C: A bank account number that is issued to the firm by its bank
D: A federal Employer Identification Number issued to a business
Why A: Refunds are issued after a return is processed and have no special code assigned to filers by request; an EIN is a business identifier, not a refund code.
Why B: A store's customer ID or loyalty number is a private marketing tool, whereas an EIN is a nine-digit tax identifier issued by the federal government.
Why C: Bank account numbers are assigned by banks to identify deposit accounts, while an EIN is assigned by the IRS and is used for tax reporting.
Why D: An Employer Identification Number is a nine-digit number the IRS issues to identify a business for tax filing, payroll reporting, and opening business bank accounts.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which business is most likely to need an EIN?
A: One that hires employees
B: A hobby with no income
C: A person washing a car
D: A child selling lemonade
Why A: Businesses with employees need an EIN to report payroll taxes, withhold income tax, and file employment forms such as Form 941 with the IRS.
Why B: A hobby with no income has no business tax filings, no employees, and no need for a separate federal employer number.
Why C: A person occasionally washing a car as a casual sole proprietor with no employees can generally use their Social Security number, so no EIN is required.
Why D: A child selling lemonade is a small casual activity without employees or formal tax reporting duties, so no EIN is needed for it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Form 941 used for?
A: Reporting contractor payments to the IRS
B: Individuals filing their yearly returns
C: Employers reporting quarterly payroll taxes
D: Applying for a license to operate in a state
Why A: Contractor payments are reported on Form 1099-NEC, while Form 941 covers wages and payroll tax withholding for employees, not independent contractors.
Why B: Individuals file annual income tax returns on Form 1040; Form 941 is filed by employers rather than by individual taxpayers.
Why C: Form 941 is the Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return, reporting wages paid, income tax withheld, and the Social Security and Medicare taxes owed each quarter.
Why D: Licenses to operate come from state or local agencies, while Form 941 is a federal IRS payroll tax return filed by employers each quarter.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a W-9 form?
A: A form employees use to set withholding, given to payroll when hired
B: A form a contractor gives a business with their taxpayer information
C: A form for filing a return, used by each person who pays tax
D: A form showing yearly wages and all the taxes already withheld
Why A: Employees use Form W-4 to tell payroll how much income tax to withhold, whereas Form W-9 is for independent contractors and vendors.
Why B: Form W-9 is completed by a contractor or vendor to give the business their name, address, and taxpayer ID so a 1099 can be issued later.
Why C: Individual income tax returns are filed on Form 1040, while Form W-9 is only an information request and is never filed as a tax return.
Why D: Form W-2 shows an employee's annual wages and taxes withheld, issued by the employer, whereas W-9 collects taxpayer information from contractors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business pays a freelancer $4,000 in a year. Which form does it generally send the freelancer?
A: Form W-2 copy
B: Form W-4 copy
C: Form 1099-NEC
D: Form 941 copy
Why A: Form W-2 is for employees who receive wages with taxes withheld, but a freelancer is an independent contractor who is not on payroll.
Why B: Form W-4 is filled out by employees to set their withholding; a business does not send it to a freelancer.
Why C: Businesses generally send Form 1099-NEC to contractors paid $600 or more in a year, so a $4,000 payment to a freelancer triggers it.
Why D: Form 941 is the employer's quarterly payroll tax return filed with the IRS, not a form sent to a freelancer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an estimated tax payment?
A: A guess about next year's tax law made by the revenue agency itself in the end
B: A refund sent by the government to people who overpaid in the year
C: A tax on estimates made by people who file their yearly returns
D: A quarterly payment of expected income tax by people without withholding
Why A: Tax agencies do not guess next year's law; estimated tax is a payment made by taxpayers themselves based on income they expect to earn.
Why B: A refund returns overpaid tax to a taxpayer, which is the opposite of an estimated payment where a taxpayer sends money in advance.
Why C: Estimated tax is not a separate tax on estimates; it is a way to prepay regular income and self-employment tax during the year.
Why D: Self-employed people and others without enough withholding pay expected income and self-employment tax in quarterly installments to the IRS to avoid underpayment penalties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sales tax permit?
A: Government permission for a seller to collect sales tax
B: A refund of sales tax to the buyers who shop at the store
C: A discount on sales tax for buyers who pay in cash
D: A tax on permits that firms must pay each year to the state
Why A: A sales tax permit is issued by the state and lets a seller legally collect sales tax from customers and remit it to the government.
Why B: Sales tax permits do not produce refunds to shoppers; they authorize the seller to collect tax, which is then sent to the state.
Why C: A permit does not discount tax for cash payers; buyers pay the legal rate whatever payment method they use.
Why D: A permit is not a tax on permits; it is an authorization, though some states charge a small fee to obtain one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is electronic invoicing?
A: Mailing invoices by post only, never online
B: Sending and receiving invoices digitally
C: Printing invoices on colored paper sheets
D: Hiding invoices from customers who owe us
Why A: Mailing paper invoices only is the traditional method that electronic invoicing replaces, so it is the opposite of sending digital invoices.
Why B: Electronic invoicing delivers invoices by email, portal, or software, which speeds delivery, lowers printing and postage costs, and makes tracking payments easier.
Why C: Printing invoices on colored paper is a stationery choice and has no connection to creating or delivering invoices in digital form.
Why D: Hiding invoices from customers would stop them from paying and is unethical; e-invoicing does the reverse by delivering bills promptly and visibly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a benefit of automated invoicing?
A: Fewer manual errors and faster collection
B: Higher costs from retyping each invoice
C: More data entry work for the staff
D: More paperwork, as each invoice is printed
Why A: Automation reduces typing mistakes and sends invoices instantly with payment reminders, which speeds collection and improves cash flow for the business.
Why B: Automation removes retyping, which lowers costs and errors; manual re-entry is a feature of non-automated invoicing.
Why C: Automated invoicing reduces data entry by creating invoices from existing records, so staff do less of it.
Why D: Automated invoicing cuts paper use by creating and sending invoices digitally, so adding printing and paperwork is the reverse of its benefit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a digital signature?
A: A scanned drawing of a pet kept on a file server
B: An electronic way to verify who signed a document
C: A printed name on a letter from a firm to a client
D: A password written on paper and kept in a safe
Why A: A scanned drawing of a pet is just an image file; it cannot identify a signer or show that a document is authentic.
Why B: A digital signature uses encryption to verify the signer's identity and that the document was not altered, and it is legally recognized under laws like the ESIGN Act.
Why C: A printed name is only typed text on paper and does not authenticate who signed or prove the document is unchanged.
Why D: A written password on paper is a login credential, not a signature, and storing it in a safe does not verify any document.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data analytics software used for in accounting?
A: Typing letters and memos for the office staff each week
B: Designing logos and brand materials for the firm each year overall
C: Printing checks only, for the vendors that a firm pays
D: Finding patterns, trends and unusual items in financial data
Why A: Typing letters and memos is word processing, a different task from analyzing financial data for patterns and risks.
Why B: Designing logos and brand materials is graphic design work done with design tools, not data analytics software used by accountants.
Why C: Printing checks is a payment function of accounting systems and is not what data analytics software is mainly built to do.
Why D: Data analytics tools scan large sets of financial data for trends, patterns, and outliers, helping accountants detect fraud, forecast results, and support decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An auditor uses software to scan all transactions for duplicate payments. What is this?
A: Inventory counting by hand each week
B: Price discrimination by sellers
C: Data analytics for fraud detection
D: Manual sampling of a few items
Why A: Counting inventory by hand is a physical, manual procedure and does not use software to scan every transaction for duplicates.
Why B: Price discrimination is a pricing practice of charging different customers different prices and has nothing to do with auditing payments.
Why C: Scanning all transactions with software to find duplicate payments is data analytics used for fraud detection, covering the whole population rather than a small sample.
Why D: Manual sampling checks only a few items by hand, which is the opposite of software that tests every transaction.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the CPA exam known for?
A: Testing typing speed and keyboard skills for office work
B: Testing accounting knowledge as part of becoming licensed
C: Testing artistic talent and the ability to draw and paint
D: Testing sales skills and the ability to persuade shoppers
Why A: Typing speed is tested in clerical or office skills assessments, while the CPA exam tests accounting, auditing, tax, and business knowledge.
Why B: The Uniform CPA Exam tests accounting, auditing, taxation, and business concepts, and passing it is one step toward earning the CPA license.
Why C: Artistic talent is judged in portfolios and art programs, which have no connection to the technical content of the CPA exam.
Why D: Sales and persuasion skills are tested in sales certifications and role-plays, not in the CPA exam, which is about accounting expertise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student likes analyzing budgets and advising managers on spending. Which role fits best?
A: Receptionist at a hotel front desk as a rule
B: Delivery driver for a courier firm
C: Management accountant or budget analyst
D: Retail cashier at a clothing store
Why A: A hotel receptionist greets guests, books rooms, and answers calls, which does not involve analyzing budgets or advising managers on spending.
Why B: A delivery driver transports packages and follows routes, which does not involve budgets, financial analysis, or advice to managers.
Why C: Management accountants and budget analysts study spending, prepare budgets and forecasts, and advise managers on cost control, matching the student's interests exactly.
Why D: A retail cashier processes sales and handles payments at the register, which does not involve analyzing budgets or advising managers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business buys office supplies for $300 cash. Which journal entry is correct?
A: Debit Cash $300; credit Supplies $300
B: Debit Expense $300; credit Capital $300
C: Debit Payable $300; credit Cash $300
D: Debit Supplies $300; credit Cash $300
Why A: This entry reverses the transaction by increasing Cash and decreasing Supplies, but paying cash for supplies lowers Cash and raises Supplies.
Why B: Buying supplies is not an expense of capital; this entry wrongly credits Capital, which would imply the owner invested $300 rather than cash being spent.
Why C: Debiting Payable would reduce a liability, but nothing was owed here because the purchase was paid for in cash on the spot.
Why D: Supplies is an asset that increases with a debit, and Cash is an asset that decreases with a credit, so both sides of the entry balance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which account type normally has a credit balance?
A: Revenue
B: Expense
C: Asset
D: Drawing
Why A: Revenue accounts increase with credits, so they normally carry credit balances, which matches the equation where revenue raises owner's equity.
Why B: Expenses increase with debits and normally have debit balances because they reduce owner's equity.
Why C: Assets increase with debits, so they normally have debit balances, which is the opposite of a credit balance.
Why D: The owner's drawing account reduces equity and increases with debits, so it has a normal debit balance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A trial balance shows total debits of $48,500 and total credits of $47,900. What does this indicate?
A: Revenue exceeds expenses by about $1,000 net
B: An error exists that must be found and corrected
C: The business is profitable, as credits are near debits
D: The books are in balance and all is well here
Why A: The $600 gap is a mismatch in the trial balance, not a measure of net income, and revenue and expenses are not what is being compared.
Why B: Debits must equal credits, so the $600 difference signals an error such as a transposition or omitted entry that must be located and corrected.
Why C: Close totals do not show profit; a trial balance only checks that debits equal credits, and a $600 difference means something is wrong.
Why D: Debits of $48,500 and credits of $47,900 are not equal, so the books are not in balance and need correcting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of posting from the journal to the ledger?
A: To prepare tax returns for the owners of the firm
B: To record bank interest earned on the cash account overall
C: To sort transaction amounts into individual accounts
D: To close the revenue accounts at the period end
Why A: Tax returns are prepared from the finished financial records; posting is an earlier bookkeeping step with no direct link to the owners' tax filings.
Why B: Bank interest earned is recorded as a transaction in the journal and posted to accounts; it is not the purpose of the posting step.
Why C: Posting copies journal entry amounts into the ledger accounts, grouping transactions by account so each account's balance can be determined.
Why D: Closing revenue accounts is done through closing entries at period end, which is a separate step from posting the journal to the ledger.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: On December 31, a company has used $1,400 of prepaid insurance that was recorded as an asset. What adjusting entry is needed?
A: No entry is needed because the insurance was prepaid in advance
B: Debit Cash $1,400 and credit Prepaid Insurance for $1,400
C: Debit Prepaid Insurance $1,400; credit Insurance Expense $1,400
D: Debit Insurance Expense $1,400; credit Prepaid Insurance $1,400
Why A: An adjusting entry is needed because part of the prepaid asset has been used up and must be recognized as an expense in the period.
Why B: The prepaid insurance was already paid, so no Cash is received; debiting Cash would incorrectly increase the cash balance.
Why C: This entry reverses the correct one, raising Prepaid Insurance and lowering expense, when used-up insurance should become an expense.
Why D: As coverage is used, the asset becomes an expense: debit Insurance Expense and credit Prepaid Insurance for $1,400, matching expense to the period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which account is closed to Income Summary at the end of the period?
A: Service Revenue
B: Accounts Payable
C: Cash on hand
D: Equipment asset
Why A: Service Revenue is a temporary account that is closed to Income Summary at period end so its balance can be transferred to owner's equity.
Why B: Accounts Payable is a liability and a permanent account, so it carries its balance forward and is not closed to Income Summary.
Why C: Cash is an asset and a permanent account; its balance carries into the next period rather than being closed out.
Why D: Equipment is a permanent asset account that remains on the balance sheet, so it is not closed to Income Summary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Revenues for the year are $82,000 and expenses are $61,500. What is the net income?
Why A: The $61,500 figure is the expense total only; net income subtracts expenses from revenue instead of reporting expenses alone.
Why B: Net income equals revenues minus expenses, so $82,000 - $61,500 = $20,500.
Why C: Adding revenue and expenses, $82,000 + $61,500 = $143,500, is incorrect because expenses must be subtracted from revenue to find income.
Why D: The $82,000 figure is total revenue before expenses are deducted, so it is not the net income.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accrual-basis accounting?
A: Recording income when cash is received and expenses when paid
B: Recording expenses when paid and revenue when ordered
C: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred
D: Recording once per decade for each business year ahead
Why A: That is cash-basis accounting; accrual records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the cash timing.
Why B: Accrual records expenses when incurred and revenue when earned, not when paid or ordered, so this mixes the two methods.
Why C: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the timing of cash, which matches income with the related costs.
Why D: Accounting is done in regular periods like months, quarters, and years, and recording once per decade would provide no useful timely information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company earned $2,000 in service revenue in December but will not be paid until January. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?
A: Next year
B: Not ever
C: February
D: December
Why A: Cash timing does not drive accrual accounting, so waiting for the January cash receipt would mean using the cash basis rather than accrual.
Why B: Earned revenue is always recorded in accrual accounting even if payment is delayed; it is booked as Accounts Receivable.
Why C: February has no tie to the service; revenue is recognized when it is earned, which was December when the work was done.
Why D: Under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned, so the $2,000 is recognized in December with a debit to Accounts Receivable and a credit to Service Revenue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the correct order of steps in the accounting cycle?
A: Journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, statements, close
B: Close, journalize, post, adjust, then prepare statements overall
C: Adjust, journalize, close, post, then prepare statements
D: Statements, journalize, post, close, the reverse order
Why A: The cycle runs from journalizing transactions, posting, preparing a trial balance, adjusting, preparing statements, and finally closing to prepare for the next period.
Why B: Closing cannot come first because closing entries need adjusted balances and finished statements, and transactions must be journalized before anything else.
Why C: Adjusting before journalizing makes no sense because there would be no recorded transactions to adjust, so this order is incorrect.
Why D: Starting with statements is impossible because statements are the output of the cycle and need journalized and posted data first.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a contra-asset account?
A: An account with a credit balance that reduces an asset
B: An account with a debit balance that records sales
C: An account with a debit balance that increases an asset
D: An account with a credit balance that records owner investments
Why A: A contra-asset such as Accumulated Depreciation or Allowance for Doubtful Accounts has a credit balance and reduces the book value of a related asset.
Why B: Sales are recorded in revenue accounts with credit balances; a contra-asset has a credit balance and reduces an asset.
Why C: A debit balance that increases an asset describes an ordinary asset account; a contra-asset does the opposite with a credit balance.
Why D: Owner investments are recorded in a capital account within equity; a contra-asset reduces an asset's value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Equipment cost $12,000 with a $2,000 salvage value and a 5-year life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?
Why A: The $12,000 figure is the original cost and ignores both salvage value and the five-year life, so it cannot be annual depreciation.
Why B: The $10,000 figure is the depreciable cost ($12,000 - $2,000), not yet divided by the five-year useful life.
Why C: The $2,400 figure divides the full cost without subtracting salvage value ($12,000 / 5), but straight-line uses cost minus salvage.
Why D: Straight-line depreciation is (cost - salvage) / life, so ($12,000 - $2,000) / 5 years = $2,000 per year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are adjusting entries needed?
A: To increase the taxes owed by the firm and its owners at the year end
B: To hide errors from the owners and the auditors of the firm for good
C: To update accounts so revenues and expenses are recorded in the proper period
D: To change prior years' books after the statements have all been issued as a rule
Why A: Adjusting entries match income and expenses to the right period, not to raise taxes, though accurate income may affect taxes.
Why B: Adjusting entries correct period accounts openly for accuracy; hiding errors from owners or auditors would be fraud rather than proper accounting.
Why C: Adjusting entries update accounts for accruals, deferrals, and depreciation so revenues and expenses appear in the period they belong to, following the matching principle.
Why D: Prior-year books are not altered after statements are issued; adjusting entries are made at the end of the current period before the statements are prepared.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Wages of $900 have been earned by employees but will be paid next period. Which adjustment is needed?
A: Debit Cash $900 and credit Wages Expense $900
B: Debit Wages Expense $900; credit Wages Payable $900
C: Debit Wages Payable $900; credit Cash $900 next period
D: No adjustment because no cash was paid out yet
Why A: This entry wrongly debits Cash and credits Wages Expense, but no cash was paid and expense should be increased, not reduced.
Why B: Earned but unpaid wages are an accrued expense, so debit Wages Expense $900 to record the cost and credit Wages Payable $900 for the liability.
Why C: Debiting Wages Payable and crediting Cash is the entry made when the wages are paid next period, not the adjusting entry now.
Why D: Accrual accounting requires recording expenses when incurred, even if no cash has been paid, so an adjustment is needed here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the post-closing trial balance contain?
A: Revenue and expense accounts
B: Permanent balance sheet accounts
C: Adjusting entries from the period
D: Income summary and drawing accounts
Why A: Revenue and expense accounts are temporary and closed to zero, so they do not appear with balances after closing.
Why B: After closing, temporary accounts have zero balances, so only permanent accounts such as assets, liabilities, and owner's capital remain on the post-closing trial balance.
Why C: Adjusting entries are made before closing; the post-closing trial balance lists just the balances left in permanent accounts.
Why D: Income summary and drawing are temporary accounts closed to zero, so they do not appear with balances.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a work sheet used for in accounting?
A: To bill customers for the goods and services that the firm sold
B: To file taxes with the state revenue office for the firm each year
C: To organize trial balance and adjustments before preparing statements
D: To record daily sales in the journal of the firm each day for the year
Why A: Customers are billed with invoices; a work sheet is an internal accounting tool and is not sent to customers.
Why B: State taxes are filed on tax forms and returns, whereas a work sheet is an informal tool and is not filed with the state.
Why C: A work sheet lays out the trial balance, adjustments, and adjusted balances in columns, helping prepare the financial statements accurately and spot errors.
Why D: Daily sales are recorded in the journal as source documents come in, while the work sheet is only a period-end planning tool.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Total owner's equity at the start of the year was $50,000. Net income was $18,000 and the owner withdrew $6,000. What is ending equity?
Why A: Ending equity equals beginning equity plus net income minus withdrawals: $50,000 + $18,000 - $6,000 = $62,000.
Why B: The $26,000 figure does not start from the $50,000 beginning equity, so it ignores the owner's existing investment that carries forward into ending equity.
Why C: The $68,000 figure adds net income to beginning equity but forgets to subtract the $6,000 withdrawal, which reduces equity.
Why D: The $74,000 figure adds both net income and withdrawals to $50,000, but withdrawals reduce equity and must be subtracted.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business sells $6,000 of goods on account with terms 2/10, n/30. What payment settles the invoice if paid on day 8?
Why A: The $6,120 figure adds the discount to the price instead of subtracting it, but a 2% discount lowers the amount the buyer owes.
Why B: The $6,000 figure is the full invoice and would be paid after the discount period; paying on day 8 earns the 2% discount.
Why C: The $5,400 figure takes a 10% reduction, but terms 2/10 mean 2% off, not 10%.
Why D: Paying within 10 days earns a 2% discount: $6,000 x 0.02 = $120, so the payment is $6,000 - $120 = $5,880.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Receivables total $80,000 and the company estimates 3% will be uncollectible. What is the bad debt estimate?
Why A: The $24,000 figure uses 30% rather than 3% of $80,000, so it overstates the estimate by a factor of ten.
Why B: Bad debt estimate = $80,000 x 3% = $2,400, the amount expected to be uncollectible and recorded in the allowance.
Why C: The $77,600 figure is receivables minus the estimate ($80,000 - $2,400), which is net realizable value rather than the bad debt estimate itself.
Why D: The $240 figure uses 0.3% instead of 3% of $80,000, putting the decimal in the wrong place.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an aging schedule show?
A: Product shelf life, how long it keeps fresh
B: Equipment age in years of use by the firm
C: Employee ages in years on the payroll
D: How long receivables have been outstanding
Why A: Shelf life concerns how long goods stay fresh, which is a product feature and has no connection to accounts receivable aging reports.
Why B: Equipment age is tracked through depreciation records and asset registers rather than an aging schedule of customer accounts.
Why C: Employee ages belong in human resources records, and an aging schedule lists customer balances rather than payroll data.
Why D: An aging schedule groups customer balances by how long they have been unpaid, such as 30, 60, or 90 days, helping estimate bad debts and guide collections.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a purchase order?
A: To prove payment was made by the buyer to the vendor firm on time overall
B: To bill the buyer for goods after they have been delivered to it
C: To authorize a vendor to deliver goods or services at stated terms
D: To record wages paid to the staff members of the firm each month
Why A: Proof of payment comes from a receipt or canceled check, while a purchase order is issued before delivery to request goods.
Why B: Billing the buyer is done with a sales invoice from the vendor, and a purchase order is created by the buyer, not the seller.
Why C: A purchase order is issued by the buyer to a vendor, listing items, quantities, prices, and terms, and it authorizes the purchase before delivery.
Why D: Wages are recorded through payroll records and journal entries, while a purchase order concerns buying goods or services from vendors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A customer's $500 account is written off under the allowance method. What is the effect on net accounts receivable?
A: No change
B: Falls by $500
C: Rises by $500
D: Falls $1,000
Why A: Under the allowance method, the write-off debits Allowance and credits Accounts Receivable, so net receivables stay the same because both fall by $500.
Why B: Net receivables would fall only if expense were recorded at write-off; under the allowance method the estimate was already expensed earlier.
Why C: A write-off removes an uncollectible account, so net receivables cannot rise from it.
Why D: The write-off is $500, not $1,000, and it leaves net accounts receivable unchanged since the allowance falls by the same amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a three-way match in accounts payable?
A: Matching three customers with three bills on the same day overall
B: Splitting a bill three ways among friends at a restaurant
C: Comparing the purchase order, receiving report and invoice
D: Paying three invoices at once with one single payment
Why A: Matching customers to bills on one day is not an accounts payable control; the three-way match deals with vendor documents.
Why B: Splitting a restaurant bill is a casual social arrangement and has nothing to do with accounts payable controls.
Why C: A three-way match compares the purchase order, the receiving report, and the vendor invoice before payment to confirm what was ordered, received, and billed.
Why D: Paying several invoices with one payment is a batch payment and does not describe the three document comparison called a three-way match.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company has $40,000 in credit sales and collects $32,000 during the period. What is the ending change in accounts receivable?
A: An increase of $8,000
B: An increase of $72,000
C: A decrease of $8,000
D: No change in sales
Why A: Receivables rise by credit sales and fall by collections, so $40,000 - $32,000 = an $8,000 increase in accounts receivable.
Why B: The $72,000 figure adds sales and collections together, but collections reduce receivables and must be subtracted from credit sales.
Why C: A decrease would occur only if collections exceeded credit sales, but here $40,000 of sales exceeded $32,000 collected.
Why D: Sales and collections differ by $8,000, so receivables did change, even though the credit sales were not changed by the collections.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit memo from a seller?
A: A bill for new goods ordered by a customer
B: A document reducing the amount a customer owes
C: A payment receipt issued by a seller to a buyer
D: A tax form that a seller files with the state
Why A: A bill for new goods is an invoice, whereas a credit memo lowers what a customer owes the seller.
Why B: A credit memo is issued by the seller to reduce a customer's balance, such as for returned or damaged goods or a pricing error.
Why C: A payment receipt confirms money received, while a credit memo reduces the amount owed without a payment being made.
Why D: Sales tax returns are filed with the state, but a credit memo is a business document sent to a customer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which statement shows revenues and expenses for a period?
A: The cash flow statement
B: The balance sheet
C: The trial balance
D: The income statement
Why A: The cash flow statement shows cash inflows and outflows from operating, investing, and financing activities, not revenues and expenses.
Why B: The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a single date rather than revenues and expenses over a period.
Why C: A trial balance lists account balances to check that debits equal credits and is not a formal financial statement of results.
Why D: The income statement lists revenues and expenses for a period and shows net income or loss, measuring profitability.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Assets total $120,000 and liabilities total $45,000. What is owner's equity?
Why A: The $165,000 figure adds liabilities to assets, but equity is found by subtracting liabilities from assets.
Why B: The $45,000 figure is the liabilities total, which is the creditors' claim on assets and not the owner's claim.
Why C: The $120,000 figure is total assets, which equals liabilities plus equity, so it is not equity alone.
Why D: Using Assets = Liabilities + Equity, equity = $120,000 - $45,000 = $75,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: On a classified balance sheet, which is a current asset?
A: Land and buildings
B: A 10-year bank loan
C: Accounts receivable
D: Owner's capital stake
Why A: Land and buildings are long-term assets used for years, so they are reported as property, plant, and equipment rather than current assets.
Why B: A 10-year bank loan is a long-term liability, not an asset at all, and certainly not a current asset.
Why C: Accounts receivable are amounts owed by customers expected to be collected within a year, so they are a current asset.
Why D: Owner's capital is an equity item on the balance sheet, not an asset, so it cannot be a current asset.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does gross profit equal?
A: Net sales plus cost of goods sold
B: Net sales minus cost of goods sold
C: Cost of goods sold minus expenses
D: Net sales minus all the expenses
Why A: Adding cost of goods sold to sales would raise the number; gross profit is found by subtracting costs from sales.
Why B: Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold, showing what remains after paying for the goods to cover operating expenses.
Why C: Subtracting expenses from cost of goods sold does not produce any profit measure, since gross profit starts with net sales.
Why D: Net sales minus all expenses is closer to net income; gross profit subtracts only cost of goods sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net sales are $200,000 and gross profit is $80,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
Why A: Gross profit = net sales - COGS, so COGS = $200,000 - $80,000 = $120,000.
Why B: The $80,000 figure is the gross profit, which is what remains after cost of goods sold is subtracted from sales.
Why C: The $280,000 figure adds gross profit to sales, but COGS is found by subtracting gross profit from sales.
Why D: The $200,000 figure is net sales, which is the starting point from which cost of goods sold is subtracted.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the current ratio?
A: Total assets divided by total sales for the year
B: Current assets divided by current liabilities
C: Net income divided by the total owner equity
D: Debt divided by total assets of the whole firm
Why A: Total assets divided by sales is an asset turnover type measure, not a liquidity ratio like the current ratio.
Why B: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, measuring whether a firm can pay obligations due within a year.
Why C: Net income divided by owner equity is return on equity, a profitability measure, not the current ratio.
Why D: Debt divided by total assets is the debt ratio, which measures leverage rather than short-term liquidity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Current assets are $90,000 and current liabilities are $60,000. What is the current ratio?
Why A: The 150,000 figure adds the two amounts, but the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, producing a small ratio.
Why B: The 0.67 figure flips the fraction ($60,000 / $90,000), but current assets belong on top.
Why C: The 30,000 figure is the difference between the amounts, which is working capital, not a ratio.
Why D: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $90,000 / $60,000 = 1.5, meaning $1.50 of liquid assets for each $1 owed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which statement explains changes in owner's equity during a period?
A: The monthly bank statement list
B: The payroll register of wages paid
C: The statement of owner's equity
D: The aging schedule of accounts
Why A: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals in the bank account and does not explain changes in owner's equity.
Why B: A payroll register lists employee wages and withholdings and does not explain changes in owner's equity.
Why C: The statement of owner's equity shows beginning capital plus investments and net income minus withdrawals, ending with the ending capital balance.
Why D: An aging schedule groups unpaid customer balances by age and does not explain changes in owner's equity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the statement of cash flows divide activities into?
A: Operating, investing and financing
B: Assets, liabilities and equity
C: Buying, selling and storing goods
D: Revenue, cost and profit centers
Why A: The cash flow statement sorts cash receipts and payments into operating, investing, and financing activities to show where cash came from and where it went.
Why B: Assets, liabilities, and equity are the balance sheet categories, not the sections of the cash flow statement.
Why C: Buying, selling, and storing goods describe business operations in general and are not the three standard cash flow sections.
Why D: Revenue, cost, and profit centers are responsibility accounting units inside a company, not cash flow statement categories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a financing activity?
A: Selling products to customers
B: Paying wages to the staff
C: Buying equipment for cash
D: Borrowing money from a bank
Why A: Selling products to customers produces cash from daily operations, so it is an operating activity.
Why B: Paying wages is a regular expense of running the business, so it is an operating activity.
Why C: Buying equipment for cash is an investing activity because it involves acquiring a long-term asset.
Why D: Financing activities involve raising or repaying funds from lenders and owners, and borrowing from a bank brings in cash through debt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does return on equity measure?
A: Net income relative to owners' investment
B: Sales relative to total assets owned
C: Cash relative to the debts of the firm
D: Expenses relative to sales for the year
Why A: Return on equity equals net income divided by owners' equity, showing how much profit is earned on the money owners have invested.
Why B: Sales relative to total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency measure that is different from return on equity.
Why C: Cash relative to debts relates to liquidity measures such as the cash ratio, not to return on equity.
Why D: Expenses relative to sales is an expense ratio or margin measure, not return on equity, which compares profit with equity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net income is $30,000 and average equity is $200,000. What is return on equity?
Why A: The 30% figure would result from dividing by $100,000, but average equity here is $200,000, so the result is lower.
Why B: The 150% figure is not possible here, because $30,000 divided by $200,000 is well below 1, so the return must be under 100%.
Why C: ROE = net income / average equity = $30,000 / $200,000 = 0.15, or 15%.
Why D: The 6.7% figure flips the fraction ($200,000 / $30,000 = 6.67), but net income belongs in the numerator.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company has current assets of $55,000 and current liabilities of $38,000. What is its working capital?
Why A: The $38,000 figure is the current liabilities alone, one component of the working capital calculation.
Why B: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $55,000 - $38,000 = $17,000, the cushion available for short-term needs.
Why C: The $93,000 figure adds the two amounts, but working capital subtracts current liabilities from current assets.
Why D: The $55,000 figure is the current assets alone, before subtracting the current liabilities owed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the role of the FASB?
A: Regulating banks in the United States today
B: Setting accounting standards in the United States
C: Setting interest rates in the United States
D: Collecting income taxes from firms and people as a rule
Why A: Regulating banks is the work of agencies like the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC, not the FASB.
Why B: The Financial Accounting Standards Board is the private body that sets US GAAP, the standards companies follow when preparing financial statements.
Why C: Interest rates are influenced by the Federal Reserve through monetary policy, not by the FASB.
Why D: Collecting income taxes is the job of the IRS and state tax agencies, not the FASB, which writes accounting standards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company records a sale before the goods ship and before the customer is obligated. Which principle is likely violated?
A: The cost principle
B: Materiality idea
C: Going concern idea
D: Revenue recognition
Why A: The cost principle says to record assets at original cost, so it does not govern when a sale is recorded.
Why B: Materiality concerns whether an amount is big enough to matter to users, not when a sale should be recognized.
Why C: Going concern assumes a business will keep operating, which has nothing to do with the timing of a sale.
Why D: Revenue is recognized when earned, such as when goods are delivered and the customer is obligated, so recording a sale earlier violates revenue recognition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the going concern assumption?
A: A business will continue operating for the foreseeable future
B: A business will close next year and stop all operating
C: A business will never lose money, as owners cover losses as a rule
D: A business will merge soon with another firm in the town
Why A: The going concern assumption presumes a business will operate long enough to carry out its plans, which justifies recording assets at cost and not at liquidation value.
Why B: Assuming the business will close next year would require liquidation accounting, which is the opposite of the going concern assumption.
Why C: Businesses can and do lose money; going concern does not guarantee profits or owners covering losses.
Why D: A merger is a specific event, and the going concern assumption makes no prediction about merging with another firm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of an audit?
A: To create the company's budget for the coming year ahead of all the owners
B: To sell products to customers and earn a profit for the owners each single year as a rule
C: To give an independent opinion on whether financial statements are fairly presented
D: To prepare the daily journal entries for each of the transactions of the firm
Why A: Budgets are prepared by management and owners, and an audit does not create a budget for the coming year.
Why B: Selling products and earning profit is the work of operations, whereas an audit is an independent review of the statements.
Why C: An audit gives an independent expert opinion on whether financial statements are fairly presented under GAAP, which builds trust for investors and lenders.
Why D: Daily journal entries are made by company bookkeepers, while auditors review the records independently after they are prepared.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An auditor issues an unqualified opinion. What does this mean?
A: The auditor refused to give an opinion on the records
B: The statements contain fraud and material errors in them
C: The statements are fairly presented in all material respects
D: The company will never fail and will always make a profit overall
Why A: Refusing to give an opinion is a disclaimer of opinion, which is different from an unqualified opinion.
