Why B: Employees work for the corporation and may hold stock, but employment alone gives no ownership; ownership comes only from holding shares of the company's stock.
Why C: Customers buy the corporation's products and services but have no ownership claim on the company unless they separately buy its shares as investors.
Why D: Suppliers sell materials and services to the corporation as business partners, but supplying goods creates no ownership; only holding shares of stock does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a board of directors?
A: A group of employees chosen by managers to run the firm
B: A group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation
C: A group of lenders that fund the firm with their large loans
D: A group of customers who vote on the firm's major decisions
Why A: Managers answer to the board, not the reverse; directors are elected by shareholders rather than chosen by managers, and they oversee the firm instead of running daily operations.
Why B: Shareholders elect directors to oversee the corporation, set major policy, appoint senior officers and protect shareholder interests, while officers handle day-to-day operations of the business.
Why C: Lenders are creditors who are repaid under loan terms; they do not form the board, which is elected by shareholders to oversee the corporation.
Why D: Customers do not vote on major decisions; the board is elected by shareholders, who are the owners, and it guides the corporation on their behalf.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A corporation's officer approves a sale that benefits the officer's own company at the expense of the corporation. Which duty is violated?
A: The duty to advertise the sale
B: The duty to hire more staff
C: The duty to audit the books
D: The fiduciary duty of loyalty
Why A: Advertising has nothing to do with the officer's self-dealing; the problem is putting personal gain ahead of the corporation, not a missing promotional duty.
Why B: Hiring staff is an operational choice and unrelated to the conflict of interest; the officer's wrong lies in favoring a personal company over the corporation.
Why C: Auditing books relates to financial controls and oversight, not to the self-dealing here, where the officer put personal interests ahead of the corporation's.
Why D: Officers and directors owe a fiduciary duty of loyalty, which requires putting the corporation's interests ahead of their own, so a self-serving sale at its expense violates it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is piercing the corporate veil?
A: Raising capital by selling new shares of stock to the public in a big offering
B: Protecting owners from all liability in every case, whatever they did
C: A court holds owners personally liable for corporate debts in certain abuses
D: Merging two companies into one larger firm under a single shared name
Why A: Selling new shares to the public is an initial or secondary public offering, a way to raise capital, and has nothing to do with disregarding corporate limited liability.
Why B: Piercing the veil is the opposite of protecting owners from all liability; it is the exception where courts remove that protection when owners abuse the corporate form.
Why C: Courts may pierce the corporate veil and hold owners personally liable when they commingle funds, ignore formalities, undercapitalize the firm or use it to commit fraud.
Why D: Combining two companies is a merger or acquisition and does not involve piercing the veil, which concerns removing owners' limited liability protection after abuse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a franchise agreement?
A: A contract allowing use of a brand and system in exchange for fees
B: A loan agreement between a bank and a business owner for funds overall
C: A contract to buy stock in a company from its current owners
D: A lease for land only, with no brand or system included in it
Why A: A franchise agreement lets the franchisee operate under the franchisor's brand, trademarks and business system in exchange for fees and royalties, subject to standards and control.
Why B: A bank loan is a financing contract that creates debt; a franchise agreement is about licensing a brand and system rather than lending money to a business owner.
Why C: Buying stock transfers a share of company ownership, while a franchise gives only the right to use a brand and system, not ownership of the franchisor.
Why D: A franchise includes the brand and operating system, so a plain land lease with neither does not qualify as a franchise agreement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A franchisee wants to change the menu without approval. Why might the franchisor object?
A: Brand consistency is part of the franchise agreement
B: Menus are not part of the business under the agreement
C: Franchise law forbids all menus from being altered
D: Franchisees own the trademark and the brand name
Why A: Franchise agreements require uniform menus, quality and branding so customers get the same experience everywhere, so the franchisor can object when a franchisee changes the menu alone.
Why B: Menus are generally part of the business and its brand standards, which the agreement controls, so claiming they fall outside the agreement is not a sound reason.
Why C: Franchise law does not forbid all menu changes; it is the franchise contract and brand standards that restrict changes without approval, and approved changes are allowed.
Why D: The franchisor owns the trademark and brand name and licenses them to the franchisee, who does not own them, which is why the franchisor can enforce standards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a limited partner?
A: A creditor of the firm who lent money to the company and is repaid before all the owners
B: An investor whose liability is limited to the amount invested and who does not manage the firm
C: A person who owns no part of the firm and has no right to its profits or to its decisions in the end
D: A partner with unlimited liability who manages the firm and makes every decision each day
Why A: That describes a creditor, who lends money and is repaid under loan terms; a limited partner is an owner-investor who shares profits rather than a lender.
Why B: A limited partner invests capital, shares in profits and risks losing only the amount invested, but cannot take part in management without risking losing that limited liability.
Why C: A limited partner does own part of the firm and shares in its profits, so a person with no ownership or profit right would not be a partner.
Why D: That describes a general partner, who manages the firm and has unlimited personal liability; a limited partner has capped liability and no management role.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an operating agreement govern in an LLC?
A: How products are shipped to customers each week
B: How customers pay for goods and services in cash
C: How the LLC is managed and how profits are shared
D: How taxes are filed by customers who buy goods
Why A: Shipping logistics are day-to-day operations handled by managers and are not the subject of an operating agreement, which sets internal rules for owners.
Why B: Customer payment methods are business operations and sales policy, not governance; the operating agreement covers owners' rights, management structure and profit sharing in the LLC.
Why C: An operating agreement sets out how an LLC is managed, each member's ownership share, voting rights, how profits and losses are divided and what happens when members leave.
Why D: Customers file their own taxes; an operating agreement governs the LLC's internal affairs among members and has nothing to do with tax filings by buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which formation document must usually be filed with the state to create a corporation?
A: A trademark application form
B: A warranty card for buyers
C: An invoice for the goods
D: Articles of incorporation
Why A: A trademark application protects a brand name or logo with the federal trademark office and does not create a corporation or give it legal existence.
Why B: A warranty card records a product guarantee for buyers and has no role in forming a corporation, which requires a filing with the state.
Why C: An invoice is a bill for goods sold, a routine business document, and plays no part in creating a corporation as a legal entity.
Why D: Articles of incorporation, filed with the state, create the corporation as a separate legal entity and set out basics such as its name, purpose, registered agent and authorized shares.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is apparent authority?
A: When a third party reasonably believes an agent has authority because of the principal's conduct
B: Authority held by a court of law over the parties to a lawsuit that is brought before it
C: When an agent holds authority that the principal expressly gave in writing
D: When an agent gains authority because the principal later approves the act
Why A: Apparent authority arises when a principal's words or conduct lead a third party to reasonably believe an agent is authorized, so the principal may be bound even without actual permission.
Why B: That describes jurisdiction, a court's power over a case and its parties, which is a procedural concept and not a form of authority held by an agent.
Why C: That describes express authority, which is stated directly; apparent authority arises from the principal's conduct that leads a third party to believe the agent has authority.
Why D: That describes ratification, where the principal approves an act after it happens; apparent authority comes from the principal's conduct before the third party relied on it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store lets a new clerk wear a manager's badge. The clerk signs a large order with a supplier. What may be the result?
A: The supplier must pay the store, as the clerk lacked leave
B: No contract is possible with the store or its staff
C: The store may be bound because of apparent authority
D: Only the clerk is bound by the supply contract signed
Why A: The clerk's lack of leave to sign does not release the supplier or the store; the supplier is entitled to rely on appearances, and the supplier would not owe the store payment.
Why B: A contract is possible here because the store's conduct gave the clerk the look of authority, so the claim that no contract can exist with the store is wrong.
Why C: Letting the clerk wear a manager's badge made the supplier reasonably believe the clerk had authority, so the store may be bound by apparent authority even without actual permission.
Why D: The clerk acted as an agent for the store, so the store can be bound rather than only the clerk, because the store's own conduct created the appearance of authority.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a principal in agency law?
A: The person who inspects the agent's work
B: The person who authorizes an agent to act
C: The person who drafts the agent's contract
D: The school leader in charge of the staff
Why A: An inspector or supervisor checks work quality but does not authorize the agent; the principal is the person on whose behalf, and with whose authority, the agent acts.
Why B: The principal is the person who authorizes an agent to act on their behalf, and the principal is bound by the agent's actions within that authority.
Why C: Drafting a contract is a lawyer's or manager's task; the principal is defined by authorizing the agent to act for them, not by writing the agent's contract.
Why D: In agency law the principal is not a school head; the word here means the party who gives an agent authority to act for them in dealings with third parties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which fact most suggests a worker is an employee rather than a contractor?
A: She uses her own tools and sets her own schedule, working for many clients
B: She works for several clients at the same time during the year
C: She sends invoices for each project and pays her own taxes each year
D: The company sets her hours and tells her exactly how to do the work
Why A: Using her own tools, setting her own schedule and working for many clients are marks of an independent contractor, not an employee, because she controls the work.
Why B: Serving several clients at once suggests independence and a contractor relationship, since employees usually work for one employer who controls their time and work.
Why C: Sending invoices and paying her own taxes are typical of independent contractors, while employers withhold taxes and pay employees through payroll.
Why D: When a company controls hours and how the work is done, the worker is likely an employee, because the right to control the manner of work is the key test.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A delivery driver causes a crash while making a delivery. Who may be liable?
A: The customer who ordered it
B: The employer and the driver
C: The customer's insurance company
D: The driver's family members
Why A: The customer who ordered the delivery did not cause the crash or control the driver, so liability falls on the driver and the employer.
Why B: Under respondeat superior an employer can be liable for torts committed by an employee within the scope of employment, and the driver is also personally liable for the crash.
Why C: The customer's insurer has no connection to the driver's negligence; liability falls on the driver and the employer under agency law.
Why D: A driver's relatives are not liable for the driver's torts on the job; responsibility rests with the driver and the employer under respondeat superior.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an at-will employment relationship?
A: Either side may end employment at any time for a lawful reason
B: Employment that always needs a reason and ends only by court order
C: Employment with no pay for the person who does the work
D: Employment for a fixed term agreed by both sides in advance
Why A: At-will employment lets either the employer or the employee end the relationship at any time, with or without notice, so long as the reason is not illegal.
Why B: At-will employment does not need any reason and does not need a court order to end; requiring cause is what a contract or union agreement typically provides.
Why C: At-will describes the right to end the job and says nothing about pay; employees under it are still entitled to lawful wages for the work done.
Why D: A fixed term is the opposite of at-will employment, where either side may end the job at any time and no set length of service is promised.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An employee is fired a week after reporting safety violations to a government agency. Which claim is most likely?
A: Trade dilution
B: Price fixing
C: Retaliation
D: Breach of terms
Why A: Trade dilution is a trademark concept about weakening a famous brand, so it has no relevance to firing a worker who reported safety problems to a government agency.
Why B: Price fixing is an antitrust violation where competitors agree on prices, which has nothing to do with discipline or termination after an employee's safety report.
Why C: Firing someone soon after they report safety violations suggests retaliation, which laws such as OSHA and whistleblower statutes prohibit, and the close timing supports that claim.
Why D: Breach of terms relates to contract duties, but the facts here, a firing right after a protected safety report, point most directly to a retaliation claim instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is real property?
A: Stock certificates and bonds held by investors
B: Furniture and other movable household items
C: A car, a truck or any other motor vehicle
D: Land and things permanently attached to it
Why A: Stocks and bonds are personal property, specifically intangible financial assets, because they are not land and are not permanently attached to land.
Why B: Furniture and movable household items are personal property since they can be moved and are not permanently attached to land or buildings.
Why C: Vehicles are movable and so count as personal property, even though they are valuable; they are not land or permanent fixtures.
Why D: Real property includes land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings, trees and fixtures, together with the rights that come with owning them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is personal property?
A: Movable items such as vehicles and equipment
B: Mineral rights beneath land, real property
C: A permanent building on a piece of land
D: Land, houses and other fixed objects on it
Why A: Personal property is anything movable and not attached to land, such as vehicles, equipment, furniture and inventory, as opposed to land and permanent fixtures.
Why B: Mineral rights beneath land are interests in real property, because they belong to the land itself and are not movable items.
Why C: A permanent building on land is real property, since it is attached to the land and not movable like personal property.
Why D: Land, houses and fixed objects on land are all real property, the opposite of personal property, which consists of movable items.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A tenant installs a movable bookshelf. At move-out, who owns it?
A: The landlord, because it is real property
B: No one may keep it after the tenant moves
C: The bank, because it holds the tenant's lease
D: The tenant, because it is personal property
Why A: A movable bookshelf is not attached to the building, so it is not real property, and the landlord has no claim to it based on that label.
Why B: The tenant may keep the bookshelf at move-out; the claim that no one may keep it has no basis in property law for a movable item.
Why C: A bank holding a lease has no ownership of a tenant's movable furniture; leases give rights to use the premises, not title to the tenant's belongings.
Why D: A movable bookshelf is personal property and not a fixture, so it stays the tenant's and the tenant may remove it when moving out.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a lease?
A: A contract to buy property permanently from the owner at a price agreed in advance in the end
B: A loan on property from a bank, repaid in monthly installments over many years
C: A contract giving someone the right to use property for a time in exchange for rent
D: A tax on property paid by the owner to the local government every single year
Why A: That describes a purchase agreement, which transfers ownership permanently; a lease only gives the right to use property for a limited time in exchange for rent.
Why B: A loan on property from a bank is a mortgage, which is a financing agreement; a lease is a contract between a landlord and a tenant.
Why C: A lease is a contract in which an owner gives another party the right to use property for a set time, usually in exchange for rent, while keeping ownership.
Why D: A tax paid on property to local government is a property tax, a levy and not a contract; a lease is an agreement between landlord and tenant.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is eminent domain?
A: A buyer's right to cancel a purchase within a few days of buying a house
B: The government's power to take private property for public use with fair payment
C: A landlord's right to evict a tenant who has not paid the rent on time
D: A bank's right to foreclose on a home when the borrower stops paying the loan in the end
Why A: A right to cancel a purchase within days of buying a home describes a rescission or cooling-off right, not eminent domain, which is a government power.
Why B: Eminent domain lets the government take private property for public use, such as roads or schools, as long as the owner receives just compensation under the Fifth Amendment.
Why C: A landlord's right to evict a nonpaying tenant is an eviction remedy under landlord-tenant law and has no connection to the government's eminent domain power.
Why D: A bank's right to foreclose on a home after nonpayment is a lender's remedy under a mortgage, while eminent domain is the government's power to take property.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A city needs a strip of private land for a new road. What must it generally provide to the owner?
A: Just compensation
B: Free city services
C: A permit to build
D: A property tax cut
Why A: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation, meaning fair market value, when the government takes private property for public use, such as a new road.
Why B: The Takings Clause requires fair payment for the land, not free services; the owner is entitled to just compensation, usually measured as market value.
Why C: A building permit allows construction and is not payment for land taken; the owner is entitled to just compensation, not a permit for a new project.
Why D: A reduction in future property taxes does not replace payment for the land taken; the Fifth Amendment requires just compensation to the owner.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an intentional tort?
A: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency over taxes
B: A wrong committed deliberately, such as assault or defamation
C: A contract breach by one side that fails to perform its part
D: A careless act with no intent to cause harm to another person
Why A: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency is an administrative or tax law matter, not a tort, which is a civil wrong that harms another person.
Why B: An intentional tort is a civil wrong committed on purpose, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment or defamation, where the person meant to act, and it can bring damages.
Why C: A contract breach is a failure to perform a promise, which is a separate area of law from torts, which are wrongs that do not depend on a contract.
Why D: Careless acts without intent to harm are negligence, not intentional torts, because an intentional tort requires that the wrongdoer meant to commit the act.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager publicly accuses an employee of stealing, knowing the claim is false. Which tort is most likely?
A: Trespass
B: Negligence
C: Conversion
D: Defamation
Why A: Trespass is unauthorized entry onto someone's land and has nothing to do with a false public accusation of theft made about an employee.
Why B: Negligence involves carelessness, but here the manager knowingly made a false statement, so the better fit is the intentional tort of defamation rather than negligence.
Why C: Conversion is the wrongful taking or use of another's property and does not describe a false statement harming an employee's reputation.
Why D: Defamation is a false statement of fact that harms someone's reputation; a knowing false public accusation of theft is a classic example of this intentional tort.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A blender sold with a defective motor injures a user. A claim that does not require proving negligence is based on:
A: Statute of frauds rule
B: Liquidated damages term
C: Strict product liability
D: Adverse possession of land
Why A: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing and has no bearing on a claim for injury caused by a defective product.
Why B: Liquidated damages is a contract term that fixes damages in advance, not a basis for a claim by an injured user against a seller.
Why C: Strict product liability holds sellers and manufacturers liable for injuries from defective, unreasonably dangerous products without the plaintiff proving negligence, only that a defect caused harm.
Why D: Adverse possession is a way to gain title to land by long, open use, and has nothing to do with injuries from defective products.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copyright?
A: Protection for trade secrets such as recipes and secret formulas kept by firms
B: Legal protection for original creative works such as books, music and software
C: Protection for brand names, logos and slogans used by a company in sales
D: Protection for inventions such as new machines and processes that work
Why A: Trade secrets such as recipes and formulas are protected by trade secret law, which depends on keeping them confidential, not by copyright protection.
Why B: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible form, such as books, music, art and software, and arises automatically when the work is created.
Why C: Brand names, logos and slogans are protected by trademark law, not copyright, which protects creative expression rather than words used to identify a source of goods.
Why D: Inventions such as machines and processes are protected by patents, which require an application, while copyright covers expressive works instead of functional inventions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fair use?
A: Renting copyrighted work to other people for a fee, without ever asking the owner first as a rule
B: Copying any work for free, forever, whatever the creator or the owner may say about it
C: Unlimited copying for profit, with no credit given to the original creators or owners
D: Limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like criticism or education
Why A: Renting copyrighted work to others for a fee without permission is not fair use; it would infringe the owner's rights, which include control over distribution.
Why B: Fair use does not allow copying any work for free forever; it is a limited defense that courts weigh by factors, regardless of what creators say.
Why C: Unlimited copying for profit without credit is infringement; fair use is limited, and commercial copying of a whole work weighs strongly against it.
Why D: Fair use permits limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching and research, judged by four factors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business copies an entire popular song for its commercial ad without permission. Is this likely fair use?
A: Yes, because it is advertising and ads may use any song
B: Yes, because it was short and only a part of the song
C: No, because it is a commercial use of a whole work
D: Yes, because songs are public property and free to all
Why A: Advertising is commercial use, and ads cannot freely use any song; using music in an ad without permission usually requires a license from the copyright holder.
Why B: The question states the business copied the entire song, so the claim that it was short and only a part contradicts the facts and weakens the fair use argument.
Why C: Copying a whole popular song for a commercial ad weighs against fair use on the purpose, amount used and market effect factors, so it likely infringes.
Why D: Songs are protected by copyright and are not public property, so using one in an ad without permission generally requires a license from the owner.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How long does a trademark generally last?
A: As long as it is used and renewed
B: Exactly 20 years from the filing
C: Until the owner retires or sells up
D: One year only, then it must end
Why A: A trademark can last indefinitely as long as the owner keeps using it in commerce and files the required maintenance renewals with the trademark office.
Why B: Twenty years is the term of a utility patent from filing, not a trademark, which can last as long as it is used and renewed.
Why C: Trademark rights do not end when the owner retires or sells; they can be sold with the business and continue as long as the mark is used.
Why D: A trademark is not limited to one year; protection continues as long as the mark remains in use and the owner makes required renewals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 about?
A: The sale of land
B: Tax filing rules
C: The sale of goods
D: Employment rules
Why A: The sale of land is governed by real property law, not the UCC, which covers movable goods and not interests in real estate.
Why B: Tax filing rules are found in tax law, not the UCC, which is a uniform set of state commercial laws.
Why C: UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods, meaning movable tangible items, and it covers formation, warranties, delivery, risk of loss and remedies for breach.
Why D: Employment rules are found in labor and employment statutes, not in the UCC, which regulates commercial transactions like sales of goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Under the UCC, a contract for the sale of goods priced at $600 or more generally must be:
A: In writing to be enforceable
B: Notarized by a public notary
C: Oral only, with no writing
D: Recorded on video and stored
Why A: The UCC statute of frauds requires a signed writing for sales of goods priced at $500 or more under the original code, and a writing is generally required to enforce larger sales.
Why B: Notarization is not required for goods contracts; a signed writing is what the UCC statute of frauds asks for, not a notary public's certificate.
Why C: An oral-only agreement for goods at this price generally cannot be enforced under the statute of frauds, so a contract resting on no writing is the weak choice here.
Why D: Video recording does not satisfy the writing requirement and is not required; the law asks for a signed written record showing the contract's key terms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A buyer tells a clerk she needs a mattress for a bad back, and the clerk recommends a specific model that worsens her pain. Which warranty may apply?
A: Merchantability, for ordinary use
B: No warranty applies to the sale
C: Title to the goods being sold
D: Fitness for a particular purpose
Why A: Merchantability is a general warranty that goods are fit for ordinary use, but here the buyer told the seller a specific need, which points to a different warranty.
Why B: Implied warranties arise automatically in sales unless properly disclaimed, so saying that no warranty applies ignores the clerk's recommendation after the buyer stated her need.
Why C: The warranty of title promises the seller owns the goods and can transfer them; it does not address whether the mattress suits the buyer's back problem.
Why D: An implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when a seller knows the buyer's special need and the buyer relies on the seller's advice to select suitable goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a 'lemon law'?
A: A law on car insurance that sets minimum cover for drivers
B: A state law protecting buyers of defective new vehicles
C: A law on sales tax charged in each state to shoppers
D: A law about fruit sold in stores and sold at markets
Why A: Car insurance minimums are set by separate state insurance laws, not by lemon laws, which protect buyers of defective vehicles rather than set insurance cover.
Why B: Lemon laws give buyers of new vehicles with substantial defects that the maker cannot fix after reasonable attempts a remedy such as a refund or replacement.
Why C: Sales tax is a separate state revenue law, whereas lemon laws deal with defective vehicles rather than taxes charged to shoppers.
Why D: Despite the name, a lemon law has nothing to do with fruit sales and instead protects consumers who buy defective new cars from the manufacturer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Truth in Lending Act require?
A: Lenders to waive all interest on their loans
B: Lenders to disclose credit costs, including APR
C: Banks to lend to everyone who asks for a loan
D: Borrowers to repay within 24 hours of the loan
Why A: The Truth in Lending Act does not require interest waivers; it requires clear disclosure of credit terms so borrowers can compare loan costs.
Why B: TILA requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the annual percentage rate and finance charges, in a standard form so consumers can compare offers.
Why C: TILA does not force banks to lend to everyone; lenders may still decide whom to approve, subject to other laws against discrimination.
Why D: TILA does not require repayment within 24 hours; it concerns disclosure of loan terms, and repayment schedules are set by the loan contract.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A lender advertises a 'low payment' loan but hides a high APR. Which law is most directly implicated?
A: The Sherman Act of 1890
B: The Fair Labor Standards Act
C: The Clean Air Act of 1970
D: The Truth in Lending Act
Why A: The Sherman Act of 1890 is an antitrust law against monopolies and price fixing and does not address disclosure of loan costs.
Why B: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules for workers and does not regulate how lenders advertise loan costs.
Why C: The Clean Air Act of 1970 addresses air pollution and environmental standards and has nothing to do with loan advertising or disclosure.
Why D: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR and other credit costs clearly, so hiding a high APR behind a low payment ad implicates it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act protect?
A: Stock prices set on the major exchanges each day
B: Business tax rates set by the state and the nation
C: Accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
D: Interest rates on savings, as offered by banks
Why A: Stock prices are set by trading and overseen by securities laws, not by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which concerns consumer credit reports.
Why B: Business tax rates are set by tax law and legislatures, not the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which covers how credit information is collected and used.
Why C: The FCRA promotes the accuracy, fairness and privacy of consumer credit information held by credit bureaus and gives consumers the right to see and dispute their reports.
Why D: Savings interest rates are set by banks and market conditions; the FCRA is about credit report accuracy and privacy rather than rates on deposits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibit?
A: Abusive, deceptive or harassing debt collection practices
B: Opening a savings account at a bank with a small deposit
C: Paying debts on time and in full each month to lenders
D: Any debt repayment plan made between a debtor and creditor
Why A: The FDCPA bans abusive, deceptive and harassing debt collection practices, such as repeated threatening calls, false statements and contact at inconvenient times or places.
Why B: Opening a savings account is a normal banking activity and is not prohibited by any law, much less the debt collection law.
Why C: Paying debts on time is encouraged and legal; the FDCPA restricts how collectors behave, not how consumers pay what they owe.
Why D: The FDCPA does not forbid repayment plans; voluntary arrangements between debtor and creditor are common and lawful, while the law targets collectors' abusive tactics.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A debt collector calls a consumer at work after being told not to and threatens arrest. What is this?
A: A likely violation of debt collection law
B: A credit report update sent to the borrower
C: A normal collection step in the process
D: A required notice about the debt owed
Why A: Calling a consumer at work after being told to stop and threatening arrest are practices the FDCPA bans, so this is a likely violation of the law.
Why B: A credit report update is a bureau action and not a collector's phone call, so it does not describe the harassing conduct in the question.
Why C: Debt collection law limits what collectors may do, and calling a workplace after a request to stop plus threatening arrest is not a normal permitted step.
Why D: A validation notice is a written statement about the debt that collectors must send; threatening arrest by phone at work is not such a notice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule for door-to-door sales?
A: Buyers must wait a year before they can cancel
B: Sellers can cancel at any time, whatever they promised
C: Buyers can cancel certain sales within three days
D: Buyers must pay twice for each sale made at the door
Why A: The Cooling-Off Rule gives buyers three days to cancel, not a year, and a year-long wait would defeat its purpose of protecting against pressure sales.
Why B: The rule protects buyers, not sellers; a seller cannot cancel whenever it likes after making a promise, since that would undermine the sale contract.
Why C: The FTC rule lets buyers cancel certain door-to-door and off-premises sales of $25 or more within three business days, helping them escape high-pressure sales.
Why D: The rule does not require double payment; it gives buyers a right to cancel and get a refund, and it does not add costs to buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a requirement of a negotiable instrument?
A: It must be a signed writing that promises to deliver goods or services on a date
B: It must be unsigned and may be left blank until the day of payment arrives for the holder overall
C: It must be notarized and filed with the county clerk before anyone can use it
D: It must be in writing, signed and contain an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount
Why A: A negotiable instrument must promise payment of money, not delivery of goods or services; a signed writing that promises other performance does not qualify under Article 3.
Why B: A negotiable instrument must be signed by the maker or drawer, so an unsigned and blank instrument fails the UCC Article 3 requirements.
Why C: Neither notarization nor filing with a clerk is required for a negotiable instrument; Article 3 requires a signed writing with an unconditional promise to pay.
Why D: Under UCC Article 3 a negotiable instrument must be a signed writing with an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, payable on demand or at a definite time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is endorsement of a check?
A: Printing the front of the check with the amount
B: Signing the back to transfer or deposit it
C: Raising the amount shown on the check
D: Voiding the check and then tearing it up
Why A: Printing on the front of the check with the amount is filling in the check by the drawer, not endorsement, which happens on the back by the payee.
Why B: Endorsement is the payee signing the back of a check, which lets the payee transfer it to another person or deposit it at a bank.
Why C: Raising the amount is alteration, a form of forgery that is illegal, and has no connection to the lawful act of endorsing a check.
Why D: Voiding and tearing up a check cancels it, whereas endorsement is a signature on the back that allows transfer or deposit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker signs her name on the back of a paycheck and loses it. What is the risk?
A: It cannot be lost or stolen by anyone
B: Only the employer can cash it as it names them
C: Anyone who finds it may be able to cash it
D: It is automatically void and worthless
Why A: Checks can be lost or stolen like any other item, so claiming that no one can take it ignores the risk created by a blank endorsement.
Why B: A paycheck names the worker as payee, not the employer, so the employer cannot cash it; the risk comes from the worker's own signature on the back.
Why C: A signature alone on the back is a blank endorsement, making the check payable to the bearer, so anyone who finds it may be able to cash or deposit it.
Why D: Losing a signed check does not void it; the check stays valid, and the employer can stop payment and reissue it if the worker acts quickly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is perfection of a security interest?
A: Making a product perfect so that it meets every quality standard set by the maker and the buyers
B: Cancelling a loan so that the borrower no longer owes the lender any money, often after a final settlement talk
C: Paying a debt early so that the lender cannot charge any more interest on the loan or the fees
D: The steps, such as filing a financing statement, that make a security interest effective against others
Why A: Perfection is a legal term from secured transactions and has nothing to do with product quality standards set by makers and buyers.
Why B: Cancelling a loan is a release or discharge of debt, whereas perfection is the step a lender takes to make its security interest effective against third parties.
Why C: Paying a debt early is prepayment of the loan, a borrower's act, and not a lender's step to protect a security interest in collateral.
Why D: Perfection is the set of steps, usually filing a financing statement or taking possession of the collateral, that make a security interest effective against other creditors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two lenders both claim the same collateral. Who generally has priority?
A: The lender who perfected first
B: The lender who lent last of all
C: The lender with the larger loan
D: Neither lender has any claim
Why A: Under UCC priority rules, the secured party who first files or perfects generally has priority in the collateral over later claimants, so the earlier perfected lender wins.
Why B: Lending last gives a lender no advantage; priority generally goes to whoever perfected first, and a later lender usually ranks behind earlier perfected ones.
Why C: The size of the loan does not decide priority; the order of filing or perfection controls, so a larger loan gives no better claim by itself.
Why D: Both lenders may have valid security interests, so neither lacking a claim is wrong; priority rules decide which one is paid first from the collateral.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)?
A: A law on imports and duties on goods coming from other countries as a rule
B: A federal law setting minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules
C: A law on stock sales and share prices on the major exchanges
D: A law on trademarks and brand names used in the retail market
Why A: Imports and duties on foreign goods are covered by customs and tariff laws, not the FLSA, which regulates pay and working conditions for workers.
Why B: The FLSA is the federal law that sets the minimum wage, overtime pay at one and a half times the regular rate over 40 hours a week, and child labor limits.
Why C: Stock sales and share prices are regulated by securities laws such as the Securities Exchange Act, not by the FLSA, which concerns wages and hours.
Why D: Trademarks and brand names are protected under the Lanham Act, and the FLSA addresses minimum wage, overtime and child labor instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A nonexempt employee works 46 hours in a week at $20 per hour. Under the FLSA, what is the minimum total pay?
Why A: $800 equals only 40 hours at $20 and ignores the 6 overtime hours, which must be paid at least one and a half times the regular rate.
Why B: $1,100 overstates the pay; the correct total is 40 times $20 plus 6 overtime hours at $30, which comes to less than $1,100.
Why C: The first 40 hours pay 40 times $20, or $800. The 6 overtime hours pay 1.5 times $20, or $30 each, for $180. The total is $980.
Why D: $920 is 46 hours times $20 at the straight rate, but the FLSA requires time and a half for the 6 hours over 40, so the minimum is higher.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act?
A: A law on retirement accounts and the pensions that are paid to workers by firms after they leave
B: A law that prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin
C: A law on workplace safety standards and the inspections of factories by federal agents each year
D: A law on minimum wage rates and the pay of workers in shops and factories nationwide for each hour worked
Why A: Retirement accounts and pensions are governed by ERISA, not Title VII, which is a civil rights law about discrimination in employment.
Why B: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits employers from discriminating in hiring, firing, pay and conditions because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin.
Why C: Workplace safety standards come from OSHA, not Title VII, which deals with discrimination and not factory inspections.
Why D: Minimum wage and hourly pay come from the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Title VII prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act require employers to do?
A: Provide reasonable accommodations for qualified employees with disabilities
B: Hire staff without holding any interviews or tests for the applicants
C: Pay everyone the same wage whatever their job or their level of skill
D: Ignore disabilities when the job tasks are set out for the workers in a team
Why A: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees with disabilities, such as modified equipment or schedules, unless doing so causes undue hardship.
Why B: The ADA does not ban interviews or tests; employers may use job-related screening, though they cannot discriminate against qualified people because of a disability.
Why C: The ADA does not require equal pay for all jobs; it prohibits discrimination and requires accommodation rather than setting identical wages for everyone.
Why D: The ADA does not tell employers to ignore disabilities; it requires considering reasonable accommodations so qualified people can perform the essential functions of the job.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An employee in a wheelchair asks for a desk adjusted to a lower height. What should the employer generally do?
A: Fire the employee because she asked for a new desk to be installed
B: Deny the request because the desk is far too costly for the firm to buy
C: Ignore the request until someone else raises it again with the firm
D: Consider and provide the accommodation unless it creates undue hardship
Why A: Firing an employee for asking for an accommodation is unlawful discrimination and retaliation under the ADA, so it is never the right response.
Why B: An employer cannot simply deny the request by calling it costly; a lower desk is a modest accommodation, and denial requires proof of undue hardship.
Why C: Ignoring the request fails the interactive process the ADA expects, in which employer and employee discuss a possible accommodation promptly and in good faith.
Why D: The ADA requires employers to consider and provide reasonable accommodations, such as an adjustable desk, unless they can show that doing so would create undue hardship.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)?
A: A law on pensions and the retirement plans that firms set up for staff and managers
B: A law banning all leave for workers who are ill or have a new baby in the family at home in this case
C: A law giving eligible employees unpaid, job-protected leave for family and medical reasons
D: A law giving paid vacation to all workers after one year of work, with full pay
Why A: Pensions and retirement plans fall under ERISA, not the FMLA, which provides leave rather than retirement benefits.
Why B: The FMLA does not ban leave; it does the opposite by guaranteeing eligible workers time off for illness or the birth of a child.
Why C: The FMLA lets eligible employees take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for family and medical reasons, such as a newborn or serious illness.
Why D: The FMLA leave is unpaid, not paid, and it does not grant vacation; paid vacation is a matter of employer policy rather than this law.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An eligible employee takes 8 weeks of FMLA leave. What must the employer generally do when she returns?
A: Fire her a few days after her return from leave
B: Demote her to a lower role after her return
C: Reduce her pay by half for the weeks she was on leave
D: Restore her to the same or an equivalent position
Why A: Firing an employee after FMLA leave would violate the law, which protects the job, so the employer cannot end her employment for taking leave.
Why B: Demoting her after leave would be interference with FMLA rights, since the law requires return to the same or an equivalent role.
Why C: FMLA leave is unpaid and cannot be penalized by a pay cut; returning employees must get equivalent pay, benefits and terms, not half pay.
Why D: The FMLA requires restoring a returning employee to the same or an equivalent position with the same pay, benefits and working conditions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of Form I-9?
A: Applying for a license to work in a regulated field in the U.S.
B: Verifying an employee's identity and eligibility to work in the U.S.
C: Reporting wages and tax withheld to the revenue agency each quarter overall
D: Setting the rate of tax withholding on each employee's pay stub
Why A: Work licenses for regulated fields are issued by state boards, not through Form I-9, which employers use to check identity and work eligibility.
Why B: Form I-9 is completed by employers and new hires to verify identity and authorization to work in the United States, with supporting documents examined within three business days.
Why C: Wages and tax withheld are reported on payroll tax forms such as Form 941 and W-2, not on Form I-9, which concerns work eligibility.
Why D: Withholding rates are set through Form W-4, which the employee fills in, while Form I-9 verifies identity and employment eligibility instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company discourages employees from discussing pay with each other. What is the likely legal concern?
A: Employees generally have a right to discuss wages
B: Pay talk can be treated as disclosing trade secrets
C: Pay discussions need written permission from human resources
D: Wage data is confidential under federal privacy law
Why A: Under the National Labor Relations Act, most employees have a protected right to discuss wages and working conditions, so discouraging such talk may be unlawful.
Why B: Wages are not trade secrets, and the National Labor Relations Act protects most employees who discuss pay, so such a rule may be unlawful.
Why C: Employees do not need permission to discuss wages with coworkers; the NLRA protects these talks, so requiring written permission may be unlawful.
Why D: No federal privacy law makes wages confidential among coworkers; the NLRA protects pay discussions, so a blanket confidentiality rule can violate employee rights.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of the Securities Act of 1933?
A: To regulate shipping routes and ports used by cargo vessels
B: To require disclosure when securities are first sold to the public
C: To ban stock trading by all firms and all investors in the nation
D: To set the minimum wage for all of the workers in the stock market
Why A: Shipping routes and ports are governed by maritime and transport law, not the Securities Act of 1933, which deals with securities offerings.
Why B: The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies selling securities to the public for the first time to register them and disclose accurate financial information to investors.
Why C: The Act does not ban stock trading; it regulates new offerings through disclosure, while trading in existing shares continues and is regulated by other laws.
Why D: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and has nothing to do with the Securities Act of 1933 and its disclosure rules.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 do?
A: Sets interest on mortgages and fixes lenders' rates
B: Regulates farm prices and the sale of crops in markets
C: Regulates imports and the duties paid at the border
D: Regulates trading of securities and created the SEC
Why A: Mortgage rates are not set by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which regulates securities trading, brokers and exchanges.
Why B: Farm prices and crop sales are covered by agricultural law, whereas the 1934 Act regulates trading in securities on exchanges.
Why C: Imports and border duties are governed by customs and trade law, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 concerns securities markets.
Why D: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading of securities on the secondary market and created the Securities and Exchange Commission to enforce the securities laws.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company executive buys stock after learning confidential merger news before the public does. What law is most likely violated?
A: Antidiscrimination laws that protect workers
B: Zoning laws about the use of land in cities
C: Securities laws against insider trading
D: Child labor laws about work by minors
Why A: Antidiscrimination laws protect workers from unfair treatment and do not address trading on confidential merger news learned as an executive.
Why B: Zoning laws control how land is used in cities and have nothing to do with trading stocks on confidential information.
Why C: Trading on material nonpublic information, like secret merger news, is insider trading, which the Securities Exchange Act and SEC Rule 10b-5 prohibit and punish.
Why D: Child labor laws limit work by minors, so they are unrelated to an executive using confidential merger news to buy stock early.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bankruptcy trustee?
A: A person appointed to manage and distribute a debtor's assets
B: A judge who presides over the bankruptcy case and decides it overall
C: A debtor's friend who offers to lend them money in need
D: A tax collector who works for the revenue agency in town
Why A: A bankruptcy trustee is appointed to collect and manage the debtor's assets and distribute proceeds to creditors according to bankruptcy law.
Why B: The judge presides over the case and issues rulings, while the trustee is a separate administrator who handles the debtor's estate and payments to creditors.
Why C: A trustee is a neutral court-supervised officer, not the debtor's friend, and does not lend the debtor money in times of need.
Why D: A tax collector works for a revenue agency, whereas a bankruptcy trustee administers the debtor's estate on behalf of the court and the creditors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy?
A: Chapter 7 is for large corporations while Chapter 13 is for small ones
B: Chapter 7 covers family farms while Chapter 13 covers city governments
C: Chapter 13 erases all debt immediately, while Chapter 7 requires a plan for repayment
D: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets while Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan
Why A: Chapter 13 is only for individuals with regular income, and Chapter 7 is open to individuals as well; corporations reorganizing usually use Chapter 11.
Why B: Family farmers use Chapter 12 and municipalities use Chapter 9; Chapter 13 is a repayment plan for individuals with regular income.
Why C: This reverses the chapters: Chapter 13 does not erase debts immediately but requires a repayment plan, while Chapter 7 liquidates assets and discharges eligible debts.
Why D: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets to pay creditors and then discharges many debts, while Chapter 13 lets an individual with regular income keep property and repay under a three to five year plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person with a steady income wants to keep her house while repaying debts over five years. Which bankruptcy chapter best fits?
A: Chapter 7
B: Chapter 11
C: Chapter 13
D: No such plan
Why A: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets and could put her house at risk, and it does not provide a multiyear repayment plan.
Why B: Chapter 11 is a reorganization used mainly by businesses with complex finances, and it is too costly and complex for an individual repaying debts over five years.
Why C: Chapter 13 lets an individual with a steady income keep her property, such as a house, while repaying debts under a court-approved plan lasting three to five years.
Why D: A plan like this does exist: Chapter 13 provides exactly this arrangement for individuals with regular income who wish to keep their home while repaying debts.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is tax avoidance?
A: Legally reducing taxes by using deductions and credits
B: Hiding income from the tax agency to pay less tax
C: Falsifying records to reduce the tax a person owes
D: Not filing a return at all for several years in a row
Why A: Tax avoidance is the lawful reduction of taxes using deductions, credits, retirement plans and other legal strategies that the tax code allows.
Why B: Hiding income from the tax agency is tax evasion, which is illegal, not tax avoidance, which remains within the law.
Why C: Falsifying records to cut a tax bill is fraud and tax evasion, a crime that can bring fines and prison, unlike lawful avoidance.
Why D: Failing to file for years is unlawful noncompliance, with penalties and possible prosecution, rather than a legal strategy to reduce taxes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business owner hides $50,000 in cash sales from the IRS. What is this?
A: A deduction
B: Tax evasion
C: Tax avoidance
D: A tax credit
Why A: A deduction is a lawful reduction of taxable income for allowed expenses; hiding cash sales is not a deduction but an unlawful omission of income.
Why B: Deliberately hiding cash sales from the IRS to pay less tax is tax evasion, a federal crime involving fraud that can lead to penalties and prison.
Why C: Tax avoidance is lawful planning that reduces taxes within the rules, whereas concealing $50,000 of income is illegal and not avoidance.
Why D: A tax credit directly reduces tax owed for qualifying items, so it is a lawful benefit and not the concealment of income described here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A government bans all imports from a specific country for political reasons. This is an:
A: Embargo
B: Subsidy
C: Merger
D: Tax cut
Why A: An embargo is a government ban on trade with a specific country, here imports, usually for political reasons, and it can be a form of sanction.
Why B: A subsidy is government financial support for a business or industry, not a ban on trade with another country.
Why C: A merger combines two companies into one, which has nothing to do with a government banning imports from a country.
Why D: A tax cut lowers taxes for people or businesses, so it is not a trade ban on goods from a specific country.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the WTO do?
A: Sets national tax rates and collects income taxes for the nation
B: Prints currency and coins for use across the whole nation
C: Sets rules for trade between nations and helps resolve disputes
D: Runs world airlines and sets the fares that passengers pay
Why A: National tax rates are set by governments and legislatures, not by the WTO, which deals with international trade rules between member countries.
Why B: Printing currency and coins is done by national governments and central banks, and the WTO has no role in making money.
Why C: The World Trade Organization sets rules for trade between nations, runs trade negotiations and helps settle disputes among its member countries.
Why D: The WTO does not run airlines or set fares; airlines are private or state firms, and the WTO focuses on trade rules among countries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)?
A: A law on tariffs and duties on goods crossing a border
B: A law that bans exports to foreign states without license
C: A law on minimum wage for workers in factories
D: A U.S. law that prohibits bribing foreign officials
Why A: Tariffs and duties are governed by customs and trade laws, not the FCPA, which targets bribery of foreign officials.
Why B: Export controls and licensing are covered by separate export laws, while the FCPA concerns improper payments to foreign government officials.
Why C: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act, so it is unrelated to the FCPA, which deals with international corruption.
Why D: The FCPA is a U.S. law that makes it illegal for U.S. companies and individuals to bribe foreign officials to win or keep business, and it requires accurate accounting records.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A U.S. company pays a foreign official to speed up a permit. Which law may be violated?
A: The ADA
B: The FCPA
C: The CAA
D: The FLSA
Why A: The ADA protects people with disabilities and does not address payments to foreign officials, so it is not the law violated here.
Why B: The FCPA prohibits U.S. companies from paying foreign officials to gain business advantages, and paying to speed up a permit may violate it unless it is a narrow routine facilitation payment.
Why C: The CAA, the Clean Air Act, concerns pollution and air quality, so it does not apply to a payment made to a foreign official.
Why D: The FLSA sets wage and hour standards for workers and has no connection to payments to foreign officials for permits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do exporters use standard shipping terms such as FOB or CIF?
A: To clarify who pays freight and bears risk during transit
B: To set tax rates for all of the exporters in the country
C: To avoid contracts with buyers in all other countries
D: To eliminate shipping costs for the buyer and the seller alike
Why A: Incoterms like FOB and CIF state who pays for freight and insurance and when risk of loss passes from seller to buyer, avoiding disputes in international sales.
Why B: Shipping terms do not set tax rates; governments set taxes and customs duties, whereas FOB and CIF allocate cost and risk between buyer and seller.
Why C: Exporters use shipping terms to define duties within a sale, not to avoid foreign buyers, and they help make international contracts clearer.
Why D: Shipping terms do not eliminate costs; they only decide who pays freight and insurance, so some party still bears these shipping expenses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a civil case, the plaintiff generally must prove the claim by:
A: A unanimous vote of the public
B: A signed confession by the party
C: Proof beyond any reasonable doubt
D: A preponderance of the evidence
Why A: Civil cases are decided by a judge or jury applying a legal standard, not by a public vote, which has no place in court.
Why B: A confession by the defendant is not required in a civil case, and plaintiffs usually prove claims with evidence, testimony and documents instead.
Why C: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the higher standard used in criminal cases, whereas civil plaintiffs only need to meet a lower burden.
Why D: In civil cases the plaintiff must show the claim is more likely true than not, called a preponderance of the evidence, which is a lower standard than in criminal cases.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is precedent?
A: A contract term fixing the price of goods
B: A prior court decision that guides later cases
C: A new law from Congress that ends past rulings
D: A tax rule applied to the sale of goods in states
Why A: Fixing the price of goods is a contract term and not a precedent, which is a legal principle from earlier court rulings.
Why B: Precedent is a prior court decision that courts follow when deciding later cases with similar facts, under the doctrine of stare decisis, which promotes consistency.
Why C: A new law from Congress is a statute, and it may change court rules, but it is not a precedent set by earlier court decisions.
Why D: Tax rules on the sale of goods are set by statutes and regulations, not by precedent, which is based on earlier judicial opinions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a statute?
A: A company policy on staff pay
B: A private contract by two parties
C: A law passed by a legislature
D: A judge's written opinion
Why A: A company policy on pay is an internal rule set by an employer, not a statute, which is a law passed by a government legislature.
Why B: A private contract between two parties binds only those parties and is not a statute, which is a public law made by a legislature.
Why C: A statute is a written law passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature, and it applies to the public within its jurisdiction.
Why D: A judge's written opinion is case law, which applies and interprets statutes, but it is not itself a statute passed by a legislature.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A federal law conflicts with a state law on the same subject. Under the Supremacy Clause, which generally prevails?
A: The federal law
B: The older law
C: The state law
D: Neither law
Why A: Under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, valid federal law overrides conflicting state law, so the federal law generally prevails when the two conflict.
Why B: The age of a law does not decide a conflict between federal and state law; the Supremacy Clause says federal law takes priority regardless of date.
Why C: The state law does not win a conflict with a valid federal law on the same subject, because the Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme.
Why D: One of the laws does prevail; the Supremacy Clause establishes that valid federal law controls over conflicting state law, so neither law winning is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the plaintiff do in a lawsuit?
A: Defends against the claim in court
B: Writes the statute for the whole court
C: Decides the case for both of the parties
D: Brings the claim against the defendant
Why A: The party who defends against the claim in court is the defendant, not the plaintiff, who is the person who starts the case.
Why B: Statutes are written by legislatures, not by plaintiffs, who only bring a case to court asking for a remedy.
Why C: The judge or jury decides the case, not the plaintiff, who is simply one of the parties asking the court to decide.
Why D: The plaintiff is the party who starts a lawsuit by filing a complaint, bringing a claim against the defendant and seeking a remedy such as damages.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Small claims courts are typically used for:
A: Federal crimes tried before a jury of twelve people at a trial
B: Constitutional appeals heard by the highest court in the land
C: Disputes involving limited dollar amounts, often without lawyers
D: Billion-dollar mergers between large companies in several industries
Why A: Federal crimes are tried in federal district courts, often before juries, and small claims courts do not hear criminal cases.
Why B: Constitutional appeals go to appellate courts and ultimately the Supreme Court, not small claims courts that handle minor money disputes.
Why C: Small claims courts handle disputes involving limited amounts of money, with simple procedures and often no lawyers, so ordinary people can resolve minor claims quickly and cheaply.
Why D: Billion-dollar mergers involve large complex transactions that belong in regulatory review or major courts, not small claims courts with low dollar limits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A salesperson knows a product has a safety defect but continues to sell it to meet quotas. What best describes this?
A: A required legal practice by firms
B: An unethical and likely illegal act
C: Good salesmanship by the seller
D: A neutral business choice by the seller
Why A: No law requires selling a product known to be defective; selling one is a legal risk, not a required practice for firms.
Why B: Knowingly selling a defective, unsafe product to meet quotas puts profit over safety and is unethical and likely illegal, exposing the firm to product liability.
Why C: Good salesmanship is honest and does not hide dangers, so knowingly selling a defective product is deceptive rather than skilled selling.
Why D: Selling a known unsafe product is not neutral, because it risks harming customers and breaches duties of honesty and safety that businesses owe.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is corporate social responsibility?
A: A government program that rewards firms for hiring workers locally
B: A company's commitment to act in ways that benefit society and the environment
C: An accounting method for reporting profit to shareholders each quarter
D: A tax loophole used by large firms to cut their yearly tax bills in the nation
Why A: Corporate social responsibility is a voluntary commitment by the company, not a government reward program for hiring; it covers broader social and environmental goals.
Why B: Corporate social responsibility is a company's commitment to act ethically and to benefit society and the environment, beyond simply maximizing profit or following the law.
Why C: Corporate social responsibility concerns ethical and social commitments, not accounting; profit reporting follows separate accounting standards and is not a form of responsibility.
Why D: CSR is not a tax loophole; it concerns ethical and social commitments, while tax loopholes are legal gaps used to reduce a tax bill.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company has two options: one legal but harmful to the community, one legal and beneficial. Which choice reflects strong ethics?
A: The cheaper option always
B: Neither option works
C: The harmful legal option
D: The beneficial option
Why A: Always choosing the cheaper option puts cost above community welfare, and it does not reflect strong ethics when a beneficial legal option exists.
Why B: Refusing both options is not reasonable here, because a legal and beneficial option exists and a company can choose it to act ethically.
Why C: Choosing a legal but harmful option puts profit ahead of the community, so it meets the law but fails the test of strong ethics.
Why D: Strong business ethics go beyond legality, so choosing the option that benefits the community, even if both are legal, shows responsibility toward stakeholders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is it important for companies to be transparent with customers?
A: It builds trust and reduces the risk of deception claims
B: It increases secrecy and cuts trust among the staff
C: It lowers quality and weakens the loyalty of customers
D: It avoids all laws and all rules in every state and city
Why A: Transparency builds customer trust and loyalty and reduces the risk of deception or false advertising claims by giving customers accurate information.
Why B: Transparency reduces secrecy and builds trust, so saying it increases secrecy and cuts trust among staff reverses its actual effect.
Why C: Transparency tends to raise trust and loyalty rather than lower quality or weaken customer loyalty, because honest dealing strengthens relationships.
Why D: Transparency does not let companies avoid laws; businesses must follow all applicable laws, and being open with customers is simply good practice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An accountant is asked to backdate a document so a deal looks compliant. What should she do?
A: Backdate it to keep the job
B: Wait and see what happens next
C: Decline and report the request
D: Backdate it but tell no one
Why A: Backdating a document to look compliant is fraud and an ethical breach, and keeping a job is no excuse for falsifying records.
Why B: Waiting and doing nothing allows a falsified record to stand and leaves the accountant exposed to professional and legal consequences.
Why C: An accountant should decline to backdate the document and report the request to a supervisor, compliance officer or authority, because honesty and professional standards come first.
Why D: Backdating secretly is still falsification, and hiding it makes the accountant complicit in fraud, which violates professional ethics and the law.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A contract says 'the entire agreement is contained in this writing.' A party later claims a prior oral promise adds a term. Under the parol evidence rule, what will a court likely do?
A: Void the entire contract automatically, as it has a merger clause as a rule
B: Exclude the earlier oral promise that contradicts the final writing
C: Add the oral promise to the contract as an extra binding term
D: Require the parties to restart negotiations from the beginning
Why A: A merger clause does not void the contract; it states the writing is the complete agreement, which is why earlier oral promises are usually excluded.
Why B: The parol evidence rule bars evidence of prior oral agreements that contradict or add to a fully integrated written contract, so the court will likely exclude the oral promise.
Why C: Adding the oral promise would defeat the merger clause and the parol evidence rule, which keep earlier oral terms out of a final written agreement.
Why D: Courts enforce the written agreement as is, so they do not usually send the parties back to renegotiate when a merger clause covers the whole deal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is anticipatory repudiation?
A: Assigning the contract to someone else, who then takes over the duties
B: Asking to renegotiate the terms of the contract politely with the other side
C: One party clearly states before performance is due that it will not perform
D: Performing the contract early, before the due date arrives for the other party
Why A: Assigning a contract transfers rights or duties to another person, which is different from refusing in advance to perform the contract.
Why B: Politely asking to renegotiate is not repudiation, because the party has not clearly stated that it will not perform its obligations.
Why C: Anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party clearly states or shows before performance is due that it will not perform, allowing the other side to treat it as a breach.
Why D: Early performance is not repudiation, because the party is carrying out its duties rather than refusing to perform them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A builder tells a homeowner in March that she will not build the June project at all. What may the homeowner do?
A: Ask the state to fine the builder instead of suing
B: Wait silently until June, then ask for a refund
C: Do nothing, since a breach cannot happen before June
D: Treat it as a breach now and seek another builder
Why A: A missed contract is a private civil matter, so the remedy is damages from the builder, not a state fine; the state does not penalize ordinary breach.
Why B: She need not wait silently until June, because after a clear repudiation the other party may treat the contract as breached right away and mitigate damages.
Why C: A clear repudiation is a breach before the due date, so the homeowner need not wait for June and may act right away.
Why D: Because the builder clearly repudiated in March, the homeowner may treat it as a breach now, hire another builder and seek damages for any extra cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is substantial performance?
A: Performance that meets the essential purpose despite minor flaws
B: Performance that misses the main purpose but is mostly finished
