Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A landlord changes the locks while a tenant is at work, with no court order. This is generally called:
A: A lawful eviction by the landlord
B: An illegal self-help eviction
C: A rent adjustment by the landlord
D: A routine repair by the landlord
Why A: A lawful eviction requires notice and a court order, so locking out a tenant without either is not lawful.
Why B: Changing locks without a court order is an illegal self-help eviction in most states, and landlords may owe damages to the tenant.
Why C: A rent adjustment changes the amount charged and does not involve excluding the tenant from the rental unit.
Why D: Changing locks is not a repair; a repair fixes defects, but here the landlord is removing the tenant's access without legal process.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a deed?
A: A mortgage payment made to the lender each month by the owner
B: A zoning map showing how land is used in the city and its suburbs
C: A legal document that transfers ownership of real property
D: A rent receipt given by the landlord to the tenant after payment
Why A: A mortgage payment goes to the lender to repay a loan, while a deed is the document that transfers ownership of real property.
Why B: A zoning map shows permitted land uses, whereas a deed is the document that transfers title between owners.
Why C: A deed is a written, signed legal document that transfers ownership of real property from the grantor to the grantee and is usually recorded.
Why D: A rent receipt only proves a rent payment, while a deed transfers ownership of real estate itself.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a quitclaim deed?
A: A deed that guarantees clear title to the buyer, with promises about past owners
B: A deed that sells a car or other motor vehicle from one person to another
C: A deed that cancels a mortgage and releases the lien on the property
D: A deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has, without warranties
Why A: A deed guaranteeing clear title with warranties is a warranty deed, whereas a quitclaim deed gives no promises about title.
Why B: A car sale is transferred by a certificate of title, not a deed, and a quitclaim deed deals with real property interests.
Why C: Canceling a mortgage and releasing a lien is done by a satisfaction or release of mortgage, which is a different document than a quitclaim deed.
Why D: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the grantor has, if any, without warranties or guarantees of clear title, and is often used between family members or to clear title defects.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A buyer wants the strongest protection about clear ownership. Which deed should she prefer?
A: A general warranty deed
B: A quitclaim deed only
C: No deed is required
D: A lease of the land
Why A: A general warranty deed gives the broadest protection, as the grantor promises clear title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor's ownership.
Why B: A quitclaim deed gives no warranties about title, so it is the weakest protection and the least suitable for a buyer wanting security.
Why C: A deed is needed to transfer title to real property, so skipping one would leave the buyer without legal ownership.
Why D: A lease grants temporary possession rather than ownership, so it gives no protection of clear title.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is title insurance?
A: Insurance against fire damage to the property that is owned by the buyer
B: Insurance on a car that covers damage from accidents on the road and fires every time
C: Insurance protecting a buyer or lender against defects in a property's title
D: Insurance on a job that pays workers when they lose their wages at work
Why A: Fire damage is covered by property or hazard insurance, whereas title insurance protects against defects in the title to the property.
Why B: Auto insurance covers vehicles and has no connection to the ownership defects that title insurance covers in real estate.
Why C: Title insurance protects a buyer or lender against losses from defects in a property's title, such as liens, forgery or errors in public records.
Why D: Lost wages from work injuries are covered by workers' compensation, which is a different insurance from title insurance on real property.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is zoning?
A: A survey tool used to measure the size of land
B: A type of loan used to buy a home or other land
C: A tax on land charged by the local government
D: Local rules controlling how land can be used
Why A: Surveys measure the size and boundaries of land, while zoning is the set of local rules controlling land use.
Why B: A home loan is a mortgage, while zoning is a set of local government rules on how land may be used.
Why C: A tax on land is a property tax, and zoning is instead a land use regulation that sets what may be built where.
Why D: Zoning is a set of local government rules controlling how land can be used, such as residential, commercial or industrial zones, and what may be built.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business wants to open a loud factory in a residential zone. What may it need?
A: A trademark registration filed for the firm
B: A zoning variance or rezoning approval
C: Nothing, as the land is private property
D: A patent application for the factory
Why A: A trademark protects brand identity and does not authorize a particular land use, so it cannot allow a factory in a residential zone.
Why B: A factory in a residential zone breaks the zoning rules, so the business would need a variance or rezoning approval from the local authority.
Why C: Private ownership does not override zoning law, so the business cannot use the land for any purpose it wants without approval.
Why D: A patent protects an invention and does not affect where the factory may be located or what zoning allows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an easement?
A: A tax break for homeowners who pay interest on a mortgage overall
B: A type of mortgage with fixed payments for thirty years
C: A right to use another person's land for a limited purpose
D: A building permit issued by the city for new construction
Why A: A mortgage interest deduction is a tax rule, while an easement is a right to use another's land for a limited purpose.
Why B: A fixed-rate mortgage is a loan; an easement is a property right and has nothing to do with loan payments.
Why C: An easement is a right to use another person's land for a limited purpose, such as a utility line or a shared driveway, without owning it.
Why D: A building permit is government permission to build, while an easement is a property right to use another's land for a limited purpose.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is adverse possession?
A: Renting land from the owner for a fixed sum paid each month under a lease
B: Buying land at an auction held by the local county government
C: Stealing a car from a parking lot in the middle of the night
D: Gaining title to land by openly occupying it for a statutory period
Why A: Renting under a lease is a permissive use with payments, whereas adverse possession is occupying land openly without the owner's consent.
Why B: Buying land at auction transfers title by purchase, whereas adverse possession gains title through long, open occupation without consent.
Why C: Stealing a car is a crime about personal property and not adverse possession, which concerns acquiring real estate title by occupation.
Why D: Adverse possession lets someone gain title by occupying land openly, continuously, exclusively and hostilely for the statutory period, often 10 to 20 years, depending on the state.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is comparative negligence?
A: A rule that reduces damages by the plaintiff's share of fault
B: A rule on rent and the amounts that landlords may charge each month
C: A rule that bans suits against any firm or any person in court
D: A rule that doubles damages if the plaintiff was partly at fault
Why A: Under comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault, so a partly at-fault plaintiff recovers less but may still recover something.
Why B: Rent rules belong to landlord-tenant law, whereas comparative negligence is a tort rule allocating fault between plaintiff and defendant.
Why C: Comparative negligence does not ban suits; it allows partly at-fault plaintiffs to recover reduced damages instead of being barred.
Why D: Comparative negligence reduces damages for the plaintiff's fault and never doubles them, so a partly at-fault plaintiff gets less.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A jury finds a plaintiff 30% at fault and awards $50,000 total damages. Under comparative negligence, what does she recover?
Why A: $15,000 is 30% of $50,000, which is the amount of the reduction, not what she recovers.
Why B: Her damages are reduced by her 30% fault: $50,000 x 0.30 = $15,000, and $50,000 - $15,000 = $35,000, which she recovers.
Why C: $5,000 does not match the calculation; 30% of $50,000 is $15,000, so the recovery is $35,000.
Why D: $50,000 ignores her fault; comparative negligence reduces the award by 30%, so she cannot recover the full amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is assumption of risk?
A: A form of insurance covering injuries that are caused by risky activities
B: A tax rule on the amount of income that a person earns during the year
C: A defense when a plaintiff knowingly accepted the danger that caused the injury
D: A contract term on rent and the dates of payment for the tenant each month as a rule
Why A: Insurance for risky activities is a different matter, while assumption of risk is a defense used when a plaintiff knowingly accepted the danger.
Why B: A tax rule on income is unrelated; assumption of risk is a tort defense to liability based on the plaintiff's knowing acceptance of danger.
Why C: Assumption of risk is a defense that can bar or reduce recovery when the plaintiff knew of and voluntarily accepted the danger that caused the injury.
Why D: A rent payment term is a contract provision, and assumption of risk is instead a defense to tort liability and not a lease term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is premises liability?
A: A tenant's duty to pay rent on time and keep the home in good repair
B: A property owner's responsibility for injuries caused by unsafe conditions
C: An agent's duty to act for a principal and follow all lawful instructions as a rule
D: A tax on buildings charged by the city every year at a flat rate of value
Why A: That describes a tenant's duties under a lease, whereas premises liability concerns an owner's responsibility for injuries from unsafe conditions.
Why B: Premises liability makes owners responsible for injuries caused by unsafe conditions they knew or should have known about, and a duty depends on whether the visitor is an invitee, licensee or trespasser.
Why C: An agent's duty to a principal belongs to agency law, whereas premises liability is a tort doctrine about injuries on someone's property.
Why D: A building tax is a government charge, but premises liability concerns an owner's responsibility for injuries on the property.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A customer is injured by a broken stair in a store that knew about it for weeks. The store's likely exposure is:
A: Only a tax penalty paid by the owner
B: Full immunity from any civil liability
C: No liability because customers should look
D: Liability for failing to repair or warn
Why A: A tax penalty is unrelated to the customer's injury; the store faces a negligence claim for a hazard it knew about and failed to fix.
Why B: Stores have no immunity from civil liability for known hazards, and a customer injured by a known defect can sue for damages.
Why C: Customers can expect reasonably safe premises, and a store that knew about a hazard for weeks cannot rely on customers to avoid it.
Why D: A store that knew of a broken stair for weeks and failed to repair or warn breached its duty of care to customers under premises liability, so it is likely liable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a nuisance in tort law?
A: An unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of land
B: A tax on land charged by the local county government each year
C: A contract term that sets the price of goods sold under the deal
D: A friendly neighbor who helps out with chores and other jobs nearby as a rule
Why A: A nuisance is an unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of land, such as noise, odors or pollution, and may support damages or an injunction.
Why B: A land tax is a government charge, and a nuisance is a tort claim about interference with use of land.
Why C: A price term in a sales contract is part of a contract, whereas a nuisance is a tort about interfering with land use.
Why D: A helpful neighbor is not a legal nuisance; the tort concerns unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is trespass?
A: A fair trade deal between two firms
B: A loan default by a borrower to a bank
C: Unauthorized entry onto another's land
D: A zoning rule for the use of the land
Why A: A fair trade deal is a lawful commercial agreement, while trespass is an unauthorized entry onto another's land.
Why B: A loan default is a breach of a financial obligation, and trespass is an intentional tort involving entry onto land.
Why C: Trespass is the unauthorized entry onto another person's land, or causing something to enter it, and it is an intentional tort even without harm.
Why D: A zoning rule regulates land use, whereas trespass is the tort of entering another's land without permission.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is tortious interference with contract?
A: Giving advice to a firm about how it should run its business
B: Intentionally causing someone to breach a contract with another
C: Signing a contract with a supplier for the sale of goods
D: Paying a bill to a supplier on the due date shown on the invoice
Why A: Giving advice to a firm is lawful consulting and does not induce a breach of a contract with another party.
Why B: Tortious interference occurs when a person intentionally and improperly causes someone to breach a contract with another party, harming the other party.
Why C: Signing a supplier contract is a normal lawful transaction, with no interference with someone else's contract.
Why D: Paying a bill on time is performing a contract, not interfering with one, so it cannot be a tort.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A competitor secretly offers a supplier a bribe to break its contract with a rival. Which tort is most likely?
A: Tortious interference with contract
B: Negligence in the way it was done
C: Defamation of the supplier's name
D: Nuisance caused by the competitor
Why A: Bribing a supplier to break its contract with a rival intentionally induces a breach, which is tortious interference with contract.
Why B: Negligence involves carelessness, while the competitor acted intentionally to cause the supplier's breach, so tortious interference fits better.
Why C: Defamation concerns false statements harming reputation, and the facts here involve a bribe to induce a breach.
Why D: Nuisance is interference with land use, whereas here the competitor induced a contract breach through a bribe.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patent's three main types in the U.S.?
A: Food, drink and tobacco
B: Red, white and blue shades
C: Land, sea and air patents
D: Utility, design and plant
Why A: Food, drink and tobacco are products and are not patent categories, which are utility, design and plant patents.
Why B: Colors are not patent types; the three U.S. types are utility, design and plant, protecting function, ornamental design and new plant varieties.
Why C: Land, sea and air are not patent categories; U.S. patents are utility, design and plant.
Why D: The three U.S. patent types are utility patents for new inventions, design patents for ornamental appearance and plant patents for new asexually reproduced plants.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a design patent protect?
A: How a product works and functions
B: A brand name and logo for a firm
C: The ornamental appearance of an item
D: A secret recipe kept by the company
Why A: How a product works and functions is protected by a utility patent, not a design patent.
Why B: Brand names and logos are protected by trademarks, while a design patent protects the ornamental look of an article.
Why C: A design patent protects the new, original, ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture, not how it works, and lasts 15 years from grant.
Why D: A secret recipe is typically protected as a trade secret and not by a patent, which requires public disclosure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company invents a new chair shape that looks distinctive. Which protection best covers its appearance?
A: A chair copyright
B: A trademark only
C: A utility patent
D: A design patent
Why A: Copyright protects creative expression and does not typically protect the useful shape of an article like a chair, so it is a weak fit.
Why B: A trademark identifies the source of goods, and it would not best protect the chair's ornamental shape by itself.
Why C: A utility patent protects how an invention works, not how it looks, so it does not best cover a chair's appearance.
Why D: A design patent protects the ornamental appearance of an article, so the distinctive chair shape is best covered by it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How long does copyright generally last for a work created by an individual today?
A: Twenty years from first filing
B: The author's life plus 70 years
C: One year after first publication
D: Five years after publication
Why A: Twenty years from filing is the term of a utility patent, not copyright, which generally lasts far longer.
Why B: For works created by an individual today, U.S. copyright generally lasts for the author's life plus 70 years after death.
Why C: One year is far too short; copyright subsists from creation and generally lasts the author's life plus 70 years.
Why D: Five years after publication is far shorter than copyright's actual term of the author's life plus 70 years.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the DMCA do?
A: Provides a process for removing infringing online content and limits platform liability
B: Taxes the sales of digital goods and services that cross state lines in the nation
C: Sets the federal minimum wage and overtime rules for people who work online from home in practice
D: Regulates the safety standards for cars and the software that runs them on the road
Why A: The DMCA creates a notice-and-takedown process for removing infringing online content and gives platforms safe harbor from liability if they comply.
Why B: Sales taxes on digital goods are governed by state tax law and the DMCA is a copyright statute.
Why C: Minimum wage and overtime rules come from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the DMCA addresses digital copyright.
Why D: Car safety standards are set by federal motor vehicle regulators, whereas the DMCA concerns copyright in digital works.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is trade dress?
A: A tax form that a business files each year to report its sales and income
B: A shipping label that shows the address of the buyer and the name of the seller in general
C: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging that identifies its source
D: Clothing worn by workers at a shop or a factory while they are on duty each day
Why A: A tax form reports sales and income to the government, while trade dress is a form of trademark protection for a product's look.
Why B: A shipping label identifies the sender and buyer, whereas trade dress identifies the source of a product by its overall appearance.
Why C: Trade dress is the overall look and feel of a product or its packaging that identifies its source, protected under trademark law if it is distinctive and nonfunctional.
Why D: Worker clothing is a uniform, and trade dress is a trademark concept covering the overall appearance of a product or packaging.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A knockoff restaurant copies the exact decor, uniforms and layout of a famous chain, causing customer confusion. Which claim might apply?
A: Trade dress infringement
B: Respondeat superior only
C: Breach of warranty claim
D: Statute of frauds claim
Why A: Copying a famous chain's decor, uniforms and layout in a confusing way can be trade dress infringement under the Lanham Act.
Why B: Respondeat superior makes employers liable for employees' acts and does not address copying a chain's distinctive look.
Why C: Breach of warranty concerns promises about goods and does not address copying of a restaurant's overall look.
Why D: The statute of frauds concerns which contracts must be in writing and has no bearing on copying a chain's appearance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a domain name dispute often called when someone registers a famous brand's name to profit?
A: Tax planning
B: Cybersquatting
C: Franchising
D: Telemarketing
Why A: Tax planning is arranging finances to reduce taxes and has no connection to registering famous brand names to profit.
Why B: Cybersquatting is registering a domain name that matches a famous brand in bad faith to profit by reselling it, and it is addressed by the ACPA.
Why C: Franchising is licensing a business model to operators, a legitimate arrangement unrelated to bad faith domain registrations.
Why D: Telemarketing is selling by phone and has no connection to domain name disputes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is diversity jurisdiction?
A: Authority over sports leagues and the rules of play for all teams that compete in them each season in this case
B: Authority over cultural groups and the way that they pass on their customs and traditions
C: Authority over disputes among employees and managers within a single firm or workplace in a state
D: Federal court authority over disputes between citizens of different states with enough money at stake
Why A: Sports leagues set their own rules, and diversity jurisdiction is a federal court power over disputes between citizens of different states.
Why B: Cultural groups are not a subject of federal jurisdiction, while diversity jurisdiction concerns parties from different states.
Why C: Disputes among employees and managers in a firm are not diversity cases, which require citizens of different states and an amount in controversy.
Why D: Diversity jurisdiction lets federal courts hear cases between citizens of different states when more than $75,000 is at stake, which prevents local bias.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A citizen of Ohio sues a citizen of Texas for $200,000 over a contract. Which court may have jurisdiction beyond state court?
A: Small claims court only, whatever the sum at stake overall
B: A federal district court under diversity jurisdiction
C: The Supreme Court as the court of first instance
D: No court can hear the case, as the sum is too big
Why A: Small claims court handles low-dollar disputes, and a $200,000 claim exceeds typical limits, so small claims is not the right court.
Why B: Ohio and Texas citizens are diverse parties and $200,000 exceeds $75,000, so a federal district court has diversity jurisdiction.
Why C: The Supreme Court hears cases mainly on appeal and has original jurisdiction only in narrow cases, not an ordinary contract dispute.
Why D: Plenty of courts can hear it: state courts, or federal court under diversity, and a large sum does not remove jurisdiction.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is venue?
A: The proper geographic location for a trial
B: The judge's salary, paid out of the budget
C: The jury's size and the number of its members
D: The lawyer's fee and how it is to be paid
Why A: Venue is the proper geographic location for a trial, usually where the parties live or the dispute arose, and it may be changed for fairness.
Why B: A judge's salary is a budget matter and has nothing to do with venue, which concerns the location of trial.
Why C: Jury size is set by procedural rules, whereas venue refers to the geographic location of the trial.
Why D: Lawyer fees are set by agreement or statute, while venue is the geographic location of the trial.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a motion to dismiss?
A: A request for a bigger jury to hear the case in the courtroom of the county
B: A request to change the judge's name on the case file before the trial starts
C: A request that the court end a case because the claim is legally insufficient
D: A request to add more parties to the case before the trial begins in the court
Why A: A larger jury is a trial matter, while a motion to dismiss asks the court to end the case for a legal defect.
Why B: Changing a judge's name makes no legal sense; a motion to dismiss asks the court to end the case because the claim is legally insufficient.
Why C: A motion to dismiss asks the court to end a case because the complaint fails to state a legally sufficient claim, even if all alleged facts are true.
Why D: Adding parties is done by a motion to join or intervene, whereas a motion to dismiss ends the case.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Both parties agree on all facts and ask the judge to decide who wins as a matter of law. Which motion fits?
A: Motion to appeal
B: Motion in limine
C: Motion to compel
D: Summary judgment
Why A: A motion to appeal is not a trial court motion on facts; an appeal asks a higher court to review a final decision.
Why B: A motion in limine asks the court to exclude certain evidence before or during trial, not to decide the case.
Why C: A motion to compel asks the court to force a party to comply with discovery requests and does not decide the case.
Why D: Summary judgment asks the court to rule for one side as a matter of law when no genuine dispute of material fact exists.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a verdict?
A: The decision of a jury on the facts of a case
B: The list of witnesses called by each side
C: The court's schedule of hearings this year overall
D: The lawyer's fee for the work on the case
Why A: A verdict is the jury's decision on the facts of a case, such as finding the defendant liable or not liable.
Why B: A witness list names the people who will testify and is not the decision of the jury.
Why C: A court schedule sets hearing dates and is not the decision on the facts, which is the verdict.
Why D: A lawyer's fee is a cost for legal services and is not a decision by the jury about the case.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an appellate court generally review?
A: New witnesses from scratch in a fresh trial
B: The jury's names and home addresses on file
C: The lawyers' fashion and the clothes they wore overall
D: Whether legal errors occurred in the lower court
Why A: Appellate courts generally do not hear new witnesses or hold a fresh trial; they review the record from the lower court.
Why B: Juror names and addresses are not what an appeals court reviews; it examines the trial record for legal errors.
Why C: Lawyers' clothing is irrelevant to appeals, which focus on legal errors in the lower court's proceedings.
Why D: Appellate courts review the record for legal errors in the lower court, and they usually defer to the trial court's findings of fact.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a default judgment?
A: A settlement reached by both sides before any trial starts
B: A judgment for the defendant when the plaintiff dies before trial
C: A judgment for the plaintiff when the defendant fails to respond
D: A jury's apology to the parties after a mistaken verdict
Why A: A pretrial settlement is an agreement between the sides, whereas a default judgment is entered when a defendant fails to respond.
Why B: A default judgment is not for the defendant when the plaintiff dies; it favors the plaintiff when the defendant does not respond.
Why C: A default judgment is entered for the plaintiff when the defendant fails to respond or appear after being properly served with the complaint.
Why D: An apology from a jury is not a legal judgment; a default judgment results from a defendant's failure to respond.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business is served with a lawsuit and ignores it for months. What may happen?
A: The case disappears and nothing happens to it
B: The court may enter a default judgment against it
C: The plaintiff must pay the business a large sum overall
D: The court cancels the law the suit was based on
Why A: A lawsuit does not vanish when ignored. The case proceeds without the defendant, so silence for months leads to a loss rather than dismissal.
Why B: Ignoring a served complaint lets the plaintiff ask for a default judgment, so the court may rule against the business without hearing its side of the dispute.
Why C: A plaintiff is the party seeking money, so it would not owe the business anything for being ignored. The default risk falls on the defendant instead.
Why D: Courts decide individual disputes and cannot cancel a statute because a defendant failed to respond. Only legislatures or constitutional rulings change the law itself.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a settlement?
A: An agreement between parties to resolve a dispute without a trial
B: A new law passed by the state legislature for the whole country
C: A jury decision reached after hearing the evidence in the case
D: A court order to arrest a person who has not paid a fine on time overall
Why A: A settlement is an agreement between the parties that resolves the dispute without a trial, usually with payment or promises, and it ends the case for both sides.
Why B: A statute passed by a legislature is a law, not a settlement. Settlements are private deals between the disputing parties, not rules that apply to a whole country.
Why C: A jury decision is a verdict reached after trial and evidence. A settlement happens by agreement, usually before any jury hears the case or decides it.
Why D: An arrest order for an unpaid fine is a court enforcement step against one person. A settlement is a voluntary agreement between parties, not a command to detain someone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is garnishment of wages?
A: A bonus that an employer adds to a worker's pay for strong results
B: A court-ordered withholding of part of pay to satisfy a debt
C: A tax refund that is paid after a person files a yearly return
D: A raise that increases a worker's hourly rate after a review period
Why A: A bonus is extra money an employer chooses to add to pay. Garnishment works the other way, taking money out of wages under a court order to pay a debt.
Why B: Garnishment is a court-ordered deduction from a worker's paycheck, sent to a creditor to satisfy a debt such as a judgment, with federal limits on how much can be taken.
Why C: A tax refund returns money to a taxpayer after a return is filed. Garnishment instead removes part of earnings to repay what the worker owes a creditor.
Why D: A raise increases the hourly rate after a review. Garnishment reduces take-home pay by court order, so it is not an increase in the worker's pay at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: After winning a money judgment, how may a creditor collect from a debtor who refuses to pay?
A: By ignoring the judgment and waiting for the debtor to pay
B: By force of arms against the debtor and his family
C: By waiting for many years and doing nothing at all
D: Through legal remedies such as wage garnishment or levies
Why A: Ignoring a judgment leaves the creditor unpaid, since a judgment alone does not move money. Waiting is not a collection method, and the law gives the creditor real tools instead.
Why B: Force against a debtor and family is unlawful and could be a crime. Creditors must use court-approved remedies, not violence or threats, to collect what is owed.
Why C: Doing nothing for many years collects nothing, and judgments can expire or lose value over time. A creditor must act using legal tools to recover the money.
Why D: After winning, a creditor may use legal remedies such as wage garnishment, bank levies or property liens to collect, all enforced through the court and sheriff, not self-help.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company's code of ethics bans gifts over $50, but a vendor offers a manager tickets worth $400. What should the manager do?
A: Accept and give a better deal to the vendor
B: Share the tickets with friends and the staff overall
C: Decline or report the offer according to policy
D: Accept it and say nothing to anyone at work
Why A: Accepting the tickets and favoring the vendor with a better deal is a bribe in effect. It breaks the $50 gift cap and corrupts fair purchasing decisions.
Why B: Sharing $400 tickets with friends and staff does not fix the problem. The gift still exceeds the $50 limit and may still sway the manager's future buying choices.
Why C: The tickets, worth $400, exceed the $50 limit eight times over. Following policy means declining the gift or reporting it, which protects the manager and the company from conflicts of interest.
Why D: Taking a $400 gift in secret breaks the $50 cap and hides a conflict of interest. Concealment makes the violation worse, because policy requires disclosure or refusal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is 'tone at the top'?
A: The company slogan and the words printed on its adverts in the daily press overall
B: Leaders' behavior and messages that set the ethical culture of an organization
C: The color of the headquarters building and the signs outside it in town
D: The volume of meetings and the loudness of voices in the large board room
Why A: A slogan or advert is marketing and says little about conduct. Tone at the top concerns how leaders actually behave, which employees watch and copy over printed words.
Why B: Tone at the top means the behavior and messages of senior leaders, which set the ethical culture because employees follow what executives do and reward, not just what they say.
Why C: The headquarters building color is decoration with no bearing on ethics. The phrase refers to leadership conduct and messaging, not the physical look of the premises or signs.
Why D: Loud meetings or voices are about volume and have no link to ethics. Tone at the top refers to the example and values that senior leaders communicate through actions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ethical relativism?
A: The view that ethics depend on cultural or personal standards
B: The view that ethics are fixed by the laws of each country
C: The view that the best action is the one with the best results
D: The practice of ignoring rules whenever they seem inconvenient
Why A: Ethical relativism holds that right and wrong depend on cultural or personal standards, so no single universal code applies to everyone, which is why it can clash with global business rules.
Why B: That is closer to legal positivism; ethical relativism says right and wrong depend on cultural or personal standards rather than on written law.
Why C: That describes consequentialism, which judges actions by outcomes; relativism instead holds that moral standards vary with culture or the individual.
Why D: Ignoring rules when inconvenient is simple rule breaking or opportunism. Relativism is a theory about where moral standards come from, not permission to skip rules at will.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm abroad is told local custom accepts small bribes to speed permits. A U.S. company is bound by which law?
A: The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)
B: The Sherman Antitrust Act
C: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act
D: The Truth in Lending Act
Why A: The FLSA governs minimum wage and overtime for workers in the U.S. It says nothing about bribing foreign officials, so it does not decide this situation.
Why B: The Sherman Act deals with monopolies and price fixing, not bribery of foreign officials, which is covered by the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
Why C: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act bars U.S. firms from bribing foreign officials, even where local custom accepts small payments, so the company must refuse despite local practice.
Why D: The Truth in Lending Act covers credit disclosures to consumers, not bribery of foreign officials by a U.S. company.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is utilitarianism in ethics?
A: Judging actions by whether the person acting had good intentions
B: Following duties and rules no matter what the consequences are
C: Avoiding all decisions that could have any effect on other people
D: Choosing the action that creates the greatest good for the greatest number
Why A: Judging by intentions is closer to intent-based ethics; utilitarianism judges actions by their results for everyone affected.
Why B: That describes deontology, which focuses on duties; utilitarianism looks at outcomes and chooses the action producing the greatest overall good.
Why C: Avoiding all decisions that affect others is impossible and is not a theory at all. Utilitarians actively choose actions by weighing how they affect everyone involved.
Why D: Utilitarianism judges actions by outcomes and picks the one producing the greatest good for the greatest number of people, so costs and benefits to all are weighed together.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is deontological ethics?
A: Doing what feels good at the time to the person acting
B: Judging actions by the greatest good for the greatest number
C: Judging actions by whether they follow moral duties or rules
D: Judging actions by the character of the person who acts
Why A: Doing what feels good to the actor is subjectivism or egoism. Deontology instead ties morality to duties and rules that bind regardless of personal feelings.
Why B: That describes utilitarianism, which weighs outcomes; deontology judges an act by whether it follows moral duties or rules.
Why C: Deontological ethics judges an action by whether it follows moral duties or rules, such as honesty, no matter the outcome, which makes the act itself the test.
Why D: That describes virtue ethics, which focuses on character; deontology judges the act itself by moral duties and rules.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager reasons, 'I should never lie, even if lying would help the company.' Which ethical approach is this?
A: Moral relativist thinking
B: Duty-based (deontological)
C: Utilitarian, by the results
D: Egoist, acting for self only
Why A: Relativism says morality varies by culture or person. A manager who says one should never lie is applying a fixed rule, not changing standards by situation.
Why B: Refusing to lie even when lying would help the company follows a fixed duty regardless of results. That is the core of duty-based, or deontological, ethics.
Why C: A utilitarian would lie if the lie produced the greatest good. The manager rejects lying even when it helps, so the reasoning is not outcome based.
Why D: An egoist acts for personal advantage. The manager is following a principle about honesty even when lying would help the company, which is not self-interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is insider information in ethics?
A: Confidential knowledge not available to the public that could influence decisions
B: A stock chart that shows how a share's price changed over a full year  on a public website
C: Public news that anyone can read in a paper or on a website, free of charge
D: A general rumor that is passed around the office without any proof or facts
Why A: Insider information is confidential, non-public knowledge that could influence decisions such as trades. Using it for gain is unethical and often illegal, as in insider trading.
Why B: A public stock chart shows past prices that anyone can view, so it is not confidential. Insider information must be non-public and capable of affecting decisions.
Why C: News anyone can read in a paper or online is public, so using it gives no unfair advantage. Insider information is defined by being unavailable to the public.
Why D: An unproven office rumor is gossip, not reliable confidential knowledge. Insider information is specific, non-public facts that could influence decisions, not baseless talk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ethics audit?
A: A tax audit in which the IRS checks that a firm paid what it owed
B: A hiring test that checks how well a job candidate knows the work
C: A product test that measures how well an item works before sale
D: A review of how well an organization follows its ethical policies
Why A: A tax audit by the IRS checks tax compliance, not ethics. An ethics audit looks at conduct against the organization's own ethical policies instead.
Why B: A hiring test measures a candidate's job knowledge and has no connection to reviewing company ethics. An ethics audit examines the organization, not an applicant.
Why C: A product test measures how well an item performs before sale. An ethics audit examines whether people and processes follow the organization's ethical policies, not product quality.
Why D: An ethics audit reviews how well an organization follows its ethical policies and codes, finding gaps and risks so that management can correct problems before harm grows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: After an ethics audit finds repeated gift-policy violations, what is the best response?
A: Hide the findings from the board and the public
B: Fire the auditor who found the problems in the audit
C: Ignore the report and carry on as before the audit
D: Retrain staff, enforce the policy and fix incentives
Why A: Hiding findings from the board and public deepens the wrongdoing and removes oversight. Repeated violations call for correction and openness, not concealment.
Why B: Firing the auditor punishes the person who exposed the problem, which is retaliation. It leaves the gift violations untouched and discourages honest reporting.
Why C: Ignoring the report leaves repeated gift violations to continue and signals that policy is not enforced. Audit findings exist so management can act on them.
Why D: Retraining staff, enforcing the policy and fixing incentives addresses the cause of repeated violations, since people break rules when training is weak or rewards push them to.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is insurable interest?
A: A tax on policies charged by the state to the holders of insurance cover each year
B: The interest rate charged on the premium when a customer pays by monthly installment
C: A financial stake in the person or property insured, so that a loss would cause real harm
D: A hobby of the insurance agent who sells the policy to the customers in town each year as a rule
Why A: A tax on policies charged by the state is a premium tax and has no relation to the holder's stake. Insurable interest is about the policyholder's financial relationship to the thing insured.
Why B: Interest charged on installment premiums is a finance cost. Insurable interest is a different idea, meaning the policyholder would suffer a real loss if the insured thing were harmed.
Why C: Insurable interest means a financial stake in the person or property insured, so a loss would cause real harm to the holder. Without it, a policy is an illegal wager.
Why D: An agent's hobby has nothing to do with the contract. Insurable interest concerns the policyholder's stake in the insured person or property, not any personal interest of the seller.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A man buys fire insurance on a neighbor's house that he does not own and has no stake in. What is the likely legal problem?
A: He lacks an insurable interest
B: The premium is too high for it
C: Fire insurance is illegal there
D: The neighbor must be the agent
Why A: He has no stake in the neighbor's house, so a loss would not harm him. Without an insurable interest the policy is void as a wager, which is the likely legal problem.
Why B: The premium level is a pricing matter and is not why the policy fails. The real legal defect is that he would suffer no loss, so he lacks insurable interest.
Why C: Fire insurance is lawful in general, and homeowners buy it all the time. The problem here is that he does not own the house or have any financial stake in it.
Why D: The neighbor does not need to be the agent. Agents sell policies and have nothing to do with validity. The flaw is that the buyer has no insurable interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is subrogation in insurance?
A: A cancellation of the policy by the insurer when the insured fails to pay the premium on time as set out in the contract
B: The insurer's right to step into the insured's shoes and recover from a responsible third party after paying a claim
C: The insured's right to a bonus payment from the insurer each year when no claims are made against the policy
D: A claim denial letter that the insurer sends to the insured after reviewing the claim, with its reasons for the decision
Why A: Cancelling for unpaid premiums is a lapse or cancellation, not subrogation. Subrogation concerns the insurer recovering money from a third party after paying a claim.
Why B: Subrogation lets the insurer step into the insured's position after paying a claim and recover the amount from the responsible third party, preventing a double recovery for the insured.
Why C: A no-claims bonus is a reward paid for claim-free years, not subrogation. Subrogation is the insurer's right to recover from whoever caused the loss after it has paid.
Why D: A denial letter explains why a claim was refused. Subrogation happens when a claim is paid, and the insurer then pursues the party at fault to get its money back.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A driver's car is damaged by another driver's negligence. After the insurer pays the repair, it sues the at-fault driver. What is this called?
A: Novation
B: Rescission
C: Subrogation
D: Arbitration
Why A: Novation replaces one party in a contract with another by agreement. It does not describe an insurer suing an at-fault driver after paying a repair claim.
Why B: Rescission cancels a contract and restores the parties to their prior positions. The insurer here is pursuing recovery from a third party, not cancelling the policy.
Why C: Subrogation allows the insurer that paid the repair to take over the insured's rights and sue the negligent driver to recover its payment, which is exactly this situation.
Why D: Arbitration is a private method of resolving disputes outside court. It names a forum, not the insurer's right to recover its payment from the driver who caused the damage.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the principle of indemnity mean in insurance?
A: The insured should earn a profit from a claim, so a loss is turned into a gain
B: The insured need not prove any loss at all when making a claim against the insurer
C: The insurer must pay double the loss whenever a claim is made by the holder of a policy
D: The insured should be restored to their pre-loss position, but not profit from the loss
Why A: Indemnity forbids profit from a loss. If an insured could earn a gain from a claim, insurance would invite deliberate losses, so the principle prevents exactly that.
Why B: Insurers pay only for actual, proven loss. Indemnity compensates a real loss, so an insured who proves nothing is owed nothing, and this option reverses the principle.
Why C: Paying double the loss would give the holder a profit, which indemnity forbids. The principle limits payment to the actual loss suffered, not more than it.
Why D: Indemnity means the insured is restored to the position held before the loss but does not profit from it, so the payout is limited to the actual loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a misrepresentation on an insurance application?
A: A false statement of a material fact that may let the insurer void the policy
B: A late payment of premium made by the insured after the due date has passed
C: An optional rider added to a policy by the insured for extra cover at an added cost
D: A request for lower rates made by the insured when applying for the cover
Why A: A misrepresentation is a false statement of a material fact on an application. Because the insurer relied on it to set terms, the insurer may void the policy or deny claims.
Why B: Paying a premium late is a payment default and can cause a lapse. It is not a false statement on the application, which is what misrepresentation means.
Why C: An optional rider is an agreed addition to coverage, openly requested and paid for. It involves no false statement, so it is not misrepresentation.
Why D: Asking for lower rates is a normal request and is not a false statement of fact. Misrepresentation requires an untrue material statement made on the application.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An applicant hides a serious prior illness on a life insurance application and dies two years later. The insurer may:
A: Refund all premiums plus a bonus to the family at once
B: Contest the claim based on material misrepresentation
C: Ignore the policy and pay the claim in full anyway
D: Pay double the claim amount to the family quickly
Why A: Hiding a serious illness is a material misrepresentation, so the insurer does not owe a bonus. Refunding premiums with extra money would reward the dishonest answer and is not required.
Why B: A hidden serious illness is a material misrepresentation, so the insurer may contest the claim, usually within the contestability period, and may deny it or void the policy.
Why C: Paying in full would ignore the false application. Because the concealed illness was material, the insurer has the right to contest the claim instead of paying automatically.
Why D: Doubling the claim has no basis in contract or law. The insurer is entitled to challenge the claim because of the concealed illness, not to pay extra.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a lease under UCC Article 2A?
A: A sale of land from one owner to another for a fixed price to be paid in cash
B: A transfer of the right to possess and use goods for a term in exchange for payment
C: A loan with no goods involved, made by a bank to a firm in need of working funds overall
D: A gift of goods from one person to another, made with no payment of any kind
Why A: A sale of land is real property law and transfers ownership. A UCC Article 2A lease covers goods, and ownership stays with the lessor, so it is not a land sale.
Why B: Under Article 2A, a lease transfers the right to possess and use goods for a term in exchange for payment, while the lessor keeps title to the goods.
Why C: A bank loan is a credit transaction involving money. An Article 2A lease involves goods that are possessed and used for payment, so a loan with no goods is not a lease.
Why D: A gift involves no payment, but a lease requires consideration in the form of rent. Article 2A leases are paid arrangements for using goods for a term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a finance lease?
A: A three-party lease in which a lessor buys goods chosen by the lessee and leases them to the lessee
B: A lease with no payments due from the lessee to the owner for the use of the goods during the term in practice
C: A lease between two cars that are parked in a lot owned by the same firm and used by staff
D: A lease of a home to a family that pays a monthly rent to the owner of the property in question
Why A: In a finance lease, a lessor buys goods the lessee selected and leases them to the lessee, creating three parties: supplier, lessor and lessee. The lessor acts mainly as a financier.
Why B: A lease with no payments from the lessee would be a gift or loan of goods. A finance lease needs rent, since the lessor is financing the equipment purchase.
Why C: Where cars are parked or who owns the lot is irrelevant. A finance lease is defined by its three parties and the lessor buying goods chosen by the lessee.
Why D: Leasing a home is a residential real estate lease governed by landlord and tenant law. A finance lease concerns goods bought by a lessor at the lessee's request.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bailee?
A: A seller of land who transfers title by deed to a buyer in a sale
B: A judge who hears a dispute over goods that were left with a keeper
C: The owner of the goods who leaves them with another party for a time
D: The party who temporarily holds another's property for a purpose
Why A: A seller of land who gives a deed is a grantor. A bailee instead holds another person's property temporarily and has possession without ownership.
Why B: A judge decides disputes and is not defined by holding goods. A bailee is the party who temporarily has possession of another's property for a specific purpose.
Why C: The owner who leaves goods with someone is the bailor, not the bailee. The bailee is the one receiving and holding the goods temporarily.
Why D: A bailee is the party who temporarily holds another's property for a purpose such as storage or repair and must return it, with title staying with the bailor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A dry cleaner loses a customer's coat through its negligence. What is the bailee's likely liability?
A: Only the cleaning fee that the customer paid for the service
B: No liability for the loss of the coat while it was in the shop
C: Responsible for the loss because it failed to use reasonable care
D: The customer's other coats, which the customer left at home on the day
Why A: Liability is not capped at the cleaning fee. A bailee who loses goods through negligence generally owes the value of the lost item, which here is the coat.
Why B: The bailee had possession and a duty of care, so the loss in the shop does not release it. Negligence creates liability to the owner for the lost coat.
Why C: A bailee for hire must use reasonable care, and the cleaner failed by losing the coat through negligence, so it is liable for the loss.
Why D: The customer's other coats stayed at home and were never in the cleaner's care. A bailee is liable only for the bailed property that it lost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a common carrier?
A: A private courier for one client, carrying parcels for that firm only
B: A passenger who rides free on a bus or train owned by the firm
C: A business that transports goods or people for the public for pay
D: A car dealer who sells new and used cars to the public in town
Why A: A private courier serving one client does not offer services to the public. A common carrier holds itself out to carry goods or people for anyone who pays.
Why B: A free rider is a passenger, not a carrier. A common carrier is the business that transports goods or people for the public for a fee.
Why C: A common carrier is a business that transports goods or people for the general public for pay, and it faces strict duties and heightened liability for what it carries.
Why D: A car dealer sells vehicles and does not transport goods or passengers for hire. A common carrier moves goods or people for the public for payment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is stoppage in transit?
A: A delivery delay of a few days caused by bad weather on the road to town every time
B: A buyer's right to cancel the order if the goods are delivered late
C: A tax on shipping charged by the government on goods carried by road
D: A seller's right to stop goods already shipped if the buyer proves insolvent
Why A: A weather delay is just a slow shipment. Stoppage in transit is a legal right of a seller to halt goods already shipped, not a delivery delay.
Why B: A buyer's right to cancel for late delivery is a rejection or cancellation remedy. Stoppage in transit is a right held by the seller, not the buyer.
Why C: A shipping tax charged by a government is a duty or levy. Stoppage in transit is a seller's remedy and has no relation to taxes on freight.
Why D: Stoppage in transit lets a seller stop goods already shipped and recall them from the carrier when the buyer is found insolvent, which prevents shipping goods to a buyer who cannot pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does COBRA allow?
A: Employees who lose coverage to continue group health insurance for a limited time at own cost
B: Free health care for life, paid for by the employer after the worker has left the firm for good
C: Paid sick leave for employees who miss work because of a long illness
D: Retirement accounts that employers must match with deposits from company funds each pay period
Why A: COBRA lets employees who lose group coverage, for example after a layoff, keep the same group health plan for a limited time by paying the premium themselves.
Why B: COBRA does not make employers pay for lifetime care. The former worker pays the premium, and coverage lasts only a limited time, not for life.
Why C: COBRA is about keeping group health insurance after job loss, not paid sick leave, which employers or other laws provide separately.
Why D: Retirement account matching is not part of COBRA, which only lets former employees continue group health coverage by paying the premium.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A laid-off worker wants to keep her employer's health plan for several months. Which law may help?
A: Sherman
B: COBRA
C: Lanham
D: Clean Air
Why A: The Sherman Act deals with antitrust and monopolies. It has nothing to do with continuing health coverage, so it would not help a laid-off worker.
Why B: COBRA lets a laid-off worker continue the employer's group health plan for a limited period if she pays the premium herself, which fits this situation.
Why C: The Lanham Act governs trademarks and false advertising. It has no role in health plans, so it cannot help a laid-off worker keep coverage.
Why D: The Clean Air Act regulates pollution and emissions. It does not address employee benefits, so it cannot help someone keep health insurance after a layoff.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does HIPAA protect?
A: Wages that employees earn for their work at a clinic or hospital
B: Stock trades that investors make on a public exchange each day
C: Import duties that businesses pay on goods brought into a port
D: The privacy and security of individuals' health information
Why A: Wages are covered by wage laws such as the FLSA. HIPAA protects medical privacy and security, not what employees earn at a clinic or hospital.
Why B: Stock trades are regulated by securities laws. HIPAA does not deal with exchanges or investors, and it focuses on health information instead.
Why C: Import duties are customs matters handled by trade law. HIPAA has no role in goods entering a port, because it is a healthcare privacy law.
Why D: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of individuals' health information, setting rules on how providers and insurers may use and share patient records.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A clinic employee posts a patient's diagnosis on social media. Which law is most likely violated?
A: The ADA
B: The FLSA
C: HIPAA
D: Lanham
Why A: The ADA prohibits disability discrimination and requires accommodations. It does not govern sharing a patient's diagnosis, so it is not the likely violation here.
Why B: The FLSA covers minimum wage and overtime. Posting a patient diagnosis is not a wage issue, so the FLSA is not the law violated.
Why C: Posting a patient's diagnosis discloses protected health information without permission, which is a classic HIPAA privacy violation by a covered entity's employee.
Why D: The Lanham Act concerns trademarks and false advertising, not patient privacy. Disclosing a diagnosis is a health privacy matter, not a trademark one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does ERISA regulate?
A: Immigration rules and visas for foreign workers overall
B: Private-sector employee pension and benefit plans
C: Workplace safety rules for factories and shops
D: Minimum wage rates for workers in the country
Why A: Immigration and visas are handled by immigration law. ERISA covers private retirement and benefit plans, so it does not regulate foreign worker entry.
Why B: ERISA regulates private-sector employee pension and benefit plans, setting standards for reporting, disclosure and fiduciary duty to protect participants' retirement and health benefits.
Why C: Workplace safety falls under OSHA. ERISA addresses pensions and benefits, so factory and shop safety rules are not within its scope.
Why D: Minimum wage is set under the FLSA. ERISA deals with employee benefit plans and pensions rather than wage rates for workers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is disparate treatment?
A: Intentionally treating an employee worse because of a protected characteristic
B: Offering training to staff on new skills and the use of new tools at work
C: Treating everyone the same way, whatever their personal traits or background every time
D: Paying everyone equally for the same work, whatever their role or title
Why A: Disparate treatment means intentionally treating an employee worse because of a protected characteristic such as race, sex or religion, and it is a core form of discrimination.
Why B: Offering training on new skills is lawful development of staff. Disparate treatment requires intentional unfavorable treatment because of a protected trait, which training is not.
Why C: Treating everyone the same is the opposite of disparate treatment. The term describes singling out an employee for worse treatment because of a protected trait.
Why D: Equal pay for the same work is lawful and expected. Disparate treatment instead involves intentionally unequal, worse treatment tied to a protected characteristic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is disparate impact?
A: A pay raise given to an employee after a good annual review by the manager of the department
B: A neutral policy that disproportionately harms a protected group without business necessity
C: A merit bonus awarded to staff who exceed their sales targets for the whole year
D: A deliberate act of harm carried out by a manager against a particular worker at the firm
Why A: A raise after a good review is lawful and unrelated to discrimination. Disparate impact concerns neutral policies that harm a protected group, not rewards for performance.
Why B: Disparate impact is a facially neutral policy that disproportionately harms a protected group without business necessity, so intent is not required to prove discrimination.
Why C: A merit bonus for exceeding targets is a lawful performance reward. Disparate impact concerns neutral rules that hurt protected groups, not rewards based on results.
Why D: A deliberate act of harm by a manager against a worker is disparate treatment because it is intentional. Disparate impact needs no intent at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company requires a physical test that screens out most women applicants but is not related to the job. Which claim may arise?
A: Defamation against the staff
B: Contract rescission for both sides
C: Disparate impact discrimination
D: A wage claim for unpaid pay
Why A: Defamation concerns false statements that harm reputation. A job-unrelated physical test that screens out women is a discrimination issue, not defamation.
Why B: Contract rescission cancels a contract. The facts describe a hiring test with an unequal effect on women, which raises discrimination, not rescission.
Why C: A physical test that screens out most women and is unrelated to the job is a neutral rule with unequal impact, which supports a disparate impact discrimination claim.
Why D: The facts involve hiring applicants, not unpaid wages. Nothing suggests pay was withheld, so a wage claim does not fit a test that screens out women.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the first step usually required before filing a federal employment discrimination lawsuit?
A: Filing a charge with the EEOC
B: Resigning from the company
C: Hiring a bank to act for you
D: Writing a will for the estate
Why A: Before a federal discrimination suit, a person generally must file a charge with the EEOC, which investigates and issues a right to sue notice that allows the case to go to court.
Why B: Resigning is not required and could even weaken a claim. The required first step is an administrative charge, not leaving the job.
Why C: Hiring a bank has no connection to discrimination claims. The needed first step is a charge filed with the EEOC, not any financial arrangement.
Why D: A will concerns an estate after death and has no role in employment claims. The usual first step is filing a charge with the EEOC.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Pregnancy Discrimination Act prohibit?
A: Hiring pregnant workers and giving them leave on request from the employer
B: Offering benefits to staff, such as health cover and paid time off work
C: Giving maternity leave to staff who have had a child or are expecting one
D: Treating a worker unfavorably because of pregnancy or related conditions
Why A: The Act does not prohibit hiring pregnant workers or giving leave. It protects them, so this option describes lawful conduct that the law actually encourages.
Why B: Offering health cover and paid time off is lawful and good practice. The Act forbids unfavorable treatment, not providing benefits to staff.
Why C: Giving maternity leave is allowed and often supports workers. The Act prohibits discrimination, not leave for those who have had or expect a child.
Why D: The Pregnancy Discrimination Act prohibits treating a worker unfavorably because of pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, in hiring, pay, promotion and other terms of employment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager refuses to promote an employee because she is expecting a baby. This is most likely:
A: A lawful business choice
B: A tax rule on wages
C: Unlawful discrimination
D: A required next step
Why A: Refusing a promotion because of pregnancy is not a legitimate business reason. It is protected status discrimination, so calling it a lawful choice is wrong.
Why B: A tax rule on wages is about payroll withholding. The refusal here concerns a promotion denied due to pregnancy, which has nothing to do with taxes.
Why C: Denying a promotion because a woman is expecting a baby is unlawful pregnancy discrimination under the Pregnancy Discrimination Act and Title VII.
Why D: Nothing in law requires a promotion to be denied for pregnancy. A required next step is a process step, whereas this is a discriminatory decision.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are employee drug-testing rules mainly based on?
A: Company policy, since drug testing is treated as a private business matter
B: Federal and state law plus the nature of the job and consent or notice
C: A federal law that requires employers to test new hires each year
D: Whatever a coworker prefers, as long as they ask the employer in good time
Why A: Company policy alone cannot decide testing; state and federal law, the nature of the job, and consent or notice set the limits on employers.
Why B: Drug-testing rules rest on federal and state law, the nature of the job, such as safety sensitive roles, and employee consent or notice, so employers cannot act at will.
Why C: No general federal law requires employers to test new hires annually; testing is governed by various laws and depends on the job and notice.
Why D: A coworker's preference has no legal weight over testing. Rules come from law, the job's nature and employee consent or notice, not from coworkers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Equal Pay Act?
A: A law requiring equal pay for equal work regardless of sex
B: A law capping all pay for every worker in every industry
C: A law on vacations and the number of days that workers may take
D: A law on taxes paid by workers and by firms on their income
Why A: The Equal Pay Act requires equal pay for equal work, meaning substantially equal jobs, regardless of sex, so employers cannot pay men and women differently for the same work.
Why B: The Act does not cap pay for any industry. It only bars sex-based pay differences for equal work, so it sets no ceiling on wages.
Why C: Vacation days are not addressed by the Equal Pay Act. It concerns pay equality between sexes, not time off for workers.
Why D: Taxes on workers and firms are covered by tax law. The Equal Pay Act deals with equal pay for equal work regardless of sex.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two employees with the same job, skills and responsibilities are paid differently solely because one is female. What law is violated?
A: The Clean Air Act
B: The Sherman Act
C: The ADA of 1990
D: The Equal Pay Act
Why A: The Clean Air Act regulates pollution. It does not address pay differences between employees, so it is not the law violated here.
Why B: The Sherman Act covers antitrust, such as monopolies and price fixing. It does not address pay differences within a firm, so it is not violated.
Why C: The ADA of 1990 prohibits disability discrimination. The facts concern pay based on sex, not disability, so it is not the relevant law.
Why D: Paying one worker less solely because she is female, for the same job, skills and responsibilities, violates the Equal Pay Act, which bars sex-based pay differences.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the minimum age to work in non-hazardous jobs under federal law, with certain limits?
Why A: Twenty-one is too high. Federal law generally allows youths aged 14 to work in non-hazardous jobs with limits, so 21 is not the minimum age.
Why B: Ten is too low for regular non-hazardous work. The federal minimum is 14 for most such jobs, though limited exceptions exist, such as farm work and child acting.
Why C: Seven is far below the federal minimum of 14. Children that young cannot generally work in non-hazardous jobs under the FLSA child labor rules.
Why D: Under federal child labor rules, the minimum age for non-hazardous jobs is 14, with limits on hours and types of work, while hazardous jobs require 18.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a 'tipped employee' rule under the FLSA?
A: Employers may pay a lower cash wage if tips bring the worker up to at least the minimum wage
B: Employers pay the full minimum wage in cash and may keep a share of tips
C: Employers may pay a lower cash wage even if tips leave the worker below minimum wage
D: Tips are illegal for employers to accept and for workers to receive in any form of work
Why A: The FLSA allows a tip credit, so an employer can pay a lower cash wage if tips raise the worker to at least the full minimum wage. Otherwise the employer makes up the difference.
Why B: Employers may not keep employees' tips; the tip credit lets them pay a lower cash wage, not the full wage plus a share of tips.
Why C: If tips do not bring the worker up to the minimum wage, the employer must make up the difference, so the cash wage cannot leave the worker below it.
Why D: Tips are legal to accept and receive. The FLSA actually sets rules for tipped employees, so saying they are illegal is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act mainly about?
A: Environmental cleanup of land and rivers that have been polluted by large factories
B: Protecting the privacy of consumers' financial information held by financial institutions
C: Trademarks and the brand names that firms register with the patent office for use in trade
D: Minimum wage rates and the overtime pay that workers earn each week on the job in factories
Why A: Environmental cleanup belongs to laws such as the Superfund Act. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act concerns financial institutions and the privacy of consumer financial data.
Why B: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to protect the privacy of consumers' financial information and to explain their information sharing practices through privacy notices.
Why C: Trademarks are registered under the Lanham Act through the patent and trademark office. Gramm-Leach-Bliley does not deal with brand names.
Why D: Minimum wage and overtime come from the FLSA. Gramm-Leach-Bliley deals with financial privacy, not wage and hour matters in factories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Bank Secrecy Act require?
A: Banks to freeze accounts of customers who owe back taxes
B: Banks to hold a minimum reserve of customer deposits
C: Banks to report large cash transactions and suspicious activity
D: Banks to disclose loan costs and finance charges to borrowers
Why A: Freezing accounts for tax debts is done through levies and legal process; the Act focuses on recordkeeping and reports to the government.
Why B: Reserve requirements are set by the Federal Reserve, while the Secrecy Act is an anti-money laundering law about reports and records.
Why C: The Bank Secrecy Act requires financial institutions to report large cash transactions, over $10,000, and suspicious activity so that regulators can detect money laundering and crime.
Why D: Loan cost disclosure falls under the Truth in Lending Act; this Act requires reports on large cash transactions and suspicious activity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person deposits $9,500 in cash on several consecutive days to avoid a $10,000 reporting threshold. This conduct is called:
A: Budgeting
B: Structuring
C: Leasing
D: Compounding
Why A: Budgeting is planning spending and income. Splitting deposits to dodge a $10,000 reporting threshold is not budgeting, and it is a crime.
Why B: Breaking up cash deposits, such as $9,500 on several days, to avoid the $10,000 reporting threshold is called structuring, and it is a federal offense even if the money is legal.
Why C: Leasing is renting an asset for a term. Making deposits below the reporting threshold has nothing to do with leasing, so it is not the right term.
Why D: Compounding is earning interest on interest. Splitting cash deposits to evade a reporting requirement is structuring, not compounding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is money laundering?
A: Depositing a paycheck into a bank account on payday each week
B: Paying a bill to a supplier or a landlord on the due date
C: Disguising illegally obtained money to make it appear legitimate
D: Washing cash in a machine to remove dirt and germs from the notes
Why A: Depositing a paycheck is routine banking with legitimate income. Money laundering requires hiding illegal origins, which is absent from a normal paycheck deposit.
Why B: Paying a supplier or landlord is a normal business payment. It has no element of disguising illegally obtained funds, so it is not laundering.
