Why A: Seventy-five percent would come from a misplaced decimal; 15,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.075, which is 7.5 percent, not 75.
Why B: A margin of 13.3 percent comes from dividing profit by 112,500 or a similar wrong base; the revenue is 200,000, so the margin is 7.5.
Why C: Profit margin equals profit divided by revenue, so 15,000 divided by 200,000 gives 0.075, which is 7.5 percent of each sales dollar kept as profit.
Why D: Fifteen percent would be profit over 100,000 of revenue, but this firm has 200,000 in revenue, so dividing 15,000 by 200,000 gives only 7.5 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a firm's break-even quantity?
A: The output where revenue is zero for the firm
B: The output that earns the largest profit for the firm
C: The output where costs are zero for the firm
D: The output where total revenue equals total cost
Why A: Revenue is not zero at break-even; a firm there sells enough to cover its costs, so revenue equals total cost, which is not a zero level.
Why B: The output that earns the largest profit is the profit-maximizing quantity, which differs from break-even, where profit is exactly zero.
Why C: Costs are never zero when a firm is producing, so break-even cannot be where costs vanish; it is where revenue matches those costs.
Why D: Break-even quantity is the output at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero, and selling any more begins to earn a profit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Fixed costs are $9,000. Each unit sells for $15 and costs $6 to make. What is the break-even quantity?
A: 600 units
B: 1,000 units
C: 9,000 units
D: 1,500 units
Why A: Six hundred units results from dividing 9,000 by 15, which ignores variable cost; the contribution per unit is 15 minus 6, giving 9 dollars.
Why B: Break-even equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit; each unit adds 15 minus 6, which is 9 dollars, so 9,000 divided by 9 gives 1,000 units.
Why C: Nine thousand units treats the fixed cost figure as the quantity; dividing 9,000 by the contribution of 9 dollars per unit gives 1,000 units.
Why D: One thousand five hundred units comes from dividing 9,000 by 6, the variable cost alone, but break-even uses the contribution of 9 dollars, giving 1,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If a firm sells above its break-even quantity, what happens?
A: It earns a profit
B: Fixed costs vanish
C: Revenue becomes zero
D: It suffers a loss
Why A: Selling above break-even means revenue exceeds total cost, so each extra unit adds to profit and the firm earns a profit.
Why B: Fixed costs do not vanish above break-even; they stay the same in total, but sales are large enough to cover them.
Why C: Revenue becomes larger, not zero, when a firm sells more units, so this contradicts what happens above the break-even quantity.
Why D: A loss happens when quantity sold is below the break-even quantity, because revenue falls short of cost, which is the opposite of this case.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do firms often use economies of scope?
A: Producing less to save paper and other materials
B: Producing related goods together lowers average cost
C: Producing only one good raises cost for the firm
D: Producing unrelated goods in different countries at once
Why A: Producing less to save paper and materials is not economies of scope, which concerns producing a range of related goods rather than cutting output.
Why B: Economies of scope arise when producing related goods together shares inputs such as staff and equipment, which lowers the average cost per product.
Why C: Producing only one good raises cost is not the concept; economies of scope come from making several related goods, not from limiting output to one.
Why D: Producing unrelated goods in different countries cannot share staff, equipment or know-how, so it does not create the savings that scope economies describe.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bakery that also sells coffee uses the same staff and counters for both. Which concept explains the lower cost?
A: Sunk costs paid
B: Price discrimination
C: Economies of scope
D: Diminishing returns
Why A: Sunk costs are payments already made that cannot be recovered, and they have no role in explaining shared staff and counters lowering cost.
Why B: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices and has nothing to do with sharing staff and counters across two products to cut costs.
Why C: Selling coffee and bread with the same staff and counters spreads inputs over related products, lowering average cost, which is an economy of scope.
Why D: Diminishing returns describe falling extra output as more input is added to a fixed amount of another input, not savings from joint production.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the long run in economics?
A: A period when firms cannot produce any goods
B: A period longer than ten years exactly for all firms
C: A period when prices never change at all in markets
D: A period long enough for all inputs to be varied
Why A: A period when firms cannot produce any goods describes no real time frame; the long run is about flexibility, and firms still produce in it.
Why B: The long run is not exactly ten years; it is defined by whether all inputs can be changed, which varies from industry to industry.
Why C: Prices can change in the long run, and the definition rests on adjusting inputs, so a period of fixed prices is not what the term means.
Why D: The long run is a period long enough for a firm to vary all its inputs, including plant size and equipment, so no inputs are fixed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the short run in economics?
A: A period when at least one input is fixed
B: A period with zero production by firms
C: A period when firms can change plant size
D: A period shorter than one calendar year
Why A: The short run is a period in which at least one input, such as plant size or equipment, is fixed, so output changes only by varying other inputs.
Why B: Production continues in the short run; it simply limits how much a firm can change, so a period of zero production is wrong.
Why C: That describes the long run, when all inputs including plant size can change; in the short run at least one input is fixed.
Why D: The short run is defined by fixed inputs, not by calendar time; its length differs across industries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens in a competitive industry when firms earn economic profit?
A: New firms enter and profit shrinks
B: Existing firms raise prices to raise profit
C: Firms exit and profit rises for others
D: The government takes the profit
Why A: Economic profit attracts new firms into a competitive industry, which raises supply and pushes down price until profit shrinks toward zero.
Why B: Competitive firms are price takers and cannot raise prices; economic profit draws in new firms, which lowers price.
Why C: Firms exit when they suffer losses, not when they earn profit, so this describes the opposite of what happens in a profitable competitive industry.
Why D: Governments do not take profit away in a competitive industry; entry by new firms is what reduces profit over time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens in a competitive industry when firms suffer losses?
A: More firms enter the market
B: Costs fall to zero for all firms
C: Some firms exit and prices rise
D: Prices fall with no limit at all
Why A: More firms entering the market happens when firms earn profit, not losses, so entry is the reverse of the response to continued losses.
Why B: Costs do not fall to zero when firms suffer losses; firms still pay for inputs, and exit rather than lower costs removes the loss.
Why C: Losses push some firms out of a competitive industry, which cuts supply and raises prices until the remaining firms earn normal profit.
Why D: Prices rise, not fall, as firms exit and supply shrinks, and they cannot fall without limit since firms leave when they lose money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the accounting equation for profit?
A: Profit equals price divided by quantity
B: Profit equals revenue minus expenses
C: Profit equals expenses minus revenue
D: Profit equals assets minus liabilities
Why A: Price divided by quantity is not the profit formula; it makes no reference to revenue or costs and would not measure what a firm keeps.
Why B: Profit equals total revenue minus total expenses, so a firm earns a profit when what it receives from sales is larger than what it spends.
Why C: Expenses minus revenue reverses the formula and gives a positive number when the firm has a loss, so it would not measure profit.
Why D: Assets minus liabilities gives equity or net worth on the balance sheet, which is a measure of ownership value rather than profit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a typical overhead cost for a retail store?
A: The cost of goods sold
B: Commissions on sales
C: The price buyers pay
D: Utilities and rent
Why A: Cost of goods sold is a direct cost tied to the products sold, not an overhead cost that stays fixed regardless of sales volume.
Why B: Commissions on sales vary with how much is sold, so they are a variable selling cost rather than a fixed overhead expense for the store.
Why C: The price buyers pay is the store's revenue, which is money coming in, so it cannot be a cost the store carries as overhead.
Why D: Utilities and rent are ongoing costs of running the store that do not depend on how much is sold, which is exactly what overhead means for a retailer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Total revenue is $500,000, cost of goods sold is $300,000 and operating expenses are $120,000. What is operating profit?
Why A: Operating profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus operating expenses, so 500,000 minus 300,000 minus 120,000 leaves 80,000 for the business.
Why B: The figure 920,000 comes from adding all three numbers together, but costs must be subtracted from revenue, not added to it, so this is wrong.
Why C: The figure 380,000 is revenue minus operating expenses only, which forgets to subtract the 300,000 cost of goods sold from the 500,000 revenue figure.
Why D: The figure 200,000 is revenue minus cost of goods sold only, which is gross profit, and it ignores the 120,000 of operating expenses still to deduct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a business do with the resources it takes in?
A: Stores them without ever using them in case prices rise
B: Burns them to heat the factory in the winter months
C: Gives them away to competitors for no payment at all
D: Turns them into goods or services that customers value
Why A: Hoarding resources unused earns nothing and wastes them, so it is not what a business does; businesses use inputs to produce something customers will pay for.
Why B: Burning resources for heat is not the purpose of taking them in; a business converts inputs into output it can sell, not simply consumes them as fuel.
Why C: Giving resources to competitors for nothing would destroy value and profit, and it is the opposite of how a business turns inputs into sellable products.
Why D: A business takes in inputs such as labor, materials and capital and transforms them into goods or services that customers value enough to pay for.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a limited partnership?
A: A partnership where no one is ever liable for debts of the firm
B: A partnership where some partners have limited liability
C: A partnership with no profit sharing among the partners
D: A partnership limited to two people and no one else
Why A: If no partner were ever liable for the firm's debts, that would describe a corporation style shield for everyone, whereas a limited partnership still needs at least one liable partner.
Why B: A limited partnership has at least one general partner with full liability and one or more limited partners whose liability stops at what they invested in the firm.
Why C: Profit sharing is normal in a limited partnership because partners agree how profits are divided, so a partnership with no sharing does not describe this form at all.
Why D: Limiting a partnership to two people is not what makes it limited; the word refers to limited liability for some partners, and any number of partners may join.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a general partnership?
A: A partnership where one partner is liable for debts, not the rest
B: A partnership run by the government of the state for the public
C: A partnership where all partners share management and liability
D: A partnership with shareholders who vote on every decision
Why A: In a general partnership every partner is personally liable for firm debts, not just one, so a single liable partner describes a limited partnership structure instead.
Why B: A general partnership is a private business owned by its partners, not a government body, and nothing about it involves running a state operation for the public.
Why C: In a general partnership all partners share in managing the business and all carry unlimited personal liability for its debts, which is what makes it general.
Why D: Shareholders who vote on every decision belong to a corporation; a general partnership has partners, not shareholders, and partners manage the firm directly themselves.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a partnership agreement?
A: A loan from a bank to a partner to fund the business
B: A tax form filed with the state, listing each partner's profits
C: A contract stating each partner's duties, shares and rights
D: A license to sell goods in the town, issued by the city
Why A: A loan from a bank is a financing contract between the lender and borrower; a partnership agreement is instead a contract among the partners themselves about running the firm.
Why B: A tax form listing partner profits is a filing made with the government after the year ends, while the partnership agreement is a private contract made among the partners.
Why C: A partnership agreement is a written contract that sets out each partner's duties, share of profits and losses, and rights, so disputes can be settled by its terms.
Why D: A license to sell goods in town is a permit issued by a city authority, which is a different document from the agreement signed privately among the partners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a disadvantage of a partnership?
A: It pays no taxes at all in any year on its profits or income
B: It cannot raise any money from partners or outside lenders
C: It must be run by a single person, who decides for all partners
D: Partners can disagree and may be liable for each other's acts
Why A: Partnerships do pay tax on profits through the partners' personal returns, so the claim that they pay no taxes at all in any year is false.
Why B: Partnerships can raise money from partners' contributions and from lenders, though often less than corporations can, so saying they cannot raise any money is an overstatement.
Why C: A partnership has two or more owners by definition, so being run by a single person who decides for all partners describes a sole proprietorship, not a partnership.
Why D: Partners can disagree over decisions, and in a general partnership each partner can be held liable for debts and acts of the other partners, which is a real weakness.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is double taxation?
A: Paying sales tax at two different stores on one purchase overall
B: Corporate profit taxed at the firm and again as dividends
C: Paying tax twice on a purchase made in one store or shop
D: Filing two tax returns in one year, state and federal
Why A: Paying sales tax at two stores covers two separate purchases, each taxed once, which is not double taxation; the term refers to the same income taxed twice.
Why B: Double taxation happens when a corporation pays tax on its profits and shareholders then pay tax again on the dividends received from those same after tax profits.
Why C: Paying tax twice on one purchase at one store does not happen under normal sales tax rules, and double taxation is about corporate profits and dividends instead.
Why D: Filing both state and federal returns means two different governments each tax income once, so it is not double taxation, which taxes the same corporate profit twice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an S corporation?
A: A corporation taxed through its owners' returns
B: A corporation taxed twice on its profits
C: A corporation owned by the state and run by it
D: A corporation formed to serve charities
Why A: An S corporation passes its income, losses and credits through to its owners, who report them on their personal returns, which avoids the corporate level of tax.
Why B: Double taxation describes a C corporation; an S corporation passes income to its owners to avoid taxation at the corporate level.
Why C: State ownership describes a government enterprise, whereas an S corporation is privately owned by shareholders and is defined by its special pass through tax status.
Why D: A corporation formed for charity is a nonprofit; an S corporation is a for-profit firm with a special pass-through tax status.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a board of directors?
A: The employees of a corporation who work for it daily overall
B: Customers who buy company stock in the open market
C: A bank that lends to the company and sets its rates
D: Elected leaders who oversee a corporation's management
Why A: Employees who work for the corporation each day are the staff, not the board; the board is a group chosen to oversee the top managers of the firm.
Why B: Customers who buy stock in the open market become shareholders, and only the shareholders elect the board, so customers as a group are not the board.
Why C: A bank that lends to the company is a creditor, not a board; the board of directors is elected by shareholders to guide and oversee management.
Why D: A board of directors is a group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation's management, set major goals and hire or replace the senior executives of the firm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a shareholder?
A: A supplier of raw materials to firms
B: A lender who holds the company's loans
C: An owner of shares in a corporation
D: A worker paid by the hour at a firm
Why A: A supplier of raw materials sells inputs to firms and is a vendor, while a shareholder owns a piece of the company through its shares of stock.
Why B: A lender holding the company's loans is a creditor who is owed repayment, whereas a shareholder is an owner with a claim on profits and assets.
Why C: A shareholder owns shares of stock in a corporation, which gives a share of ownership, a claim on profits through dividends, and usually a vote on key matters.
Why D: A worker paid by the hour is an employee earning wages, which does not make that person an owner; shareholders hold stock and are the owners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stakeholder?
A: Owners who invest money in the firm
B: Anyone affected by a business's decisions
C: Rivals that sell similar goods
D: Managers who run the daily work
Why A: Owners are one stakeholder group, but stakeholders include anyone affected by the firm, so this is too narrow.
Why B: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or with an interest in a business's decisions, including employees, customers, suppliers, owners and the local community around it.
Why C: Rivals can be affected, but stakeholders also include employees, customers, suppliers and communities.
Why D: Managers are stakeholders, but the term is wider and includes anyone affected by or with an interest in the firm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is vertical integration?
A: A firm owning several stages of its supply chain
B: A firm selling to many countries around the world
C: A firm splitting into smaller units over time
D: Two rivals merging at the same stage of production
Why A: Vertical integration means a firm owns several stages of its supply chain, such as supplying inputs, making the product and selling it directly to customers.
Why B: Selling to many countries is international expansion, which concerns where a firm sells, not whether it owns more than one stage of its supply chain.
Why C: A firm splitting into smaller units is a breakup or spin off, which is the reverse of integrating stages of production under one owner.
Why D: Two rivals merging at the same stage of production is horizontal integration, whereas vertical integration joins different stages of the supply chain under one owner.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is horizontal integration?
A: Selling part of the company to new outside investors
B: Merging with a competitor at the same stage of production
C: Opening a store in a new country on another continent
D: Buying a supplier of raw materials to control early steps
Why A: Selling part of the company to outside investors raises capital and changes ownership, but it does not combine firms at the same stage of production.
Why B: Horizontal integration is when a firm merges with or buys a competitor operating at the same stage of production, which raises market share and cuts duplicate costs.
Why C: Opening a store in a new country is geographic expansion, which does not involve merging with a competitor at the same stage of the supply chain.
Why D: Buying a supplier of raw materials to control early steps is vertical integration, since it moves backward along the supply chain rather than across to a competitor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a merger?
A: Two companies combining into one
B: A company paying a dividend out
C: A company closing its doors for good
D: One company splitting into two firms
Why A: A merger is when two companies agree to combine into a single new or surviving firm, usually to gain scale, share markets or reduce costs.
Why B: A company paying a dividend simply distributes part of its profit to shareholders, and nothing is combined with another company in that event.
Why C: A company closing its doors is a shutdown or liquidation, which ends the business instead of joining it with another firm as a merger does.
Why D: One company splitting into two firms is a breakup or spin off, which is the opposite of a merger, where two firms join to form one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an acquisition?
A: A firm hiring a new CEO for the job
B: A firm closing a branch in another city
C: One company buying control of another
D: Two firms agreeing to share a logo
Why A: Hiring a new CEO is a management change inside one firm and does not transfer control of the company to another firm as an acquisition does.
Why B: Closing a branch is a cost cutting or restructuring step within one company, and no other company gains control of it, so it is not an acquisition.
Why C: An acquisition occurs when one company buys enough of another to take control of it, and the target usually becomes part of the buyer or its subsidiary.
Why D: Two firms sharing a logo might be a branding or licensing deal, but neither firm buys control of the other, so it is not an acquisition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hostile takeover?
A: A strike by employees against the company's owners
B: A theft of company property by a group of staff members
C: An acquisition both sides welcome, with managers in favor
D: An acquisition the target company's management opposes
Why A: A strike by employees is a labor dispute between workers and owners and has nothing to do with another company buying control of the target.
Why B: Theft of company property by staff is a crime committed inside the firm and is unrelated to one company seeking to take over another firm.
Why C: An acquisition that both sides welcome with managers in favor is a friendly takeover, which is the opposite of a hostile one.
Why D: A hostile takeover is an acquisition that the target company's management opposes, so the buyer goes straight to shareholders or buys up shares to win control.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business plan's executive summary?
A: A list of every employee's pay
B: A legal contract with investors
C: A short overview of the whole plan
D: A full set of financial statements
Why A: A list of every employee's pay would be part of a detailed payroll or staffing section, not a short summary that introduces the whole business plan.
Why B: A legal contract with investors is a separate document, such as an investment agreement, and an executive summary is only a summary of the plan itself.
Why C: The executive summary is a short overview of the whole business plan, placed first, that gives readers the key points such as the idea, market and financial needs.
Why D: A full set of financial statements is a long, detailed section of the plan, whereas the executive summary is brief and only highlights the main financial points.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a franchisee?
A: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others overall
B: A supplier of the brand's goods and materials to outlets
C: A customer of the brand who buys its products every week
D: A person who buys the right to run a business under a brand
Why A: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others is the franchisor, not the franchisee, who is the person buying the right to use that brand.
Why B: A supplier of goods and materials sells products to outlets, which is a vendor role, while a franchisee is the person who runs a branded outlet under a license.
Why C: A customer buys the brand's products, while a franchisee is a business owner who pays for the right to operate an outlet under the brand's name and system.
Why D: A franchisee is a person or firm that buys the right to run a business under an established brand, paying fees and following the franchisor's methods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a franchisor?
A: The company that licenses its brand and system to others
B: The bank that lends to the outlet owner for startup as a rule
C: The person who runs the local outlet and pays a fee
D: The customer who buys the product from the outlet
Why A: A franchisor is the company that owns a brand and licenses its name, products and business system to franchisees, who pay fees and often royalties to use them.
Why B: A bank that lends to the outlet owner is a lender, which is a different role from the franchisor that owns the brand and licenses its system.
Why C: The person who runs the local outlet and pays a fee is the franchisee, not the franchisor, who grants the license and receives the fee.
Why D: The customer who buys the product from the outlet is a consumer, and has no role in owning or licensing the brand as a franchisor does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a royalty?
A: A fine for breaking a rule of the brand owner
B: A payment for the ongoing use of a brand or idea
C: A tax on imported goods at the border post
D: A payment for one-time labor made once a job is done
Why A: A fine for breaking a rule is a penalty for misconduct, whereas a royalty is an agreed payment for the continuing use of someone's brand or idea.
Why B: A royalty is a payment made to the owner of a brand, patent or creative work for the ongoing right to use it, often a share of sales.
Why C: A tax on imported goods at the border is a tariff or customs duty paid to the government, not a royalty paid to the owner of an idea.
Why D: A one time payment for labor after a job is done is a wage or fee, whereas a royalty keeps being paid as long as the brand or idea is used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is entrepreneurship's role in an economy?
A: Creating new businesses, jobs and ideas
B: Printing the nation's money supply
C: Setting official prices for all goods
D: Collecting income taxes from workers
Why A: Entrepreneurs start new businesses, which creates jobs, brings new products and ideas to market, and helps drive competition and growth in an economy.
Why B: Printing the nation's money supply is done by the central bank and the treasury, not by entrepreneurs, whose role is starting and growing new businesses.
Why C: Setting official prices for goods is price control by a government, while entrepreneurs operate in markets where prices come from supply and demand.
Why D: Collecting income taxes from workers is a task for tax authorities, whereas entrepreneurs create firms and jobs, which indirectly generate the income that gets taxed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which agency enforces federal rules against false advertising?
A: The Social Security Agency
B: The Federal Reserve Board
C: The Federal Trade Commission
D: The Bureau of Labor Statistics
Why A: The Social Security Agency pays retirement and disability benefits and does not police advertising claims, so it does not enforce rules against false advertising.
Why B: The Federal Reserve Board sets monetary policy and supervises banks, and it has no job enforcing federal rules against deceptive advertising by businesses.
Why C: The Federal Trade Commission enforces federal rules on unfair and deceptive practices, including false advertising, and can order firms to stop and pay penalties.
Why D: The Bureau of Labor Statistics collects data on jobs, wages and prices; it is a statistics agency with no power to enforce advertising rules.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission require of public companies?
A: Fixed prices for their products sold
B: Regular, accurate financial disclosures
C: Hiring a set number of new workers
D: A guaranteed profit each year for firms
Why A: The SEC does not set product prices, because prices come from markets, and its role is to protect investors by requiring honest information from public companies.
Why B: The SEC requires public companies to file regular, accurate financial disclosures so investors can judge the firm, and it can punish fraud and misleading reports.
Why C: The SEC does not tell companies how many workers to hire, as hiring is a management decision, and its rules focus on investor information and fair markets.
Why D: No agency can guarantee a profit each year to firms, since profit depends on market conditions, and the SEC only requires honest reporting, not results.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is deregulation?
A: Taxing an industry far more heavily than before
B: Taking over an industry entirely by the state
C: Adding more rules to an industry for stricter standards
D: Reducing government rules that apply to an industry
Why A: Taxing an industry far more heavily is a tax increase, not deregulation, which removes or relaxes government rules instead of adding financial burdens.
Why B: Taking over an industry entirely by the state is nationalization, which increases government control, whereas deregulation reduces the rules that apply to an industry.
Why C: Adding more rules for stricter standards is regulation, or re-regulation, and it is the opposite of deregulation, which reduces the rules a government imposes.
Why D: Deregulation means the government reduces or removes rules that apply to an industry, often to encourage competition, lower costs and give firms more freedom to operate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a common argument for regulating pollution?
A: Clean air is a private good for each person
B: Pollution raises company profit for everyone
C: Firms ignore costs they push onto others
D: Markets always price pollution correctly
Why A: Clean air is a public good that people share and cannot be easily excluded from, not a private good, and this is why markets alone struggle to protect it.
Why B: Pollution does not raise profit for everyone; it imposes costs on third parties, and the harm to society is the main reason regulation is argued for.
Why C: Firms often ignore the costs of pollution that fall on other people, called negative externalities, so regulation makes them account for the damage they cause.
Why D: Markets do not always price pollution correctly, because polluters do not pay for the harm to others, and this market failure is what regulation targets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A carbon tax is designed to:
A: Remove all costs from firms in the market
B: Make polluters pay for the harm they cause
C: Ban all production of energy for good
D: Reward firms that pollute with extra emissions
Why A: A carbon tax does not remove costs from firms; it adds a cost to emitting carbon so that firms have a reason to cut their emissions.
Why B: A carbon tax makes polluters pay for the harm their emissions cause, turning an outside cost into a price they must weigh, which pushes them to pollute less.
Why C: A carbon tax raises the cost of emitting carbon but does not ban energy production, and firms may keep producing if they pay the tax.
Why D: Rewarding polluters with extra emissions is the opposite of a carbon tax, which penalizes emissions by charging a tax on each unit of carbon released.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tradable pollution permit?
A: A right to emit a set amount that can be bought and sold
B: A free pass to pollute without limit whenever a firm wishes
C: A fine for emitting any pollution into the air or water
D: A ban on all emissions from any firm in the nation
Why A: A tradable pollution permit gives a firm the right to emit a set amount, and firms can buy or sell permits, so total pollution stays under a cap.
Why B: A pass to pollute without limit would defeat the purpose, since permits set a cap on emissions and each permit allows only a fixed quantity.
Why C: A fine for emitting pollution is a penalty, not a permit; a permit is an allowance to emit a set amount that can be traded between firms.
Why D: A ban on all emissions would stop production completely, whereas permits allow limited pollution under a cap and let firms trade the right to emit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a government-provided public good?
A: A designer jacket
B: A restaurant meal
C: A concert ticket
D: National defense
Why A: A designer jacket is a private good that individuals buy for themselves, and sellers can exclude those who do not pay, so it is not a public good.
Why B: A restaurant meal is a private good that only the buyer consumes, and the restaurant can refuse service to anyone who does not pay for it.
Why C: A concert ticket is a private good because only ticket holders can attend, so non payers are excluded, which means it is not a public good.
Why D: National defense is a public good that protects everyone at once; one person's protection does not reduce another's, and nobody can easily be excluded from it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might the government give a subsidy to a positive externality such as vaccination?
A: Vaccines cost nothing to make, so price them low
B: Society gains more than the buyer alone gets
C: Vaccines harm third parties in the market
D: Markets over-supply vaccines to all buyers
Why A: Vaccines cost real money to make, so the claim that they cost nothing is false; the subsidy exists because society gains from vaccination beyond what buyers get.
Why B: Vaccination gives benefits to others by reducing the spread of disease, so society gains more than the buyer alone, and a subsidy raises vaccination toward the best level.
Why C: Vaccines protect third parties by cutting disease spread, so they create benefits to others rather than harm, which is why a subsidy is used and not a tax.
Why D: Markets tend to under supply vaccines because buyers ignore the benefit to others, so a claim of over supply gets the direction of the problem backward.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main purpose of an excise tax on tobacco?
A: Lower the price for all buyers
B: Encourage smoking to raise revenue
C: Raise revenue and discourage use
D: Replace all income taxes soon
Why A: An excise tax on tobacco raises the price for buyers, not lowers it, and the goal is to discourage use while collecting revenue.
Why B: Encouraging smoking is the opposite of public health goals; the tax raises the price of tobacco so that fewer people smoke while bringing in government revenue.
Why C: An excise tax on tobacco raises revenue for the government and also raises the price of cigarettes, which discourages use, especially among price sensitive buyers and young people.
Why D: An excise tax on one product cannot replace all income taxes, since tobacco sales are far too small to fund the whole government budget.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a user fee?
A: A charge for using a government service
B: A loan from the state to a firm or person
C: A fine for breaking the law or a rule
D: A tax paid by every citizen each year
Why A: A user fee is a charge paid by those who use a particular government service, such as a park entrance fee or a toll, so users help fund it.
Why B: A loan from the state to a firm or person is credit that must be repaid, and a user fee is a charge for using a service.
Why C: A fine for breaking the law is a penalty for wrongdoing, whereas a user fee is a price for using a government service legally.
Why D: A tax paid by every citizen each year is a general tax, while a user fee is paid only by people who actually use a service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Federal Trade Commission do about mergers?
A: Forces all firms to merge into one company
B: Sets the price of merged firms' goods each year
C: Approves every merger without any review
D: Reviews those that might reduce competition
Why A: The FTC does not force firms to merge; it checks proposed mergers and can challenge those that harm competition, which is the opposite of forcing combinations.
Why B: The FTC does not set the price of merged firms' goods, because prices are set by firms in markets, and its role is to review deals for competition effects.
Why C: The FTC does review mergers and may block or set conditions on them, so saying it approves every merger without any review is plainly false.
Why D: The FTC reviews mergers that might reduce competition and can challenge or block them, so that consumers are protected from higher prices and fewer choices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What was the purpose of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
A: Set the minimum wage for all workers
B: Regulate food labels on packaged goods
C: Break up monopolies and ban price fixing
D: Create the income tax for the government
Why A: The minimum wage is set by other laws, such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the Sherman Act has nothing to do with worker pay.
Why B: Food labeling is regulated by laws such as the Food and Drug Act and later labeling laws, which came well after and differ from the Sherman Act.
Why C: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was passed to break up monopolies and ban price fixing and other practices that restrain trade and reduce competition.
Why D: The income tax was created by other laws and the Sixteenth Amendment, while the Sherman Act focused on competition and had no role in creating a tax.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patent?
A: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
B: Exclusive rights to a brand name or a logo
C: Exclusive rights to a book, song or film for life
D: A license to open a store in a town or city
Why A: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to make, use and sell an invention for a set period, commonly twenty years in the United States.
Why B: Exclusive rights to a brand name or logo are called a trademark, which is a different kind of intellectual property from a patent on an invention.
Why C: Exclusive rights to a book, song or film are called a copyright, which lasts for the author's life plus years, and it is not a patent.
Why D: A license to open a store in a town is a local business permit, whereas a patent protects an invention and has nothing to do with store openings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do patents sometimes create temporary monopolies?
A: Patents set price ceilings by law for goods
B: Only the holder may sell the invention for a time
C: Patents let any firm copy the invention at any time
D: Patents end all competition permanently in markets
Why A: Patents do not set price ceilings; they grant exclusive rights, and the holder is free to set the price, which can be high during the protected period.
Why B: A patent lets only the holder sell the invention for a set time, which gives a temporary monopoly that rewards the inventor before competitors can copy it.
Why C: If any firm could copy the invention at any time, there would be no exclusive right, so a patent does the opposite of allowing free copying.
Why D: Patents expire after a fixed term, so they cannot end competition permanently, and after expiry other firms may copy the invention and compete freely.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copyright?
A: A guarantee of a work's quality given to the buyers
B: A license to sell goods abroad for a firm or person
C: A tax on creative workers such as authors and artists
D: The legal right to control copies of an original work
Why A: A guarantee of quality is a warranty given by a seller, while a copyright protects the creator's right to control copies of an original work.
Why B: A license to sell goods abroad is an export license, which is a trade permit and has no link to protecting an original creative work.
Why C: A copyright is not a tax on creative workers; it is a legal protection that benefits authors and artists by controlling who may copy their work.
Why D: A copyright is the legal right of a creator to control the copying and distribution of an original work, such as a book, song, film or software.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act regulate?
A: Minimum wage and overtime
B: Bank deposit insurance
C: Stock market trading rules
D: Product safety labels
Why A: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the federal minimum wage and requires overtime pay, usually one and a half times pay beyond forty hours a week.
Why B: Bank deposit insurance is provided by the FDIC under banking law, and it is separate from the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers wages and hours.
Why C: Stock market trading rules come from the securities laws and the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers pay and hours of employees.
Why D: Product safety labels are covered by consumer protection laws and agencies, whereas the Fair Labor Standards Act deals with employee wages, hours and child labor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Occupational Safety and Health Act aim to do?
A: Guarantee all job promotions
B: Limit the number of workers hired
C: Set the price of insurance cover
D: Keep workplaces safe and healthy
Why A: No law can guarantee job promotions, which depend on performance and employer decisions, and the Occupational Safety and Health Act deals with workplace safety instead.
Why B: The Act does not limit how many workers a firm hires; it sets safety and health standards that apply to workplaces whatever the size of the staff.
Why C: Setting the price of insurance cover is not what the Act does; its purpose is to make workplaces safe and healthy through standards and inspections.
Why D: The Occupational Safety and Health Act aims to keep workplaces safe and healthy by setting standards, requiring employers to fix hazards, and allowing inspections by OSHA.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act require of employers?
A: Closing offices that lack ramps and lifts
B: Reasonable accommodations for qualified workers
C: Paying disabled workers more than all others
D: Hiring only workers with disabilities for openings
Why A: The Americans with Disabilities Act does not close offices lacking ramps; it requires reasonable accommodations and removal of barriers where this can be done without undue hardship.
Why B: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities, such as changes to equipment or schedules, unless it causes undue hardship.
Why C: The ADA bans discrimination and does not require paying disabled workers more than others; they must be paid on the same basis as comparable workers.
Why D: The ADA does not require hiring only workers with disabilities; it forbids discrimination against qualified people and says nothing about reserving all openings for them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a government contract?
A: A license to operate a business in a state or county for a year overall
B: A subsidy paid to households to help pay for food and housing
C: An agreement for a firm to supply goods or services to government
D: A tax form for firms that sell goods to the state each year
Why A: A license to operate a business in a state is a permit issued by authorities, which differs from a contract where a firm agrees to supply the government.
Why B: A subsidy paid to households for food and housing is a transfer payment or welfare benefit, not an agreement for a firm to supply the government.
Why C: A government contract is an agreement in which a firm supplies goods or services to the government, such as building a road or providing equipment, for a set payment.
Why D: A tax form for firms selling to the state is a filing document, while a government contract is the agreement under which the firm supplies goods or services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How do government purchases affect GDP?
A: They are a component of total spending
B: They are ignored in the GDP figures
C: They only affect imports of goods
D: They are subtracted from the GDP total
Why A: Government purchases are one component of GDP, along with consumption, investment and net exports, so they count as part of total spending on output.
Why B: Government purchases are not ignored; they are counted in GDP as the G in the expenditure formula, since the government buys goods and services too.
Why C: Government purchases affect more than imports, because they are spending on domestic output, and they directly add to GDP as one part of total spending.
Why D: Government purchases are added to GDP, not subtracted, because they are spending on newly produced goods and services, such as roads, schools and defense.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the multiplier effect of government spending?
A: Spending equals the tax collected, so the budget is balanced
B: Spending can raise total output by more than its own size
C: Spending raises output by just the amount that was spent
D: Spending crowds out private spending by the same amount
Why A: The multiplier effect is not about balancing the budget; it describes how spending is re-spent through the economy, and it does not require taxes to equal spending.
Why B: The multiplier effect means a round of government spending becomes income for others, who spend part of it again, so total output can rise by more than the original amount.
Why C: The multiplier means output rises by more than the original spending, because recipients re-spend part of what they receive.
Why D: Full crowding out is an extreme view; the multiplier effect says spending is re-spent and raises output by more than the first round.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the federal minimum wage meant to do?
A: Guarantee full employment for all
B: Cap how much any worker can earn
C: Set a floor for pay under the law
D: Replace all collective bargaining
Why A: A minimum wage cannot guarantee full employment, because it sets a pay floor but does not create jobs, and some argue it can reduce them.
Why B: The minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, so it does not cap how much a worker can earn; workers may be paid more than it.
Why C: The federal minimum wage sets a legal floor under pay, so employers covered by the law cannot pay less than that hourly amount to covered workers.
Why D: The minimum wage does not replace collective bargaining, because unions still negotiate pay and conditions above the legal floor for their members.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tariff's usual effect on domestic producers?
A: It exposes them to more foreign competition
B: It bans them from exporting goods abroad
C: It sets their prices by law for each good
D: It shields them from foreign competition
Why A: A tariff raises the price of imports, which lowers foreign competition for domestic producers, so saying it exposes them to more competition gets the effect backward.
Why B: A tariff taxes imported goods and does not restrict a country's own exports, so it does not ban domestic producers from selling goods abroad.
Why C: A tariff is a tax on imports and does not set domestic producers' prices by law, since those firms remain free to set their own prices.
Why D: A tariff raises the price of imported goods, so domestic producers face less competition from abroad, which shields them and lets them sell more or charge more.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a quota's usual effect on the price of an imported good?
A: It tends to rise
B: It becomes zero
C: It tends to fall
D: It stays pegged
Why A: A quota limits the quantity of an import, which reduces supply, and with demand unchanged the price of the imported good tends to rise.
Why B: A quota limits supply and does not make the price zero; a price of zero would mean the good is free, which cannot result from restricting quantity.
Why C: A quota cuts the supply of the imported good, and less supply with the same demand pushes the price up, not down, so falling prices is wrong.
Why D: A quota does not peg the price to a fixed level; it limits quantity, and the market price still moves, rising when supply is restricted.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is nationalization?
A: A firm selling shares to the public for the first time
B: The government taking ownership of a private industry
C: A firm merging with a competitor from abroad to cut costs
D: A firm moving to another country to avoid taxes
Why A: A firm selling shares to the public for the first time is an initial public offering, which changes ownership but does not move a private industry into government hands.
Why B: Nationalization is the government taking ownership of a private industry or firm, so that the state owns and often runs it, sometimes with compensation to owners.
Why C: A firm merging with a foreign competitor is an international merger between private companies, and the government does not take ownership of it.
Why D: A firm moving to another country is relocation, often called offshoring, and the government does not take ownership of any industry in doing so.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is privatization?
A: A firm going out of business for good this year
B: A firm hiding its profits from the tax office
C: The state taking over a private firm and running it
D: Selling government-owned assets to private owners
Why A: A firm going out of business is a closure or bankruptcy, which ends the company rather than moving government owned assets into private hands.
Why B: A firm hiding profits from the tax office is tax evasion, which is illegal, and it has no connection with selling government owned assets to private owners.
Why C: The state taking over and running a private firm is nationalization, which is the opposite of privatization, where the government sells or hands over assets.
Why D: Privatization means selling government owned assets or enterprises to private owners, which moves ownership and often operation of a business from the state to the private sector.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does real GDP adjust for?
A: Changes in tax rates paid
B: Changes in exchange rates
C: Changes in the price level
D: Changes in population size
Why A: Real GDP does not adjust for tax rates; it removes the effect of price changes so that output in different years can be compared fairly.
Why B: Exchange rates affect trade values but real GDP does not adjust for them; it adjusts for the price level using a base year's prices.
Why C: Real GDP adjusts for changes in the price level, using constant prices from a base year, so that a rise in GDP shows more output and not just higher prices.
Why D: Population size is not part of the real GDP adjustment; adjusting for population gives GDP per capita, which is a different measure from real GDP.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Nominal GDP rises 6% while prices rise 2%. About how much did real GDP grow?
Why A: An 8% figure comes from adding 6% and 2%, but inflation must be subtracted from nominal growth to find real growth, so 8% is wrong.
Why B: A 12% figure comes from multiplying 6% by 2, which has no meaning here; real growth is nominal growth minus inflation, not a product of the two.
Why C: A 2% figure is just the inflation rate and ignores the nominal growth, but real growth equals 6% minus 2%, which is more than 2%.
Why D: Real GDP growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation, so 6% minus 2% gives about 4%, showing that output rose by 4% after removing the price effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a GDP deflator?
A: A device that reduces unemployment in cities
B: A price index that covers all goods in GDP
C: A rule that caps inflation at a set level
D: A tool that lowers a firm's taxes by a set sum
Why A: A GDP deflator is not a device that reduces unemployment; it is a statistical measure of prices and has no power to change the labor market.
Why B: The GDP deflator is a price index that covers all goods and services included in GDP, and it is used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP.
Why C: A rule capping inflation at a set level would be a policy or target, but the GDP deflator is just a measure of price changes, not a rule.
Why D: A tool that lowers a firm's taxes is a tax measure, but the GDP deflator is a price index used to measure inflation across the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Consumer Price Index track?
A: Wages paid to workers in all sectors of firms
B: Prices producers get for goods sold to dealers
C: Prices of a basket of goods households buy
D: Stock market values of large firms each day
Why A: Wages paid to workers are tracked by wage and earnings data, while the Consumer Price Index follows the prices households pay for a typical basket of goods.
Why B: Prices producers receive for goods sold to dealers are tracked by the Producer Price Index, which is a different measure from the Consumer Price Index.
Why C: The Consumer Price Index tracks the prices of a basket of goods and services that households typically buy, and it is the main gauge of inflation for consumers.
Why D: Stock market values are measured by stock indexes such as the S&P 500, whereas the CPI measures the cost of goods and services households buy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The CPI was 250 last year and is 260 this year. What was the inflation rate?
Why A: Inflation is the change in CPI divided by last year's CPI, so 260 minus 250 is 10, and 10 divided by 250 gives 0.04, or 4%.
Why B: A 26% figure takes the new CPI value as a percent, but inflation is the change divided by the old CPI, which here is 10 over 250.
Why C: A 2.5% figure divides the 10 point change by 400, which is not the right base; the base should be last year's CPI of 250, giving 4%.
Why D: A 10% figure uses the 10 point change as if it were a percent, but it must be divided by the old CPI of 250 to give 4%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is core inflation useful?
A: It ignores all price changes in the economy
B: It counts only food and energy prices today
C: It predicts stock prices by removing energy
D: It leaves out volatile food and energy prices
Why A: Core inflation does not ignore all price changes; it removes only the volatile food and energy prices so that the underlying trend in other prices is easier to see.
Why B: Core inflation excludes food and energy prices instead of counting only them, so saying it counts only food and energy prices gets the definition reversed.
Why C: Core inflation is a measure of price trends, not a tool for predicting stock prices, and removing energy does not give it that purpose.
Why D: Core inflation leaves out volatile food and energy prices, which swing with weather and oil markets, so policymakers can see the underlying inflation trend more clearly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the labor force participation rate?
A: The share of jobs that are full time in the economy
B: The share of working-age people who are working or looking
C: The share of workers who are unemployed in the labor force
D: The share of workers in unions across the whole nation
Why A: The share of jobs that are full time describes job quality, not the participation rate, which looks at how many working age people are in the labor force.
Why B: The labor force participation rate is the share of working age people who are either working or actively looking for work, out of the total working age population.
Why C: The share of workers who are unemployed in the labor force is the unemployment rate, which is a different measure from the participation rate.
Why D: The share of workers in unions is the union membership rate, which tells us about labor organization and not about how many people are in the labor force.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might the unemployment rate fall even if no new jobs appear?
A: Discouraged workers leave the labor force
B: Taxes rise on all workers in the nation
C: Prices fall across the whole economy
D: More people join the labor force to seek work
Why A: If discouraged workers give up and leave the labor force, they are no longer counted as unemployed, so the unemployment rate can fall even though no new jobs appeared.
Why B: Tax increases on workers do not directly change how the unemployment rate is counted, and they would not make it fall without any new jobs appearing.
Why C: Falling prices across the economy do not by themselves reduce the share of people counted as unemployed, and no new jobs means no direct fall.
Why D: More people joining the labor force to seek work raises the number of job seekers, which tends to push the unemployment rate up, not make it fall.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the underemployment problem?
A: Workers earn more than expected, above what firms planned
B: Workers have no jobs at all in the whole economy right now
C: Workers hold jobs below their skills or hours wanted
D: Workers retire early by choice well before age sixty
Why A: Workers who earn more than expected is a positive outcome and not underemployment, which refers to people not fully using their skills or hours.
Why B: Having no jobs at all describes unemployment, while underemployment means people do have jobs but those jobs are below their skills or fewer hours than wanted.
Why C: Underemployment is when workers hold jobs below their skill level or work fewer hours than they want, so labor is not being fully used even though they have work.
Why D: Retiring early by choice is a decision to leave the labor force and does not describe workers who want more hours or better matched jobs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a leading indicator?
A: A statistic that tends to change before the economy does
B: A statistic that tends to change after the economy does
C: A statistic made up by a leader of the firm each month
D: A statistic that moves at the same time as the economy
Why A: A leading indicator is a statistic that tends to change before the economy changes, such as new housing permits, so it can help forecast turning points.
Why B: That describes a lagging indicator, such as the unemployment rate; a leading indicator changes before the economy turns.
Why C: A leading indicator is not a number made up by a firm's leader; it is a measured economic statistic whose changes tend to come before the economy's.
Why D: That describes a coincident indicator, such as industrial production; a leading indicator changes ahead of the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a coincident indicator?
A: A statistic that moves long after the economy does
B: A statistic that moves before the economy does each year
C: A statistic that moves with the economy at the same time
D: A statistic that has no timing link to the economy
Why A: A statistic that moves long after the economy does is a lagging indicator, so it is not a coincident indicator, which moves at the same time.
Why B: A statistic that moves before the economy does is a leading indicator, whereas a coincident indicator moves at the same time as the economy does.
Why C: A coincident indicator moves with the economy at the same time, such as industrial production or employment, so it shows where the economy is now.
Why D: A statistic with no timing link to the economy would not be an indicator at all, whereas a coincident indicator moves in step with the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is generally a lagging indicator?
A: Stock prices each day
B: The unemployment rate
C: New housing permits
D: Consumer confidence
Why A: Stock prices are generally a leading indicator because they tend to move before the economy changes, as investors look ahead to future profits.
Why B: The unemployment rate is generally a lagging indicator because firms hire or lay off workers only after the economy has already turned up or down.
Why C: New housing permits are generally a leading indicator because builders apply for permits before construction, which happens ahead of the economy's changes in activity.
Why D: Consumer confidence is generally a leading indicator because households that feel hopeful or worried change their spending plans before the economy itself shifts.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a rising consumer confidence index suggest?
A: Prices will fall for certain
B: Unemployment must be rising
C: Households may spend less
D: Households may spend more
Why A: Rising confidence does not guarantee that prices will fall; it signals optimism about the economy, which tends to raise spending, and that can push prices up.
Why B: Rising consumer confidence suggests households feel secure about jobs and income, so it does not point to rising unemployment, which would lower confidence instead.
Why C: When confidence rises, households feel better about the future and tend to spend more, not less, so predicting reduced spending reverses the usual relationship.
Why D: A rising consumer confidence index suggests households feel better about jobs and income, so they may spend more, which can lift demand and economic growth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Index of Leading Economic Indicators try to do?
A: Count the firms in the economy each month
B: Measure the national debt in the economy
C: Set the interest rate for the whole economy
D: Signal turning points in the business cycle
Why A: Counting the firms in the economy is a business census task and not the aim of the Index of Leading Economic Indicators, which forecasts changes in activity.
Why B: The national debt is measured by the Treasury from government borrowing records, and it is not what the Index of Leading Economic Indicators tries to measure.
Why C: Interest rates are set by the central bank and by markets, not by an index, since the Index of Leading Economic Indicators only gives forecasting signals.
Why D: The Index of Leading Economic Indicators combines several data series to signal turning points in the business cycle, such as upcoming peaks and troughs, before they occur.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the trade deficit?
A: A fall in the exchange rate level
B: Government spending above revenue
C: Imports exceeding exports in value
D: Exports exceeding imports in value
Why A: A fall in the exchange rate is a depreciation of the currency, which is different from a trade deficit, defined as imports exceeding exports.
Why B: Government spending above revenue is a budget deficit, which is a different concept from the trade deficit that compares imports with exports.
Why C: A trade deficit occurs when the value of a country's imports is greater than the value of its exports over a period, so it buys more than it sells abroad.
Why D: Exports exceeding imports in value is a trade surplus, which is the opposite of a trade deficit, where imports are the larger amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A country exports $400 billion and imports $450 billion. What is its trade balance?
A: A surplus of $50 billion
B: A deficit of $50 billion
C: A zero balance, no deficit
D: A deficit of $850 billion
Why A: A surplus needs exports to exceed imports, but here exports of 400 are below imports of 450, so the balance is negative and not a surplus.
Why B: The trade balance is exports minus imports, so 400 minus 450 equals negative 50, which is a deficit of 50 billion dollars.
Why C: A zero balance would require exports and imports to be equal, but 400 billion is not equal to 450 billion, so there is a gap of 50.
Why D: The figure 850 billion comes from adding exports and imports together, but the trade balance is found by subtracting imports from exports, which gives a deficit of 50.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the current account measure?
A: A country's trade in goods and services plus income flows
B: The number of firms in the country at a given time
C: The money in a person's checking account after bills are paid
D: The country's yearly budget for all public services
Why A: The current account measures a country's trade in goods and services plus income flows and transfers with the rest of the world, so it shows its net external position.
Why B: The number of firms in a country is a business count and has nothing to do with the current account, which tracks flows of trade and income.
Why C: Money in a person's checking account is a personal bank balance, while the current account is a national measure of trade and income flows with other countries.
Why D: A country's yearly budget for public services is a government spending plan, not the current account, which records international trade, income and transfers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recession's effect on tax revenue?
A: It stays unchanged
B: It typically falls
C: It rises sharply
D: It turns into zero
Why A: Tax revenue does not stay unchanged in a recession, because incomes and spending fall and so do income and sales tax receipts for the government.
Why B: In a recession, incomes, profits and spending fall, so the income, corporate and sales taxes collected typically fall, and this is called an automatic stabilizer effect.
Why C: A recession lowers incomes and sales, so tax revenue falls rather than rises sharply, and a sharp rise would be typical of strong growth.
Why D: Tax revenue falls in a recession but does not drop to zero, since people and firms still earn income and make purchases that are taxed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a yield curve compare?
A: Profits of different firms across the economy
B: Wages in different cities across the country
C: Interest rates on bonds with different maturities
D: Prices of different brands of the same product overall
Why A: Profits of different firms are compared in company reports, whereas a yield curve compares interest rates on bonds that differ by their time to maturity.
Why B: Wages in different cities are compared in labor market data, and a yield curve has nothing to do with wages or city differences.
Why C: A yield curve compares interest rates on bonds, usually government bonds, with different maturities, and its shape helps show what investors expect for the economy.
Why D: Prices of different brands of the same product are compared by shoppers, but a yield curve plots bond interest rates against time to maturity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an inverted yield curve often signal?
A: A coming boom in output and sales
B: An end to inflation as prices stop rising
C: No change in the economy for years
D: A higher chance of a coming recession
Why A: A coming boom is typically linked to a normal upward sloping yield curve, whereas an inverted curve has often come before slowdowns and not before booms.
Why B: An inverted curve does not mean inflation is ending; it means short term rates are above long term rates, which has often come before a recession.
Why C: An inverted yield curve points to a possible change in the economy, because short term rates exceed long term rates, so it does not signal years of no change.
Why D: An inverted yield curve, with short term rates above long term rates, has often come before recessions, so it signals a higher chance of a coming recession.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the personal savings rate?
A: The share of disposable income that households save
B: The share of spending on housing and food each year
C: The share of income paid in taxes each year to the state
D: The interest rate on savings accounts at banks
Why A: The personal savings rate is the share of disposable income that households save instead of spend, which shows how much of their income they set aside.
Why B: The share of spending on housing and food describes a spending pattern, whereas the savings rate measures the part of disposable income that is saved.
Why C: The share of income paid in taxes is the tax rate, but the personal savings rate looks at what households keep after taxes and do not spend.
Why D: The interest rate on savings accounts is what banks pay depositors, which is different from the savings rate, the share of income households save.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is retail sales data used to show?
A: How many stores close each year in the nation
B: How many workers stores hire each year
C: How much stores pay in rent each month
D: How much consumers are spending at stores
Why A: Store closings are tracked in business closure data, but retail sales data measures the dollar value of what consumers spend at stores.
Why B: How many workers stores hire is employment data, while retail sales data measures the spending that consumers do at stores.
Why C: Rent paid by stores is a cost of business, and retail sales data tracks revenue from consumer purchases, not stores' costs.
Why D: Retail sales data shows how much consumers are spending at stores, which is a key sign of consumer demand and so of the strength of the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) gauge?
A: The average wage of workers across the nation
B: The number of banks in the whole country today
C: The health of manufacturing and service activity
D: The price of homes in the whole country, on average
Why A: The average wage of workers is measured in earnings data, while the PMI is a survey based index on business activity in manufacturing and services.
Why B: The number of banks in a country is a count from banking regulators, and it is not what the Purchasing Managers' Index is designed to gauge.
Why C: The PMI is based on surveys of purchasing managers and gauges the health of manufacturing and service activity, with a reading above 50 showing expansion.
Why D: The price of homes is measured by house price indexes, whereas the PMI gauges business activity in manufacturing and services based on manager surveys.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between a tariff and a quota?
A: A tariff limits imports while a quota taxes them instead
B: A tariff taxes imports; a quota limits their amount
C: Both mean the same thing in the law of trade and tariffs
D: Both pay exporters directly in cash each year of trade
Why A: This reverses the definitions, because a tariff is a tax on imports and a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports.
Why B: A tariff is a tax placed on imports, which raises their price, while a quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported.
Why C: The two are not the same, since a tariff raises government revenue through a tax and a quota caps quantities, so their effects differ.
Why D: Neither tariffs nor quotas pay exporters in cash; both restrict imports, and a payment to exporters would instead describe an export subsidy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an export subsidy?
A: Government support that makes exports cheaper abroad
B: A fine for exporters who break the trade rules
C: A ban on exports of all goods and services abroad overall
D: A tax on exports of all goods and services abroad
Why A: An export subsidy is government support, such as payments or tax breaks, that lowers the cost of exports, so the goods can be sold cheaper in foreign markets.
Why B: A fine for exporters who break trade rules is a penalty for violations, while an export subsidy is a support payment that helps exporters.
Why C: A ban on exports of all goods is an export embargo, which stops exporting, whereas an export subsidy encourages more exporting by cutting the cost.
Why D: A tax on exports is an export duty, which makes exports more costly, whereas an export subsidy lowers the cost and so is the opposite.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do economists often oppose export subsidies?
A: They lower prices at home and help all
B: They always raise efficiency in trade
C: They remove all trade barriers for good
D: They distort trade and cost taxpayers
Why A: Export subsidies lower prices for foreign buyers, not for people at home, and taxpayers pay for them, so the claim that they help all is wrong.
Why B: Export subsidies do not always raise efficiency, because they push production toward goods that may not be made at lowest cost, so the word always is wrong.
Why C: Export subsidies add a distortion to trade and do not remove barriers, so they do not lead to freer trade and may invite retaliation.
Why D: Economists oppose export subsidies because they distort trade by artificially lowering export prices, and taxpayers must fund them, which wastes resources and can harm other countries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main benefit of comparative advantage?
A: Countries gain by trading what they produce at lower opportunity cost
B: Countries gain by selling more than they buy from abroad
C: Countries gain by making the goods that they use most
D: Countries gain by taxing imports to shield domestic firms from rivals
