Why C: The price in dollars changes with the exchange rate, so it cannot stay at $110 per euro after the euro rises to $1.20, making the item cost $120.
Why D: The item does not become worthless, since it still sells in Europe and in dollar terms the price merely rises from $110 to $120 as the euro strengthens.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is purchasing power parity?
A: The idea that exchange rates adjust so identical goods cost the same across countries
B: A tax on imports that is added to the price of goods from other countries at the border
C: A trade deficit that arises when a country buys more than it sells abroad each year
D: A trade bloc in which member countries agree to lower their tariffs on each other
Why A: Purchasing power parity says exchange rates adjust until identical goods cost the same across countries, so currency values reflect relative price levels over the long run.
Why B: A tax on imports at the border is a tariff, which is a trade policy tool and not purchasing power parity, which links exchange rates to relative prices.
Why C: A trade deficit arises when a country imports more than it exports, which is a balance of trade concept and differs from purchasing power parity.
Why D: A trade bloc with lower mutual tariffs is a free trade area or customs union, which differs from purchasing power parity, a theory linking exchange rates to price levels.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Under the Big Mac Index idea, a burger costs $5 in the U.S. and 400 yen in Japan. What exchange rate would equalize prices?
A: 80 yen per dollar
B: 5 yen per dollar
C: 2,000 yen per dollar
D: 400 yen per dollar
Why A: For prices to be equal, 400 yen must equal $5, so one dollar buys 400 divided by 5, which is 80 yen, making 80 yen per dollar the equalizing rate.
Why B: An exchange rate of 5 yen per dollar would make the $5 burger cost only 25 yen, far below the 400 yen price in Japan, so prices would not be equal.
Why C: At 2,000 yen per dollar the $5 burger would cost 10,000 yen, much more than the 400 yen Japanese price, so this rate does not equalize the burgers.
Why D: At 400 yen per dollar the $5 burger would cost 2,000 yen, which is five times the 400 yen price in Japan, so the rate would not equalize prices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a capital account?
A: A trade permit issued to firms that export goods abroad
B: A tax account kept by the revenue agency for each firm
C: A bank account in a capital city, held by a firm that trades overall
D: The part of the balance of payments tracking investment flows
Why A: A trade permit for exporters is a license, not a capital account, which records cross border financial flows such as investment, loans and purchases of assets.
Why B: A tax account held by a revenue agency is an administrative record and has no link to the capital account in the balance of payments.
Why C: A bank account in a capital city is just a deposit account in a place, whereas the capital account is a balance of payments category and not a bank account.
Why D: The capital account is the part of the balance of payments that tracks investment flows, such as foreign investment and financial transfers, between a country and the rest of the world.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is trade diversion in a customs union?
A: Increasing trade with everyone around the world by cutting taxes and fees on goods and services
B: Shifting imports from a lower-cost outside country to a higher-cost member country because of tariffs
C: Replacing higher-cost domestic production with cheaper imports from a partner inside the union
D: Raising tariffs on goods traded between member countries to protect local producers
Why A: Increasing trade with everyone by cutting taxes describes general trade creation or liberalization, not trade diversion, which shifts imports toward member countries inside the union.
Why B: Trade diversion occurs when a customs union's common tariff shifts imports from a cheaper outside country to a higher cost member, so efficiency falls and consumers may lose.
Why C: That describes trade creation, which improves efficiency; trade diversion shifts imports from a cheaper outside country to a costlier member.
Why D: A customs union removes tariffs among members; trade diversion happens because of the common external tariff against outsiders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A strong dollar generally makes U.S. exporters:
A: Unaffected, because exchange rates never change what foreign buyers pay  for goods
B: More competitive, because their goods cost less in foreign currency
C: Less competitive abroad because their goods cost more in foreign currency
D: Tax free, because exports are exempt from all foreign import duties
Why A: Exchange rates matter greatly to foreign buyers, since a stronger dollar raises the foreign currency price of U.S. goods, so exporters are affected and not unaffected.
Why B: A strong dollar makes U.S. goods cost more in foreign currency, not less, so exporters become less competitive, and this option gets the direction of the effect wrong.
Why C: A strong dollar means each dollar buys more foreign currency, so U.S. goods cost more abroad, which reduces foreign demand and makes exporters less competitive.
Why D: Exports are not tax free because of a strong dollar, and foreign countries may charge import duties on them, which is unrelated to the exchange rate's effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a currency peg?
A: A free-floating rate that moves with the market
B: A fixed exchange rate tied to another currency
C: A tax on money held in banks and other places
D: A coin design chosen by the central bank
Why A: A free floating rate moves with the market, which is the opposite of a peg, since a peg fixes the exchange rate to another currency rather than letting it move.
Why B: A currency peg is a fixed exchange rate tied to another currency, such as a country's money set at a stated rate to the dollar, and the central bank defends it.
Why C: A tax on money held in banks is a levy on deposits and is not a peg, which concerns the exchange rate between currencies and not a tax.
Why D: A coin design is about the look of money and has no link to exchange rate policy, whereas a currency peg fixes the exchange rate to another currency.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does devaluation do to a country's exports?
A: Makes them dearer abroad
B: Has no effect on exports
C: Bans them from sale abroad
D: Makes them cheaper abroad
Why A: Devaluation lowers the currency's value, so exports become cheaper for foreign buyers rather than dearer, which means this option has the effect reversed.
Why B: Devaluation does affect exports, because a weaker currency lowers their price in foreign currency and tends to raise foreign demand, so there is a clear effect.
Why C: Devaluation does not ban exports from being sold abroad, and instead it makes them cheaper in foreign currency, which usually increases sales to foreign buyers.
Why D: Devaluation lowers a currency's value, so each unit of foreign currency buys more of it, making a country's exports cheaper abroad and typically raising the quantity sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A country devalues its currency to boost exports. A risk of this policy is:
A: Banning imports from abroad for good
B: Zero effect on import prices at home
C: Higher import prices and inflation
D: Lower import prices and deflation
Why A: Devaluation does not ban imports, and imports continue but at higher prices in home currency, so banning them for good is not a risk of devaluing.
Why B: Devaluation does change import prices, because a weaker home currency makes foreign goods cost more at home, so zero effect on import prices is wrong.
Why C: A weaker currency makes imports cost more in home currency, which can raise the general price level, so the risk of devaluation is higher import prices and inflation.
Why D: Devaluation raises, not lowers, the home currency price of imports, so it tends to cause inflation rather than deflation, which makes this option the reverse of the truth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A country's nominal GDP is $2,200 billion and the GDP deflator is 110 (base 100). What is real GDP?
A: $2,000 billion
B: $2,090 billion
C: $110 billion
D: $2,420 billion
Why A: Real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the deflator over 100, so 2,200 divided by 1.10 is $2,000 billion, which removes the effect of price increases.
Why B: The figure of $2,090 billion results from subtracting 5 percent of nominal GDP, but the right method divides 2,200 by 1.10, which gives exactly $2,000 billion.
Why C: An answer of $110 billion just repeats the deflator as if it were output, but real GDP is 2,200 divided by 1.10, or $2,000 billion.
Why D: Multiplying 2,200 by 1.10 gives $2,420 billion, but that inflates the figure, and real GDP divides nominal GDP by the deflator, giving $2,000 billion.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: GDP was $800 billion last year and $840 billion this year with no price change. What is the growth rate?
Why A: A 40% growth rate would need GDP to rise by $320 billion, but the rise is only $40 billion, and 40 divided by 800 is 5 percent.
Why B: A 16% rate would need GDP to rise by $128 billion, but it rose by $40 billion, and 40 divided by 800 gives 5 percent, not 16.
Why C: A 4% rate would require a rise of $32 billion on 800, but GDP rose by $40 billion, and 40 divided by 800 equals 5 percent.
Why D: Growth equals the change divided by the starting value, so 840 minus 800 is 40, and 40 divided by 800 equals 0.05, which is 5 percent real growth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Consumption is $600, investment $150, government $200, exports $90 and imports $110. What is GDP?
Why A: GDP equals C plus I plus G plus net exports, so 600 plus 150 plus 200 plus 90 minus 110 gives 930, since net exports are minus 20.
Why B: The figure of $1,040 adds imports to the total instead of subtracting them, but GDP counts net exports, which are exports minus imports, so the right total is $930.
Why C: An answer of $900 leaves out the balance of trade, but net exports of minus 20 must be added to 950, giving the correct total of $930.
Why D: The figure of $1,150 adds both exports and imports to spending, but imports must be subtracted from GDP, and the right sum is 950 minus 20, which is $930.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is net exports?
A: Exports plus imports
B: Exports minus imports
C: Taxes minus spending
D: Imports minus exports
Why A: Exports plus imports is the total volume of trade, and it does not measure the balance, so it is not net exports, which subtract imports from exports.
Why B: Net exports equals exports minus imports, showing the trade balance, and a positive value is a surplus while a negative value is a deficit.
Why C: Taxes minus spending is a government budget balance, which concerns fiscal policy and not net exports, which compare sales abroad with purchases from abroad.
Why D: Imports minus exports reverses the formula and gives the trade deficit as a positive number, whereas net exports are defined as exports minus imports.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the inflation rate formula?
A: Old price index divided by the new price index, as a percent
B: New price index plus old price index, all divided by two years in general
C: (New price index minus old price index) divided by old price index
D: New price index times old price index, divided by the year
Why A: Dividing the old price index by the new one gives a ratio below one when prices rise, and it does not measure the change, so it is not the inflation rate.
Why B: Adding the new and old indexes and dividing by two gives an average of the two, which is not a rate of change, so it cannot measure inflation.
Why C: Inflation is the percentage change in the price index, found as the new index minus the old index, divided by the old index, then multiplied by 100.
Why D: Multiplying the two indexes and dividing by the year has no meaning as a rate of change, so it cannot be the inflation formula, which uses the difference over the old value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The CPI rises from 240 to 252. What is the inflation rate?
Why A: An answer of 4.8% comes from dividing the change of 12 by 252, the new index, but inflation divides by the old index of 240, giving 5 percent.
Why B: A rate of 12% just reports the change in index points, which is 12, but inflation divides that change by the old index of 240, giving 5 percent.
Why C: A rate of 50% is far too high, since the index rose only from 240 to 252, and 12 divided by 240 gives 0.05, which is 5 percent.
Why D: Inflation equals the change divided by the old index, so 252 minus 240 is 12, and 12 divided by 240 equals 0.05, or 5 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker earns $50,000 and the CPI rises from 200 to 210. What salary keeps the same purchasing power?
Why A: Keeping purchasing power means scaling pay by the CPI ratio, so 50,000 times 210 divided by 200 gives $52,500, which is a 5 percent raise.
Why B: A salary of $55,000 is a 10 percent raise, but prices rose only 5 percent, since the CPI moved from 200 to 210, so the right salary is $52,500.
Why C: A salary of $50,500 is only a 1 percent raise, which falls short of the 5 percent price increase, so purchasing power would drop below its earlier level.
Why D: A salary of $51,000 is a 2 percent raise, less than the 5 percent price rise from 200 to 210, so the worker would still lose purchasing power.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the unemployment rate exclude?
A: People who are unemployed and looking for work during the past four weeks
B: Part-time workers who want more hours but cannot find any extra work at all every time
C: People not in the labor force, such as discouraged workers who stopped looking
D: Employed workers who hold a full-time job at a firm that pays their wages
Why A: People who are unemployed and looking for work are counted as unemployed, so the rate includes them rather than excluding them, which makes this option wrong.
Why B: Part time workers who want more hours are counted as employed, so this group is not excluded in the headline unemployment rate, though broader measures include them.
Why C: The unemployment rate leaves out people not in the labor force, such as discouraged workers who stopped looking, so they are not counted as unemployed even without jobs.
Why D: Employed full time workers are part of the labor force and are counted as employed, so they are in the denominator and are not excluded from the rate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Population 16+ is 1,000, labor force is 650 and unemployed are 52. What is the unemployment rate?
Why A: A figure of 52% would treat the 52 unemployed as if they were a share of 100, but the rate divides 52 by the labor force of 650, giving 8 percent.
Why B: The unemployment rate equals the unemployed divided by the labor force, so 52 divided by 650 equals 0.08, which is 8 percent of the labor force.
Why C: A rate of 5.2% divides 52 by the population of 1,000, but the rate uses the labor force of 650 as the base, and 52 over 650 is 8 percent.
Why D: A figure of 65% is the participation rate, which is 650 divided by 1,000, and not the unemployment rate, which is 52 divided by 650, or 8 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Using the same figures (population 1,000; labor force 650), what is the labor force participation rate?
Why A: A figure of 52% does not use the labor force figure of 650, and participation equals the labor force divided by the population, which is 650 over 1,000, or 65 percent.
Why B: A figure of 35% is the share of the population outside the labor force, which is 350 over 1,000, but the participation rate is the 650 who are in it.
Why C: A figure of 8% is the unemployment rate, found from 52 divided by 650, and not participation, which compares the labor force of 650 with the population of 1,000.
Why D: Participation equals the labor force divided by the population aged 16 and over, so 650 divided by 1,000 gives 0.65, or 65 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Gini coefficient?
A: A measure of income inequality from 0 (equal) to 1 (most unequal)
B: A measure of GDP growth over time in a country or a region
C: A measure of trade between countries over time in a given year
D: A measure of inflation across prices of goods and services in a country
Why A: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale from 0, where everyone has equal income, to 1, where one person holds all income, so a higher value means more inequality.
Why B: GDP growth over time is measured by the percentage change in output, which is not the Gini coefficient, a number that summarizes how unevenly income is distributed.
Why C: Trade between countries is measured by exports, imports and the balance, none of which is the Gini coefficient, which describes inequality within a population.
Why D: Inflation is measured with price indexes such as the CPI, and the Gini coefficient does not track prices, since it measures how unequal incomes are.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Lorenz curve show?
A: The exchange rate between two currencies over a period of several months in the end
B: The cumulative share of income held by cumulative shares of the population
C: The rate of inflation in an economy over the course of a full year
D: The price of oil per barrel across the markets of the world today
Why A: An exchange rate between two currencies is a price, and the Lorenz curve is not about currencies, as it plots how income is distributed across a population.
Why B: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income held by cumulative shares of the population, and its distance from the line of equality shows inequality.
Why C: Inflation is the rate of price increase, and the Lorenz curve does not track prices, because it shows income distribution across households and not changes over time.
Why D: The price of oil is a commodity price, and it is not the subject of the Lorenz curve, which graphs the cumulative share of income against the population.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If the Lorenz curve is far below the line of equality, income distribution is:
A: Perfectly equal
B: Irrelevant
C: Highly unequal
D: Impossible
Why A: Perfect equality would put the Lorenz curve right on the line of equality, so a curve far below the line cannot mean income is perfectly equal.
Why B: The shape of the Lorenz curve is highly relevant, since it is the standard picture of how unequal incomes are, so calling it irrelevant is wrong.
Why C: A Lorenz curve far below the line of equality means the poorer groups hold a small share of income, so distribution is highly unequal and the Gini value is high.
Why D: A Lorenz curve far below the line is a real, observable outcome in many countries, so calling the distribution impossible is wrong, and it shows high inequality.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the poverty line used for?
A: Measuring how unevenly income is divided across households in a nation
B: Identifying households with income below a level needed for basic needs
C: Calculating the average price of a basket of consumer goods
D: Setting tax rates for households using a single rate for everyone in the nation
Why A: That describes inequality measures such as the Gini index; the poverty line is an income threshold for basic needs.
Why B: The poverty line is an income level needed for basic needs, and it is used to identify households whose income falls below it and so may qualify for aid.
Why C: That describes the consumer price index; the poverty line is an income threshold used to identify households in poverty.
Why D: Tax rates are set by law and vary with income, so the poverty line is not used to set a single rate for everyone, since it is an income threshold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The reserve requirement is 10%. A bank receives a $1,000 deposit. What is the maximum amount it can lend?
Why A: Lending $10,000 from a $1,000 deposit would be ten times the deposit, which no bank can do, since it must hold back reserves and can lend only $900.
Why B: A bank cannot lend the full $1,000, because a 10 percent reserve requirement means it must hold $100 back, so only the other $900 can be lent.
Why C: With a 10% reserve requirement the bank holds $100 in reserve, 10 percent of $1,000, and may lend the remaining $900 out to borrowers.
Why D: A figure of $100 is the required reserve, which is 10 percent of the deposit, and not the amount that can be lent, which is the other $900.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: With a 10% reserve requirement, what is the simple money multiplier?
Why A: The simple money multiplier equals one divided by the reserve ratio, so 1 divided by 0.10 equals 10, meaning each dollar of reserves can support ten dollars of deposits.
Why B: A multiplier of 100 would need a reserve ratio of 1 percent, but the requirement here is 10 percent, so one divided by 0.10 gives 10, not 100.
Why C: A value of 0.1 is the reserve ratio itself, and the multiplier is its inverse, so one divided by 0.1 gives 10, not 0.1.
Why D: A multiplier of 1 would mean a 100 percent reserve requirement with no lending, but at 10 percent the multiplier is 1 divided by 0.10, which is 10.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: With a 20% reserve requirement, a new $5,000 deposit could expand the money supply by up to:
Why A: A figure of $4,000 is the 80 percent that can be lent in the first round, but total expansion is the deposit times the multiplier, which is much larger.
Why B: An amount of $100,000 would need a multiplier of 20, which implies a 5 percent reserve ratio, but a 20 percent requirement gives a multiplier of 5.
Why C: An amount of $1,000 is the required reserve, which is 20 percent of $5,000, and not the potential expansion, which is the deposit times the multiplier of 5.
Why D: The multiplier is 1 divided by 0.20, which is 5, so a $5,000 deposit could expand the money supply by up to 5 times 5,000, which is $25,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fractional reserve banking?
A: Banks keep only a portion of deposits in reserve and lend out the rest
B: Banks hold all deposits and make no loans to anyone in the economy in practice
C: Banks lend nothing at all to firms or households in the nation
D: Banks destroy money whenever they accept a deposit from a customer
Why A: Fractional reserve banking means banks keep only a portion of deposits in reserve and lend out the rest, which lets the banking system expand the money supply.
Why B: Fractional reserve banks hold only part of deposits, and they do lend, so a bank holding all deposits and making no loans is full reserve banking instead.
Why C: Banks do lend to firms and households under fractional reserve banking, and that lending is how they earn interest, so saying they lend nothing is false.
Why D: Banks do not destroy money when they accept deposits, and instead lending out part of each deposit helps create more money in the system, which is the opposite effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bank run?
A: A promotion where a bank offers a gift for each new loan that is signed by a customer
B: A race held by bankers to see who can open the most new accounts in a month and win a prize in general
C: A situation where many depositors withdraw funds at once because they fear the bank will fail
D: A deposit drive that banks hold each spring to attract new savers and new retail customers
Why A: A gift promotion for new loans is a marketing campaign and has nothing to do with a bank run, which is a panic where depositors rush to take out money.
Why B: A race among bankers to open accounts is a sales contest, not a bank run, which is a rush by depositors to withdraw money from a bank.
Why C: A bank run happens when many depositors withdraw funds at once because they fear the bank will fail, and since banks lend most deposits, they may run out of cash.
Why D: A deposit drive attracts new savers to a bank, which is the opposite of a bank run, where customers rush to withdraw their money out of fear.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the FDIC do to reduce bank runs?
A: Closes all banks that are in trouble in the whole nation
B: Prints money for banks that run short of cash on hand
C: Sets interest rates on loans that banks make to firms
D: Insures deposits so depositors need not rush to withdraw
Why A: The FDIC does not close all troubled banks across the nation, and it insures deposits and handles failed banks in an orderly way to prevent panic.
Why B: Printing money is done by the Treasury and the central bank, and the FDIC does not print money for banks, since its role is deposit insurance.
Why C: Interest rates on loans are set by banks and markets, with the central bank steering policy rates, so the FDIC does not set them, as its role is insurance.
Why D: The FDIC insures deposits up to a limit, so depositors know their money is safe even if the bank fails and have no reason to rush to withdraw it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is quantitative easing?
A: Banning bank loans so that spending in the economy slows down quickly
B: A central bank buying large amounts of assets to lower long-term rates
C: Raising taxes on households so that the government can pay down its debt
D: Cutting spending on public programs so the federal budget is balanced
Why A: Banning bank loans would shrink credit and slow spending, but quantitative easing does the opposite, as the central bank buys assets to ease credit and boost the economy.
Why B: Quantitative easing is when a central bank buys large amounts of assets, such as bonds, to lower long term interest rates and encourage borrowing and spending.
Why C: Raising taxes to pay down debt is a fiscal policy of the government, but quantitative easing is a monetary policy action carried out by the central bank.
Why D: Cutting public programs to balance the budget is fiscal austerity, which differs from quantitative easing, a central bank policy of buying assets to lower long term rates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: To fight high inflation, the Fed would most likely:
A: Raise the federal funds rate
B: Lower the federal funds rate
C: Buy large amounts of bonds
D: Cut the reserve requirement
Why A: To fight high inflation the Fed would raise the federal funds rate, which makes borrowing costlier, slows spending and demand, and so helps bring price increases down.
Why B: Lowering the federal funds rate would make borrowing cheaper and boost spending, which would add to inflation instead of reducing it, so it fits a recession.
Why C: Buying large amounts of bonds adds money and lowers rates, which stimulates demand and could worsen inflation, so it is a tool for fighting weak growth instead.
Why D: Cutting the reserve requirement lets banks lend more, which expands the money supply and could push prices higher, so it would not be used to fight high inflation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the relationship between bond prices and interest rates?
A: They are unrelated to each other
B: They stay fixed until bonds mature
C: They move in opposite directions
D: They rise and fall together
Why A: Bond prices and interest rates are linked, because a bond's fixed payments are worth less when new bonds pay higher rates, so they are not unrelated.
Why B: Bond prices change daily in the market; they respond to interest rate changes rather than staying fixed until maturity.
Why C: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions, since when rates rise existing bonds with lower fixed payments lose value and their prices fall.
Why D: When interest rates rise, existing bonds with lower payments lose value, so the two move in opposite directions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bond pays 3% while new bonds pay 5%. What happens to the older bond's price?
A: No change
B: It falls
C: It is zero
D: It rises
Why A: The older bond pays 3 percent while new bonds pay 5 percent, so buyers would not pay full price for it, and its price cannot stay unchanged.
Why B: Because new bonds pay 5 percent and the older bond pays only 3 percent, buyers demand a discount, so the older bond's price falls until its yield is competitive.
Why C: The older bond still pays interest and has a maturity value, so its price is not zero, and it only trades at a discount to remain competitive.
Why D: A price rise would happen if rates fell below 3 percent, but new bonds pay a higher 5 percent, so the older bond becomes less attractive and its price falls.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the real interest rate?
A: The tax rate on all income earned by firms
B: The nominal rate plus inflation, the full cost
C: The inflation rate only, with nothing else
D: The nominal rate minus the inflation rate
Why A: The tax rate on firm income is a separate idea, and the real interest rate is a measure of borrowing cost after adjusting for inflation, not a tax.
Why B: Adding inflation to the nominal rate would overstate the return, since the real rate subtracts inflation, so this formula has the sign backwards.
Why C: The inflation rate alone is the rise in prices, and it ignores the nominal interest rate, so it cannot be the real interest rate on its own.
Why D: The real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus the inflation rate, showing the true return on lending or cost of borrowing after the loss of purchasing power.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A loan has a 7% nominal rate and inflation is 3%. What is the real interest rate?
Why A: A figure of 21% multiplies the 7 percent and 3 percent together, but the real rate is found by subtracting inflation from the nominal rate, which gives 4 percent.
Why B: A figure of 3% just repeats the inflation rate, but the real rate is the 7 percent nominal rate minus 3 percent inflation, which equals 4 percent.
Why C: The real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus inflation, so 7 percent minus 3 percent gives 4 percent, the true return after the loss of purchasing power.
Why D: A figure of 10% adds inflation to the nominal rate, but the real rate subtracts it, so 7 percent minus 3 percent is 4 percent, not 10 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.8. What is the spending multiplier?
Why A: A multiplier of 0.2 is the marginal propensity to save, which equals 1 minus 0.8, and not the spending multiplier, which is one divided by that number.
Why B: The spending multiplier equals 1 divided by (1 minus MPC), so 1 divided by 0.2 equals 5, meaning each extra dollar of spending raises output by up to five dollars.
Why C: A value of 1.25 is 1 divided by 0.8, which uses the MPC instead of the marginal propensity to save, and the correct divisor is 0.2, giving 5.
Why D: A value of 0.8 is the marginal propensity to consume itself and not the multiplier, which is 1 divided by 1 minus 0.8, so it equals 5.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: With a multiplier of 4, an increase of $50 billion in government spending raises total output by up to:
A: $12.5 billion
B: $54 billion
C: $50 billion
D: $200 billion
Why A: A figure of $12.5 billion divides $50 billion by the multiplier of 4, but the multiplier works the other way, so the increase must be multiplied by 4.
Why B: A figure of $54 billion adds 4 to $50 billion, but a multiplier scales the change by multiplication, so the effect is 4 times $50 billion, which is $200 billion.
Why C: A rise of only $50 billion would mean a multiplier of 1, but the given multiplier of 4 magnifies the initial spending, so output rises by $200 billion.
Why D: The change in output equals the multiplier times the change in spending, so 4 times $50 billion gives up to $200 billion of added output.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the marginal propensity to save?
A: The share of additional income that is saved
B: The share that is spent on goods and services
C: The share that is taxed by the state and nation
D: The share that is lent out to borrowers
Why A: The marginal propensity to save is the share of additional income that is saved, and it equals 1 minus the marginal propensity to consume.
Why B: The share of extra income spent on goods and services is the marginal propensity to consume, which is the counterpart of saving, not the saving share itself.
Why C: The share of extra income paid in taxes is the marginal tax rate, which is a different measure from the marginal propensity to save.
Why D: Lending out income to borrowers is not what the marginal propensity to save measures, since it is the share of extra income that is saved and not spent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is aggregate demand?
A: Demand for one product in a single market during a given year of trade in general
B: Supply of labor offered by workers at each wage rate in a market
C: The total demand for goods and services in an economy at each price level
D: The money supply held by banks and the central bank at a given time
Why A: Demand for one product in one market is ordinary market demand, whereas aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in the whole economy.
Why B: The supply of labor is a factor market concept showing how many hours workers offer at each wage, which differs from aggregate demand for output.
Why C: Aggregate demand is the total demand for goods and services in an economy at each price level, made up of consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.
Why D: The money supply is the amount of money held in the economy, which is a separate concept from aggregate demand, the total spending on goods and services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is aggregate supply?
A: The total output firms are willing to produce at each price level
B: The tax base of the nation, which is the total of taxable incomes
C: The trade balance of the country, which is exports less imports
D: Demand for money held by households and by firms at any time
Why A: Aggregate supply is the total output firms are willing to produce at each price level, and it reflects production costs, technology and the resources available in the economy.
Why B: The tax base is the total of taxable incomes, which is a fiscal concept, and it differs from aggregate supply, the total output firms will supply.
Why C: The trade balance is exports less imports, which is a different concept from aggregate supply, which shows how much firms will produce at each price level.
Why D: Demand for money is the amount that households and firms want to hold, which is a monetary concept and not aggregate supply, the output firms will produce.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A surge in oil prices raises production costs across the economy. What happens to short-run aggregate supply?
A: It does not shift at all in this case of rising costs
B: It shifts right, lowering prices and raising output
C: It becomes vertical, so output stays fixed at any price
D: It shifts left, raising prices and lowering output
Why A: Higher oil prices raise costs for firms across the economy, so short run aggregate supply cannot stay put, and it shifts as costs change.
Why B: A rightward shift would mean firms produce more at each price, but higher costs cut output and raise prices, so the shift is to the left, not right.
Why C: Short run aggregate supply does not become vertical when oil prices jump, and it simply shifts left, as higher costs reduce output at each price level.
Why D: A surge in oil prices raises production costs, so firms supply less at each price level, shifting short run aggregate supply left, which raises prices and lowers output.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An increase in consumer confidence raises spending. What happens to aggregate demand?
A: It shifts left
B: It shifts right
C: It becomes zero
D: It is unchanged
Why A: A leftward shift would mean less spending at each price level, but greater consumer confidence raises spending, so aggregate demand moves the other way.
Why B: More consumer confidence raises consumption at every price level, so aggregate demand shifts right, which tends to increase output and push the price level up.
Why C: Aggregate demand does not fall to zero when confidence rises, since higher confidence raises spending, and demand only moves to the right.
Why D: Aggregate demand does change when consumer confidence rises, because consumption is a component of it, so it shifts right and does not stay unchanged.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is potential GDP?
A: Output in a recession, when firms cut back their production
B: The output an economy can produce at full employment of resources
C: Last year's output, which has already been produced and sold in this case
D: Government spending on goods and services in a given year
Why A: Output in a recession is below potential, and potential GDP refers instead to what the economy can produce when its resources are fully employed.
Why B: Potential GDP is the output an economy can produce at full employment of its resources, using its available labor, capital and technology without causing rising inflation.
Why C: Last year's output is past actual GDP and may differ from potential GDP, which is what the economy could produce at full employment this year.
Why D: Government spending is one component of GDP and is not potential GDP, which measures the full employment level of output for the whole economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recessionary gap?
A: High inflation across the economy
B: No unemployment in the whole economy
C: Actual output below potential output
D: Actual output above potential output
Why A: High inflation tends to appear when output is above potential in an inflationary gap, so it does not describe a recessionary gap, where output is below potential.
Why B: A recessionary gap tends to involve high unemployment, so claiming that there is no unemployment in the economy contradicts what such a gap means.
Why C: A recessionary gap exists when actual output is below potential output, so resources such as labor are underused and unemployment is above its natural level.
Why D: Actual output above potential output is an inflationary gap, which pushes up prices, and it is the opposite of a recessionary gap.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Output is below potential and unemployment is high. Which policy fits?
A: Expansionary policy such as tax cuts or more spending
B: Contractionary policy such as tax rises or less spending
C: No policy is ever needed in any such case at all
D: A ban on trade with all other countries at once
Why A: With output below potential and unemployment high, expansionary policy such as tax cuts or more government spending raises demand, output and jobs to close the gap.
Why B: Contractionary policy such as tax rises or spending cuts would lower demand further, and it would deepen the recession, so it suits an overheated economy.
Why C: Policy is useful here, since output is below potential and unemployment is high, so saying no policy is ever needed ignores a case where stimulus can help.
Why D: A ban on trade would cut exports and imports and would harm output, so it is not a sensible policy for closing a gap with output below potential.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is supply-side economics?
A: The view that prices are fixed by law for all goods in the economy
B: The view that markets always fail and need the state to run all of them
C: The view that demand is everything and that taxes and rules have no effect on output
D: The view that lower taxes and fewer regulations boost production and growth
Why A: Fixed prices set by law describe price controls, which are not supply side economics, a view focused on raising production through taxes and regulation.
Why B: Saying markets always fail and the state must run them describes central planning, which is far from supply side economics, which favors lower taxes and freer markets.
Why C: Supply side economics does not claim that taxes and rules have no effect on output, and it argues the opposite, that they strongly affect incentives to produce.
Why D: Supply side economics holds that lower taxes and fewer regulations raise incentives to work, save and invest, and so boost production and long run growth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which economist is most associated with arguing that government spending can stabilize recessions?
A: John Maynard Keynes
B: Milton Friedman
C: Adam Smith, 1776
D: Karl Marx, 1867
Why A: John Maynard Keynes argued that government spending can raise demand and stabilize recessions, which is why Keynesian economics supports fiscal stimulus in downturns.
Why B: Milton Friedman is linked with monetarism, the view that the money supply is the main driver of inflation, and he was skeptical of using government spending to stabilize.
Why C: Adam Smith wrote in 1776 on markets and the invisible hand, long before the idea of using government spending to stabilize recessions arose.
Why D: Karl Marx wrote in 1867 about capitalism and class conflict, and he is not known for arguing that government spending can stabilize recessions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which economist is most associated with the idea of the invisible hand?
A: John Keynes
B: Karl Marx
C: Paul Samuelson
D: Adam Smith
Why A: John Keynes is known for arguing that government spending can stabilize recessions, not for the invisible hand, which comes from an earlier writer.
Why B: Karl Marx is known for critiquing capitalism and for his theory of class conflict, rather than for the invisible hand idea of self interested markets.
Why C: Paul Samuelson wrote a well known economics textbook and worked on modern economic theory, but the invisible hand idea comes from a much earlier author.
Why D: Adam Smith introduced the invisible hand in The Wealth of Nations, describing how individuals pursuing their own interest can promote the good of society through markets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is monetarism?
A: The view that government spending is the main driver of inflation and output in the short run
B: The view that wages set by unions are the main driver of inflation in the economy
C: The view that the money supply is the main driver of inflation and output in the short run
D: The view that taxes cause all inflation and the money supply has no effect on prices
Why A: That describes a Keynesian-style view; monetarism holds that changes in the money supply are the main driver of inflation and output.
Why B: Monetarists see inflation as caused by money supply growth rather than union wages, so this does not describe monetarism.
Why C: Monetarism holds that the money supply is the main driver of inflation and of output in the short run, a view associated with Milton Friedman.
Why D: Monetarists do not say taxes cause all inflation, and they say the money supply is central, so denying any effect of money on prices contradicts the view.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If the money supply grows much faster than output, what is the likely long-run result?
A: Zero unemployment
B: Higher inflation
C: No change in prices
D: Lower inflation
Why A: Growing the money supply much faster than output does not bring zero unemployment, since the long run effect is mainly on prices and not on lasting job gains.
Why B: When money grows much faster than output, more money chases the same goods, so the long run result is a rise in the price level, which is higher inflation.
Why C: Prices tend to rise when money growth outpaces output, so saying there is no change in prices ignores the link between money and inflation.
Why D: Faster money growth than output growth raises prices and does not lower inflation, so lower inflation is the opposite of what is likely to occur.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is hyperinflation?
A: Falling prices that last for many years in a row
B: Stable prices that stay almost flat for many years
C: Extremely rapid and out-of-control price increases
D: A small price increase of a few percent in a year
Why A: Falling prices lasting many years are deflation, which is the opposite of hyperinflation, an extreme and rapid rise in prices.
Why B: Prices that stay almost flat describe price stability, which is the opposite of hyperinflation, in which prices rise extremely fast.
Why C: Hyperinflation is extremely rapid and out of control price increases, often more than 50 percent a month, which wipes out savings and the value of money.
Why D: A small price rise of a few percent a year is mild inflation, which is normal and far below the extreme rates that define hyperinflation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the national debt vs. the deficit?
A: The debt is foreign borrowing while the deficit is borrowing from citizens
B: The deficit measures spending while the debt measures tax collected
C: They are identical and mean the same thing in public finance
D: The debt is the total owed while the deficit is the annual shortfall
Why A: The debt is the total of all past borrowing from any lender, and the deficit is the yearly shortfall; neither is defined by who lends.
Why B: The deficit is the yearly gap when spending exceeds revenue, and the debt is the total owed from past borrowing, not tax collected.
Why C: The debt and the deficit are different, since the debt is a stock of past borrowing, and the deficit is a yearly flow, so they are not identical.
Why D: The national debt is the total amount owed from past borrowing, while the deficit is the annual shortfall when spending exceeds revenue, and deficits add to the debt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A government runs deficits of $300 billion in each of three years with no surplus years. What happens to the national debt?
A: It falls by about $900 billion
B: It rises by about $900 billion
C: It stays the same each year
D: It disappears over a few years
Why A: Deficits add to the national debt, so three years of $300 billion deficits cannot make it fall, as borrowing increases the total owed.
Why B: Each deficit adds to the debt, so with no surplus years three deficits of $300 billion raise the national debt by about 3 times 300, or $900 billion.
Why C: The debt cannot stay the same while the government keeps borrowing $300 billion each year to cover deficits, because each deficit adds to the amount owed.
Why D: Debt does not disappear from running deficits, and borrowing adds to it, so after three years of $300 billion deficits the debt is higher by about $900 billion.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does marginal analysis mean?
A: Comparing the extra benefit of an action with its extra cost
B: Comparing the average cost of an action with its average price
C: Choosing the option that has the lowest total cost of production
D: Comparing the total benefit of an action with its total cost
Why A: Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit of an action with its extra cost, and if marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost the action is worth taking.
Why B: Marginal analysis looks at the extra benefit and extra cost of one more unit, not at averages.
Why C: Choosing the lowest total cost ignores benefits; marginal analysis weighs the extra benefit against the extra cost.
Why D: That is total analysis; marginal analysis compares only the added benefit and added cost of one more unit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student can earn $9 more per hour by working a third shift but loses an hour of study valued at $11. Should she work?
A: Yes, because costs do not matter when the pay is higher than before overall
B: It cannot be decided from the facts that are given in the question
C: Yes, because $9 is positive and any positive gain is worth taking
D: No, because the marginal cost of $11 exceeds the marginal benefit of $9
Why A: Costs matter in every choice, and here the $11 cost of lost study exceeds the $9 gain, so ignoring costs would lead to a bad decision.
Why B: The question gives the marginal benefit of $9 and the marginal cost of $11, which is enough to decide, since cost exceeds benefit by $2.
Why C: A positive gain alone is not enough, because the extra $9 must be compared with the $11 value of lost study, and the $2 net loss means no.
Why D: She should not work, since the marginal cost of $11 for lost study is more than the marginal benefit of $9 in pay, leaving her $2 worse off.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Giffen good?
A: A rare inferior good whose demand rises when its price rises
B: A luxury good whose demand rises when people's incomes go up a lot
C: A public good that everyone can use without paying for it directly
D: A free gift that a store hands out to a customer who buys something
Why A: A Giffen good is a rare inferior good for which demand rises when its price rises, because the income effect outweighs the substitution effect, as with a staple food.
Why B: A luxury good has demand that rises as income rises, which is a different idea, since a Giffen good has demand that rises when its own price rises.
Why C: A public good is one people can use without paying and without reducing its availability to others, which is unrelated to a Giffen good's unusual demand.
Why D: A free gift is a promotional giveaway, not a Giffen good, which is an inferior good whose demand rises as its price goes up.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a luxury good?
A: A good everyone needs and buys in large amounts each week of the year
B: A good whose demand rises more than proportionally as income rises
C: A good with no price attached to it in any store or shop in town
D: A good that is given away free to all who come to the shop to ask for it
Why A: A good everyone needs and buys regularly is a necessity, not a luxury, since the demand for a luxury rises faster than income and is not constant.
Why B: A luxury good has demand that rises more than proportionally as income rises, so its income elasticity is greater than one, as with fine jewelry or sports cars.
Why C: A good with no price is a free good, and a luxury good does have a price, often a high one, so this option does not describe it.
Why D: A good given away free is not a luxury good, which is typically costly and bought with extra income, and its demand rises more than income does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Income rises 10% and demand for restaurant meals rises 20%. Income elasticity of demand is:
A: 0.5, so meals are a necessity
B: 30, so meals are inferior goods
C: 2, so meals behave like a luxury
D: 10, so meals are perfectly elastic
Why A: Income elasticity is 20 divided by 10, which equals 2, not 0.5; a value of 0.5 would mean demand rose only 5 percent.
Why B: Dividing gives 20 over 10 equals 2, not 30; adding the two percentages is the wrong operation, and inferior goods would show a negative elasticity anyway.
Why C: Income elasticity equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income, so 20 divided by 10 equals 2; a value above 1 marks a luxury.
Why D: The 10 is just the income change, not the ratio; the correct ratio of 20 to 10 is 2, and perfectly elastic describes price responses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a monopoly's pricing power?
A: The inability to set a price on the goods that it chooses to sell to buyers
B: The ability to raise price because many rivals sell the same product
C: The ability to set price above marginal cost because there are no close substitutes
D: The ability to cut price below marginal cost to attract more buyers
Why A: Inability to set price describes a price taker in perfect competition; a monopoly is the sole seller and can choose its own price instead.
Why B: Many rivals selling the same product describes competition, which limits price; a monopoly has pricing power because it has no close substitutes.
Why C: With no close substitutes, a monopolist faces the whole market demand curve and can pick a price above marginal cost, which is the source of its market power.
Why D: A monopolist maximizes profit by pricing above marginal cost, not below it; cutting below marginal cost would lose money on each unit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly typically charges:
A: A lower price and more output
B: No price at all in the market
C: The same price and output as before
D: A higher price and produces less
Why A: A lower price with more output is the competitive outcome; the monopolist restricts quantity to raise price, so this describes the opposite of monopoly behavior.
Why B: A monopoly sells its good at a positive price, because it wants revenue; charging nothing would earn no profit and is not typical monopoly behavior.
Why C: Price and output change when a market becomes a monopoly, because the firm sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charges more than a competitive firm would.
Why D: A monopoly sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, which gives a smaller quantity and a price above the competitive level, creating a deadweight loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An airline charges business travelers more than leisure travelers for similar seats. This is:
A: Collusion among rivals
B: Price discrimination
C: Dumping of goods
D: A tariff on exports
Why A: Collusion is rival firms agreeing to fix prices or output; one airline charging different customer groups different prices is not an agreement among competitors.
Why B: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same product based on willingness to pay; business travelers will pay more, so the airline charges them more.
Why C: Dumping means selling goods in a foreign market below cost or below the home price; it concerns international trade, not different fares for different traveler types.
Why D: A tariff is a tax on imported goods collected by a government, not a pricing tactic used by an airline across traveler groups.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a duopoly?
A: A market with exactly two sellers
B: A market with many sellers, one buyer
C: A market with two buyers, one seller
D: A market with one seller, many buyers
Why A: The prefix duo means two, so a duopoly is a market dominated by exactly two sellers, who must consider each other's pricing and output choices.
Why B: Many sellers facing one buyer describes a monopsony, which is a buyer-side market power structure, not a duopoly, which counts sellers and has exactly two.
Why C: Two buyers facing one seller does not define a duopoly; the term counts sellers, and a lone seller would more closely resemble a monopoly.
Why D: One seller with many buyers describes a monopoly, not a duopoly; a duopoly requires exactly two competing sellers sharing the market between them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are many natural monopolies regulated?
A: To limit prices and protect consumers while allowing efficient single-firm service
B: To ban the service that natural monopolies provide to all customers in an area overall
C: To raise prices for customers who have no alternative supplier to turn to
D: To remove all competition from every market in the economy as a whole nation
Why A: A natural monopoly has high fixed costs so one firm serves the market cheapest; regulators cap prices to protect consumers while keeping the efficiency of single-firm service.
Why B: Regulation does not aim to ban the service; utilities like water and power are essential, so regulators oversee them rather than prohibit them.
Why C: Regulators want to restrain prices, not raise them; customers lacking an alternative supplier are exactly why oversight exists, to prevent overcharging.
Why D: A natural monopoly already faces little competition because one firm is cheapest; regulation limits its power in that single market and does not remove competition everywhere.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a main function of money?
A: A medium of exchange
B: A source of insurance
C: A legal contract
D: A form of ownership
Why A: Money serves as a medium of exchange, letting people trade goods and services without barter, which requires a double coincidence of wants.
Why B: Insurance transfers risk through premiums and claims; money does not insure anyone against losses, so this is not one of money's main functions.
Why C: A legal contract is an enforceable agreement between parties, a different thing from money; money can settle contract obligations, but that is not its function.
Why D: Ownership is a property right in an asset; money can purchase ownership, but being a form of ownership is not one of money's core functions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the time value of money mean?
A: A dollar in the future is worth more than a dollar today
B: Interest earned on savings is taxed at the same rate as wages
C: Money keeps its value best when it is held as cash
D: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future
Why A: That reverses the concept; a dollar today can earn interest, so it is worth more than the same dollar received later.
Why B: Tax treatment of interest is unrelated to the time value of money, which says money today is worth more than money later.
Why C: Cash loses buying power through inflation and earns no interest, which is why money today can be worth more when invested.
Why D: A dollar today can be invested to earn interest, so it grows to more than a dollar later; this is why present money is valued above future money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to the purchasing power of cash kept under a mattress when inflation is 3 percent a year?
A: No change
B: It doubles
C: It falls
D: It rises
Why A: Cash under a mattress earns no interest while prices rise 3 percent a year, so the same cash buys fewer goods; its purchasing power does change.
Why B: Doubling would require far higher inflation or large returns; with 3 percent inflation and no interest, cash buys slightly less each year, never twice as much.
Why C: Prices rise 3 percent a year while idle cash stays the same amount, so each dollar buys fewer goods and services; purchasing power falls.
Why D: Purchasing power rises only when prices fall or income grows; with 3 percent inflation and zero interest on mattress cash, purchasing power falls rather than rises.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A deposit of $2,000 earns 4 percent interest compounded annually. What is the balance after 2 years?
Why A: $2,080.00 is only one year of interest, 2,000 times 1.04; the second year's growth is missing, so the balance after 2 years is higher.
Why B: Compounding gives 2,000 times 1.04 squared, which is 2,000 times 1.0816, or $2,163.20; year two earns interest on year one's interest as well.
Why C: $4,163.20 wrongly adds the full $2,000 principal a second time; interest should only add 163.20 to the original deposit of $2,000.
Why D: $2,160 uses simple interest, 2,000 plus 2 times 80; compounding adds interest on the first year's $80, giving $2,163.20 instead, a $3.20 difference.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the opportunity cost of spending $100 today instead of saving it?
A: Nothing, because spending is free
B: The $100 itself plus its sales tax
C: The growth the $100 could have earned
D: The interest on a credit card loan
Why A: Spending is never free in economic terms, because the money could have been saved or used elsewhere; opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up.
Why B: The $100 itself is the price paid, not the opportunity cost; sales tax is part of the price, while the forgone alternative use of money is the cost.
Why C: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative; by not saving the $100, you give up the interest or growth it could have earned.
Why D: Credit card interest is a cost of borrowing, which is unrelated to spending your own cash; the forgone gain from saving that same money is the relevant cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a store of value?
A: Savings held in a bank account
B: A paper receipt from a shop
C: A coffee bought in the morning
D: A gift card used the same day
Why A: A bank account holds purchasing power safely until needed later, and often earns interest; keeping value across time is exactly what a store of value does.
Why B: A paper receipt only proves a past purchase and has no lasting purchasing power; it cannot be exchanged for goods, so it does not store value.
Why C: A coffee is consumed within minutes, so its value disappears rapidly; it is a consumption item, not something that keeps purchasing power for use later.
Why D: A gift card used the same day acts as a payment tool right away rather than holding value over time, so it does not serve as a store of value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Real income is nominal income adjusted for:
A: Hours worked
B: Taxes only
C: Tax rates
D: Inflation
Why A: Hours worked measure labor effort and are not an adjustment applied to nominal income; real income adjusts for price changes, not time spent working.
Why B: Taxes reduce after-tax income, but real income is specifically about purchasing power; adjusting nominal income for taxes only gives disposable income, not real income.
Why C: Tax rates are a policy variable, not a price level; real income removes the effect of rising prices, and tax rates do not appear in that calculation.
Why D: Real income is nominal income divided by a price index, so it shows how many goods the money buys; this adjusts for inflation and measures purchasing power.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How long is a short-term financial goal generally?
A: More than 30 years
B: Less than a year
C: It has no time frame
D: Exactly 10 years
Why A: More than 30 years is a very long horizon, typical of retirement planning or paying off a mortgage, which are long-term goals, not short-term ones.
Why B: Short-term goals are typically achieved within a year, such as building a small emergency fund or buying a gadget, so less than a year fits the definition.
Why C: Financial goals are defined by time frames, and a short-term goal has a deadline within about a year; a goal with no time frame is not SMART.
Why D: Exactly 10 years sits in the long-term range, because short-term goals finish within about a year; a ten-year goal like a down payment is long-term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does SMART stand for in SMART goals?
A: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
B: Saved, Managed, Audited, Reported and Taxed yearly
C: Secure, Mutual, Approved, Real and Tested yearly
D: Simple, Modest, Average, Regular and Timely, in order
Why A: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound; these five qualities make a goal clear, trackable, realistic, meaningful and tied to a deadline.
Why B: Saved, Managed, Audited, Reported and Taxed is an invented phrase; SMART is a goal-setting framework, not an accounting process with audits and tax reports.
Why C: Secure, Mutual, Approved, Real and Tested is made up and does not describe goals; SMART refers to Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound qualities.
Why D: Simple, Modest, Average, Regular and Timely is not the framework; SMART's letters stand for qualities that make goals actionable, not for average or modest ones.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is net worth calculated?
A: Assets plus liabilities
B: Savings divided by income
C: Income minus expenses
D: Assets minus liabilities
Why A: Adding assets and liabilities double counts what you own and what you owe; liabilities reduce net worth, so they must be subtracted from assets rather than added.
Why B: Savings divided by income gives a savings rate, a ratio showing how much of income is saved; it is not a measure of net worth in dollars.
Why C: Income minus expenses gives cash flow or surplus for a period; net worth is a snapshot of total wealth, using what you own less what you owe.
Why D: Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe, so assets minus liabilities; a positive result means owning more than owing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student has $600 saved and needs $2,400 for a car in 12 months. She saves $150 a month. What will happen?
A: She will be $600 short again
B: She will have $600 left over
C: She will reach exactly $2,400
D: She will be $300 short again
Why A: She has 600 plus 12 times 150, which is 600 plus 1,800 equals 2,400; she is not short, so a $600 shortfall is wrong.
Why B: Her total is 600 plus 1,800, which equals exactly 2,400, the cost of the car; nothing is left over, so a $600 surplus is wrong.
Why C: Twelve months at $150 adds $1,800, and with the $600 already saved the total is $2,400, matching the car's price exactly, so she reaches the goal.
Why D: A $300 shortfall would need only $1,500 of new savings; she saves 12 times 150, which is $1,800, plus $600 gives $2,400 and no shortfall.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which expense is discretionary?
A: Groceries each month
B: A streaming subscription
C: An insurance premium payment
D: Rent payment each month
Why A: Groceries are a basic need for food each month, so they count as essential spending; discretionary expenses are optional items you could cut without hardship.
Why B: A streaming subscription is a want that can be cancelled without harming health or housing, so it is discretionary spending a person may cut when budgets are tight.
Why C: Insurance premiums protect against major financial loss and are often required by law or lenders, such as car coverage, so they are not freely optional.
Why D: Rent pays for housing, an essential and usually fixed cost that is not optional; discretionary spending refers to items a person can skip, unlike rent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is generally the first priority when starting a financial plan?
A: Buy a luxury item or two
B: Pay for vacations on credit
C: Invest everything in one stock
D: Build a small emergency fund
Why A: Buying luxury items first spends money before any safety net exists; a sound financial plan starts with security rather than extra purchases for pleasure.
Why B: Paying for vacations on credit creates debt and interest charges before basics are secure; a financial plan should avoid borrowing for optional spending, especially early on.
Why C: Putting everything in one stock concentrates risk heavily; a plan begins with safety first and diversification later, so betting it all on one company is unwise.
Why D: A small emergency fund covers surprise costs like repairs or job loss, preventing debt; it is usually the first step before investing or larger goals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a budget variance?
A: The total of all of a person's outstanding debts
B: The difference between planned and actual amounts
C: The amount of interest earned on a savings account
D: The total cost of a loan including the interest
Why A: The total of all debts owed is a person's total liabilities, not a budget variance; variance compares planned figures with what was actually spent or earned.
Why B: Budget variance is the actual amount minus the planned amount for a category; a gap shows where spending or income differed from the plan.
Why C: Interest earned on savings is investment income and has nothing to do with comparing a plan with actual results, which is what variance measures.
Why D: The total cost of a loan with interest is the repayment amount, a borrowing concept; variance is about planned versus actual budget figures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit union?
A: A member-owned, not-for-profit financial cooperative
B: A for-profit stock brokerage firm for investors
C: A company that sells insurance and annuities to families
D: A government agency that sets interest rates for loans
Why A: A credit union is owned by its members and runs as a not-for-profit cooperative, often giving better rates and lower fees than banks that pay shareholders.
Why B: A stock brokerage is a for-profit firm that trades securities for investors; credit unions are member-owned cooperatives that take deposits and make loans.
Why C: Insurance companies sell insurance and annuities; a credit union is a deposit and lending institution owned by its members, so insurance is not its core service.
Why D: Government agencies, such as the Federal Reserve, set policy rates; credit unions are private member cooperatives that lend at their own rates and are not government agencies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does FDIC insurance protect?
A: Credit card debt owed
B: Cryptocurrency holdings
C: Deposits at insured banks
D: Stock market holdings
Why A: Credit card debt is a liability owed by the cardholder; FDIC insurance protects depositors' money in banks and does not cover amounts owed on cards.
Why B: Cryptocurrency is not a bank deposit, so FDIC insurance does not cover it; the insurance applies only to deposit accounts at insured banks.
Why C: The FDIC insures deposits at member banks, currently up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, so if a bank fails, depositors get their money back.
Why D: Stocks and mutual funds can lose value and are not covered by FDIC insurance; the agency protects bank deposits, not investment market losses of any kind.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A checking account is mainly designed for:
A: Borrowing money long term
B: Long-term investing
C: Earning high interest
D: Everyday transactions
Why A: Borrowing long term is the purpose of loans like mortgages, not a checking account, which holds your own deposited money for spending and bill paying.
Why B: Long-term investing happens in brokerage and retirement accounts; checking accounts pay little or no interest and are built for access to cash, not growth.
Why C: Checking accounts usually pay very low or no interest; high earnings are found in savings accounts, certificates of deposit and investments, not everyday accounts.
Why D: Checking accounts support everyday transactions such as paying bills, using a debit card and writing checks, with easy and frequent access to your money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When is an overdraft fee charged?
A: When the account earns interest at the end of the month as a rule
B: When the account is first opened at the bank branch
C: When a payment or withdrawal exceeds the available balance
D: When a deposit is made into the account by the owner
Why A: Interest earned is a benefit paid to the customer, not a fee; overdraft fees arise when spending exceeds funds, not when interest is credited to the account.
Why B: Opening an account does not trigger an overdraft; there is no negative balance at that point, and fees at opening are not overdraft charges.
Why C: An overdraft happens when a payment or withdrawal is bigger than the money in the account, so the bank covers it and charges a fee.
Why D: A deposit adds money to the account and raises the balance, so it cannot cause an overdraft; overdrafts come from taking out more than is available.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does ATM stand for?
A: Account transfer method
B: Automated teller machine
C: Automatic tax manager
D: Authorized trading market
Why A: ATM does not stand for account transfer method; the letters stand for automated teller machine, a device that lets customers deposit or withdraw cash on their own.
Why B: ATM stands for automated teller machine, a self-service terminal that lets customers withdraw cash, deposit funds and check balances without a human bank teller.
Why C: Automatic tax manager is not what ATM means; these machines handle cash and account transactions, and they have nothing to do with managing taxes for customers.
Why D: Authorized trading market is a made-up phrase; an ATM is a cash machine and has no connection to stock trading or financial exchanges.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which provider typically sells stocks and bonds to individual investors?
A: A brokerage firm
B: A credit union
C: A payday lender
D: A pawn shop loan
Why A: A brokerage firm is licensed to buy and sell securities for clients, so individual investors use one to trade stocks, bonds and funds.
Why B: A credit union takes deposits and makes loans for its members; it is not primarily a seller of stocks and bonds to individual investors.
Why C: A payday lender makes short, costly loans due on the next payday; it does not sell securities, so it is the wrong provider for investing.
Why D: A pawn shop lends money against personal items kept as collateral; it has no license or business of selling stocks and bonds to investors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is often true of online-only banks?
A: They offer customers no way to reach their accounts online
B: They may offer lower fees because they have no branches to run
C: They are not insured under any program at all by the state
D: They require customers to visit a branch in person each month overall
Why A: Online-only banks are accessed through websites and apps, so customers can reach their accounts online anytime; saying they offer no online access is plainly false.
Why B: Without branches to staff and maintain, online banks have lower costs and can pass savings on as lower fees and higher rates for customers.
Why C: Reputable online banks are FDIC insured just like traditional banks, up to the legal limit, so claiming no insurance at all is inaccurate and misleading.
Why D: Online-only banks have no branches, so they require no branch visits; deposits and transfers are handled digitally, making a monthly visit requirement impossible to apply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is diversification?
A: Selling everything when prices fall
B: Borrowing money to buy more stock
C: Timing the market to buy low
D: Spreading investments to reduce risk
Why A: Selling everything when prices fall locks in losses and does nothing to spread holdings across assets; diversification means owning many different investments instead of reacting to drops.
Why B: Borrowing to buy stock is leverage and increases risk; diversification spreads investments across assets to reduce risk.
Why C: Timing the market is an attempt to predict prices and does not spread risk; diversification holds many different investments.
