Why B: The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time: divide 72 by the annual interest rate, so at 8% money doubles in roughly 72 / 8 = 9 years.
Why C: Finding a monthly loan or lease payment needs an amortization formula or a calculator using rate, term and amount, and the Rule of 72 is not designed for it.
Why D: Tax owed on interest depends on your tax bracket and the interest amount, and the Rule of 72 only estimates growth time, so it cannot calculate any tax.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Using the Rule of 72, about how long will it take money earning 6% to double?
A: 6 years
B: 8 years
C: 72 years
D: 12 years
Why A: Six years would be the answer only if you divided 36 by 6; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by the rate, so 72 / 6 is 12, not 6.
Why B: Eight years comes from dividing 72 by 9, which would be a 9% rate; at the stated 6% rate, 72 / 6 gives a doubling time of 12 years.
Why C: Seventy-two years confuses the constant with the answer; the Rule of 72 requires dividing 72 by the interest rate of 6, which gives 12 years, not 72.
Why D: Using the Rule of 72, divide 72 by the rate: 72 / 6 = 12, so money earning 6% a year takes about 12 years to double.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the time value of money?
A: A dollar in the future is worth more than a dollar today
B: Time has no effect on money at any point in the future
C: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future
D: Money loses all value at midnight each night of the year
Why A: This reverses the idea; money today can be invested to earn interest, so a dollar in the future is worth less in present terms, not more.
Why B: Time does affect money; because of inflation and the chance to earn interest, a dollar's value changes over time, so saying time has no effect is wrong.
Why C: The time value of money says a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can be invested and earn interest or returns.
Why D: Money does not lose all value at midnight each night; its value changes gradually through inflation and interest, so this claim has no basis in economics or in practice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is purchasing power?
A: The number of cards in a wallet or purse at any one time
B: The size of a store's inventory held in the back rooms
C: The amount of money a person earns each year at work in total
D: The amount of goods and services a unit of money can buy
Why A: The number of cards in a wallet describes what a person carries, which has nothing to do with how many goods and services a unit of money can buy.
Why B: The size of a store's inventory in its back rooms is a business stock measure, unrelated to what a unit of money is able to purchase for consumers.
Why C: What a person earns each year is income, not purchasing power; purchasing power depends on how far each dollar goes at current prices, not on total earnings.
Why D: Purchasing power is the quantity of goods and services one unit of money can buy, and it falls when prices rise through inflation, even if your income stays the same.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the annual percentage rate (APR) on a loan?
A: The yearly cost of borrowing with certain fees
B: The amount borrowed from a bank by the buyer
C: The number of years that a loan lasts for
D: The amount of the first monthly payment on the loan
Why A: APR expresses the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage and includes certain fees along with interest, so it lets you compare loans on a consistent basis.
Why B: The amount borrowed from a bank is the loan principal, not the APR; APR is a percentage rate that measures the yearly cost of that borrowing.
Why C: The number of years a loan lasts is its term, which is a different feature from APR, a percentage describing the yearly cost of borrowing.
Why D: The first monthly payment is a dollar amount worked out from the principal, rate and term, while APR is an annual percentage and not a payment amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a fixed interest rate?
A: A rate that changes with market conditions over time
B: A rate that drops each year as the balance falls
C: A rate that stays the same for the whole loan term
D: A rate that applies to a short introductory period
Why A: A rate that changes with market conditions is a variable or adjustable rate; a fixed rate is defined by staying unchanged, so this describes the opposite product.
Why B: A fixed rate does not fall as the balance falls; it stays the same for the whole loan term, which makes payments predictable.
Why C: A fixed interest rate stays the same for the whole loan term, so the borrower can predict payments and is protected if market interest rates rise later.
Why D: A rate that lasts for a short introductory period is a teaser rate that later changes; a fixed rate stays unchanged for the full loan term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a variable interest rate?
A: A rate that stays the same for the full loan term
B: A rate that can change over time with a benchmark
C: A rate that is free of charge to the borrower
D: A rate set by the borrower alone on any loan
Why A: A rate that stays the same for the full loan term is a fixed rate; a variable rate is defined by the fact that it can change.
Why B: A variable rate can move up or down over time because it is tied to a benchmark or index, so the borrower's payments may change with the market.
Why C: Variable rates are not free of charge; the borrower still pays interest, and the rate simply floats with a benchmark, so the cost of borrowing is not removed.
Why D: The borrower does not set the rate alone; lenders set it, usually as a benchmark plus a margin, so the idea that the borrower decides is mistaken.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit score?
A: A number that shows the total balance a person owes on loans
B: A number that is assigned by the employer to each worker
C: A number that shows how many times a person applied for credit
D: A number that estimates how likely a borrower is to repay debts
Why A: A credit score estimates how likely someone is to repay debts; it is not a total of what is owed, though balances are one factor in the calculation.
Why B: Employers do not assign credit scores to workers; the scores come from credit bureaus and scoring models using your borrowing and repayment history, not from the workplace.
Why C: The number of credit applications is a small input called inquiries; the score itself combines payment history, balances and other factors to estimate repayment risk.
Why D: A credit score is a number that estimates how likely a borrower is to repay debts, based on history such as payments, balances and account age.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which factor has the largest effect on a FICO credit score?
A: Payment history
B: Your income
C: Your street name
D: Your age group
Why A: Payment history carries the most weight in a FICO score, about 35%, because lenders care most about whether you have paid past debts on time.
Why B: Income is not part of a FICO score calculation at all, so it cannot be the biggest factor; payment history, which carries about 35%, is.
Why C: Your street name is not a factor in a FICO credit score; the score uses payment history, amounts owed, length of history, new credit and credit mix.
Why D: Age group is not used in FICO scoring, and using it would be unlawful discrimination; payment history is the factor with the largest weight, not demographics.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is credit utilization?
A: The number of credit cards you have applied for
B: The share of available credit that you are using
C: The age of your oldest account on file with a bank
D: The total interest you have paid on a loan
Why A: The number of cards you applied for relates to new credit and hard inquiries, which is a different scoring factor from credit utilization, a ratio of balances to limits.
Why B: Credit utilization is the share of your available credit that you are currently using, calculated by dividing total balances by total limits, and lower is better.
Why C: The age of your oldest account measures credit history length, a separate scoring factor, and says nothing about how much of your available credit is in use.
Why D: Total interest paid on a loan is a cost of borrowing and is not a ratio of balance to limit, so it is not credit utilization.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person has a $5,000 credit limit and a $2,000 balance. What is the utilization rate?
Why A: 250% inverts the ratio; utilization is balance divided by limit, so $2,000 / $5,000 is 0.40, and 250% would come from dividing the limit by the balance.
Why B: 25% would result from dividing $2,000 by $8,000 or similar; the correct calculation uses the $5,000 limit, and $2,000 / $5,000 is 40 percent, not 25 percent.
Why C: Utilization equals balance divided by credit limit: $2,000 / $5,000 = 0.40, so the person is using 40% of available credit, which is fairly high for scoring.
Why D: 60% is the share of credit that remains unused ($3,000 of $5,000); utilization measures the part in use, which is $2,000 / $5,000 = 40%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a good strategy to build credit responsibly?
A: Miss payments to save some cash for later
B: Pay bills on time and keep balances low
C: Max out cards and pay only the minimum
D: Open many new cards at once each month
Why A: Missing payments hurts your payment history, the biggest scoring factor, and brings late fees, so it damages credit and does not build it responsibly.
Why B: Paying bills on time builds a strong payment history, and keeping balances low keeps credit utilization down; these are the two habits that most improve a credit profile.
Why C: Maxing out cards drives utilization very high, and paying only the minimum keeps balances and interest growing, both of which lower your score and cost more money.
Why D: Opening many new cards at once creates multiple hard inquiries and lowers your average account age, which tends to reduce your score rather than build it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hard inquiry?
A: A question asked by a teller at the bank branch
B: A bill that arrives late in the mail each month
C: A credit check made when you apply for new credit
D: A check you make on your own credit report, no effect
Why A: A teller asking a question at a branch is ordinary customer service and has no relation to credit reports; a hard inquiry is a lender checking your credit.
Why B: A bill that arrives late in the mail is a delivery problem, not a credit event, and it is unrelated to the term hard inquiry.
Why C: A hard inquiry is a credit check made by a lender when you apply for new credit, and it can slightly lower your score for a time.
Why D: A check you make on your own credit report is a soft inquiry, which has no effect on your score, so it is not a hard inquiry.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How long can most negative items stay on a credit report?
A: Up to seven years
B: Only one year
C: They vanish at once
D: Twenty years or more
Why A: Most negative items, such as late payments and collections, can stay on a credit report for up to seven years, though bankruptcies may remain as long as ten.
Why B: One year is far too short; most negative marks remain on the report for several years, up to seven, so their harm to credit lasts much longer.
Why C: Negative items do not vanish at once; they stay for years unless found to be errors, so waiting seven years or disputing mistakes is the real path.
Why D: Twenty years or more is too long for most items; the law limits most negative entries to seven years, and even bankruptcy usually drops off after ten.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a cosigner?
A: A person who lends money without interest to a friend in need
B: A person who approves a bank's paperwork for the buyer
C: A person who inspects collateral for the lender at the bank
D: A person who agrees to repay a loan if the borrower does not
Why A: Lending money to a friend without interest is a personal loan, not cosigning; a cosigner guarantees someone else's loan from the lender and does not lend anything.
Why B: Approving a bank's paperwork is a clerical job, but a cosigner is not a bank employee; they sign the loan and become legally responsible for repaying it.
Why C: Inspecting collateral for a lender is the work of an appraiser or inspector, not a cosigner, whose role is to promise repayment if the borrower fails.
Why D: A cosigner signs the loan and agrees to repay it if the borrower does not, which helps borrowers with weak credit but puts the cosigner's own credit at risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a minimum payment on a credit card?
A: The fee for using the card at any shop or store
B: The smallest payment due to stay in good standing
C: The amount of your credit limit, the most you owe
D: The total balance you owe on the card this month
Why A: A fee for using the card at shops is not what a minimum payment is; stores generally do not charge you per use, and this payment is a required amount.
Why B: The minimum payment is the smallest amount you must pay by the due date to keep the account in good standing and avoid late fees, though interest still accrues.
Why C: The credit limit is the maximum you may borrow on the card, not the smallest payment due; a minimum payment is a small portion of the balance owed.
Why D: The total balance owed is the statement balance; paying that clears the debt, while the minimum payment is only a small required portion of it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why does paying only the minimum on a credit card cost more over time?
A: The bank raises the principal each month by a set sum
B: The card turns into a savings account after a year
C: Minimum payments reduce your credit limit to zero
D: Interest keeps accruing on the remaining balance
Why A: The bank does not raise your principal each month by a set sum; the balance grows only because unpaid interest accumulates, and new purchases or fees are separate.
Why B: A credit card never turns into a savings account after a year; it remains a revolving loan, and unpaid balances continue to charge interest at the stated rate.
Why C: Minimum payments do not reduce your credit limit to zero; the limit is set by the issuer, and paying on time does not shrink it.
Why D: Paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance unpaid, so interest keeps accruing on it month after month, and the total cost over time rises sharply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a grace period on a credit card?
A: Time to pay in full without interest
B: Time when the bank forgives all debt
C: Time when interest is doubled each month
D: Time when the card cannot be used at all
Why A: A grace period is the time you have after the billing cycle to pay the balance in full without being charged interest on new purchases.
Why B: A grace period does not mean the bank forgives debt; you still owe the full balance, and only the interest charge is avoided if you pay on time.
Why C: Interest is not doubled during a grace period; the grace period is designed to avoid interest, whereas penalty rates or late fees are what raise costs.
Why D: A grace period does not block card use; you can keep making purchases, and the term refers to time allowed to pay without interest, not a suspension.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a late fee?
A: A fee for opening a new card account
B: A tax on interest income earned each year
C: A charge for paying after the due date
D: A reward for paying early off the bill
Why A: A fee for opening a new card account is an annual or setup fee, which is a different charge from a late fee tied to a missed due date.
Why B: A tax on interest income is charged by the government on what you earn, whereas a late fee is charged by a lender when your payment is overdue.
Why C: A late fee is a charge applied when you pay a bill after its due date, and it can also trigger higher interest rates and damage your credit.
Why D: Paying early may earn goodwill, but a late fee is a penalty and not a reward, so this option contradicts the meaning of the term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is debt consolidation?
A: Combining several debts into a single loan or payment
B: Borrowing from a friend to cover several small debts
C: Splitting one debt into many smaller debts at once
D: Ignoring debts until they disappear on their own
Why A: Debt consolidation combines several debts into one loan or payment, often with a lower rate or one due date, which can simplify repayment and reduce stress.
Why B: Borrowing from a friend to cover small debts only moves the obligation to a person; it is not the formal process of merging debts into one loan.
Why C: Splitting one debt into many smaller debts is the reverse of consolidation, which merges several debts into one, and it makes management harder instead of easier.
Why D: Ignoring debts does not make them disappear; interest and fees grow, collections may begin, and credit suffers, so this is not consolidation or any real repayment plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which debt-repayment method pays off the smallest balance first for motivation?
A: The avalanche method
B: The snowball method
C: The rollover method
D: The deferral method
Why A: The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first to save the most money, so it does not start with the smallest balance as the question describes.
Why B: The snowball method pays off the smallest balance first while making minimum payments on the others, which gives quick wins that keep people motivated to continue.
Why C: A rollover is generally moving funds from one retirement account to another, and it is not a standard method for deciding which debt to pay off first.
Why D: A deferral postpones a payment to a later date, and it is not a repayment strategy that targets the smallest balance first for motivation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which debt-repayment method targets the highest interest rate first to save the most money?
A: The snowball method
B: The random method
C: The minimum-only method
D: The avalanche method
Why A: The snowball method pays off the smallest balance first for motivation, not the highest rate, so it can cost more interest than the avalanche approach.
Why B: A random method follows no plan, so it cannot reliably target the highest rate first, and it will usually pay more interest than a deliberate approach.
Why C: Paying only the minimum on every debt keeps balances and interest growing for years, so it saves the least money rather than the most.
Why D: The avalanche method sends extra payments to the debt with the highest interest rate first, which minimizes total interest paid and usually clears all debts at the lowest cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is liquidity?
A: How risky an asset is to hold
B: How much interest an asset earns
C: How easily an asset becomes cash
D: How large an asset is in size
Why A: How risky an asset is to hold describes its risk level, which is separate from liquidity; a risky asset can be very liquid, like a volatile stock.
Why B: How much interest an asset earns is its yield or return, not its liquidity; some highly liquid assets, like cash, earn little or no interest.
Why C: Liquidity measures how easily and quickly an asset can be converted into cash without losing much value, so cash is most liquid and real estate is much less so.
Why D: The size of an asset describes its value or scale, not how quickly it converts to cash; large assets such as buildings are often quite illiquid.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which asset is the most liquid?
A: Land
B: Coins
C: A house
D: Cash
Why A: Land can take months to sell and the price is uncertain, so it is among the least liquid assets rather than the most liquid.
Why B: Coins are close to cash, but they must be sold or exchanged as collectibles, and cash itself needs no conversion, so coins rank below cash.
Why C: A house can take weeks or months to sell and involves fees, so it is far less liquid than cash, which is spendable immediately.
Why D: Cash is already money and can be spent immediately without conversion or loss of value, which makes it the most liquid asset of all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does diversification mean?
A: Spending money on many different purchases
B: Moving money only into cash and savings
C: Spreading money over investments to cut risk
D: Putting all your money in one single investment
Why A: Spending money on many different purchases is simply consumption and offers no risk reduction for savings; diversification refers to spreading investments, not shopping for different items.
Why B: Moving money only into cash and savings concentrates holdings in one type of asset, which does not spread risk across investments and can lose value to inflation.
Why C: Diversification means spreading money across different investments so that a loss in one is offset by others, which reduces the overall risk of the portfolio.
Why D: Putting all your money in one single investment is the opposite of diversification and exposes you to the full loss if that one investment fails.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the relationship between risk and return?
A: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
B: Risk and return are unrelated to each other in finance
C: Lower-risk investments tend to offer the highest potential returns
D: Risky assets are insured, so their returns are protected
Why A: Risk and return are linked: investments that offer the chance of higher returns, such as stocks, usually carry more risk of loss than safer options like savings.
Why B: Risk and return are closely related in finance; investors demand higher potential returns for taking more risk, so saying they are unrelated is incorrect.
Why C: Low-risk investments such as savings accounts offer lower returns; the chance of higher returns usually requires taking more risk, so this reverses the relationship.
Why D: Risky assets such as stocks are not insured against market losses; their values can fall, which is exactly why they are called risky.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inflation risk?
A: The risk that taxes rise next year for most savers
B: The risk that rising prices reduce the value of savings
C: The risk that a stock pays no dividend in a year
D: The risk that a bank closes its doors for good one day overall
Why A: A rise in taxes next year is tax risk, which is separate from inflation risk, the danger that rising prices erode what your savings can buy.
Why B: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices reduce the purchasing power of savings, so money held at a low interest rate can buy less over time.
Why C: A stock paying no dividend is a company payout risk, unrelated to inflation risk, which concerns the general rise in prices across the whole economy.
Why D: A bank closing is institution risk, which deposit insurance largely covers, and it is unrelated to inflation risk, the loss of purchasing power as prices rise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a negative real interest rate mean?
A: Interest is higher than inflation, so savings grow
B: Interest is paid daily to the account holder
C: Interest is exactly zero for the whole year
D: Inflation is higher than the interest rate earned
Why A: Interest higher than inflation gives a positive real interest rate, in which savings grow in purchasing power, so this describes the opposite of a negative real rate.
Why B: Interest paid daily describes how often interest is credited, which is a compounding schedule and says nothing about whether the real rate is positive or negative.
Why C: A zero interest rate for the year is a nominal rate of zero, and the real rate depends on inflation, so this does not define a negative real rate.
Why D: A negative real interest rate means inflation is higher than the interest rate earned, so savings lose purchasing power even though the nominal balance may be growing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A savings account pays 2% while inflation is 3%. What is the approximate real return?
A: About -1%
B: About 0%
C: About +5%
D: About +1%
Why A: The approximate real return is the interest rate minus inflation: 2% - 3% = -1%, so savings lose about one percent of purchasing power each year.
Why B: A real return of 0% would require inflation equal to the 2% interest rate; with inflation at 3%, subtracting gives -1%, not zero.
Why C: Plus 5% adds the two rates together, which is the wrong operation; the real return subtracts inflation from the interest rate, giving 2% - 3% = -1%.
Why D: Plus 1% reverses the subtraction, taking 3% - 2%; the real return is interest minus inflation, which is 2% - 3% = -1%, a loss of buying power.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a barter system?
A: Using a credit card to buy goods and pay later
B: Selling stocks for cash at a brokerage firm
C: Trading goods or services directly without money
D: Paying taxes with gold coins at the local office
Why A: Using a credit card to buy goods and pay later is credit, which still involves money; barter involves no money or credit at all, only direct exchange.
Why B: Selling stocks for cash at a brokerage is an ordinary financial transaction that uses money, so it is not barter, which avoids money entirely.
Why C: A barter system is one in which people trade goods or services directly for other goods or services without using money as a medium of exchange.
Why D: Paying taxes with gold coins would still use a form of money, so it does not describe barter, which exchanges goods and services without any money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fiat money?
A: Money that has no legal status in the nation
B: Money that has value because a government says so
C: Money that exists only in video games and online worlds
D: Money backed by gold held in a vault at the bank
Why A: Fiat money is legal tender, so it does have legal status; the claim that it has none contradicts the definition of money declared by a government.
Why B: Fiat money has value because a government declares it legal tender and people trust it, not because it is backed by a physical commodity such as gold.
Why C: Money that exists only in video games is in-game currency with no legal status, so it is not fiat money, which is issued and backed by a government.
Why D: Money backed by gold describes a commodity-backed or gold standard currency; fiat money is the opposite, because it relies on government decree and public trust instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cryptocurrency?
A: A paper currency printed by a state
B: A coin made of silver and other metals
C: A bank deposit insured by the FDIC
D: A digital currency using cryptography
Why A: A paper currency printed by a state is government fiat money like the dollar, while cryptocurrency is digital and is not issued by any central government or bank.
Why B: A coin made of silver and other metals is a physical commodity coin; cryptocurrency has no physical form and exists only as digital records on a network.
Why C: A bank deposit insured by the FDIC is a regulated bank product, but cryptocurrency holdings are not insured by the FDIC and are not bank deposits.
Why D: Cryptocurrency is a digital currency that uses cryptography to secure transactions and to control the creation of new units, usually recorded on a blockchain without a central bank.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are cryptocurrencies considered risky for savings?
A: Values can swing sharply and are not FDIC insured
B: Their value is set daily by the Federal Reserve
C: They are printed by the Treasury in limited amounts
D: They are covered by FDIC insurance up to a limit
Why A: Cryptocurrency prices can swing sharply in short periods and holdings are not FDIC insured, so a saver could lose much of their money, which makes them risky.
Why B: No central bank sets cryptocurrency prices; they move with trading demand, which is why values can swing sharply and make them risky for savings.
Why C: Treasury does not print cryptocurrency; it is created by software networks, and its value rests on demand and trust, which adds risk for savers.
Why D: Cryptocurrency holdings are not covered by FDIC insurance, so if the price drops or an exchange fails, the saver can lose the money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a budget surplus used for in smart personal finance?
A: Spending it all at once on wants, with none saved
B: Hiding it from the bank and the tax office
C: Building savings, paying down debt or investing
D: Burning it for safety reasons at the end of the year
Why A: Spending a surplus all at once on wants, with nothing saved, wastes the chance to improve your finances and is not what smart personal finance recommends.
Why B: Hiding a surplus from the bank and the tax office is dishonest and may be illegal, and it brings no financial benefit like saving or investing does.
Why C: A budget surplus is best used to build savings, pay down debt or invest, because each of these improves long-term financial security and net worth.
Why D: Burning money destroys its value for no reason and is illegal in many places, so it is never a sensible use of a budget surplus.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a monetary policy tool the Fed uses to influence interest rates?
A: Hiring more bank tellers for branches
B: Setting the federal funds rate target
C: Printing school textbooks to give away
D: Collecting income taxes from workers
Why A: Hiring more bank tellers is a decision made by individual banks about staffing and has no effect on the Fed's control of interest rates.
Why B: The Fed sets a target for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, which influences borrowing costs across the whole economy.
Why C: Printing school textbooks is unrelated to monetary policy; the Fed does not do this, and giving away books does not change interest rates or the money supply.
Why D: Collecting income taxes is done by the IRS as part of fiscal policy, and it is not a monetary policy tool that the Fed uses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When the Fed raises interest rates, what typically happens to the cost of loans?
A: It falls
B: It is zero
C: It rises
D: No change
Why A: Loan costs do not fall when the Fed raises rates; higher benchmark rates make funds more expensive for banks, and that cost is passed on to borrowers.
Why B: Loan costs do not become zero when the Fed raises rates; borrowing stays costly, and the interest charged generally moves up with the Fed's target.
Why C: When the Fed raises interest rates, borrowing costs for banks increase, so loans such as mortgages, car loans and credit cards typically become more expensive.
Why D: Loan costs do change when the Fed acts, because the federal funds rate influences prime and other lending rates, so no change is generally not accurate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a depreciating asset?
A: An asset that holds steady value, such as a savings balance
B: An asset that rises in value over time, such as land
C: An asset that is worthless on the day of purchase
D: An asset that loses value over time, such as a new car
Why A: An asset that holds steady value does not depreciate; depreciation means a decline in value from age, wear or obsolescence, as with a new car.
Why B: An asset that rises in value over time is an appreciating asset, which is the opposite of a depreciating asset that loses value.
Why C: Not every depreciating asset is worthless on the day of purchase; most lose value gradually, so a new car keeps a large share of its price at first.
Why D: A depreciating asset loses value over time through wear, age or obsolescence, and a new car is a classic example because it loses value as it is driven.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an appreciating asset?
A: An asset that tends to gain value, like real estate
B: An asset that is rented out only to tenants and firms
C: An asset that loses value each year, like a car
D: An asset that cannot be sold to anyone at any price
Why A: An appreciating asset tends to gain value over time, and real estate is a common example because land and buildings often rise in price over many years.
Why B: Renting an asset out to tenants describes an income property, which is a use of an asset, and it does not tell you whether the asset gains value.
Why C: An asset that loses value each year, like a car, is a depreciating asset, which is the opposite of appreciating, so this option describes the wrong idea.
Why D: An asset that cannot be sold at any price is illiquid or worthless, not appreciating; an appreciating asset has a market and a rising value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is insurance?
A: A tax paid on risky activities and hobbies
B: A contract protecting against loss for premiums
C: A loan used to buy a home or other property
D: A savings account that earns high interest each year
Why A: A tax on risky hobbies is a government charge, whereas insurance is a private contract in which you pay to transfer the risk of loss to someone else.
Why B: Insurance is a contract in which you pay premiums and the insurer agrees to cover certain losses, which protects you from large unexpected financial hardship.
Why C: A loan to buy a home is a mortgage, which is borrowing to purchase property, and it does not protect you from loss as insurance does.
Why D: A savings account earns interest on your deposits and does not transfer risk, whereas insurance charges premiums to cover potential losses, so it is not a savings product.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a premium?
A: The amount you pay for an insurance policy
B: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
C: The maximum the insurer will pay out in total
D: The amount you must pay before coverage starts
Why A: The premium is the amount you pay, monthly or yearly, to the insurer to keep a policy active and to have coverage when a loss happens.
Why B: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payout or benefit, not the premium, which is what the policyholder pays into the policy.
Why C: The maximum the insurer will pay in total is the policy limit or coverage limit, which is a different term from the premium you pay.
Why D: The amount you must pay before coverage starts is the deductible, and the premium is the regular price paid to keep the policy in force.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a deductible?
A: The maximum amount the insurer pays
B: The fee for filing a claim late
C: The monthly payment for coverage
D: What you pay before insurance pays
Why A: The maximum amount the insurer pays is the coverage limit, which caps the insurer's side, whereas the deductible is the amount the policyholder pays first.
Why B: A fee for filing a claim late is a penalty some policies may impose, but it is not the deductible, which is the share you pay first.
Why C: The monthly payment for coverage is the premium, which keeps the policy active, while the deductible is a separate amount paid only when you make a claim.
Why D: A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket on a covered loss before the insurance company begins to pay its share of the claim.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If you choose a higher deductible, what usually happens to your premium?
A: It increases
B: It becomes zero
C: It decreases
D: No change
Why A: A higher deductible means you take on more of the risk yourself, so the insurer charges less; the premium decreases, not increases, when the deductible goes up.
Why B: The premium does not become zero with a higher deductible; you still pay a regular premium for coverage, though it is usually lower than before.
Why C: Choosing a higher deductible lowers your premium, because you agree to cover more of the initial loss and the insurer expects to pay out less often.
Why D: The premium does change with the deductible, since insurers price coverage by how much of the loss they must pay, so a higher deductible lowers the premium.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a claim?
A: A fee for buying a policy from an agent
B: A request to an insurer after a covered loss
C: A discount for safe driving over the year
D: A rule that forbids certain coverage in a policy
Why A: A fee for buying a policy from an agent is a commission or policy fee, while a claim is a request made after a loss occurs.
Why B: A claim is a formal request to the insurer for payment after a covered loss, such as an accident, theft or fire, so the insurer can pay under the policy.
Why C: A discount for safe driving is a premium reduction for good behavior, which is separate from a claim, a request to be paid after a loss.
Why D: A rule that forbids certain coverage is an exclusion in the policy, whereas a claim is the request you make to receive payment for a covered loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main purpose of auto liability insurance?
A: To pay for injuries and damage you cause to other people
B: To pay for damage caused by theft, fire or storms
C: To pay for routine maintenance like oil changes and tires
D: To repair your own car after a crash you cause
Why A: Auto liability insurance pays for injuries and property damage you cause to others in an accident, which protects your assets from lawsuits and large bills if you are at fault.
Why B: Damage from theft, fire or storms is handled by comprehensive coverage; liability insurance pays for injuries and property damage you cause to other people.
Why C: Routine maintenance such as oil changes and tires is the owner's expense, and insurance covers sudden losses, so liability coverage does not pay for regular upkeep.
Why D: Repairing your own car is the job of collision coverage; liability insurance pays for harm you cause to other people and their property.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does collision coverage pay for?
A: Medical bills for passengers in your car
B: Routine tire replacements and oil
C: Damage from hail, fire or flooding
D: Damage to your car in an accident
Why A: Medical bills for passengers fall under medical payments or injury coverage; collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after an accident.
Why B: Routine tire replacements and oil changes are normal maintenance costs, which collision coverage does not pay for, since it responds only to accident damage.
Why C: Damage from hail, fire or flooding is covered by comprehensive coverage; collision pays for damage from crashes with other vehicles or objects.
Why D: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car when it is damaged in an accident, whether you hit another car or an object, regardless of fault.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does comprehensive auto coverage pay for?
A: Damage from a crash you cause to another car
B: Damage from non-collision events like theft
C: Injuries to other drivers on the same road
D: Routine oil changes and new tire swaps
Why A: Damage from a crash you cause to another car falls under liability coverage, not comprehensive, which pays for non-collision losses to your own vehicle.
Why B: Comprehensive coverage pays for damage to your car from events other than collisions, such as theft, fire, vandalism, hail or hitting an animal, after the deductible.
Why C: Injuries to other drivers caused by you are covered by bodily injury liability, which is a separate coverage from comprehensive, which protects your own car.
Why D: Routine oil changes and new tire swaps are maintenance costs that you pay yourself, and comprehensive coverage pays only for sudden, unexpected damage and theft.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is renters insurance?
A: Coverage for the landlord's income and the building
B: Coverage for the building itself and the land under it
C: A renter's belongings and liability, not the building
D: Coverage for unpaid rent only owed to the landlord
Why A: Renters insurance does not cover the landlord's income or building; the landlord carries a separate policy for the property, while you insure your own items.
Why B: The building and land under it are the landlord's responsibility, and the landlord's policy covers them, whereas renters insurance protects the tenant's own belongings and liability.
Why C: Renters insurance covers a tenant's personal belongings and liability if someone is hurt or you cause damage, but it does not cover the building itself.
Why D: Renters insurance does not pay unpaid rent owed to the landlord; rent is a contract obligation, and the policy protects your belongings and liability instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does homeowners insurance usually cover?
A: Flood and earthquake damage to the house
B: Routine upkeep like repainting and lawn care
C: The home, belongings and liability for accidents
D: Mortgage payments if the owner loses a job
Why A: Flood and earthquake damage are excluded from standard homeowners policies and need separate coverage, so this does not describe what a typical policy covers.
Why B: Routine upkeep is the owner's responsibility; homeowners insurance pays for sudden losses such as fire or theft, not regular maintenance.
Why C: Homeowners insurance usually covers the dwelling, personal belongings and liability for accidents on your property, giving broad protection against many common losses.
Why D: Homeowners insurance protects the property and liability; it does not make mortgage payments if the owner loses a job, which would need a different product.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which disaster is typically NOT covered by a standard homeowners policy?
A: Burglary
B: Flooding
C: A blaze
D: Tornado
Why A: Theft is normally covered by a standard homeowners policy, so it is not the excluded event the question asks about.
Why B: Flooding is typically excluded from a standard homeowners policy, so owners in flood-prone areas must buy separate flood insurance, for example through the NFIP.
Why C: Fire is one of the main perils a standard homeowners policy covers, so it is not the event the question asks about.
Why D: Wind damage from storms is usually covered by standard homeowners insurance, though some coastal areas have separate wind deductibles, so it is not generally excluded.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is health insurance?
A: A savings plan meant for retirement
B: A discount at grocery stores near you
C: A loan to pay medical bills for you
D: Coverage for part of medical costs
Why A: A savings plan meant for retirement describes an IRA or 401(k), not health insurance, which is designed to share the costs of medical care.
Why B: A discount at grocery stores is a store loyalty program, and health insurance is a contract that pays part of your medical bills, not food costs.
Why C: A loan to pay medical bills is borrowing that must be repaid in full, whereas health insurance spreads costs through premiums and pays part of the bills.
Why D: Health insurance is coverage in which an insurer pays part of your medical costs in return for premiums, reducing your exposure to large and unexpected bills.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copayment (copay)?
A: A fixed amount you pay for a covered service, such as a doctor visit
B: The monthly amount you pay to keep your insurance policy active
C: The amount you must pay before your insurance starts to pay
D: A tax on medical care that patients pay each year to the state
Why A: A copay is a fixed amount you pay for a covered service, such as a $25 doctor visit, and the insurer then pays the rest of the allowed charge.
Why B: The monthly amount paid to keep a policy active is the premium; a copay is a separate fixed fee paid when you receive a service.
Why C: The amount paid before coverage begins is a deductible; a copay is a fixed fee paid for a covered service, such as a doctor visit.
Why D: A tax on medical care paid to the state is not a copay; a copay is paid to the provider under your insurance plan, not to the government.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is coinsurance in health insurance?
A: A flat fee paid at every visit to the doctor's office
B: A percentage of costs you share after the deductible
C: The monthly premium payment you make to the insurer
D: A fine for using an out-of-network doctor for care
Why A: A flat fee at every visit describes a copayment, not coinsurance, which is a percentage of the cost rather than a fixed dollar amount.
Why B: Coinsurance is a percentage of covered costs that you share with the insurer after meeting the deductible, such as paying 20% while the plan pays 80%.
Why C: The monthly premium is the regular price paid to keep the policy active, whereas coinsurance is a percentage share of costs when you actually use care.
Why D: A fine for using an out-of-network doctor is a penalty or higher cost-sharing, and it is not the same thing as coinsurance, a percentage share of covered costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an out-of-pocket maximum?
A: The total of your premiums for each year
B: The most an insurer will pay in a lifetime
C: The least you must pay for insurance each year
D: The most you pay in a year for covered care
Why A: The total of premiums for the year is what you pay to keep coverage, but the out-of-pocket maximum counts only deductibles, copays and coinsurance for covered care.
Why B: The most an insurer will pay in a lifetime is a lifetime benefit limit, which caps the insurer's payments and is different from the cap on what you pay.
Why C: The least you must pay for insurance each year is not a defined term, whereas an out-of-pocket maximum is a ceiling on what you pay, not a floor.
Why D: An out-of-pocket maximum is the most you pay in a year for covered care, after which the insurer pays 100% of covered costs, protecting you from catastrophic bills.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is life insurance?
A: Coverage paying beneficiaries when the insured dies
B: Coverage that pays for car repairs after a crash
C: Coverage that pays for health care when you fall ill
D: Coverage that pays when you retire from your job
Why A: Life insurance pays a death benefit to chosen beneficiaries when the insured person dies, which helps replace income and cover expenses such as funerals, debts and daily living costs.
Why B: Coverage that pays for car repairs after a crash is auto insurance, specifically collision coverage, and it has no relation to the death of the insured.
Why C: Coverage that pays for health care when you fall ill is health insurance, a separate product from life insurance, which pays out only upon death.
Why D: A payment when you retire from your job comes from a pension or retirement plan, while life insurance pays beneficiaries after the death of the insured person.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between term life and whole life insurance?
A: Term builds cash value you can borrow against; whole life does not
B: Term covers a lifetime; whole life covers a set period of years
C: Term covers a set period; whole life covers a lifetime and builds cash value
D: Both pay the death benefit to the owner while the insured is alive
Why A: Whole life is the policy that builds cash value you can borrow against; term insurance is pure protection for a set period and builds none.
Why B: This swaps the two products; term insurance covers a set number of years, while whole life covers the insured for life and builds cash value.
Why C: Term life covers a set period such as 20 years, while whole life covers the insured's lifetime and builds cash value, which makes whole life much more expensive.
Why D: A death benefit is paid to the beneficiary after the insured dies, not to the owner during life, and both term and whole life pay it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is disability insurance?
A: Coverage that pays your taxes in full each year
B: Coverage replacing income if you cannot work
C: Coverage that pays for a new car after a crash
D: Coverage that pays for vacations and trips
Why A: Paying your taxes in full each year is not what disability insurance does; it replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you working.
Why B: Disability insurance replaces a portion of your income if you cannot work because of illness or injury, which helps you pay bills during a long recovery.
Why C: Paying for a new car after a crash is the job of auto insurance, specifically collision coverage, and disability insurance covers lost income instead.
Why D: Paying for vacations and trips is not covered by insurance for disability; travel insurance is a different product, and disability coverage is meant to replace lost wages.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an umbrella policy?
A: Extra liability coverage beyond other limits
B: Coverage for storm damage to a home
C: Coverage for jewelry and valuables
D: Coverage for your medical bills after illness
Why A: An umbrella policy provides extra liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies, protecting your assets against large lawsuits or claims that exceed those limits.
Why B: Storm damage to a home falls under homeowners insurance; an umbrella policy adds extra liability protection above the limits of other policies.
Why C: Coverage for jewelry and valuables is personal property insurance; an umbrella policy provides extra liability coverage once other policy limits are used up.
Why D: Medical bills are paid by health insurance; an umbrella policy is extra liability coverage that protects assets from large lawsuits above other limits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is risk avoidance?
A: Setting aside savings for a possible loss in the future
B: Buying insurance to cover a loss from fire, theft or flood overall
C: Reducing the chance of a loss by taking safety steps first
D: Choosing not to engage in an activity that could cause a loss
Why A: Setting aside savings for a possible loss is risk retention, because you plan to pay the loss yourself, rather than avoiding the activity altogether.
Why B: Buying insurance to cover fire, theft or flood losses is risk transfer, since the insurer takes on the financial burden, rather than avoiding the risk.
Why C: Reducing the chance of a loss by taking safety steps is risk reduction, such as installing smoke detectors, rather than avoiding the activity altogether.
Why D: Risk avoidance means choosing not to engage in an activity that could cause a loss, such as not skydiving, which removes the chance of that loss entirely.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is risk transfer?
A: Avoiding a risky activity entirely for good
B: Reducing risk through safety steps in daily life
C: Shifting the financial burden to an insurer
D: Accepting the risk and paying losses yourself
Why A: Avoiding a risky activity entirely is risk avoidance, in which you remove the exposure, whereas risk transfer moves the financial burden to someone else.
Why B: Reducing risk through safety steps is risk reduction, such as wearing seat belts, which lowers the chance or size of loss rather than shifting it.
Why C: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, most often an insurer, in exchange for paying a premium to the company.
Why D: Accepting the risk and paying losses yourself is risk retention, which is the opposite of transfer because the cost stays with you instead of moving elsewhere.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is risk retention?
A: Avoiding the risky activity altogether for good
B: Installing safety devices in the home or car
C: Accepting a risk and paying losses yourself
D: Buying insurance so an insurer pays the loss
Why A: Avoiding the risky activity altogether is risk avoidance, in which you eliminate the exposure, rather than retention, in which you accept the risk.
Why B: Installing safety devices in the home or car is risk reduction, because it lowers the chance or size of loss rather than accepting the whole risk.
Why C: Risk retention means knowingly accepting a risk and paying any resulting losses yourself, often through savings or a deductible, instead of insuring or avoiding it.
Why D: Buying insurance so an insurer pays the loss is risk transfer, because it moves the cost to another party, which is the opposite of retention.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is risk reduction?
A: Steps that lower the chance or size of loss
B: Refusing to participate in any risky activity
C: Ignoring the risk altogether and hoping
D: Paying a premium so an insurer takes the loss
Why A: Risk reduction means taking steps that lower the chance or size of a loss, such as installing smoke alarms or driving carefully, while still carrying the activity.
Why B: Refusing to take part in any risky activity is risk avoidance, which removes the exposure completely rather than lowering the chance or size of a loss.
Why C: Ignoring the risk and hoping nothing happens is not a strategy; it is neglect, and it does nothing to lower the chance or size of a loss.
Why D: Paying a premium so an insurer takes the loss is risk transfer, which moves the financial burden to another party rather than reducing the chance of loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A family installs smoke detectors and a fire extinguisher at home. Which risk strategy is this?
A: Risk avoidance
B: Risk retention
C: Risk transfer
D: Risk reduction
Why A: Risk avoidance would mean not owning the home or not using fire at all, but installing detectors keeps the home and lowers the danger instead.
Why B: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying losses yourself, but detectors and extinguishers are active steps to reduce the loss, not simply accepting it.
Why C: Risk transfer would mean buying insurance so an insurer pays the loss, while detectors and extinguishers are safety equipment that the family owns and uses itself.
Why D: Installing smoke detectors and a fire extinguisher lowers the chance and damage of a fire, which is risk reduction, a strategy of taking safety steps.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an insurance exclusion?
A: A discount for good behavior on the road
B: A situation the policy does not cover
C: The amount you pay each month for cover
D: A cap on the number of claims you make
Why A: A discount for good behavior on the road is a safe driver discount that lowers a premium, which is the opposite of an exclusion that limits coverage.
Why B: An exclusion is a situation, event or item that the policy specifically does not cover, such as flood damage in a standard homeowners policy.
Why C: The amount paid each month for cover is the premium, which keeps the policy in force, and an exclusion is a limit on what the policy covers.
Why D: A cap on the number of claims is a claim limit, which differs from an exclusion, an event or cause the policy never covers at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stock?
A: A promise to repay a debt on time
B: A deposit held at a bank or a union
C: A loan made to a company by a lender
D: A share of ownership in a company
Why A: A promise to repay a debt on time describes a bond or loan, where you are a lender, and a stock gives ownership instead of a repayment promise.
Why B: A deposit held at a bank or credit union is a savings product that earns interest, not a share of ownership in a business like a stock.
Why C: A loan made to a company by a lender is debt, such as a bond, whereas a stock buyer becomes a part owner, not a creditor.
Why D: A stock is a share of ownership in a company, so stockholders can profit from price gains and dividends and may have voting rights on company matters.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bond?
A: A type of insurance policy for assets that pays on damage
B: A share of ownership in a public company or a large firm
C: A loan made by an investor to a company or government
D: A savings account at a local bank or credit union near you
Why A: A type of insurance policy that pays on damage is not a bond; a bond is a debt security issued to raise money, not a protection contract.
Why B: A share of ownership in a public company is a stock, not a bond, because bondholders are lenders and do not become owners of the firm.
Why C: A bond is a loan made by an investor to a company or government, which pays interest over time and returns the principal at maturity.
Why D: A savings account at a local bank is a deposit product held by the bank, whereas a bond is a security sold to investors by a borrower.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mutual fund?
A: A savings account with a fixed rate of interest, insured
B: A pool of investors' money buying a mix of securities
C: A single stock held by one person or one firm only
D: A loan from a group of friends or family members
Why A: A savings account with a fixed rate and insurance is a bank deposit, not a mutual fund, which holds securities whose value can rise or fall.
Why B: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and uses it to buy a diversified mix of securities such as stocks and bonds, managed by professionals.
Why C: A single stock held by one person is direct ownership, whereas a mutual fund pools many investors' money and holds many securities, giving broader diversification.
Why D: A loan from a group of friends or family is informal borrowing and has no connection to a mutual fund, which invests pooled money in securities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an exchange-traded fund (ETF)?
A: A basket of securities traded like a stock
B: A loan sold on the stock exchange to buyers
C: A single company's bond held by one investor
D: A bank account that pays no interest at all
Why A: An ETF is a basket of securities, such as stocks or bonds, that trades on an exchange like a single stock, so its price changes all day.
Why B: A loan sold on the stock exchange is a debt security, not an ETF, which holds a basket of investments and trades like a stock.
Why C: A single company's bond held by one investor is one security, but an ETF holds many securities in one fund, which gives diversification.
Why D: An ETF is an investment fund and not a bank account; it holds securities that can rise or fall, while bank accounts typically pay at least some interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a dividend?
A: Interest paid on a bank deposit
B: A tax paid on stock gains each year
C: A fee paid to a broker each year
D: A share of company profits paid out
Why A: Interest paid on a bank deposit is the return on a savings account, whereas a dividend is a share of a company's profit paid to shareholders.
Why B: A tax paid on stock gains is a capital gains tax owed to the government, whereas a dividend is money the company pays to shareholders.
Why C: A fee paid to a broker each year is a cost paid by the investor, but a dividend is a payment the investor receives from a company.
Why D: A dividend is a portion of a company's profits paid out to shareholders, usually in cash on a regular schedule such as every quarter.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a capital gain?
A: A dividend paid by a company to its owners
B: Profit from selling an asset above its cost
C: Interest paid on a savings account each month
D: Money earned from a paycheck at a job each week
Why A: A dividend paid by a company to its owners is income from profits, which differs from a capital gain, the profit made by selling an asset higher.
Why B: A capital gain is the profit you make when you sell an asset, such as a stock or a house, for more than you paid for it.
Why C: Interest paid on a savings account each month is interest income, not a capital gain, because no asset was sold at a higher price.
Why D: Money earned from a weekly paycheck is wage income from working, whereas a capital gain comes from selling an asset for more than its purchase cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a capital loss?
A: A bank fee for low balance on a checking account
B: A drop in your paycheck from a job each week
C: A loss from selling below the purchase price
D: A tax refund that the government sends back
Why A: A bank fee for a low balance is a service charge on an account, and a capital loss comes from selling an investment at a lower price.
Why B: A drop in your paycheck is a reduction in wages, not a capital loss, which arises only when you sell an asset for less than you paid.
Why C: A capital loss occurs when you sell an asset, such as a stock, for less than its purchase price, and it may offset taxable gains.
Why D: A tax refund sent back by the government is money returned to you, so it is the opposite of a loss and is unrelated to capital losses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does dollar-cost averaging mean?
A: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
B: Waiting for the lowest price to buy shares
C: Investing everything at once on a hunch alone
D: Selling shares when prices fall to a low level
Why A: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, such as monthly, regardless of price, so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when high.
Why B: Waiting for the lowest price to buy is market timing, which is very hard to do and is the opposite of investing on a fixed schedule.
Why C: Investing everything at once on a hunch is a lump sum approach based on a guess, whereas dollar-cost averaging spreads purchases over time at regular intervals.
Why D: Selling shares when prices fall locks in losses and is the reverse of dollar-cost averaging, which continues buying a fixed amount at regular intervals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor puts $100 into a fund each month. Prices are $10, $20, then $10. What happens to the average cost per share compared with the average price?
A: The average cost equals the highest price paid during the whole period
B: The average cost cannot be known until the fund is sold by the investor
C: The average cost is lower, because more shares are bought when prices are low
D: The average cost per share is the same, because the same amount is spent each month
Why A: The highest price paid is $20, but you spend the same $100 each month and buy more shares at $10, so your average cost is well below $20.
Why B: The average cost can be calculated at any time as total dollars spent divided by total shares bought, so it does not depend on selling the fund.
Why C: You buy 10, 5 and 10 shares for $300 total, an average cost of $12, which is below the $13.33 average price, because more shares are bought when prices are low.
Why D: Spending the same amount each month does not make the average cost equal to the average price; $300 buys 25 shares, an average cost of $12, below the average price of $13.33.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is asset allocation?
A: Selling all investments at once to raise cash
B: Choosing the cheapest broker in the whole market
C: Putting everything into one stock that will surely rise
D: Dividing investments among stocks, bonds and cash
Why A: Selling all investments at once to raise cash is liquidation, not asset allocation, which means deciding how to divide your money among asset classes.
Why B: Choosing the cheapest broker is a cost decision about where to invest, but asset allocation is about how to divide money among types of investments.
Why C: Putting everything into one stock is the opposite of allocating across assets, and no stock is certain to rise, so this concentrates the risk heavily.
Why D: Asset allocation means dividing your investments among asset classes such as stocks, bonds and cash, so the mix matches your goals, time horizon and risk tolerance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is rebalancing a portfolio?
A: Selling everything and starting over each year
B: Adjusting holdings back to the target mix of assets
C: Buying only the best performer of the past year
D: Ignoring the portfolio for years and years on end overall
Why A: Selling everything and starting over each year is a costly restart that triggers taxes and fees, whereas rebalancing only adjusts holdings back toward a target mix.
Why B: Rebalancing means adjusting your holdings back to your target mix of assets, such as selling some winners and buying laggards, to keep your intended risk level.
Why C: Buying only last year's best performer chases past returns and concentrates risk, which is the opposite of restoring a balanced target mix of assets.
Why D: Ignoring a portfolio for years lets the mix drift away from its target and changes risk, so it is the opposite of rebalancing, which is regular maintenance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which investor would most likely hold a higher share of stocks?
A: A young investor saving for retirement in 40 years
B: A person saving for a car to buy next year or soon
C: A person with no time to wait for any gains at all
D: A retiree who needs the money next month for costs
Why A: A young investor saving for retirement 40 years away has a long time horizon to ride out market dips, so a higher share of stocks suits them.
Why B: Someone saving for a car purchase next year needs the money soon and cannot wait out a market drop, so safer assets suit them better than stocks.
Why C: A person with no time to wait for gains has a short horizon, which makes volatile stocks risky for them, so they would hold fewer stocks.
Why D: A retiree who needs money next month for costs requires stable, liquid assets and cannot risk a stock decline, so a high share of stocks is unsuitable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a time horizon?
A: How long an investor expects to hold before needing money
B: The time it takes to open an account at a bank branch
C: The time a stock market is open each day for trading
D: The date a company was founded and first listed for sale overall
Why A: A time horizon is how long an investor expects to keep money invested before needing it, which helps decide how much risk to take.
Why B: The time it takes to open an account is a matter of paperwork and has nothing to do with how long money stays invested before it is needed.
Why C: The hours a stock market is open each day are trading hours, which are separate from an investor's time horizon, the length of time until money is needed.
Why D: The date a company was founded and listed is company history, not the investor's time horizon, which is about how long the investor expects to hold money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is risk tolerance?
A: How much a stock paid last year in total
B: How many accounts a person holds in banks
C: How much a person earns each year from a job
D: How much loss an investor can accept calmly
Why A: How much a stock paid last year is its past dividend or return, which says nothing about how much loss an investor can accept calmly.
Why B: How many accounts a person holds describes their account count, and it does not measure their ability or willingness to accept investment losses without panic.
Why C: How much a person earns each year is income, and while it affects risk capacity, it is not the same as risk tolerance, which is about comfort with loss.
Why D: Risk tolerance is how much loss, or how large a swing in value, an investor can accept calmly, without panicking and selling at the worst time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an employer match in a 401(k)?
A: A fine for contributing too much to the plan
B: Money the employer adds to your contributions
C: A loan from the employer that you must repay
D: A tax paid on contributions to the account
Why A: An employer match is not a fine; contributing more than the plan limit may bring a tax penalty, but the match is a benefit the company adds.
Why B: An employer match is money the employer adds to your 401(k) contributions, often a percentage of your pay, which is effectively free money and boosts retirement savings.
Why C: A loan from the employer that you must repay is a plan loan, whereas an employer match is a contribution you keep and do not repay.
Why D: A tax paid on contributions is not an employer match; a match is extra money the employer adds to your account to reward saving.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Your employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. You earn $40,000 and contribute 6%. How much does the employer add?
Why A: $2,400 is the full 6% of salary that you contribute ($40,000 x 0.06); the employer adds only 50% of that amount, which is $1,200, not the whole $2,400.
Why B: $4,800 would be 12% of salary or double your contribution; the employer matches half of your $2,400, so it adds only $1,200, which is far less.
Why C: You contribute 6% of $40,000, which is $2,400, and the employer matches 50% of that, so it adds $2,400 x 0.5 = $1,200.
Why D: $600 would be 50% of a 3% contribution; you actually contribute 6%, or $2,400, and the match is 50% of that, so the employer adds $1,200.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an IRA?
A: A bank loan for retirees who own their homes outright
B: An insurance policy for retirement paying out at sixty-five
C: A retirement account anyone with earned income can open
D: A government tax form used to report retirement income
Why A: An IRA is not a bank loan for retirees; it is an account for saving for retirement, and no one borrows money through it.
Why B: An IRA is an account that holds investments, not an insurance policy that pays out at sixty-five, and the balance depends on contributions and investment growth.
Why C: An IRA is an individual retirement account that anyone with earned income can open, with tax advantages depending on whether it is a traditional or Roth IRA.
Why D: A government tax form to report retirement income is something like Form 1099-R, whereas an IRA is an actual account where retirement savings are held.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main feature of a Roth IRA?
A: Contributions are tax-deductible now and retirement withdrawals are taxed
B: You must begin taking required withdrawals at age 73
C: It is a plan offered by an employer with a company match
D: Contributions are after-tax money and qualified withdrawals are tax-free
Why A: Tax-deductible contributions with taxed withdrawals describe a traditional IRA, not a Roth IRA, which reverses the timing and taxes money before it goes in.
Why B: Roth IRAs have no required withdrawals during the owner's life; the main feature is after-tax contributions with tax-free qualified withdrawals in retirement.
Why C: A Roth IRA is opened by an individual with earned income, not offered through an employer, and there is no company match on contributions.
Why D: A Roth IRA is funded with after-tax money, so contributions are not deductible, but qualified withdrawals in retirement, including the growth, come out tax-free.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main feature of a traditional IRA?
A: Contributions may be deductible and withdrawals in retirement are taxed
B: Contributions are limited to the amount your employer matches
C: It pays a fixed interest rate set by the federal government
D: Contributions are made after tax and retirement withdrawals are tax-free
Why A: A traditional IRA allows tax-deductible contributions for many savers, with withdrawals in retirement taxed as income, so you get the tax break now and pay later.
Why B: IRA contribution limits are set yearly by law and are not tied to an employer match, which is a feature of workplace plans like a 401(k).
Why C: An IRA is an account type, not an investment with a set rate; returns depend on what the saver invests in, and the government sets no rate.
Why D: Contributions made with after-tax dollars and tax-free withdrawals describe a Roth IRA, which reverses the tax timing of a traditional IRA, so it is the wrong account.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What penalty usually applies to early withdrawals from retirement accounts before age 59½?
A: A 1% bonus paid to you each year
B: A 10% extra tax plus income tax
C: A free refund of the tax you paid
D: No penalty, as the money is yours
Why A: An early withdrawal does not earn a 1% bonus; retirement accounts discourage early withdrawals with penalties, and no bonus is paid for taking money before 59 and a half.
Why B: Withdrawing from a retirement account before age 59 and a half usually brings an extra 10% tax penalty on top of ordinary income tax owed.
Why C: A free refund of the tax you paid is not given for early withdrawals; the government instead adds a penalty to discourage taking the money early.
Why D: There is generally a penalty, even though the money is yours, because the tax advantages are meant for retirement, so withdrawing early usually costs an extra 10%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a 529 plan?
A: A plan for buying insurance for the family
B: A loan program for homebuyers and renters
C: A retirement plan for employees of one firm
D: A tax-advantaged education savings plan
Why A: A plan for buying insurance for the family is not a 529; a 529 plan is a savings vehicle designed for education costs.
Why B: A loan program for homebuyers and renters is housing finance, whereas a 529 plan lets families save for education with tax advantages.
Why C: A retirement plan for employees of one firm describes a 401(k), whereas a 529 plan is used to save for education expenses.
Why D: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings plan for education costs, where earnings grow tax-deferred and withdrawals for qualified education expenses are tax-free.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an annuity?
A: A fee for opening an IRA account at a bank
B: A short-term stock trade made within a day
C: A contract paying income, often in retirement
D: A type of checking account that pays a flat fee
Why A: A fee for opening an IRA account is an account charge, whereas an annuity is a contract with an insurer that pays out income over time.
Why B: A short-term stock trade made within a day is day trading, which is a speculative activity and not a contract that pays regular income.
Why C: An annuity is a contract, usually with an insurance company, that pays a stream of income, often used to provide steady money in retirement.
Why D: A type of checking account that pays a flat fee is not an annuity; an annuity is an insurance contract that pays income over time.
