Why D: Your own accidents regardless of fault describe collision coverage, but uninsured motorist coverage only applies when another driver without insurance causes the harm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is homeowners insurance?
A: A mortgage payment you make to your bank each month in general
B: A property tax charged on land and buildings owned
C: A policy for renters who lease flats from landlords
D: A policy that covers the home, belongings and liability
Why A: A mortgage payment repays a home loan to a bank, which differs from homeowners insurance, a policy that protects the house and belongings.
Why B: A property tax is charged by the local government on land and buildings, and it is not insurance, which protects against loss.
Why C: A policy for renters is renters insurance, which covers belongings and liability of tenants, while homeowners insurance is meant for those who own the home.
Why D: Homeowners insurance covers damage to the home, personal belongings and liability for injuries on the property, up to policy limits and subject to exclusions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does whole life insurance provide?
A: Coverage that pays medical bills for illness
B: Income replacement if the owner becomes disabled
C: Lifelong coverage with a cash value component
D: Coverage for a set term, ending after some years
Why A: Paying medical bills describes health insurance; whole life insurance pays a death benefit and builds cash value over the insured's lifetime.
Why B: Replacing income after a disability is what disability insurance does; whole life pays a death benefit to the beneficiary and builds cash value.
Why C: Whole life provides coverage for your entire life as long as premiums are paid, and it builds a cash value that you can borrow against.
Why D: Coverage for a set term ending after some years is term life insurance, which is different from whole life that lasts for life.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Who is a beneficiary on a life insurance policy?
A: The insurer that issues the policy to you
B: The person who receives the death benefit
C: The doctor who treats the insured person
D: The agent who sold you the life policy
Why A: The insurer is the company that issues the policy and pays the claim, whereas the beneficiary is the person who receives the payout.
Why B: The beneficiary is the person or entity named in the policy to receive the death benefit when the insured person dies.
Why C: A doctor treats the insured person and has no claim to the benefit, so the doctor is not the beneficiary.
Why D: The agent who sold the policy earns a commission and is not the beneficiary, who is the person named to receive the payout.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of insurance?
A: To prevent all losses from ever happening to the policyholder
B: To transfer the financial risk of a loss to an insurer for a premium
C: To avoid paying taxes on income earned by workers and by firms
D: To guarantee profits to every policyholder who buys a plan each year
Why A: Insurance cannot prevent losses from happening, since it only pays for part or all of the cost afterward, so the claim of preventing all losses is wrong.
Why B: The purpose of insurance is to transfer the financial risk of a possible loss to an insurer in exchange for paying a premium.
Why C: Insurance is not a way to avoid taxes, since premiums are a cost and the purpose is to cover losses and not to cut taxes.
Why D: Insurance does not guarantee profit to policyholders, because it pays only for covered losses, and most people pay premiums without ever filing a claim.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is self-insurance?
A: Borrowing from friends when a loss occurs, repaying later
B: Ignoring risk and hoping that no loss will occur
C: Buying a policy from an insurer to cover any loss
D: Setting aside money to cover potential losses yourself
Why A: Borrowing from friends after a loss is just taking a loan, whereas self-insurance means setting aside your own money in advance to cover possible losses.
Why B: Ignoring risk and hoping no loss occurs is not self-insurance, because there is no plan or funds ready to cover a loss.
Why C: Buying a policy from an insurer is ordinary insurance, which transfers risk, while self-insurance means you keep the risk and cover it yourself.
Why D: Self-insurance means setting aside money, such as an emergency fund, to pay for potential losses yourself rather than buying a policy from an insurer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Affordable Care Act marketplace?
A: A stock exchange for trading shares in public companies
B: A bank that lends money to people who need to buy health plans
C: An exchange where individuals can compare and buy health plans
D: A tax office that processes returns for the state each year
Why A: A stock exchange trades company shares, while the Affordable Care Act marketplace is a place to compare and buy health insurance plans.
Why B: The marketplace is not a bank and makes no loans, and it simply lets people shop for health plans and see any subsidies for which they qualify.
Why C: The marketplace is an exchange where individuals and families can compare and buy health plans, and many qualify for subsidies that lower the premium.
Why D: A tax office processes returns, but the marketplace is where health plans are chosen, and it is not a government revenue office.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a health maintenance organization (HMO)?
A: A plan that generally requires using in-network providers and referrals
B: A bank that holds the savings of members in a local area of a city
C: A plan with no network of doctors and no referrals needed at all
D: A pharmacy that sells medicines and health goods to the public each day
Why A: An HMO generally requires you to use in-network providers and to get referrals from a primary care doctor to see specialists, in exchange for lower costs.
Why B: An HMO is a type of health plan and not a bank, and it does not hold savings accounts for members.
Why C: A plan with no network and no referrals describes the opposite of an HMO, which depends on a defined network and referral rules.
Why D: An HMO is a health plan, not a pharmacy, so it does not sell medicines to the public, though it may cover prescriptions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a preferred provider organization (PPO)?
A: A plan with no coverage for doctors or hospitals in any network at all
B: A plan with more flexibility to see out-of-network providers at higher cost
C: A pharmacy that sells medicines and health goods to the public in town
D: A bank that lends money to patients who need to pay for their health plans overall
Why A: A plan with no coverage for doctors or hospitals would be pointless, whereas a PPO provides coverage and a network of preferred providers.
Why B: A PPO offers more flexibility, letting you see out-of-network providers without a referral, though you usually pay more than for in-network care.
Why C: A PPO is a health plan and not a pharmacy, so it does not sell medicines directly to people in town.
Why D: A PPO is a health plan and not a bank, and it does not lend money to patients to help pay for their own plans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is it important to keep financial records?
A: They prevent saving money for the future or for goals
B: They increase debt over time and cut your savings
C: They are never needed by anyone for any purpose at all overall
D: They support taxes, budgeting and proof of transactions
Why A: Records support saving and planning by showing where money goes, so claiming they prevent saving is false and goes against their purpose.
Why B: Good records help control debt and savings, and they do not increase debt, since tracking spending lets you spot problems and cut costs.
Why C: Records are needed for taxes, disputes, loans and insurance claims, so claiming no one ever needs them for any purpose is plainly false.
Why D: Keeping records supports filing taxes, budgeting and proving transactions, so you can track spending, resolve disputes and answer audits with evidence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How long should you generally keep tax returns and supporting documents?
A: Six months after you file, then they can be shredded
B: Until you receive your refund, then discard them
C: At least three years, longer in some cases
D: One year, since audits end after that
Why A: Six months is too short; the tax agency can audit returns for years, so documents should be kept at least three years and longer in some cases.
Why B: Receiving a refund does not end the audit window; you need your own records to support deductions if the agency asks questions years later.
Why C: The usual guidance is to keep returns and supporting documents at least three years, since that is the normal audit window, and longer in some cases.
Why D: Audits and amended returns can happen after one year; the usual guidance is to keep returns and supporting documents at least three years.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a will?
A: A legal document stating how your property is distributed after death
B: A tax return that reports a person's income to the government
C: A bank form that lets a customer name who else may use an account
D: A loan contract that sets the payments a borrower must repay each month
Why A: A will is a legal document that states how your property is to be distributed after your death and who will manage the estate.
Why B: A tax return reports income and taxes to the government, and it is unrelated to the distribution of property after death.
Why C: A bank form that lets someone use an account describes a joint account or authorized user agreement, which is different from a will.
Why D: A loan contract sets the repayment terms for a borrower, while a will states how your belongings are passed on after you die.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Alex owns assets worth $60,000 and owes $22,000. What is Alex's net worth?
Why A: $82,000 adds the debts to the assets, but net worth is assets minus liabilities, so you subtract the $22,000 owed from the $60,000 owned.
Why B: Net worth equals assets minus liabilities, so $60,000 minus $22,000 gives $38,000, which is what Alex would have left after paying every debt.
Why C: $60,000 is only the value of Alex's assets, and it ignores the $22,000 of debts that must be subtracted to find net worth.
Why D: $22,000 is only the amount Alex owes, and net worth requires subtracting that from the $60,000 of assets, giving $38,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an asset?
A: A credit card balance owed
B: A mortgage balance still owed
C: A student loan balance
D: A savings account balance
Why A: A credit card balance owed is money you must pay to the issuer, which makes it a liability and not an asset.
Why B: A mortgage balance still owed is a debt to the lender, so it is a liability and not something you own.
Why C: A student loan balance is money you owe, so it is a liability that reduces your net worth rather than increasing it.
Why D: A savings account balance is money that you own and can use, so it is an asset that adds to your net worth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a liability?
A: A savings account
B: A house you own outright
C: An auto loan balance
D: A retirement account
Why A: A savings account is money you own, so it is an asset and not a liability, since you do not owe it to anyone.
Why B: A house you own outright is something of value that you hold, so it is an asset, and no debt remains on it.
Why C: An auto loan balance is money you owe to a lender, which makes it a liability that subtracts from your net worth.
Why D: A retirement account holds savings that belong to you, so it is an asset and not a debt that you owe.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a SMART financial goal?
A: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
B: Secret, mild, active, rare and trivial goals for each year
C: Sudden, major, awkward, rich and thin goals for each year
D: Simple, minor, average, random and tiny, for a short plan
Why A: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, which makes it clear enough to plan for and to track over time.
Why B: Secret, mild, active, rare and trivial do not describe SMART goals, since secret and trivial goals would be hard to plan or measure.
Why C: Sudden, major, awkward, rich and thin are not the SMART terms, and these words would not help anyone set a workable goal.
Why D: Simple, minor, average, random and tiny are not what the letters stand for, which are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best SMART goal?
A: Spend less money on random things whenever it is possible to do so as a rule
B: Save $1,800 for a laptop by December by setting aside $150 per month
C: Be rich someday, with no plan and no clear way to reach the goal
D: Save more someday when you have the time and a spare moment or two
Why A: Spending less on random things is vague, with no amount or deadline, so it is not specific, measurable or time-bound, and fails the SMART test.
Why B: Saving $1,800 for a laptop by December at $150 a month is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, since 12 months times $150 equals $1,800.
Why C: Being rich someday has no amount, plan or deadline, so it is neither specific nor measurable and does not meet the SMART standard.
Why D: Saving more someday has no amount and no date, which makes it vague and impossible to measure, so it is not a SMART goal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a short-term financial goal?
A: A goal that takes thirty years to reach
B: A goal with no set timeline at all, ever
C: A goal for retirement in forty years
D: A goal to achieve within about a year
Why A: A goal that takes thirty years to reach is a long-term goal, not a short-term one, which is reached within about a year.
Why B: A goal with no timeline is not short-term, because short-term goals have a clear timeframe, and having no end date makes progress hard to track.
Why C: A goal for retirement in forty years is a long-term goal, since short-term goals are completed in about a year or less.
Why D: A short-term financial goal is one you aim to reach within about a year, such as building a small emergency fund or paying off a card.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a long-term financial goal?
A: A weekend purchase of a movie ticket or a meal out overall
B: Saving for lunch or a snack at the end of the week
C: A goal that takes many years to reach, such as retirement
D: A monthly bill paid to a utility company or lender
Why A: A weekend movie ticket or meal out is a small near-term expense, so it is a short-term spending item and not a long-term goal.
Why B: Saving for lunch or a snack at the end of the week is a very short-term need and not a goal that takes years.
Why C: A long-term financial goal takes many years to reach, such as retirement, buying a home or paying for a child's college education.
Why D: A monthly bill paid to a utility or lender is a recurring expense and not a goal, and it is settled within weeks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is opportunity cost in personal finance?
A: The value of the next best alternative you give up
B: The price of a product at the time it is bought overall
C: The interest on a loan or credit card balance
D: The sales tax on a purchase made at the store
Why A: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice, such as the other way you could spend money.
Why B: The price of a product at purchase is its cost, and opportunity cost is the value of what you give up by choosing it.
Why C: Interest on a loan or card balance is a financing cost, which is a real payment and is different from the value of a forgone alternative.
Why D: Sales tax is an added charge on a purchase and is a cost you actually pay, while opportunity cost concerns the alternative you give up.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a scam?
A: A legitimate investment offered by a registered firm
B: A bank statement showing deposits and withdrawals
C: A deceptive scheme to steal money or information
D: A government benefit paid to people who qualify
Why A: A legitimate investment from a registered firm is lawful and transparent, so it is the opposite of a scam, which aims to deceive.
Why B: A bank statement is an ordinary record of deposits and withdrawals, and it is a true account of activity and not a deceptive scheme.
Why C: A scam is a deceptive scheme meant to steal money or personal information, often by posing as a trusted business, agency or person.
Why D: A government benefit paid to qualifying people is a lawful program and not a trick, so it is not a scam.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: You get a text saying your bank account is locked and to click a link to log in. What should you do?
A: Reply with your PIN and the number on the front of your card
B: Click the link at once to unlock your account before it is closed
C: Forward it to friends and ask them to check the link for you
D: Contact the bank using a known phone number or app, not the link
Why A: Replying with your PIN and the number on your card gives a criminal what is needed to steal from you, so never do that.
Why B: Clicking the link at once is exactly what the scammer wants, because the link probably leads to a fake site that steals your login details.
Why C: Forwarding the message to friends spreads the scam and puts them at risk, and they cannot safely judge a suspicious link for you.
Why D: Contact the bank using a phone number or app you already know and trust, not the link in the text, which may be a phishing attempt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A promise of guaranteed high returns with no risk is a sign of:
A: Possible investment fraud
B: A government bond fund
C: A bank savings product
D: A safe, high-return plan
Why A: Guaranteed high returns with no risk are a classic sign of possible investment fraud, because real investments with higher returns always carry some risk of loss.
Why B: A government bond fund is a real investment with modest returns and some risk, and it does not promise guaranteed high returns without risk.
Why C: A bank savings product pays modest interest and is insured up to limits, and it does not promise high returns without any risk.
Why D: A safe, high-return plan with no risk does not exist in legitimate markets, because higher returns come with higher risk, so the promise is a warning sign.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a strong password practice?
A: Sharing it with friends so they can log in for you whenever they like
B: Using a long, unique password for each account with a password manager
C: Keeping it in a text file named passwords on your desktop
D: Using a favorite word with a number added at the end
Why A: Sharing a password with friends lets others access your accounts and money, and it is unsafe even if you trust them.
Why B: A long, unique password for each account, stored in a password manager, means one breach cannot unlock your other accounts, so this is the strong practice.
Why C: A plainly named text file is easy for malware or anyone with access to the computer to find, so it offers little protection for your accounts.
Why D: A word with a number added is easy to guess and often reused; a strong password is long and unique for each account.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is two-factor authentication?
A: Logging in twice with the same password each time you visit
B: Using two passwords of different lengths for the one account overall
C: Using two forms of proof, such as a password and a code, to log in
D: Using two banks at once to hold your funds for extra safety
Why A: Logging in twice with the same password is still one factor, because both entries rely on the same secret that could be stolen.
Why B: Two passwords of different lengths are still the same kind of factor, something you know, so this does not meet the two-factor idea.
Why C: Two-factor authentication requires two different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code sent to your phone, which makes stolen passwords far less useful.
Why D: Holding funds at two banks is a way of spreading money around and has nothing to do with proving your identity at login.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)?
A: A bank that lends money to the general public of the nation
B: A credit bureau that tracks the scores of consumers and firms overall
C: A stock exchange that lists the shares of public companies
D: A federal agency that protects consumers in financial products
Why A: The CFPB is a federal agency and not a bank, so it does not lend money to the public, and its role is protection.
Why B: Credit bureaus such as Equifax, Experian and TransUnion track credit scores, whereas the CFPB is a regulator that oversees how financial companies treat consumers.
Why C: A stock exchange lists shares of public companies, and the CFPB is a consumer protection agency that does not run a market.
Why D: The CFPB is a federal agency that protects consumers in financial products and services, taking complaints and enforcing rules on lenders, banks and credit reporting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an annual percentage rate on a credit card most closely tied to?
A: The rewards rate paid on the card
B: The yearly cost of carrying a balance
C: The credit limit set for the card
D: The annual fee only, charged once a year
Why A: The rewards rate is what you earn back on purchases and is a separate feature, not the interest rate measured by the APR.
Why B: The APR reflects the yearly cost of carrying a balance on the card, and it shows how much interest you pay if you do not pay in full.
Why C: The credit limit is the most you can borrow on the card, and it is not what the annual percentage rate measures.
Why D: The annual fee is a separate flat charge, whereas the APR is about interest, so it is not tied only to the yearly fee.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an annual fee?
A: A yearly charge some credit cards impose for having the card
B: A late fee charged when a payment is made after its due date
C: Interest on balances that are carried over from month to month
D: A tax charged by the government on each credit card each year
Why A: An annual fee is a yearly charge that some credit cards impose simply for holding the card, whether or not you carry a balance.
Why B: A late fee is charged when a payment arrives after its due date, which is a different charge from the yearly fee for having a card.
Why C: Interest on balances carried from month to month is the finance charge, and the annual fee is a separate flat yearly cost.
Why D: An annual fee is set by the card issuer and is not a government tax, so the claim that it is a tax is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which strategy pays off multiple debts fastest in interest terms?
A: Paying the lowest-interest debt first, clearing the smallest rate
B: Paying only minimums on all of the debts each month for years
C: Paying extra toward the highest-interest debt first (avalanche)
D: Ignoring debts and hoping they go away on their own someday
Why A: Paying the lowest-interest debt first leaves the costliest balances growing faster, so you pay more interest overall than if you target the highest rate.
Why B: Paying only minimums on all debts keeps balances alive for years and lets interest pile up, which is slower and more costly than extra payments.
Why C: The avalanche method puts extra money toward the highest-interest debt first while paying minimums elsewhere, which cuts total interest cost and clears debt fastest in dollar terms.
Why D: Ignoring debts lets interest and fees grow and can lead to collections and credit damage, so debts never go away on their own.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the debt snowball method?
A: Skipping payments for several months in a row or more
B: Paying off the smallest debts first to build momentum
C: Taking on more debt each month to cover the old debts
D: Paying off the largest debt first, whatever the rest are
Why A: Skipping payments brings late fees, interest and credit damage, so it does not help clear debt and is not the snowball method.
Why B: The debt snowball method pays off the smallest debts first while making minimum payments on the others, which builds momentum and motivation as each balance disappears.
Why C: Taking on more debt each month to cover old debts only grows the problem, so it is the reverse of the snowball method.
Why D: Paying off the largest debt first is not the snowball method, which begins with the smallest balance, to build momentum through quick wins.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is bankruptcy?
A: A legal process for people who cannot repay debts
B: A tax credit for people who owe a great deal of tax
C: A savings plan for people who want to build wealth
D: A type of loan offered to people with poor credit
Why A: Bankruptcy is a court process that lets people or businesses who cannot repay their debts get relief by discharging or restructuring what they owe.
Why B: A tax credit reduces tax owed and has nothing to do with court proceedings for debts that someone is unable to repay.
Why C: A savings plan builds wealth over time, which is the opposite of bankruptcy, a legal remedy used after debts become unmanageable.
Why D: Bankruptcy is not a loan product at all, and poor-credit loans are just borrowing, not a court process for debt relief.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a student loan's key difference between federal and private?
A: Private loans offer income-driven repayment while federal loans depend on the lender
B: Federal loans are issued by colleges while private loans come from the government
C: Federal loans are forgiven after graduation while private loans must be repaid
D: Federal loans offer income-driven repayment while private loans depend on the lender
Why A: This swaps the two; federal loans carry government protections like income-driven repayment, while private loans vary by lender.
Why B: Federal student loans are funded by the government and private loans come from banks and other lenders, so this description reverses who issues them.
Why C: Federal loans must be repaid; they may be deferred or forgiven only under specific programs, not simply because the borrower graduates.
Why D: Federal loans come with government protections such as income-driven repayment, deferment and forgiveness options, while private loan terms are set by each lender.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does FAFSA stand for?
A: Free Application for Federal Student Aid
B: Free Account for Financial Savings Accounts
C: Funds for Americans' Student Aid fund
D: Federal Agency for Financial Student Accounts
Why A: FAFSA stands for Free Application for Federal Student Aid, the form used to apply for federal grants, work-study and student loans.
Why B: This invents a savings account meaning, but FAFSA is an aid application and has nothing to do with opening savings accounts.
Why C: This names a made-up fund, but FAFSA is an application form for federal aid, not a pool of money for Americans.
Why D: FAFSA is not a federal agency, and the word Application in the real name shows it is a form rather than an agency.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a scholarship?
A: A credit card with a rewards program attached
B: A student loan that must be repaid with interest overall
C: A tax on students who attend college each year
D: Money for education that does not need to be repaid
Why A: A credit card with rewards is a borrowing tool for purchases and carries no connection to money awarded to pay for education.
Why B: A student loan has to be repaid with interest, whereas a scholarship is a gift of money that never needs repayment.
Why C: Scholarships are awards paid to students, not a tax charged on them, so this reverses the actual meaning of the word.
Why D: A scholarship is money awarded for education based on merit, need or other criteria, and it does not have to be repaid.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a grant?
A: A credit line that must be repaid in full with interest, over a set term
B: Money given for education or projects that typically does not have to be repaid
C: A loan with interest that must be repaid in monthly installments to the bank in the end
D: A tax that students pay on the money they receive for college each year
Why A: A credit line repaid in full with interest describes a loan, while a grant is money given that normally needs no repayment.
Why B: A grant is money given for education or a project by a government or organization, and it typically does not have to be repaid.
Why C: A loan repaid in installments with interest describes borrowing, which is the opposite of a grant that does not usually require repayment.
Why D: Grants are not taxes charged to students; they are gifts of money for education, so this describes a levy instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a lease?
A: A loan to buy stock in a company that is listed on an exchange
B: Buying with cash at the time of sale, paying the full price up front
C: A contract to use property for a set period in exchange for payments
D: A tax form that must be filed by every renter in the state each year
Why A: Buying stock is an investment in a company, whereas a lease is a rental agreement for using property such as a car or apartment.
Why B: Paying the full price in cash at the time of sale is an outright purchase, while a lease is use of property over time.
Why C: A lease is a contract giving someone the right to use property, such as an apartment or car, for a set period in exchange for payments.
Why D: A tax form is a government filing, but a lease is a contract between owner and user, and renters are not all required to file one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a downside of leasing a car compared with buying?
A: You pay for major repairs after the warranty ends
B: You can sell the car to a buyer whenever you like
C: You do not build ownership and may face mileage limits
D: You must pay the full price of the car on signing day
Why A: Most leases are short enough to stay under warranty, so major repair bills are not the typical downside; the real drawbacks are no ownership and mileage limits.
Why B: A leased car belongs to the lessor, so you cannot sell it freely; lacking ownership is part of the downside of leasing.
Why C: Leasing builds no ownership, because you only pay to use the car, and mileage caps with penalties are common, which are real downsides.
Why D: Leases usually need only a smaller upfront payment plus monthly payments; paying the full price on signing day describes a cash purchase.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a down payment?
A: An upfront portion of the purchase price paid in cash
B: A late fee charged on a payment made after the due date
C: The final payment on a loan or a lease contract
D: Interest charged on a loan by the lender each year
Why A: A down payment is the portion of the purchase price paid upfront in cash, which lowers the amount that must be borrowed.
Why B: A late fee is a penalty for paying after the due date, and it is unrelated to the upfront money paid at purchase.
Why C: The final payment on a loan is a payoff or balloon payment made at the end, whereas a down payment is made at the start.
Why D: Interest is the lender's yearly charge for borrowing, and it is paid over time rather than as an upfront share of the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A $200,000 home requires a 10% down payment. How much is the down payment?
Why A: $180,000 is 90 percent of the home price, which is the amount financed after a 10 percent down payment, not the down payment itself.
Why B: Ten percent of $200,000 is 0.10 times 200,000, which equals $20,000, so that is the required down payment on the home.
Why C: $200,000 is the entire price of the home, which would be a 100 percent down payment, not the 10 percent required here.
Why D: $2,000 is only 1 percent of $200,000, so it comes from misplacing the decimal point when taking 10 percent of the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is private mortgage insurance (PMI)?
A: Insurance for the house against fire, wind and theft for the owner
B: Insurance for the borrower's death, paying off the mortgage
C: A tax on mortgages that lenders collect from borrowers each year
D: Insurance protecting the lender when the down payment is under 20%
Why A: Insurance on the house against fire, wind and theft is homeowners insurance, which protects the property, while PMI protects the lender.
Why B: Insurance that pays off a mortgage when the borrower dies is mortgage life insurance, a different product from PMI, which covers lender default risk.
Why C: PMI is an insurance premium paid by the borrower, not a government tax, and lenders collect it only to protect themselves.
Why D: PMI protects the lender if the borrower defaults, and it is typically required when the down payment is less than 20 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a fixed-rate mortgage?
A: A loan with no interest charged to the borrower at any time
B: A loan whose interest rate stays the same for the whole term
C: A loan for a car that is paid back in equal parts over years
D: A loan whose rate changes with the market each year of its term
Why A: Every loan charges interest, and a fixed-rate mortgage does too, so a loan with no interest charged at any time is wrong.
Why B: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for the entire term, so the principal and interest payment stays predictable throughout the loan.
Why C: A car loan paid in equal parts describes an installment loan for a vehicle, which is not the definition of a home mortgage.
Why D: A rate that changes with the market describes an adjustable-rate mortgage, which is the opposite of a fixed-rate loan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM)?
A: A loan with a fixed rate for the whole life of the term
B: A loan with no rate attached to it at any point in time
C: A loan for a car with a rate that can never change in any year
D: A loan whose interest rate can change after an initial period
Why A: A rate that stays fixed for the whole term describes a fixed-rate mortgage, which is the opposite of an adjustable-rate loan.
Why B: Every mortgage carries an interest rate, so a loan with no rate at all cannot be an adjustable-rate mortgage.
Why C: An ARM is a home loan whose rate can change, so a car loan whose rate never changes does not describe it.
Why D: An ARM starts with an initial rate for a set period, then the rate adjusts periodically based on a market index.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is equity in a home?
A: The property tax paid each year to the city
B: The mortgage amount that you still owe on the home
C: The home's value minus the mortgage balance owed
D: The down payment only, the sum paid at the purchase
Why A: Property tax is a yearly charge paid to local government, and it is a cost of owning a home rather than the owner's stake.
Why B: The mortgage amount still owed is the debt against the home, which is subtracted from value to find equity rather than being equity.
Why C: Home equity is what the owner actually holds in the property, calculated as the current value of the home minus the mortgage balance still owed.
Why D: The down payment is only the starting part of equity, because equity also grows as principal is paid and as the home appreciates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A home is worth $250,000 and the mortgage balance is $180,000. What is the owner's equity?
Why A: Equity equals value minus mortgage balance, so $250,000 minus $180,000 is $70,000, which is the share of the home the owner holds.
Why B: $180,000 is the mortgage balance still owed, which is subtracted from the home value, not the amount of equity.
Why C: $250,000 is the market value of the home, and equity requires subtracting the $180,000 owed, so this ignores the loan.
Why D: $430,000 comes from adding the value and the loan, but equity is found by subtracting the mortgage balance from the value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is closing cost?
A: The home price agreed upon by the buyer and seller overall
B: The down payment made by the buyer to the seller
C: Fees paid at the completion of a real estate purchase
D: Monthly rent paid by the tenant to the landlord
Why A: The agreed home price is the purchase price, which is separate from closing costs, the extra fees paid at completion of the sale.
Why B: The down payment is part of the purchase price paid upfront, while closing costs are additional fees for services such as title and appraisal.
Why C: Closing costs are fees paid when a real estate purchase is completed, including lender charges, title insurance, appraisal and recording fees.
Why D: Monthly rent from tenant to landlord is an ongoing housing cost, while closing costs are one-time fees at the end of a purchase.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Leo earns $2,500 a month after taxes. Using the 50/30/20 guideline, how much should go to savings and debt repayment?
Why A: Under 50/30/20, savings and debt repayment get 20 percent, and 20 percent of $2,500 is 0.20 times 2,500, which equals $500.
Why B: $750 is 30 percent of $2,500, which is the wants share of the guideline, not the savings and debt repayment share.
Why C: $1,250 is 50 percent of $2,500, which is the needs share of the guideline, not the savings and debt repayment share.
Why D: $250 is only 10 percent of $2,500, which is half of the 20 percent that the guideline assigns to savings and debt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A family spends $1,400 on rent, $500 on food and $300 on utilities from $3,500 of monthly income. What share of income goes to these needs?
A: Is 40 percent
B: Is 63 percent
C: Is 37 percent
D: Is 100 percent
Why A: Forty percent would be about $1,400 divided by $3,500, which counts only rent and leaves out the food and utilities in the total.
Why B: Needs total $1,400 plus $500 plus $300, which is $2,200, and $2,200 divided by $3,500 is about 0.63, or 63 percent of income.
Why C: Thirty-seven percent is what is left over, 100 minus 63, so it is the share of income not spent on these needs.
Why D: One hundred percent would mean needs use all of the $3,500, but $2,200 is only about 63 percent of that income.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Tia budgets $60 a week for groceries but spends $72. What is the variance for the week?
A: $12 under budget
B: $132 over budget
C: $6 over budget
D: $12 over budget
Why A: Spending $72 against a $60 budget is more than planned, so the variance is over budget and not under budget as stated.
Why B: $132 adds the budget and the spending together, but variance is the difference between them, which is $72 minus $60, or $12.
Why C: $6 is half of the real difference, and subtracting $60 from $72 gives $12, not $6.
Why D: Variance is actual minus budget, so $72 minus $60 equals $12, and since spending exceeded the plan, it is over budget.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these should be recorded first in a monthly budget?
A: Gifts
B: Dining
C: Income
D: Concerts
Why A: Gifts are a variable, optional spending category that is planned only after income is known, so it should not be recorded first.
Why B: Dining out is a discretionary expense that depends on how much income is available, so it is not the first line.
Why C: Income comes first because every spending and saving amount in a budget depends on how much money is available to allocate.
Why D: Concerts are an optional entertainment cost, planned only after income and necessities are known, so they are not recorded first.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might someone use a budgeting app?
A: To remove the need to check any bank statements all year
B: To increase income automatically without working extra hours
C: To guarantee that spending will never exceed income
D: To track spending automatically and see where money goes
Why A: A budgeting app does not remove the need to check bank statements, since statements are still needed to verify transactions and catch errors.
Why B: An app tracks money but cannot raise pay automatically, because income only grows through work, raises or other earnings.
Why C: No app can guarantee that spending stays under income, because the user still decides what to buy and when to stop.
Why D: Budgeting apps connect to accounts and categorize transactions automatically, which shows where money goes and helps people stay within their plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student's monthly income is $900 and fixed expenses are $600. How much is left for variable spending and savings?
Why A: Money left after fixed expenses is $900 minus $600, which equals $300 available for variable spending and savings each month.
Why B: $150 is half of the real remainder, and subtracting the $600 of fixed expenses from $900 gives $300 instead.
Why C: $1,500 adds the income and the fixed expenses together, but what is left over requires subtracting expenses from income.
Why D: $600 is the amount of fixed expenses themselves, not the remainder, which is $900 minus $600, or $300.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best way to handle a bill that comes only once a year, such as car registration?
A: Borrow from a friend on the day that the bill is due
B: Save a small amount each month in a sinking fund
C: Ignore it until the bill arrives, then use a card
D: Skip the bill and hope that no one will notice
Why A: Borrowing from a friend on the due date creates a debt and strain on a relationship when the bill could be planned for.
Why B: A sinking fund spreads an annual bill over monthly deposits, so for a $600 bill saving $50 a month covers it when due.
Why C: Ignoring the bill until it arrives and then using a card adds interest and debt, when saving ahead would avoid it.
Why D: Skipping the bill risks penalties, fines or loss of registration, and someone is certain to notice, so it is not a sound plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a cash-flow statement for a household?
A: A record of money coming in and going out over a period
B: A document that shows the value of the family home
C: A forecast of the prices of goods in shops over the next year
D: A list of everything the household owns and owes on one date
Why A: A cash-flow statement tracks inflows and outflows of money over a period, showing whether the household takes in more than it spends.
Why B: The value of the family home belongs on a balance sheet or appraisal, not in a statement tracking money moving in and out.
Why C: A forecast of shop prices is an economic projection, whereas a household cash-flow statement records the family's own income and spending over time.
Why D: A list of everything owned and owed on one date is a net worth or balance sheet statement, not a cash-flow statement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A household's monthly income is $4,000 and expenses are $3,200. What is the savings rate?
A: 8 percent
B: 80 percent
C: 20 percent
D: 25 percent
Why A: Eight percent would come from a savings of $320, but savings here are $800, which is a larger share of income.
Why B: Eighty percent is the share of income that goes to expenses, $3,200 divided by $4,000, not the share that is saved.
Why C: Savings are $4,000 minus $3,200, or $800, and $800 divided by $4,000 equals 0.20, so the household saves 20 percent of income.
Why D: Twenty-five percent comes from dividing $800 by $3,200, the expenses, but the savings rate divides by income, which is $4,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a sign that a budget needs to be changed?
A: Bills are paid before the due date
B: Income matches what was expected
C: Savings goals are being met on time
D: Spending is repeatedly above income
Why A: Paying bills early shows the budget is working well, so it gives no reason to change the plan.
Why B: When income matches expectations, the budget's assumptions hold true and the plan does not need revising.
Why C: Meeting savings goals on time shows the budget is succeeding, so there is no reason to change it.
Why D: Spending that repeatedly exceeds income means the plan is unrealistic or too loose, so categories or amounts need to be changed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a windfall?
A: A loan received from a bank at a low rate of interest
B: An unexpected sum of money, such as a bonus or inheritance
C: A regular payment received each month from an employer
D: A bill that arrives once a year, such as property tax on a home
Why A: A bank loan at a low rate is borrowed money that must be repaid, whereas a windfall is unexpected money you receive.
Why B: A windfall is an unexpected sum of money, like a bonus, tax refund, gift or inheritance, that was not part of regular income.
Why C: A regular monthly payment from an employer is a paycheck, which is expected, so it is not an unexpected windfall.
Why D: A yearly bill such as property tax is an expense that can be planned in advance, not unexpected money that arrives.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a smart use of a $1,000 windfall if a person has credit card debt at 22 percent interest?
A: Put it in a plain savings account
B: Lend it to a friend to repay later
C: Spend all of it on a vacation trip
D: Pay down the credit card balance
Why A: A plain savings account pays far less than the 22 percent charged on the card debt, so the debt costs far more than savings earn.
Why B: Lending to a friend risks never being repaid and earns nothing, while the credit card debt keeps charging 22 percent interest.
Why C: Spending it all on a vacation adds nothing to financial health, and the 22 percent card interest would keep growing on the balance.
Why D: Paying down the card gives a guaranteed return equal to the 22 percent interest avoided, which beats nearly any savings account or investment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person earns $18 an hour and works 30 hours a week. What is the gross weekly pay?
Why A: $600 would be about $20 an hour times 30 hours, but the wage is $18 an hour, not $20.
Why B: Gross weekly pay is hourly rate times hours, so $18 times 30 equals $540 before any taxes or deductions are taken out.
Why C: $1.67 comes from dividing 30 by 18, but pay is found by multiplying the hourly wage by the hours worked.
Why D: $48 comes from adding $18 and 30 hours, but wages are multiplied by hours, so adding the two numbers is meaningless.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker earns $15 an hour and receives time-and-a-half for overtime. What is the pay for one overtime hour?
Why A: Time-and-a-half means 1.5 times the regular wage, so $15 times 1.5 equals $22.50 for each overtime hour worked.
Why B: $15 is just the regular hourly wage, and overtime at time-and-a-half must pay more than the normal rate.
Why C: $16.50 adds only 10 percent to the wage, but time-and-a-half adds 50 percent, which is $7.50 on $15.
Why D: $30 is double time, two times the $15 wage, whereas time-and-a-half is 1.5 times the wage, or $22.50.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a bank's routing number identify?
A: The date the account was opened by the owner
B: The individual account of the bank's customer
C: The bank or credit union holding the account
D: The branch manager who approved the account
Why A: The date an account was opened is recorded in bank files, but it has no role in the routing number.
Why B: The individual customer account is identified by the account number, while the routing number is shared by all of a bank's accounts.
Why C: A routing number is a nine-digit code that identifies the bank or credit union holding the account so payments are routed correctly.
Why D: A routing number does not identify a manager or any person, only the financial institution where the account is held.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bank statement shows an ending balance of $1,200. Outstanding checks total $150 and a deposit of $100 is in transit. What is the adjusted bank balance?
Why A: Adjusted balance equals $1,200 minus $150 in outstanding checks plus $100 deposit in transit, which gives $1,150 after both adjustments.
Why B: $1,300 adds the deposit but also adds back the checks instead of subtracting them, and neither treatment is correct.
Why C: $1,450 adds both the $150 in checks and the $100 deposit to the balance, but outstanding checks must be subtracted.
Why D: $1,050 subtracts the $150 in checks and then also subtracts the $100 deposit, but a deposit in transit must be added.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which bank account typically pays the least interest?
A: A money market type account
B: A five-year CD at a bank
C: A standard checking account
D: A high-yield savings account
Why A: Money market accounts usually pay more than checking, because they hold larger balances and earn better rates than basic accounts.
Why B: A five-year CD locks money in for a long term and normally pays one of the higher rates among bank products.
Why C: Standard checking accounts are built for everyday spending and typically pay little or no interest, so they pay the least.
Why D: High-yield savings accounts are designed to pay rates well above standard accounts, so they pay far more than checking.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a joint account?
A: An account held in the name of a business
B: An account shared by a bank with the state
C: An account that holds money for a minor child
D: An account owned by two or more people
Why A: An account held in a business name is a business account; a joint account is shared by two or more individuals who each have access.
Why B: A bank does not share an account with the state, and a joint account is held by customers who share ownership.
Why C: An account holding money for a minor child is a custodial account; a joint account is owned by two or more people who share access.
Why D: A joint account is owned by two or more people, who can each deposit and withdraw, such as spouses or partners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an electronic funds transfer (EFT)?
A: A coin deposit made at a machine in a shop
B: Moving money between accounts electronically
C: A paper check mailed to a payee for deposit
D: A cash deposit made in person at a branch
Why A: Depositing coins at a machine in a shop is a physical cash deposit, not an electronic movement of funds between accounts.
Why B: An EFT moves money between accounts electronically, as with direct deposit, online bill pay or ACH transfers, without paper checks or cash.
Why C: A paper check is a physical instrument, which is the older method that electronic transfers replaced, so it is not an EFT.
Why D: A cash deposit made in person is physical money handed to a teller, which is not an electronic transfer of funds.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should you do if your debit card is lost?
A: Post the card number on social media
B: Report it to your bank right away
C: Wait weeks before telling the bank
D: Tell no one and hope no one finds it
Why A: Posting the card number on social media would let thieves use it, so it exposes you to fraud instead of protecting you.
Why B: Reporting a lost debit card right away lets the bank block it and limits your liability for any unauthorized charges.
Why C: Waiting weeks lets thieves keep spending, and delaying the report can raise your liability from $50 to $500 or more.
Why D: Telling no one and hoping lets anyone who finds the card drain your account, so you lose protection by doing nothing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Under federal rules, how quickly must you report a lost debit card to limit your liability to $50?
A: Within two business days
B: Within one year of loss
C: Never, as the bank pays all
D: Within thirty days of loss
Why A: Reporting within two business days limits liability to $50 under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, while later reports can cost much more.
Why B: One year is far too late, since waiting beyond 60 days after the statement can leave you liable for all losses.
Why C: The bank does not pay everything automatically, since your liability depends on how quickly you report, so waiting indefinitely offers no protection.
Why D: Reporting within thirty days raises liability to as much as $500, so only a report inside two business days holds it to $50.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bank's service charge?
A: Interest paid by the bank on the balance of the account overall
B: A tax collected by the government on bank deposits
C: A reward for opening an account, such as a free gift
D: A fee for maintaining an account or for specific services
Why A: Interest paid by the bank on a balance is earnings for the customer, while a service charge is a cost charged to the customer.
Why B: A government tax on deposits is not a service charge, which is a fee the bank itself sets for its services.
Why C: A reward for opening an account is a bonus or promotion paid to the customer, which is the reverse of a charge.
Why D: A service charge is a fee a bank imposes for maintaining an account or for services like wire transfers, overdrafts and paper statements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action best avoids monthly account fees?
A: Closing and reopening the account every month
B: Making many small withdrawals to keep the balance low
C: Keeping the minimum balance the account requires
D: Overdrawing the account so the bank sees activity
Why A: Closing and reopening the account each month adds paperwork and can trigger new fees, and it does nothing to waive monthly charges.
Why B: Making many small withdrawals keeps the balance low, which is the very thing that triggers monthly fees on accounts with a minimum.
Why C: Many accounts waive monthly fees if you keep a required minimum balance, so meeting it is the surest way to avoid them.
Why D: Overdrawing the account causes overdraft fees and negative balances, which add charges rather than avoiding monthly account fees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a custodial account?
A: An account owned jointly by a married couple
B: An account opened by a school for a student
C: An account managed by an adult for a minor's benefit
D: An account that is managed by a bank for its own staff
Why A: An account owned by a couple is a joint account; a custodial account is run by an adult for the benefit of a minor.
Why B: Schools do not open custodial accounts; an adult such as a parent sets one up and manages it until the child reaches the age of majority.
Why C: A custodial account is managed by an adult, the custodian, for the benefit of a minor until the child reaches the age of majority.
Why D: Accounts managed by a bank for its own staff are internal accounts, not custodial accounts, which exist to benefit minors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a high-yield savings account?
A: A savings account that charges a fee each time that money is deposited
B: A savings account that pays a higher interest rate than a standard one
C: A savings account that pays no interest but offers free checks for its owner
D: A savings account that can be opened only with a very large deposit of cash
Why A: Charging a fee for each deposit would make an account worse, whereas a high-yield savings account offers a better interest rate.
Why B: A high-yield savings account pays a higher interest rate than a standard savings account, so balances grow faster with the same deposit.
Why C: Paying no interest contradicts the name, since high-yield accounts exist to pay more interest, and free checks are not the point.
Why D: High-yield accounts commonly have low or no minimums, so requiring a very large deposit is not part of the definition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Maria deposits $1,200 at 3 percent simple interest for 2 years. How much interest does she earn?
Why A: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, so $1,200 times 0.03 times 2 gives $72 earned over the two years.
Why B: $36 is the interest for only one year, $1,200 times 0.03, and the question asks for two years, which doubles it.
Why C: $1,272 is the total balance at the end, principal plus the $72 of interest, and the question asks only for the interest.
Why D: $720 comes from using 30 percent rather than 3 percent, which puts the decimal point in the wrong place by one digit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A borrower has a credit limit of $8,000 and a balance of $2,000. What is the credit utilization ratio?
A: 10 percent
B: 400 percent
C: 75 percent
D: 25 percent
Why A: Ten percent would need a balance of $800, but the balance here is $2,000, which is a bigger share of the $8,000 limit.
Why B: Four hundred percent flips the fraction, $8,000 divided by $2,000, but utilization is the balance divided by the limit.
Why C: Seventy-five percent is the unused credit, $6,000 of $8,000, but utilization measures the share that is used, not the share left.
Why D: Utilization equals balance divided by limit, so $2,000 divided by $8,000 is 0.25, or 25 percent of available credit used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action would most likely raise a credit score over time?
A: Paying all bills on time and keeping balances low
B: Opening many new credit cards in a short period of time
C: Maxing out cards each month and paying only the minimum
D: Closing the oldest account to shorten history
Why A: On-time payments are the biggest factor in a score, and keeping balances low lowers utilization, so both habits raise a score over time.
Why B: Opening many cards quickly creates several hard inquiries and lowers average account age, which usually hurts a score in the short term.
Why C: Maxing out cards pushes utilization very high, and paying only the minimum keeps balances high, both of which lower a score.
Why D: Closing the oldest account shortens credit history and lowers available credit, which tends to reduce a score instead of raising it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit report?
A: A list of grocery purchases kept in a household notebook
B: A record of a person's borrowing and repayment history
C: A statement of the balance of a person's savings account
D: A document that shows how much a person earns each year
Why A: Grocery purchases kept in a household notebook are personal records, whereas a credit report is compiled by credit bureaus about borrowing.
Why B: A credit report records a person's borrowing and repayment history, including accounts, balances, payment record and inquiries, as compiled by credit bureaus.
Why C: A savings balance statement comes from your bank, and it is not part of what a credit report records about debts.
Why D: Income is not listed on a credit report, which is about borrowing history and not about how much a person earns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit limit?
A: The number of cards you are allowed to hold at a time
B: The total interest that you will pay over the life of the card
C: The minimum payment you must make each month to stay open
D: The maximum amount a lender allows you to borrow on a card
Why A: The number of cards you hold is not the limit; a credit limit is the dollar amount available on a single card.
Why B: Total interest over the life of a card is a cost that varies with balances and time, not a limit set by the lender.
Why C: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due each month, which is a separate figure from the credit limit.
Why D: A credit limit is the maximum amount the lender lets you borrow on a card, and going over it can bring fees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A card has a 24 percent APR. About how much interest per month is charged on a $1,000 balance?
A: About $240
B: About $200
C: About $20
D: About $2
Why A: $240 is the interest for a full year at 24 percent on $1,000, not for one month, so it is twelve times too high.
Why B: $200 would come from 20 percent a month, but 24 percent APR divided by 12 months is 2 percent a month.
Why C: Monthly interest is 24 percent divided by 12, or 2 percent, and 2 percent of $1,000 is about $20 each month.
Why D: $2 would be 0.2 percent of $1,000, which misplaces the decimal, since 2 percent of $1,000 is $20.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a charge-off?
A: When a borrower is given extra time to repay with no penalty at all
B: When a lender raises the credit limit of a good customer today
C: When a borrower pays off a debt early and the lender cancels the account
D: When a lender gives up on collecting a debt and writes it off as a loss
Why A: Extra time to repay with no penalty is a forbearance or grace arrangement, not a charge-off, which is a lender's accounting loss.
Why B: Raising the credit limit of a good customer is an upgrade, and it has nothing to do with a debt written off.
Why C: Paying a debt off early closes the account in good standing, whereas a charge-off happens when the borrower has not paid.
Why D: A charge-off is when a lender gives up on collecting and writes the debt off as a loss, though the borrower still owes it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a collection account?
A: A list of coins that a person has gathered as a hobby
B: A past-due debt that has been turned over to a collector
C: A savings account banks use to collect small deposits
D: A credit card account with a low interest rate and no fee
Why A: A hobby coin collection has nothing to do with credit, and a collection account is a debt, not a set of coins.
Why B: A collection account is a past-due debt that the original lender has turned over to a collector, and it harms credit.
Why C: Banks do not use savings to collect small deposits as collection accounts, which are overdue debts in the hands of collectors.
Why D: A low-rate card with no fee is a favorable product, while a collection account signals unpaid debt and damages credit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibit?
A: Charging interest on any loan made to a customer today
B: Reporting debts to the credit bureaus every single month
C: Abusive, deceptive or harassing debt collection practices
D: Opening a savings account at a bank with a small cash deposit
Why A: The Act does not ban interest on loans, because lenders may legally charge interest, and it governs how collectors behave.
Why B: Reporting debts to credit bureaus is lawful and common, and the Act does not forbid creditors from doing it.
Why C: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bans abusive, deceptive and harassing collection tactics such as threats, false statements and repeated calls at unreasonable hours.
Why D: Opening a savings account is ordinary banking and unrelated to debt collection, which is the only thing the Act regulates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A collector calls a consumer at midnight and threatens arrest for a credit card debt. What is this?
A: Likely illegal harassment under debt collection law
B: A requirement of the card contract allowing night calls
C: A normal collection step that debt collectors take
D: A courtesy reminder that the law itself encourages
Why A: Calling at midnight and threatening arrest breaks the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, since collectors may not call at odd hours or make false threats.
Why B: Card contracts cannot override federal law, so no agreement can allow harassing night calls or arrest threats by a collector.
Why C: Debt collectors must follow the law, and calling at midnight with threats of arrest is not a normal or permitted step.
Why D: The law does not encourage this behavior; it prohibits threats and calls at unreasonable hours, so it cannot be a courtesy reminder.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Truth in Lending Act require lenders to disclose?
A: The salary of each of the lender's employees today
B: The names of the lender's largest competitors in town
C: The home addresses of every other borrower of the lender overall
D: The cost of credit, including the APR and finance charges
Why A: Employee salaries are private business information, and lenders are not required to disclose them under the Truth in Lending Act.
Why B: Competitors' names are marketing information, and the Act does not require lenders to disclose them to borrowers.
Why C: Other borrowers' addresses are private data that lenders must protect, so disclosing them would violate privacy and not the Act's purpose.
Why D: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the APR, finance charges and the total of payments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a finance charge?
A: The amount a borrower repays as principal, with no interest
B: The total cost of borrowing, including interest and fees
C: The monthly rent a borrower pays for a home or a flat
D: The tax a borrower pays to the state for taking out a loan
Why A: Principal is the amount borrowed and repaid, but a finance charge is the added cost of borrowing, not the principal itself.
Why B: A finance charge is the total cost of borrowing, including interest and fees like origination or service charges, which the borrower pays.
Why C: Monthly rent for a home is a housing cost and has no link to the cost of borrowing money.
Why D: A finance charge is paid to the lender as part of the credit cost, rather than a tax paid to the state.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit card's penalty APR?
A: A higher rate that may apply after a late or missed payment
B: A bonus rate that applies to new cardholders for the first year
C: A fee that is charged for using the card abroad each time
D: A lower rate given to customers who pay their bills early
Why A: A penalty APR is a higher interest rate that the card issuer may apply after a late or missed payment, per the card terms.
Why B: A bonus rate for new cardholders is an introductory or promotional APR, which is low, while a penalty APR is high.
Why C: A fee for using the card abroad is a foreign transaction fee, which is a flat charge and not an interest rate.
Why D: A penalty APR raises the rate after misbehavior, so a lower rate for early payers is the reverse of what it does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an introductory 0 percent APR offer?
A: A rate that stays low until the card is closed
B: A rate that is charged on purchases made abroad
C: A temporary low rate offered when you open a card
D: A rate set for customers who pay on time each month
Why A: An introductory rate is temporary and ends after a set number of months, so a rate that stays low until closing does not describe it.
Why B: A rate on purchases abroad is not an introductory rate, because foreign charges usually bring fees and the offer applies to the card generally.
Why C: An introductory 0 percent APR is a temporary low rate offered when you open a card, and it ends after months.
Why D: A reward for paying on time is not an introductory offer; an introductory 0 percent APR is a temporary rate offered when you open a new card.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person has a 0 percent APR for 12 months followed by 22 percent. What is the best plan?
A: Plan to pay the balance before the promotional period ends
B: Spend as much as possible in the promotional period
C: Ignore the date when the rate will change, as it is minor overall
D: Close the account on the last day without paying anything
Why A: Paying the balance before the 0 percent period ends avoids the 22 percent rate, so you borrow for free and avoid interest.
Why B: Spending as much as possible builds a large balance that will start costing 22 percent interest once the promotion ends.
Why C: The rate change is significant, because a balance left after 12 months will begin accruing 22 percent interest, so the date matters.
Why D: Closing the account without paying leaves the debt unpaid, which invites late fees, collections and damage to the credit score.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a co-borrower?
A: A person who repays a loan only if the main borrower fails
B: A person who approves a loan for a bank and its senior staff in the end
C: A person who shares equal responsibility for a loan from the start
D: A person who lends money to a borrower without any interest
Why A: A person who pays only if the main borrower fails is a co-signer, whereas a co-borrower shares responsibility from the beginning.
Why B: Approving a loan on behalf of a bank is the job of a loan officer or underwriter, not a co-borrower.
Why C: A co-borrower applies with the main borrower and shares equal legal responsibility for repaying the loan from the start.
Why D: A person who lends money to a borrower without interest is a lender or a generous friend, not a co-borrower on a loan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a student loan deferment?
A: A penalty charged to students who miss a payment on any loan or term
B: A permanent cancellation of the whole loan with nothing left to pay back overall
C: A higher interest rate for borrowers who study abroad for each year
D: A period when payments are paused, sometimes without interest building up
Why A: A penalty for missing a payment is a late fee, which is unrelated to deferment, a pause in payments.
Why B: Deferment does not cancel a loan, so the borrower must still repay it later, and cancellation is called discharge or forgiveness.
Why C: Deferment has nothing to do with studying abroad or a higher interest rate, because it is a pause granted for eligible situations.
Why D: Deferment pauses payments, for example while in school or unemployed, and on some federal loans interest does not build up during the pause.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between federal and private student loans?
A: Federal loans must be repaid in full within one year of graduation, whatever one earns
B: Federal loans carry government terms and protections while private ones use lenders
C: Private loans are backed by the government and federal loans are not
D: Federal loans require a credit check and a cosigner while private loans do not
Why A: Federal loans have long repayment terms, often ten years or more, and are not due in full one year after graduation.
Why B: Federal loans have terms and protections set by the government, such as income-driven repayment and deferment, while private loans come from banks with lender-set terms.
Why C: Federal loans are the ones backed by the government; private loans come from banks and other lenders without those protections.
Why D: Many federal loans need no credit check or cosigner, while private lenders usually require both, so this description is backwards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student takes a $10,000 loan at 5 percent simple interest for 4 years. How much interest will accumulate in total?
Why A: $500 is the simple interest for only one year, $10,000 times 0.05, and the loan runs for four years.
Why B: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, so $10,000 times 0.05 times 4 gives $2,000 of total interest.
Why C: $12,000 is the principal plus the $2,000 of interest, which is the total repaid, and the question asks only for interest.
Why D: $20,000 does not follow from any step, because multiplying $10,000 by 5 percent for 4 years gives only $2,000 in interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is loan amortization?
A: Paying the loan off in one lump sum on the first day of term
B: Paying only the interest on a loan for years and never reducing principal
C: Canceling the loan when the borrower asks for it, with no fee
D: Paying off a loan through regular payments of principal and interest
Why A: A lump-sum payment on day one is a single payoff, whereas amortization spreads payments over the life of the loan.
Why B: Paying only interest and never reducing principal is an interest-only loan, while amortization gradually reduces the principal balance too.
Why C: Canceling a loan on request is simply early termination, which is a different matter from the scheduled repayment that amortization describes.
Why D: Amortization pays off a loan through regular payments that cover interest and principal, so the balance falls to zero by the end.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is generally true of a longer loan term?
A: Zero interest, since time reduces the borrowing cost
B: Higher monthly payments and less total interest
C: Lower monthly payments but more total interest
D: The same total interest as a shorter loan term
Why A: A longer term does not make interest zero, since interest accrues for more months, which usually raises the total cost.
Why B: A longer term spreads payments out, which lowers each monthly payment, so claiming higher payments with less interest is backwards.
Why C: A longer term stretches the principal over more months so the payments are smaller, but interest accrues longer and totals more.
Why D: Total interest depends on the time the balance is outstanding, so a longer term costs more in interest than a short one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A car loan of $12,000 at 6 percent for 5 years has a lower monthly payment than the same loan for 3 years. Why would some borrowers still pick the 3-year loan?
A: It costs less total interest
B: It leaves a higher final balance
C: It has a lower rate every time
D: It avoids paying any interest
Why A: The 3-year loan has a higher payment but pays interest for fewer months, so the total interest cost is lower than with 5 years.
Why B: A shorter loan pays down principal faster, so the final balance is lower, which makes a higher final balance wrong.
Why C: The rate is the same 6 percent in both cases, so the 3-year loan does not carry a lower rate, and the savings come from time.
