Why B: A savings or checking account lets you withdraw quickly without penalty and is usually insured, so it is the best place for money you may need within days.
Why C: Retirement funds of stocks and bonds are meant for decades and can fall in value. Early withdrawal also brings penalties, which makes them unsuitable for near-term needs.
Why D: A single speculative stock can drop sharply in just a few days. Money needed soon should never be exposed to that much risk, so it is unsuitable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a good reason to keep savings in an account separate from your checking account?
A: It reduces the temptation to spend it
B: It makes keeping a budget unnecessary
C: It prevents all deposits from being made
D: It raises your credit score right away
Why A: Keeping savings in a separate account puts a small barrier between you and the money, so you are less tempted to spend it on impulse and the balance can grow.
Why B: A budget is still needed to plan income and spending; a separate savings account is one tool that helps by making the money harder to spend.
Why C: A separate savings account does not stop deposits. You can still deposit into it, and it is simply set apart from daily spending money.
Why D: Opening a savings account does not change your credit score; the real benefit is that separation reduces the temptation to spend the money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main drawback of a long-term CD?
A: It pays no interest during the term
B: It loses all value in the term
C: It has no insurance of any kind
D: Penalties if you withdraw early
Why A: CDs do pay interest during the term, usually at a fixed rate that is higher than ordinary savings. Paying nothing is not a drawback that applies.
Why B: CDs do not lose their value during the term. Deposits are normally insured up to limits and the principal is safe, so total loss is not a real drawback.
Why C: CDs at insured banks and credit unions are protected by FDIC or NCUA insurance up to set limits. Having no insurance of any kind is therefore not true.
Why D: A CD locks your money for a fixed term, so withdrawing early usually triggers a penalty, often some months of interest. That lack of flexibility is its main drawback.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Compare two savings accounts: one earns 1 percent and one earns 4 percent on $10,000 for one year. About how much more interest does the 4 percent account pay?
Why A: $30 would be the gap if the rates were 0.1 and 0.4 percent. The gap here is 3 percentage points on $10,000, which gives $300.
Why B: The difference is 4 percent minus 1 percent, or 3 percentage points. Three percent of $10,000 is $300, so the higher account pays about $300 more in one year.
Why C: $500 would require a 5 percentage point gap, such as 1 percent against 6 percent. The real gap is 3 points, and 3 percent of $10,000 is $300.
Why D: $3,000 would be a 30 percent difference in rates. The gap here is only 3 percentage points, and 3 percent of $10,000 comes to $300.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the benefit of an automatic transfer to savings?
A: It increases the interest rate on your account
B: It lets you skip paying your monthly bills
C: It protects your savings from inflation
D: It saves consistently without relying on willpower
Why A: Automatic transfers do not change the interest rate; they move money on a schedule so you save regularly without relying on willpower.
Why B: Automatic transfers move money into savings; they do not pay bills for you, and bills still need to be handled separately.
Why C: An automatic transfer is only a way of moving money and does not protect savings from inflation; it simply builds the habit of saving consistently.
Why D: An automatic transfer moves money to savings on a schedule, so you save steadily without having to remember or decide each time, which takes willpower out of the process.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean to buy and hold?
A: Buying investments and keeping them for the long term
B: Selling investments soon after a small gain
C: Moving money into whichever fund did best last quarter
D: Buying investments with borrowed money and selling soon
Why A: Buy and hold means purchasing investments and keeping them for many years, riding out ups and downs, which avoids frequent trading costs and taxes and favors long-term growth.
Why B: Selling soon after a small gain is short-term trading; buy and hold means keeping investments for many years to ride out market ups and downs.
Why C: Moving into last quarter's top fund is performance chasing; buy and hold keeps investments through ups and downs without frequent switching.
Why D: Buying with borrowed money and selling soon is margin trading for short-term gain. Buy and hold uses your own money and keeps the investment for the long term.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which investment mix suits a goal one year away?
A: All in a start-up business that has no revenue yet at all
B: All in a single speculative stock held for one year or more
C: Safe, liquid options such as a savings account or short-term CD
D: All in a long-term growth fund that may fall in value in the year
Why A: A start-up with no revenue is extremely risky and could lose everything within the year. A goal only one year away needs safety of principal, not speculation.
Why B: A single speculative stock can fall sharply in one year, and there is little time to recover. A one-year goal calls for safer and more stable choices.
Why C: For a goal one year away, safety and easy access matter most, so savings accounts or short-term CDs protect the principal and still earn some interest.
Why D: Long-term growth funds can lose value in any given year, and one year is too short to recover from a drop. They suit goals many years away.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to your total interest if you pay extra on a loan each month?
A: You pay less total interest and finish sooner
B: Interest is unchanged, extra payments do not help
C: You pay more interest, as the balance falls slowly
D: The loan is canceled at once by the bank
Why A: Extra payments reduce the principal faster, so less interest accrues each month. The loan is paid off sooner and the total interest cost falls.
Why B: Extra payments do help. They cut the principal, and since interest is charged on the remaining balance, a smaller balance means less interest is owed.
Why C: Extra payments make the balance fall faster, not slower, so you pay less interest overall. Claiming that interest rises gets the effect backwards.
Why D: Extra payments do not cancel a loan at once. The bank only applies them to reduce what you owe, and the loan ends when the balance reaches zero.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a prepayment penalty?
A: A fine for paying late on a monthly bill or loan
B: A fee some lenders charge for paying off a loan early
C: A tax on loans paid to the state by a lender each year
D: A reward for paying early on a loan from a bank
Why A: A fine for paying late is a late fee. A prepayment penalty is the opposite situation, charged when you pay off a loan too early, not too late.
Why B: A prepayment penalty is a fee some lenders charge when you pay off all or part of a loan early, because they lose the interest they expected to earn.
Why C: A tax paid to the state by a lender is not a prepayment penalty. This fee is charged to the borrower by the lender for early payoff.
Why D: Lenders do not reward early payment with this term. A prepayment penalty is a cost to the borrower, not a reward, so this has the meaning reversed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an I bond (Series I savings bond)?
A: A bond that pays a fixed rate for thirty years to holders
B: A bond issued by a company to fund its factories, repaid yearly
C: A bond issued by a foreign government to raise funds
D: A U.S. savings bond with a rate that adjusts for inflation
Why A: A bond paying a fixed rate for thirty years describes a long-term Treasury bond. An I bond differs because its rate adjusts with inflation, not staying fixed.
Why B: A bond issued by a company to fund factories is a corporate bond. An I bond is a savings bond issued by the U.S. Treasury, not a business.
Why C: Bonds issued by a foreign government to raise funds are foreign sovereign bonds. An I bond is issued by the U.S. government, not by another country.
Why D: An I bond is a U.S. savings bond whose interest combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate, so its value keeps pace with rising prices and protects buying power.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might someone choose a Roth IRA over a traditional IRA?
A: It has an employer match on contributions
B: Contributions are deductible, withdrawals are taxed
C: Qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free
D: It must be opened through your employer
Why A: A Roth IRA is an individual account and has no employer match; people choose it mainly because qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
Why B: This describes a traditional IRA, where contributions may be deductible and withdrawals are taxed. Roth contributions are made after tax, so that is the opposite.
Why C: Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement, including the growth, are tax-free. This is the main reason people choose it.
Why D: A Roth IRA is opened by an individual at a brokerage or bank, not through an employer, and workers of any age with earned income may use one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: At what age can most people withdraw from an IRA without an early-withdrawal penalty?
Why A: Age 40 is far too early. Withdrawals before 59 and a half generally trigger a 10 percent penalty plus income tax, unless a special exception applies.
Why B: Age 70 is later than needed. The penalty ends at 59 and a half, though required withdrawals eventually begin in the seventies for most people.
Why C: Age 50 is still before 59 and a half, so a withdrawal would normally face the 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty unless an exception applies.
Why D: The standard rule lets people withdraw from an IRA without the 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty once they reach age 59 and a half, though ordinary income tax may apply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a required minimum distribution (RMD)?
A: The minimum amount that must be withdrawn from certain retirement accounts after a set age
B: The fee charged to withdraw funds early from a plan, set by the plan's rules each year
C: The maximum amount that may be withdrawn each year from any retirement account by the holder
D: The smallest deposit allowed in a retirement account each year, set by the plan sponsor
Why A: An RMD is the minimum amount you must withdraw each year from certain retirement accounts, like traditional IRAs, once you reach a set age, so that tax-deferred money eventually gets taxed.
Why B: The fee charged for early withdrawal is the early-withdrawal penalty, usually 10 percent. An RMD is a mandatory withdrawal later in life, not a penalty fee.
Why C: An RMD is a minimum that must be withdrawn, not a maximum cap. You may withdraw more than the required amount, so the maximum description is wrong.
Why D: An RMD relates to withdrawals, not deposits. The smallest deposit allowed is a different matter set by the plan, while an RMD forces money out of the account.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Social Security?
A: A loan program for homebuyers who are first-time buyers in a town
B: A federal program that pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits
C: A private savings account that each worker owns, with no help from the state
D: A tax on investment gains and capital sales for workers and firms
Why A: Loans for first-time homebuyers are offered by lenders and housing agencies. Social Security is a benefits program funded by payroll taxes and is not a loan program.
Why B: Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes that pays monthly retirement, disability and survivor benefits to eligible workers and their families.
Why C: Social Security is not a private account. It is a government program funded by current payroll taxes, and workers do not own individual balances in it.
Why D: A tax on investment gains is a capital gains tax. Social Security is funded by payroll taxes and pays benefits instead of taxing investments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should most people not rely only on Social Security for retirement?
A: It is paid to every citizen at 18 years of age and older
B: It is a private account that grows fast, so benefits cover expenses
C: Benefits typically replace only part of pre-retirement income
D: It pays more than a worker's final salary or wage in all cases
Why A: Social Security is not paid to everyone at 18. Benefits depend on work history and age, and retirement benefits start no earlier than 62.
Why B: Social Security is a government program, not a private account, and its benefits are modest. They are meant to supplement other savings and not fully cover expenses.
Why C: Benefits typically replace only about 40 percent of pre-retirement earnings for an average worker, so people also need personal savings, pensions or retirement accounts to maintain their lifestyle.
Why D: Benefits are based on past earnings and are almost always lower than a final salary. Saying it pays more in all cases is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker's gross pay is $2,000. Federal tax is $200, FICA is $153 and state tax is $60. What is the net pay?
Why A: $2,413 would be gross pay plus the deductions, which adds when it should subtract. Net pay is gross pay minus every tax withheld from the check.
Why B: $1,800 subtracts only the federal tax of $200 and ignores FICA and state tax. Net pay must subtract all three deductions from gross pay.
Why C: Total deductions are $200 plus $153 plus $60, which is $413. Subtracting from $2,000 gives a net pay of $1,587.
Why D: $413 is the total of the deductions, not the pay. Net pay is what remains after subtracting them from $2,000, which is $1,587.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The employee share of FICA is 7.65 percent. How much is withheld from a $2,000 paycheck?
Why A: The employee share is 7.65 percent of $2,000, and $2,000 times 0.0765 equals $153. That amount is withheld for Social Security and Medicare.
Why B: $15.30 comes from a misplaced decimal, using 0.765 percent instead of 7.65 percent. The correct calculation, $2,000 times 0.0765, gives $153.
Why C: $765 would be 38.25 percent of $2,000. FICA is 7.65 percent of pay, so the withholding is $153 and not $765.
Why D: $1,847 is the pay left after FICA, which is $2,000 minus $153. The question asks how much is withheld, and that is $153.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do FICA taxes fund?
A: Highway and road construction
B: Social Security and Medicare
C: National defense and military
D: Public schools and libraries
Why A: Highways and roads are paid mainly from fuel taxes and general funds. FICA taxes are dedicated payroll taxes with different purposes.
Why B: FICA taxes are payroll taxes that fund Social Security, which pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits, and Medicare, which provides health coverage mainly for people age 65 and older.
Why C: National defense is paid from general federal revenue such as income taxes. FICA taxes are earmarked for Social Security and Medicare, not the military.
Why D: Public schools and libraries are funded largely by state and local taxes such as property taxes. FICA is a federal payroll tax for Social Security and Medicare.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A taxpayer in the 22 percent bracket has a $1,000 deduction. How much tax does it save?
Why A: $780 is what remains of the $1,000 after paying the 22 percent. A deduction saves tax equal to the deduction times the rate, not the leftover.
Why B: A $1,000 saving would only occur with a credit. A deduction lowers taxable income, so the tax saved is $1,000 times 22 percent, which is $220.
Why C: $22 would be 22 percent of $100. A $1,000 deduction at a 22 percent bracket saves $1,000 times 0.22, which is $220, not $22.
Why D: A deduction reduces taxable income, not the tax directly. At a 22 percent bracket, $1,000 times 0.22 gives $220 of tax saved.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A taxpayer has a $1,000 tax credit. How much does it reduce the tax owed?
Why A: A credit does reduce tax. A $0 reduction would ignore that a credit lowers the tax bill dollar for dollar, so $1,000 of credit saves $1,000.
Why B: A tax credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, so a $1,000 credit cuts the tax bill by the full $1,000, unlike a deduction that lowers income.
Why C: $220 is the saving from a $1,000 deduction at a 22 percent bracket. A credit works directly on the tax owed, so it saves the full $1,000.
Why D: $100 would be 10 percent of the credit. A credit reduces the tax owed by its full value, so a $1,000 credit saves $1,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is withholding?
A: A savings plan at work offered by employers to staff
B: A fee charged by the bank for cashing a paycheck each time
C: Income tax taken from a paycheck and sent to the government
D: Money an employer keeps from the paycheck as a bonus for itself
Why A: A savings plan at work is a retirement plan like a 401(k). Withholding is tax taken out of pay, not a savings program offered by employers.
Why B: Banks may charge fees for cashing checks, but that is not withholding. Withholding is the tax an employer takes from pay and sends to the government.
Why C: Withholding is income tax that employers take out of each paycheck and send to the government on the worker's behalf, as a prepayment of the tax owed for the year.
Why D: Employers send withheld money to the government and do not keep it. Withholding is a tax payment, not a bonus for the employer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker gets a large refund every spring. What does this suggest about withholding?
A: Too much tax was withheld from paychecks all year
B: Taxes do not apply to refunds in any year at all
C: No tax was withheld during the year by the employer
D: Too little tax was withheld from paychecks all year
Why A: A large refund means more tax was taken from paychecks than was owed, so the government returns the extra. It is effectively an interest-free loan to the government.
Why B: Refunds are not taxes. The refund is the return of overpaid tax, so saying taxes do not apply to refunds misses what it indicates about withholding.
Why C: If no tax were withheld, the worker would likely owe tax at filing and not receive a refund. A large refund shows too much was withheld.
Why D: Too little withholding would produce a balance due when filing, not a refund. A large refund shows the opposite, which is that too much was withheld.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student earned $3,000 from a summer job and had $0 tax withheld. What should they check?
A: Nothing, since students never file tax returns on any earned income
B: Whether the employer is a nonprofit group or a for-profit firm today overall
C: Let their employer file for them, as the firm sends in each return
D: Whether they must file a return and whether they can claim any refund
Why A: Students do not automatically avoid filing. Whether a return is required depends on income and filing status, and filing may be needed to claim refunds.
Why B: Whether the employer is a nonprofit or a for-profit firm does not decide filing duties. The worker's income, status and withholding matter instead.
Why C: Employers do not file returns for workers. They report wages on a W-2, but each person must file their own return if required or to claim a refund.
Why D: The student should check whether income requires a return and whether filing could produce a refund. With $0 withheld, no refund is likely, but filing may still be needed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A freelancer earns $5,000 with no tax withheld. What should the freelancer plan for?
A: Paying tax only if the freelancer wishes
B: Paying estimated taxes and self-employment tax
C: A refund automatically, as freelancers are employees
D: Nothing, because freelance income is tax free
Why A: Paying tax is not optional. Self-employment income is taxable and must be reported, and ignoring it can bring penalties and interest from the tax authority.
Why B: With no withholding, a freelancer must pay estimated taxes during the year, plus self-employment tax of 15.3 percent for Social Security and Medicare on net earnings.
Why C: Freelancers are self-employed, not employees, so no employer withholds tax. A refund does not come automatically, and they usually owe tax at filing.
Why D: Freelance income is taxable like other income. Saying it is tax free is false, and ignoring it can lead to penalties for underpayment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Who is responsible for paying self-employment tax?
A: The government alone
B: Their customers, who pay it
C: The self-employed person
D: Their suppliers or buyers
Why A: The government does not pay self-employment tax for workers. It collects the tax from the self-employed person, who must pay both the employer and employee share.
Why B: Customers pay for the work, but they do not pay the freelancer's self-employment tax. The self-employed person must calculate and pay it on their own net earnings.
Why C: Self-employed people pay self-employment tax themselves, covering both the employer and employee halves of Social Security and Medicare, since there is no employer to share it.
Why D: Suppliers and buyers have no legal duty to pay a self-employed person's tax. The obligation rests on the self-employed worker, who reports and pays it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Form 1040?
A: A form used to report payments to contractors
B: A form used to set withholding at work each year
C: A form used by employers to report wages to employees
D: The standard individual federal income tax return
Why A: Reporting payments to contractors is done with Form 1099-NEC. Form 1040 is the individual return filed by taxpayers, not an information form.
Why B: Setting withholding at work is done with Form W-4. Form 1040 is filed at tax time to report income and compute tax owed.
Why C: Employers report wages to employees on Form W-2. Form 1040 is the return that individuals file themselves, not an employer's wage report.
Why D: Form 1040 is the standard federal individual income tax return, where taxpayers report income, claim deductions and credits, and calculate the tax owed or the refund due.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the filing deadline for most individual federal returns?
A: April 15 (or the next business day)
B: January 1, at the start of the year
C: July 4, the national holiday day
D: December 31, the last day of the year
Why A: The usual deadline for most individual federal returns is April 15, moving to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday.
Why B: January 1 is the start of the tax year, and returns for the prior year are not due then. Most filers have until mid-April.
Why C: July 4 is a holiday with no link to tax filing. The standard deadline is April 15, though extensions can move it later.
Why D: December 31 ends the tax year, but returns are filed afterward. The deadline for most individuals falls on April 15 of the following year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tax bracket?
A: A range of income taxed at a particular rate
B: A fee for filing a tax return late, added on
C: A form used to claim a refund from the state
D: A type of tax-exempt bond issued by cities
Why A: A tax bracket is a range of taxable income that is taxed at a particular rate. The US system has several brackets, with higher rates on higher slices of income.
Why B: A fee for filing late is a late-filing penalty. A bracket is a range of income taxed at one rate, not a charge for lateness.
Why C: A form used to claim a refund is a return. A tax bracket is a range of income, and it has nothing to do with claiming refunds.
Why D: Tax-exempt bonds issued by cities are municipal bonds. A tax bracket is an income range with a rate, not a type of bond.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If a raise pushes part of your income into a higher bracket, what happens?
A: You must pay back your raise to the government in full or in part
B: Your earlier income is taxed at the average of both rates
C: Your take-home pay falls below what you earned before the raise
D: Only the income in the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate
Why A: You never have to pay back a raise because of brackets. Only the extra income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so you still gain.
Why B: Brackets are marginal, so earlier income stays at its lower rates and is not averaged with the higher one; only the income in the higher bracket gets the higher rate.
Why C: A raise never lowers take-home pay because only the extra income in the higher bracket is taxed more; you still keep part of every added dollar.
Why D: The system is marginal, so only income inside the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate. Income below stays at lower rates, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a use tax?
A: A tax on using public roads, paid when drivers buy fuel overall
B: A tax on goods bought out of state for use in your state
C: A tax on using the internet at home or at an office
D: A tax on using a library at a school or a college
Why A: Taxes on fuel for road use are excise taxes collected at the pump. A use tax applies to goods bought elsewhere and used in your own state.
Why B: A use tax is owed on goods bought out of state, such as online, when no sales tax was charged, so it matches the sales tax you would have paid at home.
Why C: There is no general tax for using the internet at home or at an office. A use tax applies to purchased goods brought into the state.
Why D: A library or a school does not charge a use tax. This kind of tax applies to goods bought out of state and used within your own state.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an excise tax?
A: A tax on investments held by firms and savers
B: A tax on the sale of homes by owners each year
C: A tax on specific goods such as fuel or tobacco
D: A tax on all income earned by workers and firms
Why A: A tax on investments held by firms and savers is a capital or income tax, not an excise tax. Excise taxes apply to particular goods and services.
Why B: A tax on the sale of homes is a transfer or capital gains tax. An excise tax is levied on specific goods or activities, not home sales.
Why C: An excise tax is charged on specific goods or activities, such as gasoline, tobacco, alcohol and airline tickets, and is often built into the price you pay.
Why D: A tax on all income of workers and firms is an income tax. An excise tax targets particular products, not broad earnings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an estate tax?
A: A tax on selling a home or other real estate overall
B: A tax on rental income earned by a landlord
C: A tax on buying real estate, paid at closing
D: A tax on transferring a dead person's property
Why A: A tax on selling a home is a capital gains or transfer tax. An estate tax is triggered by death and applies to the property left behind.
Why B: A tax on rental income is an income tax paid by the landlord. An estate tax applies to inherited wealth, not to income earned from rentals.
Why C: A tax paid when buying real estate is a transfer or recording tax at closing. An estate tax is about passing property after death.
Why D: An estate tax is charged on the transfer of a deceased person's property to heirs, and in the US applies only to estates above a high exemption amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a capital gains tax?
A: A tax on interest paid on a savings account by a bank
B: A tax on gifts given to others by one person to another in general
C: A tax on profit from selling an asset for more than its cost
D: A tax on wages and salaries paid to workers each year
Why A: A tax on interest paid by a bank is income tax on interest. A capital gains tax applies to profit from selling an asset, not to interest.
Why B: A tax on gifts is a gift tax. Capital gains tax applies when an asset such as stock or property is sold for more than it cost.
Why C: A capital gains tax is charged on the profit you make when you sell an asset, such as stocks or property, for more than you paid for it.
Why D: A tax on wages and salaries is an income or payroll tax. Capital gains tax applies to profit from selling assets, not to earnings from work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do long-term capital gains often have lower tax rates than short-term gains?
A: Long-term gains are deferred until the investor reaches age 65
B: The tax law favors assets held longer than one year
C: Short-term gains are taxed twice, which raises their rate
D: The rates are the same for both types of gains
Why A: Long-term gains are taxed in the year the asset is sold, not deferred to a certain age; the lower rate rewards holding for more than a year.
Why B: Tax law gives lower rates to gains on assets held longer than a year, which encourages long-term investing, while short-term gains are taxed at ordinary income rates.
Why C: Short-term gains are taxed once at ordinary income rates; they are not taxed twice, and the difference is that long-term gains get lower special rates.
Why D: The rates differ. Short-term gains are taxed at ordinary income rates, while long-term gains get lower special rates, so saying they are the same is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tax-exempt organization?
A: An organization, such as a charity, that does not pay certain taxes
B: A business that pays no taxes of any kind because it serves the public good
C: A government office that sells bonds to the public for the state
D: A company that is too small to pay tax on its income in the year
Why A: A tax-exempt organization, such as a charity, church or school, is recognized by law as not required to pay certain taxes, like federal income tax, on activities tied to its mission.
Why B: Tax-exempt groups are not free of all taxes. They may still pay payroll taxes, and taxes on unrelated business income, so saying any kind is overstated.
Why C: A government office selling bonds is a government agency or issuer. A tax-exempt organization is a nonprofit entity recognized by law, not a bond seller.
Why D: Small size alone does not make a company exempt. Businesses owe tax on income whatever their size, while exempt status depends on legal qualification as a nonprofit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens if you underpay your taxes and do not file an extension?
A: You receive a bonus refund anyway
B: The debt is erased by the tax agency
C: Nothing, as the agency does not check
D: You may owe penalties and interest
Why A: Underpaying brings a bill, not a bonus. Nobody receives a refund for tax they failed to pay, so this outcome is the opposite of what happens.
Why B: Tax debts are not erased by the agency. The amount stays owed, and penalties and interest grow until it is paid or settled by a formal process.
Why C: The tax agency does check returns through matching and audits. Assuming nothing happens is a risky mistake, since unpaid tax is eventually discovered and charged.
Why D: Without payment or an extension, unpaid tax accrues late-payment penalties and interest, so you owe more over time. Filing an extension does not extend the time to pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When might a taxpayer itemize deductions rather than take the standard deduction?
A: When their income is higher than average
B: When allowed expenses exceed the standard amount
C: When they are filing for the first time
D: When they want to pay more tax, so they itemize
Why A: Itemizing depends on whether deductible expenses exceed the standard deduction, not on income level, so a high earner with few expenses should still take the standard deduction.
Why B: Itemizing makes sense when your allowed expenses, such as mortgage interest, state taxes and charity, add up to more than the standard deduction, which lowers taxable income further.
Why C: Filing for the first time does not make itemizing better; the choice depends on whether allowed expenses add up to more than the standard deduction.
Why D: Itemizing lowers taxable income and reduces tax, so wanting to pay more tax is no reason. The choice should depend on which deduction is larger.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a W-9 form?
A: A form a contractor gives a business with their taxpayer information
B: A form employees use to set withholding at their new job each year overall
C: A form that shows an employee's yearly wages and the tax withheld
D: A form to request an extension of the tax filing date from the IRS
Why A: A W-9 is the form an independent contractor gives a business, listing their name, address and taxpayer identification number so the business can report payments on Form 1099.
Why B: Employees use a W-4 to set withholding at a new job. A W-9 is for contractors and has nothing to do with withholding choices.
Why C: The form showing an employee's yearly wages and tax withheld is a W-2. A W-9 supplies a contractor's taxpayer information instead.
Why D: An extension of the filing date is requested with Form 4868. A W-9 gives a contractor's taxpayer details to a business, not a request to the IRS.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Form 1099-NEC used for?
A: Reporting stock sales and gains on trades overall
B: Reporting wages to employees at year end
C: Reporting payments to independent contractors
D: Reporting a gift made to a family member
Why A: Reporting stock sales and gains uses Form 1099-B, issued by brokers. A 1099-NEC reports non-employee pay such as fees paid to contractors.
Why B: Wages paid to employees are reported on Form W-2. A 1099-NEC is used for non-employees, so reporting wages to employees is the wrong form.
Why C: Form 1099-NEC reports payments of $600 or more made to independent contractors and other non-employees, so the payee can report the income and pay tax on it.
Why D: Gifts are not reported on this form. Large gifts may need a gift tax return, Form 709, but 1099-NEC concerns payments for services by non-employees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is earned income?
A: Money from interest and dividends only, paid to investors overall
B: Money from selling a car at a profit to a private buyer
C: Money from working, such as wages and self-employment income
D: Money from gifts given by relatives and close friends
Why A: Interest and dividends are investment income, which is not earned income. Earned income comes from working, so this answer leaves out wages and self-employment pay.
Why B: Profit from selling a car is a capital gain, not pay for work. Earned income comes from working, such as wages or self-employment, not from asset sales.
Why C: Earned income is money from working, including wages, salaries, tips and net self-employment income. It is the basis for credits like the EITC and for IRA contributions.
Why D: Gifts from relatives are not earned, since no work was done to receive them. Earned income arises from labor, such as wages or running a business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is passive income?
A: Money earned with little day-to-day effort, such as rental income
B: A tax refund from the government after the filing of a return overall
C: Wages from a full-time job at a firm, paid each month by it
D: Money received as a gift from relatives, not earned by work
Why A: Passive income comes from activities needing little day-to-day effort, such as rental property or limited partnerships. It differs from wages because ongoing work is not required.
Why B: A tax refund returns overpaid tax and is not income from an activity. Passive income is money earned from sources such as rentals with little regular effort.
Why C: Wages from a full-time job are earned income because they require regular work. Passive income needs little ongoing effort, so wages do not qualify.
Why D: A gift is money received without work, but it is not passive income. Passive income comes from assets or businesses like rentals that earn money with little effort.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tax-advantaged account?
A: An account with no fees of any kind for the account owner
B: An account that pays no interest on the balance held in it
C: An account the government runs for citizens who have no savings
D: An account with special tax treatment, such as an IRA or 529
Why A: Fees can apply to tax-advantaged accounts. The term describes tax treatment, not fee levels, so saying there are no fees of any kind is wrong.
Why B: Tax-advantaged accounts generally do pay interest or earn returns. The advantage concerns taxes, not interest, so an account paying none does not fit.
Why C: An account run by the government for people without savings is a welfare program. A tax-advantaged account is open to savers and has special tax treatment.
Why D: A tax-advantaged account offers special tax treatment, such as deductible contributions or tax-free growth. Examples include IRAs, 401(k) plans, HSAs and 529 college savings plans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the three functions of money?
A: Spending, borrowing and lending of money each year
B: Medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value
C: Only a way to decorate a wallet, with little other use
D: Saving, investing and taxing of money by the state
Why A: Spending, borrowing and lending are uses of money, not its functions. The three functions are medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
Why B: Money works as a medium of exchange for buying goods, a unit of account for pricing them, and a store of value that holds purchasing power over time.
Why C: Money is a practical economic tool and not decoration. Its real functions are exchange, measuring value and storing value, so this answer is not a function.
Why D: Saving, investing and taxing are activities involving money, not its functions. Money itself serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inflation?
A: A general rise in prices over time
B: A rise in the value of a currency
C: A rise in interest rates on loans
D: A general fall in prices over time
Why A: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in the overall price level over time, which reduces what each dollar can buy. It is usually measured by an index like CPI.
Why B: A rising currency value is appreciation, which makes money buy more; inflation is a general rise in prices that makes money buy less.
Why C: Higher loan interest rates are a change in the cost of borrowing; inflation is a general rise in the price level across the economy.
Why D: A general fall in prices over time is deflation, the opposite of inflation. Inflation means prices rise on average across the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Prices rise 3 percent in a year while your pay rises 2 percent. What happened to your buying power?
A: No change
B: It doubled
C: It fell
D: It rose
Why A: Buying power changes when prices and pay grow at different rates. Prices rose 3 percent while pay rose only 2 percent, so there was a change.
Why B: Buying power cannot double when pay lags prices. Pay rose 2 percent against 3 percent price growth, so the effect is a small decline.
Why C: Prices rose faster than pay, 3 percent versus 2 percent, so your pay buys fewer goods than before. Your real income fell by about 1 percent.
Why D: Buying power rises only if pay grows faster than prices. Here pay rose 2 percent against 3 percent price growth, so it fell and did not rise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If prices double over time, what happens to the value of a dollar?
A: It buys twice as much now
B: It buys about half as much
C: It buys the same amount
D: It becomes worthless at once
Why A: If prices double, each dollar buys less, not more. Buying twice as much would require prices to fall by half instead.
Why B: If prices double, each dollar buys only about half as many goods as before. Purchasing power falls in proportion to the rise in the price level.
Why C: Doubled prices mean a dollar buys less. It cannot buy the same amount, because the same goods now cost twice as much.
Why D: Money loses purchasing power but does not become worthless at once. A dollar still buys something, only about half as much if prices double.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?
A: A measure of interest rates charged by the banks each year
B: A measure of employment levels across the nation as a whole
C: A measure of the profits of companies, from all firms' earnings
D: A measure of price changes for a basket of goods and services
Why A: Interest rates charged by banks are measured by rate surveys, not CPI. CPI tracks the prices consumers pay, not borrowing costs.
Why B: Employment levels are measured by the unemployment rate and jobs reports. CPI measures price changes, not how many people hold jobs.
Why C: Company profits are reported in earnings statements. CPI follows consumer prices and is not a measure of corporate profit.
Why D: The CPI tracks the change in prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by typical urban consumers, and it is the standard gauge of inflation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Federal Reserve?
A: A government agency that collects taxes
B: A stock exchange for trading shares
C: The central bank of the United States
D: A commercial bank that lends for profit
Why A: Collecting taxes is the job of the IRS and other revenue agencies. The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supervises banks instead.
Why B: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE or Nasdaq, trades shares. The Federal Reserve does not run a market for shares but sets monetary policy.
Why C: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It sets monetary policy, supervises banks, and works to keep prices stable and employment high.
Why D: The Fed does not operate to earn profit from lending. It acts as the central bank and as lender of last resort, with policy goals instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to borrowing costs when the Fed raises interest rates?
A: They tend to rise
B: They stay the same
C: They tend to fall
D: They disappear
Why A: When the Fed raises its rates, banks pay more to borrow, so loan rates on mortgages, cards and car loans tend to rise, and borrowing becomes more costly.
Why B: Borrowing costs do not stay fixed when the Fed raises rates. Banks pass higher funding costs on, so consumer loan rates usually move upward in response.
Why C: Rates tend to fall when the Fed lowers rates, not raises them. A rise in the policy rate pushes loan rates up and makes borrowing costlier.
Why D: Borrowing costs never vanish when the Fed raises rates. Higher policy rates make loans more costly, and interest remains part of every loan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a real interest rate?
A: The highest rate that a bank may charge today
B: The rate printed on a loan agreement, unadjusted
C: The interest rate that applies to real estate loans
D: The nominal interest rate adjusted for inflation
Why A: The highest rate a bank may charge is a usury cap, which is a legal limit. The real rate is a measure that adjusts for inflation.
Why B: The rate printed on a loan agreement is the nominal rate. The real rate corrects that figure for inflation, so unadjusted is the opposite meaning.
Why C: A rate on real estate loans is a mortgage rate. The real interest rate is a different idea that accounts for inflation and has no link to property.
Why D: The real interest rate is the nominal rate minus the inflation rate. It shows the true gain in purchasing power that an investor earns, or the cost a borrower pays.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A savings account pays 3 percent and inflation is 2 percent. What is the approximate real rate?
A: About 0 percent
B: About 1 percent
C: About 6 percent
D: About 5 percent
Why A: A real rate near zero would need inflation near 3 percent. With 2 percent inflation, the nominal 3 percent leaves about 1 percent after adjusting.
Why B: The real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation, so 3 percent minus 2 percent equals about 1 percent. Your savings gain only a little buying power.
Why C: Six percent would come from adding 3 and 2 and then doubling the sum. The real rate subtracts inflation, giving 3 minus 2, or about 1 percent.
Why D: Five percent adds inflation to the nominal rate. Inflation erodes returns, so you subtract it, and 3 minus 2 gives a real rate near 1 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean for money to be liquid?
A: It is held in a bank account for savings
B: It earns a steady interest payment each month
C: It is held in real estate for many years
D: It can be spent or converted to cash quickly
Why A: Holding money in a bank account does not define liquidity, since some bank accounts, such as long-term CDs, are hard to access without penalty.
Why B: Earning interest does not make money liquid; liquidity means how quickly an asset can be spent or turned into cash without losing much value.
Why C: Real estate takes time and effort to sell, so it is illiquid; liquid money can be spent or converted to cash quickly.
Why D: Liquidity describes how quickly an asset can be spent or turned into cash without losing much value. Cash and checking balances are highly liquid, while property is not.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recession's effect on household finances?
A: Job losses and lower incomes become more likely
B: Jobs become easier to find for most workers
C: Prices fall to zero, so households buy goods free
D: Wages always rise for all workers in the nation
Why A: In a recession, businesses cut costs and lay off workers, so job losses and lower incomes become more likely for households, which strains budgets.
Why B: In a recession jobs become harder to find, not easier. Employers cut hiring while many people search for work, so this answer reverses the effect.
Why C: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. Some prices fall or rise more slowly, but goods are never free, and households still must pay.
Why D: Wages do not always rise in a recession. Pay often stagnates or is cut and hours are reduced, so this claim is false for most workers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is gross domestic product (GDP)?
A: The total amount of exports only from the country each year
B: The total money held by the government at the central bank
C: The total value of goods and services produced in a country
D: The total wages paid to workers in a country each year
Why A: Exports are only one part of a nation's output, and GDP counts everything produced at home, including goods and services sold domestically, so exports alone cannot be the total.
Why B: Money held by the government at the central bank is a balance sheet item and says nothing about how much the whole economy produces during a year.
Why C: GDP adds up the market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a period, usually a year, which is exactly this definition.
Why D: Wages paid to workers make up only part of income in an economy, and GDP measures total output value, which also includes profits, rents, and taxes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is supply and demand?
A: A government plan to set all prices and wages for firms and for workers in the nation
B: The relationship between how much is offered and how much is wanted at various prices
C: A list of items for sale in a store, with the price of each one and its stock level
D: A tax on goods sold abroad, paid by the exporters to the government when they leave the port
Why A: A government plan that sets all prices and wages describes central planning, not supply and demand, where prices move freely as buyers and sellers respond to each other.
Why B: Supply and demand describes how the quantity sellers offer and the quantity buyers want both change with price, and the price settles where these two meet.
Why C: A list of items with prices and stock levels is just a store inventory sheet, and it does not explain how prices are set by buyers and sellers.
Why D: A tax on goods sold abroad is an export duty, which is a government policy tool and has nothing to do with how markets balance supply and demand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When demand for a product rises and supply stays the same, what usually happens to its price?
A: It falls
B: It rises
C: It is zero
D: No change
Why A: If demand rises while supply stays fixed, more buyers chase the same goods, so sellers can charge more and the price does not fall.
Why B: With more buyers competing for an unchanged supply, shortages push sellers to raise the price until the amount wanted again matches the amount available, so the price rises.
Why C: A price of zero would only occur when a good is free and plentiful, which is the opposite of what happens when demand increases against fixed supply.
Why D: Prices respond to the balance of supply and demand, so a rise in demand with fixed supply must move the price, and it will not stay unchanged.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a monopoly?
A: A market with many sellers of similar goods in practice
B: A market with a few large sellers and many buyers
C: A market owned by the customers and their families
D: A market with one seller and no close substitutes
Why A: A market with many sellers of similar goods is described as competitive, and it is nearly the opposite of a monopoly, where only one seller exists.
Why B: A few large sellers and many buyers describes an oligopoly, in which several firms share the market, so it is not a monopoly, which has just one seller.
Why C: A market owned by customers and their families describes a cooperative style of ownership and says nothing about the number of sellers or the lack of substitutes.
Why D: A monopoly has a single seller and no close substitutes, so buyers have nowhere else to go, which gives the seller strong power over price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor puts $100 into a fund each month. Prices are $10, $5, then $10. How many shares are bought in total?
A: 30 shares
B: 25 shares
C: 40 shares
D: 20 shares
Why A: Thirty shares is wrong because it adds the prices incorrectly or counts only two months; the three purchases are 10 shares, 20 shares, and 10 shares, which total 40.
Why B: Twenty-five shares does not match any sum of the three purchases; $100 buys 10 shares at $10, 20 shares at $5, and 10 shares at $10, giving 40.
Why C: Each month buys $100 divided by the price: 10 shares at $10, 20 shares at $5, then 10 shares at $10, and 10 plus 20 plus 10 equals 40 shares.
Why D: Twenty shares is only the purchase made in the cheap $5 month; it ignores the 10 shares bought in each of the other two months, so the total is really 40.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If you invest $200 a month at an average of 6 percent, which factor most affects your final balance?
A: The length of time you invest
B: The day of the week you invest
C: The brand of your bank checkbook
D: The color of the bank statement
Why A: With regular monthly contributions at a given return, compounding works longer on early deposits, so the length of time invested has the largest effect on the final balance.
Why B: The day of the week you invest has almost no effect over decades, because returns depend on growth over years and not on which weekday a deposit is made.
Why C: The brand of a checkbook has no effect on investment growth, since the balance depends on contributions, returns, and time and not on the stationery you use.
Why D: The color of a bank statement is only cosmetic and cannot change returns, so it cannot affect how large the final balance becomes after years of saving.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a target-date retirement fund?
A: A fund that moves toward riskier stocks as a retirement date nears
B: A fund that pays a fixed income to retirees each month
C: A fund that shifts toward safer assets as a retirement date nears
D: A fund that holds one mix of assets until its target date
Why A: This reverses the glide path; a target-date fund becomes more conservative, shifting toward bonds and cash as the retirement year gets closer.
Why B: A target-date fund is an investment fund that adjusts its mix over time; it does not promise a fixed monthly income to retirees.
Why C: A target-date fund starts with more stocks for growth and gradually moves toward bonds and cash as the chosen retirement year approaches, lowering risk when it matters most.
Why D: A target-date fund changes its mix of stocks and bonds as the target year nears, so holding one unchanged mix does not describe it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is it risky to chase last year's top-performing fund?
A: Top funds must by law repeat their results
B: Fees rise after a strong year
C: Top funds hold too many stocks
D: Past gains often fail to repeat later on
Why A: No law requires a top fund to repeat its results, and returns often fall back toward average the next year, so assuming repeat performance is a mistake.
Why B: Fund fees do not automatically rise after a good year; the risk of chasing winners is that past performance does not predict future results.
Why C: Holding many stocks is a form of diversification, not a risk; chasing last year's winner is risky because strong past results often do not repeat.
Why D: Past performance does not guarantee future results, because markets change and luck plays a role, so chasing last year's winner can lead to disappointing returns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stop-loss order?
A: An order to buy at the lowest price of the year
B: An order to sell when a price falls to a set level
C: An order that prevents all trades from being made
D: An order to buy when prices rise by a set amount
Why A: Buying at the lowest price of the year would need perfect hindsight, and a stop-loss is a sell instruction, not a buy order, so this definition does not fit.
Why B: A stop-loss order automatically becomes a sell order once the price drops to the level you set, which limits how much you can lose on a position.
Why C: A stop-loss order does not block trading; it is a specific instruction placed with a broker, and it only triggers a sale when the stated price is reached.
Why D: An order to buy after prices rise by a set amount is a buy-stop order, whereas a stop-loss is a sell order that triggers when prices fall.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is margin investing?
A: Borrowing money from a broker to buy securities
B: Investing only your own cash and none borrowed
C: Investing on the edges of the market for small moves
D: Investing in a savings account at a local bank
Why A: Margin investing means borrowing money from a broker to buy more securities than your cash would allow, which magnifies both potential gains and potential losses on the position.
Why B: Using only your own cash with no borrowing is the opposite of margin investing, which by definition involves a loan from the broker to buy securities.
Why C: Margin has nothing to do with the edges of the market or small price moves; it refers to a loan from a broker used to purchase securities.
Why D: Putting money in a savings account at a local bank is ordinary saving, and it involves no borrowing from a broker, so it is not margin investing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main risk of buying stocks on margin?
A: Margin loans are free of any interest charge
B: Your losses are capped at ten percent
C: Losses can exceed your original investment
D: The broker guarantees your profit each time
Why A: Margin loans do charge interest, so calling them free is false, and the interest cost adds to the losses an investor may face on a falling position.
Why B: Losses are not capped at ten percent; because you borrow to buy more, a fall in price can wipe out your money and leave you owing more.
Why C: Because the broker's loan must be repaid in full, a sharp price drop can cause losses larger than the original investment, which is the main risk of margin.
Why D: Brokers never guarantee profits on margin trades; they lend money and expect repayment with interest whether the investment gains or loses, so the investor carries all the risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a stock's ticker symbol do?
A: A rating for the company's debt load
B: A tax number for the company's filings
C: A password to log in to a broker's site
D: Identifies a listed company in trading
Why A: A rating of a company's debt load comes from credit rating agencies, while a ticker symbol is just a short code used to name the stock in markets.
Why B: A tax number used on a company's filings is an identification number for tax authorities, and it is a different thing from the short letters used in trading.
Why C: A ticker symbol is a public code for a stock, not a password, and it gives no access to anyone's broker account or login.
Why D: A ticker symbol is a short code of letters that identifies a listed company or fund when orders are placed and prices are quoted on the exchange.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mutual fund's net asset value (NAV)?
A: The yearly fee of the fund and its managers to hold it
B: The per-share value of the fund's assets minus liabilities
C: The total number of investors in the fund at year end
D: The price printed on a stock certificate held by the first buyer
Why A: A yearly fee to hold a fund is its expense ratio, not NAV, which instead measures the value of one share based on the fund's assets and liabilities.
Why B: NAV is found by subtracting the fund's liabilities from its assets and dividing by the number of shares, giving the per-share value at which mutual fund shares trade.
Why C: The number of investors in a fund is a count of shareholders and has no role in the NAV calculation, which uses assets, liabilities, and shares outstanding.
Why D: A price printed on a stock certificate is the par or original issue figure for a stock, and a mutual fund's NAV is recalculated each day from its holdings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do many experts suggest low-cost index funds for long-term investors?
A: They offer broad diversification and low fees
B: They are insured by the government against loss
C: They carry no market risk as they hold many stocks
D: They guarantee that they will beat the market
Why A: Index funds hold hundreds of companies in one fund and charge very low fees, so investors get wide diversification at low cost, which suits long-term goals.
Why B: Index funds are not insured against loss by the government; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, while fund values rise and fall with the markets they track.
Why C: Holding many stocks reduces company-specific risk but not market risk, so an index fund can still fall sharply when the whole market declines.
Why D: An index fund aims to match the market, not beat it, so no guarantee of outperformance exists, and it will rise and fall roughly in line with its index.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stock's volatility?
A: How much and how quickly its price moves up and down
B: How long the company has existed, counted in years overall
C: How much dividend it pays out to holders each year
D: How many shares exist in the whole market today
Why A: Volatility describes how much and how quickly a price swings up and down, with higher volatility meaning bigger and faster changes and therefore more uncertainty for holders.
Why B: The age of a company in years has no link to volatility, since young and old firms can both have stable or wildly moving share prices.
Why C: Dividends paid to holders are called the dividend, and volatility measures price movement, so how much a company pays out does not define volatility.
Why D: The number of shares in the whole market is not a measure of price movement, so it does not describe volatility, which is about swings in price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes an aggressive portfolio?
A: A high share of cash and short-term bonds
B: Mostly Treasury bonds held to maturity
C: A high share of stocks seeking growth
D: Mostly CDs and money market funds
Why A: A high share of cash and short-term bonds is a cautious, low-risk mix and describes a conservative portfolio, which is the opposite of aggressive.
Why B: Mostly Treasury bonds held to maturity is a cautious, low-risk approach; an aggressive portfolio holds a high share of stocks seeking growth.
Why C: An aggressive portfolio puts a high share in stocks, accepting larger swings and the chance of bigger losses in exchange for higher expected long-term growth.
Why D: CDs and money market funds are safe and low-return, so a portfolio built from them is conservative rather than aggressive.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes a conservative portfolio?
A: Mostly new company stocks bought for rapid growth
B: A larger share of bonds and cash to protect principal
C: Mostly speculative stocks of young firms, risking loss
D: Mostly options contracts on shares and bonds in funds
Why A: New company stocks bought for rapid growth describe an aggressive, risk-seeking approach, which is the opposite of a conservative portfolio that aims to protect savings.
Why B: A conservative portfolio holds more bonds and cash so that the original amount invested is less likely to fall, accepting lower growth in return for stability.
Why C: Speculative stocks of young firms carry a high risk of loss, so a portfolio made of them is aggressive and does not match a conservative goal.
Why D: Options contracts are complex and risky instruments that can lose all their value quickly, so a portfolio mostly made of them would not be conservative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor has 10 years until needing money for a home. What mix is generally reasonable?
A: All in one start-up company that has no profits and no sales
B: All in speculative stocks until the money is needed for the home overall
C: All in cash for the whole ten years until the home is bought
D: A balance of stocks and bonds that shifts safer as the date nears
Why A: Putting everything in one start-up with no profits or sales is extreme concentration, so a single failure could erase the savings needed for the home purchase.
Why B: All speculative stocks until the money is needed risks a large loss right before the purchase, with no time to recover, which is unsuitable for a ten year goal.
Why C: All cash for ten years is safe from market drops but may lose purchasing power to inflation, so it gives up growth that a ten year horizon can capture.
Why D: With ten years to go, a mix of stocks and bonds gives some growth, and moving gradually toward safer holdings as the purchase date nears protects the money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' mean for investing?
A: Spread out investments
B: Concentrate on winners
C: Keep cash handy
D: Put your money in eggs
Why A: The saying means spreading money across many different investments, so that if one performs badly, the others can offset the loss and the overall risk falls.
Why B: Concentrating on winners puts more eggs in one basket; the saying advises spreading money across different investments to reduce risk.
Why C: Keeping cash handy is about liquidity; the eggs saying advises diversifying so that one poor performer cannot ruin the whole portfolio.
Why D: The eggs are a metaphor, not a literal suggestion to buy eggs, and the advice concerns splitting investments among assets and not about spending on groceries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is a hot tip from social media risky for investing?
A: Tips are reviewed by regulators before they are posted
B: Tips are illegal to read or to pass on to others
C: Tips come from licensed advisors who have studied the stock
D: Tips may be false, promotional or part of a scheme
Why A: Regulators do not review social media posts before publication, so tips can be false, paid promotions or part of a scheme.
Why B: Reading or sharing a tip is not illegal in itself; the risk is that the tip may be misleading, promotional, or a scheme meant to trap investors.
Why C: Many tips come from anonymous accounts with no license or research and some have hidden interests, so acting on them without checking is risky.
Why D: Social media tips can be false, paid promotions, or part of pump-and-dump schemes, so acting on one without research can lead to large and quick losses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is dividend reinvestment?
A: Spending dividends on bills and food
B: Using dividends to buy more shares
C: Returning dividends to the company
D: Sending dividends to a charity
Why A: Spending dividends on bills and food is using them as income and does not reinvest them, because reinvesting means putting the money back into the investment.
Why B: Dividend reinvestment uses the dividends paid out to buy additional shares, which grows the number of shares owned and lets future dividends compound over time.
Why C: Returning dividends to the company would cancel the payout and is not reinvestment, which buys more shares for the investor and not for the company.
Why D: Sending dividends to a charity is a donation of the income, so the investor gets no extra shares and it is not dividend reinvestment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bond with a $1,000 face value is bought at $950. What is this called?
A: Buying on margin
B: Buying at a premium
C: Buying at a discount
D: Buying at par value
Why A: Buying on margin means borrowing from a broker to buy securities, and it has nothing to do with paying less than face value for a bond.
Why B: A premium means paying more than the $1,000 face value, but $950 is below that amount, so this purchase is not at a premium.
Why C: The bond has a face value of $1,000 and was bought for $950, which is less than face value, and buying below face value is called buying at a discount.
Why D: Buying at par means paying exactly the $1,000 face value, but $950 is $50 lower, so this is not a purchase at par.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is yield?
A: The fee a broker charges for each trade made for you by phone
B: The income an investment returns, as a percent of its price or cost
C: The total number of shares an investor owns in a single company every time
D: The date a bond matures and the principal is repaid to holders
Why A: A fee charged by a broker for executing a trade is a commission, which is a cost and not the income an investment returns as a percent of price.
Why B: Yield measures the income an investment returns, such as interest or dividends, as a percent of its price or cost, which lets investors compare different investments.
Why C: The total number of shares an investor owns is their holding or position size, and it says nothing about the income earned as a percent of price.
Why D: The date a bond matures and repays principal is its maturity date, and it is different from yield, which measures income relative to the investment's price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between saving and investing?
A: Saving has more risk than investing, since a bank can lose your money
B: Saving seeks growth with risk while investing prioritizes safety and access
C: Saving is done through a broker while investing is done at a bank
D: Saving prioritizes safety and access while investing seeks growth with risk
Why A: Saving is generally the lower risk choice, such as an insured bank account, so saying it has more risk than investing reverses the real relationship.
Why B: This swaps the two ideas; saving is for safety and easy access, while investing accepts risk in order to seek growth over a longer period.
Why C: Saving usually happens in bank accounts and investing usually happens through a broker, so this reverses where each is done.
Why D: Saving keeps money safe and easy to reach for near-term needs, while investing accepts the chance of loss in order to seek growth over a longer time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor's portfolio is 80 percent stocks and 20 percent bonds. Stocks fall 10 percent and bonds are unchanged. About how much does the portfolio fall?
A: About 8 percent
B: About 2 percent
C: About 18 percent
D: About 10 percent
Why A: Stocks are 80 percent of the portfolio, so a 10 percent drop costs 0.80 times 10, which is 8 percent, while the unchanged bonds add no loss.
Why B: Two percent would come from 20 percent times 10 percent, which applies the stock drop to the bond share, but it is stocks that fell, and they are 80 percent.
Why C: Eighteen percent comes from adding 8 and 10, which double counts; only the stock portion fell, and 80 percent times 10 percent gives just 8 percent.
Why D: A 10 percent portfolio loss would need every holding to fall 10 percent, but bonds were unchanged and are 20 percent of the portfolio, so the loss is only 8 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why can frequent trading hurt returns?
A: It is not legal to do so
B: It removes all risk of loss
C: Fees and taxes reduce gains
D: It always lifts returns for you
Why A: Frequent trading is legal, so it is not true that it is against the law, although it may cost investors more money than they expect.
Why B: Trading does not remove risk; every trade still exposes the investor to price changes, and frequent trading can add costs on top of the existing risk.
Why C: Each trade can bring commissions, spreads, and taxes on short-term gains, which reduce the net return, so more trading often leaves investors with less money.
Why D: Frequent trading does not always lift returns, since costs and mistimed trades can reduce them, and studies show active traders often earn less than buy-and-hold investors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is comparison shopping a smart habit?
A: It is required by law for shoppers
B: It helps find the best price and value
C: It guarantees the lowest price in the world
D: It removes the need for a budget plan
Why A: No law requires shoppers to compare prices; it is a personal habit people adopt because it saves money, so legal requirement is not the reason it is smart.
Why B: Comparing prices and quality across stores or brands helps a shopper find the best value for their money, and this saving is why the habit is smart.
Why C: Comparison shopping cannot guarantee the lowest price in the world, because nobody can check every seller, but it does improve the chance of a good deal.
Why D: A budget is still needed because comparison shopping only affects the price of each purchase, and it does not control the total amount that you spend.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A 16 oz bottle costs $3.20 and a 24 oz bottle costs $4.20. Which is the better unit price?
A: The 16 oz bottle at $0.20 an ounce, the dearer
B: The 16 oz bottle, since $3.20 is the lower price
C: Neither, since both cost about $0.19 an ounce
D: The 24 oz bottle at about $0.175 per ounce
Why A: The 16 oz bottle costs $3.20 divided by 16, which is $0.20 an ounce, and that is higher than the larger bottle's unit price, so it is not the better buy.
Why B: The lower total price does not mean the better value; the smaller bottle costs $0.20 an ounce, while the 24 oz bottle costs about $0.175.
Why C: The bottles do not cost the same per ounce; $3.20 divided by 16 is $0.20, while $4.20 divided by 24 is $0.175, so the larger bottle is cheaper.
Why D: Dividing $4.20 by 24 ounces gives $0.175 per ounce, which is lower than the $0.20 per ounce for the smaller bottle, so the 24 oz size is better value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A coupon takes $10 off a purchase of $50 or more. A shopper has $46 in items and considers adding a $4 item to use it. Is it a good idea?
A: Yes always, as coupons are free money and buying more only saves
B: No, because coupons cannot be used on purchases of $50 or more
C: Only if she needed the extra item, since she still pays $40
D: Yes, because the item becomes free of charge to her once she buys
Why A: Coupons are not free money if you buy something you do not need; adding a $4 item just to save $10 means spending more than before, so always is wrong.
Why B: The coupon requires a purchase of $50 or more, so it can be used at $50 and above; saying it cannot be used there reverses the rule.
Why C: Adding the $4 item brings the total to $50, the coupon cuts it to $40, so she pays less than $46, but this helps only if she wanted the item.
Why D: The item is not free; she still pays $40 for $50 of goods, so the extra $4 item is only partly offset by the coupon and costs her real money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is buying on impulse?
A: Purchasing without planning
B: Purchasing at a discount
C: Purchasing only listed items
D: Purchasing online or in store
Why A: Buying on impulse means purchasing something without planning ahead, often on a sudden urge, rather than because the item was on a list or budget.
Why B: A discount describes the price of an item and not the reason for buying, since people can plan purchases of discounted goods, so it is not an impulse buy.
Why C: Purchasing only listed items is the opposite of impulse buying, because sticking to a shopping list is a planned approach to spending.
Why D: Shopping online or in a store describes where someone buys and not why, so both can be planned or impulsive and neither defines buying on impulse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a need and not a want?
A: A concert ticket
B: A new video game
C: Basic groceries
D: A streaming plan
Why A: A concert ticket is entertainment, which is nice to have but not required for survival or basic living, so it is a want and not a need.
Why B: A new video game is a leisure purchase that people can live without, so it is classified as a want and not as a basic need.
Why C: Basic groceries supply the food a person must eat to live and stay healthy, so they are a need and not simply something that is wanted.
