Why A: SIPC does not cover market losses, so full value is never guaranteed; it only restores missing cash and securities, up to $500,000 per customer, when a brokerage fails.
Why B: SIPC never covers losses from falling prices or bad investment choices; it responds only to a failed brokerage firm, so claiming it covers all losses is false.
Why C: SIPC has no weekend or holiday condition; its protection depends on the brokerage failing, not on the calendar, and still excludes losses caused by a market decline.
Why D: SIPC protects customers when a brokerage fails and assets go missing, not when prices drop; a market-driven fall in value is investment risk the investor bears alone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A retiree who needs steady income soon would most likely choose:
A: A more conservative mix of bonds and stable assets
B: Borrowing to buy more stocks on margin accounts
C: All speculative penny stocks that may gain quickly
D: Only options trading and futures trading in funds
Why A: A retiree needing steady income soon cannot afford large swings, so a conservative mix of bonds and stable assets protects principal while providing predictable interest and dividend income.
Why B: Margin means borrowing to buy more stocks, which magnifies losses; a retiree with little time to recover cannot safely take that kind of leveraged risk.
Why C: Penny stocks are highly speculative and can lose most of their value quickly; a retiree needing steady income soon cannot rely on such unpredictable, risky holdings.
Why D: Options and futures are complex, leveraged instruments that can produce large losses and no regular income, so they suit speculation rather than a retiree's need for stability.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is compound interest?
A: A fee on loans paid by borrowers to the lender each year
B: Interest earned on both the original amount and past interest
C: A tax on interest earned on savings and deposits each year
D: Interest earned only on the original amount, never on past interest
Why A: That describes a loan fee, meaning ordinary interest paid by a borrower to a lender; compound interest instead means interest also earns interest, which grows savings faster over time.
Why B: Compound interest is earned on the original principal plus all interest already added, so each period's interest is larger than the last and growth accelerates over time.
Why C: A tax on interest income is just a tax; compound interest is a growth mechanism for the balance itself, not a levy charged by the government.
Why D: Interest earned only on the original amount is simple interest; compound interest differs precisely because past interest is added to the base and also earns interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: $1,000 grows at 10% compounded annually. What is the value after 2 years?
Why A: $1,100 is only the value after one year ($1,000 x 1.10); a second year of growth is still needed, so it understates the two-year result.
Why B: $2,000 would require doubling in two years, which needs 100% growth; at 10% compounded, $1,000 reaches only $1,210, far short of that figure.
Why C: Year one gives $1,000 x 1.10 = $1,100, and year two gives $1,100 x 1.10 = $1,210, because the second year earns interest on interest.
Why D: $1,200 treats growth as simple interest, adding $100 twice; compounding adds 10% of $1,100 in year two, which is $110, giving $1,210 instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: At a 6% annual return, about how long does money take to double by the Rule of 72?
A: 6 years
B: 12 years
C: 1 year
D: 72 years
Why A: Six years comes from using the rate as the time; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by the rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years, not 6.
Why B: The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time as 72 divided by the annual rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years for money growing at 6% a year.
Why C: One year would require a 72% return, since 72 / 72 = 1; at 6% the formula gives 72 / 6 = 12 years instead.
Why D: Seventy-two years confuses the numerator with the answer; the rule divides 72 by the 6% rate, which gives 12 years rather than the number 72 itself.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inflation risk to investors?
A: The chance a stock splits into two shares, each of half value
B: The chance a bank closes its doors for good one day
C: The chance that returns do not keep up with rising prices
D: The chance of a tax audit by the revenue agency this year
Why A: A stock split divides one share into several of lower price without changing total value; inflation risk concerns prices of goods rising faster than investment returns, which erodes purchasing power.
Why B: A bank closing is institutional or credit risk, usually addressed by deposit insurance; inflation risk is about rising prices reducing what your money can buy over time.
Why C: Inflation risk is the chance that investment returns fail to outpace rising prices, so real purchasing power shrinks even when the account balance is growing in nominal terms.
Why D: An audit is a tax compliance event that has nothing to do with price levels; inflation risk is the loss of purchasing power when prices rise faster than returns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is rebalancing a portfolio?
A: Selling everything and starting over in cash
B: Ignoring the portfolio for years on end
C: Buying only the best performer of the year
D: Adjusting holdings back to the target mix
Why A: Selling everything and moving to cash abandons the plan and may trigger taxes; rebalancing keeps the existing strategy and only restores the original mix of assets.
Why B: Ignoring a portfolio lets winners grow into an oversized share and shifts risk unnoticed; rebalancing is the opposite, an active periodic check that restores the intended weights.
Why C: Buying only the best performer concentrates risk and chases past returns; rebalancing usually trims winners and adds to laggards so the portfolio returns to its target allocation.
Why D: Rebalancing means selling assets that have grown too large and buying those that have shrunk, which returns the portfolio to its target allocation and keeps risk at the intended level.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The bid is $19.95 and the ask is $20.05. What is the spread?
Why A: The spread is the ask minus the bid, so $20.05 - $19.95 = $0.10, which is the cost a trader pays to buy and sell immediately.
Why B: $20.00 is roughly the midpoint of the bid and ask, not their difference; subtracting $19.95 from $20.05 gives a spread of only $0.10.
Why C: $40.00 comes from adding the bid and ask ($19.95 + $20.05); the spread requires subtraction, which gives $0.10, not the sum of the two quotes.
Why D: $1.00 is ten times too large; the ask of $20.05 minus the bid of $19.95 is only $0.10, a narrow spread typical of a liquid stock.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bond's maturity date?
A: The date interest is calculated each year
B: The date when the issuer repays the face value
C: The date the bond is rated by a rating agency
D: The date the bond is first sold by the firm
Why A: Interest calculation or payment dates are separate from maturity; maturity is the final date when the issuer repays the face value, not a yearly interest date.
Why B: The maturity date is when the bond ends and the issuer must repay the principal, called the face or par value, to the bondholder in full.
Why C: Rating agencies assess a bond at issuance and afterward on their own schedule; that is unrelated to maturity, which is the date principal is repaid.
Why D: The first sale of a bond is its issue date; maturity comes at the end of the bond's life, when the issuer repays the face value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is credit rating?
A: An assessment of a borrower's ability to repay debt
B: A tax assessment made by the revenue agency each year
C: A ranking of a stock's price from highest to lowest
D: A list of dividends paid by a firm in the past year
Why A: A credit rating is an independent assessment of how likely a borrower is to repay debt on time, with grades such as AAA down to D.
Why B: Tax assessments are done by revenue agencies for property or income; a credit rating evaluates a borrower's capacity to repay debt, not what taxes are owed.
Why C: Ranking stock prices from high to low is a price list; a credit rating measures a borrower's repayment ability and applies to debt issuers, not share prices.
Why D: A record of past dividends is a dividend history; credit ratings concern how reliably a borrower can pay interest and principal, not what a firm paid shareholders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is volatility?
A: The total number of shares traded over a day
B: The fees on a trade made through a broker or app
C: The average price over a year for the stock
D: How much and how quickly prices move up and down
Why A: Total shares traded in a day is trading volume; volatility measures how much and how quickly prices change, regardless of how many shares trade hands.
Why B: Trade fees are commissions or costs of transacting; volatility describes price movement of the asset itself, not what a broker or app charges to execute orders.
Why C: An average price over a year is a mean price; volatility measures how far prices swing around that average, not the average value itself.
Why D: Volatility measures the size and speed of price changes; a highly volatile asset swings sharply up and down, which means higher uncertainty and typically greater risk for holders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the risk-return tradeoff?
A: Lower risk usually comes with higher expected returns
B: Risk and return are unrelated to each other overall
C: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
D: Risk matters for stocks but has no link to bond returns
Why A: This reverses the tradeoff: safer investments usually offer lower expected returns, and investors accept higher risk only in hope of earning more.
Why B: Risk and return are closely linked; investors demand extra expected return for taking on added risk, so calling them unrelated contradicts a basic principle of investing.
Why C: The risk-return tradeoff says that to seek higher potential returns, investors generally must accept higher risk, including a greater chance of losing money along the way.
Why D: Bonds follow the same tradeoff; longer maturities and weaker credit carry more risk and so pay higher yields to compensate investors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which asset class typically has the highest long-run risk and return?
A: Savings
B: Stocks
C: Cash only
D: T-bills
Why A: Savings accounts offer stable, insured balances with low interest, so they carry low risk and low return, the opposite of the highest long-run risk and return.
Why B: Stocks have historically delivered the highest long-run returns among common asset classes but with the largest price swings, so they carry the greatest risk and reward together.
Why C: Cash is the safest, most liquid asset with minimal return, so it has the lowest long-run risk and return rather than the highest.
Why D: Treasury bills are short-term government securities with very low default risk and modest yields, so they sit near the bottom of the risk and return scale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What role does an underwriter play in an IPO?
A: Audits the company only, and signs a report on its books overall
B: Insures deposits at banks for the savers in the nation
C: Sets tax rates for the firm and its owners in the state
D: Helps price the offering and sells the shares to investors
Why A: Auditing and signing off on financial statements is the job of an independent accountant; the underwriter instead helps price the offering and sells the new shares.
Why B: Deposit insurance is provided by the FDIC for banks; an underwriter has no role in insuring savers and instead manages the sale of new securities.
Why C: Tax rates are set by governments, not underwriters; an underwriter advises on offering price and distributes shares to investors in an IPO.
Why D: In an IPO, the underwriter, usually an investment bank, advises on price, buys or markets the shares, and sells them to investors, often taking on some risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the NYSE?
A: A government agency that regulates trading of stocks
B: A U.S. bank that lends money to firms and homes alike
C: The New York Stock Exchange, a major U.S. stock exchange
D: A credit bureau that reports on borrowers' debts and bills
Why A: The NYSE is a private marketplace, not a government agency; regulation of trading comes from the SEC, while the NYSE simply operates the exchange.
Why B: Lending to firms and households is done by banks; the NYSE is a marketplace where shares trade and does not make loans.
Why C: NYSE stands for the New York Stock Exchange, one of the largest U.S. stock exchanges, where buyers and sellers trade shares of listed companies.
Why D: Credit bureaus such as Equifax track borrowers' debt histories; the NYSE is a stock exchange where listed company shares are bought and sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Nasdaq known for listing?
A: Many technology and growth companies
B: Mostly government bonds and Treasury bills
C: Mainly oil, gas and mining companies
D: Mainly farm commodity contracts and futures
Why A: Nasdaq is known for listing many technology and growth companies, including large names in software, semiconductors, and biotechnology, which gives it a strong tech identity.
Why B: Nasdaq is a stock exchange, and Treasury securities are sold by the government through auctions; Nasdaq is known for technology and growth companies.
Why C: Nasdaq lists companies from many industries but is best known for technology and growth firms, not for energy and mining producers.
Why D: Commodity futures trade on dedicated futures exchanges, while Nasdaq is a stock market famous for listing technology and growth companies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Dow Jones Industrial Average?
A: A bond index covering the whole bond market
B: An index of small companies with prices added up
C: An index of 500 firms in the whole U.S. market
D: A price-weighted index of 30 large U.S. companies
Why A: The Dow tracks 30 stocks, not bonds; a bond index would measure debt securities, while the Dow follows large U.S. company shares only.
Why B: The Dow holds 30 large, established companies, not small ones; it is price-weighted, but small company indexes such as the Russell 2000 track smaller firms.
Why C: An index of 500 U.S. firms describes the S&P 500; the Dow has only 30 companies, so the count of firms does not match.
Why D: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of 30 large U.S. companies, meaning higher-priced stocks have more influence on the index level than lower-priced ones.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the S&P 500?
A: A market-cap-weighted index of 500 large U.S. companies
B: An index of 30 companies with prices added and divided
C: An index of bonds issued by large U.S. firms and states
D: A government agency that rates the whole stock market
Why A: The S&P 500 holds 500 large U.S. companies and weights each by market capitalization, so bigger firms influence the index more than smaller ones do.
Why B: An index of 30 firms using a divisor and price weighting describes the Dow, not the S&P 500, which has 500 stocks weighted by size.
Why C: The S&P 500 contains stocks, not bonds; a bond index would track debt issued by corporations and governments, which is a different product.
Why D: The S&P 500 is a stock index, not an agency; it measures large company performance and does not rate or regulate anything in markets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company has 5 million shares trading at $40. What is its market capitalization?
B: $20 million
C: $200 million
D: $8 million
Why A: $125,000 comes from dividing $5 million by $40, which is meaningless here; market cap multiplies shares by price, so 5,000,000 x $40 = $200 million.
Why B: $20 million would apply to a $4 share price (5 million x $4); at $40 the calculation of 5,000,000 x $40 gives $200 million.
Why C: Market capitalization equals shares outstanding times price per share, so 5,000,000 x $40 = $200,000,000, which is $200 million for the whole company.
Why D: $8 million would be 200,000 shares at $40 or 5 million shares at $1.60; with 5,000,000 shares at $40 the product is $200 million.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a market correction?
A: A tax change affecting investors and firms
B: A decline of 10% or more from a recent peak
C: A rule change affecting the whole market
D: A 50% crash in stock prices over a week
Why A: A tax change is a policy event; a market correction describes price behavior, specifically a decline of at least 10% from a recent high.
Why B: A correction is a drop of 10% or more from a recent peak, smaller than a bear market, which is a decline of 20% or more.
Why C: A rule change is regulatory; a correction refers to falling prices after a rise, not to any change in the rules governing the market.
Why D: A 50% crash in a week is far more extreme than a correction; a correction is a moderate decline of roughly 10% or more from a recent peak.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the VIX often called?
A: The jobs index
B: The CPI index
C: The fear gauge
D: The dividend index
Why A: The jobs index concerns employment data; the VIX instead measures expected stock market volatility, which is why it is known by a different nickname.
Why B: The CPI measures consumer price inflation and is published by the government; the VIX tracks implied volatility in S&P 500 options and carries a different nickname.
Why C: The VIX is called the fear gauge because it rises when investors expect large market swings and buy protection, and it falls during calm, confident periods.
Why D: Dividends are cash payments from companies; the VIX does not measure dividends at all, since it reflects expected volatility from S&P 500 option prices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock is quoted bid $24.90 and ask $25.10. What is the bid-ask spread?
Why A: $0.10 is half the real gap; the spread is the ask minus the bid, so $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20, not $0.10.
Why B: $25.00 is near the midpoint of the two quotes, not their difference; subtracting the bid from the ask yields $0.20 instead.
Why C: $50.00 adds the bid and ask ($24.90 + $25.10); the spread is a difference, so the correct calculation is $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20.
Why D: The bid-ask spread equals the ask minus the bid, so $25.10 - $24.90 = $0.20, which represents the transaction cost of trading in and out immediately.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: You own a stock at $60 and place a stop-loss at $54. The price falls to $54. What happens?
A: The order is triggered and the stock is sold at the next available price
B: The stock is delisted from the exchange by the broker at once and for good
C: Nothing happens to the stock until the price rises again in the market
D: You buy more shares at the lower price and hold them for a while
Why A: When the price touches the $54 stop, the stop order becomes a market order and sells at the next available price, which may differ slightly from $54.
Why B: A stop-loss triggers a sale order, not a delisting; delisting is an exchange decision about a company and has nothing to do with the investor's order.
Why C: The order is triggered when the price falls to $54, so something does happen; waiting for a price rise would defeat the purpose of a stop-loss.
Why D: A stop-loss is a sell order, not a buy order; it exits the position to limit losses rather than adding shares at the lower price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a day order?
A: An order that lasts for a whole week if it is not filled first
B: An order that expires at the end of the trading day if not filled
C: An order that never expires and stays open until the investor cancels it
D: An order that lasts for a whole year if it is not filled first
Why A: A day order lasts only until the market closes on the day it is placed, not a week; longer-lasting instructions are called good-til-canceled orders.
Why B: A day order is valid only for the current trading session and expires at the end of the trading day if it has not been filled.
Why C: An order that stays open until the investor cancels it is a good-til-canceled order, not a day order, which expires automatically at the close.
Why D: A day order does not last a year; it ends at the close of that trading day if unfilled, so a year-long duration is incorrect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor shorts 100 shares at $50 and buys them back at $42. Ignoring costs, what is the profit?
Why A: $5,000 would be the dollar value of 100 shares at $50, not the profit; profit equals the price drop per share ($8) times 100 shares.
Why B: A short seller profits when the price falls: ($50 - $42) x 100 shares = $8 x 100 = $800, ignoring costs.
Why C: $80 uses the $8 drop but forgets to multiply by 100 shares; the correct profit is $8 x 100 = $800.
Why D: $4,200 is the cost to buy back the 100 shares at $42; profit is the difference between the sale and buyback, ($50 - $42) x 100 = $800.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a circuit breaker in markets?
A: A tax on trades made by day traders and funds each year
B: An electrical switch that cuts power to the trading floor overall
C: A type of order placed by a broker for a client of a bank
D: A rule that temporarily halts trading after a large decline
Why A: Circuit breakers are not taxes; they are exchange rules that pause trading when prices fall sharply, giving investors time to absorb information and avoid panic.
Why B: Though the name sounds electrical, a market circuit breaker is not a power switch; it is a trading rule that triggers halts after sharp declines.
Why C: Order types, such as limit or stop orders, are instructions from clients; a circuit breaker is a market-wide rule, not an order a broker places.
Why D: A circuit breaker temporarily halts trading after a large decline, such as a 7% drop in the S&P 500, to calm panic selling and let investors reassess.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is high-frequency trading?
A: Using fast algorithms to make many trades in fractions of a second
B: Holding stocks for several years to earn long-term gains
C: Trading by mail between firms and investors in the whole nation in the end
D: Placing large trades by hand through a broker each morning
Why A: High-frequency trading uses powerful computers and fast algorithms to place a very large number of orders in fractions of a second, often profiting from tiny price differences.
Why B: That describes buy-and-hold investing; high-frequency trading is the opposite, placing huge numbers of orders in fractions of a second.
Why C: High-frequency trading is electronic and measured in milliseconds or microseconds; trading by mail is far too slow to match that description.
Why D: Hand-placed orders are slow and manual, while high-frequency trading relies on computer algorithms and fast connections to act in milliseconds.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock at $120 undergoes a 3-for-1 split. What is the approximate price after the split?
Why A: $360 multiplies the price by 3, but a 3-for-1 split divides the price by 3; $120 / 3 = $40 per share.
Why B: $117 subtracts 3 from the price, which is not how a split works; the price is divided by the split ratio, so $120 / 3 = $40.
Why C: A 3-for-1 split triples the share count and divides the price by 3, so $120 / 3 = $40, leaving total company value unchanged.
Why D: $123 adds 3 to the price, which has no basis in a split; dividing $120 by the ratio of 3 gives about $40 per share.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: You own 50 shares before a 2-for-1 split. How many shares do you own after?
A: 100 shares
B: 50 shares
C: 25 shares
D: 52 shares
Why A: A 2-for-1 split doubles the number of shares, so 50 shares x 2 = 100 shares, while the price per share is cut in half.
Why B: Staying at 50 shares would mean no split occurred; a 2-for-1 split doubles holdings to 100 shares, with the price halving so total value stays the same.
Why C: Dividing 50 by 2 gives 25, which would describe a reverse split; in a 2-for-1 forward split the share count doubles to 100.
Why D: Adding 2 shares to get 52 misreads the ratio; a 2-for-1 split multiplies shares by 2, so 50 shares become 100 shares.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a reverse stock split?
A: A merger of two firms into one larger company, with their shares swapped
B: A dividend paid out of profits to each holder of a share every year
C: A company reduces its share count and raises the share price proportionally
D: A company increases its share count and lowers the share price proportionally
Why A: A merger combines two firms into one; a reverse split changes the share count of a single company and does not combine businesses or swap shares between firms.
Why B: A dividend distributes profit to shareholders as cash or stock; a reverse split does not pay anything, it only changes the share count and price.
Why C: A reverse split reduces the number of shares outstanding and raises the price per share proportionally, such as 1-for-10, leaving total company value unchanged.
Why D: Increasing the share count while lowering the price describes a forward stock split; a reverse split does the opposite by cutting shares and raising price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)?
A: A credit bureau that collects and reports a person's borrowing history  every month
B: The federal agency that regulates securities markets and protects investors
C: A stock exchange where investors buy and sell shares of companies there
D: A private bank that lends money to companies and individual savers
Why A: A credit bureau compiles consumer credit histories; the SEC regulates securities markets, enforces disclosure rules, and protects investors, which is a different mission altogether.
Why B: The SEC is the federal agency that regulates securities markets, enforces securities laws, and protects investors by requiring companies and professionals to disclose accurate information.
Why C: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE, is a marketplace for trading shares; the SEC is a regulator that oversees exchanges rather than operating one.
Why D: The SEC is a government regulator, not a private bank, and it does not lend money; its role is overseeing markets and enforcing securities laws.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is SIPC?
A: A tax agency that collects taxes on investment gains from the public  each April
B: A bank insurer that protects deposits when a commercial bank closes
C: A stock index that follows the price of shares of large companies
D: An organization that protects customers' securities if a brokerage fails
Why A: Taxes on investment gains are collected by the IRS; SIPC is a nonprofit that protects customers' assets if a brokerage firm fails.
Why B: Bank deposits are insured by the FDIC; SIPC is separate and covers securities and cash at failed brokerage firms, not at commercial banks.
Why C: A stock index tracks prices of selected companies; SIPC is not an index, it is a protection organization for customers of failed brokerage firms.
Why D: SIPC is the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which helps return customers' cash and securities, up to $500,000, when a member brokerage fails or assets go missing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Does SIPC protection cover losses from falling stock prices?
A: Yes, it repays losses when a stock falls below its purchase price
B: Yes, once the price falls past a set percentage of its value
C: No, it covers missing assets if a broker fails, not market losses
D: No, it protects against bank failures, not brokerage failures
Why A: SIPC does not cover market declines; it only restores missing cash and securities when a brokerage firm fails.
Why B: No percentage trigger exists, since SIPC never pays for falling prices; it protects customers only when a brokerage fails and assets go missing.
Why C: SIPC protects against missing assets when a brokerage fails but never against falling prices; market losses are an ordinary investment risk the investor must bear.
Why D: Bank deposits are protected by the FDIC; SIPC is the program that covers customers when a brokerage firm fails and assets are missing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Securities Act of 1933 mainly about?
A: Insuring deposits at banks and credit unions up to a limit
B: Regulating trading on exchanges and the conduct of brokers each day
C: Setting tax rates for individuals and companies each year
D: Requiring disclosure when securities are first sold to the public
Why A: Deposit insurance came from the Banking Act of 1933 and later the FDIC; the Securities Act of 1933 is about disclosure when securities are first sold.
Why B: Regulating exchange trading and broker conduct is the job of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; the 1933 Act focuses on new issues.
Why C: Tax rates are set by tax legislation, such as the Internal Revenue Code; the Securities Act of 1933 addresses securities registration and disclosure instead.
Why D: The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies to register new securities and give investors accurate disclosure when shares are first sold to the public in the primary market.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 mainly about?
A: Regulating trading in the secondary market and creating the SEC
B: Setting minimum wage rates for workers in the whole nation in the end
C: Regulating new issues only, when first sold to the public
D: Insuring deposits at banks and credit unions up to a limit
Why A: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading of existing securities in the secondary market and created the SEC to enforce those rules.
Why B: Minimum wage is covered by labor law such as the Fair Labor Standards Act; the 1934 Act concerns securities trading and created the SEC.
Why C: Regulating new issues when first sold describes the Securities Act of 1933; the 1934 Act covers trading after issuance and created the SEC.
Why D: Bank deposit insurance is handled by the FDIC, created in 1933; the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs securities trading, not deposits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What did the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 target?
A: Bank deposits and savings accounts in the whole nation
B: Corporate accounting fraud and financial reporting accuracy
C: Import duties on goods coming from other countries abroad overall
D: Consumer loans from banks and credit card firms alike
Why A: Bank deposits are covered by banking laws and the FDIC; Sarbanes-Oxley focuses on public company accounting and financial reporting, not savings accounts.
Why B: Sarbanes-Oxley followed scandals such as Enron and WorldCom, and it targeted corporate accounting fraud by requiring accurate financial reporting, stronger internal controls, and executive accountability.
Why C: Import duties are tariffs set by trade policy; Sarbanes-Oxley deals with corporate governance and financial reporting at public companies, not trade taxes.
Why D: Consumer lending is regulated by laws on credit and banking; Sarbanes-Oxley addresses accounting fraud and reporting at public companies instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What did the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 respond to?
A: The Great Depression of the 1930s in the whole nation in general
B: The 2008 financial crisis, by adding financial regulation
C: The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s in tech stocks
D: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency
Why A: The Great Depression led to the 1933 and 1934 securities acts; Dodd-Frank came much later, in 2010, in response to a more recent crisis.
Why B: Dodd-Frank, enacted in 2010, responded to the 2008 financial crisis by adding oversight of banks and markets, creating the CFPB, and imposing new rules on derivatives.
Why C: The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s helped lead to reforms around 2002 such as Sarbanes-Oxley, not to the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010.
Why D: Dodd-Frank is broad financial legislation, not a response to a tax dispute; it addressed systemic risk and consumer protection after the 2008 crisis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio?
A: Debt divided by equity for the whole firm
B: Earnings divided by share price, the inverse
C: Dividends divided by price per share held
D: Share price divided by earnings per share
Why A: Debt divided by equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of leverage; the P/E ratio instead compares a stock's price with its earnings per share.
Why B: Earnings divided by share price is the earnings yield, which is the inverse of P/E; P/E itself puts the price in the numerator.
Why C: Dividends divided by price is the dividend yield; the P/E ratio uses earnings per share, not dividends, in the denominator against share price.
Why D: The P/E ratio equals share price divided by earnings per share, showing how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual earnings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock trades at $60 and earnings per share are $4. What is the P/E ratio?
Why A: 240 results from multiplying $60 by $4; P/E requires division, so $60 / $4 = 15, not the product of the two numbers.
Why B: 56 comes from subtracting $4 from $60; the P/E ratio divides price by earnings per share, giving $60 / $4 = 15 instead.
Why C: P/E equals price divided by earnings per share, so $60 / $4 = 15, meaning investors pay $15 for each $1 of annual earnings.
Why D: 0.067 is the earnings yield, $4 / $60, which is the inverse; P/E divides price by earnings, giving $60 / $4 = 15.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company earns $2 million net income with 500,000 shares outstanding. What is EPS?
Why A: EPS equals net income divided by shares outstanding, so $2,000,000 / 500,000 = $4.00 earned per share.
Why B: $40 would result from an arithmetic slip, such as treating $20 million as net income; with $2 million and 500,000 shares, EPS is $4.00.
Why C: $0.25 is the inverse, 500,000 / $2,000,000; EPS divides income by shares, so $2,000,000 / 500,000 = $4.00, not a quarter dollar.
Why D: $1,000 is far too high; dividing $2 million by 500,000 shares gives $4.00, since $2,000,000 / 500,000 = 4.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock pays $2 per share in annual dividends and trades at $50. What is the dividend yield?
Why A: 25% comes from inverting the fraction, $50 / $2 = 25; dividend yield is dividend divided by price, so $2 / $50 = 4%.
Why B: Dividend yield equals annual dividend divided by price, so $2 / $50 = 0.04, or 4%, the cash return from dividends alone.
Why C: 2% would require a $1 dividend on a $50 stock; with a $2 dividend the calculation is $2 / $50 = 4%.
Why D: $100 multiplies the dividend by the price ($2 x $50); yield is a percentage found by dividing $2 by $50, which gives 4%, not a dollar amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the payout ratio?
A: Profit divided by revenue for the year
B: Debt divided by assets owned by the firm overall
C: The share of earnings paid out as dividends
D: Price divided by earnings per share held
Why A: Profit divided by revenue is the net profit margin, which measures profitability; the payout ratio measures how much of earnings is distributed as dividends.
Why B: Debt divided by assets is a leverage measure called the debt ratio; the payout ratio concerns dividends relative to earnings, not borrowing.
Why C: The payout ratio equals dividends divided by earnings, showing what share of profit goes to shareholders and how much the company retains for growth.
Why D: Price divided by earnings per share is the P/E ratio, a valuation measure; the payout ratio compares dividends paid with net earnings instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company earns $5 per share and pays $2 in dividends. What is its payout ratio?
Why A: Payout ratio equals dividends divided by earnings, so $2 / $5 = 0.40, or 40%, meaning the company pays out two-fifths of earnings.
Why B: 7% results from an unrelated calculation; the payout ratio divides the $2 dividend by $5 of earnings per share, which gives 40%.
Why C: 60% is the retention ratio, the share of earnings kept, which is $3 / $5; the payout ratio is $2 / $5 = 40%.
Why D: 250% inverts the fraction, $5 / $2 = 2.5; the payout ratio divides dividends by earnings, so $2 / $5 = 40%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the price-to-book ratio compare?
A: Price to sales for the whole firm in the year
B: Price to dividend for the whole firm each year
C: Debt to equity for the whole firm in the year
D: Market price per share to book value per share
Why A: Price to sales compares price with revenue per share; price-to-book compares market price per share with the book value per share on the balance sheet.
Why B: Price to dividend relates to yield and is not price-to-book; the P/B ratio uses book value, meaning assets minus liabilities, per share.
Why C: Debt to equity measures leverage; price-to-book is a valuation ratio that compares a stock's market price with the accounting value of equity per share.
Why D: Price-to-book compares market price per share with book value per share, showing how much investors pay relative to the company's net assets on its books.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is return on equity (ROE)?
A: Net income divided by shareholders' equity
B: Revenue divided by equity for the year
C: Net income divided by sales, the profit margin
D: Equity divided by assets for the whole firm
Why A: ROE equals net income divided by shareholders' equity, showing how much profit a company generates from the money its owners have invested.
Why B: Revenue divided by equity is not a standard profitability measure; ROE uses net income in the numerator, not sales, to measure profit earned on equity.
Why C: Net income divided by sales is the profit margin; ROE divides net income by shareholders' equity, so the denominator makes the difference.
Why D: Equity divided by assets is the equity ratio, which shows financing structure; ROE measures profit relative to equity, with net income on top.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm has net income of $3 million and shareholders' equity of $20 million. What is ROE?
Why A: 6.7% results from inverting or misreading the numbers; ROE is net income divided by equity, so $3 million / $20 million = 15%.
Why B: ROE equals net income divided by shareholders' equity, so $3 million / $20 million = 0.15, or 15%.
Why C: 23% does not follow from the data; dividing $3 million by $20 million gives 0.15, which is 15%, not 23%.
Why D: 60% is far too high; ROE is $3 million / $20 million = 0.15, so only 15 cents of profit per dollar of equity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm has current assets of $600,000 and current liabilities of $400,000. What is the current ratio?
Why A: 100,000 matches no valid calculation here; the current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5, which is a ratio rather than a dollar figure.
Why B: 0.67 inverts the ratio ($400,000 / $600,000); the current ratio puts current assets on top, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5.
Why C: 200,000 is the dollar difference ($600,000 - $400,000), known as working capital; the current ratio divides instead of subtracting, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5.
Why D: The current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities, so $600,000 / $400,000 = 1.5, meaning $1.50 of liquid assets for each $1 owed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is intrinsic value?
A: The IPO price paid by the first buyers of the shares
B: The current market price on the day it is traded by investors
C: The estimated true worth of an asset based on fundamentals
D: The par value printed on the face of the stock certificate
Why A: An IPO price is what first buyers paid, set by supply and demand at issue; intrinsic value is an estimate of true worth from fundamentals.
Why B: The current market price is what investors pay now; intrinsic value is a separate estimate of what the asset is truly worth, which may differ.
Why C: Intrinsic value is the estimated true worth of an asset, found by analyzing fundamentals such as earnings, cash flows, and growth, regardless of the quoted market price.
Why D: Par value is a nominal legal figure printed on a certificate and often unrelated to worth; intrinsic value is based on fundamentals, not a printed number.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do support and resistance levels describe?
A: Tax brackets for income earned by workers each year of work overall
B: Dividend dates set by the board of directors each year
C: Price levels where a security tends to stop falling or rising
D: Interest rates charged by banks on loans to firms and homes
Why A: Tax brackets are income tax bands for workers; support and resistance are price levels on a chart, so this option confuses taxation with technical analysis.
Why B: Dividend dates are corporate calendar events; support and resistance refer to prices where buying or selling pressure has tended to halt a trend.
Why C: Support is a price level where falling prices tend to stop, and resistance is a level where rising prices tend to stall, both used in technical analysis.
Why D: Interest rates charged on loans are credit pricing; support and resistance describe price behavior on a chart, not borrowing costs from banks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is beta?
A: A profit margin shown on the income statement of a firm overall
B: A credit rating given to a firm by a rating agency
C: A dividend measure used by analysts to rank firms
D: A measure of a stock's volatility relative to the market
Why A: A profit margin is an income statement ratio; beta is a market-risk measure comparing a stock's price movement with the overall market.
Why B: A credit rating gauges borrowers' repayment ability; beta instead measures how sensitive a stock's returns are to market movements.
Why C: Beta is not a dividend measure; it compares a stock's price swings with the market, while dividend measures such as yield or payout ratio concern income.
Why D: Beta measures a stock's volatility relative to the market; a beta above 1 means it swings more than the market, and below 1 means less.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock has a beta of 1.5. If the market rises 10%, the stock is expected to rise about:
Why A: 6.7% results from dividing 10% by 1.5; beta multiplies the market move, so 1.5 x 10% = 15%, not a division.
Why B: Expected move equals beta times the market move, so 1.5 x 10% = 15%, meaning the stock is expected to rise more than the market.
Why C: A 10% rise would fit a beta of 1.0; with a beta of 1.5 the stock amplifies the market's move to about 15%.
Why D: 1.5% mistakes the beta for a percentage; multiplying the beta of 1.5 by the market's 10% rise gives 15%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A stock has a beta of 0.5. If the market falls 8%, the stock is expected to fall about:
Why A: Expected move equals beta times the market move, so 0.5 x 8% = 4%; a low-beta stock falls only half as much as the market.
Why B: 12% would result from 1.5 x 8%, a beta of 1.5; with a beta of 0.5 the stock moves only half of the market's 8%.
Why C: An 8% fall would fit a beta of 1.0; a beta of 0.5 means the stock is expected to fall by half the market's decline, which is 4%.
Why D: 16% would result from a beta of 2.0 (2 x 8%); the given beta of 0.5 halves the move, giving 0.5 x 8% = 4%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is alpha in investing?
A: Return in excess of what the market would predict for the risk taken
B: Market volatility, which shows how much prices rise and fall in a single day
C: A dividend that a company pays to its shareholders each quarter
D: A tax that investors pay on the profit they earn when they sell shares
Why A: Alpha is the return earned above what the market and the investment's risk would predict, so a positive alpha suggests the manager added value beyond market exposure.
Why B: Volatility describes price swings, and the measure relative to the market is beta; alpha is excess return after adjusting for risk, not a measure of daily swings.
Why C: A quarterly payment to shareholders is a dividend; alpha is a performance measure for excess return and has nothing to do with company payouts.
Why D: A tax on profit from selling shares is capital gains tax; alpha is a measure of risk-adjusted excess return, not a tax paid by investors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Sharpe ratio measure?
A: Trading volume levels
B: Risk-adjusted return
C: Debt level of a firm
D: Dividend yield rates
Why A: Trading volume counts shares traded and is unrelated to the Sharpe ratio, which compares a portfolio's excess return with the risk it took on.
Why B: The Sharpe ratio measures risk-adjusted return, dividing excess return over the risk-free rate by standard deviation, so higher values show more return per unit of risk.
Why C: Debt level of a firm is measured by leverage ratios such as debt-to-equity; the Sharpe ratio evaluates investment performance relative to its risk.
Why D: Dividend yield is annual dividends divided by price; the Sharpe ratio instead evaluates how much return an investment delivers for each unit of risk taken.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the efficient market hypothesis?
A: The idea that prices follow a fixed pattern that can be predicted
B: The idea that company insiders set prices to match their forecasts
C: The idea that bargains are easy to find with careful research
D: The idea that prices already reflect all available information
Why A: The hypothesis says prices move randomly as new information arrives, so patterns cannot be used to predict them and beat the market.
Why B: Prices are set by the trading of many investors reacting to information, not by insiders deciding where a stock should trade.
Why C: The hypothesis argues the opposite: because prices already reflect known information, finding bargains consistently is very difficult even with careful research.
Why D: The efficient market hypothesis states that prices already reflect all available information, so it is very difficult to consistently beat the market using known facts.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is portfolio rebalancing?
A: Adding more money to the best-performing holding
B: Moving funds into whatever asset rose last month
C: Adjusting holdings back to target allocations
D: Selling everything in the account at once
Why A: That lets one winner grow even larger and pushes the portfolio further from its targets; rebalancing trims the winners and restores the planned mix.
Why B: Chasing last month's winner is performance chasing, which ignores the target mix; rebalancing returns the portfolio to its planned proportions.
Why C: Portfolio rebalancing means adjusting holdings back to target allocations, usually by selling assets that have grown too large and buying those that have fallen behind.
Why D: Selling the whole account at once ends the investment plan and may create taxes; rebalancing only trims and adds enough to restore the original proportions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A 60/40 stock/bond portfolio drifts to 70/30 after a stock rally. To rebalance, an investor would:
A: Buy more stocks to push it further
B: Do nothing and just wait for it
C: Sell bonds only and buy none
D: Sell some stocks and buy bonds
Why A: Buying more stocks would push the portfolio even further from 60/40, increasing risk; rebalancing requires moving back toward the target mix, not away from it.
Why B: Doing nothing leaves the allocation at 70/30, with more risk than intended; rebalancing is an active step that restores the 60/40 target.
Why C: Selling bonds only and buying none would reduce the bond share below the 30% it already has, moving even further from the 40% target.
Why D: The portfolio is now 70% stocks instead of 60%, so selling some stocks and buying bonds brings it back to the 60/40 target.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which asset class has historically offered higher long-term returns but more volatility?
A: Stocks
B: Cash
C: T-bills
D: Savings
Why A: Stocks have historically earned higher long-term returns than bonds or cash, but they also swing more in price, so they combine higher return with greater volatility.
Why B: Cash is stable but earns little, often less than inflation, so it has low volatility and low returns, the reverse of higher returns with more volatility.
Why C: Treasury bills are safe, short-term, low-yield securities with minimal price swings, so they do not offer high long-term returns with high volatility.
Why D: Savings accounts offer stable balances with low interest, so they have both low returns and low volatility, unlike stocks, which pair higher returns with larger swings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is time horizon in investing?
A: The tax year, which is the twelve months used when filing a tax return each year
B: The length of time an investor expects to hold an investment before needing the money
C: The market's hours, which are the times when trades can be made each trading day
D: The stock's age, which is the number of years since the company was founded  by its owners
Why A: The tax year is a reporting period for filing returns and has nothing to do with investing goals; time horizon is how long money will be invested.
Why B: Time horizon is the length of time an investor expects to hold an investment before needing the money, and it guides how much risk is appropriate.
Why C: Market hours are the trading times of an exchange; time horizon refers to an investor's own holding period, not when trades can be made.
Why D: A stock's age is the number of years since a company was founded; time horizon concerns the investor's plan, not the history of the company.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A 25-year-old saving for retirement in 40 years can typically take:
A: Less equity risk because a downturn would be hard to recover from
B: Mostly short-term bills to keep the savings safe from change
C: More equity risk since there is time to recover from downturns
D: Mostly cash held in a savings account for safety
Why A: With 40 years to invest, a young saver has ample time to recover from downturns, so a higher equity share is usually suitable.
Why B: Short-term bills pay low returns that may trail inflation over four decades, which wastes the growth a long time horizon allows.
Why C: With 40 years until retirement, a young saver has time to recover from downturns, so holding more equities for higher expected growth is typically appropriate.
Why D: Cash earns little and loses buying power to inflation, a heavy cost over 40 years for someone who could afford to hold growth assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A retiree needing money next year should most likely hold:
A: All aggressive growth stocks
B: Mostly stable, liquid assets
C: Illiquid land and houses
D: Only speculative options
Why A: Aggressive growth stocks can fall sharply, and a retiree needing money next year would have little time to recover, so all-aggressive holdings are unsuitable.
Why B: Needing money next year calls for stable assets that can be sold quickly at predictable prices, so mostly stable, liquid holdings suit a retiree.
Why C: Land and houses are illiquid and can take months to sell, so they are a poor fit for someone needing cash within a year.
Why D: Speculative options can expire worthless, wiping out the entire investment, which is a poor choice for a retiree who needs funds next year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is yield to maturity?
A: The total return on a bond held until it matures
B: The tax rate on bond interest paid to holders
C: The coupon rate only, the yearly interest paid overall
D: The stock dividend paid each year to holders
Why A: Yield to maturity is the total annualized return on a bond if held until it matures, counting coupons, any price gain or loss, and reinvestment of interest.
Why B: A tax rate on bond interest concerns taxation; yield to maturity measures the bond's total expected annual return when held until maturity, not what is owed.
Why C: The coupon rate alone is only the annual interest on face value; yield to maturity also reflects the price paid and the gain or loss at maturity.
Why D: A stock dividend is a payment on equity; yield to maturity applies to bonds and measures total return from interest and price change to maturity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A $1,000 bond has a 6% coupon. How much interest does it pay each year?
Why A: $6 would be 0.6% of $1,000; a 6% coupon pays 6% x $1,000 = $60 per year, so $6 is ten times too small.
Why B: $600 would be a 60% coupon; the correct calculation is 6% x $1,000 = $60, so $600 is ten times too large.
Why C: $1,060 is the face value plus one year's interest, which is what the holder gets at maturity in the final year, not the annual interest alone.
Why D: Annual interest equals the coupon rate times face value, so 6% x $1,000 = $60 per year, usually paid in two $30 installments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bond's face (par) value?
A: The market price of the bond
B: The broker fee charged on it
C: The amount repaid at maturity
D: The annual interest paid on it
Why A: The market price is what the bond currently trades for and can differ from par; face value is the fixed amount repaid at maturity.
Why B: A broker fee is a transaction cost and is unrelated to the bond's face value, which is the principal that the issuer returns at maturity.
Why C: Face or par value is the amount the issuer repays at maturity, and it is also the base on which the coupon interest is calculated.
Why D: The annual interest payment is the coupon, computed as coupon rate times face value; it is not itself the face value that is repaid at maturity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean when a bond trades at a discount?
A: Its price is above face value
B: It has defaulted on debts
C: Its price is below face value
D: It is given away free of charge
Why A: A price above face value is a premium, not a discount; a discount bond trades below face value, usually because yields have risen since issue.
Why B: Trading at a discount does not mean default; many healthy bonds trade below par when market rates rise above their coupon rates.
Why C: A bond trades at a discount when its market price is below its face value, so a buyer pays less than the amount repaid at maturity.
Why D: A discount describes a lower market price, not a giveaway; buyers still pay money, and they receive the face value at maturity plus interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a lower bond credit rating signal?
A: Higher default risk
B: No risk involved
C: Guaranteed repayment
D: Lower default risk
Why A: A lower credit rating signals higher default risk, meaning investors face a greater chance the issuer will fail to pay interest or principal, so they demand higher yields.
Why B: Every bond carries some risk, and a lower rating signals more risk, not none; no risk involved contradicts what ratings are designed to show.
Why C: No rating guarantees repayment; a lower rating suggests a higher chance of default, so claiming guaranteed repayment is the reverse of what the signal means.
Why D: Lower default risk would be indicated by a higher rating such as AAA; a lower rating suggests the opposite, a greater chance of default.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are junk bonds?
A: Government bonds that are backed by the full faith of the federal government overall
B: Insured bonds that guarantee the investor will be repaid if the issuer fails
C: Zero-risk bonds that pay a high rate with no chance of losing any money
D: Bonds rated below investment grade with higher yields and higher default risk
Why A: Government bonds backed by full faith are the safest category, such as Treasuries, and are not junk; junk bonds are rated below investment grade.
Why B: Junk bonds are not insured or guaranteed; they carry high default risk, which is why issuers must offer higher yields to attract buyers.
Why C: No bond is zero-risk with a high rate; junk bonds pay more precisely because investors can lose money if the issuer defaults.
Why D: Junk bonds, also called high-yield bonds, are rated below investment grade, so they pay higher yields to compensate for a greater chance the issuer defaults.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is duration in bond investing?
A: The credit rating of the issuer of the bond in the market
B: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes
C: The issuer's age in years since the firm was first founded in this case
D: The coupon payment made to the holder each year in cash form
Why A: The issuer's credit rating measures default risk, not duration; duration instead measures how much a bond's price changes when interest rates move.
Why B: Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes; a longer duration means the price falls more when rates rise and rises more when rates fall.
Why C: An issuer's age has no bearing on duration, which is a calculation based on a bond's cash flows and timing, not on how old the firm is.
Why D: The coupon payment is annual interest on face value; duration is a different measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to rate changes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Treasury bill?
A: A mutual fund holding many bonds and notes for investors
B: A stock issued by a firm and traded on major exchanges
C: A long-term corporate bond that pays interest twice a year overall
D: A short-term U.S. government debt security sold at a discount
Why A: A fund that holds many bonds is a bond mutual fund; a Treasury bill is a single short-term government debt security, not a pooled fund.
Why B: A stock represents ownership in a company; a Treasury bill is debt issued by the U.S. government, so it pays no dividends and trades differently.
Why C: A Treasury bill matures in one year or less and pays no coupons, so it is not a long-term corporate bond paying interest twice a year.
Why D: A Treasury bill is a short-term U.S. government debt security, maturing in a year or less, sold at a discount and redeemed at face value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are municipal bonds?
A: Bonds issued by corporations to raise money for their business needs
B: Bonds issued by states and local governments, often with tax-exempt interest
C: Stocks of cities that pay dividends to the residents of each town or city
D: Bonds issued by the federal government, whose interest is taxed by every state
Why A: Corporate bonds come from companies; municipal bonds are issued by states, cities, and local governments to finance public projects, so this option names the wrong issuer.
Why B: Municipal bonds are issued by states and local governments to fund public projects, and their interest is often exempt from federal income tax, which makes them attractive to high earners.
Why C: Municipal bonds are debt, not stocks; cities do not issue shares and the holders receive interest, not dividends, so this describes no real product.
Why D: Federal government bonds are Treasuries, which are exempt from state tax; municipal bonds come from states and localities and often have tax-exempt interest.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a call provision on a bond?
A: A voting right held by common stockholders only
B: The investor's right to sell the bond back to the issuer
C: The issuer's right to redeem the bond before maturity
D: A dividend right held by preferred shareholders
Why A: Voting rights belong to common stockholders and are unrelated to bonds; a call provision lets the bond issuer redeem the bond early.
Why B: The investor's right to sell the bond back to the issuer is a put provision; a call provision gives that right to the issuer.
Why C: A call provision gives the issuer the right to redeem the bond before maturity, often when interest rates have fallen, so the issuer can refinance more cheaply.
Why D: Dividend rights for preferred shareholders concern stock, not bonds; a call provision is a bond feature that lets the issuer repay early.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What rights do common shareholders typically have?
A: Voting rights and a claim on residual assets
B: Priority claim over bondholders on company assets
C: A fixed dividend set when the shares are issued
D: Fixed interest paid each year to holders
Why A: Common shareholders typically vote on directors and major corporate matters and hold a residual claim on assets after creditors and preferred holders are paid.
Why B: Bondholders and other creditors are paid before common shareholders in a liquidation, so common holders hold only a residual claim.
Why C: A fixed set dividend is a feature of preferred stock; common dividends are decided by the board and can change or stop.
Why D: Fixed interest payments are a feature of bonds; common shareholders instead receive variable dividends, if any, and share in residual assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In liquidation, who is paid first?
A: Employees' bonuses paid out before other claims
B: Creditors, including bondholders, before shareholders
C: The CEO and other top managers of the firm itself
D: Common shareholders before any of the other creditors
Why A: Bonuses are not senior claims; in liquidation, secured creditors and other creditors are paid before shareholders, and ordinary bonuses do not outrank them.
Why B: In liquidation, creditors, including bondholders, must be paid before shareholders, because debt holders have a legal claim while shareholders hold only a residual claim.
Why C: Managers have no special priority in liquidation; unpaid wages aside, payment order starts with creditors and ends with shareholders, not with top executives.
Why D: Common shareholders come last in liquidation, after creditors and preferred holders, so they cannot be paid ahead of the other creditors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor buys a call with a $50 strike for a $3 premium. At expiration the stock is $48. What is the loss per share?
Why A: $0 would be correct only if the premium were free; the buyer paid $3 and the option expires worthless since $48 is below the $50 strike.
Why B: $2 is the gap between the strike and stock price ($50 - $48), but the call is out of the money and worthless, so the loss is the whole premium.
Why C: The call has no value at $48 because it is below the $50 strike, so the buyer loses only the $3 premium paid, per share.
Why D: $50 is the strike price, not the loss; a call buyer's maximum loss is limited to the premium paid, which is $3 per share.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor buys a call with a $40 strike for a $2 premium. At expiration the stock is $48. What is the profit per share?
Why A: $10 ignores the premium and overstates the gain; the payoff is $48 - $40 = $8, then subtract the $2 premium, which leaves $6.
Why B: $8 is the intrinsic value ($48 - $40) before subtracting the $2 premium paid; profit is the payoff minus the cost, which gives $6.
Why C: $2 is only the premium paid, which is the cost, not the profit; the option is worth $8 at expiration, so net profit is $8 - $2 = $6.
Why D: The call pays $48 - $40 = $8 at expiration, and subtracting the $2 premium paid gives a net profit of $6 per share.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is hedging?
A: Taking a position to offset the risk of another
B: Ignoring risk and hoping for the best outcome
C: Increasing risk to chase higher returns each year
D: Day trading for small gains several times each day
Why A: Hedging means taking an offsetting position, such as buying a put against a stock holding, to reduce the risk of another investment or exposure.
Why B: Ignoring risk is the opposite of hedging; hedging is a deliberate step to protect against losses, not a hope for a good outcome.
Why C: Increasing risk to chase returns is speculation or leverage; hedging aims to reduce risk, even if it limits some of the potential gain.
Why D: Day trading means frequent buying and selling for small gains, which is speculation; hedging is a protective strategy that offsets risk elsewhere.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a REIT?
A: A bank account that is insured and earns a small yearly return for savers
B: A credit card that gives rewards on travel and hotel purchases made online
C: A type of bond that pays a fixed rate of interest to the people who hold it  each year
D: A real estate investment trust that owns or finances income-producing property
Why A: An insured account that earns a small return describes a savings account or certificate; a REIT is a company that owns property and trades like a stock.
Why B: A rewards credit card is a payment product; a REIT is an investment vehicle that owns or finances real estate and passes income to investors.
Why C: A REIT is not a bond with a fixed rate; it is a real estate company that distributes most of its income as dividends to shareholders.
Why D: A REIT is a real estate investment trust that owns or finances income-producing property and must distribute most of its income to shareholders, offering real estate exposure without buying buildings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is net asset value (NAV)?
A: A fund's assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding
B: A fund's fees and costs charged each year to all of its holders
C: A stock's market price on the day it is traded by investors
D: A bond's coupon rate paid to holders each year in cash or by check
Why A: NAV equals total assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding, giving the per-share value of a fund, usually calculated at the end of each trading day.
Why B: Fees and costs charged to holders are the fund's expense ratio; NAV is the per-share value of the fund's net assets, not its costs.
Why C: A stock's market price is set by trading, whereas NAV is calculated from the value of a fund's holdings less its liabilities, per share.
Why D: A bond's coupon rate is its stated interest; NAV applies to funds and measures net assets per share, so it has no link to coupons.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A fund has $90 million in assets, $10 million in liabilities and 4 million shares. What is NAV?
Why A: $25 would result from dividing $100 million by 4 million; NAV subtracts liabilities first, so ($90 million - $10 million) / 4 million = $20.
Why B: $320 results from multiplying $80 million by 4 rather than dividing; NAV divides net assets by shares, so $80 million / 4 million = $20.
Why C: NAV equals assets minus liabilities divided by shares, so ($90 million - $10 million) / 4 million = $80 million / 4 million = $20 per share.
Why D: $22.50 ignores the liabilities; dividing the full $90 million by 4 million shares gives $22.50, but NAV uses net assets of $80 million, giving $20.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How do ETFs differ from mutual funds in trading?
A: Mutual funds trade all day long on exchanges like stocks do, ETFs once
B: ETFs trade throughout the day on exchanges while mutual funds price once per day
C: ETFs trade once per month on the exchange at a fixed time of the day each month in the end
D: They are identical in every way, including how and when they trade, each day
Why A: This reverses the facts; ETFs trade throughout the day on exchanges like stocks, while mutual funds are bought or sold at one price after the close.
Why B: ETFs can be bought and sold at market prices all day on exchanges, whereas mutual funds are priced once per day at the net asset value.
Why C: ETFs trade continuously during market hours, not once per month; a monthly fixed-time trade has no basis in how exchange-traded funds work.
Why D: ETFs and mutual funds differ in trading: ETFs trade on exchanges all day, while mutual funds are priced once daily, so calling them identical is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hedge fund?
A: A type of insurance product sold to wealthy investors in the open market
B: A private investment pool using varied strategies, often for wealthy investors
C: A public savings account open to anyone who wants to deposit money safely in practice
D: A bond that pays interest to holders on a fixed date every single year
Why A: Insurance is a risk transfer product; a hedge fund is an investment pool that uses varied strategies, usually open only to wealthy or institutional investors.
Why B: A hedge fund is a private pooled investment that uses varied strategies, such as leverage and short selling, and is generally open to accredited or wealthy investors.
Why C: A public savings account open to anyone is a bank product; hedge funds are private, less regulated, and limited to qualified investors.
Why D: A bond pays fixed interest on set dates; a hedge fund is a pooled investment vehicle using flexible strategies rather than a single debt instrument.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a penny stock?
A: A blue-chip stock of a large and stable company
B: A high-priced stock trading at a large dollar amount
C: A government bond issued by the Treasury of the nation
D: A low-priced, speculative stock of a small company
Why A: A blue-chip stock belongs to a large, stable, established company; a penny stock is the opposite, a low-priced, risky share of a small firm.
Why B: A penny stock has a low price, typically under $5, not a high price; high-priced shares of large firms are not what the term describes.
Why C: Treasury debt is a government bond, not a stock; a penny stock is a share of a small company that trades at a very low price.
Why D: A penny stock is a low-priced, speculative share of a small company, often thinly traded and volatile, so investors can lose much of their money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a registered investment adviser (RIA)?
A: A bank teller who handles deposits and withdrawals daily
B: A credit bureau that tracks borrowing history for lenders overall
C: A firm or person registered to give investment advice for a fee
D: A stock exchange where shares of public firms are traded
Why A: A bank teller handles deposits and withdrawals for customers; a registered investment adviser is a firm or person registered to provide investment advice for compensation.
Why B: A credit bureau tracks borrowing history for lenders; an RIA gives investment advice to clients and is registered with the SEC or a state.
Why C: An RIA is a firm or individual registered with the SEC or a state to give investment advice for a fee, and owes clients fiduciary duty.
Why D: A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares trade; an RIA is a professional adviser to clients, not a place where securities are traded.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a custodian in investing?
A: A financial institution that holds clients' securities for safekeeping
B: A company's janitor who cleans the offices of the firm each night
C: A stock picker who selects shares for the clients of a large firm
D: A tax agency that collects taxes from firms and individuals each year overall
Why A: A custodian is a financial institution, often a bank or trust company, that holds clients' securities for safekeeping and handles settlement, so assets stay separate from the adviser.
Why B: A janitor cleans offices; in investing, a custodian is a financial institution that keeps clients' securities safe, so the word has a different meaning here.
Why C: Picking shares for clients is the work of a portfolio manager or adviser; a custodian holds and safeguards the assets but does not choose investments.
Why D: Taxes are collected by revenue agencies; a custodian in investing safeguards securities for clients and does not collect taxes from anyone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a clearinghouse?
A: A grocery store that sells food and drink to the public each day of the week in the end
B: An institution that settles trades by ensuring buyers and sellers meet obligations
C: A tax office that processes returns for the state and the nation each year
D: A company that prints stock certificates for firms and investors in a city
Why A: A grocery store sells food; a clearinghouse is a financial institution that stands between buyers and sellers to settle trades and reduce counterparty risk.
Why B: A clearinghouse settles trades by confirming details and ensuring buyers and sellers meet their obligations, which reduces the risk that one side defaults on the deal.
Why C: Tax returns are processed by revenue offices; a clearinghouse handles settlement of securities trades, not taxes for states or the nation.
Why D: Printing stock certificates is a transfer or printing service; a clearinghouse completes trades by matching, settling, and guaranteeing the obligations of both parties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does T+1 settlement mean?
A: Settles in one year after the date of the trade
B: Settles instantly on the same day as the trade is made
C: A trade settles one business day after the trade date
D: Settles in one month after the date of the trade
Why A: T+1 means one business day, not one year; a settlement taking a year would make trading impractical, and the T stands for trade date.
Why B: Same-day settlement is called T+0; T+1 means settlement occurs one business day after the trade date, so it is not instant.
Why C: T+1 settlement means a trade settles one business day after the trade date, when cash and securities change hands, a standard in U.S. markets.
Why D: One month would be T+30; T+1 adds a single business day to the trade date, which is far shorter than a month.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a conflict of interest in investing?
A: A type of stock that pays high dividends to all of its holders
B: A tax rule that applies to investors who sell shares at a profit
C: A market holiday when the exchanges are closed for the whole day by law
D: A situation where an advisor's interests could compromise client advice
