Why C: Distance between branch offices is a geographic measure, which has no bearing on how many employees one manager supervises.
Why D: Span of control is how many employees one manager supervises directly, which affects the number of management levels and the amount of attention each worker receives.

Question: What is the chain of command?
A: The order in which products are shipped
B: The list of all of the company suppliers

D: The sequence of tax filings each year
Why A: The order of product shipments is a logistics matter, whereas the chain of command describes who reports to whom in the organization.
Why B: A list of suppliers is a purchasing record, not the reporting structure that the chain of command represents.
Why C: The chain of command is the line of authority from the top to the bottom of an organization, showing who reports to whom.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager hands a team member an important project, explains the goal and gives authority to make decisions, then checks in at milestones. This is:
A: Effective delegation

C: Downsizing the staff
D: Strict micromanaging
Why A: Giving a project, a clear goal, decision authority and milestone check-ins is effective delegation, because responsibility and authority are handed over while oversight stays appropriate.
Why B: Abdication means dropping the task with no follow-up, but this manager explains goals and checks in at milestones, so responsibility is not abandoned.
Why C: Downsizing means cutting staff, which is not what happens here, since the manager is assigning work to a team member.
Why D: Micromanaging means controlling every detail, but this manager gives decision authority and checks in only at milestones, which is the opposite behavior.

Question: What is micromanagement?
A: Giving employees freedom to decide how they work

Why A: Giving employees freedom to decide how they work is empowerment, which is the opposite of micromanagement.
Why B: Micromanagement is controlling every small detail of employees' work, which reduces morale, slows progress and signals a lack of trust.
Why C: Micromanagement is not about company size, since it describes a management behavior that can occur in organizations of any size.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is empowerment?
A: Hiring only managers for every open position in the company

Why A: Hiring only managers does not give employees authority, and a company with only managers would have no one to do the work.
Why B: Empowerment means giving employees the authority and resources to make decisions, which improves motivation, speed and ownership of results.
Why C: Removing decision rights takes authority away, which is the opposite of empowerment, which expands what employees may decide.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mission statement?

Why A: A schedule of shifts is an operational roster, which does not explain why the organization exists, as a mission statement does.

Why C: A mission statement is a short statement of an organization's purpose, describing what it does, whom it serves and why it exists.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vision statement?
A: A report of the daily sales made at each store in the chain
B: A description of what the company did last year and its results overall
C: A list of current employees and their job titles in the firm
D: A picture of what the organization wants to become in the future
Why A: Daily sales reports are operating data, not a vision, which describes the future the organization hopes to create.
Why B: A description of last year's results is a history or annual report, whereas a vision statement looks forward.
Why C: A list of employees and job titles is an organizational record, not an expression of what the organization wants to be.
Why D: A vision statement describes what the organization wants to become in the future, giving everyone a long-term picture to work toward.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a SWOT analysis?
A: An assessment of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
B: A review of stocks, wages, offers and trends over the past year
C: A review of suppliers, workers, owners and traders who deal with it
D: A review of sales, wages, orders and taxes for the full year
Why A: SWOT analysis assesses strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, helping an organization examine internal and external factors before planning strategy.
Why B: Stocks, wages, offers and trends do not match the SWOT letters, so this option names the wrong concepts for the acronym.
Why C: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders are not what the letters in SWOT stand for, so this list is incorrect.
Why D: Sales, wages, orders and taxes is an invented expansion, because SWOT actually stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which item is an external factor in a SWOT analysis?
A: A new competitor entering the market
B: A skilled and loyal workforce on staff

D: Outdated company equipment in the plant
Why A: A new competitor entering the market comes from outside the company, so it is an external threat in a SWOT analysis.
Why B: A skilled and loyal workforce exists inside the company, so it is an internal strength and not an external factor.
Why C: A strong brand reputation is built by the company itself, which makes it an internal strength instead of an external factor.
Why D: Outdated equipment in the plant is an internal weakness, since it is within the company's control and not an outside condition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is strategic planning?
A: Choosing today's lunch break time for staff

Why A: Choosing a lunch time is a minor daily scheduling matter, not strategic planning, which deals with long-term direction.
Why B: Strategic planning sets long-term goals and the path to reach them, guiding the organization's direction over several years.
Why C: Fixing a broken machine is a maintenance task and an immediate operational concern, not long-term strategic planning.
Why D: Daily work schedules are short-term operational planning, whereas strategic planning concerns the long-term direction of the organization.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is operational planning?
A: Setting a five-year vision for the whole firm
B: Choosing the company mission for the year
C: Planning daily activities for short-term goals
D: Deciding to merge with another firm next year
Why A: A five-year vision is long-term strategic planning, which is broader than operational planning, which covers short-term activities.
Why B: Choosing the company mission is a strategic matter set at the top, not the day-to-day focus of operational plans.
Why C: Operational planning covers daily activities that support short-term goals, turning the strategy into specific tasks for teams.
Why D: Merging with another firm is a major strategic decision, not a routine operational plan for daily work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a goal that is SMART?
A: Simple, Mild, Average, Relaxed and Tentative goals
B: Silent, Moving, Active, Rapid and Tough steps for staff
C: Secret, Modest, Automatic, Random and Temporary goals only
D: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound
Why A: Simple, mild, average, relaxed and tentative are invented words, since SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Why B: Silent, moving, active, rapid and tough do not describe SMART goals, so this option gives the wrong words for the acronym.
Why C: Secret, modest, automatic, random and temporary are not the SMART terms, and such vague traits would not make a goal clear.
Why D: SMART stands for specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, which describes goals clear enough to act on and track.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best example of a SMART goal?
A: Try to sell more as soon as possible
B: Improve things when you can, no deadline
C: Be the best company ever in our industry
D: Raise monthly sales 10% in six months
Why A: Selling more as soon as possible is vague, with no number or fixed date, so it fails the specific and measurable tests.
Why B: Improving things with no deadline lacks a time limit and a measure, so it cannot be a SMART goal.
Why C: Being the best company ever is not measurable or time-bound, and it is hard to define or achieve.

Question: What is management by objectives (MBO)?

Why A: MBO is a process in which managers and employees agree on goals together and then review progress, which produces clear and shared targets.
Why B: MBO rests on goals agreed jointly by managers and employees and reviewed together, not goals imposed by managers with punishment attached.
Why C: Deciding goals in secret contradicts MBO, which relies on managers and employees agreeing on goals and discussing progress together.
Why D: MBO involves managers working with employees to agree on goals, so leaving managers out of the process does not match it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a budget in management?

Why A: A contract with a supplier is a purchasing agreement, not a budget, which is a plan for money coming in and going out.
Why B: A report of past mistakes is a review, whereas a budget looks ahead and sets expected income and expenses.
Why C: A budget is a plan of expected income and expenses, which lets managers allocate money and later compare actual results against it.
Why D: A list of birthdays is a personnel record with no financial content, so it cannot be a budget.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager compares actual spending to the budget and finds a department is $5,000 over. What is this difference called?
A: A premium
B: A variance
C: A markup
D: A dividend
Why A: A premium is an extra amount paid, as with insurance or a higher price, and not the gap between actual and budgeted spending.
Why B: A variance is the difference between actual and budgeted amounts, so spending $5,000 over budget is called an unfavorable variance.
Why C: A markup is an amount added to cost to set a selling price, which is not used to describe budget differences.
Why D: A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders, which has no connection to comparing spending with a budget.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is decision making?

B: Carrying out a plan once it is chosen
C: Predicting what will happen in the future
D: Choosing the best course from alternatives
Why A: Gathering information is one step that supports a decision, but decision making is the act of choosing among alternatives.
Why B: Carrying out a plan is implementation, which comes after the decision has been made.
Why C: Forecasting is a planning tool that can inform a choice, but decision making means selecting a course from alternatives.
Why D: Decision making is choosing the best course of action from alternatives, which involves weighing options against goals and likely outcomes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the first step in a typical decision-making process?
A: Evaluating all the final results
B: Choosing the final option up front
C: Defining the problem to be solved
D: Implementing the best solution
Why A: Evaluating the final results is a late step that comes after implementation, not the first step in the process.
Why B: Choosing the final option up front skips analysis, so the decision would be made before the problem is understood.
Why C: Defining the problem comes first, because the options and criteria can only be chosen once the problem to be solved is clear.
Why D: Implementing the best solution occurs after the problem is defined and options are weighed, so it cannot be the first step.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the correct order of steps in decision making?
A: Define, gather facts, find options, choose, act, review
B: Choose, implement, define, gather information, then review
C: Implement, choose, gather facts, define, evaluate
D: Evaluate, implement, choose, define, gather facts
Why A: The correct order is define the problem, gather facts, find options, choose, act and review, which moves logically from understanding to evaluation.
Why B: Choosing before defining the problem and gathering information puts the decision first, which is illogical and risks solving the wrong problem.
Why C: Implementing before choosing or defining the problem reverses the sequence, because action should follow analysis and selection.
Why D: Evaluating first, before the problem is defined or any facts exist, makes no sense, because there is nothing to evaluate yet.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is groupthink?
A: A team brainstorming many new ideas together overall

C: A team splitting into smaller groups to work
D: A team using data to decide its next steps
Why A: Brainstorming many new ideas together is healthy creative work, but groupthink is the opposite, where the group suppresses ideas.
Why B: Groupthink occurs when a group agrees to avoid conflict even if the decision is wrong, so critical thinking and dissent are suppressed.
Why C: Splitting into smaller groups is a way of organizing work, and it does not describe the pressure to agree in groupthink.
Why D: Using data to decide is a rational approach, while groupthink is driven by pressure to agree and not by evidence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is brainstorming?
A: Criticizing every suggestion at once so only the best stay

D: Generating many ideas without judging them right away
Why A: Criticizing every suggestion at once is the opposite of brainstorming, which delays judgment so that people feel free to share ideas.
Why B: Writing a report alone is individual work, but brainstorming is a group activity for producing many ideas.
Why C: Choosing a single idea and dropping the others ends idea generation early, whereas brainstorming gathers many ideas first.
Why D: Brainstorming generates many ideas without judging them right away, which encourages creativity and gives the group more options to evaluate later.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a policy?
A: A general guideline that directs decisions and actions
B: A step-by-step set of instructions for a single task or job
C: A list of products that the company sells each year
D: A single rule for one situation only at the firm
Why A: A policy is a general guideline that directs decisions and actions, giving managers and employees a consistent framework within which to act.
Why B: Step-by-step instructions for a single task describe a procedure, which is more specific than a broad policy.
Why C: A list of products sold is a catalog and not a guideline that directs how decisions are made in the company.
Why D: A rule for one situation only is narrower than a policy, which is a general guide covering many similar situations.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a procedure?
A: A broad guideline for firm decisions
B: A step-by-step guide to doing a task
C: A company's long-term mission goals
D: A list of customer names and phones
Why A: A broad guideline for decisions describes a policy, whereas a procedure gives the specific steps for carrying out a task.
Why B: A procedure is a step-by-step guide to doing a task, which helps employees complete work consistently and correctly.
Why C: Long-term mission goals belong to strategic planning, not to procedures, which describe how a specific task is carried out.
Why D: A list of customer names and phones is a contact directory, not a set of instructions for performing a task.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is organizational culture?
A: The company's legal documents and contracts
B: The company's art collection on display
C: Shared values and behaviors in a company
D: The list of the company's main products
Why A: Legal documents and contracts are formal records, whereas organizational culture means the shared values and behaviors that shape how people act.
Why B: An art collection is decoration and not culture in the management sense, which concerns shared values, beliefs and behaviors.
Why C: Organizational culture is the shared values and behaviors in a company, which shape how people work together and make decisions.
Why D: A list of main products describes what the company sells, not the values and behaviors that make up its culture.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an organizational chart?
A: A chart of monthly sales by region
B: A chart of customer complaints by month
C: A diagram of reporting relationships
D: A chart of company profits by year
Why A: Monthly sales by region is a sales report, not a chart showing who reports to whom in the organization.

Why C: An organizational chart is a diagram of reporting relationships, showing positions, levels and who reports to whom.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a functional organizational structure?
A: Grouping employees by the product they make
B: Grouping staff by specialty, like marketing
C: Grouping employees by age and seniority
D: Having no structure at all in the firm
Why A: Grouping by product describes a divisional structure, not a functional one, which groups employees by specialty.
Why B: A functional structure groups staff by specialty, such as marketing, finance or operations, so people with similar skills work together.
Why C: Grouping by age and seniority is not a recognized structure, and functional structures group people by the work they do.
Why D: Having no structure at all is not a functional structure, which has clear departments organized by specialty.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a flat organization?
A: Few management levels and wide spans
B: A structure with many layers of managers
C: Decisions made at the top of the firm
D: A structure that groups staff by product line
Why A: A flat organization has few management levels and wide spans of control, which speeds communication and gives employees more autonomy.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tall organization?
A: A structure with much taller employees
B: A structure that is run by one person
C: A structure with few levels of management
D: Many management levels and narrow spans
Why A: Employee height has nothing to do with organizational structure, since the word tall refers to the number of management levels.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A start-up with 12 employees wants quick decisions and easy communication. Which structure fits best?

C: A flat structure with few management levels

Why A: A tall structure adds layers that slow decisions and communication, which does not suit a 12-person start-up that wants speed.

Question: What is a matrix organization?

Why A: A matrix organization uses teams and combines functions with projects, so a structure with no teams does not describe it.

Why C: A single manager for everyone describes a very simple structure, not a matrix with two reporting lines.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a team?
A: A single person who works alone on a job with no help ever
B: A group of people who work together toward a common goal
C: A group of competitors who fight for the same buyers
D: A group of people who happen to be in the same building
Why A: A single person working alone is an individual, not a team, since a team requires multiple people working together.

Why C: Competitors who fight for the same buyers are rivals and not teammates, since a team shares goals and cooperates.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main benefit of teamwork?

Why A: Teamwork combines different skills and viewpoints, which helps the group solve problems better than individuals working separately.

Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Tuckman's stages of team development in order are:
A: Performing, norming, storming, forming
B: Storming, forming, performing, norming
C: Norming, forming, performing, storming
D: Forming, storming, norming, performing
Why A: Performing, norming, storming, forming reverses the real order, because teams must form before they can perform.
Why B: Storming, forming, performing, norming puts the stages in the wrong order, since forming is always the first stage.
Why C: Norming, forming, performing, storming is not Tuckman's sequence, since forming comes first and performing comes last.
Why D: Tuckman's order is forming, storming, norming and performing, as the team moves from meeting, to conflict, to agreement, to productivity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: During the 'storming' stage of team development, what typically happens?
A: Members disagree and compete over roles and approaches
B: Members meet for the first time and are polite to all
C: Members work together smoothly with no conflict at all
D: Members disband the team after the first month of work
Why A: In the storming stage members disagree and compete over roles and approaches, which is a normal part of group development.
Why B: Meeting for the first time and being polite describes the forming stage, which comes before storming.
Why C: Working smoothly with no conflict describes the performing stage, whereas storming is marked by conflict.
Why D: Disbanding after a month is not a Tuckman stage in storming, where the team works through disagreements to get stronger.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a performance appraisal?
A: A list of company policies and rules
B: A formal review of an employee's work
C: A report on customer complaints per month
D: A review of the company's yearly profit
Why A: A list of policies and rules is a handbook, whereas a performance appraisal evaluates how well an employee is doing their job.
Why B: A performance appraisal is a formal review of an employee's work, which gives feedback and supports pay, training and promotion decisions.
Why C: A report on customer complaints measures service issues across the business, not a review of an individual's work.
Why D: A review of company profit is a financial analysis and not an evaluation of an employee's performance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should feedback be specific and timely?
A: So reviews become much longer
B: So managers avoid future talks
C: So employees know what to change
D: So employees feel more nervous
Why A: Making reviews longer is not the aim, since feedback should be brief and clear rather than padded.
Why B: Avoiding future talks would defeat feedback, which is meant to encourage ongoing communication between managers and employees.
Why C: Specific and timely feedback tells employees exactly what to change while the events are fresh, which helps them improve.
Why D: Making employees nervous harms morale and learning, whereas feedback should be clear and constructive so employees can improve.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a key performance indicator (KPI)?
A: A list of the main competitors
B: A measurable value tied to a goal
C: A confidential personnel file
D: A product's price tag in a store
Why A: A list of competitors is market information, not a performance measure tied to the organization's goals.
Why B: A KPI is a measurable value tied to a goal, which shows how well an organization or person is progressing toward targets.
Why C: A confidential personnel file stores employee records, which is not a metric for tracking progress toward goals.
Why D: A price tag is the cost of a product, not a performance measure, which is what a KPI is.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is total quality management (TQM)?
A: A way to cut staff to the minimum number needed
B: A rule to inspect only at the end of production
C: A tax on poor products sold by a firm to buyers
D: Continuous improvement for customer satisfaction
Why A: Cutting staff to a minimum is downsizing, not TQM, which aims at quality across all processes and people.
Why B: Inspecting only at the end of production is a late check, whereas TQM builds quality into every stage of production.
Why C: A tax on poor products is not part of TQM, which is a management approach and not a government charge.
Why D: TQM is continuous improvement for customer satisfaction, involving all employees in reducing defects and improving processes every day.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which Japanese term refers to continuous, small improvements?
A: Kaizen
B: Sushi
C: Origami
D: Haiku
Why A: Kaizen is the Japanese term for continuous, small improvements, which is widely used in quality management and lean manufacturing.
Why B: Sushi is a Japanese food and not a management term, so it cannot name the practice of continuous small improvements.
Why C: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding, and it has nothing to do with business improvement.
Why D: Haiku is a form of Japanese poetry, not a term for continuous improvement in business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is crisis management?
A: Ignoring problems until they disappear
B: Hiding information from the public view
C: Preparing for and handling sudden threats
D: Blaming the first employee who is found
Why A: Ignoring problems until they vanish is neglect, whereas crisis management involves preparing for and responding to threats.
Why B: Hiding information from the public usually worsens a crisis and damages trust, so it is not crisis management.
Why C: Crisis management means preparing for and handling sudden threats, so organizations can limit harm and recover quickly.
Why D: Blaming the first employee found does not resolve the crisis, and it avoids dealing with the actual threat.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is change management important?
A: It guarantees every change succeeds
B: It removes the need for communication
C: It prevents any change from happening
D: It helps people adopt new processes
Why A: Change management cannot guarantee that every change succeeds, since outcomes depend on many factors, but it improves the chances.
Why B: It increases the need for communication, since explaining the change to people is central to the process.
Why C: Change management does not prevent change, since its purpose is to guide people through a change that is happening.
Why D: Change management helps people adopt new processes by communicating, training and supporting them, which reduces resistance and improves results.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Employees resist a new software system. Which management step best reduces resistance?
A: Cancel all communication with the staff
B: Explain why, train and invite feedback
C: Force the change with no explanation
D: Punish employees who ask questions
Why A: Cutting off communication increases fear and rumors, which makes resistance stronger instead of reducing it.
Why B: Explaining why, giving training and inviting feedback addresses employees' concerns and builds understanding, which reduces resistance to the new system.
Why C: Forcing the change without explanation breeds resentment and confusion, which usually raises resistance.
Why D: Punishing questions silences concerns and harms trust, so resistance goes underground and grows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does corporate governance refer to?
A: The company's cafeteria menu each week
B: The company's advertising plan and budget
C: The rules by which a company is directed
D: The government's tax policy for firms
Why A: A cafeteria menu is a facilities matter, not the system of rules by which a company is directed.
Why B: An advertising plan and budget is part of marketing, not the governance structure of the company.
Why C: Corporate governance refers to the rules and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, including the board and shareholder rights.
Why D: Government tax policy is set by government authorities, not by the company, and it is not corporate governance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is leadership?
A: The ability to influence and guide others toward a shared goal
B: The ownership of a company's shares by its founders alone
C: The skill of working alone on every task in the whole firm
D: The authority to give orders without explaining them to anyone
Why A: Leadership is the ability to influence and guide others toward a shared goal, which is accomplished through vision, communication and example.
Why B: Owning a company's shares is about ownership, which is not the same as influencing and guiding people.
Why C: Working alone on every task is the opposite of leadership, which depends on guiding other people.
Why D: Giving orders without explanation describes only an autocratic style, and not leadership in general, which involves guiding people toward shared goals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between a leader and a manager?
A: There is no real difference between them
B: Leaders handle budgets; managers set vision
C: Leaders hold formal authority; managers hold none
D: Leaders inspire; managers organize and control
Why A: There is a real difference, because leaders inspire and set direction while managers organize and control resources.
Why B: This reverses the usual distinction, since leaders set direction and inspire while managers handle budgets and organization.
Why C: Managers hold formal authority over resources and staff, and leaders can influence others without any formal title.
Why D: Leaders inspire and set direction, while managers organize and control work, which is the usual distinction between the two roles.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an autocratic leadership style?
A: The leader shares decisions equally and lets all vote on choices
B: The leader makes decisions alone with little input from the team
C: The leader lets the team decide everything about its own work
D: The leader has no authority over the staff or the whole team
Why A: Sharing decisions equally and voting describes a democratic style, which is the opposite of autocratic leadership.
Why B: An autocratic leader makes decisions alone with little input from the team, keeping control and speed but risking low morale.
Why C: Letting the team decide everything is laissez-faire leadership, not autocratic, where the leader holds decision control.
Why D: A leader with no authority is not autocratic, since autocratic leaders hold strong authority over their staff.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a democratic (participative) leadership style?
A: The leader copies a competitor in the same market
B: The leader avoids decisions and lets the group drift
C: The leader invites team input before making decisions
D: The leader decides alone without asking the team first
Why A: Copying a competitor is imitation and not a leadership style, so it does not describe democratic or participative leadership.
Why B: Avoiding decisions and letting the group drift describes laissez-faire leadership, not the participative approach of democratic leaders.
Why C: A democratic leader invites team input before making decisions, which improves commitment and draws on the group's knowledge.
Why D: Deciding alone without asking is autocratic behavior, which is the opposite of participative leadership.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a laissez-faire leadership style?
A: The leader gives the team wide freedom
B: The leader asks the team for input on choices
C: The leader inspires with a shared vision
D: The leader rewards people for meeting targets
Why A: Laissez-faire leaders give the team wide freedom, so group members make most decisions and work with little direction.
Why B: Asking for input and sharing decisions is democratic leadership, whereas laissez-faire leaders leave decisions mostly to the team.
Why C: Inspiring with a vision is transformational leadership, not the hands-off approach of laissez-faire.
Why D: Rewarding performance against targets is transactional leadership, which involves active management rather than a hands-off approach.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is transformational leadership?
A: Managing routines and schedules
B: Inspiring followers toward a shared vision
C: Letting followers do whatever they like
D: Making decisions without asking the team
Why A: Managing routines is a task of management; transformational leadership inspires change and a shared vision, not daily scheduling.
Why B: Transformational leadership inspires followers toward a shared vision, motivating them to go beyond their own interests and exceed expectations.
Why C: Letting followers do whatever they like is laissez-faire, which gives no inspiring direction.
Why D: Deciding without the team is autocratic, whereas transformational leaders engage followers and inspire them toward a shared vision.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is transactional leadership?
A: Avoiding direction altogether in the team
B: Serving the needs of all followers first
C: Using rewards and penalties to drive goals
D: Inspiring people through a shared vision
Why A: Avoiding direction describes laissez-faire leadership, whereas transactional leaders actively set expectations and respond with consequences.
Why B: Serving followers' needs first is servant leadership, and transactional leaders focus on exchanges instead.
Why C: Transactional leadership uses rewards and penalties to drive goals, exchanging pay or recognition for performance that meets the stated expectations.
Why D: Inspiring through a shared vision describes transformational leadership, not transactional leadership, which relies on exchanges.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is servant leadership?
A: Putting followers' needs first
B: Giving orders without explanation
C: Making followers serve the leader
D: Hiring servants for the office
Why A: Servant leadership puts followers' needs first, so the leader helps people grow and succeed so that they can do their best work.
Why B: Giving orders without explanation is autocratic behavior, which is the opposite of servant leadership.
Why C: Making followers serve the leader reverses the idea, since in servant leadership the leader serves the team.
Why D: Hiring servants for the office is a literal misreading, because servant leadership is a leadership philosophy and has nothing to do with domestic staff.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A team is highly skilled and self-motivated and needs little supervision. Which style is likely to work well?
A: Constant close micromanagement
B: Strict autocratic control of tasks
C: Silence and no support at all
D: Laissez-faire or delegating style
Why A: Close micromanagement wastes the abilities of a skilled, self-motivated team, frustrates its members, and adds supervision effort that the group simply does not need to do good work.
Why B: Strict autocratic control removes the autonomy that skilled, self-driven people value, so it stifles their initiative and creates resentment when they need little direction anyway.
Why C: Giving silence and no support at all is neglect, not delegation; even independent teams need resources, clear goals, and a leader available when problems arise.
Why D: A laissez-faire or delegating style fits a skilled, self-motivated team, because members can manage their own tasks, so the leader trusts them and steps back while staying available for support.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A new team with little experience faces an emergency. Which style may be most effective?
A: A hands-off style with no direction given
B: A directive style that gives clear instructions
C: A style that waits for everyone to vote on what to do
D: A style that ignores the problem and the people
Why A: A hands-off style gives no direction, which fails an inexperienced team in an emergency because they lack the knowledge to act alone and time is short.
Why B: A directive style gives clear instructions, which suits a new, inexperienced team in an emergency because they need quick, specific guidance and there is no time for debate or learning by trial.
Why C: Waiting for everyone to vote wastes precious time in an emergency, and an inexperienced team may lack the knowledge to vote well, so decisive direction works better.
Why D: Ignoring both the problem and the people abandons the team entirely; a leader must respond to an emergency, and this approach provides no guidance, support, or action at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is situational leadership?
A: Letting followers choose the leader each day
B: Choosing leaders based on their job titles
C: Adapting style to followers and the situation
D: Using a style based on the leader's personality
Why A: Situational leadership has nothing to do with followers choosing a new leader every day; it is about the leader changing style, not about electing leaders.
Why B: Situational leadership concerns how a leader adapts style, not how leaders are chosen or what titles they hold.
Why C: Situational leadership means adapting your style to the readiness of followers and the demands of the situation, so the leader directs, coaches, supports, or delegates as conditions require.
Why D: Situational leadership matches style to follower readiness and the task, not to the leader's own personality.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which trait is most associated with effective leaders?
A: Indifference
B: Secrecy
C: Stubbornness
D: Integrity
Why A: Indifference means not caring about people or results, which damages morale and trust; effective leaders show concern and engagement instead of being detached or uninterested in others.
Why B: Secrecy breeds suspicion and weakens trust, so it is associated with poor leadership; effective leaders are open and transparent with their teams about goals and decisions.
Why C: Stubbornness is an unwillingness to listen or change, which blocks good ideas and adaptation, so it marks weak leaders rather than effective ones who stay open to input.
Why D: Integrity, meaning honesty and consistent moral principles, is the trait most linked to effective leaders because followers trust and follow leaders who do what is right and keep their word.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is emotional intelligence?
A: Managing your emotions and those of others
B: The ability to memorize large amounts of data
C: The ability to speak several languages
D: The ability to avoid feelings entirely
Why A: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and understand and influence the emotions of others, which helps leaders build relationships and handle conflict well.
Why B: Memorizing large amounts of data is a memory skill, not emotional intelligence, which concerns awareness and management of feelings in yourself and other people instead of recall of facts.
Why C: Speaking several languages is a language ability, not emotional intelligence; the concept is about understanding and handling emotions, not about how many languages someone can use.
Why D: Emotional intelligence does not mean avoiding feelings; it means being aware of and managing them well, so avoiding feelings entirely is the opposite of the skill.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is empathy?
A: Sharing another person's feelings
B: Agreeing with everything someone says
C: Feeling superior to other people
D: Ignoring other people's feelings
Why A: Empathy is understanding and sharing another person's feelings, seeing a situation from their view, which helps leaders connect with people and respond with real care and understanding.
Why B: Agreeing with everything someone says is flattery or giving in, not empathy; you can understand and respect a person's feelings while still disagreeing with their opinion.
Why C: Feeling superior to others is arrogance, which blocks understanding; empathy requires treating others as equals and caring about how they feel, not looking down on them.
Why D: Ignoring other people's feelings is the lack of empathy, the exact opposite; empathy means noticing and caring about what others feel in a given situation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is active listening?
A: Interrupting to give your own advice fast
B: Waiting for your turn to talk, not to listen
C: Checking your phone while someone speaks
D: Fully focusing on a speaker, then replying
Why A: Interrupting to give advice quickly shows you are not truly listening; active listening means letting the speaker finish and understanding the message before you respond with anything of your own.
Why B: Waiting for your turn to talk means you are planning your reply instead of absorbing the message, so it is passive or poor listening, not active listening.
Why C: Checking your phone while someone speaks splits your attention and signals disrespect; active listening requires giving the speaker your full focus without distractions during the conversation.
Why D: Active listening means giving the speaker your full attention, understanding the message, and then replying thoughtfully, which shows respect and helps avoid misunderstandings in the conversation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is constructive feedback?
A: Praise with no details about what went well at work
B: Specific, respectful input meant to help someone improve
C: Silence about problems until they grow much worse
D: Harsh criticism of a person's character in front of the team
Why A: Praise with no details gives the person nothing specific to repeat or improve, so it is not constructive; useful feedback needs clear examples about what was done well.
Why B: Constructive feedback is specific, respectful input aimed at helping someone improve, giving clear examples of what to keep or change so the person can grow and perform better.
Why C: Staying silent about problems lets them grow worse and denies the person a chance to improve, so it provides no feedback at all and is not constructive.
Why D: Harsh criticism of someone's character in front of the team attacks the person instead of the behavior and humiliates them, which hurts morale and does not help improvement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which statement is the best example of constructive feedback?
A: You never do anything right at all
B: Do better next time and try harder
C: Your report was clear; add cost data
D: Your report was bad and too long
Why A: Saying "you never do anything right" is a vague, absolute attack on the person; it gives no specific detail and no path to improve, so it is not constructive.
Why B: "Do better next time and try harder" is vague and offers no specifics about what to change or how, so the person cannot act on it; it is not constructive.
Why C: "Your report was clear; add cost data" names a specific strength and one specific improvement in a respectful tone, so the person knows exactly what to keep and what to add.
Why D: "Your report was bad and too long" is a blunt judgment with no specific guidance; it gives little to act on and sounds harsh, so it is not constructive feedback.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vision in leadership?
A: An eye test for all managers at the firm
B: A list of this month's expenses for the firm
C: A prediction of next week's weather in the city
D: A picture of a future that inspires people
Why A: A vision has nothing to do with eyesight or eye tests for managers; in leadership it means a mental picture of the desired future for the organization, not physical sight.
Why B: A list of this month's expenses is a financial record of the past, not a vision; a vision describes an inspiring future the organization wants to reach.
Why C: A weather prediction concerns forecasting next week's conditions and is unrelated to the organization; a leadership vision is an inspiring image of the organization's long-term future instead.
Why D: A vision is a picture of a desirable future that inspires and guides people, giving the team a shared direction and a reason to work toward common goals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is communicating a vision important?
A: It increases confusion among the staff and the team
B: It lets leaders avoid decisions for a very long time
C: It aligns people around common goals and motivates action
D: It keeps the vision secret so only managers know the plan
Why A: Communicating a vision should reduce confusion by giving people clear direction; saying it increases confusion for the staff gets the purpose backward, since clarity is the entire point.
Why B: Communicating a vision does not let leaders avoid decisions; a vision guides decisions, so leaders must still make them, and avoiding decisions for a long time would hurt the organization.
Why C: Sharing the vision aligns people around common goals and motivates them to act, because they understand where the organization is heading and why their work matters to it.
Why D: Keeping the vision secret so only managers know the plan defeats its purpose; a vision must be shared widely so everyone can understand it and work toward it together.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is motivation?
A: The pay a worker receives each month
B: The drive that causes a person to act
C: The hours worked in a typical work week
D: The result of a yearly performance review
Why A: Pay is only one possible reward and not the definition of motivation; motivation is the internal drive to act, and money is just one outside factor that may influence it.
Why B: Motivation is the drive or force that causes a person to act, to start, direct, and keep up effort toward a goal, whether the source is inside or outside.
Why C: The hours worked in a typical week measure time spent, not the drive behind the effort; someone can work long hours with low motivation, so hours do not define motivation.
Why D: A yearly performance review is an evaluation event, not a definition of motivation; motivation is the inner drive that leads people to act, not the result of a review.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need comes first?
A: Physiological needs
B: Self-actualization
C: Belonging and love
D: Esteem and respect
Why A: Physiological needs such as food, water, air, and sleep sit at the base of Maslow's hierarchy, so they come first and must be met before higher needs matter.
Why B: Self-actualization is at the very top of Maslow's hierarchy, so it comes last; people pursue it only after the lower needs are satisfied, not first.
Why C: Belonging and love is the third level of Maslow's hierarchy, above physiological and safety needs, so it cannot come first; basic survival needs must be met before it.
Why D: Esteem and respect is the fourth level of Maslow's hierarchy, well above the basics, so it does not come first; physiological needs at the bottom must be satisfied before it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the correct order of Maslow's hierarchy from bottom to top?
A: Esteem, belonging, safety, physiological, self-actualization
B: Safety, esteem, belonging, physiological, self-actualization
C: Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualization
D: Self-actualization, esteem, belonging, safety, physiological
Why A: This order puts esteem first and physiological fourth, which reverses the pyramid and leaves out proper placement of safety; Maslow places physiological needs at the bottom and self-actualization at the top.
Why B: This list puts safety before physiological needs and esteem before belonging, so two levels are swapped; Maslow's correct order is physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, then self-actualization.
Why C: Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, then self-actualization is Maslow's correct order from bottom to top, moving from basic survival needs up to personal growth and fulfillment at the peak.
Why D: This order is completely reversed, starting with self-actualization and ending with physiological needs; Maslow's pyramid runs from physiological at the bottom up to self-actualization at the top.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, which is a hygiene factor?
A: Challenging, creative work
B: Salary and working conditions
C: Opportunity for career growth
D: Recognition for achievement
Why A: Challenging, creative work is a motivator in Herzberg's theory because it provides satisfaction through the job itself, so it is not a hygiene factor like pay or conditions.
Why B: Salary and working conditions are classic hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory; they prevent dissatisfaction when adequate but do not by themselves create real motivation or lasting satisfaction among workers.
Why C: Opportunity for career growth is a motivator in Herzberg's theory, since it provides a sense of achievement and advancement, and is not a hygiene factor like pay or conditions.
Why D: Recognition for achievement is a motivator in Herzberg's theory, because it satisfies a need for esteem and accomplishment, whereas hygiene factors concern surroundings such as pay and policies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: According to Herzberg's theory, which is a motivator?
A: Recognition and advancement
B: Company policies and rules
C: Job security and benefits
D: A salary and pay raises
Why A: Recognition and advancement are motivators in Herzberg's theory, since they come from the work itself and create real satisfaction, achievement, and a drive to perform better.
Why B: Company policies and rules are hygiene factors; they can cause dissatisfaction when poor but do not motivate, so they are not Herzberg motivators.
Why C: Job security and benefits are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction when adequate, but they do not produce lasting motivation, so they are not Herzberg motivators.
Why D: Salary and pay raises are hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory; they remove dissatisfaction when fair but do not by themselves motivate, so they are not motivators.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is intrinsic motivation?
A: Motivation that comes from rewards given by others, such as pay, praise or prizes
B: Motivation that comes from fear of punishment or the loss of a job
C: Motivation that comes from a lack of choices at work or in daily life
D: Motivation that comes from inside, such as enjoyment or pride in the work
Why A: Motivation from rewards given by others such as pay, praise, or prizes is extrinsic motivation, because the source is outside the person rather than inside them.
Why B: Motivation from fear of punishment or job loss is extrinsic, driven by outside pressure and threats, not by an inner interest in the work itself.
Why C: Lacking choices at work or in life describes constraint, not a source of inner drive; intrinsic motivation comes from within, not from having no options.
Why D: Intrinsic motivation comes from inside the person, such as enjoyment, curiosity, or pride in the work, so the activity itself is rewarding without needing outside rewards or pressure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is extrinsic motivation?
A: Motivation that comes from outside rewards such as pay or praise
B: Motivation that comes from curiosity about the task itself
C: Motivation that comes from enjoying the task for its own sake
D: Motivation that comes from personal interest and love of the work
Why A: Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards such as pay, praise, grades, or prizes, so the person acts to earn something external instead of for personal enjoyment of the task.
Why B: Curiosity about the task itself is an inner source of drive, which makes it intrinsic motivation rather than extrinsic, where the reward comes from outside the person.
Why C: Enjoying a task for its own sake is intrinsic motivation, since the reward is the activity itself, while extrinsic motivation depends on outside rewards.
Why D: Personal interest and love of the work come from within the person, so they describe intrinsic motivation, not extrinsic motivation which relies on outside rewards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student volunteers at a shelter because it feels meaningful. This is an example of:
A: Extrinsic motivation
B: Intrinsic motivation
C: Friendly competition
D: Pressure from a boss
Why A: Extrinsic motivation relies on outside rewards like pay or praise; a student volunteering because it feels meaningful is driven by inner values, not an external reward.
Why B: Volunteering because it feels meaningful is driven by inner satisfaction and values rather than outside rewards, which is the definition of intrinsic motivation.
Why C: Friendly competition involves comparing yourself with others for a contest; nothing in the example mentions competing, since the student acts only because the work feels meaningful.
Why D: Pressure from a boss would be an outside force; a student volunteering at a shelter has no boss pushing them, and the stated reason is that it feels meaningful.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a role model?
A: A person who only gives orders
B: A person who models clothing
C: A person others admire and copy
D: A person who ignores values
Why A: A person who only gives orders is a commander, not a role model; role models earn admiration through their example, character, and behavior rather than by simply issuing commands.
Why B: A person who models clothing is a fashion model, which is a different meaning of the word; in leadership a role model is someone whose behavior others look up to.
Why C: A role model is a person whose behavior, values, and success others admire and copy, so they influence people by example instead of by giving orders.
Why D: A person who ignores values cannot be a good role model, because others should not copy that behavior; role models are admired for upholding strong values and setting an example.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean to lead by example?
A: Copying other leaders blindly without any thought of your own
B: Avoiding all responsibility for results and for the team
C: Telling others to do what you will not do yourself at work
D: Showing the behavior and standards you expect from others
Why A: Copying other leaders blindly without thought is imitation, not leading by example; leading by example means your own behavior shows the standards you expect, not borrowing others' actions.
Why B: Avoiding responsibility for results and for the team is the opposite of leading by example; leaders who dodge responsibility set a poor model for everyone around them.
Why C: Telling others to do what you will not do yourself is hypocrisy, which destroys credibility; leading by example means doing yourself what you ask of others.
Why D: Leading by example means showing the behavior and standards you expect from others through your own actions, which builds credibility and encourages people to follow your lead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accountability in leadership?
A: Owning decisions and their results
B: Avoiding decisions and their results
C: Blaming others for poor results
D: Taking credit only for success
Why A: Accountability means owning your decisions and their results, good or bad, and accepting responsibility for outcomes instead of shifting blame, which builds trust with the team.
Why B: Avoiding decisions and their results is the opposite of accountability; accountable leaders face outcomes and take responsibility for what happens as a result of their choices.
Why C: Blaming others for poor results shifts responsibility away, which is the opposite of accountability; accountable leaders accept their own part in outcomes instead of pointing fingers at the team.
Why D: Taking credit only for success ignores failures; true accountability means accepting responsibility for both good and bad results, not just the parts that make you look good.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is trust in a team?
A: Fear of consequences for making a mistake at work
B: Belief that no one will ever disagree with the group overall
C: Confidence that members will act honestly and reliably
D: Reliance on rumors and gossip from the office staff
Why A: Fear of consequences for mistakes describes a climate of anxiety, which undermines trust; trust means feeling safe, so fear is the opposite of trust within a team.
Why B: Believing no one will ever disagree is unrealistic and unhealthy; trust allows honest disagreement because members feel safe, so it is not the absence of disagreement.
Why C: Trust in a team is confidence that members will act honestly and reliably, doing what they say and caring about the group, which lets people cooperate and take risks.
Why D: Reliance on rumors and gossip spreads unverified claims and damages relationships; trust rests on honesty and reliable behavior, so gossip erodes it instead of building it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A leader promises to approve vacation requests but later refuses without explanation. What is the likely effect?
A: Trust in the leader grows
B: Nothing changes for the team
C: Employees become more motivated
D: Trust in the leader declines
Why A: Trust cannot grow when a leader breaks a promise without explanation; broken commitments make employees doubt the leader's word, so trust falls rather than rises.
Why B: Something has clearly changed; refusing a promised approval without explanation makes employees feel misled, so saying nothing changes ignores the likely damage to trust and morale.
Why C: Employees are unlikely to feel more motivated after a promise is broken without explanation; feeling cheated usually lowers motivation and engagement instead of raising it.
Why D: Breaking a promise without explanation shows the leader is unreliable, so employees stop believing the leader's word, and trust in the leader declines as a result.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is conflict resolution?
A: Punishing everyone involved in the dispute equally
B: Finding a solution that settles a disagreement fairly
C: Ignoring a disagreement until it ends by itself in time
D: Taking sides without listening to either person
Why A: Punishing everyone involved equally ignores who is at fault and does not address the cause of the disagreement; conflict resolution seeks a fair settlement, not equal punishment.
Why B: Conflict resolution is finding a solution that settles a disagreement fairly, addressing the causes so the parties can move forward and keep working together productively.
Why C: Ignoring a disagreement until it ends by itself is avoidance, which often lets tension grow; conflict resolution means actively working to settle the issue.
Why D: Taking sides without listening to either person is unfair and increases resentment; resolution requires hearing both parties and reaching a fair outcome, not choosing a side blindly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a win-win solution?
A: An outcome that benefits all parties in a disagreement
B: An outcome decided by chance such as a coin toss
C: An outcome where both sides lose something of value
D: An outcome where one side wins and the other side loses
Why A: A win-win solution is an outcome that benefits all parties in a disagreement, so each side gets something it needs and the relationship stays intact.
Why B: Deciding by chance, such as a coin toss, is random and does not meet the needs of either side, so it is not a win-win solution.
Why C: An outcome where both sides lose something is a lose-lose result, which is the opposite of win-win, where both parties gain something of value.
Why D: An outcome where one side wins and the other loses is win-lose, which leaves one party unhappy, while a win-win outcome benefits everyone involved.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two team members disagree about how to split a task. What is the best first step for a leader?
A: Remove both people from the team and replace them at once
B: Choose a side right away without hearing the reasons
C: Tell them to stop talking about it for good in the office
D: Listen to both sides and help them find a shared solution
Why A: Removing both people and replacing them at once is an extreme reaction that wastes skills and does not address the cause; a leader should first understand the problem.
Why B: Choosing a side right away without hearing reasons is unfair and may punish the wrong person; a good leader gathers information before deciding anything about the dispute.
Why C: Telling them to stop talking about it does not resolve the disagreement; it just hides the issue so resentment grows, and the task split remains unsettled.
Why D: The best first step is to listen to both sides and help them reach a shared solution, which is fair, respects both people, and addresses the real cause of the disagreement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is mentoring?
A: A formal punishment for repeated mistakes
B: A test given to new hires on their first day
C: An experienced person guides a newer one
D: A job title for a senior manager role
Why A: A formal punishment for mistakes describes discipline, not mentoring; mentoring is supportive guidance meant to help a person grow, not a penalty for errors.
Why B: A test given to new hires on their first day is an assessment, not mentoring; mentoring is an ongoing relationship where someone experienced offers advice and support.
Why C: Mentoring is a relationship in which an experienced person guides and advises a newer or less experienced one, sharing knowledge to help them grow and succeed in their career.
Why D: A job title for a senior manager role names a position, not an activity; mentoring is the guidance an experienced person gives a newer one, whatever their title.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is coaching?
A: Ordering someone to do tasks and checking each step
B: Improving skills through guidance and feedback
C: Writing a policy manual for the company's staff
D: Firing poor performers from the firm each year
Why A: Ordering someone to do tasks and checking each step is micromanagement or direct supervision; coaching develops skills through guidance and feedback instead of giving constant commands and inspection.
Why B: Coaching is improving someone's skills and performance through guidance, questions, and feedback, helping them reach their own potential rather than just telling them what to do.
Why C: Writing a policy manual for staff is documentation work, not coaching; coaching is a personal process of developing skills through guidance and feedback with an individual.
Why D: Firing poor performers each year is a dismissal practice, not coaching; coaching aims to help people improve through guidance, not to remove them from the company.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stakeholder in a leadership context?
A: A company's main competitor in the same market
B: A stake used to mark property lines in a field
C: Only the one person who makes the final decision
D: Anyone affected by or interested in a decision
Why A: A main competitor sits on the other side of the market, so it is not a stakeholder; stakeholders are those affected by or interested in the organization's decisions.
Why B: A stake used to mark property lines is a literal wooden post; it has nothing to do with the leadership meaning of stakeholder, which refers to people.
Why C: Stakeholders are not limited to one decision maker; many people can be affected by a decision, and the definition covers everyone with an interest, not just one person.
Why D: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in a decision, such as employees, customers, owners, or community members, so leaders must consider their needs when choosing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ethical leadership?
A: Leading by hiding mistakes from the whole team at all
B: Leading in ways that are honest, fair and respect others
C: Leading by whatever brings the fastest profit for the firm
D: Leading by favoring friends and close allies at work
Why A: Hiding mistakes from the team is dishonest and breaks trust, so it is unethical; ethical leaders admit errors and are open with their team about what happened.
Why B: Ethical leadership means leading in ways that are honest, fair, and respectful of others, so the leader's actions follow sound moral values and earn trust from followers.
Why C: Choosing whatever brings the fastest profit can justify harming people or cutting corners; ethical leadership weighs fairness and honesty, not profit alone, so this is not ethical.
Why D: Favoring friends and close allies is unfair treatment that undermines trust and morale; ethical leaders treat people fairly and judge them on merit rather than personal connection.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A leader discovers that a team member padded expense reports. The ethical response is to:
A: Hide it from the rest of the company
B: Spread rumors about the person widely
C: Follow policy, fairly and consistently
D: Ignore it because the amount is small
Why A: Hiding the padding from the company covers up dishonest behavior, which is itself unethical and may make the leader complicit; the matter should be handled openly under policy.
Why B: Spreading rumors about the person is unprofessional and unfair, harms their reputation outside of any proper process, and is not how an ethical leader handles wrongdoing.
Why C: Following policy fairly and consistently is the ethical response; it treats the person the same as anyone else, respects due process, and upholds honesty in expense reporting.
Why D: Ignoring the padding because the amount is small excuses dishonesty and sends the message that small violations are fine, which weakens standards and treats people inconsistently.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean to be adaptable as a leader?
A: Adjusting approach when conditions or needs change
B: Changing your mind every minute for no reason at all
C: Refusing to change plans no matter what happens
D: Avoiding new ideas from the team and from others
Why A: Being adaptable means adjusting your approach when conditions or needs change, so you can respond to new situations and still keep the team moving toward its goals.
Why B: Changing your mind every minute for no reason is erratic and confuses the team; adaptability means changing for good reasons when conditions change, not constant random flip-flopping.
Why C: Refusing to change plans no matter what happens is rigidity, the opposite of adaptability, since adaptable leaders respond to new information and conditions.
Why D: Avoiding new ideas from the team and from others shuts out useful input, which is the opposite of adaptable; adaptable leaders stay open to change and fresh suggestions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a common mistake of new leaders?
A: Doing everything themselves, not delegating
B: Asking the team for ideas before deciding
C: Setting clear goals and deadlines for others
D: Giving regular feedback to team members often
Why A: Doing everything themselves instead of delegating is a common new leader mistake, because it overloads the leader, wastes the team's talents, and keeps people from growing.
Why B: Asking the team for ideas before deciding is a good practice that builds buy-in and uses their knowledge, so it is not a mistake of new leaders.
Why C: Setting clear goals and deadlines is good leadership because it gives direction and accountability, so it is a strength and not a common mistake of new leaders.
Why D: Giving regular feedback to team members often is a good habit that helps people improve and feel supported, so it is not a common mistake of new leaders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is peer pressure?
A: A tax on income earned by working adults
B: Pressure from a group to act a certain way
C: A handbook rule that tells students how to act
D: Orders from a boss to do tasks at work daily
Why A: A tax on income earned by working adults is an income tax; peer pressure has nothing to do with taxes and concerns influence from people in a group.
Why B: Peer pressure is pressure from a group of people, often of similar age or status, to act or think a certain way in order to fit in.
Why C: A handbook rule that tells students how to act is formal policy from an authority; peer pressure comes from equals in a group, not from written rules.
Why D: Orders from a boss are authority-based instructions, not peer pressure; peer pressure comes from people at the same level, such as classmates or coworkers, wanting you to conform.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a parliamentary procedure used for?
A: Hiring staff for open jobs in firms
B: Filing taxes for the firm each year
C: Running meetings in an orderly way
D: Choosing products and prices each year
Why A: Hiring staff for open jobs is a human resources function, not the purpose of parliamentary procedure, which sets the rules for how formal meetings are conducted.
Why B: Filing taxes for the firm each year is an accounting task, unrelated to parliamentary procedure, which is a set of rules for running meetings and making group decisions.
Why C: Parliamentary procedure is a set of rules used to run meetings in an orderly, fair way, so that business gets done and every member has a chance to be heard.
Why D: Choosing products and prices each year is a business strategy task, not what parliamentary procedure covers; it governs how meetings are run, not what a company sells.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In parliamentary procedure, what is a motion?
A: A written minutes record of each meeting
B: A count of the votes cast by all members
C: A physical move by a member from one chair
D: A formal proposal that a group take action
Why A: A written record of each meeting is called the minutes, not a motion; a motion is a proposal that members bring forward for the group to consider.
Why B: A count of the votes cast is a tally or vote result, not a motion; a motion is the proposal on which members vote.
Why C: A physical move by a member from one chair is simply changing seats; in parliamentary procedure, a motion is a formal proposal for the group to take action.
Why D: In parliamentary procedure, a motion is a formal proposal that the group take a specific action, which members make so it can be discussed and voted on.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In parliamentary procedure, what must happen after a motion is made?
A: It is passed by the chair with no vote
B: It is immediately tabled by the chair
C: It is cancelled by the whole group
D: It needs a second before discussion
Why A: A chair cannot pass a motion without a vote; the group decides by voting, so this skips the required steps of a second and discussion.
Why B: A motion is not automatically tabled by the chair; tabling is a separate motion that members must propose and the group must approve, so it does not happen immediately.
Why C: A motion is not cancelled automatically by the whole group; it stays pending until it is seconded, debated, and voted on, or withdrawn by its maker.
Why D: After a motion is made, it needs a second from another member before discussion begins, which shows at least two members want the group to consider the proposal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are meeting minutes?
A: The official written record of a meeting
B: The length of time a meeting lasts in total
C: A prediction of future meetings and dates
D: A list of attendees' hobbies and pastimes
Why A: Meeting minutes are the official written record of a meeting, noting who attended, what was discussed, what motions were made, and what decisions the group reached.
Why B: The length of time a meeting lasts is just its duration; minutes are a written record of what happened, not a measure of how many minutes passed.
Why C: A prediction of future meetings and dates would be a schedule or calendar; minutes record what already happened at a past meeting instead of forecasting the future.
Why D: A list of attendees' hobbies has no business purpose; minutes record the official business of a meeting, such as attendance, motions, and decisions, not personal interests.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an agenda?
A: A record of past decisions kept in the files
B: A list of topics to be covered in a meeting
C: A list of rules for employees and managers
D: A summary of financial results for the year
Why A: A record of past decisions kept in the files describes minutes or archives; an agenda looks ahead and lists what will be covered at an upcoming meeting.
Why B: An agenda is a list of the topics to be covered in a meeting, usually in order, which keeps discussion organized and focused on the items that matter.
Why C: A list of rules for employees and managers is a policy or code of conduct; an agenda is specific to a meeting and lists topics to be discussed.
Why D: A summary of financial results for the year is a financial report; an agenda lists topics for a meeting and does not summarize finances.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which practice makes a meeting more productive?
A: Letting discussions run on forever with no end
B: Starting without a plan, an agenda or a clock
C: Sharing an agenda in advance and keeping to time
D: Inviting everyone in the firm regardless of role
Why A: Letting discussions run on forever with no end wastes time and loses focus, so meetings become unproductive; a productive meeting keeps to a limit and reaches decisions.
Why B: Starting without a plan, agenda, or clock leads to wandering talk and wasted time, so the meeting lacks direction and is less productive, not more.
Why C: Sharing an agenda in advance and keeping to time lets people prepare and focus on the key topics, so the meeting stays on track and ends with results.
Why D: Inviting everyone in the firm regardless of role crowds the meeting with people who have no part in the topic, which wastes their time and slows decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is public speaking confidence built through?
A: Reading from a script only
B: Memorizing without meaning
C: Practice and preparation
D: Avoiding all audiences
Why A: Reading from a script only does not build confidence, because it keeps the speaker tied to the page and unable to connect with the audience or handle surprises.
Why B: Memorizing without meaning leaves the speaker lost if one word is forgotten, so it adds anxiety instead of confidence; understanding the content is what builds real confidence.
