B: A documented set of steps for performing a routine task consistently
C: A company slogan used in advertising and printed on the products it sells
D: A pay scale that lists the wages for each job grade in the company
Why A: A one-time suggestion is an informal idea raised once, whereas an SOP is a standing written procedure that people follow repeatedly, so a single suggestion cannot be an SOP.
Why B: An SOP is a documented set of steps for doing a routine task the same way every time, which keeps quality and safety consistent across staff.
Why C: A slogan is a marketing phrase used in advertising and on packaging, while an SOP is an internal instruction document. The two serve entirely different purposes.
Why D: A pay scale lists wages by job grade and belongs to compensation management. An SOP instead describes steps for performing a task, so this does not match.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is kaizen?
A: A budgeting tool used to plan yearly spending
B: A one-time overhaul done by outside consultants
C: A legal term used in contracts and court filings
D: A philosophy of continuous small improvements
Why A: A budgeting tool plans spending for a year, while kaizen is about improving work methods continuously. Kaizen is a philosophy of improvement, not a financial planning document.
Why B: Kaizen is not a one-time overhaul. Its core idea is steady, ongoing small changes by everyone, whereas a single consultant-led makeover is a big, one-off change.
Why C: Kaizen is a Japanese management concept, not a legal term. Contracts and court filings use different vocabulary, so this has no connection to the word's real meaning.
Why D: Kaizen is the Japanese philosophy of continuous small improvements made by all employees over time, which gradually raises quality and efficiency without needing large, disruptive changes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Six Sigma?
A: A hiring plan that sets out how many workers to recruit
B: A sales method used to close deals with new customers
C: A logo style used in the branding of the company's products
D: A data-driven approach to reduce defects and variation
Why A: A hiring plan sets recruitment numbers and is an HR planning tool. Six Sigma is a quality method focused on reducing defects, so recruitment targets are unrelated to it.
Why B: A sales method closes deals with customers, but Six Sigma is a process-quality approach. It targets production and service defects, not selling techniques or deal closing.
Why C: A logo style is a branding choice. Six Sigma is a statistical quality approach, so a visual identity has no link to it despite the sigma symbol.
Why D: Six Sigma is a data-driven approach that measures processes to cut defects and variation, aiming for about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, which improves quality.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is lean management?
A: Delaying work until the very last minute before it is due
B: Cutting staff only, to lower the cost of running the firm
C: Eliminating waste while delivering value to customers
D: Making products slimmer and lighter to cut shipping costs
Why A: Lean management removes waste and does not mean delaying work. Putting tasks off until the deadline usually creates rushed output and idle time, which lean specifically tries to avoid.
Why B: Lean is about waste removal while delivering value, not simply cutting staff. Layoffs alone can harm quality and morale, so a staff-cutting-only view misses the point.
Why C: Lean management means eliminating waste such as extra steps, idle time and defects while still delivering value to customers, which improves efficiency without lowering what the customer receives.
Why D: Lean refers to a management approach, not to making products physically slimmer or lighter. Product size and shipping weight are unrelated to waste elimination in processes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is benchmarking?
A: Comparing your performance to best practices of leading organizations
B: Copying products illegally from rivals and selling them at a lower price
C: Building benches for parks and other public places in the city
D: Ignoring competitors and the market while looking only at your own firm
Why A: Benchmarking compares your performance and processes with best practices of leading organizations, which shows where gaps exist and how to improve, so this is the accurate definition.
Why B: Benchmarking is a legal, open comparison of practices and results. Copying rivals' products illegally is theft or infringement, which is a different and unlawful act.
Why C: Building benches is a construction or public works activity. The word only sounds similar, and benchmarking is a management practice of measuring performance against others.
Why D: Benchmarking requires looking closely at competitors and the market for best practices. Ignoring them and looking only inward is the opposite of comparing against leaders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between a manager and a leader?
A: Managers set the vision while leaders handle schedules and budgets
B: Managers handle processes and tasks while leaders inspire and set direction
C: Managers are chosen by employees while leaders are appointed by owners
D: Managers work for the owners while leaders work for the customers
Why A: This reverses the roles: leaders set the vision and inspire people, while managers handle schedules, budgets and processes.
Why B: Managers focus on processes, tasks and getting things done, while leaders inspire people and set direction. This captures the common distinction between the two roles accurately.
Why C: Neither role depends on who selects the person; the difference lies in function, with managers running processes and leaders setting direction.
Why D: Both roles can serve the owners and customers; the real distinction is process and tasks for managers versus direction and inspiration for leaders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an autocratic leader?
A: A leader who asks the team to vote on each decision
B: A leader who delegates everything to the team and stays away
C: A leader who makes decisions alone and expects compliance
D: A leader who gives total freedom to the team without direction
Why A: A leader who has the team vote on each decision is democratic or participative, not autocratic, since an autocrat keeps decision power rather than sharing it.
Why B: Delegating everything and staying away describes a laissez-faire leader. An autocratic leader stays in control and directs the work instead of stepping back.
Why C: An autocratic leader makes decisions alone, with little or no input from the team, and expects staff to comply with the orders given.
Why D: Giving the team total freedom with no direction is laissez-faire. Autocratic leaders do the opposite by controlling decisions tightly, so this does not describe them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a democratic (participative) leader?
A: A leader who involves the team in decisions
B: A leader who focuses on rewards for meeting targets
C: A leader who lets staff choose tasks freely
D: A leader who decides alone, with no input
Why A: A democratic or participative leader involves team members in decisions by seeking their input and ideas, which builds ownership and commitment while the leader still guides the process.
Why B: Rewarding the meeting of targets is transactional leadership; a democratic leader asks the team for input before deciding.
Why C: Letting staff choose tasks freely is laissez-faire; a democratic leader still guides the team while inviting its input.
Why D: Deciding alone with no input is autocratic leadership, the opposite of democratic leadership, which is built on involving the team in the decision.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In an emergency requiring an immediate decision, which leadership style is often most appropriate?
A: No leadership
B: Democratic
C: Laissez-faire
D: Autocratic
Why A: Having no leadership in an emergency wastes scarce time and leaves people without direction, so it is the least appropriate response when an immediate decision is required.
Why B: Democratic decision making takes time for discussion and consensus, which an emergency does not allow. It suits calm situations rather than ones needing an immediate decision.
Why C: Laissez-faire leaves decisions to the team with little direction, which risks confusion and delay when a fast, clear call is needed during an emergency.
Why D: The autocratic style lets one leader decide quickly and give clear orders without debate, which is often the most suitable approach when an immediate decision is required in an emergency.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A leader who gives a highly skilled team freedom to choose its approach is using which style?
A: Bureaucratic
B: Laissez-faire
C: Autocratic
D: Charismatic only
Why A: Bureaucratic leadership relies on strict rules and procedures, which limits freedom. It does not describe a leader who lets a skilled team choose its own approach.
Why B: Laissez-faire leaders give a capable, skilled team freedom to choose its own methods, with little interference, which works well when members are experienced and self-motivated.
Why C: An autocratic leader keeps decisions and control, which is the opposite of giving a skilled team freedom to select how it works.
Why D: Charismatic leadership relies on personal charm to inspire, not on handing over freedom. The word "only" also makes it too narrow to describe the hands-off approach given here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is charismatic leadership?
A: Leading through paperwork and written orders, not charm
B: Leading through rules and procedures written in manuals
C: Leading through personal charm and the ability to inspire
D: Leading through fear and punishments handed out to workers
Why A: Leading through paperwork and written orders describes a bureaucratic style. Charismatic leadership depends on personal charm and inspiration, which the question states directly, not on documents.
Why B: Leading through rules and procedures in manuals is bureaucratic leadership. Charismatic leaders rely on their personality and ability to inspire rather than on written rules.
Why C: Charismatic leadership uses personal charm and the ability to inspire followers, who are drawn to the leader's vision and enthusiasm rather than to rules or rewards alone.
Why D: Leading through fear and punishment is coercive, not charismatic. Charismatic leaders attract followers through admiration and inspiration, not threats or penalties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a component of emotional intelligence?
A: Memorized facts
B: Self-awareness
C: Speed typing
D: Math skill
Why A: Memorized facts measure knowledge recall, not emotional intelligence, which concerns understanding and managing emotions in oneself and others rather than storing information.
Why B: Self-awareness, the ability to recognize your own emotions and their effect on others, is one of the core components of emotional intelligence alongside self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.
Why C: Speed typing is a technical skill with no link to recognizing or managing emotions, so it is not a component of emotional intelligence.
Why D: Math skill is a cognitive ability tied to analytical intelligence, not to emotional intelligence, which covers awareness and management of feelings and relationships.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is integrity in leadership?
A: Being popular with the staff and the customers
B: Being strict about rules and deadlines at all times
C: Being wealthy enough to pay for the needs of the team
D: Being honest and consistent in values and actions
Why A: Being popular is about being liked, which can change with the situation. Integrity is about moral principles, so popularity does not define it.
Why B: Being strict about rules and deadlines is discipline or rigidity. Integrity concerns honesty and moral consistency, which a strict person may or may not show.
Why C: Wealth has no bearing on integrity. A leader's honesty and values do not depend on money, so being wealthy enough to pay for the team's needs is irrelevant.
Why D: Integrity in leadership means being honest and keeping values and actions consistent, so people can trust the leader to do what is right and say what is true.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'leading by example' mean?
A: Modeling the behavior you expect of others
B: Delegating all tasks while taking the credit
C: Telling others what to do from a distance
D: Rewarding those who follow your instructions
Why A: Leading by example means modeling the behavior you expect from others, such as arriving on time and working hard, so your actions match your words and set the standard.
Why B: Delegating everything and taking credit is the opposite of leading by example, because it shows the leader sets a poor standard and avoids sharing recognition.
Why C: Giving directions from a distance does not show the expected behavior; leading by example means doing the work yourself.
Why D: Rewarding compliance is a form of incentive, whereas leading by example means showing the behavior you want through your own actions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is vision in leadership?
A: A yearly budget that lists the money the team plans to spend and earn
B: A clear picture of a desirable future that guides and inspires others
C: Good eyesight that helps a manager read reports and spot small errors
D: A to-do list of tasks that employees should finish by the end of the week
Why A: A yearly budget lists planned spending and income, which is a financial plan. Vision in leadership is a picture of a desirable future, not a budget document.
Why B: Vision in leadership is a clear picture of a desirable future that guides decisions and inspires people to work toward a shared goal.
Why C: Good eyesight is a physical ability and has nothing to do with leadership vision, which is a figurative idea about the future, not about reading reports.
Why D: A weekly to-do list covers short-term tasks, whereas vision is a long-term picture of a desirable future that gives direction and inspiration beyond daily or weekly tasks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is power in organizations?
A: A budget set by the company each year
B: A job title only, shown on a business card
C: The ability to influence others' behavior
D: Electricity used to run machines in the plant
Why A: A budget is a financial plan for money, not power. Power in organizations is about the ability to influence people, not about yearly spending limits.
Why B: A job title shows position and can support formal authority, but power is the ability to influence behavior, which does not depend on a title alone.
Why C: Power in organizations is the ability to influence the behavior of others, whether through position, expertise, rewards, coercion or personal appeal, so this is the correct definition.
Why D: Electricity running machines is the physical meaning of power, not the organizational meaning, which refers to influence over people rather than energy supply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is legitimate power?
A: Power from charm and personal appeal
B: Power from rewards that managers give
C: Power from expertise and special skills
D: Power that comes from a formal position
Why A: Power from charm and personal appeal is referent or charismatic power. Legitimate power comes from a formal position, not from being liked or admired.
Why B: Power from rewards is reward power. Legitimate power comes from holding a formal position, not from the ability to hand out rewards.
Why C: Power from expertise and special skills is expert power. Legitimate power is based on position, so skill does not create it.
Why D: Legitimate power comes from a formal position in the organization, such as manager or supervisor, which gives the holder the recognized right to direct others.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is expert power?
A: Influence based on specialized knowledge or skill
B: Power from title or rank in the company's hierarchy
C: Power from punishment by taking away rewards
D: Power from charm and personal appeal with others
Why A: Expert power is influence based on specialized knowledge or skill, so people follow someone because they trust that person's competence in a field.
Why B: Power from title or rank is legitimate power. Expert power stems from knowledge and skill, not from the position held in the hierarchy.
Why C: Power from taking away rewards or punishing is coercive power, not expert power, which depends on skill and knowledge rather than threats.
Why D: Power from charm and personal appeal is referent power. Expert power comes from specialized knowledge and skill, not from being liked.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is referent power?
A: Influence based on admiration and personal connection
B: Power from force or the threat of punishment at work
C: Power from expertise and special skills in a field
D: Power from position or title in the organization
Why A: Referent power is influence based on admiration, respect and personal connection, so people follow a leader they identify with and want to be like.
Why B: Power from force or the threat of punishment is coercive power. Referent power is about admiration and personal connection, not fear.
Why C: Power from expertise and special skills is expert power. Referent power comes from admiration and connection to a person, not from competence.
Why D: Power from position or title is legitimate power. Referent power is built on personal admiration, so it does not require any formal rank.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is coercive power?
A: Influence from expertise and special skill
B: Influence based on the ability to punish
C: Influence from charm and personal appeal
D: Influence from rewards given to workers
Why A: Influence from expertise and skill is expert power. Coercive power rests on the ability to punish, not on knowledge.
Why B: Coercive power is influence based on the ability to punish, such as discipline, demotion or dismissal, so people comply because they fear negative consequences.
Why C: Influence from charm and personal appeal is referent power. Coercive power depends on threats and punishment rather than on being liked.
Why D: Influence from rewards is reward power, which is the opposite approach. Coercive power works through the threat of punishment and not through giving benefits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is reward power?
A: Influence from title or rank in the firm
B: Influence from expertise gained by knowledge
C: Influence from fear of being punished at work
D: Influence based on the ability to give rewards
Why A: Influence from title or rank is legitimate power. Reward power is based on the ability to give rewards, not on position alone.
Why B: Influence from expertise gained through knowledge is expert power. Reward power depends on controlling things people value, such as raises, bonuses and praise.
Why C: Influence from fear of being punished is coercive power, which is the opposite of reward power, since reward power uses benefits instead of threats.
Why D: Reward power is influence based on the ability to give rewards such as raises, bonuses, promotions or praise, so people comply to gain those benefits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best example of constructive feedback?
A: 'Your report was bad, and you should have done much better on it overall.'
B: 'Whatever, it's fine, I did not read it but I am sure that it will do.'
C: 'Your report was clear, but adding data in section two would make it stronger.'
D: 'You always mess up, and this latest report is the proof that you do not care.'
Why A: Calling a report bad and saying it should be better gives no specific detail about what to fix, so it is vague criticism, not constructive feedback.
Why B: Saying it is fine without reading the report gives no real feedback at all. It shows indifference and offers nothing the employee can use to improve.
Why C: This feedback is specific, balanced and actionable. It notes a strength, then suggests adding data in section two, so the employee knows exactly how to improve the report.
Why D: Saying someone always messes up and does not care is a personal attack with a sweeping judgment. It offers no specific improvement and will damage trust.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vision versus a mission?
A: A vision is where an organization wants to go while a mission is why it exists and what it does
B: A vision is a yearly budget plan while a mission is a list of the firm's products and prices
C: A vision is the firm's slogan used in ads while a mission is its legal name on filings
D: A vision is what the firm does today while a mission is where it wants to be in ten years
Why A: A vision describes where an organization wants to go in the future, while a mission states why it exists and what it does today, so this contrast is accurate.
Why B: A vision describes a desired future, not a budget, and a mission states purpose rather than listing products and prices.
Why C: A vision is the future the firm aims for and a mission is its purpose; neither is a slogan or a legal name.
Why D: This swaps the terms: a vision looks ahead to a desired future, and a mission describes current purpose and activity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How do leaders shape organizational culture?
A: Through the office layout and the dress code
B: Through the number of meetings they schedule
C: Through the values they model, reward and communicate
D: Through the products the firm decides to make
Why A: Layout and dress code are small signals; culture is shaped mainly by what leaders model, reward and communicate through their behavior.
Why B: Meeting counts do not set values; employees learn culture by watching what leaders do, reward and say.
Why C: Leaders shape culture through the values they model in their own behavior, the behaviors they reward, and what they communicate, because employees copy what leaders do.
Why D: Product choices reflect strategy; culture is set by the values leaders model, reward and communicate to employees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is change management?
A: Making coins at the mint for use as money in the economy of the nation overall
B: Avoiding all change, so that the firm keeps doing things the same way
C: Changing management staff only so that new leaders replace old ones
D: A structured approach to helping people and organizations adapt to change
Why A: Making coins at a mint is a government function related to currency, not business. Change management concerns helping people and organizations adjust to new ways of working.
Why B: Avoiding all change is the opposite of change management, which exists to plan and guide change so the organization can adapt, not to keep things the same.
Why C: Replacing managers is a staffing action, not change management. The field deals with how people and processes adapt to any change, not merely who holds the leadership posts.
Why D: Change management is a structured approach for helping people and organizations adapt to change, using planning, communication and support so new methods are adopted smoothly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a common cause of resistance to change?
A: Too much communication tires the staff
B: Fear of the unknown or loss of control
C: Clear benefits shown to the staff
D: Early involvement of all the staff
Why A: Too much communication is rarely a cause of resistance. Resistance usually grows when communication is lacking, and tiredness from updates is not the typical reason people resist.
Why B: Fear of the unknown or of losing control is a common cause of resistance, because people worry about job security, new skills and changed routines.
Why C: Clear benefits shown to staff reduce resistance rather than cause it, since people are more willing to accept a change when they see its value.
Why D: Early involvement reduces resistance by giving staff a voice and ownership, so it works against resistance and cannot be a common cause of it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action best reduces resistance to a major change?
A: Announcing it suddenly with no warning to the staff
B: Keeping it secret from employees until the last day
C: Forcing it without input from the staff affected
D: Explaining the reasons and involving employees early
Why A: Announcing a change suddenly gives people no time to adjust and increases fear and resistance, so surprise is likely to make the problem worse.
Why B: Keeping a change secret until the last day builds distrust and rumors, which raises resistance rather than reducing it.
Why C: Forcing a change without staff input leaves affected employees feeling powerless, which fuels resistance, so it does not help the change succeed.
Why D: Explaining the reasons and involving employees early builds understanding and ownership, which lowers fear and resistance, so it is the best action here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the steps in Kotter's change model beginning?
A: Celebrate wins
B: End the change
C: Create urgency
D: Anchor changes
Why A: Celebrating wins is a later step in Kotter's model, after short-term wins have been created. The model begins with building urgency instead.
Why B: Ending the change is not a step in Kotter's model, which finishes with embedding the change in culture rather than stopping it.
Why C: Kotter's eight-step model begins with creating a sense of urgency, so people see why change is needed now and become motivated to act.
Why D: Anchoring changes in the culture is the final step of Kotter's model, not the first. It comes only after the change has been built and shown to work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Tuckman's model of team development?
A: Forming, storming, norming, performing
B: Planning, buying, selling and billing
C: Hiring, firing, paying and training
D: Start, stop, wait, go, and repeat
Why A: Tuckman's model describes the stages a team moves through as it develops, namely forming, storming, norming and performing, so this is the correct list.
Why B: Planning, buying, selling and billing are business transactions, not stages of how a team develops, so they do not describe Tuckman's model.
Why C: Hiring, firing, paying and training are human resource activities, not the group development stages that Tuckman identified.
Why D: Start, stop, wait, go and repeat are not Tuckman's stages. His model names forming, storming, norming and performing as the sequence of team development.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: During the 'storming' stage of team development, teams typically experience:
A: Perfect harmony among members
B: Conflict as members assert views
C: Introductions only as members meet
D: Dissolution of the team soon
Why A: Perfect harmony is not typical of storming. Harmony appears later, in norming and performing, once members have worked through differences.
Why B: Storming is the stage where members assert their views and compete over roles and ideas, so conflict is typical at this stage of team development.
Why C: Introductions as members meet describe the forming stage, which comes before storming, when people are polite and still getting to know one another.
Why D: Dissolution comes at the adjourning stage, when the team ends. Storming happens early in development, when members are still working out how to cooperate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: During the 'norming' stage, teams typically:
A: Disband and go their separate ways soon
B: Meet for the first time and learn names
C: Establish shared norms and cooperate more
D: Argue constantly about the roles and goals
Why A: Disbanding is the adjourning stage, at the end of the team's life. Norming happens earlier, after storming, when the team is still working together.
Why B: Meeting for the first time and learning names is the forming stage, which comes before norming in the sequence of team development.
Why C: In norming, teams establish shared norms, resolve earlier conflicts, and begin to cooperate more, building trust and cohesion as members accept roles and ground rules.
Why D: Arguing constantly about roles and goals describes the storming stage, which precedes norming, where members start to settle those disagreements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: During the 'performing' stage, teams typically:
A: Work effectively toward goals with high trust
B: Meet for the first time and agree on the plan
C: Fight over roles and fight over goals again
D: End the project and disband the group for good
Why A: In the performing stage the team works effectively toward its goals with high trust, clear roles and strong cooperation, which is why productivity is highest at this stage.
Why B: Meeting for the first time and agreeing on a plan describes forming, the first stage, which comes well before a team reaches performing.
Why C: Fighting over roles and goals describes storming, an earlier stage, whereas performing teams have already settled such issues and work smoothly.
Why D: Ending the project and disbanding the group is the adjourning stage, which follows performing rather than describing it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A team skips raising concerns about a risky plan because everyone wants harmony. This is:
A: Healthy debate
B: Delegation
C: Benchmarking
D: Groupthink
Why A: Healthy debate involves openly raising concerns and disagreement, but this team stays silent to keep harmony, so it is the opposite of healthy debate.
Why B: Delegation means assigning tasks to others. The team here suppresses concerns about a risky plan, which has nothing to do with handing off work.
Why C: Benchmarking is comparing performance with best practices. Staying quiet about a risky plan to keep harmony is a group decision flaw, not a comparison method.
Why D: Groupthink is when a group values harmony over critical thinking, so members hide concerns and a risky plan goes ahead without proper challenge.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How can leaders prevent groupthink?
A: Punish disagreement so members learn to obey
B: Encourage dissent and invite outside views
C: Limit discussion to the leader's own ideas
D: Seek only agreement and avoid outside views
Why A: Punishing disagreement teaches members to stay quiet and obey, which is exactly what causes groupthink, so it makes the problem worse.
Why B: Encouraging dissent and inviting outside views brings in critical thinking and fresh information, which breaks the pressure for false harmony and prevents groupthink.
Why C: Limiting discussion to the leader's own ideas shuts out other perspectives and strengthens conformity, which increases the risk of groupthink instead of preventing it.
Why D: Seeking only agreement and avoiding outside views is how groupthink develops, because the group never tests its plan against different opinions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is diversity in the workplace?
A: Everyone being alike in background, age and views at the firm
B: Differences among people in background, experience and perspective
C: Hiring people with the same training and similar views
D: Having staff spread across several office locations
Why A: Everyone being alike in background, age and views is uniformity, the opposite of diversity, which means including real differences among people.
Why B: Diversity in the workplace means differences among people in background, experience and perspective, such as age, gender, culture and skills, which can improve ideas.
Why C: Hiring people with the same training and views creates sameness; diversity means including a range of backgrounds, experience and perspectives.
Why D: Locations describe where people work, not how they differ; diversity concerns differences in background, experience and perspective.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inclusion?
A: Hiring one person from a minority group to fill a single open post only as a rule
B: Counting employees by background and recording the numbers in a report
C: Excluding some people from the group so that others feel more at ease
D: Creating an environment where all people feel valued and able to participate
Why A: Hiring one person from a minority group for one post is tokenism. It does not create an environment where all people feel valued and able to participate.
Why B: Counting employees by background and reporting the numbers measures diversity but does not mean people feel valued, so it is a count, not inclusion.
Why C: Excluding some people is the opposite of inclusion. Inclusion means involving everyone, so leaving people out to make others comfortable defeats the purpose.
Why D: Inclusion means creating an environment where all people feel valued, respected and able to participate fully, whatever their background, so their contributions are used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is corporate social responsibility (CSR)?
A: A company's plan to raise profit by cutting costs and prices
B: Avoiding laws and rules that limit what a company may do in the market
C: A company's commitment to operate ethically and contribute to society
D: A company's practice of donating a share of profits to its owners
Why A: Cutting costs to raise profit is a financial strategy, whereas CSR means acting ethically and contributing to society beyond profit.
Why B: Avoiding laws and rules is unethical and often illegal, whereas CSR is a commitment to responsible behavior beyond simply following regulations.
Why C: CSR is a company's commitment to operate ethically and contribute to society, including care for employees, communities and the environment, beyond making a profit.
Why D: Paying profits to owners is a dividend, not CSR, which is about ethical operation and benefit to society.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a code of conduct?
A: Written guidelines on expected behavior within an organization
B: A secret code used by staff to send private messages inside the firm
C: A pay plan that sets the wages and bonuses for each level in the firm
D: A product list that shows the goods that the company makes and sells
Why A: A code of conduct is a set of written guidelines on expected behavior within an organization, so employees know the standards for ethical and professional conduct.
Why B: A code of conduct is not a secret code for private messages. It is a public document that states expected behavior, not a way of hiding communication.
Why C: A pay plan sets wages and bonuses and is a compensation document. A code of conduct sets behavior standards, so the two are unrelated.
Why D: A product list shows what the company makes and sells. A code of conduct covers how employees should behave, not what is sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a whistleblower?
A: A person who reports wrongdoing within an organization
B: A sports referee only, who calls fouls in a match
C: A manager who sets goals and assigns the work to staff
D: A rule breaker who is caught breaking the rules of the firm
Why A: A whistleblower is a person who reports wrongdoing, such as fraud or safety violations, within or outside an organization, often to authorities or higher management.
Why B: A sports referee calls fouls in a match, which is a different role. A whistleblower reports misconduct inside an organization, and is not limited to sports.
Why C: A manager who sets goals and assigns work is doing normal supervision, not whistleblowing, which means exposing wrongdoing instead of directing the work of staff.
Why D: A whistleblower is the person who reports a rule breaker, not the rule breaker. The role is to expose misconduct, not to commit it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ethical dilemma?
A: A scheduling issue in which two meetings are set for the same hour and room
B: A clear rule to follow that tells staff exactly what to do in each case
C: A budget error in which the totals for costs do not add up correctly
D: A situation where choosing among options involves conflicting moral values
Why A: Two meetings booked at the same time is a scheduling conflict that can be solved with logistics. It does not involve conflicting moral values, so it is not an ethical dilemma.
Why B: A clear rule telling staff exactly what to do removes the difficulty, whereas a dilemma arises when the right course is unclear and values conflict.
Why C: A budget error where totals do not add up is an accounting mistake, which can be corrected, and it does not involve a moral choice.
Why D: An ethical dilemma is a situation where choosing among options involves conflicting moral values, so every choice has some ethical cost and no option is fully right.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager learns a supplier overcharged the company but the supplier is the boss's friend. What is the best ethical step?
A: Retaliate against the supplier
B: Report it through proper channels
C: Ignore it and say nothing to anyone
D: Hide the invoice to keep the supplier
Why A: Retaliating against the supplier is a hostile act that does not fix the overcharge and may be unethical or illegal, so it is not the best step.
Why B: Reporting the overcharge through proper channels is honest, protects the company's money, and does not depend on the friendship, so it is the best ethical step.
Why C: Ignoring the overcharge lets the company lose money and puts personal loyalty above duty, which is an ethical failure by omission.
Why D: Hiding the invoice to protect the supplier is concealment that could count as fraud, and it harms the company, so it is clearly unethical.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is selection?
A: Attracting applicants through ads and job fairs
B: Terminating employees who break the rules of the firm
C: Choosing the best candidate from the applicant pool
D: Training new staff in the skills needed for the job
Why A: Attracting applicants through ads and job fairs is recruitment, which comes before selection. Selection starts once there is a pool of applicants to choose from.
Why B: Terminating employees who break rules is discipline or dismissal, which happens after hiring, so it is not selection.
Why C: Selection is the process of choosing the best candidate from the applicant pool, using tools such as interviews, tests and reference checks to decide who gets the job.
Why D: Training new staff in the skills for the job is orientation and development, which comes after selection, once the person has been chosen.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an advantage of internal recruitment?
A: It brings brand new ideas from fresh eyes
B: It is always slower and costs much more money
C: It rewards employees and saves training time
D: It costs more and takes longer than other options
Why A: Bringing in brand new ideas from fresh eyes is a benefit of external recruitment, since internal candidates already know the organization and its current thinking.
Why B: Internal recruitment is not always slower or costlier. It usually saves time and money, so the claim that it is slower and more expensive is wrong.
Why C: Internal recruitment rewards employees with promotion opportunities, which boosts morale, and it saves training time because the person already knows the firm.
Why D: Internal recruitment usually costs less and is faster than hiring outsiders, since it avoids ads and long orientation, so costing more and taking longer is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an advantage of external recruitment?
A: It rewards current staff with promotions
B: It requires no screening of any applicant overall
C: It always costs less than internal hiring
D: It brings fresh ideas and skills from outside
Why A: Rewarding current staff with promotions is an advantage of internal recruitment, not external recruitment, which looks outside the organization for candidates.
Why B: External recruitment still needs screening of applicants, since candidates are unknown, so saying no screening is required is wrong.
Why C: External hiring often costs more because of ads and recruiters, so it does not always cost less than internal hiring.
Why D: External recruitment brings in new ideas, skills and experience from outside the organization, which can improve the firm and widen the pool of candidates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a behavioral interview question?
A: A question asking candidates to describe past actions in real situations
B: A yes/no question that can be answered with one single word only
C: A hypothetical riddle that tests how well the candidate solves puzzles
D: A salary question about the pay that the candidate wants in the new job overall
Why A: A behavioral interview question asks candidates to describe past actions in real situations, because past behavior is a good predictor of how someone will act in future.
Why B: A yes or no question gives little information about behavior. Behavioral questions ask for detailed stories, so a one-word answer does not fit them.
Why C: A hypothetical riddle tests puzzle-solving rather than past behavior, and behavioral questions ask about real events the candidate has already experienced.
Why D: A salary question concerns the pay a candidate wants, which is about compensation, not about describing past actions, so it is not behavioral.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a behavioral interview question?
A: 'What would you do if...?' which asks about an imaginary case
B: 'Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict with a coworker.'
C: 'Are you a team player, and do you like working with others?'
D: 'Where do you live, and how far is your home from our office?'
Why A: "What would you do if...?" is a hypothetical or situational question about an imaginary case. A behavioral question asks about something that really happened.
Why B: "Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict" asks for a real past example, which is how behavioral questions are phrased and why they predict future behavior.
Why C: Asking if someone is a team player invites a simple yes or no. A behavioral question would ask for a specific example of teamwork in the past.
Why D: Where someone lives and how far the office is concerns logistics, not past behavior, so it is not behavioral and could raise fairness issues.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which interview question is generally illegal to ask?
A: 'Are you planning to have children?'
B: 'Why do you want to join our firm?'
C: 'What are your strengths and skills?'
D: 'Can you work some evenings a week?'
Why A: Asking about plans to have children is generally illegal because it can lead to discrimination based on sex, family status or pregnancy, and it is unrelated to job ability.
Why B: Asking why someone wants to join the firm is a normal, lawful question about motivation and interest in the role, so it is allowed.
Why C: Asking about strengths and skills is a standard job-related question that helps judge fit, so it is legal and appropriate.
Why D: Asking about availability for evenings is a lawful job-related question, as long as it is asked of all candidates and relates to the real schedule.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a background check?
A: A skill test that checks how well a candidate can do the tasks of a job
B: Verification of a candidate's history such as employment and criminal record
C: A review of a building to check its safety and its fire exits before staff move in
D: A pay review in which the manager looks at salaries to see whether raises are due
Why A: A skill test checks how well a candidate can do job tasks, while a background check verifies a candidate's history, so these two are different.
Why B: A background check verifies a candidate's history, such as past employment, education and criminal record, to confirm the information given and reduce hiring risk.
Why C: Reviewing a building for safety and fire exits is a facility inspection, not a check on a candidate, so it is unrelated to a background check.
Why D: A pay review looks at salaries to decide on raises, which concerns current employees, not the verification of a new candidate's history.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an applicant tracking system (ATS)?
A: A payroll system that pays the staff and records hours worked
B: A time clock that staff use to punch in and out of a shift
C: Software that manages job applications and screens resumes
D: A chat tool that lets employees send quick messages to each other
Why A: A payroll system pays staff and records hours, which is a different HR function. An ATS handles job applications during hiring, not salaries.
Why B: A time clock lets staff punch in and out of a shift, which tracks attendance. An ATS tracks applicants during recruitment instead.
Why C: An applicant tracking system is software that manages job applications and screens resumes, helping recruiters store, sort and follow candidates through the hiring process.
Why D: A chat tool for quick messages is a communication app. An ATS is hiring software that tracks applicants, so messaging is not its purpose.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a fringe benefit?
A: A salary raise only, given to staff each year for good work
B: A fine charged to staff who break the rules of the company
C: A penalty given to staff who arrive late for work too often
D: A non-wage reward such as health insurance or paid time off
Why A: A salary raise only is a wage increase, which is direct pay. A fringe benefit is a non-wage reward, so it differs from salary.
Why B: A fine charged for breaking rules is a penalty, which is the opposite of a reward, so it cannot be a fringe benefit.
Why C: A penalty for lateness is a disciplinary action. Fringe benefits are extras that employees gain, not punishments given for poor conduct.
Why D: A fringe benefit is a non-wage reward, such as health insurance, retirement contributions or paid time off, that adds to total compensation beyond regular pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A sales rep earns 5% commission on $80,000 in sales. What is her commission?
Why A: Commission is 5% times $80,000, which is 0.05 x 80,000 = $4,000, so this is the correct amount for her commission.
Why B: $400 is only 0.5% of $80,000, which is a decimal slip. Five percent is 0.05, and 0.05 x 80,000 gives $4,000, not $400.
Why C: $16,000 would be 20% of $80,000, which is 0.20 x 80,000. The rate here is 5%, so 0.05 x 80,000 is $4,000, not $16,000.
Why D: $80,005 simply adds 5 to the sales figure, which misreads a percentage as a flat amount. Five percent of $80,000 is $4,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a performance review?
A: A budget review of what the firm spent last year
B: A sales report of what the firm sold over the past year
C: A review of a product by a customer who has bought it
D: A periodic evaluation of an employee's performance
Why A: A budget review looks at the firm's spending, which is a finance matter. A performance review evaluates an individual employee's work.
Why B: A sales report records what the firm sold, which is a business result. A performance review evaluates the work of an employee, so this is different.
Why C: A customer's review of a product is feedback on goods. A performance review is conducted by an employer to assess an employee, not a product.
Why D: A performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee's performance, usually done yearly, that gives feedback, sets goals and informs pay and promotion decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the halo effect in performance reviews?
A: Using data only to rate each worker, with no personal input
B: Letting one positive trait influence overall evaluation
C: Rating everyone low because of one bad trait or event
D: Rating accurately across all traits for the whole period
Why A: Using data only to rate workers is an objective method, not the halo effect, which is a bias caused by letting one impression color the rest.
Why B: The halo effect is letting one positive trait influence the overall evaluation, so a person who excels at one thing is rated high in everything else.
Why C: Rating everyone low because of one bad trait is the opposite bias, called the horn effect, since the halo effect works through a positive trait.
Why D: Rating accurately across all traits for the whole period is good practice, not a bias, so it is the absence of the halo effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the recency effect in performance reviews?
A: Ignoring all events that happened in the whole review period
B: Rating by tenure, so that longer-serving staff always get the top score
C: Overweighting recent events rather than the whole review period
D: Considering the whole year with each month weighted equally
Why A: Ignoring all events from the review period would ignore evidence entirely, whereas the recency effect focuses too much on the latest events.
Why B: Rating by tenure, where longer service gives the top score, is seniority bias, not recency bias, which is about the timing of events.
Why C: The recency effect is overweighting recent events instead of the whole review period, so the last few weeks wrongly count more than the full year.
Why D: Considering the whole year with each month weighted equally is the fair method that avoids recency bias, so it is the cure, not the effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is job enlargement?
A: Reducing tasks to give workers less to do each day
B: Adding more tasks of a similar level to a job
C: Adding higher authority such as power to hire
D: Cutting hours to save pay costs for the firm
Why A: Reducing tasks to give workers less to do is job reduction or simplification, not enlargement, which increases the number of tasks in a job.
Why B: Job enlargement adds more tasks of a similar skill level to a job, which widens it horizontally and reduces monotony without raising authority.
Why C: Adding higher authority such as the power to hire is job enrichment, which deepens the job vertically, so it differs from enlargement.
Why D: Cutting hours to save pay costs is a cost measure, not a redesign of job tasks, so it has nothing to do with enlargement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is job sharing?
A: One person holding two jobs with two different employers
B: Sharing salary with a boss who pays a cut to staff
C: Sharing office space among workers who have no desk
D: Two part-time employees splitting one full-time position
Why A: One person holding two jobs with different employers is dual employment, whereas job sharing splits one position between two people at one employer.
Why B: Sharing salary with a boss is not job sharing, which divides duties and pay of a single full-time position between two part-time employees.
Why C: Sharing office space among workers is desk sharing or hot desking, which concerns space, not splitting a single job between people.
Why D: Job sharing is when two part-time employees split one full-time position, dividing the duties, hours and pay between them, which gives staff flexibility.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is telecommuting?
A: Working from a remote location using technology
B: Working in a phone booth on a landline phone
C: Selling phones and phone plans to customers
D: Commuting by train to the main office each day
Why A: Telecommuting is working from a remote location, such as home, using technology like the internet and phones to stay connected with the workplace.
Why B: Working in a phone booth on a landline is not telecommuting, which relies on modern technology to do office work from a remote place.
Why C: Selling phones and plans is a retail job, not telecommuting. The word means working remotely using technology, whatever the occupation.
Why D: Commuting by train means traveling to the office, which is the opposite of telecommuting, where the worker avoids the daily trip by working remotely.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a collective bargaining agreement?
A: A sales contract in which a buyer agrees to purchase goods in bulk from a seller
B: A lease in which a company rents office space from a building owner for a fixed term
C: A contract negotiated between employers and a union covering pay and conditions
D: A personal loan that an employee takes from the company credit union to buy a car
Why A: A bulk purchase contract is a sales agreement between buyer and seller. A collective bargaining agreement is negotiated between employers and a union on work terms.
Why B: A lease for office space is a property contract between a company and a landlord, not an agreement about pay and conditions for union members.
Why C: A collective bargaining agreement is a contract negotiated between an employer and a union covering pay, hours and working conditions for the represented employees.
Why D: A personal loan from a credit union is a financial contract for one employee. A collective bargaining agreement covers groups of workers through their union.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a labor union?
A: A government agency that makes laws about the pay and hours of all workers
B: A customer club that gives discounts and rewards to loyal shoppers of a firm
C: A company owner group that meets to vote on the strategy of the business each year
D: An organization of workers that bargains with employers for better conditions
Why A: A government agency that makes labor laws is a regulator. A labor union is an organization of workers, not a government body.
Why B: A customer club gives discounts to loyal shoppers, which is a marketing program. A labor union represents workers, not customers.
Why C: A group of owners voting on strategy is a board or shareholder body. A union is made up of workers, not owners.
Why D: A labor union is an organization of workers that bargains with employers for better pay, hours and working conditions, giving employees a collective voice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a grievance procedure?
A: A pay system that sets the wages and bonuses for all the workers
B: A formal process for employees to raise and resolve complaints
C: A way to fire workers who break the rules, in a series of steps
D: A hiring process in which candidates apply and then interview
Why A: A pay system that sets wages and bonuses is a compensation structure. A grievance procedure handles complaints, so it has no role in setting pay.
Why B: A grievance procedure is a formal process for employees to raise and resolve complaints about treatment or conditions, ensuring issues are heard and addressed fairly.
Why C: A series of steps to fire workers who break rules is a disciplinary process. A grievance procedure instead lets employees raise their own complaints.
Why D: A hiring process in which candidates apply and interview is recruitment and selection, which has nothing to do with handling employee complaints.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is downsizing?
A: Hiring more staff to raise output
B: Opening new branches in the market
C: Reducing the workforce to cut costs
D: Raising salaries for all workers
Why A: Hiring more staff to raise output is expansion, which is the opposite of downsizing, as downsizing reduces the number of employees.
Why B: Opening new branches is growth in locations and often adds staff, which is the opposite of downsizing, which shrinks the organization.
Why C: Downsizing is reducing the workforce to cut costs, often through layoffs or early retirements, in order to make the organization leaner or more profitable.
Why D: Raising salaries for all workers increases costs, whereas downsizing aims to cut costs by reducing the number of employees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is outsourcing?
A: Contracting work to an outside company
B: Hiring interns for the summer months
C: Moving offices to a new building or city
D: Doing all work in-house, no outside help
Why A: Outsourcing means contracting work to an outside company instead of doing it in-house, often to cut costs or use specialist skills.
Why B: Hiring summer interns adds temporary staff to the firm's own payroll, so it is not outsourcing, which uses an outside company to do work.
Why C: Moving offices changes location, not who does the work. Outsourcing means giving tasks to an outside company, not moving to a new place.
Why D: Doing all work in-house with no outside help is the opposite of outsourcing, which relies on external firms for some tasks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an employee assistance program (EAP)?
A: A sales program that trains staff to close deals with customers
B: A training schedule that lists the dates of courses for new staff as a rule
C: A pay plan that sets how much money each employee earns each year
D: A confidential service offering counseling and support to employees
Why A: A sales program that trains staff to close deals is sales training. An EAP offers confidential support for personal and work problems.
Why B: A training schedule lists course dates for staff. An EAP is a support service that gives counseling, so a schedule does not match.
Why C: A pay plan sets how much each employee earns. An EAP is a confidential support service, not a compensation structure.
Why D: An employee assistance program is a confidential service offering counseling and support to employees for personal or work-related issues such as stress, family, health or substance problems.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a probationary period?
A: To delay pay for new hires until they have worked for a full year
B: To end the job of a new hire after the first week without any notice
C: To evaluate a new hire's fit and performance before permanent status
D: To punish new hires who make a mistake by cutting their pay at once
Why A: A probationary period does not delay pay for a year. New hires are paid from the start, while the period usually lasts only a few months.
Why B: Ending a new hire's job after the first week without notice is not the purpose. The period is for fair evaluation, not instant dismissal.
Why C: A probationary period lets the employer evaluate a new hire's fit and performance before granting permanent status, and lets the employee judge the job too.
Why D: The period is not meant to punish mistakes by cutting pay. It exists to assess fit and performance, with support, not to reduce wages.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is employee engagement?
A: The level of commitment and enthusiasm employees have for their work and organization
B: A work schedule that lists each employee's start and end times for every day of the week
C: A promise that is made before a wedding or other formal celebration between two people
D: A pay level that rises each year an employee has worked at a firm, set by the employer
Why A: Employee engagement is the level of commitment and enthusiasm that employees have for their work and organization, which drives productivity, retention and quality.
Why B: A work schedule lists start and end times and is a scheduling tool. Engagement refers to commitment and enthusiasm, not hours of work.
Why C: A promise before a wedding is the social meaning of the word engagement. In business, employee engagement means commitment to work, not a marriage promise.
Why D: A pay level that rises with years of service is a seniority-based pay scale, whereas engagement is about commitment and enthusiasm, not wages.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the first step in the problem-solving process?
A: Evaluate all of the results
B: Identify and define the problem
C: Implement a solution at once
D: Choose a solution right away
Why A: Evaluating results comes last in problem solving, after a solution has been carried out, so it cannot be the first step.
Why B: The first step is to identify and define the problem, because a solution cannot be chosen until the real problem is clearly understood.
Why C: Implementing a solution at once skips defining the problem and weighing options, which risks wasting effort on the wrong issue, so it is not first.
Why D: Choosing a solution right away skips defining the problem and gathering information, so the choice may be poor. This step comes after analysis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which step in problem solving comes right after defining the problem?
A: Implement the chosen solution now
B: Gather information and identify causes
C: Evaluate results before gathering facts
D: Celebrate the success with the whole team
Why A: Implementing the solution comes later, after the causes are known and options are weighed. Doing it right after defining the problem skips analysis.
Why B: After defining the problem, you gather information and identify causes, so that the later solution addresses the real source of the problem.
Why C: Evaluating results before gathering facts is out of order, because results appear only after a solution is implemented, not directly after problem definition.
Why D: Celebrating success is a final step, if at all, and cannot come right after defining a problem that has not been solved yet.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram used for?
A: Scheduling shifts for workers on the shop floor each week
B: Budgeting for the costs of a project over the next year
C: Tracking sales of each product in each store by month
D: Identifying possible causes of a problem by category
Why A: Scheduling shifts is done with rosters or scheduling software. A fishbone diagram is a cause analysis tool, so it does not plan work hours.
Why B: Budgeting for a project's costs uses financial planning tools, not a fishbone diagram, which maps out possible causes of a problem.
Why C: Tracking sales by product and store uses reports or charts of sales data. A fishbone diagram looks at causes, not sales figures.
Why D: A fishbone or Ishikawa diagram identifies possible causes of a problem by category, such as people, methods, machines and materials, helping teams find root causes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Pareto chart based on?
A: The 80/20 principle that a few causes produce most effects
B: The idea that most effects come from many small causes
C: The rule that the middle values in data are most common
D: The idea that effects arrive in a repeating pattern each year
Why A: A Pareto chart is based on the 80/20 principle, which says that a few causes produce most of the effects, so effort goes to the vital few.
Why B: A Pareto chart shows the opposite: a few causes account for most effects, so effort should target those vital few.
Why C: That describes a bell-shaped normal distribution; a Pareto chart ranks causes to show that a few matter most.
Why D: Seasonal patterns are a different analysis; a Pareto chart ranks causes by size to show which few produce most effects.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager finds 80% of customer complaints come from 20% of product types. Which tool/principle does this reflect?
A: Benchmarking rivals
B: Groupthink in a team
C: The Pareto principle
D: Delegation of tasks
Why A: Benchmarking compares your practices with rivals or leaders. It does not explain why 20% of products cause 80% of complaints.
Why B: Groupthink is a team decision flaw caused by pressure to agree. It has nothing to do with the distribution of complaints among products.
Why C: The Pareto principle states that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes, which matches 80% of complaints coming from 20% of product types.
Why D: Delegation means handing tasks to others. It is not a principle for analyzing how complaints are concentrated in a small share of products.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is opportunity cost?
A: The price paid for goods and services in the open market
B: The value of the best alternative given up when making a choice
C: The interest cost on a loan over the length of the loan term in general
D: A tax paid on the sale of a good or service to a buyer today
Why A: The price paid for goods is simply the money cost, not the opportunity cost, which measures the value of what you give up by choosing.
Why B: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up when making a choice, so it measures what you lose by choosing one option over another.
Why C: Interest on a loan is a financing cost, not opportunity cost, which is about alternatives forgone, not about the charge for borrowing money.
Why D: A tax on the sale of a good is a government charge, not opportunity cost, which concerns the next best use of resources that you give up.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bias in thinking?
A: A neutral view of all sides and the facts
B: A formula used to compute costs and sales
C: A fact that anyone can verify by checking
D: A systematic tendency that skews judgment
Why A: A neutral view of all sides and facts is objectivity, which is the opposite of bias, since bias distorts how we see information.
Why B: A formula used to compute costs and sales is a calculation tool. A bias in thinking is a mental tendency, not a formula.
Why C: A fact that anyone can verify is objective information, whereas a bias is a leaning that distorts judgment and is not verifiable fact.
Why D: A bias in thinking is a systematic tendency that skews judgment, causing people to favor certain ideas or conclusions without good reason.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager only reads reports that support her preferred plan. This is:
A: Objective thinking
B: Critical thinking
C: Confirmation bias
D: Delegation of work
Why A: Objective thinking weighs all evidence fairly. A manager reading only reports that support her plan is selective, so this is not objective.
Why B: Critical thinking examines evidence from all sides. Reading only supportive reports avoids challenge, so it is the opposite of critical thinking.
Why C: Confirmation bias is seeking only information that supports what you already believe, which matches the manager reading only reports backing her preferred plan.
Why D: Delegation means assigning work to others. The manager's selective reading of reports is a thinking bias, not a way of sharing tasks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is anchoring bias?
A: Relying too heavily on the first piece of information encountered
B: Using many sources to check the facts from different views
C: Sailing a boat on open water, where the anchor holds it in place overall
D: Ignoring all numbers and data that are given at the start
Why A: Anchoring bias is relying too heavily on the first piece of information encountered, such as an initial price, when making later judgments and decisions.
Why B: Using many sources to check facts from different views is good practice that reduces bias, so it is the opposite of anchoring.
Why C: Sailing and anchoring a boat is the physical meaning of the word. Anchoring bias is a mental habit of fixating on first information.
Why D: Ignoring numbers and data given at the start is the reverse of anchoring bias, in which the first information has too much influence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
A: Continuing a course because of past investment rather than future value
B: Budgeting carefully so that future costs are the only ones considered
C: Cutting losses early once it is clear the project will not succeed
D: Ignoring all costs, whether they were paid in the past or are still to come
Why A: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing a course because of past investment instead of future value, ignoring that money already spent cannot be recovered.
Why B: Budgeting so that only future costs count is the correct way to avoid the fallacy, so it describes sound reasoning, not the fallacy.
Why C: Cutting losses early once a project is clearly failing is rational and is the opposite of the sunk cost fallacy.
Why D: Ignoring all costs, past or future, would be careless. The fallacy is specifically letting past costs drive decisions, not ignoring every cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company keeps funding a failing project because it already spent $2 million. This is:
A: Opportunity cost thinking
B: The sunk cost fallacy
C: Benchmarking firms
D: Sound investing rules
Why A: Opportunity cost thinking compares the value of the best alternative forgone. Funding a failing project because of past spending is not that kind of reasoning.
Why B: Continuing to fund a failing project because $2 million was already spent is the sunk cost fallacy, since that money is gone whatever happens next.
Why C: Benchmarking compares performance against other firms. It does not explain why a company keeps funding a failing project because of money already spent.
Why D: Sound investing looks at future returns, not past spending. Throwing more money at a failing project because of $2 million spent is poor reasoning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ad hominem attack?
A: Addressing the argument with facts and reasons
B: Asking a question about the facts of the argument
C: Citing evidence to support the points in the argument
D: Attacking the person rather than their argument
Why A: Addressing the argument with facts and reasons is a valid response, whereas an ad hominem attack targets the person instead of the argument.
Why B: Asking a question about the facts is a legitimate way to test an argument, not an attack on the person who made it.
Why C: Citing evidence to support the points in an argument is proper reasoning, so it is not an ad hominem attack.
Why D: An ad hominem attack targets the person making the argument rather than the argument itself, which is a fallacy because it avoids the real issue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a false dilemma?
A: Listing facts to support the whole argument
B: Asking for ideas from the whole team first
C: Presenting only two options when more exist
D: Offering many options so the person can choose
Why A: Listing facts to support an argument is sound reasoning and not a false dilemma, which wrongly limits the choices available.
Why B: Asking the team for ideas first is a way to widen options, so it is the opposite of a false dilemma.
Why C: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist, wrongly forcing a choice and hiding other possible solutions or middle ground.
Why D: Offering many options lets the person choose freely, so it is the reverse of a false dilemma, which limits choices artificially.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a slippery slope fallacy?
A: A budget rule that limits how much each department may spend in a year in practice
B: A proven chain of events in which each step is shown to cause the next
C: A skiing term for a steep hill that skiers go down quickly in winter
D: Claiming one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without proof
Why A: A budget rule that limits department spending is a financial control. The slippery slope fallacy is a flaw in reasoning, not a spending policy.
Why B: A proven chain of events in which each step causes the next is valid reasoning. A slippery slope is the claim made without proof.
Why C: A steep ski hill is the literal meaning of the words. The slippery slope fallacy is an argument error, not a feature of winter sports.
Why D: The slippery slope fallacy claims that one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without proof, assuming a chain of events that has not been shown.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between fact and opinion?
A: They are identical, as both can be proven true by evidence
B: A fact is a feeling that a person has about a topic or event
C: A fact can be verified while an opinion is a personal view
D: An opinion can be proved, while a fact is only a view
Why A: Facts and opinions are not identical. A fact can be proven with evidence, while an opinion is a personal belief that cannot be proven in that way.
Why B: A fact is not a feeling. Feelings are subjective, whereas a fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true.
Why C: A fact can be verified with evidence, while an opinion is a personal view or judgment that may differ between people, which is the key difference.
Why D: This reverses the terms. Facts, not opinions, can be proved, and opinions are views, so the statement mixes up the two ideas.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a fact?
A: The company's revenue grew 8% last year according to its report
B: Our brand is the most trusted name among shoppers
C: That design is ugly and poorly made in the view of many people
D: The office is a great place to spend a workday
Why A: Revenue grew 8% last year according to its report is a specific claim that can be checked against the report, so it is a verifiable fact.
Why B: Trusted is a judgment that cannot be checked without a stated measure, so this is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact.
Why C: Calling a design ugly and poorly made is a matter of taste and judgment, not a measurable claim, so it is an opinion.
Why D: Great is a matter of personal view and cannot be verified, so it is an opinion, unlike a figure that can be checked in a report.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How can you evaluate the credibility of a source?
A: Choose the first result shown by the search engine on the page
B: Check the author's expertise, evidence and potential bias
C: Trust anything online since all posts on the web are checked
D: Prefer the loudest voice, as the most confident speaker wins
Why A: The first search result is not always the most credible, since ranking reflects popularity or advertising and not accuracy, so choosing it blindly is unreliable.
Why B: Checking the author's expertise, evidence and potential bias is the standard way to judge credibility, since it tests who wrote it and why.
Why C: Not everything online is checked. Many posts have no review process, so trusting anything on the web leads to misinformation.
Why D: Confidence or loudness is not evidence. A confident speaker may still be wrong, so preferring the loudest voice does not test credibility.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a primary source?
A: A summary of other works by a historian
B: An original firsthand account or data
C: A textbook that reviews other works
D: A commentary on other written works
Why A: A summary of other works by a historian is a secondary source, since it interprets earlier material rather than being firsthand.
