Why B: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and with 5 values the middle one is the third, which is 5, so the median is 5.
Why C: The value 5.6 is the mean, since 3 + 9 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 28 and 28 / 5 = 5.6, but the question asks for the median, which is 5.
Why D: Sorted, the numbers are 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and 7 is the fourth value, one place past the middle; the median is the third value, 5.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the range of a data set?
A: The sum of all values in the data set
B: The most common value in the data set
C: The largest value minus the smallest value
D: The middle value of the whole data set overall
Why A: The sum of all values is found by adding them and gives a total, not a measure of spread; the range is the largest value minus the smallest.
Why B: The most common value is the mode, which measures frequency; the range instead measures spread by subtracting the smallest value from the largest value.
Why C: The range is the largest value minus the smallest value, which shows the total spread from the lowest point to the highest point in the data.
Why D: The middle value of the data is the median, which measures center; the range measures spread by finding the gap between the extremes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A set of exam scores is 62, 70, 75, 88 and 95. What is the range?
Why A: The value 75 is the median (the middle of the five sorted scores), not the range; the range is 95 - 62 = 33.
Why B: The value 78 is not the difference between any extremes; the range is the highest score minus the lowest, so 95 - 62 = 33, not 78.
Why C: The value 157 comes from adding the largest and smallest, 95 + 62, but the range subtracts them, so 95 - 62 = 33.
Why D: The range is the largest score minus the smallest score, so 95 - 62 = 33, which shows how far apart the highest and lowest results are.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does standard deviation measure?
A: How spread out values are around the mean
B: The most common value in the data set
C: How many values are in a set of numbers
D: The middle of the data when it is sorted
Why A: Standard deviation measures how far the values typically sit from the mean, so a small value means tightly clustered data and a large one means widely spread data.
Why B: The most common value is the mode, which is a measure of frequency; standard deviation instead describes how spread out the values are around the mean.
Why C: The number of values in a set is the sample size or count, which has no part in standard deviation, as that measures spread around the mean.
Why D: The middle of sorted data is the median, a measure of center; standard deviation measures spread, which is a different property of the data set.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two classes have the same mean score. Class A has a small standard deviation and Class B a large one. What does this tell you?
A: Class A scored higher on average
B: Class B's scores are more spread out
C: Class A's scores are more spread out
D: Both classes have identical scores
Why A: The question says both classes share the same mean, so neither scored higher on average; the standard deviation tells you about spread and not about the average.
Why B: A large standard deviation means the scores lie far from the mean on average, so Class B, with the larger value, has the more spread out scores.
Why C: Class A has the small standard deviation, so its scores are clustered close to the mean and are less spread out, not more, than Class B's.
Why D: Different standard deviations show that the score distributions differ, so the classes cannot have identical scores even though they share the same mean.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a population in statistics?
A: The number of people in a city only each year
B: The result of a survey taken in a town
C: A small group chosen for the study sample
D: The entire group you want to learn about
Why A: A population is not limited to counting people in a city; it is the whole group of interest, and a count of residents is just one possible example.
Why B: The result of a survey is data, not a population; a population is the entire group you want to learn about, and a survey only draws from it.
Why C: A small group chosen for a study is a sample, not a population; the population is the whole group from which the sample comes.
Why D: In statistics a population is the entire group you want to learn about, such as all students in a country, whether or not everyone is measured.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sample in statistics?
A: A part of a population used to learn about the whole
B: A single value in a data set that is far from others
C: The entire group being studied and asked each question
D: A chart of the findings of a survey in a school
Why A: A sample is a subset taken from the population and used to draw conclusions about the whole, since measuring every member is often too costly or slow.
Why B: A single value far from the others is an outlier, not a sample; a sample is a group of observations drawn from the population.
Why C: The entire group being studied is the population, not the sample; a sample is only the part of that group that actually gets measured or asked.
Why D: A chart of survey findings is a way of displaying results, not a sample; the sample is the set of people or items actually chosen and measured.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is random sampling used?
A: It removes the need for any data to be collected
B: It lets the researcher pick favorites from the group
C: It gives every member a fair chance of being chosen
D: It guarantees the sample is the biggest possible
Why A: Random sampling still requires data to be collected from the chosen members; it is a method for selecting who is measured and does not remove data collection.
Why B: Letting the researcher pick favorites introduces bias, which is exactly what random sampling avoids by making the choice depend on chance and not on preference.
Why C: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which keeps the sample fair and makes it more representative of the whole group.
Why D: Random sampling does not guarantee the biggest possible sample; sample size is chosen separately, while randomness only decides who is picked, so this reason is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A survey about school lunches only asks students eating in the cafeteria. What is the main problem?
A: The data is too clean to be useful for the survey
B: The mean was calculated wrongly, using too few numbers
C: Too many questions asked of each student in class
D: Sampling bias, because other students are left out
Why A: Data being clean is a good thing and is not the problem here; the real flaw is that only cafeteria students are asked, which leaves other students out.
Why B: No mean has been calculated wrongly in this scenario; the flaw lies in who was asked, since students outside the cafeteria were never included in the survey.
Why C: The problem is not the number of questions per student; the problem is who was surveyed, since only cafeteria eaters were asked and everyone else was excluded.
Why D: Asking only students who eat in the cafeteria excludes those who bring lunch or eat elsewhere, so the sample is not representative, which is sampling bias.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is correlation?
A: A proof that one variable causes another to change in time
B: A relationship in which two variables tend to change together
C: A way of removing outliers from a data set before analysis
D: A random error in a data set that is caused by chance alone overall
Why A: Correlation shows that variables move together but cannot prove that one causes the other, so describing it as proof of causation is a common mistake.
Why B: Correlation describes a relationship in which two variables tend to change together, whether both rise or one rises while the other falls, without implying a cause.
Why C: Removing outliers is a data-cleaning step and is unrelated to correlation, which measures how strongly two variables are linked to one another in the data.
Why D: A random error caused by chance is noise or variance, not correlation, which is a pattern of two variables changing together in a consistent way.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in summer. What is the best conclusion?
A: Ice cream causes sunburn because of the sugar it contains
B: Sunburn causes ice cream sales as burned people buy cold treats
C: They are correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn
D: The data must be wrong because both cannot rise together
Why A: Sugar in ice cream does not cause sunburn; sunburn comes from ultraviolet sun exposure, so the shared rise in summer is not evidence that one causes the other.
Why B: Burned people do not drive ice cream sales in any meaningful way; both rise because summer heat and sun act as a third factor, not because one causes the other.
Why C: Both rise in summer because of a common cause, hot sunny weather, so they are correlated without ice cream causing sunburn, which is the best conclusion.
Why D: Two variables can easily rise together when a common factor like summer weather drives both, so the data is not wrong, and this claim is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a normal distribution?
A: A bell-shaped curve with most values near the mean
B: A curve with all of the values equal to each other
C: A straight line rising steadily over the years
D: A scatter of random points that shows no clear pattern
Why A: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped curve in which most values cluster near the mean and fewer values appear farther out in the tails.
Why B: If all values were equal there would be no spread at all, but a normal distribution is a bell curve with values spread around the mean.
Why C: A straight rising line is a linear trend over time and is not a distribution of values, so it does not describe a normal distribution.
Why D: A random scatter with no pattern is not a normal distribution, which has a clear symmetric bell shape with values concentrated around the mean.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a normal distribution, about what share of values lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
A: About 68%
B: About 95%
C: About 50%
D: About 100%
Why A: By the empirical rule, about 68% of values in a normal distribution fall within one standard deviation of the mean, on both sides combined.
Why B: About 95% is the share within two standard deviations of the mean, not one; within one standard deviation the figure is roughly 68%.
Why C: The 50% figure is the share of values above or below the mean alone; within one standard deviation on both sides it is about 68%.
Why D: A share of 100% would require infinitely wide limits, because a normal curve has tails that extend outward; within one standard deviation it is about 68%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hypothesis in a statistical test?
A: A chart showing the results of a survey or a test
B: A claim about a population that can be tested with data
C: A proven fact that needs no testing, from a textbook
D: A sample of the population chosen at random for study overall
Why A: A chart of results is a visualization, not a hypothesis; a hypothesis is a claim about a population that data can be used to test.
Why B: A hypothesis is a claim about a population that can be tested with data, such as saying the average height is 170 cm.
Why C: A hypothesis is not a proven fact; it is a statement that may be supported or rejected by data, so it must be open to testing.
Why D: A random sample of the population is data collected for study, not a hypothesis, which instead is a testable claim about the population itself.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a small p-value (such as 0.01) suggest?
A: The sample is too small to use in any real test of a claim
B: The null hypothesis is certainly true and the result is chance
C: The result would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true
D: The data has no errors of any kind in it at all in the set
Why A: A p-value does not measure sample size; a small p-value means the observed result would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, not that the sample is too small.
Why B: A small p-value points away from the null hypothesis being true and does not show that the result is chance; it suggests the result would be rare under that null.
Why C: A small p-value means data this extreme would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, which is evidence against the null hypothesis, not proof of it.
Why D: A p-value says nothing about whether the data is free of errors; it only measures how surprising the result would be if the null hypothesis were true.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a confidence interval?
A: The most common value in a sample drawn from the group studied
B: The time needed to collect data from the sample group in a survey
C: A guarantee that the estimate is exact and has no error at all
D: A range likely to contain the true value of a population measure
Why A: The most common value in a sample is the mode, which is a single summary number, whereas a confidence interval is a range built around an estimate.
Why B: The time needed for collecting data has nothing to do with a confidence interval, which is a statistical range for an estimate and not a duration.
Why C: A confidence interval does not guarantee exactness; it reflects uncertainty by giving a range, and the true value could still lie outside the interval.
Why D: A confidence interval is a range of values, calculated from sample data, that is likely to contain the true value of the population measure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is exploratory data analysis (EDA)?
A: Training a model on all of the data and then testing it on the same data
B: Publishing the final report to the public with the charts and tables
C: Deleting data that looks unusual without checking why it is so
D: Examining data with summaries and charts to find patterns and problems
Why A: Training and testing on the same data is a modeling mistake that hides overfitting, whereas exploratory analysis means examining data to find patterns and problems.
Why B: Publishing a final report is the last stage of a project, after the exploration is done, and does not describe examining data to find patterns.
Why C: Deleting unusual data without checking why is poor practice; exploratory analysis investigates unusual values first, to learn whether they are errors or real signals.
Why D: Exploratory data analysis uses summaries and charts to understand the data, spot patterns, and find problems like missing values or outliers before building a model.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: Why do analysts use a histogram?
A: To show the parts of a whole as slices of a circle
B: To show how two variables move together over time
C: To show how values are distributed across ranges
D: To show a list of exact names and values in a table
Why A: Slices of a circle describe a pie chart, which shows parts of a whole, whereas a histogram shows how values are distributed across ranges.
Why B: Showing how two variables move together over time calls for a line or scatter chart, not a histogram, which displays a single variable's distribution.
Why C: A histogram groups values into ranges, called bins, and shows how many fall in each, so it reveals the shape of a distribution.
Why D: Listing exact names and values is the job of a table, not a histogram, which summarizes counts in ranges with bars rather than listing individual entries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: Which chart is best for showing the relationship between two numeric variables?
A: A word cloud
B: A scatter plot
C: A pie chart
D: A table of text
Why A: A word cloud displays word frequency by text size and does not plot two numeric variables against each other, so it cannot show their relationship.
Why B: A scatter plot places each observation as a point using two numeric variables on the axes, so patterns such as trends or clusters in their relationship show clearly.
Why C: A pie chart shows parts of a single whole, not the relationship between two numeric variables, so it cannot display how one changes with the other.
Why D: A table of text lists words and values without plotting them, so it makes the relationship between two numeric variables hard to see at a glance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: Which chart is best for showing change over time?
A: A line chart
B: A pie chart
C: A scatter plot
D: A histogram plot
Why A: A line chart connects points in time order, which makes rises, falls and trends over time easy to see, so it is the best choice here.
Why B: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts at one moment and has no time axis, so it cannot display change over time.
Why C: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, and while it can show time on an axis, a line chart shows the trend more clearly.
Why D: A histogram displays how values are distributed in ranges and has no time axis, so it does not show how a value changes over time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is feature scaling?
A: Removing every column from the data set to save space
B: Making a chart larger on the screen for the audience
C: Adjusting numeric values so they have comparable ranges
D: Increasing the number of rows in a table for the model overall
Why A: Removing columns would reduce the features available and does not change numeric ranges; feature scaling adjusts values so features share comparable ranges.
Why B: Making a chart larger changes how it looks on screen and has no effect on the data values, whereas feature scaling adjusts numeric values in the data itself.
Why C: Feature scaling adjusts numeric values, for example by normalizing to 0 through 1, so that features have comparable ranges and none dominates the model unfairly.
Why D: Adding rows changes the amount of data, not the range of values; feature scaling transforms the numbers in each column so that their ranges are comparable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is a feature in a data set used for machine learning?
A: An input variable that describes each example
B: The final answer a model predicts after training
C: The computer a model runs on at the firm
D: The name of the data file saved on a hard disk
Why A: A feature is an input variable that describes each example, such as the size of a house, and the model uses these inputs to learn patterns.
Why B: The final answer a model predicts is the label or target, not a feature; features are the inputs that the model uses to make that prediction.
Why C: The computer a model runs on is hardware, not a feature; in a data set, a feature is a column that describes each example.
Why D: The name of a data file is metadata about storage and is not a feature, which is a variable that describes each example for the model.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is a label (target) in supervised learning?
A: A chart legend that explains the colors in a graph
B: A comment typed by a programmer in the code
C: An input column describing each example in the data
D: The correct answer the model learns to predict
Why A: A chart legend explains colors in a graph and has nothing to do with learning; a label in supervised learning is the correct answer for each example.
Why B: A comment typed in code is documentation for programmers, not a label; in supervised learning, a label is the correct answer the model learns to predict.
Why C: An input column describing each example is a feature, not a label; the label is the output value the model is trained to predict.
Why D: In supervised learning the label, or target, is the correct answer attached to each training example, and the model learns to predict it from the features.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: In a data set predicting house prices, which column is the label?
A: The square footage
B: The sale price
C: The bedroom count
D: The year built
Why A: Square footage is an input that describes a house and helps predict the price, so it is a feature and not the label being predicted.
Why B: The sale price is what the model is trying to predict from the other columns, so it is the label (target), while the others serve as features.
Why C: Bedroom count describes the house and is used as an input to predict price, which makes it a feature rather than the label.
Why D: The year built is another input describing the house that helps estimate price, so it is a feature, whereas the price itself is the label.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: Why is data split into training and test sets?
A: To avoid using labels at all in the model's data
B: To remove all outliers automatically from the data
C: To make the data set smaller so it takes less room on disk
D: To check how well a model works on data it has not seen
Why A: Splitting data does not remove the need for labels, since both training and test sets keep their labels so that predictions can be checked against true answers.
Why B: Splitting does not remove outliers; outlier handling is a separate cleaning step, while the split exists to test the model on unseen data.
Why C: The purpose of the split is not to save disk space; both parts together hold the same data, so the total size is unchanged.
Why D: A test set holds data the model never saw during training, so scoring on it shows how well the model works on new data and reveals overfitting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on test data. What does this suggest?
A: Underfitting
B: Faster training
C: Overfitting
D: A perfect model
Why A: Underfitting means poor results on both training and test data, but here training accuracy is high at 99%, so underfitting does not fit this pattern.
Why B: Faster training is about computation time and says nothing about the gap between 99% on training data and 60% on test data.
Why C: A big gap between 99% on training data and 60% on test data shows the model memorized training examples and fails to generalize, which is overfitting.
Why D: A perfect model would score well on test data too; 60% on unseen data is far from perfect, so the model does not generalize and is not perfect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: A model scores poorly on both the training data and the test data. What is the likely problem?
A: Overfitting
B: Underfitting
C: Perfect accuracy
D: Data leakage
Why A: Overfitting gives high scores on training data and low scores on test data, but here both scores are poor, so overfitting is not the problem.
Why B: Poor results on both training and test data mean the model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data, which is underfitting.
Why C: Perfect accuracy would mean high scores, but the model performs poorly on both sets, so this cannot describe the situation in the question.
Why D: Data leakage usually makes test scores look unrealistically good, because test information slips into training, so it does not explain poor results on both sets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is accuracy in classification?
A: The share of predictions that are correct
B: The size of the model file on the disk
C: The time a model takes to make its predictions
D: The number of features used in the model
Why A: Accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions, so it is the share of predictions that are correct.
Why B: The size of the model file on disk is a storage measure and does not reflect how many predictions are correct, which is what accuracy measures.
Why C: The time a model takes to predict is speed or latency, not accuracy, which is about how many predictions turn out to be correct.
Why D: The number of features is a property of the input data, not a measure of quality; accuracy is the share of correct predictions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: A model makes 90 correct predictions out of 120. What is its accuracy?
Why A: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions, so 90 / 120 = 0.75, which is 75%.
Why B: The value 30% is the share of errors in the other direction only if misread; the actual error rate is 30 / 120 = 25%, and accuracy is 75%.
Why C: An accuracy of 120% is impossible because it cannot exceed 100%; the calculation 90 / 120 gives 0.75, which is 75%.
Why D: The number 90 is the count of correct predictions, not a percentage; dividing by 120 predictions gives 90 / 120 = 75% as the accuracy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: Why can accuracy be misleading when 99% of cases are one class?
A: Accuracy falls to near zero when one class dominates
B: Accuracy cannot be calculated when the classes are unbalanced
C: A model that always predicts the common class scores 99%
D: The model must have learned the rare class very well
Why A: Accuracy rises, not falls, in this case, because predicting the common class is correct 99% of the time. That high score hides missed rare cases.
Why B: Accuracy can still be calculated with unbalanced classes; the problem is that the number can look high without the model detecting the rare class.
Why C: If 99% of cases belong to one class, a model that always predicts that class is right 99% of the time while never finding the rare class.
Why D: A 99% score does not show that the rare class was learned. A model that always predicts the common class gets 99% while missing each rare case.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is a confusion matrix?
A: A list of all of the training data used by the model
B: A table of confusing column names in the data
C: A chart of the weather in the region over a year
D: A table comparing predicted and actual classes
Why A: A list of all training data is just the data set; a confusion matrix is a table that compares predicted classes with actual classes.
Why B: A confusion matrix is not about confusing column names; it counts how often the model confuses one class for another in its predictions.
Why C: A chart of the weather over a year has nothing to do with evaluating a model; a confusion matrix tabulates predicted against actual classes.
Why D: A confusion matrix is a table with predicted classes on one axis and actual classes on the other, showing correct predictions and the types of errors.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is a false positive?
A: The model predicts no and is right about it
B: The model predicts yes, but the true answer is no
C: The model predicts no, but the true answer is yes
D: The model predicts yes and is right about it
Why A: Predicting no and being right is a true negative, since both the prediction and the reality are negative, so it is not a false positive.
Why B: A false positive occurs when the model predicts yes but the true answer is no, which means it raised a false alarm.
Why C: Predicting no when the true answer is yes is a false negative, a missed case, which is the opposite error of a false positive.
Why D: Predicting yes and being right is a true positive, because the prediction matches reality, so it is a correct result and not a false positive.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is a false negative?
A: The model predicts no and is right about it
B: The model predicts no, but the true answer is yes
C: The model predicts yes and is right about it
D: The model predicts yes, but the true answer is no
Why A: Predicting no and being right is a true negative, since the prediction matches reality, so this is a correct result and not a false negative.
Why B: A false negative occurs when the model predicts no but the true answer is yes, which means the model missed a real positive case.
Why C: Predicting yes and being right is a true positive, a correct outcome, so it cannot be a false negative, which is a missed positive case.
Why D: Predicting yes when the true answer is no is a false positive, a false alarm, which is the opposite error of a false negative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What does precision measure?
A: Of all real positives in the data, how many were found
B: How many features the model uses in its training
C: Of the cases predicted positive, how many really were
D: How fast the model runs on a computer at work today
Why A: Finding all the real positives in the data describes recall, not precision; precision looks only at the cases the model predicted as positive.
Why B: The number of features is about the model's inputs and does not measure how reliable its positive predictions are, which is what precision measures.
Why C: Precision is the share of cases predicted positive that really are positive, so it shows how trustworthy the model's positive predictions are.
Why D: Speed of the model is a performance measure for run time and has nothing to do with correctness of positive predictions, which precision measures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What does recall measure?
A: How long the model takes to train on the data
B: Of predicted positives, how many were correct
C: How much memory the model uses to run its tasks
D: Of all real positives, how many the model found
Why A: Training duration is about time and cost, not about finding positives; recall measures how many of all real positives the model manages to find.
Why B: The share of predicted positives that are correct is precision, which looks at predictions; recall instead looks at the real positives in the data.
Why C: Memory use is a resource measure and says nothing about how many real positive cases the model finds, which is what recall measures.
Why D: Recall is the share of all real positives that the model found, so a high recall means few real positive cases were missed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is regression used to predict?
A: A numeric value such as a price or temperature
B: The best chart type for showing the results
C: A category such as spam or not spam for each email
D: A group of similar customers in a market
Why A: Regression predicts a numeric value, such as a price or a temperature, which is why it is used for continuous outcomes.
Why B: The best chart for results is a visualization decision, not something a regression model predicts; regression predicts a numeric value.
Why C: Predicting a category like spam or not spam is classification, not regression, which outputs numbers rather than classes.
Why D: Grouping similar customers is clustering, an unsupervised task, whereas regression predicts a numeric value from input features.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Topic: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI
Question: What is classification used to predict?
A: The time of day at which the data is collected
B: A new random data set of unlabeled records
C: A category or class such as spam or not spam
D: A continuous number like income or a house price
Why A: The time of day data was collected is a detail about the data, not a prediction target type; classification predicts a category or class.
Why B: Classification does not generate new random data sets; it assigns each input to a category, such as spam or not spam.
Why C: Classification predicts a category or class for each example, such as spam or not spam, so the output is a label from a fixed set.
Why D: Predicting a continuous number like income or a house price is regression, not classification, which instead assigns inputs to categories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is artificial intelligence (AI)?
A: Programs that follow fixed steps to convert files from one format to another
B: Robots that repeat a fixed assembly motion without sensing their surroundings
C: Any computer connected to the internet through a modem or a cable
D: Computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human intelligence
Why A: Converting file formats follows fixed steps with no learning or reasoning. AI means systems that perform tasks usually needing human intelligence.
Why B: A machine repeating a fixed motion does not reason or learn. AI means systems that perform tasks that usually need human intelligence.
Why C: Being connected to the internet describes networking, and many connected computers use no AI at all, so this does not define AI.
Why D: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images and making decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
A: Machine learning is one way of building AI by learning from data
B: Machine learning is a type of hardware that runs AI programs faster
C: AI is a narrow type of machine learning built from fixed rules
D: Machine learning needs a person to write each rule, while AI learns from data
Why A: Machine learning is one approach to building AI in which systems learn patterns from data, so ML is a subset of the wider field of AI.
Why B: Machine learning is a method, not hardware. It is one way of building AI in which systems learn from data.
Why C: This reverses the relationship. AI is the broader field, and machine learning is one approach within it that learns from data.
Why D: That swaps them. Machine learning learns patterns from data instead of relying on hand-written rules, and it is one approach within AI.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is narrow (weak) AI?
A: AI that can do any task a human can do
B: AI designed to do one specific task well
C: AI that is too small to be useful at all
D: AI that has human feelings and goals
Why A: An AI that can do any task a human can do is general AI, not narrow AI, which is built for one specific task.
Why B: Narrow, or weak, AI is designed to do one specific task well, such as recognizing faces or recommending movies, and cannot move freely to unrelated tasks.
Why C: Narrow AI is not defined by size or usefulness; many narrow systems are very useful and powerful at their one task, so this definition is wrong.
Why D: Human feelings and goals describe a hypothetical conscious machine, which does not exist; narrow AI is simply focused on one task without feelings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is general AI (AGI)?
A: An AI used by the military to guide drones and plan missions in war zones
B: An AI freely available online to anyone with a computer and an internet link as a rule
C: An AI designed for only one task, such as playing chess or sorting mail
D: A hypothetical AI able to learn and perform any intellectual task a human can
Why A: Military use describes where an AI might be applied, not what general AI is, which is defined by its ability to do any intellectual task.
Why B: Free online availability concerns access and cost, not capability, so it does not define general AI, which is about broad human-level ability.
Why C: An AI built for one task such as chess or sorting mail is narrow AI, which is the opposite of general AI.
Why D: General AI, or AGI, is a hypothetical system that could learn and perform any intellectual task a human can, and no such system exists today.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of narrow AI?
A: A system that recommends movies based on viewing history
B: A printer that prints a page from a computer file
C: A calculator that adds two numbers and shows the sum
D: A machine that can do every human job as well as a worker
Why A: A system that recommends movies from viewing history is built for one specific task, which makes it an example of narrow AI.
Why B: A printer that prints a file follows fixed instructions and does not learn or reason, so it is ordinary machinery and not narrow AI.
Why C: A calculator performs fixed arithmetic with set rules and no learning or judgment, so it is not usually counted as AI at all.
Why D: A machine that can do every human job would be general AI, which is hypothetical, not narrow AI, which handles one specific task.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an algorithm?
A: A random list of words used in a dictionary or a book
B: A type of computer screen used to display graphics and video
C: A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem
D: A file that stores photos taken with a phone or camera
Why A: A random list of words is not a procedure; an algorithm is a precise set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.
Why B: A computer screen is hardware for displaying output, whereas an algorithm is a sequence of instructions that solves a problem.
Why C: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, such as a recipe a computer can follow.
Why D: A file storing photos is data storage and not a set of instructions, so it does not describe an algorithm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a model in machine learning?
A: The data used to train and test the algorithm
B: The result of training an algorithm on data
C: A person who tests software for bugs and errors
D: A toy version of a computer made for children
Why A: The data used to train and test is the data set, not the model; the model is what you get after training an algorithm on data.
Why B: A model in machine learning is the result of training an algorithm on data, and it holds the learned patterns used to make predictions.
Why C: A person who tests software is a tester, not a model; in machine learning, a model is the trained system that makes predictions.
Why D: A toy version of a computer for children has no relation to machine learning, where a model is the output of training an algorithm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is training in machine learning?
A: Feeding data to an algorithm so it learns patterns
B: Teaching employees how to use a new program at work
C: Deleting old data from the system to free up space
D: Printing the model's results on paper for managers
Why A: Training means feeding data to an algorithm so that it learns patterns, producing a model that can then be used to make predictions.
Why B: Teaching employees to use a program is staff training, which is a different meaning of the word and unrelated to machine learning.
Why C: Deleting old data to free space is housekeeping, and it does not teach an algorithm anything, so it is not training in machine learning.
Why D: Printing results on paper is reporting, and it does not help an algorithm learn; training in machine learning means learning patterns from data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inference (prediction) in AI?
A: Collecting the first data set used to train the model
B: Using a trained model to make a prediction on new data
C: Cleaning errors from data before it is used to train
D: Building the model's code in a programming language
Why A: Collecting the first data set is part of data preparation before training, not inference, which means using a trained model on new data.
Why B: Inference, or prediction, means using an already trained model to make a prediction on new data it has not seen before.
Why C: Cleaning errors from data is a preparation step done before training, and it does not involve making predictions, so it is not inference.
Why D: Writing the model's code is development work and not inference, which happens after the model is trained and is used to predict.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a chatbot?
A: A tool for editing spreadsheets and charts used by analysts
B: A robot that cleans floors in homes and offices
C: A program that talks with users through text or voice
D: A device that stores passwords for your accounts
Why A: A tool for editing spreadsheets and charts is analysis software, not a chatbot, which is a program that converses with users.
Why B: A robot that cleans floors is a household machine and not a chatbot, which is software that carries on a conversation.
Why C: A chatbot is a program that talks with users through text or voice, answering questions or carrying out requests in a conversation.
Why D: A device that stores passwords is a password manager, which is a security tool and not a chatbot that holds conversations.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recommendation system?
A: A system that prints personal letters for customers
B: A system that deletes unused files from a hard drive overall
C: A system that blocks all advertisements on websites
D: A system that suggests items a user may like using data
Why A: Printing personal letters is a document task and does not involve suggesting items, which is what a recommendation system does.
Why B: Deleting unused files is storage cleanup and does not suggest anything to users, so it is not a recommendation system.
Why C: Blocking advertisements is the job of an ad blocker, which is the opposite of suggesting items a user may like.
Why D: A recommendation system uses data about users and items to suggest things a user may like, such as movies, songs or products.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is automation?
A: Doing every task by hand with no help from machines
B: Storing data in the cloud for use at a much later time overall
C: Using technology to perform tasks with little human input
D: Writing a program in a notebook by hand with a pen
Why A: Doing every task by hand with no help from machines is manual work, which is the opposite of automation.
Why B: Storing data in the cloud is a storage practice and does not mean machines perform tasks with little human input, as automation does.
Why C: Automation means using technology to perform tasks with little human input, such as a machine sorting parcels or software sending routine messages.
Why D: Writing a program by hand in a notebook is just a way of drafting code and does not itself perform any task automatically.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which task is the best candidate for automation with AI?
A: Sorting thousands of support emails into categories
B: Comforting a grieving customer in person at the store
C: Choosing a company's mission and its core values
D: Deciding whether a new law is fair to citizens
Why A: Sorting thousands of emails into categories is repetitive, high-volume and rule-driven, which suits AI very well and saves human time.
Why B: Comforting a grieving customer needs human empathy and presence, which AI cannot truly offer, so it is a poor candidate for automation.
Why C: Choosing a mission and core values calls for human judgment about purpose and ethics, so it is not a good task for AI automation.
Why D: Deciding whether a law is fair involves moral reasoning and social values, which should rest with people, so AI is a poor fit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is natural language processing (NLP)?
A: AI that helps computers store text files on a hard disk
B: AI that helps computers understand and use human language
C: AI that helps computers recognize faces in photos online overall
D: AI that helps computers move robots in a factory line
Why A: Storing text files on a disk is a file storage task and does not involve understanding language, which is what NLP is for.
Why B: Natural language processing is AI that helps computers understand and use human language, for example in translation, chatbots and text summaries.
Why C: Recognizing faces in photos is computer vision, which works with images, whereas NLP works with human language in text and speech.
Why D: Moving robots on a factory line is robotics and control, which is a different area from NLP, which handles human language.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is computer vision?
A: AI that improves screen brightness on a monitor display
B: AI that enables computers to speak in a natural voice
C: AI that checks eyesight in people at an eye clinic
D: AI that enables computers to interpret images and video
Why A: Improving screen brightness is a display feature and has no relation to interpreting what is in images, which is computer vision.
Why B: Speaking in a natural voice is speech synthesis, a language task, not computer vision, which deals with images and video.
Why C: Checking eyesight at an eye clinic is a medical test of human vision and does not describe AI that interprets images.
Why D: Computer vision is AI that enables computers to interpret images and video, for example by recognizing objects, faces or text in pictures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is speech recognition?
A: Converting video into audio only
B: Converting spoken words into text
C: Converting images into text files
D: Converting text into spoken words
Why A: Converting video to audio is a media conversion that does not turn speech into text, so it is not speech recognition.
Why B: Speech recognition converts spoken words into text, which lets voice assistants and dictation tools understand what a person has said.
Why C: Converting images into text files describes optical character recognition, which reads text from pictures and not from spoken audio.
Why D: Converting text into spoken words is speech synthesis, or text-to-speech, which is the reverse of speech recognition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is generative AI?
A: AI that creates new content such as text, images or music
B: AI that predicts a number, such as next month's sales total
C: AI that sorts incoming emails into spam and inbox groups
D: AI that finds unusual transactions in a bank's records
Why A: Generative AI creates new content such as text, images or music, based on patterns it learned from its training data.
Why B: Predicting a number is a forecasting task, not creating new content. Generative AI produces new text, images or music from patterns in training data.
Why C: Sorting emails into groups is classification of existing items. Generative AI creates new content such as text, images or music.
Why D: Finding unusual records is anomaly detection and creates nothing new. Generative AI produces new text, images or music.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a large language model (LLM)?
A: A device that records speech and plays it back through a small speaker
B: A program that translates one language into another at borders and airports
C: A model trained on huge amounts of text to generate and understand language
D: A dictionary stored in a database of words and their meanings for readers
Why A: A device that records and plays back speech is an audio recorder and has nothing to do with a language model trained on text.
Why B: Translating at borders describes a translation service and not an LLM, which is a model trained on huge amounts of text.
Why C: A large language model is trained on huge amounts of text, which lets it generate and understand language, answer questions and write content.
Why D: A dictionary lists words and meanings and cannot generate new text, whereas an LLM learns language patterns from huge text collections.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hallucination in generative AI?
A: A very fast response from the system to a user
B: A correct answer with sources cited in full
C: A request to restart the system when it stops
D: A confident answer that is false or made up
Why A: A fast response is about speed and says nothing about accuracy, whereas a hallucination is a confident answer that is false or made up.
Why B: A correct answer with sources cited is reliable output, which is the opposite of a hallucination, where the answer is false.
Why C: A request to restart the system is a technical prompt or error message and has nothing to do with the false content of a hallucination.
Why D: A hallucination is a confident answer that is false or made up, such as an invented fact or a citation to a source that does not exist.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a prompt?
A: The data used to train the AI before use
B: The input or instruction given to an AI system
C: The code that runs the AI on a large server
D: The final answer an AI gives back to the user
Why A: The data used to train the AI is its training data, which is provided before use, while a prompt is the input given at use.
Why B: A prompt is the input or instruction given to an AI system, such as a question or a task description, that tells it what to do.
Why C: The code that runs the AI is the software, not the prompt, which is just the text or instruction that a user supplies.
Why D: The final answer an AI gives back is the output or response, not the prompt, which is the input the user provides.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which prompt is likely to get the most useful answer?
A: Do the thing that I asked about earlier and make it good enough
B: Write something about the topic that you think I might like to read
C: Summarize this article in three bullet points for a high school student
D: Tell me something interesting about anything you know of in the world in the end
Why A: Do the thing I asked earlier gives no content or context, so the model cannot know the task and the answer is unlikely to be useful.
Why B: Write something about the topic is vague, with no subject, length or format, so the model must guess and the answer may not be useful.
Why C: This prompt names the task (summarize), the format (three bullet points) and the audience (a high school student), giving clear detail that leads to a useful answer.
Why D: Tell me something interesting about anything is open-ended with no goal, format or audience, so the response is unfocused and may not help the reader.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Turing test?
A: A test of whether a machine can act so like a human that people cannot tell the difference
B: A test of how much data a model can store and the speed of its disk in the system
C: A test of how fast a computer processes data, using a fixed set of standard calculations and timers
D: A test of a computer's memory size and how fast its screen can refresh each second
Why A: The Turing test checks whether a machine can behave so much like a human in conversation that people cannot tell the difference, which is the standard test of machine intelligence.
Why B: Storage capacity and disk speed are hardware measures, whereas the Turing test checks whether a machine's behavior can pass for human behavior.
Why C: Processing speed is measured with benchmarks, not the Turing test, which is about whether a machine can imitate a human so well that it is indistinguishable.
Why D: Memory size and screen refresh rate are hardware specifications, and neither relates to the Turing test, which judges whether a machine can pass as human.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a benefit of AI for businesses?
A: Perfect fairness in the results it gives
B: Setup costs lower than a simple spreadsheet
C: Removal of any need for human oversight
D: Faster analysis of large amounts of data
Why A: AI can carry bias from its training data, so fair results are not assured. A real benefit is faster analysis of large amounts of data.
Why B: AI usually costs more to set up, needing data, computing power and skilled staff. A real benefit is faster analysis of large amounts of data.
Why C: Businesses still need human oversight to check AI results and handle errors, so AI does not remove that need, and this claim is false.
Why D: One real benefit of AI for businesses is faster analysis of large amounts of data, which saves time and can reveal useful patterns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a limitation of current AI systems?
A: They work well on tasks unlike their training
B: They need no data to learn how to do a task well
C: They depend on the quality of their training data
D: They get tired and slow down after long use
Why A: Performance drops on tasks unlike the training data, so this is not a strength. A real limitation is dependence on the quality of training data.
Why B: AI systems learn from data, so they cannot learn a task well with no data; this statement is false, though it is phrased as an ability.
Why C: A real limitation of current AI is that its performance depends on the quality of its training data, since poor or biased data leads to poor results.
Why D: AI systems do not tire the way people do. A real limitation is that results depend on the quality of their training data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an expert system?
A: A program that predicts prices by learning from past sales
B: A program that uses rules from human experts to make decisions
C: A program that generates random music for a video game level
D: A program that lets experts chat with each other online
Why A: That describes a machine learning model that learns from data. An expert system applies rules gathered from human experts to make decisions.
Why B: An expert system uses rules gathered from human experts to make decisions or give advice in a specific field, such as medical diagnosis.
Why C: Generating random music for a game is a creative generation task and does not apply expert knowledge, so it is not an expert system.
Why D: That is a communication tool and makes no decisions. An expert system applies rules from human experts to decide or advise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a rule-based system?
A: A system that learns its own rules from data automatically over time
B: A system with no instructions at all and no logic built in
C: A system that changes its rules randomly each time it runs
D: A system that follows explicit if-then rules written by people
Why A: Learning its own rules from data describes machine learning, whereas a rule-based system follows rules that people have written in advance.
Why B: A system with no instructions and no logic could not operate, so it cannot be a rule-based system, which depends on explicit rules.
Why C: A rule-based system follows fixed rules, so it behaves predictably; changing rules at random each run is the opposite of how it works.
Why D: A rule-based system follows explicit if-then rules written by people, so its behavior is predictable and easy to trace to a specific rule.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a robot?
A: A machine that can sense, decide and act, often by following programs
B: Any computer connected to the internet, such as a laptop, a phone or a server
C: A screen that displays charts and tables of numbers for managers
D: A program that only stores data and cannot take any action at all
Why A: A robot is a machine that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do and act, often by following programs that control its movements.
Why B: A laptop, phone or server is a computer connected to the internet, but it does not sense and act physically, so it is not a robot.
Why C: A screen that displays charts and tables is an output device that shows information and does not sense, decide or act as a robot does.
Why D: A program that only stores data and cannot act is not a robot, which must be able to take actions in the physical world.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?
A: Everyday devices connected to the internet that share data
B: A kind of social media account used to post photos and videos
C: A list of websites that are saved as bookmarks in a browser
D: A network of only large computers kept in data centers
Why A: The Internet of Things means everyday devices, such as thermostats, watches and appliances, that are connected to the internet and share data.
Why B: A social media account for posting photos is a service for people, whereas the Internet of Things links physical devices that exchange data.
Why C: A list of bookmarked websites is a browser feature and not a network of connected devices, which is what the Internet of Things is.
Why D: The Internet of Things includes small everyday devices like sensors and appliances, so a network of only large data center computers does not describe it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why does AI often need a lot of data?
A: Data lets the computer avoid power
B: Patterns are learned from many examples
C: Data makes the computer run cooler
D: Data replaces the need for algorithms
Why A: Data does not let a computer avoid power; AI training actually uses a lot of electricity, so this reason is wrong.
Why B: AI learns by finding patterns, and the more varied examples it sees, the better it can learn those patterns and generalize to new cases.
Why C: Data does not cool the computer; the heat comes from processing, so a bigger data set tends to increase the workload.
Why D: Data does not replace algorithms, because an algorithm is still needed to learn from the data; both are required for machine learning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a spreadsheet used for?
A: Sending video calls to coworkers across the globe each week as a rule
B: Protecting computers from viruses and other malware attacks
C: Organizing, calculating and analyzing data in rows and columns
D: Editing photographs for a website and marketing materials
Why A: Video calls are made with conferencing software, not a spreadsheet, which is a tool for working with data in rows and columns.
Why B: Protecting computers from viruses is the job of security software, not a spreadsheet, which organizes and analyzes data.
Why C: A spreadsheet organizes, calculates and analyzes data in rows and columns, using formulas and functions to total values or find averages.
Why D: Editing photographs is done with image-editing software, and a spreadsheet is designed for working with data in rows and columns instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which spreadsheet function adds a range of numbers?
A: COUNT
B: MAX
C: IF
D: SUM
Why A: COUNT tells you how many cells contain numbers, not their total, so it does not add the values together as SUM does.
Why B: MAX returns the largest value in a range and does not add numbers, so it cannot give the total of the range.
Why C: IF tests a condition and returns one of two results, so it is a logic function and does not add a range of numbers.
Why D: SUM adds all the numbers in a range, for example =SUM(A1:A10), which makes it the right function for finding a total.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which spreadsheet function finds the average of a range?
A: MIN
B: SUM
C: ROUND
D: AVERAGE
Why A: MIN returns the smallest value in the range, not the average, so it does not describe the center of the data.
Why B: SUM adds all the values in a range to give a total, and without dividing by the count it is not the average.
Why C: ROUND changes a number to a chosen number of decimal places and does not calculate any average of a range.
Why D: AVERAGE adds the numbers in a range and divides by how many there are, so it returns the mean of the range.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does =COUNTIF(B2:B10,"Yes") return?
A: An error because the word Yes is only text
B: The number of cells in the range that equal Yes
C: The sum of the cells in the range B2 to B10
D: The word Yes repeated nine times in a column overall
Why A: COUNTIF accepts text criteria, so the word Yes works fine and does not cause an error; it counts the cells that match.
Why B: COUNTIF counts the cells in B2:B10 that equal the word Yes, so it returns the number of cells in the range that match.
Why C: Summing the cells would need the SUM function; COUNTIF counts matching cells and does not add up their values.
Why D: COUNTIF returns a number, not text, so it never repeats the word Yes; it only reports how many cells in the range match.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does SQL stand for?
A: System Quality Levels
B: Simple Query Language
C: Structured Query Language
D: Secure Query Logic Set
Why A: SQL does not stand for System Quality Levels; that phrase does not name any database language, and SQL is the language used to query data.
Why B: Simple Query Language is not the official name; SQL actually stands for Structured Query Language, and the word simple is not part of it.
Why C: SQL stands for Structured Query Language, the standard language for storing, retrieving and managing data in relational databases.
Why D: Secure Query Logic Set is not a real expansion; SQL stands for Structured Query Language, and it is not defined by security features.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the SQL command SELECT do?
A: Retrieves data from a table
B: Changes existing values
C: Adds a new row to a table
D: Deletes a table permanently
Why A: SELECT retrieves data from a table, letting you choose which columns and rows to read without changing the stored data.
Why B: Changing existing values is done with UPDATE, not SELECT, which only reads data and leaves the table unchanged.
Why C: Adding a new row is done with INSERT, not SELECT, which only retrieves data that is already stored in the table.
Why D: Deleting a table is done with DROP, not SELECT, which is a read-only command that never removes a table.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which SQL query returns all rows from a table named orders where the total is over 100?
A: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 100;
B: SELECT total FROM orders ORDER BY;
C: INSERT INTO orders WHERE total > 100;
D: DELETE FROM orders WHERE total > 100;
Why A: SELECT * returns all columns, FROM orders names the table, and WHERE total > 100 keeps only rows where the total is over 100.
Why B: This query returns only the total column, has no filter for totals over 100, and has an incomplete ORDER BY clause, so it fails.
Why C: INSERT adds new rows and does not read existing ones; it also cannot use a WHERE filter in that form, so it does not return rows.
Why D: DELETE removes the matching rows from the table instead of returning them, so it does the opposite of what the question asks for.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the SQL clause ORDER BY do?
A: Removes duplicates
B: Counts the rows
C: Sorts the results
D: Joins two tables
Why A: Removing duplicates is done with DISTINCT, not ORDER BY, which changes the order of rows and keeps all of them.
Why B: Counting rows is done with COUNT, not ORDER BY, which only arranges the rows in a certain order.
Why C: ORDER BY sorts the results by one or more columns, in ascending order by default or descending when you add DESC.
Why D: Joining tables is done with JOIN, not ORDER BY, which only sorts rows and does not combine data from other tables.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a SQL JOIN do?
A: Renames a column in a table of data to a new name
B: Sorts a single table of data by the date field only
C: Deletes the second table from the database when queried
D: Combines rows from two tables based on related columns
Why A: Renaming a column is done with an alias or ALTER, not JOIN, which combines data from two tables using related columns.
Why B: Sorting a single table is the job of ORDER BY, while JOIN works with two tables and does not sort rows.
Why C: JOIN does not delete anything; it only reads data, and deleting a table uses a different command such as DROP.
Why D: A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on related columns, such as a customer ID that appears in both tables.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which programming language is widely used for data science?
A: Latin
B: Python
C: Braille
D: Morse code
Why A: Latin is a human language used long ago and is not a programming language, so it cannot be used to analyze data.
Why B: Python is widely used for data science because of its readable syntax and strong libraries such as pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn.
Why C: Braille is a tactile writing system for people with visual impairment, not a programming language, so it is not used for data science.
Why D: Morse code is a signaling system of dots and dashes, not a programming language, so it is not used in data science.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a library in programming?
A: A collection of ready-made code that programmers can reuse
B: A file that deletes errors from the code every time it runs
C: A screen that displays results of the program to the user
D: A building that stores books for readers to borrow and read
Why A: A library is a collection of ready-made code that programmers can reuse, saving them from writing common functions from scratch.
Why B: A library does not delete errors; the code inside it can have bugs, and using one does not automatically fix errors in a program.
Why C: A screen that displays results is an output device, not a library, which is a package of reusable code.
Why D: A building that stores books is a physical library, but in programming the term means reusable code, so this meaning is wrong here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is pandas in Python?
A: A library for drawing 3D video games on screen
B: A library for working with tables of data
C: A tool for sending emails to clients and staff
D: A way to play music files on a computer
Why A: Drawing 3D video games is the work of graphics engines, whereas pandas is a Python library for working with tables of data.
Why B: Pandas is a Python library for working with tables of data, offering tools to load, clean, filter and summarize data frames.
Why C: Sending email is the job of mail tools and libraries such as smtplib, not pandas, which is built for handling table data.
Why D: Playing music files is the job of audio software, not pandas, which is a library that handles tables of data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Jupyter notebook?
A: A paper notebook for taking notes, with ruled lines on each page
B: A type of database server that stores tables of records
C: An interactive document that mixes code, results and text
D: A device that records lectures in a classroom or hall
Why A: A Jupyter notebook is software, not paper; it is an interactive document, so a ruled paper notebook does not describe it.
Why B: A database server stores records and answers queries, whereas a Jupyter notebook is a document that mixes code, results and text.
Why C: A Jupyter notebook is an interactive document that mixes code, results and text, so analysts can run code and explain findings in one place.
Why D: A device that records lectures is hardware and has no connection to Jupyter, which is software for running code in a document.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data visualization software used for?
A: Writing legal contracts for a law firm
B: Encrypting passwords stored in a database
C: Backing up files to the cloud each night
D: Turning data into charts and dashboards
Why A: Writing legal contracts is done with word processors or legal tools, whereas data visualization software turns data into charts and dashboards.
Why B: Encrypting passwords is a security task, and visualization software does not encrypt anything; it displays data as charts and dashboards.
Why C: Backing up files to the cloud is the job of backup software, not visualization tools, which present data in charts.
Why D: Data visualization software turns data into charts and dashboards, which makes patterns and trends easier to see and share with others.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a dashboard?
A: A database that holds large tables of raw records
B: A program that predicts future sales from past data
C: A display that shows key figures and charts at a glance
D: A list of all passwords used by the staff of a firm as a rule
Why A: Raw tables are storage, not a quick view. A dashboard displays key figures and charts at a glance.
Why B: Predicting is the job of a forecasting model. A dashboard displays key figures and charts at a glance so performance is easy to monitor.
Why C: A dashboard shows key figures and charts on one screen at a glance, so people can monitor performance quickly without reading raw tables.
Why D: A list of passwords is a security risk and is not a dashboard, which displays business figures and charts, not credentials.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cloud computing?
A: Computing that needs no electricity or any other power supply overall
B: Computing that uses a single local machine in an office
C: Computing that only works during bad weather conditions
D: Using remote servers on the internet to store and process data
Why A: Cloud computing still needs electricity, since servers in data centers consume large amounts of power, so no-power computing is impossible.
Why B: Using a single local machine in an office is traditional on-premises computing, and cloud computing instead uses remote servers.
Why C: Cloud computing works in any weather; the word cloud is only a metaphor for the internet and has nothing to do with the sky.
Why D: Cloud computing means using remote servers on the internet to store and process data instead of relying only on a local computer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a major benefit of using the cloud for AI projects?
A: Access to large computing power without buying hardware
B: Models that train faster with no usage fees
C: Data that is stored on the user's own laptop
D: Models that fix their own training data errors
Why A: The cloud gives access to large computing power, such as many processors, without buying hardware, which suits AI projects that need heavy computation.
Why B: Cloud services charge fees for usage, so there are costs. The real benefit is access to large computing power without buying hardware.
Why C: Cloud data lives on remote servers, not the user's laptop. The benefit is large computing power without buying hardware.
Why D: Cloud platforms supply computing power but do not repair data errors. Accuracy still depends on the data and the model.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an API?
A: A type of computer screen used to show graphics
B: A set of rules that lets programs talk to each other
C: A kind of database table that stores customer names
D: A tool for printing reports from a database with headings
Why A: A computer screen is a display device, whereas an API is a set of rules that lets programs talk to each other.
Why B: An API is a set of rules that lets different programs talk to each other, for example a weather service sending data to an app.
Why C: A database table stores records and is not an API, which is an interface through which software requests and exchanges data.
Why D: Printing reports with headings is a reporting feature; an API instead defines how software components request and exchange data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a GPU often used for in AI?
A: Storing the user's passwords in a secure vault on the machine
B: Keeping time for the computer clock so files are dated
C: Running many calculations in parallel to train models faster
D: Providing power to the monitor and other devices at a desk
Why A: Storing passwords is done by a password manager or secure storage, and GPUs have no role as vaults for user credentials.
Why B: Keeping time for the computer clock is the job of the system clock hardware, not the GPU, which does heavy calculations.
Why C: A GPU runs many calculations in parallel, which speeds up the matrix math in AI and lets models be trained much faster than on a CPU.
Why D: Providing power to the monitor is the job of the power supply, whereas a GPU is a processor, so this answer is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is version control, such as Git, used for?
A: Controlling how fast a program runs on a computer
B: Tracking changes to code and files over time
C: Blocking unauthorized users from the network
D: Choosing the next release date for the team
Why A: Controlling how fast a program runs is a performance setting and not version control, which tracks changes to code and files.
Why B: Version control tracks changes to code and files over time, so you can see who changed what and return to an earlier version.
Why C: Blocking unauthorized users from a network is done by firewalls and access controls, not version control, which records file history.
Why D: Choosing the next release date is a project planning decision, and version control does not schedule anything; it records changes to files.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A teammate overwrites your code by mistake. How does version control help?
A: It rewrites the code automatically for you
B: It deletes the teammate's account from the system
C: It makes overwriting impossible, even by mistake
D: You can restore an earlier version of the files
Why A: Version control does not rewrite code automatically; it stores the history of changes so that people can choose what to restore.
Why B: Version control does not delete the teammate's account; that is an administrator action, and it works with files, not user accounts.
Why C: Version control cannot prevent a person from overwriting a file by mistake, but it keeps history, so saying overwriting is impossible is false.
Why D: Version control saves earlier versions of the files, so after a mistaken overwrite you can restore a previous version and recover the lost code.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is open-source software?
A: Software whose code is publicly available to use and modify
B: Software that runs only offline on a single computer
C: Software that cannot be changed by any user or company
D: Software that costs the most money, as top engineers write it
Why A: Open-source software has publicly available code that anyone may use, study, modify and share, subject to its license terms.
Why B: Open-source software is not defined by running offline, since much of it runs on networks and online servers, so this definition is wrong.
Why C: Open-source software can be changed by users, because its code is open, so saying it cannot be changed is the opposite of the truth.
