Why D: Open-source software is often free and open to use, so it is not defined as the most expensive software, and cost is not the idea.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ETL process?
A: Extract, transform and load data into a destination
B: Edit, test and launch a website in three release steps
C: Enter, track and log expenses for a business firm
D: Encrypt, tag and lock files on a computer or server
Why A: ETL stands for extract, transform and load, the standard way to pull data from sources, clean and reshape it, and place it into a target system.
Why B: Editing, testing and launching a website describes a software release cycle, not ETL, which is about moving and reshaping data between systems rather than publishing web pages.
Why C: Entering, tracking and logging expenses is bookkeeping work done by a business, and none of those steps match the extract, transform and load stages that define ETL.
Why D: Encrypting, tagging and locking files is a security task for protecting storage, while ETL is a data integration process that does not aim to lock anything.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data warehouse?
A: A device that cleans data from a computer by wiping a disk
B: A program that edits photos and adds filters for social media in general
C: A central store of data collected from many sources for reporting
D: A building for storing boxes and pallets before they ship out
Why A: A device that wipes a disk is a data eraser or sanitizer, which destroys data, while a data warehouse is built to keep and organize data for analysis.
Why B: Photo editing and filter programs work on images for social media, and they have no role in storing combined business data for reporting, which is what a warehouse does.
Why C: A data warehouse gathers data from many source systems into one central store, organized so analysts can run reports and queries across the whole organization.
Why D: A building holding boxes and pallets is a physical goods warehouse, and the word here is only borrowed, since a data warehouse stores digital records, not shipping stock.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data pipeline?
A: A list of all employees and their pay for the whole year
B: A series of steps that moves data from source to destination
C: A pipe carrying water to the servers in a data center to cool
D: A chart that shows pipeline pressure in oil and gas lines
Why A: A list of employees and yearly pay is a payroll report, which is a static record of values, not a series of steps that moves data between systems.
Why B: A data pipeline is a series of automated steps that collects data from a source, processes it, and delivers it to a destination such as a warehouse.
Why C: A water pipe cooling servers is physical plumbing for hardware, and it carries no data, while a data pipeline moves information through software stages.
Why D: A chart of pressure in oil and gas lines is an engineering display for physical pipelines, and it has nothing to do with moving data between computer systems.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does no-code AI tools allow users to do?
A: Train very large models on a supercomputer for free
B: Rewrite the source code of existing AI software
C: Remove the need for any thinking by the user
D: Build simple AI solutions without writing programs
Why A: No-code tools do not give free computing power. They let users build simple AI solutions with visual blocks instead of writing programs.
Why B: Editing source code requires programming skills. No-code tools let users build simple AI solutions without writing programs.
Why C: No-code tools reduce programming effort but cannot remove thinking, because users still must define the problem, choose data and judge whether the results make sense.
Why D: No-code AI tools offer visual interfaces and prebuilt components so people can build simple AI solutions such as classifiers or chatbots without writing programs themselves.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which tool would most likely be used to build and train a neural network in Python?
A: TensorFlow or PyTorch
B: A music player app
C: A web browser app
D: A word processor app
Why A: TensorFlow and PyTorch are Python libraries made for defining, building and training neural networks, which is why they are the usual choices for deep learning work.
Why B: A music player plays audio files and has no features for defining layers, computing gradients or training a neural network, so it cannot do this job.
Why C: A web browser displays pages and runs websites, but it is not a framework for building or training neural networks in Python code.
Why D: A word processor is made for writing and formatting documents, and it offers no tools for model layers, training loops or numerical computing with Python.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is machine learning?
A: A way for people to learn about machines, through classes taught at a factory
B: A way for computers to learn patterns from data instead of being told every rule
C: A type of computer that has no software installed on its disk and no operating system
D: A way to store data on a hard drive for later use by the staff of a firm
Why A: Machine learning is not about people studying machines in classes at a factory, since the learner is the computer system, and the learning comes from data.
Why B: Machine learning lets computers find patterns in data and use them to make predictions, instead of having programmers write out every rule by hand beforehand.
Why C: A computer without software or an operating system cannot run anything, so it is not machine learning, which is a method that runs as software on normal systems.
Why D: Storing data on a hard drive is data storage, and while ML uses stored data, saving files for later use does not mean a system learns anything.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is supervised learning?
A: Learning in a classroom with a teacher and a text
B: Learning by trial and error with rewards and penalties overall
C: Learning from examples that include the correct answers
D: Learning from unlabeled data with no labels at all
Why A: Classroom learning with a teacher and a text is human education, and the word supervised in machine learning refers to labeled examples, not to a person teaching in a room.
Why B: Learning by trial and error with rewards and penalties describes reinforcement learning, a different type, because supervised learning uses examples that already contain the right answers.
Why C: Supervised learning trains a model on examples that include the correct answers, called labels, so it can learn to predict the answer for new inputs.
Why D: Learning from data with no labels is unsupervised learning, so it is the opposite of supervised learning, which depends on labeled examples with known answers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is unsupervised learning?
A: Learning with a human grading every step
B: Learning from labeled examples and answers
C: Learning by earning rewards and penalties
D: Finding patterns in data that has no labels
Why A: Having a human grade every step is not what defines unsupervised learning, because the term means the data has no labels, not that a grader checks each step.
Why B: Learning from labeled examples with answers is supervised learning, so it is the opposite of unsupervised learning, where the data has no answers attached.
Why C: Learning by earning rewards and penalties is reinforcement learning, which uses feedback from actions, while unsupervised learning has no reward signal and no labeled answers.
Why D: Unsupervised learning looks for structure such as groups or patterns in data that has no labels, so there are no correct answers given in advance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is reinforcement learning?
A: Learning by copying a textbook word for word from a page
B: Learning by grouping unlabeled data into similar clusters
C: Learning from a fixed set of labeled examples prepared in advance
D: Learning by trying actions and receiving rewards or penalties
Why A: Copying a textbook word for word is memorizing, not reinforcement learning, which improves behavior through feedback from actions taken in an environment instead of copying text.
Why B: Grouping unlabeled data into similar clusters is clustering, a form of unsupervised learning, and it involves no actions or rewards, which reinforcement learning needs.
Why C: Learning from a fixed set of prepared labeled examples is supervised learning, while reinforcement learning has no fixed answer key and learns from the results of actions.
Why D: Reinforcement learning has an agent try actions and receive rewards or penalties, gradually learning which choices lead to the best total reward over time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which type of machine learning is used to group customers into similar segments without labels?
A: Unsupervised learning (clustering)
B: Supervised classification only
C: Reinforcement learning methods
D: Manual spreadsheet sorting by hand
Why A: Grouping customers into similar segments with no labels is clustering, which is a task of unsupervised learning, since the groups are discovered from the data itself.
Why B: Supervised classification needs labeled examples that name the right segment for each customer, but this question says there are no labels, so it cannot be used.
Why C: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and penalties from actions, which does not fit grouping customers by similarity when no labels or rewards exist.
Why D: Sorting a spreadsheet by hand is manual work and not a type of machine learning, so it does not count as a learning method at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which type of machine learning would best predict whether an email is spam using many labeled emails?
A: No learning at all
B: Supervised learning
C: Unsupervised learning
D: Reinforcement learning
Why A: No learning at all would mean a fixed rule or guess, so it cannot predict spam well, whereas a model trained on labeled emails can learn the spam signals.
Why B: Supervised learning trains on emails already labeled spam or not spam, so the model learns from the right answers and then predicts labels for new emails.
Why C: Unsupervised learning works without labels, so it would ignore the spam tags the question gives, and it is better suited to grouping than to predicting a known label.
Why D: Reinforcement learning learns from rewards through actions in an environment, which is not the case for predicting a known label from many already labeled emails.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is clustering?
A: Deleting duplicate rows from data
B: Predicting a single number from data
C: Grouping similar data points together
D: Labeling emails as spam or not spam
Why A: Deleting duplicate rows is data cleaning called deduplication, and it does not group points by similarity, which is what clustering means.
Why B: Predicting a single number from data is regression, a supervised task, while clustering does not predict a value and instead finds groups in the data.
Why C: Clustering groups data points so that points in the same group are more similar to each other than to points in other groups, without needing labels.
Why D: Labeling emails as spam or not spam is classification, which needs known labels for training, and clustering does not assign preset labels like these.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a decision tree?
A: A list of company managers and their direct reports in an org chart
B: A model that makes predictions by following a series of yes/no questions
C: A table of numbers only, with no questions or any other kind of text in it
D: A tree that grows in a data center near the cooling system for the servers
Why A: An org chart of managers and reports is a company hierarchy diagram, not a model, so it makes no predictions even though it has a tree shape.
Why B: A decision tree predicts by following a series of yes or no questions about the input, moving down branches until it reaches a leaf with the answer.
Why C: A table of numbers with no questions describes plain data, but a decision tree is a model built from branching questions that lead to a prediction.
Why D: A physical tree near a data center cooling system has nothing to do with machine learning, and a decision tree is a model, not a plant.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a random forest?
A: A model that combines many decision trees to improve accuracy
B: A single very deep decision tree that is trained once on the data
C: A tree-planting program for firms that want to offset carbon
D: A forest of data servers kept cool in a mountain region
Why A: A random forest builds many decision trees on varied samples of the data and combines their votes, which improves accuracy and reduces overfitting compared with one tree.
Why B: A single very deep tree trained once is just one decision tree and often overfits, while a random forest uses many trees together for better results.
Why C: A tree-planting program for carbon offsets is about the environment, and random forest is the name of a machine learning method, not a program that plants trees.
Why D: A forest of servers kept cool in mountains is not a machine learning model, because random forest is an algorithm that combines decision trees, not a place for hardware.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is k-nearest neighbors (k-NN)?
A: A method for deleting nearby files from a computer disk
B: A method for finding a neighborhood on a map of a city
C: A method that predicts using only the farthest examples in the data
D: A method that predicts using the closest examples in the data
Why A: Deleting nearby files from a disk is file management, while k-NN is a prediction method that uses neighbors in the data and removes nothing from a disk.
Why B: Finding a neighborhood on a city map is navigation, and the word neighbors in k-NN refers to similar data points, not to places on a map.
Why C: Using only the farthest examples would give the least similar data points, so it reverses the method, since k-NN relies on the nearest examples to the new point.
Why D: k-NN predicts by finding the k closest examples to a new point and using their labels or values, such as a majority vote, to decide the answer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is linear regression?
A: A method that draws a pie chart from a set of data
B: A method that sorts words alphabetically in a list
C: A method that fits a straight line to predict a number
D: A method that groups data into clusters of similar items
Why A: A pie chart is a way to display shares of a whole, and linear regression is a prediction method, so drawing pie charts does not describe it.
Why B: Sorting words alphabetically is a basic data task and has nothing to do with predicting numbers, which is the purpose of linear regression.
Why C: Linear regression fits a straight line to data so it can predict a number, such as price from size, by reading the value from the line.
Why D: Grouping data into clusters of similar items is clustering, an unsupervised task, while linear regression is supervised and predicts a number rather than forming groups.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A linear regression equation is price = 50 + 20 × size. What is the predicted price when size is 3?
Why A: A result of 70 comes from adding 50 and 20, which uses size 1 and ignores that the slope must be multiplied by the size of 3.
Why B: Substituting size 3 gives 50 plus 20 times 3, which is 50 plus 60, and that equals 110, the predicted price.
Why C: A result of 170 comes from multiplying 50 plus 20 by 3 as one group, but the multiplication applies only to the size term, so the sum is 110.
Why D: A result of 60 comes from computing only 20 times 3 and forgetting the intercept of 50, but the full equation adds both, giving 110 in total.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is logistic regression commonly used for?
A: Predicting the probability of a category such as yes or no
B: Sorting files by size and date on a computer hard disk in the end
C: Drawing a map of the roads and towns in a large region
D: Predicting a house price from its size and location
Why A: Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1 for a category, which makes it a standard choice for yes or no questions such as spam or churn.
Why B: Sorting files by size and date is basic file management, and logistic regression is a statistical model for predicting categories, not a tool for ordering files.
Why C: Drawing a map of roads and towns is cartography, which has no link to logistic regression, a model that estimates the probability of a category.
Why D: Predicting a house price from size and location produces a number, which is a task for linear regression, whereas logistic regression predicts the probability of a category.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a neural network?
A: A group of people who share ideas about a topic online daily overall
B: A network of cables and routers linking the office computers
C: A website that stores brain scans for medical research teams
D: A model made of connected layers of nodes inspired by the brain
Why A: A group of people sharing ideas online is a social network, and the word network here means a human community, not the layered model used in machine learning.
Why B: A network of cables and routers is computer networking hardware, which carries data between devices and does not learn patterns the way a neural network does.
Why C: A website storing brain scans is a medical data archive, while a neural network is a computing model that only takes loose inspiration from the brain.
Why D: A neural network is a model built from connected layers of nodes, loosely inspired by brain neurons, that learns patterns by adjusting the links between them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is deep learning?
A: Learning that avoids all computers and uses books only
B: Learning that takes a long time to study, such as a degree overall
C: Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers
D: Learning with a very small data set of ten rows or fewer
Why A: Learning without computers using books only is ordinary study, whereas deep learning is a machine learning method that runs on computers and uses large amounts of data.
Why B: A long degree program is deep study by a person, but deep learning refers to the many layers in a neural network, not to the time spent studying.
Why C: Deep learning is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, which lets the model learn complex patterns from large amounts of data such as images.
Why D: Deep learning usually needs large data sets, so a very small set of ten rows or fewer is the opposite of how it is normally used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a neural network, what are weights?
A: Numbers that determine how strongly inputs influence each node
B: The speed of the internet link between servers and computers overall
C: The size of the data file saved on the computer's hard disk
D: The physical weight of the computer in kilograms on a scale
Why A: Weights are numbers on the connections between nodes that set how strongly each input affects a node, and training adjusts them to improve predictions.
Why B: The speed of a network link between servers is bandwidth, which is a hardware measure and has no role in how a neural network handles its inputs.
Why C: The size of a data file on disk is a storage measure, while weights are learned numbers inside the model that scale the inputs.
Why D: The physical weight of a computer in kilograms is a hardware fact, and the weights of a neural network are mathematical values, not a measure of mass.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does gradient descent do?
A: Splits the data into training and test groups
B: Adds new features to the data to improve results
C: Adjusts model parameters step by step to reduce error
D: Sorts features alphabetically so columns are easy to find
Why A: Splitting data is a preparation step. Gradient descent adjusts model parameters step by step to reduce error.
Why B: Adding features is feature engineering. Gradient descent changes model parameters in small steps that lower the error.
Why C: Gradient descent changes model parameters in small steps in the direction that lowers the error, repeating until the loss is as small as it can get.
Why D: Sorting features alphabetically is a layout choice that changes nothing about the model error, so it is not what gradient descent does during training.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a loss function?
A: A tool that deletes data from a table or a file
B: A measure of how wrong a model's predictions are
C: A count of how many features exist in the data set
D: A measure of how fast a model runs and how much memory
Why A: A tool that deletes data is a data removal command, but a loss function is a number that measures prediction error and does not alter any table or file.
Why B: A loss function measures how wrong a model's predictions are compared with the true values, giving training a number it tries to make smaller.
Why C: Counting the features in a data set gives its width, which is a description of the data, while a loss function scores the quality of predictions.
Why D: How fast a model runs and how much memory it uses are performance costs, but a loss function measures prediction error, not speed or memory.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hyperparameter?
A: A column of the data set that holds the target values
B: A chart label that names the axes of a graph in a report
C: A value the model learns during training from the data fed in
D: A setting chosen before training, such as learning rate
Why A: A column holding the target values is the label or target column of the data, which the model predicts, and it is not a setting chosen by the builder.
Why B: A chart label naming axes is part of a graph in a report, and has no connection to the settings that control how a model trains.
Why C: A value the model learns from the data during training is a parameter such as a weight, while a hyperparameter is set by the builder beforehand.
Why D: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training starts, such as the learning rate or number of layers, and the model does not learn it from data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the learning rate?
A: How big a step the model takes when updating during training
B: How often data is backed up to a server in the cloud daily
C: How many rows are in the data set used to train the model
D: How fast a person learns a new tool when given a manual to read
Why A: The learning rate sets how large a step the model takes when it updates its parameters, so a high rate moves fast and a low rate moves slowly.
Why B: How often data is backed up to the cloud is a backup schedule, which is an operations choice and has no link to how a model updates itself.
Why C: The number of rows in a data set is its size, and the learning rate does not count rows and instead controls the size of each update step.
Why D: How fast a person learns a tool is human skill, but in machine learning the learning rate is a training setting that controls the size of update steps.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cross-validation?
A: Checking a model only once on the data it learned from
B: Validating a user's password twice at login for safety
C: Comparing two different programming languages for a project
D: Testing a model on several different splits of the data
Why A: Checking a model only once on the data it learned from tells little about new data and hides overfitting, while cross-validation tests on data held out of training.
Why B: Validating a password twice at login is a security step for sign in, and it has nothing to do with checking how well a model performs.
Why C: Comparing two programming languages is a software choice, and cross-validation is a way to estimate model performance, not a way to compare languages.
Why D: Cross-validation splits the data into several parts, trains on some and tests on the rest, repeating so every part is tested, which gives a reliable estimate of performance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data leakage?
A: Data being stolen by hackers from a company server at night
B: Information from the test set accidentally influencing training
C: Data being stored in two places, so a copy is left on another disk
D: Data being deleted by mistake from a table or a file in use
Why A: Data stolen by hackers is a security breach, which is a different issue, since data leakage in machine learning is a modeling mistake that makes results look too good.
Why B: Data leakage happens when information from the test set accidentally influences training, which makes the performance look better than it will be on truly new data.
Why C: Data stored in two places is duplication or redundancy, and it does not describe the modeling error where test information flows into training.
Why D: Data deleted by mistake is data loss, which removes information, while data leakage is the opposite problem of unwanted information reaching the training process.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is bias in a machine learning model?
A: A model's favorite color in a chart or a report page
B: A model's file size on a disk or in a cloud account
C: Systematic error that leads to unfair or skewed results
D: A model's speed of training, which depends on the data size
Why A: A favorite color in a chart is a design choice and has nothing to do with the bias that affects model results.
Why B: A model's file size is a storage measure, and bias concerns whether predictions are systematically unfair or skewed, not how large the file is.
Why C: Bias in a model is systematic error that leads to unfair or skewed results, often caused by unbalanced or unrepresentative training data.
Why D: Training speed depends on data size and hardware, which is a performance matter, while bias is about skewed or unfair predictions and not about speed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hiring model trained on past data that favored men tends to rank women lower. What is the most likely cause?
A: Too little electricity
B: Bias in the training data
C: A broken keyboard cable
D: Too many colors in the charts
Why A: Too little electricity might stop a computer from running, but it cannot make a model favor men over women in its rankings, so it is not the cause.
Why B: A model trained on past data that favored men learns that pattern, so bias in the training data is the most likely cause of ranking women lower.
Why C: A broken keyboard cable affects typing input and has no way to shape how a trained model ranks men and women, so it is unrelated.
Why D: Too many colors in charts affects how reports look, and it cannot change the ranking decisions of a model, which come from the patterns in training data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is feature engineering?
A: Building a physical machine that sorts and counts items overall
B: Deleting all inputs from a model and starting it over
C: Creating or choosing input variables that help a model learn
D: Writing documentation for the model and its code base
Why A: Building a physical machine that sorts items is mechanical engineering, while feature engineering works on the input variables used to train a model.
Why B: Deleting all inputs and restarting would leave the model with no information, whereas feature engineering improves the inputs it already has or builds new ones.
Why C: Feature engineering means creating or choosing input variables, such as turning a date into day of week, so that they help the model learn useful patterns.
Why D: Writing documentation is useful for a project, but it does not change the inputs given to a model, so it is not feature engineering.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is dimensionality reduction?
A: Reducing the number of features while keeping important information
B: Reducing the number of rows to zero in a data set to save time in practice
C: Making charts two-dimensional only and never using 3D views
D: Making a data set smaller on the disk by compressing the files
Why A: Dimensionality reduction cuts the number of features while keeping the important information, which makes data simpler to handle and often speeds up training.
Why B: Reducing the number of rows to zero would leave no data at all, and dimensionality reduction works on the features, which are the columns, not the rows.
Why C: Making charts two-dimensional is a display choice, whereas dimensionality reduction changes the number of features in the data used by a model.
Why D: Compressing files makes them smaller on disk but keeps every feature, while dimensionality reduction cuts the number of features used in the analysis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a training set?
A: A set of machines in a gym used for training
B: The portion used to check final performance
C: A set of instructions for users of a new course
D: The portion of data used to teach the model
Why A: A set of machines in a gym is exercise equipment, and the training set in machine learning is data, not a group of physical machines.
Why B: The portion used to check final performance is the test set, which is held back, and the training set is the part used to teach the model.
Why C: A set of instructions for users of a course is teaching material for people, while a training set is a part of the data given to the model.
Why D: The training set is the portion of data used to teach the model, since the model adjusts its parameters by learning patterns from these examples.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a validation set used for?
A: Tuning a model and choosing settings during development
B: Printing the final report of the study for all managers
C: Storing backups of the data on a server in another city
D: Teaching the model first with the labeled examples
Why A: A validation set is used to tune a model and choose settings such as hyperparameters during development, without touching the test set that is saved for the end.
Why B: Printing a final report for managers is communication of results, and it is not the purpose of a validation set, which is used while building the model.
Why C: Storing backups in another city is data protection, which has no connection to validation, since a validation set is a part of data used to compare model settings.
Why D: Teaching the model first with labeled examples is the job of the training set, whereas the validation set is used afterward to tune and compare settings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should the test set be kept separate until the end?
A: So the model can learn from it faster, as more examples help
B: So it gives an honest check of how the model performs on new data
C: So it uses less memory on the computer during the training run
D: So no one can see the data until the very last step of the work as a rule
Why A: Letting the model learn from the test set would contaminate it, and a model that trains on test data gives scores that look better than they really are.
Why B: Keeping the test set separate until the end gives an honest estimate of how the model will perform on new data it has never seen.
Why C: Memory use is not the reason, since the test set is kept apart to avoid bias in the score, not to save memory during the training run.
Why D: The point is not secrecy from people, since the test set is kept unused in training so the final score is a fair measure, not hidden from viewers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is transfer learning?
A: Transferring money between accounts at a bank or a credit union
B: Copying a file to a USB drive to carry it to another computer
C: Reusing a model trained on one task as a starting point for another
D: Moving a model to another computer so it can run on a faster processor
Why A: Moving money between bank accounts is a financial transaction, and transfer learning in AI is about reusing a trained model, not about funds.
Why B: Copying a file to a USB drive only moves data from one place to another, and it does not reuse learned knowledge as transfer learning does.
Why C: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on one task as a starting point for another task, which saves time and data compared with training from nothing.
Why D: Moving a model to a faster computer is deployment or hardware migration, but transfer learning reuses what a model already learned for a new task, not where it runs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is model deployment?
A: Writing the model's documentation and a guide to it for users as a rule
B: Training a model on more data to raise its accuracy over time
C: Deleting a model after training to free up room on the server
D: Putting a trained model into use so people or systems can use it
Why A: Writing documentation and a guide helps users understand a model, but it does not put the model into use, which is what deployment means.
Why B: Training on more data to raise accuracy is part of model development, which happens before deployment, since deployment is about using the trained model in practice.
Why C: Deleting a model after training would remove it from use, whereas deployment makes a trained model available so it can serve real users or systems.
Why D: Model deployment means putting a trained model into use, for example in an app or service, so that people or other systems can get its predictions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why must deployed models be monitored over time?
A: Software licenses expire and stop the model from running
B: Hardware wears out quickly and corrupts the stored model
C: Real-world data can change and make predictions less accurate
D: Models improve automatically without data or any updates
Why A: Licenses are not the reason for monitoring. Real-world data can change, making predictions less accurate over time.
Why B: Stored models do not wear out or corrupt this way. Monitoring is needed because real-world data can change and lower accuracy.
Why C: Real-world data can change over time, so a deployed model's predictions may become less accurate, and monitoring detects this early so the model can be updated.
Why D: Models do not improve by themselves without new data or updates, since a deployed model stays fixed unless people retrain it, which is why monitoring matters.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is concept drift?
A: A change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes over time
B: A slow internet connection that delays pages from loading on a screen
C: A change in office layout when desks are moved around to new places
D: A flickering computer screen caused by a loose cable or a weak card
Why A: Concept drift is a change over time in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, so a model that once predicted well may become less accurate.
Why B: A slow internet connection delays page loading, which is a network issue and has no link to how a model's input and output relationship changes.
Why C: A change in office layout is about workspace and furniture, whereas concept drift is a change in the pattern a model has learned from data.
Why D: A flickering screen from a loose cable is a hardware fault, and concept drift describes a shift in the data pattern, not a display problem.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is overfitting?
A: A model that uses too little storage space on the disk where it is saved
B: A model learning the training data too closely and failing on new data
C: A model that is too simple to learn the patterns that are present in the data
D: A model that runs too fast and so cannot be trusted by the users who see it
Why A: Using too little storage space is a resource matter, but overfitting concerns how a model learns, so file storage on a disk does not define it.
Why B: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, and then does poorly on new data it has not seen.
Why C: A model too simple to learn the patterns in the data is underfitting, which is the opposite problem to overfitting, where the model is too closely fitted.
Why D: Running fast does not make a model overfit or untrustworthy, since overfitting is about poor performance on new data after memorizing the training set.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action helps reduce overfitting?
A: Training for much longer on the same data again
B: Adding many irrelevant features to the data
C: Using only a few training examples for the model
D: Using more training data or simplifying the model
Why A: Training much longer on the same data lets the model memorize it even more, so it tends to increase overfitting and not reduce it.
Why B: Adding many irrelevant features gives the model more noise to memorize, which raises the risk of overfitting instead of lowering it.
Why C: Using only a few training examples makes it easier for a model to memorize them, so this tends to worsen overfitting.
Why D: More training data gives the model more variety, and a simpler model has less room to memorize noise, so both steps help reduce overfitting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ensemble method?
A: Splitting data into a single column to save space
B: Using a single very large model trained once on all data
C: Playing music during training to keep the staff calm
D: Combining several models to get a better prediction
Why A: Splitting data into a single column to save space changes how data is stored, and it has no link to combining models, which is what an ensemble does.
Why B: A single very large model trained once is not an ensemble, because an ensemble uses several models whose outputs are combined for a better result.
Why C: Playing music during training has no effect on a model, and an ensemble method is about combining models and not about the mood of the staff.
Why D: An ensemble method combines several models, for example by voting or averaging, so the group gives a better prediction than most single models alone would.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recommender system based on collaborative filtering?
A: One that filters spam from emails and blocks bad links
B: One that suggests items similar in description to what the user viewed
C: One that suggests items liked by users with similar tastes
D: One that suggests the items that sold best this week
Why A: Filtering spam from emails is a classification task for security, and it has nothing to do with suggesting items based on what similar users liked.
Why B: That is content-based filtering, which compares item features. Collaborative filtering uses the preferences of users with similar tastes.
Why C: Collaborative filtering suggests items that users with similar tastes liked, using patterns in ratings or behavior across many users to predict what someone will enjoy.
Why D: Suggesting best sellers uses overall popularity, not personal taste. Collaborative filtering recommends items liked by users with similar tastes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A streaming service suggests a show because people with similar watch histories enjoyed it. This is an example of:
A: Speech recognition AI
B: Collaborative filtering
C: Data encryption tools
D: Rule-based programming
Why A: Speech recognition AI turns spoken words into text, which is a different task from suggesting a show based on what similar viewers watched.
Why B: Suggesting a show because people with similar watch histories enjoyed it is collaborative filtering, which recommends items using the preferences of similar users.
Why C: Data encryption tools protect information by scrambling it, which is a security task and does not produce show suggestions for viewers.
Why D: Rule-based programming follows fixed rules written by people, while this suggestion comes from patterns found across many viewers, which is collaborative filtering.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is perception in AI?
A: A system's ability to interpret sensory input such as images or sound
B: A system's ability to print documents and send them to a printer
C: A system's ability to rewrite its own hardware to run much faster
D: A system's ability to store large files on its internal disk drives overall
Why A: Perception in AI is a system's ability to interpret sensory input such as images or sound, which lets it make sense of what is around it.
Why B: Printing documents and sending them to a printer is an output task, while perception is about understanding input from the world.
Why C: Rewriting its own hardware to run faster is not how AI systems work and has nothing to do with perception, which is interpreting sensory input.
Why D: Storing large files on internal disk drives is a storage function, whereas perception is the ability to interpret sensory input such as images or sound.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is object detection?
A: Counting pages in a book or a long report
B: Finding spelling mistakes in a typed document
C: Finding and labeling objects inside an image
D: Detecting power failures in an electric grid
Why A: Counting pages in a book is a simple counting task on documents, and object detection works on images to find and label things in them.
Why B: Finding spelling mistakes is a text checking task, while object detection looks at pictures, not typed documents, to find items.
Why C: Object detection finds objects inside an image and labels them, usually marking each one with a box, such as a car or a person.
Why D: Detecting power failures in a grid is an engineering monitoring task, and object detection is a computer vision task that finds objects in images.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is image classification?
A: Printing an image on paper with a color laser printer
B: Assigning a label to a whole image, such as cat or dog
C: Making an image larger by zooming in on the screen
D: Drawing a box around every object in an image, with a label
Why A: Printing an image on paper is an output task for a printer, and image classification is an AI task that assigns a label to a picture.
Why B: Image classification assigns one label to a whole image, such as cat or dog, based on what the picture mostly shows.
Why C: Zooming in on a screen only changes how large an image looks, and it does not assign a label to the picture, which classification does.
Why D: Drawing a box around every object with a label is object detection, while image classification gives one label to the whole image without locating objects.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is optical character recognition (OCR)?
A: Converting video into photos, frame by frame
B: Converting speech into written text files
C: Converting text into spoken audio files
D: Converting text in images into editable text
Why A: Converting video into photos frame by frame is video processing, and OCR reads text found in images instead of splitting video into pictures.
Why B: Converting speech into written text is speech recognition, which works on audio, while OCR works on images that contain printed or written text.
Why C: Converting text into spoken audio is speech synthesis, which goes in the opposite direction from OCR, which reads text from an image.
Why D: OCR converts text in images, such as scanned pages or photos of signs, into editable text that a computer can search and change.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is knowledge representation?
A: Organizing information so that a computer can use it to reason
B: Deleting information that the computer cannot easily store
C: Showing information on a large screen to a big audience
D: Storing information in a notebook kept on a shelf in an office
Why A: Knowledge representation organizes information in a form that a computer can use to reason, such as facts, rules or graphs, so it can draw conclusions.
Why B: Deleting information that cannot be stored easily would lose knowledge, whereas knowledge representation structures information so that a computer can use it.
Why C: Showing information on a large screen is a display task, and it does not organize facts into a form a computer can reason with.
Why D: Storing information in a notebook on a shelf keeps it on paper, where a computer cannot use it, so it is not knowledge representation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a knowledge graph?
A: A chart of student grades in a school for the whole school year as a rule
B: A network of connected facts about things and their relationships
C: A graph of a company's profits over the past few years in total
D: A list of definitions in alphabetical order, kept in a book
Why A: A chart of student grades summarizes school results and is not a network of facts, which is what a knowledge graph is.
Why B: A knowledge graph is a network of connected facts about things and their relationships, with nodes for entities and links showing how they relate.
Why C: A graph of company profits is a business chart showing numbers over time, while a knowledge graph links entities and their relationships.
Why D: A list of definitions in alphabetical order is a glossary or dictionary, and it does not link facts to each other the way a knowledge graph does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is logical reasoning in AI?
A: Copying text from the web into a document
B: Guessing without any facts at all or proof
C: Drawing conclusions from facts and rules
D: Storing data in a list on a computer disk
Why A: Copying text from the web into a document is data entry and does not involve drawing conclusions, which is what logical reasoning means.
Why B: Guessing without facts or proof is the opposite of logical reasoning, which depends on facts and rules to reach valid conclusions.
Why C: Logical reasoning in AI draws conclusions from known facts and rules, so if the facts are true and the rules are valid, the result follows.
Why D: Storing data in a list on a disk is storage and does not draw conclusions from facts and rules, which defines logical reasoning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A rule says: all invoices over $1,000 need approval. An invoice is $1,500. What does a reasoning system conclude?
A: It must be deleted
B: It must be paid now
C: It needs no approval
D: It needs approval
Why A: Deleting the invoice is not supported by the rule, which only says invoices over $1,000 need approval, so nothing in it calls for deletion.
Why B: The rule says nothing about paying the invoice now, and it only requires approval first, so a reasoning system cannot conclude it must be paid.
Why C: Since 1,500 is greater than 1,000, the rule applies, so saying it needs no approval contradicts the rule and the system would not reach that conclusion.
Why D: The invoice is $1,500, which is over $1,000, so the rule applies and the reasoning system concludes that it needs approval.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an embedding in AI?
A: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of data such as a word
B: A password stored in code and hidden from the users of a site
C: A video placed on a website to explain a product to its visitors in the end
D: A photo added inside a document by a user to illustrate a report
Why A: An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of data such as a word, so similar items get similar vectors.
Why B: A password hidden in code is a secret credential, which is a security matter and not a numeric representation of meaning, as an embedding is.
Why C: A video placed on a website to explain a product is media content, and the word embedding here means a vector, not a page element.
Why D: A photo added inside a document is an embedded image in the everyday sense, but an embedding in AI is a vector of numbers for meaning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are embeddings useful?
A: They permanently remove all errors from the text
B: They make data impossible to read for the user
C: They replace the need for training a model
D: They let models measure how similar items are
Why A: Embeddings do not remove errors from text, since they are numeric representations of meaning, and nothing about them permanently corrects mistakes in the words.
Why B: Embeddings are made for models to use, and they do not hide data from the user, so making data unreadable is not their purpose.
Why C: Models still need training to use embeddings well, so embeddings help the work but they do not replace training a model.
Why D: Embeddings place similar items close together as vectors, so models can measure how similar items are, which helps in search, recommendations and clustering.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a search algorithm in AI?
A: A way of hiding a website from search engines
B: A method for exploring options to find a solution
C: A program that prints search results on paper
D: A tool for deleting search history from a browser
Why A: Hiding a website from search engines is a web publishing setting, and a search algorithm in AI explores options to find a solution.
Why B: A search algorithm in AI explores possible options step by step, such as paths or moves, to find a solution to a problem.
Why C: Printing search results on paper is an output task for a printer, and it does not explore options the way an AI search algorithm does.
Why D: Deleting search history is a privacy action in a browser, while an AI search algorithm explores options to solve a problem.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A navigation app finds the shortest route between two cities. Which AI idea does it use?
A: Generating new roads on the map to shorten each trip
B: Converting speech into text for the driver to read
C: Searching over possible paths to find the best one
D: Compressing the map image to save room on the phone
Why A: Generating new roads would change the map, but a navigation app does not build roads, and it only looks for the best route over roads that exist.
Why B: Converting speech into text is speech recognition, which may help with voice commands, but it is not how the app finds the shortest route.
Why C: A navigation app searches over the possible paths between two cities and picks the best one, such as the shortest, which is the search idea in AI.
Why D: Compressing the map image saves storage, which is a file task, and it does not help the app find the shortest route between two cities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is sentiment analysis?
A: Using AI to find whether text expresses positive, negative or neutral feelings
B: Translating text from one language to another for a global audience of readers
C: Checking text for spelling mistakes and fixing grammar in a long document
D: Counting the words in a document and the pages in each file saved by the user
Why A: Sentiment analysis uses AI to decide whether text expresses positive, negative or neutral feelings, which is useful for reviews, posts and customer messages.
Why B: Translating text between languages is machine translation, which changes the language of the text and does not measure whether the feelings expressed are positive or negative.
Why C: Checking spelling and grammar is proofreading, which fixes writing errors and does not decide whether the text shows positive or negative feelings.
Why D: Counting words and pages is simple document statistics, which measures size, and does not tell whether the writer feels positive or negative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company runs reviews through sentiment analysis. Which result would a negative score suggest?
A: The reviews are too short to be read by the software
B: Customers are very happy with the product or service
C: The reviews were in French so the software failed
D: Customers are unhappy with the product or service
Why A: Reviews being too short would cause missing or weak results, but a negative score says something about the feeling in the text, not about its length.
Why B: Customers who are very happy would give positive text and a positive score, so a negative score suggests the opposite of this.
Why C: A failure on French text would show up as an error or missing result, while a negative score is a valid result showing negative feelings.
Why D: A negative sentiment score suggests that the reviews express negative feelings, so customers are unhappy with the product or service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is speech synthesis?
A: Removing noise from audio files
B: Recognizing spoken words as text
C: Creating spoken audio from text
D: Recording a live conversation call
Why A: Removing noise from audio files is audio cleaning or noise reduction, which improves a recording and does not create speech from written text.
Why B: Recognizing spoken words as text is speech recognition, which is the reverse of speech synthesis, since synthesis starts from text and produces audio.
Why C: Speech synthesis creates spoken audio from text, often called text to speech, and it is used in voice assistants and screen readers.
Why D: Recording a live conversation call captures sound that already exists, whereas speech synthesis generates new spoken audio from written text with a computer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sensor in an AI system?
A: A program that edits videos by adding titles and music overall
B: A device that collects information from the environment
C: A screen that shows results of the work to the user
D: A tool that stores data from the system for later use
Why A: A program that edits videos is software for media editing, and it does not collect information from the environment, which is the role of a sensor.
Why B: A sensor is a device that collects information from the environment, such as a camera, microphone or radar, and passes it to the AI system.
Why C: A screen that shows results is an output device, while a sensor is an input device that gathers information about the surroundings.
Why D: A tool that stores data for later use is a storage device, and a sensor instead gathers new information from the environment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A self-driving car uses cameras and radar. What stage of AI is this?
A: Perception of the environment
B: Writing its own manual first
C: Storing old files on a disk
D: Reporting its profits to owners
Why A: Using cameras and radar to sense the surroundings is perception, the stage in which an AI system gathers and interprets data about its environment.
Why B: Writing its own manual does not describe cameras and radar, which are sensing tools used to understand the road and not to produce documents.
Why C: Storing old files on a disk is a data storage task, and it does not describe how cameras and radar are used to sense the road.
Why D: Reporting profits to owners is a business reporting task and has no link to the cameras and radar that a self-driving car uses to sense its surroundings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is planning in AI?
A: Choosing a sequence of actions to reach a goal
B: Scheduling employee holidays for the year
C: Printing a plan on paper for the whole team
D: Writing a company's yearly budget with finance
Why A: Planning in AI means choosing a sequence of actions to reach a goal, such as a robot working out the steps to move an object.
Why B: Scheduling employee holidays is a human resources job, and although it is called planning in daily speech, AI planning means choosing actions to reach a goal.
Why C: Printing a plan on paper is a document task that outputs a file, whereas AI planning is the process of working out which actions to take.
Why D: Writing a yearly budget is a finance task, and AI planning is about picking actions that reach a goal, not about preparing budgets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is uncertainty in AI reasoning?
A: A guarantee that all answers are right, as the system uses strict logic
B: Not being sure of facts or outcomes, often handled with probability
C: A feeling that machines have when they are about to fail or crash
D: A rule that blocks all decisions made by managers or by the staff
Why A: Uncertainty is the opposite of a guarantee that all answers are right, since strict logic cannot promise this when facts are missing or unclear.
Why B: Uncertainty means not being sure of facts or outcomes, and AI systems often handle it with probability, for example by giving a likelihood instead of a sure answer.
Why C: Machines do not have feelings of dread before a crash, so uncertainty in AI is about incomplete knowledge and not an emotion.
Why D: Uncertainty is not a rule that blocks manager decisions, because it describes how sure a system is about facts, and systems still make decisions under it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data privacy?
A: Backing up customer records so they can be restored after a failure
B: Making data as large as possible so that it fills the whole disk drive
C: Making sure stored data is accurate and kept up to date in the system
D: Protecting personal information from being misused or seen by the wrong people
Why A: Backups protect against data loss, which is availability. Data privacy means protecting personal information from misuse or from being seen by the wrong people.
Why B: Making data as large as possible has no link to privacy, which is about who can access personal information and how it is used, not about size.
Why C: That describes data quality. Data privacy means protecting personal information from being misused or seen by the wrong people.
Why D: Data privacy means protecting personal information from being misused or seen by the wrong people, and giving individuals some control over how their data is used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is personally identifiable information (PII)?
A: Information that is true for everyone in a group
B: Information that is always encrypted by default
C: Information that can identify a specific person
D: Information that is deleted after use by the firm
Why A: Information true for everyone in a group is general knowledge and does not point to one person, while PII is data that can identify a specific person.
Why B: Information being encrypted by default is a protection feature, and it does not define PII, which is data that could identify a person whether or not it is encrypted.
Why C: PII is information that can identify a specific person, such as a name, address, phone number or national ID, alone or when combined with other data.
Why D: Information deleted after use is about retention, which is a different matter, and data can be PII whether or not a firm deletes it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these is PII?
A: A person's home address and phone number
B: The weather forecast for today in your town
C: The number of days in a week or a month
D: The average price of milk in a store
Why A: A home address and phone number can identify a specific person and reach them, so this is PII that needs protection.
Why B: The weather forecast for a town is public information about a place and does not identify any person, so it is not PII.
Why C: The number of days in a week or a month is a general fact and says nothing about any person, so it is not PII.
Why D: The average price of milk is a statistic about a product that does not point to a person, so it does not count as PII.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is anonymization of data?
A: Adding a person's name to every record to trace it
B: Removing or hiding details that identify individuals
C: Making data larger by adding more rows to the table
D: Copying data to a public site for anyone to see
Why A: Adding names to every record would make people easier to identify, which is the opposite of anonymization, which aims to hide identities.
Why B: Anonymization removes or hides details that identify individuals, such as names and ID numbers, so the data can be used with a lower privacy risk.
Why C: Adding more rows increases data volume and does not protect identities, so it is not anonymization, which is about hiding who the records describe.
Why D: Copying data to a public site makes it available to anyone, which puts privacy at risk and does not anonymize anything.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why can supposedly anonymous data still identify people?
A: Computers can read minds and so they can find out who anyone is from nothing
B: Anonymous data is stored on public servers where search engines copy it freely
C: The people in the data later give their names to the researchers who study it
D: Combining details such as birth date, zip code and gender can single someone out
Why A: Computers cannot read minds, and re-identification happens when data already holds details that can be matched, not because machines know things from nothing.
Why B: Where data is stored is not the cause. Re-identification happens when details such as birth date, zip code and gender are combined to single someone out.
Why C: Researchers do not need names from participants. Combining details like birth date, zip code and gender can single someone out.
Why D: Combining details such as birth date, zip code and gender can single someone out, because few people share the same combination, so anonymized data can still be linked to a person.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is informed consent in data collection?
A: People are required to share all data with any firm that asks
B: Data is collected without telling anyone, then used for any purpose
C: People understand how their data will be used and agree to it
D: People are tricked into sharing data they would keep private
Why A: Informed consent is voluntary, so a requirement to share all data with any firm that asks contradicts it, since people must be free to agree or refuse.
Why B: Collecting data without telling anyone and using it for any purpose breaks informed consent, which requires that people know and agree beforehand.
Why C: Informed consent means people understand how their data will be collected and used and then agree to it, which keeps data collection fair and open.
Why D: Tricking people into sharing private data removes real consent, since informed consent depends on honest information and a free choice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the principle of data minimization?
A: Delete data after first use and keep no copy
B: Collect as much data as possible each day
C: Share data with every partner firm we know
D: Collect only the data you actually need
Why A: Deleting data after first use with no copy is an extreme retention rule, but data minimization means collecting only what is needed, not erasing at once.
Why B: Collecting as much data as possible each day is the opposite of data minimization, which limits collection to what a purpose actually requires.
Why C: Sharing data with every partner firm increases exposure of personal information, and data minimization aims to limit data use, not spread it widely.
Why D: Data minimization means collecting only the data you actually need for a stated purpose, which lowers privacy risk and the harm if a breach occurs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data breach?
A: A rule that limits how long a company may keep customer records on file
B: An incident in which private data is accessed or exposed without permission
C: A software update that fixes errors in a program used by the staff
D: A chart that shows sales by region and by month for the whole company
Why A: That describes a retention policy, which is a planned rule. A data breach is an incident where private data is accessed or exposed without permission.
Why B: A data breach is an incident in which private data is accessed or exposed without permission, whether by an attack, a mistake or a lost device.
Why C: Updates are planned maintenance that fix errors. A data breach is an incident in which private data is accessed or exposed without permission.
Why D: A chart of sales by region and month is a business report that shows results and does not describe an incident of unauthorized access.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company discovers hackers stole customer emails. What should it do first?
A: Contain the breach and notify affected people as required
B: Blame the customers for the attack and delay any contact
C: Hide the problem from customers so as not to harm the name
D: Delete the evidence of the attack and carry on as usual
Why A: The right first step is to contain the breach to stop further loss and notify affected people as required, so they can protect themselves.
Why B: Blaming customers and delaying contact is wrong and unethical, because customers did not cause the attack and they need prompt notice to protect themselves.
Why C: Hiding the problem from customers breaks trust and often the law, since many rules require prompt notice, so concealment makes the harm worse.
Why D: Deleting evidence of the attack destroys what investigators need and may be illegal, and carrying on as usual leaves the weakness open to attackers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is encryption?
A: Deleting data permanently from all of the company's servers
B: Copying data to another drive for use as a backup copy
C: Scrambling data so only authorized people can read it
D: Making data easier for all to read by removing passwords
Why A: Deleting data permanently from servers is erasure, which removes the data, whereas encryption keeps the data and scrambles it so only authorized people can read it.
Why B: Copying data to another drive is a backup, which keeps another copy of the data and does not scramble it or limit who can read it.
Why C: Encryption scrambles data using a key so only authorized people with the key can read it, which protects it if it is stolen or intercepted.
Why D: Removing passwords makes data easier for anyone to read, which weakens protection, while encryption does the opposite by making data unreadable without the key.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is multi-factor authentication?
A: Requiring two or more ways to prove identity before access
B: Writing a password on a note and sticking it on a screen overall
C: Sharing a password with a team to make access easier
D: Using one very long password only, changed once a year
Why A: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more ways to prove identity, such as a password plus a code, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
Why B: Writing a password on a note on a screen exposes it to anyone who sees it, which is poor security and not a second factor.
Why C: Sharing a password with a team weakens security and gives one factor to many people, while multi-factor authentication adds independent proofs of identity for one person.
Why D: A single long password is still only one factor, so even changed yearly it does not meet the two or more proofs that multi-factor authentication needs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does GDPR protect?
A: Trade secrets of European firms under union law
B: The speed of the European internet networks today
C: Personal data of people in the European Union
D: The prices of goods in Europe and their taxes
Why A: GDPR protects personal data of individuals and not the trade secrets of firms, which are covered by other business laws, so this option misstates its scope.
Why B: GDPR is a data protection law and does not regulate how fast European networks run, so the speed of the internet is outside its scope.
Why C: GDPR is the European Union law that protects the personal data and privacy of people in the EU, and it gives them rights over their data.
Why D: Goods prices and taxes are matters of trade and tax law, and GDPR deals with personal data, so it does not set prices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does CCPA give California residents?
A: A right to see anyone's data held by any company in any country at will
B: Rights to know about, delete and opt out of the sale of their personal data
C: A right to free internet access at home from any provider in the state
D: A right to avoid all taxes on goods and services sold online in the state in the end
Why A: CCPA covers personal data held by businesses that meet its rules, so it does not let residents see anyone's data from any company in any country.
Why B: CCPA gives California residents the right to know what personal data is collected, to delete it, and to opt out of its sale.
Why C: CCPA is a privacy law and does not provide internet service, so free access at home from any provider is not one of its rights.
Why D: CCPA does not exempt anyone from taxes on online sales, since it is about personal data privacy and has no effect on tax duties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does COPPA protect?
A: Prices of online goods and services
B: Online privacy of adults over 65
C: Copyrights on music and film works
D: Online privacy of children under 13
Why A: Prices of online goods are a consumer and trade matter, while COPPA is a law about the privacy of children online, so it does not cover prices.
Why B: COPPA protects children, not adults over 65, so this option names the wrong group, because the law centers on the online privacy of young children.
Why C: Copyrights on music and film are covered by copyright law, and COPPA is a privacy law, so the similar sounding name does not mean it covers copyright.
Why D: COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, protects the online privacy of children under 13 by requiring parental consent before sites collect their personal data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does HIPAA protect?
A: The privacy of voter choices in an election
B: The privacy of bank accounts and the records overall
C: The privacy and security of health information
D: The privacy of school grades and test scores
Why A: Voter choices are protected by election laws and the secret ballot, and HIPAA is a law about health information, so it does not cover voting.
Why B: Bank accounts and financial records are covered by financial privacy laws, whereas HIPAA covers health information, so this option names the wrong subject.
Why C: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of health information, such as medical records held by providers and insurers, and sets rules on who may see them.
Why D: School grades and test scores fall under education privacy law, FERPA, and HIPAA covers health information, so this option mixes up the two laws.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does FERPA protect?
A: The privacy of bank records and accounts
B: The privacy of student education records
C: The privacy of medical records at hospitals
D: The privacy of phone calls and texts
Why A: Bank records and accounts are covered by financial privacy rules, not FERPA, which is an education privacy law, so this option names the wrong area.
Why B: FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, protects the privacy of student education records, such as grades, and gives students and parents rights over them.
Why C: Medical records at hospitals are protected by health privacy law, HIPAA, and FERPA covers education records, so this option confuses the two laws.
Why D: Phone calls and texts are covered by communications and wiretap laws, which differ from FERPA, a law that deals with student education records.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is AI ethics?
A: Principles about developing and using AI in fair, safe and responsible ways
B: Rules for buying AI hardware such as chips and servers for a company
C: A method for storing AI models on a server in a safe and secure data center
D: Rules that make AI run faster on a computer by using better chips now
Why A: AI ethics is the set of principles about developing and using AI in fair, safe and responsible ways, so that it benefits people and avoids harm.
Why B: Rules for buying AI hardware are purchasing policy, and AI ethics deals with how AI is built and used and its effects on people.
Why C: Storing AI models in a secure data center is a security and operations task, and it does not address fairness, safety or responsibility, which define ethics.
Why D: Making AI run faster with better chips is a performance goal, whereas AI ethics is about whether AI is used fairly, safely and responsibly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is algorithmic bias?
A: An algorithm that writes poetry and songs for the readers of a magazine
B: An algorithm that runs quickly and so gives groups different results
C: An algorithm with no input data and so no way to give an output
D: Unfair outcomes from an algorithm that favors or harms certain groups
Why A: An algorithm writing poetry describes a creative use of AI, and it does not describe unfair outcomes for groups, which is what algorithmic bias means.
Why B: Running quickly does not cause bias, because bias comes from skewed data or design choices, and speed alone does not make results differ across groups.
Why C: An algorithm with no input data could not produce results at all, so it cannot be biased, and this option describes a broken system and not bias.
Why D: Algorithmic bias is when an algorithm produces unfair outcomes that favor or harm certain groups, often because of skewed training data or flawed design choices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A loan model approves fewer applicants from one neighborhood even when finances are equal. What is the likely issue?
A: Better accuracy
B: Faster processing
C: Algorithmic bias
D: Data compression
Why A: Better accuracy would mean the model predicts well for everyone, but approving fewer applicants from one neighborhood with equal finances points to unfair treatment, so accuracy is not the issue.
Why B: Faster processing concerns speed, and it would not explain why equally qualified applicants from one neighborhood are approved less often, which is an issue of fairness.
Why C: Approving fewer applicants from one neighborhood when finances are equal shows an unfair pattern against a group, which is algorithmic bias, often from skewed data.
Why D: Data compression reduces file size and has no effect on who is approved, so it cannot explain unequal approval for equal finances.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which step best reduces bias in an AI system?
A: Collecting as much data as possible from the easiest sources
B: Hiding the data sources from users and testers during review
C: Training until the model scores perfectly on its training data
D: Using diverse, representative data and testing results across groups
Why A: Volume from easy sources can still miss groups and repeat bias. Reducing bias needs diverse, representative data and tests across groups.
