Why B: Hiding sources makes bias harder to spot. Reducing bias needs diverse, representative data and testing results across groups.
Why C: A perfect training score suggests overfitting and does not check fairness. Reducing bias needs diverse, representative data and tests across groups.
Why D: Using diverse, representative data and testing results across groups helps find and fix unfair patterns, which is the best way to reduce bias.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is transparency in AI?
A: Being open about how a system works and makes decisions
B: Hiding how a system works from users and from regulators
C: Making the screen see-through so users can look inside
D: Using only small data sets that fit in one spreadsheet
Why A: Transparency means being open about how a system works and makes decisions, so users and regulators can understand, question and check its results.
Why B: Hiding how a system works from users and regulators is the opposite of transparency, which depends on openness about how the system makes decisions.
Why C: Making a screen see-through is a literal reading of the word, but transparency in AI is about being open on how the system works.
Why D: Using only small data sets has no link to openness about how decisions are made, which is what transparency in AI is about.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is explainable AI?
A: AI that refuses to answer questions so it never errs
B: AI whose decisions can be understood by people
C: AI that explains jokes and puzzles to its users
D: AI that is hidden from users and from auditors
Why A: An AI that refuses to answer questions is not explainable, and avoiding answers does not make its decisions understandable, so this does not match the idea.
Why B: Explainable AI means the decisions of the system can be understood by people, with clear reasons given for why it produced a result.
Why C: An AI that explains jokes and puzzles describes a task it performs, but explainable AI is about making the AI's own decisions understandable.
Why D: An AI hidden from users and auditors is the opposite of explainable, because explainability means people can see and understand how decisions are made.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accountability in AI?
A: Clear responsibility for the outcomes an AI system causes
B: Counting the money spent on AI projects each year by firms
C: Blaming the computer for every error that ever occurs
D: Hiding who built the system from the public and from users
Why A: Accountability in AI means there is clear responsibility for the outcomes an AI system causes, so someone answers for its results and for fixing harm.
Why B: Counting the money spent on AI projects is financial accounting, which tracks costs, and it does not assign responsibility for what an AI system does.
Why C: Blaming the computer for every error avoids human responsibility, whereas accountability requires that people or organizations answer for the system.
Why D: Hiding who built the system defeats accountability, since people need to know who is responsible for the outcomes in order to hold them to account.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An AI tool wrongly denies a customer's claim. Who should be accountable?
A: Only the software itself and its code
B: The customer who made the claim to the firm
C: The organization that deployed the tool
D: No one, as the work was fully automated
Why A: Software cannot be held responsible, because it has no legal duty or ability to make amends, so blaming only the code leaves no accountable party.
Why B: The customer only made a claim and did not build or run the tool, so blaming the customer for a wrong denial shifts responsibility to the wrong party.
Why C: The organization that deployed the tool chose to use it and benefits from it, so it is accountable for wrong outcomes such as a wrongly denied claim.
Why D: Automation does not remove responsibility, because people and organizations choose and run these tools, so saying no one is accountable fails customers who are harmed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a deepfake?
A: A fast video format that loads in a browser without any delay for the viewer
B: A very deep database that stores records in many nested levels of folders
C: A real video with captions added to show what each person says on screen
D: Fake media created by AI that makes someone appear to say or do something
Why A: A fast video format is a technical file type for streaming, and deepfake refers to fake media made by AI, not to loading speed.
Why B: A deep database with nested folders is a storage structure, and the deep in deepfake comes from deep learning, not from levels of folders.
Why C: A real video with captions is genuine footage with text added, while a deepfake is synthetic media that shows something that never happened.
Why D: A deepfake is fake media created by AI, often a video or audio clip, that makes someone appear to say or do something they never did.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are deepfakes an ethical concern?
A: They are impossible to create with any software
B: They can deceive people and damage reputations
C: They cannot be shared online by any user or any firm
D: They always improve public safety by warning people
Why A: Deepfakes can be created with many readily available tools, so saying they are impossible to make is false, and that ease is part of the concern.
Why B: Deepfakes can deceive people and damage reputations, since realistic fake video or audio can spread false claims about a person and erode trust in real media.
Why C: Deepfakes can be shared online like other media, so saying nobody can share them is false, and wide sharing is why they can cause harm.
Why D: Deepfakes do not always improve safety, and warning people is not their usual use, since they are more often used to mislead, scam or harass.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is copyright concern with AI training data?
A: Whether creators' work was used without permission
B: Whether the data is too clean to use in a model
C: Whether the model is named correctly by its makers
D: Whether the computer running the model is large enough
Why A: The copyright concern is whether creators' work was used without permission to train AI, since models may learn from books, art or code that creators own.
Why B: Data being too clean is not a copyright question, as copyright asks whether the data was used with permission, not how tidy it is.
Why C: Whether the model is named correctly is a matter of branding and labels, and copyright concerns are about the use of creators' work.
Why D: The size of the computer running the model is a hardware matter and has no link to whether the training data was used with permission.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which practice respects creators when using AI-generated content?
A: Selling others' work without asking for their consent
B: Removing the creator's name from the work before sharing it
C: Checking permissions and giving proper credit where required
D: Copying any work found online and passing it off as your own
Why A: Selling others' work without consent violates their rights and disrespects creators, so it is the opposite of a practice that respects them.
Why B: Removing the creator's name before sharing hides who made the work and denies credit, which disrespects creators and can break the terms of use.
Why C: Checking permissions and giving proper credit where required respects the rights of creators, and keeps the use of AI content legal and fair.
Why D: Copying work found online and passing it off as your own is plagiarism, which steals credit and breaks copyright, so it fails to respect creators.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is human oversight in AI?
A: Turning off all computers in the office at the end of the day
B: People reviewing and being able to override AI decisions
C: Hiding AI outputs from people so that they cannot review them
D: Letting the AI run with no review by people at all times
Why A: Turning off computers at the end of the day is an office routine, and it does not involve people reviewing or controlling what an AI decides.
Why B: Human oversight means people review AI decisions and can override them, so a person keeps control and can correct mistakes before harm results.
Why C: Hiding AI outputs from people prevents any review, so it removes oversight and does the opposite of what human oversight is meant to do.
Why D: Letting the AI run with no review by people removes oversight altogether, and errors or bias could go uncaught, so this is the absence of human oversight.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which decision is most appropriate to keep under human review rather than fully automating?
A: Sorting incoming emails into folders
B: Spell checking a long draft report
C: Resizing images for a website page
D: Denying a person's medical treatment
Why A: Sorting incoming emails into folders is a low-stakes task where a mistake is easy to fix, so full automation is acceptable and review is not essential.
Why B: Spell checking a draft is low-risk, and a wrong suggestion is easy to spot and undo, so it does not need to be kept under human review.
Why C: Resizing images for a web page is routine and low-risk, with errors easy to see and fix, so it does not need human review.
Why D: Denying medical treatment can seriously harm a person, so a human should review the decision and be able to override it instead of leaving it fully automated.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is surveillance concern with AI?
A: Making videos higher resolution so cameras capture more detail
B: Making screens brighter so that they are easier to see
C: Making cameras cheaper to buy for homes and small shops
D: Tracking people's activities in ways that can invade privacy
Why A: Making videos higher resolution is an improvement in image quality, and it does not by itself describe the privacy worry of tracking what people do.
Why B: Brighter screens help people see content more easily, which is a display feature and has no link to the tracking of people.
Why C: Cheaper cameras for homes and shops are a cost matter, and they are not the concern, which is the tracking of people by AI.
Why D: Surveillance concern with AI is about tracking people's activities, for example with face recognition, in ways that can invade their privacy and limit their freedom.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store uses face recognition on every shopper without telling them. What is the main concern?
A: It may invade privacy without consent
B: It makes the whole store much quieter
C: It guarantees better service for all
D: It lowers the price of goods for all
Why A: Using face recognition on shoppers without telling them may invade their privacy without consent, which is the main concern raised by this scenario.
Why B: Face recognition does not make a store quieter, and noise level has no link to the concern, which is about people being identified without being told.
Why C: Nothing guarantees better service from face recognition, and even if it helped, doing it without telling shoppers still raises privacy and consent problems.
Why D: Nothing here suggests lower prices, and cheaper goods would not remove the concern that shoppers are being identified without their knowledge or consent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data ownership?
A: Who pays for the internet at the main office
B: Who has rights to control and use a set of data
C: Who stores the data on a shelf or in a cabinet
D: Who deletes the data first in the firm each year
Why A: Who pays for the internet at the office is a billing question and does not say who has rights to control and use a set of data.
Why B: Data ownership is about who has rights to control and use a set of data, including who may share it, sell it or change it.
Why C: Who stores data on a shelf or in a cabinet only describes where it is kept, and holding data does not mean having the rights to control it.
Why D: Who deletes the data first each year is a task assignment, and ownership is about rights and control over the data, not who performs deletion.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a privacy policy?
A: A chart of server speed over time that shows how fast pages load for users overall
B: A password for a website that lets users sign in and see their own account
C: A statement explaining how an organization collects, uses and protects data
D: A rule that blocks websites that do not agree to the terms of the user
Why A: A chart of server speed over time is a performance report that shows how fast pages load, and it does not explain how data is handled.
Why B: A password lets users sign in to an account, which is an access tool, and it does not describe how an organization treats personal data.
Why C: A privacy policy is a statement explaining how an organization collects, uses and protects data, so people can understand what happens to their information.
Why D: A privacy policy does not block websites that refuse terms, since it is a notice from an organization about its data practices, not a blocking rule.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Before signing up for an app, what should a user check about their data?
A: How many stars the app has in the store
B: What data is collected and how it is shared
C: Nothing, since all apps are identical in design
D: How much storage space the app needs on the phone
Why A: Star ratings reflect user opinion of features, not data handling. A user should check what data is collected and how it is shared.
Why B: Before signing up, a user should check what data is collected and how it is shared, since this shows the privacy risks they are accepting.
Why C: Apps differ in what data they collect and share, so saying they are all identical is false, and checking nothing leaves a user unaware of risks.
Why D: Storage size says nothing about privacy. A user should check what data is collected and how it is shared.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is phishing?
A: A hobby of catching fish in a lake or a river on weekends
B: A method of encrypting files so that only the owner can read
C: A scam that tricks people into giving away sensitive information
D: A kind of data chart used to show shares of a total as slices in the end
Why A: Catching fish with a rod is a hobby spelled similarly, but phishing in computing is a scam and not an outdoor activity.
Why B: Encrypting files so only the owner can read them is a protection method, while phishing is an attack that tries to trick people.
Why C: Phishing is a scam that tricks people into giving away sensitive information, such as passwords or card numbers, often with fake emails or sites that look real.
Why D: A chart showing shares of a total as slices is a pie chart, which is a data display, and it has no link to phishing scams.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An email from 'IT' asks you to enter your password on a strange link. What should you do?
A: Not click and report the email
B: Reply with your password now
C: Click and enter your password now
D: Forward it to all coworkers
Why A: Not clicking and reporting the email is right, because an unexpected request for a password on a strange link is typical of phishing, and reporting helps protect others.
Why B: Replying with your password gives it directly to a possible attacker, and real IT staff do not ask for passwords by email, so this is unsafe.
Why C: Clicking and entering your password on a strange link sends it to a possible scam site, which gives attackers access to your account.
Why D: Forwarding the email to all coworkers spreads the phishing message and puts more people at risk, so it should be reported through proper channels instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the principle of fairness in AI?
A: Systems should return results as fast as the hardware allows
B: Systems should use as much personal data as they can collect
C: Systems should favor large companies over small ones in the market
D: Systems should treat people equitably and avoid discrimination
Why A: Speed is a performance goal, not fairness. Fairness means treating people equitably and avoiding discrimination.
Why B: Collecting more personal data raises privacy risk and does not ensure equal treatment. Fairness means treating people equitably and avoiding discrimination.
Why C: Favoring large companies over small ones is unequal treatment, which goes against fairness, since fair systems do not give one group an unearned advantage.
Why D: Fairness in AI means systems should treat people equitably and avoid discrimination, so decisions do not disadvantage people because of traits such as race or gender.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best reason to audit an AI system regularly?
A: To remove the need for rules and for human review of results
B: To find errors, bias or harmful outcomes that appear over time
C: To make the system more costly, since each audit adds expense overall
D: To keep users from seeing results of the system's work tasks
Why A: Audits add oversight rather than replace it, so removing rules and human review of results would raise risk and is the opposite of what an audit is for.
Why B: Regular audits catch errors, bias and harmful outcomes that creep in as data, users and conditions change, which makes ongoing checks of a deployed AI system worthwhile.
Why C: Expense is a side effect of auditing, never its goal, and a reason that aims at higher cost is not a sound justification for checking an AI system.
Why D: Audits examine whether the system behaves well and fairly, so hiding its results from users would reduce transparency and does nothing to find problems in its work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is responsible AI?
A: Building AI that earns the highest profit for its owners
B: Using AI that is the newest and most advanced model available
C: Building and using AI that is safe, fair and accountable
D: Hiding AI use from regulators and from the public at large
Why A: Profit is a business goal, not a standard of responsibility. Responsible AI is built and used to be safe, fair and accountable.
Why B: Being the newest says nothing about safety or fairness. Responsible AI is safe, fair and accountable.
Why C: Responsible AI means designing and using systems that are safe, fair and accountable, so that people can trust them and someone answers for the harms they may cause.
Why D: Hiding AI use from regulators and the public removes transparency and accountability, which are core parts of responsible AI, so it describes irresponsible behavior instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean to be data literate?
A: Being able to type very fast and to write long reports without any errors
B: Being able to memorize large tables of numbers and repeat them
C: Being able to buy data cheaply from sellers in any market that sells it
D: Being able to read, understand and question data and its conclusions
Why A: Typing speed and report length have nothing to do with data skills, and error-free writing says nothing about whether someone can interpret or question numbers and charts.
Why B: Memorizing large tables is not data literacy, since the skill is understanding and judging data, and recalling numbers from memory does not show that anyone grasps their meaning.
Why C: Buying data cheaply is a commercial skill and says nothing about understanding it, so purchasing ability does not make a person able to read or question data.
Why D: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand and question data and the conclusions drawn from it, which lets people spot weak evidence and misleading claims.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bar chart starts its vertical axis at 90 instead of 0 to exaggerate a small difference. What is this?
A: A misleading visualization
B: A data cleaning step done
C: A way to protect privacy
D: A fair chart of the data
Why A: Starting the vertical axis at 90 instead of 0 makes a small gap look large, which distorts the picture and so makes this chart a misleading visualization.
Why B: Data cleaning means fixing errors, duplicates or missing values in the data itself, while changing where an axis starts only alters how the chart looks to viewers.
Why C: Privacy protection involves masking or removing personal details, and a truncated axis hides nothing about individuals, so it has no connection to protecting anyone's data.
Why D: A fair chart shows differences at honest scale, usually with the axis starting at zero for bars, so a chart exaggerating a small gap is not fair.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data-driven decision?
A: A choice made by the loudest voice in the whole room
B: A choice based on analysis of data rather than guesswork
C: A choice made without any information, based on a guess overall
D: A choice made by flipping a coin in the main office
Why A: A decision driven by the loudest voice rests on influence and not evidence, so it is not based on analysis of data and does not qualify as data-driven.
Why B: A data-driven decision relies on analysis of relevant data to guide the choice, which reduces guesswork and lets the reasoning be checked by others afterward.
Why C: A choice made with no information is a guess by definition, and data-driven decisions are the opposite because they depend on evidence gathered and analyzed first.
Why D: Flipping a coin is pure chance and uses no data at all, so it cannot be called a decision based on analysis of evidence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A manager sees that sales rose after a new ad and says the ad caused the rise. What should an analyst check?
A: Nothing, because timing proves cause and a rise after an ad shows it worked
B: Whether the ad cost more than the one used the previous year
C: Whether other factors, such as seasons or promotions, could explain it
D: Whether the ad was shown on more channels than competitors used
Why A: Timing alone does not prove cause, because events can follow each other by coincidence, so concluding the ad worked without any further checks is a classic correlation error.
Why B: Ad cost does not show what caused the rise. The analyst should check whether other factors, such as seasons or promotions, could explain it.
Why C: An analyst should test for confounders such as seasons, promotions or price changes that could also explain the rise before claiming that the ad caused higher sales.
Why D: Channel counts compared to competitors do not test other causes. The analyst should check whether seasons, promotions or other factors explain the rise.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the median?
A: The spread of the data around a mean
B: The average of all of the data values
C: The value that appears most often here
D: The middle value of a sorted data set
Why A: The spread of data around a mean describes variation, such as standard deviation, and not the median, which is a measure of the center of the data.
Why B: The average of all values is the mean, found by adding them and dividing by the count, and is a different measure from the median.
Why C: The value that appears most often is the mode, which can differ from the median, so this describes a different measure of center.
Why D: The median is the middle value once the data are sorted, with half the values below it and half above, which makes it a resistant measure of center.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Incomes in a town are 30, 32, 35, 36 and 500 (in thousands). Which measure best represents a typical income?
A: The median
B: The maximum
C: The mean
D: The range
Why A: With one extreme value of 500, the median of 30, 32, 35, 36 and 500 is 35, which stays close to most incomes and so represents a typical person best.
Why B: The maximum is 500, which is far above the other four incomes, so it describes only the single extreme value and not a typical income in the town.
Why C: The mean is (30+32+35+36+500)/5 = 633/5 = 126.6, which is pulled far above four of the five incomes by the outlier and so misleads here.
Why D: The range is 500 - 30 = 470, which measures spread and not a typical income, so it cannot represent what a typical person in the town earns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is standard deviation?
A: The average of the values, found by adding them up
B: The count of values in a data set that are above the mean
C: The middle of the data after it is sorted from low to high
D: A measure of how spread out values are around the mean
Why A: Adding values and dividing by their count gives the mean, which measures the center of the data, whereas standard deviation measures how far values spread from that center.
Why B: Counting the values above the mean is a simple tally and says nothing about how far values lie from the mean, which is what standard deviation measures.
Why C: The middle of sorted data is the median, a measure of center, so it describes a different statistic from standard deviation, which measures spread.
Why D: Standard deviation measures how spread out values are around the mean, so a larger value means the data are more scattered and a smaller one means they cluster closely.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two classes have the same mean score. Class A has a standard deviation of 2 and Class B has 15. Which is more consistent?
A: Class B
B: Class A
C: No mean
D: Identical
Why A: Class B has a standard deviation of 15, much larger than 2, so its scores are more scattered around the shared mean and it is less consistent.
Why B: With equal means, the smaller standard deviation signals less spread, and Class A at 2 is far tighter than Class B at 15, so Class A is more consistent.
Why C: Both classes do have a mean, since the question says they share one, so the claim of no mean is false and answers nothing about consistency.
Why D: The classes share a mean but differ in spread, 2 versus 15, so their score patterns are not identical and consistency clearly differs between them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a normal distribution, about what share of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean?
A: About 68%
B: About 99.7%
C: About 50%
D: About 10%
Why A: The empirical rule says about 68% of values in a normal distribution fall within one standard deviation of the mean, with 95% within two and 99.7% within three.
Why B: About 99.7% of values lie within three standard deviations of the mean, not one, so this figure belongs to a much wider interval than the one asked about.
Why C: Fifty percent is the share below the mean in a symmetric distribution and not the share within one standard deviation, which is about 68% in a normal distribution.
Why D: Ten percent is far too small, since the central region within one standard deviation holds about 68% of a normal distribution, which is most of the values.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a population versus a sample?
A: Two names for the same thing in the field of statistics
B: A graph versus a table of data in a report that is printed
C: The full group of interest versus a subset drawn from it
D: A subset versus the full group, where the sample is the larger
Why A: Population and sample are different ideas, since a sample is only part of the population, so calling them two names for one thing is wrong in statistics.
Why B: Population and sample describe groups of subjects or items being studied, not display formats, so comparing them to a graph and a table confuses data with its presentation.
Why C: A population is the entire group of interest, while a sample is a smaller subset drawn from it and used to learn about the whole group.
Why D: This reverses the definitions, because a sample is the smaller subset and the population is the full group, so the sample cannot be the larger of the two.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is sampling bias?
A: A random sample drawn from every member of the population
B: A sample with no data in it, so that nothing can be measured
C: A very large sample that includes thousands of people in a town
D: A sample that systematically does not represent the population
Why A: A random sample drawn from every member gives each person a fair chance, which reduces bias, so this describes a sound method and not sampling bias.
Why B: An empty sample has no data and so cannot be measured, but sampling bias concerns samples that exist yet misrepresent the population, so this does not fit.
Why C: Large size does not cure bias, since a huge sample from the wrong group still misleads, and size alone is not what sampling bias means.
Why D: Sampling bias happens when the way a sample is chosen systematically leaves out or overweights some groups, so results do not represent the whole population.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A survey about school lunches only asks students in the cafeteria line. What problem does this create?
A: Many variables
B: Sampling bias
C: Pure randomness
D: No problem at all
Why A: Many variables is not the issue here, since the flaw lies in who was asked and not in how many measures were collected in the survey.
Why B: Surveying only students in the cafeteria line leaves out those who bring lunch or skip it, so the sample misrepresents all students, which is sampling bias.
Why C: The choice of only cafeteria-line students is not random, since it follows a clear pattern of who is included, so pure randomness does not describe the problem.
Why D: Asking only one group leaves out students who may feel differently about lunches, so there is a real problem, and saying there is none ignores the bias created.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. What is the best conclusion?
A: Sunburn causes ice cream sales, because burned people go out to buy a cold treat
B: Ice cream causes sunburn because of the sugar and the cold inside it
C: They are correlated, likely because of a shared cause such as hot weather
D: They are unrelated, since the two have no link in the data at all
Why A: Sunburn does not cause ice cream sales, because both simply rise with summer heat, and burned people buying a cold treat is an unsupported story about cause.
Why B: Ice cream does not cause sunburn, since sunburn comes from sun exposure, and the sugar and cold in the treat have no effect on skin damage.
Why C: The two rise together, which is a correlation, and a shared cause such as hot weather explains both, so correlation here does not mean one causes the other.
Why D: The data show both rising in summer, so they are related in a measurable way, and calling them unrelated ignores the correlation that the numbers show.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is conditional probability?
A: The probability of an event given that another has occurred
B: A random guess made by an analyst with no data at hand
C: The chance an event never happens, however often tried
D: The sum of all probabilities in a sample space of events as a rule
Why A: Conditional probability is the chance of an event given that another event has already occurred, written P(A given B), and it changes how likely A is judged to be.
Why B: A random guess with no data is not a probability calculation, and conditional probability is a precise measure that depends on a stated known event.
Why C: An event that never happens has probability zero, which is a fixed value and not conditional probability, which depends on another event having occurred.
Why D: All probabilities across a sample space add to 1, which is a rule about totals and does not define the chance of one event given another.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A fair die is rolled. What is the probability of an even number?
Why A: A fair die has 3 even faces out of 6, namely 2, 4 and 6, so the probability of rolling an even number is 3/6 = 1/2.
Why B: One in six is the chance of a single specific face, but there are 3 even faces, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2 and not 1/6.
Why C: One third would match only 2 favorable faces out of 6, but the even faces are 2, 4 and 6, which makes 3 of 6 or 1/2.
Why D: Two thirds would need 4 favorable faces out of 6, but only 3 faces are even, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2 and not 2/3.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a p-value?
A: The size of the sample used in the test, shown as a count of the people in it who took part
B: The mean of the data, found by adding all the values and dividing by their count
C: The probability the null hypothesis is true, given the data from the sample table
D: The probability of results at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true
Why A: Sample size is the count of observations in the test, which is a separate quantity from a p-value, which measures how surprising the results would be under the null.
Why B: The mean is found by adding values and dividing by their count and describes the center of the data, not the evidence against a null hypothesis.
Why C: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, which is a common misreading, because it assumes the null is true and asks about the data.
Why D: A p-value is the probability of seeing results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis is true, so small values count as evidence against it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hypothesis test used for?
A: Cleaning missing values from a data set before an analysis
B: Judging whether data provide enough evidence against a claim
C: Drawing charts only, to show the results of an analysis to others
D: Collecting data without a plan, to see what turns up in it
Why A: Cleaning missing values is data preparation done before analysis, and it does not test any claim about a population or weigh evidence against a stated hypothesis.
Why B: A hypothesis test weighs how well sample data support or contradict a claim about a population, deciding whether the evidence is strong enough to doubt the claim.
Why C: Drawing charts only displays results and does not weigh evidence about a claim, so it is not what a hypothesis test is used for.
Why D: Collecting data with no plan is aimless exploration, whereas a hypothesis test starts with a stated claim and uses data to check it against a standard.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A data set has the same customer listed twice. What cleaning step applies?
A: Delete the whole data table
B: Rename one copy of the customer
C: Remove the duplicate record
D: Move the copy to a new table
Why A: Deleting the whole table would destroy all the valid records along with the repeat, which is far too drastic when only one repeated entry needs fixing.
Why B: Renaming leaves two records for one customer and still double counts them. The standard fix is to remove the duplicate record.
Why C: Removing the duplicate record keeps one entry per customer and stops that customer from being counted twice, which is the standard cleaning step for repeated rows.
Why D: Moving the copy keeps the customer counted twice across the data. The standard fix is to remove the duplicate record.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows how two numeric variables relate?
A: A word cloud
B: A bar chart
C: A pie chart
D: A scatter plot
Why A: A word cloud shows how often words appear in text, so it cannot display how two numeric variables relate to each other.
Why B: A bar chart compares values across categories, which does not show how two numeric variables move together, so it is the wrong tool for this question.
Why C: A pie chart shows parts of one whole, so it cannot display a relationship between two numeric variables across many observations.
Why D: A scatter plot places each observation as a point by its two values, so patterns such as trends, clusters and correlation between the variables become visible.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows the distribution of one numeric variable?
A: A histogram
B: A pie chart
C: A scatter plot
D: A line chart
Why A: A histogram groups one numeric variable into bins and shows how many values fall in each, which displays the shape of its distribution.
Why B: A pie chart shows shares of a whole across categories, so it cannot show how the values of a numeric variable are spread across a range.
Why C: A scatter plot shows the relation between two variables, so it does not display the distribution of a single numeric variable.
Why D: A line chart usually tracks values over time or an ordered sequence, and it does not group a numeric variable into bins to show its distribution.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data dictionary?
A: A backup of the data kept on a safe server
B: A list of English words with their meanings overall
C: A document describing each field in a data set
D: A chart of the data shown as a set of bars
Why A: A backup is a stored copy kept for recovery, which protects the data but does not explain what each field in the data set means.
Why B: An English dictionary lists general words and meanings, while a data dictionary documents the specific fields of one data set, so the two serve different purposes.
Why C: A data dictionary describes each field in a data set, including its name, type, meaning and allowed values, so that users read and use the data correctly.
Why D: A chart of bars displays values visually, but a data dictionary is a text description of fields and not a graph of the data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is normalization of data?
A: Hiding columns from view in a table or sheet
B: Rescaling values to a common range or structure
C: Deleting all values from the data set at once
D: Randomly shuffling rows so the record order changes
Why A: Hiding columns only changes what is visible in a table and leaves the values and their scale unchanged, so it is not normalization.
Why B: Normalization rescales values to a common range or organizes data into a consistent structure, so that features or tables can be compared and used together.
Why C: Deleting all values removes the data entirely, which defeats the purpose, since normalization changes scale or structure while keeping the information that the data contain.
Why D: Shuffling rows only changes their order and leaves every value untouched, so it does not rescale the data or give it a common structure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Heights are in centimeters and incomes in dollars. Why scale both before some models?
A: To make the data secret from all others
B: To remove all variation from the data set
C: To change the data's meaning for analysts
D: So large-valued features do not dominate
Why A: Scaling is a technical step and does not hide anything, so keeping data secret from others is not the reason for putting heights and incomes on one scale.
Why B: Scaling keeps the differences between values and just changes their units, so it does not remove variation, and a model still needs that variation to learn.
Why C: Scaling puts features on similar ranges without changing what the data mean, so the claim that it alters meaning for analysts is wrong.
Why D: Incomes in dollars are numerically far larger than heights in centimeters, so unscaled they can dominate distance-based models, and scaling lets each feature contribute fairly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a missing value strategy called when you fill gaps with the average?
A: Data encryption
B: Mean imputation
C: Feature scaling
D: Outlier removal
Why A: Encryption protects data by scrambling it and has nothing to do with filling gaps, so it is not the name for replacing missing values with an average.
Why B: Mean imputation fills missing values with the average of the observed values in that column, which keeps the row in the data instead of dropping it.
Why C: Feature scaling changes the range of values and does not fill in empty cells, so it is a different step from imputing missing data.
Why D: Outlier removal deletes extreme values, but filling gaps with the average adds values instead of removing them, so the two steps are not the same.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is SQL used for?
A: Querying and managing data in relational databases
B: Writing music for songs and films in a studio
C: Editing video clips for films and online posts overall
D: Designing logos and brand marks for new firms
Why A: SQL is a language for querying and managing data stored in relational databases, letting users select, filter, join and update rows in tables.
Why B: Writing music is a creative task done with audio software, and SQL is a database language with no role in composing songs or film scores.
Why C: Video editing needs software for cutting and arranging footage, while SQL works with tables of data and cannot edit clips or posts.
Why D: Logo design is a visual art done with graphics tools, whereas SQL is used for working with stored data and is not a design tool.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which SQL clause filters rows?
A: ORDER BY
B: SELECT
C: WHERE
D: FROM
Why A: ORDER BY sorts the rows of a result into a chosen order, but it does not remove any rows, so it does not filter them.
Why B: SELECT chooses which columns appear in the output, and it does not decide which rows are kept, so it is not the filtering clause.
Why C: WHERE sets a condition that each row must meet, so only matching rows are returned, which makes it the SQL clause that filters rows.
Why D: FROM names the table or tables the data come from and does not apply a condition to rows, so it does not filter them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Python commonly used for in data science?
A: Analysis, visualization and building models
B: Driving cars manually on roads to collect data
C: Painting walls in homes and offices by hand
D: Cooking recipes for meals in a home kitchen
Why A: Python is widely used in data science for analysis, visualization and building models, thanks to libraries such as pandas, matplotlib and scikit-learn.
Why B: Python is a programming language and cannot drive a car by hand, so manual driving to collect data is not a use of Python.
Why C: Painting walls is manual work with no link to programming, so it is not something Python is used for in data science.
Why D: Cooking meals in a kitchen has no connection to Python, which is a programming language used for data work and not for preparing food.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a spreadsheet pivot table used for?
A: Writing programs in code for use on a computer
B: Sending email messages to clients and staff
C: Summarizing and grouping data by categories
D: Drawing images and sketches by hand on paper
Why A: Writing programs is done in code editors, while a pivot table summarizes data in a sheet and does not create software for a computer.
Why B: Email is sent through mail software, and a pivot table does not send messages to clients or staff, since its job is to summarize data.
Why C: A pivot table summarizes and groups data by categories, letting users total, count or average values by region, product or date without writing formulas.
Why D: Drawing by hand on paper is unrelated to spreadsheets, so it is not the purpose of a pivot table, which works on rows of data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: You need total sales by region from a long table. Which tool is quickest?
A: A word processor
B: A pivot table
C: A calendar
D: A photo editor
Why A: A word processor is built for writing documents and does not total values by group, so it would be slow and awkward for this task.
Why B: A pivot table groups rows by region and sums the sales for each in a few clicks, which makes it the quickest tool for this question.
Why C: A calendar organizes dates and events and cannot summarize numbers by region, so it is the wrong tool for finding total sales.
Why D: A photo editor changes images and cannot add up sales figures from a table, so it is unsuited to totaling sales by region.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes a data pipeline?
A: A password manager that stores and fills in logins for your accounts
B: A water pipe for servers that carries coolant through the data center in general
C: A single chart that shows one set of numbers from the data set
D: Automated steps that move and transform data from source to destination
Why A: A password manager stores and fills in logins, which is a security tool and not a series of steps that moves and changes data.
Why B: A water pipe carrying coolant is physical cooling equipment, and a data pipeline is software that moves data, so the name is only a loose metaphor.
Why C: A single chart shows one set of numbers and does not move or transform data between systems, so it is not a data pipeline.
Why D: A data pipeline is a set of automated steps that extract, move and transform data from a source to a destination, so it arrives ready for use.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is artificial intelligence?
A: A database of facts that people can search for answers to questions
B: A robot with a metal body only, which can walk and carry out tasks on its own
C: Computer systems performing tasks that usually need human intelligence
D: Any machine with a screen that displays pictures or text to a user
Why A: A database of facts stores information that people look up, but it does not perform tasks needing intelligence, so it is not artificial intelligence itself.
Why B: AI does not need a metal body, since most AI is software with no physical form, so limiting it to walking robots is far too narrow.
Why C: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks that usually require human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, learning from data and making decisions.
Why D: A machine with a screen only displays content, and having a display says nothing about performing tasks that need human-like intelligence, so it does not define AI.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A spam filter improves by studying thousands of labeled emails. This is:
A: Supervised machine learning
B: Reinforcement learning
C: Unsupervised clustering
D: Rule-based programming
Why A: Studying thousands of labeled emails to learn which are spam is supervised machine learning, because the labels guide the model toward the right answers.
Why B: Reinforcement learning uses rewards from actions, not labeled examples. Learning from labeled emails is supervised learning.
Why C: Unsupervised clustering finds groups in data with no labels, but these emails are labeled spam or not spam, so this is not unsupervised.
Why D: Rule-based programming uses rules written by people instead of learning from examples. Labeled emails make this supervised machine learning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store groups customers by buying habits without predefined categories. This is:
A: Manual sorting of the customer lists
B: Unsupervised learning (clustering)
C: Reinforcement learning methods
D: Supervised classification only
Why A: Sorting by hand means a person sets the groups, but here the store finds groups itself from buying habits, so this is not manual sorting.
Why B: Grouping customers by similar buying habits with no predefined categories or labels is unsupervised learning, specifically clustering, since the algorithm finds the groups on its own.
Why C: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and penalties from actions, which does not match grouping customers by their buying habits.
Why D: Supervised classification needs labeled categories set in advance, but the scenario says there are none, so supervised classification does not apply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which task is most associated with deep learning?
A: Sorting a short list of names
B: Adding two numbers together
C: Storing a file on a hard disk
D: Recognizing objects in images
Why A: Sorting a short list of names is a simple routine solved by a standard algorithm, so it needs no deep learning.
Why B: Adding two numbers is basic arithmetic with fixed rules, so it requires no neural network and is not tied to deep learning.
Why C: Storing a file is a function of the operating system and disk, and it involves no learning of patterns from data.
Why D: Recognizing objects in images is a classic deep learning task, because neural networks with many layers learn visual features directly from large sets of pictures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is training data?
A: Data kept secret from the model
B: Data used only after deployment
C: Data that is deleted after each use
D: Data used to teach a model patterns
Why A: Training data is given to the model so it can learn from it, which is the opposite of keeping the data secret from the model.
Why B: Data used only after deployment would be live input and not training data, because training happens before deployment to teach the model.
Why C: Deleting data after each use does not describe training data, which is kept and used repeatedly so the model learns from it.
Why D: Training data is the set of examples used to teach a model patterns, so it can later make predictions on new inputs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is test data used for?
A: Checking how well a trained model performs on unseen examples
B: Cleaning the model by removing old code and unused files
C: Hiding errors in the results so that nobody notices them
D: Training the model on the examples it will learn from first overall
Why A: Test data is held back from training and used to measure how well the trained model performs on examples it has not seen.
Why B: Cleaning code and files is housekeeping and has nothing to do with evaluating a model, which is what test data is for.
Why C: Test data is meant to reveal errors honestly, so hiding errors from others would defeat its purpose of showing true performance.
Why D: Training is done with the training set, and test data is kept separate so that it can check the model on new examples.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on new data. What is the likely problem?
A: Great fit
B: Overfitting
C: A faster PC
D: Underfitting
Why A: A great fit would score well on both training and new data, but a drop from 99% to 60% shows the opposite, so this is not a great fit.
Why B: Scoring 99% on training data but 60% on new data shows the model memorized the training set and fails to generalize, which is overfitting.
Why C: A faster computer changes how quickly a model runs and does not explain a large gap between training and new data scores.
Why D: Underfitting gives poor scores on training data too, but this model scores 99% on training data, so it does not fit the pattern described.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is underfitting?
A: A model that memorizes noise in the training data
B: A model with extra features that it does not need
C: A model too simple to capture the pattern in the data
D: A model that is accurate on training data and new data
Why A: Memorizing noise in training data is overfitting, which is the opposite problem, since an underfit model is too simple and misses the real pattern.
Why B: Extra unneeded features tend to add complexity and risk overfitting, whereas underfitting comes from a model that is too simple to capture the pattern.
Why C: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the pattern in the data, so it performs poorly on both training data and new data.
Why D: A model accurate on both training and new data fits well, so it is a good result and not underfitting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action can help reduce overfitting?
A: Remove the test set from the data entirely
B: Add noise labels to the training data set
C: Use more training data or simplify the model
D: Memorize the training set so the model is exact
Why A: The test set is needed to measure generalization honestly, so removing it hides overfitting instead of reducing it.
Why B: Adding noisy labels makes the training data worse and tends to push a model to memorize errors, which raises overfitting.
Why C: More training data helps a model learn general patterns and a simpler model has less capacity to memorize noise, so both reduce overfitting.
Why D: Memorizing the training set is overfitting itself, and it makes the model fail on new data, so it cannot help reduce it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a feature in machine learning?
A: A bug in the code that makes the program stop working
B: An input variable used by a model to make predictions
C: A chart title shown above the graph in a report page
D: The model's final answer, shown to the user at the end
Why A: A bug stops a program from working correctly, but a feature in machine learning is an input used for prediction, so the two are unrelated.
Why B: A feature is an input variable, such as size or age, that a model uses to make predictions, and a model typically takes several of them.
Why C: A chart title labels a graph, but a feature in machine learning is a data input, so a title is not what the word means here.
Why D: The model's final answer is its output or prediction, which is different from a feature, since features are the inputs that the model uses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a label?
A: A column name only, shown at the top
B: A chart legend that explains colors in a graph
C: A random number picked by the computer
D: The correct output for a training example
Why A: A column name is a header, but a label in machine learning is the answer to be predicted, so a name shown at the top is not the meaning.
Why B: A chart legend explains colors on a graph, which is a plotting term, and a label in machine learning is the known output for an example.
Why C: A label is not random and is set by the data, so a random number picked by the computer does not describe it.
Why D: A label is the correct output for a training example, such as spam or not spam, which the model learns to predict from the features.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In predicting house prices from size and location, what is the label?
A: The house price
B: The size in feet
C: The location
D: The seller's name
Why A: The house price is what the model is trying to predict from size and location, so it is the label, or target, of this problem.
Why B: The size in feet is an input used to predict price, which makes it a feature and not the label that the model predicts.
Why C: The location is also an input used to predict the price, so it is a feature, and the label is the output being predicted.
Why D: The seller's name is not part of the problem and does not help predict price, and it is neither the target nor a useful feature.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is classification?
A: Predicting which category an item belongs to
B: Removing data from a table or a file on disk
C: Grouping data without labels into clusters
D: Predicting a number, such as a house price
Why A: Classification is a supervised task that predicts which category an item belongs to, such as spam or not spam, or which type of flower a photo shows.
Why B: Removing data from a table is a data editing step and does not assign items to categories, which is what classification does.
Why C: Grouping data without labels into clusters is unsupervised clustering, whereas classification uses known labeled categories to predict the class of a new item.
Why D: Predicting a number, such as a house price, is regression, not classification, which instead predicts a category label.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is regression?
A: Grouping items into categories
B: Storing data on a disk
C: Predicting a category label
D: Predicting a numeric value
Why A: Grouping items into categories describes classification or clustering, whereas regression predicts a numeric value from input features.
Why B: Storing data on a disk is a storage function with no learning or prediction involved, so it is not regression.
Why C: Predicting a category label is classification, and regression is the other main supervised task, which predicts a number.
Why D: Regression predicts a numeric value, such as price, temperature or sales, from input features, which separates it from classification that predicts categories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Predicting tomorrow's temperature is which type of task?
A: Encryption
B: Classification
C: Regression
D: Clustering
Why A: Encryption scrambles data to protect it and is not a type of prediction task, so it does not describe forecasting a temperature.
Why B: Classification predicts a category, but tomorrow's temperature is a number on a continuous scale, so it is not a classification task.
Why C: Predicting tomorrow's temperature means estimating a numeric value, which is regression, since the output is a number on a continuous scale.
Why D: Clustering groups similar items without labels and does not predict a specific number, so it does not match forecasting a temperature.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accuracy?
A: The speed of a model on the hardware
B: The share of predictions that are correct
C: The size of a model file on a hard disk
D: The cost of training a model on servers
Why A: The speed of a model on hardware is its performance in time, not accuracy, which measures how often predictions are right.
Why B: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct, found by dividing correct predictions by the total number of predictions made.
Why C: The size of a model file measures storage, which has nothing to do with how often predictions are correct, which is accuracy.
Why D: The cost of training is a resource measure and not a measure of correctness, so it does not define accuracy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Only 1% of transactions are fraud. A model that always says 'not fraud' is 99% accurate. Why is this misleading?
A: It never catches any fraud
B: It flags too many honest sales
C: It was tested on too little data
D: It uses far too much data
Why A: The model never flags a single fraud case, so it is useless for its real purpose even though 99 of every 100 transactions are legitimate, which gives the high score.
Why B: The model says not fraud for everything, so it flags no honest sales. The problem is that it misses all fraud despite its 99% accuracy.
Why C: Test size is not the issue. The 99% score comes from fraud being rare, while the model misses each fraud case.
Why D: The amount of data used is not the issue, since the 99% comes from class imbalance, with fraud being only 1% of cases, and not from data quantity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do precision and recall measure?
A: Training time and storage, the two measures of how long a model takes to train and how much room it uses
B: Size and color of data, the two properties that decide how a chart looks to the audience and how it prints in most cases
C: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are right, recall is the share of actual positives found
D: Speed and cost of a model, the two measures of how fast it runs and how much it costs to operate each year
Why A: Training time and storage are resource measures, whereas precision and recall measure the quality of a model's positive predictions, so this answer describes something different.
Why B: Size and color of data describe how data or a chart looks and say nothing about prediction quality, which is what precision and recall measure.
Why C: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are right, and recall is the share of actual positives the model finds, so they show different kinds of error.
Why D: Speed and cost describe how a model runs and what it costs, while precision and recall measure how correct its positive predictions are and how many positives it finds.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hiring model trained mostly on past male hires favors men. What is this?
A: Random noise in the whole data
B: Perfect fairness, as past hires show
C: Hardware failure in a data server
D: Bias inherited from training data
Why A: The bias follows a clear pattern in favor of men, so it is systematic and not random noise, since noise would not favor one group.
Why B: Favoring men because past hires were mostly men repeats historical imbalance and is not fair, so calling it perfect fairness is wrong.
Why C: Hardware failure would cause crashes or corrupted outputs and not a consistent preference for one gender, so it cannot explain the pattern.
Why D: The model learned the imbalance in past hiring from its training data and reproduces it, which is bias inherited from training data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data anonymization?
A: Deleting the analysis once the project has ended
B: Removing or masking personal identifiers from data
C: Selling data to anyone who asks, names left out
D: Adding names to data records to track each person
Why A: Deleting the analysis removes work results and does nothing to protect personal identities in the data, so it is not anonymization.
Why B: Anonymization removes or masks personal identifiers such as names and ID numbers so that individuals cannot easily be identified from the data.
Why C: Selling data to anyone who asks is a privacy risk, and leaving names out does not make a sale responsible or define anonymization.
Why D: Adding names makes records easier to trace back to individuals, which is the opposite of anonymization, so it increases privacy risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does informed consent mean for data collection?
A: Data is collected by default always, with no choice
B: Data is sold in secret to firms that pay the most
C: People understand and agree to how their data is used
D: Data is taken without telling people, then used as it likes
Why A: Collecting data by default with no choice removes the person's say, so it is not informed consent, which requires a real option.
Why B: Selling data in secret means people are unaware of its use, so there is no informed consent, since consent requires knowing what happens.
Why C: Informed consent means people understand how their data will be used and freely agree to it before it is collected.
Why D: Taking data without telling people and using it as one likes gives them no knowledge or choice, so it violates informed consent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An app collects location data but never tells users. Which principle is violated?
A: Accuracy of data and updates
B: Transparency and consent
C: Backup policy for the files
D: Data compression of files
Why A: Accuracy and updates concern data quality, but the problem here is that users were never told about collection, which breaks a different principle.
Why B: Collecting location data without telling users breaks transparency and consent, since people have a right to know what is gathered and agree to it.
Why C: A backup policy concerns data protection against loss and has no bearing on whether users were told about the location data collection.
Why D: Data compression reduces file size and has nothing to do with informing users, so it is not the principle violated by secret collection.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is human oversight important for high-stakes AI decisions such as loans?
A: To remove all automation from the process at once
B: To make the AI slower for no reason at all
C: To hide the process from the public and the users
D: To catch errors and bias and keep accountability
Why A: Human oversight does not aim to remove all automation, since automation still brings benefits, and the goal is to add review where decisions are high-stakes.
Why B: Oversight is not meant to slow the AI for no reason, and any added review step exists to catch mistakes in decisions that affect people.
Why C: Hiding the process would reduce transparency and trust, but oversight adds checks on loans and similar decisions, so concealment is not its purpose.
Why D: Human oversight lets people catch errors and bias in high-stakes decisions such as loans and keeps someone accountable for outcomes that affect lives.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a misleading graph?
A: A chart that distorts data, for example by a truncated axis
B: A chart with accurate scales showing the real values
C: A chart with a title placed above the graph in a report as a rule
D: A chart with clear labels on both of its axes and title
Why A: A misleading graph distorts the data it shows, for example by cutting off the axis so differences look larger than they are.
Why B: A chart with accurate scales and real values represents the data honestly, which makes it a fair graph and not a misleading one.
Why C: A title above a graph is a normal feature that helps readers, and placing it there does not distort the data in any way.
Why D: Clear labels on both axes and a title help readers understand the chart, so they make it more honest and not misleading.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0, making a small gap look huge. What is this?
A: A correct and honest scale, showing real numbers
B: A truncated axis that exaggerates differences
C: A normal distribution of the data values
D: A log scale that grows by powers of ten each step
Why A: Starting the axis at 95 hides most of the bar's height, so the scale is not honest, and a small gap is made to look large.
Why B: A truncated axis starts above zero, which cuts off the base of the bars and exaggerates differences, so a small gap looks huge to viewers.
Why C: A normal distribution describes the shape of data values and not how an axis is drawn, so it is unrelated to the scale problem.
Why D: A log scale grows by powers of ten and has an evenly spaced multiplicative axis, whereas this axis simply starts at 95 and cuts the bars.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data provenance?
A: The color of a chart that is used to show a trend
B: The speed of a query that runs on a database server
C: The record of where data came from and how it changed
D: The size of a file that is stored on a hard disk drive
Why A: The color of a chart is a design choice and says nothing about where data came from, which is what provenance records.
Why B: Query speed measures performance of a database server and has nothing to do with the origin or history of the data.
Why C: Data provenance is the record of where data came from and how it has changed along the way, which supports trust and traceability.
Why D: File size is a storage measure and does not tell where data originated or what was done to it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why does the source of a data set matter?
A: It affects reliability, bias and appropriate use
B: It sets the file format used for storage
C: It determines how many rows the data set holds
D: It decides which software opens the data set
Why A: The source affects how reliable the data are, what biases they may carry and whether they suit the intended use, so it matters to analysts.
Why B: The source does not set the file format. It matters because it affects reliability, bias and whether the data suits the intended use.
Why C: Row count comes from collection, not from the source's identity. Source matters because it affects reliability, bias and appropriate use.
Why D: Software choice is unrelated to data quality. The source matters because it affects reliability, bias and appropriate use.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a dataset?
A: A type of chart that shows values as bars, lines or slices on a graph
B: A single number that sums up the data, such as the mean or the total
C: A computer program that processes data into charts and other reports
D: A structured collection of data, often arranged in rows and columns
Why A: A chart displays data and is not the data itself, so it is not a dataset, which is the underlying collection of values.
Why B: A single number such as a mean or total summarizes data and is not a collection of records, so it does not define a dataset.
Why C: A program that processes data is software, whereas a dataset is the data it works on, so these are different things.
Why D: A dataset is a structured collection of data, often arranged in rows for records and columns for variables, ready for analysis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a table of data, what is a row usually called?
A: A record or observation
B: A variable or column
C: A formula in a cell
D: A header at the top
Why A: In a table each row usually holds one record, also called an observation, such as one customer or one sale, with a value per column.
Why B: A variable or column runs vertically down the table and holds one attribute for every record, so it is not a row.
Why C: A formula in a cell is a calculation in a spreadsheet, which is different from a row, a full line of values for one record.
Why D: A header sits at the top and names the columns, so it is a label for the data and not a row of records.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a table of data, what is a column usually called?
A: An observation or row
B: A database table
C: A record or a row
D: A variable or field
Why A: An observation, or row, runs across the table, whereas a column runs down it, so this describes a row and not a column.
Why B: A database table is the whole structure holding many rows and columns, so a single column is only a part of a table.
Why C: A record or row runs across the table, so it is the other dimension, and a column is not called a record.
Why D: A column usually holds one variable, also called a field, such as age or city, with one value for every record in the table.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is structured data?
A: Audio recordings made on a phone or a microphone
B: Data organized in a fixed format such as tables
C: Free-form text such as emails and notes in a file
D: Photos and videos taken with a phone or camera
Why A: Audio recordings have no fixed table layout and are unstructured data, so they do not fit the definition of structured data.
Why B: Structured data is organized in a fixed format, such as rows and columns in a table, which makes it easy to search and analyze.
Why C: Free-form text such as emails and notes has no fixed fields, which makes it unstructured and not structured.
Why D: Photos and videos are stored as pixel or frame data with no table of fields, so they are unstructured.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is unstructured data?
A: Rows in a table arranged in a fixed set of columns and labels
B: A spreadsheet that holds numbers and text in labeled cells and rows
C: Data without a predefined format, such as images, audio and free text
D: A SQL table that stores each record in a fixed layout of rows and columns
Why A: Rows with a fixed set of columns and labels describe structured data, which is the opposite of unstructured data that lacks a fixed layout.
Why B: A spreadsheet with labeled cells and rows has a clear structure, so it is structured data and not unstructured.
Why C: Unstructured data has no predefined format or fixed fields, as with images, audio and free text, so it needs special methods to analyze.
Why D: A SQL table stores records in a fixed layout of rows and columns, which is the definition of structured data, not unstructured.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is semi-structured data?
A: A strict database table with fixed rows and columns and set types
B: A plain image file such as a photo or a scan with no data fields
C: A random guess made by an analyst about the data without checking it
D: Data with some organization but no rigid table, such as JSON or XML
Why A: A strict table with fixed rows, columns and set types is fully structured, so it is not semi-structured, which lacks a rigid layout.
Why B: A plain image with no data fields is unstructured, and semi-structured data has tags or keys that give it some organization.
Why C: A guess made without checking is an assumption and not a type of data, so it has no link to semi-structured data.
Why D: Semi-structured data has some organization, such as tags or key-value pairs, but no rigid table, and JSON and XML files are common examples.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a categorical variable represent?
A: A label or group such as color or city
B: A date only, with no other detail
C: A calculation result such as a total
D: A measurable amount in a data table
Why A: A categorical variable represents a label or group, such as color or city, and its values name categories and are not measured amounts.
Why B: A date is only one possible kind of value, so saying a categorical variable is a date only is far too narrow and wrong.
Why C: A calculation result such as a total is a number, which is numerical and not a category label.
Why D: A measurable amount is a numerical variable, whereas a categorical variable names a group or label, so this describes the other type.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a numerical variable represent?
A: A group name or a category label in data
B: A color name such as red or blue in a column
C: A quantity that can be measured or counted
D: A text label for each record in the table
Why A: A group name or category label is a categorical variable, not numerical, since numerical variables hold quantities that can be measured or counted.
Why B: A color name such as red or blue is a category label, which makes it categorical and not a numerical quantity.
Why C: A numerical variable represents a quantity that can be measured or counted, such as height, price or number of students, and supports arithmetic.
Why D: A text label for each record names or describes it and is categorical, so it does not represent a measured quantity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a discrete variable?
A: Temperature in degrees now
B: Number of students in a class
C: Height of a student on a scale
D: Time to run a mile in minutes
Why A: Temperature can take any value in a range, including decimals, so it is continuous and not a discrete variable.
Why B: The number of students is counted in whole numbers and cannot be fractional, so it takes separate values and is a discrete variable.
Why C: Height can take any value within a range, such as 150.3 cm, so it is a continuous variable and not discrete.
Why D: Time to run a mile can be any value in minutes, including fractions, so it is continuous and not discrete.
