Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a continuous variable?
A: Weight of a package
B: Number of pets owned
C: Siblings in the home
D: Number of cars owned
Why A: Weight of a package can take any value within a range, including fractions, so it is measured and not counted, which makes it continuous.
Why B: The number of pets owned is counted in whole numbers, so it is a discrete variable and not continuous.
Why C: Siblings in the home are counted as whole numbers, so this is a discrete variable, since nobody has 1.5 siblings.
Why D: The number of cars owned is a count in whole numbers, so it is discrete and not a continuous variable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ordinal variable?
A: A date shown as day, month and year in a column of a table
B: A number with equal spacing such as a measured weight or height overall
C: A random label given to each item with no order at all in it
D: A category with a meaningful order, such as small, medium, large
Why A: A date shown as day, month and year describes a point in time, which is not an ordered category, so this is not an ordinal variable.
Why B: A number with equal spacing such as weight or height is a measured quantity and so is numerical, not ordinal, which is a ranked category.
Why C: A random label with no order is a nominal category, and ordinal data require a meaningful order, so this does not fit.
Why D: An ordinal variable is a category with a meaningful order, such as small, medium and large, though the gaps between levels are not exactly equal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data type 'boolean'?
A: A date and time stamp value
B: A value that is true or false
C: A decimal number such as 3.14
D: A word or a text value in a cell
Why A: A date and time stamp records a moment and is a datetime type, so it does not hold just a true or false value.
Why B: A boolean type holds one of two values, true or false, which makes it useful for yes or no flags and conditions in code and data.
Why C: A decimal number such as 3.14 is a float type, which holds numeric values, so it is different from a boolean with two states.
Why D: A word or text value is a string type, so it is a different data type from a boolean that holds only true or false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a string in programming?
A: A true or false value
B: A whole number value
C: A sequence of characters
D: A decimal number value
Why A: A true or false value is a boolean, which holds only two states, whereas a string holds a sequence of characters.
Why B: A whole number value is an integer type and holds counts and not text, so it is not a string.
Why C: A string is a sequence of characters, such as letters, digits and symbols, used to store text like names and messages in a program.
Why D: A decimal number value is a float type used for numbers with fractions, so it is not a string, which holds text.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is metadata?
A: A backup copy of all the data
B: Raw measurements from sensors
C: A graph of the results of data
D: Data that describes other data
Why A: A backup copy is a duplicate of the data kept for recovery, so it is not metadata, which describes the data and does not copy it.
Why B: Raw measurements from sensors are primary data and not metadata, which gives information about data such as its source, time or format.
Why C: A graph of the results is a visualization of data, so it is not metadata, which describes other data and does not display it.
Why D: Metadata is data that describes other data, such as a file's author, date created, size or format, which helps people find and understand it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a primary data source?
A: Data collected directly for a specific purpose
B: A textbook or library copy of the data used
C: Data from an old report written by others
D: Data copied from a website and cleaned by an analyst
Why A: Primary data are collected directly by the researcher for a specific purpose, such as through a survey, interview or experiment, so the collector controls how it is gathered.
Why B: A textbook or library copy was gathered earlier by other people, so it is a secondary source and not primary data.
Why C: Data from an old report written by others was collected by someone else, which makes it secondary and not primary.
Why D: Data copied from a website was collected earlier by someone else, so even after cleaning it is secondary and not primary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a secondary data source?
A: A survey you design and run yourself
B: Interviews you conduct yourself with customers
C: Data originally collected by someone else
D: An experiment you run on your own team
Why A: A survey you design and run yourself is primary data, since you collect it directly, so it is not a secondary source.
Why B: Interviews you conduct yourself are collected first-hand, which makes them primary data and not secondary.
Why C: Secondary data were originally collected by someone else for another purpose, such as published reports or public datasets, and are reused for new analysis.
Why D: An experiment you run on your own team produces first-hand data, so it is a primary source and not secondary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A school surveys 100 of its 2,000 students. What is the 100 students?
A: Parameter
B: A sample
C: A census
D: Population
Why A: A parameter is a value describing a whole population, such as its mean, and not the group of students surveyed, so it does not name them.
Why B: The 100 students surveyed are a subset drawn from the 2,000 students at the school, which makes them a sample of the population.
Why C: A census would survey all 2,000 students, but only 100 were surveyed, so this group is a sample and not a census.
Why D: The population is all 2,000 students at the school, and the 100 surveyed are only a part of that group.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is random sampling?
A: Picking volunteers only, who sign up on their own to take part
B: Picking friends and family of the researcher to answer questions as a rule
C: Picking the easiest people to reach and to ask for answers
D: Selecting members so that each has an equal chance of being chosen
Why A: Volunteers who sign up on their own are a self-selected group, which is not random and can bias results.
Why B: Friends and family of the researcher are chosen for convenience and are not an equal-chance selection, so this is not random sampling.
Why C: Picking the easiest people to reach is convenience sampling, which gives some people no chance of being chosen, so it is not random.
Why D: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected, which helps the sample represent the whole group fairly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A survey on school lunch is given only to students who eat in the cafeteria. What is the likely problem?
A: Sampling bias
B: Perfect sample
C: A larger sample
D: No problem
Why A: Surveying only cafeteria students leaves out students who eat elsewhere, so the sample is unrepresentative, which is sampling bias.
Why B: A sample missing students who eat elsewhere is not perfect, because it does not represent all students, so calling it perfect is wrong.
Why C: The problem is who is included, not how many, so a larger sample drawn the same way would keep the same bias.
Why D: Surveying only cafeteria students leaves out other students, so there is a clear problem, and the claim of no problem ignores it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stratified sample?
A: A sample of only volunteers, who sign up themselves to answer
B: A sample taken from each subgroup in proportion to its size
C: A sample of one person picked by the researcher from the group
D: A sample from one class in the school, picked by the teacher
Why A: A sample of only volunteers is self-selected and does not reflect the subgroups of the population in proportion, so it is not stratified.
Why B: A stratified sample draws from each subgroup in proportion to its size, so each group is fairly represented in the final sample.
Why C: A single person picked by the researcher is far too small and not drawn from each subgroup, so it is not a stratified sample.
Why D: A sample from one class at one school covers just one group and ignores the others, so it is not stratified.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a census?
A: A random guess about the size of a population
B: A chart of the results of a poll in a town
C: A survey of every member of a population
D: A survey of a sample drawn at random here
Why A: A guess about the size of a population is an estimate and not a count, while a census collects data from every member.
Why B: A chart of poll results shows data and is not a way of collecting it, whereas a census is a survey of everyone.
Why C: A census surveys every member of a population instead of just a sample, giving complete data but usually at higher cost and effort.
Why D: A survey of a random sample covers only part of the population, so it is a sample survey and not a census.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a survey question that is leading?
A: A neutral question worded so that it favors no particular answer
B: A question worded to push respondents toward a particular answer
C: A short question that takes only a few seconds to read and answer
D: A multiple-choice question that has several answers listed
Why A: A neutral question favors no answer, which is the opposite of a leading question, so it cannot be the one that pushes respondents.
Why B: A leading question is worded to push respondents toward a particular answer, which biases the results and makes them less reliable.
Why C: A short question is not leading because of its length, since wording that steers the answer is what makes a question leading.
Why D: Listing several answers is the multiple-choice format and says nothing about steering respondents, so it does not make a question leading.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is response bias?
A: When respondents give inaccurate answers due to wording or social pressure
B: A perfect survey in which every answer is true and carefully given  by every person
C: A random error that occurs by chance and does not follow a pattern
D: A sampling rule that decides which people will be asked to respond
Why A: Response bias occurs when respondents give inaccurate answers because of wording, social pressure or the wish to please, which distorts the survey results.
Why B: A survey where every answer is true and carefully given would have no response bias, so this describes the absence of the problem.
Why C: A random error occurs by chance with no pattern, but response bias follows a pattern, so these are different kinds of survey error.
Why D: A sampling rule decides who is asked, which concerns sampling and not how people answer, so it is not response bias.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the mean of a dataset?
A: The middle value in the sorted data set of numbers
B: The largest value in the data set of numbers
C: The most common value in the data set of numbers
D: The sum of values divided by the number of values
Why A: The middle value in sorted data is the median, so this is a different measure of center from the mean.
Why B: The largest value is the maximum, which is not a measure of center, so it is not the mean of the data.
Why C: The most common value is the mode, so this is a different measure from the mean, which uses every value.
Why D: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values, so it is the usual average and uses every value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 12?
Why A: The mean is the sum divided by the count, so 4+8+6+10+12 = 40 and 40/5 = 8, which means 6 is not the mean.
Why B: Forty is the sum of the values and not the mean, because the sum must still be divided by 5 values to give 8.
Why C: The sum is 4+8+6+10+12 = 40, and dividing by the 5 values gives a mean of 8.
Why D: Ten is the largest number but the mean is 40/5 = 8, so ten overstates the average.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the median of 3, 9, 5, 7 and 11?
Why A: Sorted, the values are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and the middle is 7, so 5 is only the second value and not the median.
Why B: Sorted, the values are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and with five values the third, 7, is the middle, so the median is 7.
Why C: Nine is the fourth of the five sorted values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, so it is not the middle, since the third value, 7, is.
Why D: With five values there is a single middle one, 7, and no averaging of two values is needed, so 7.5 is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the median of 2, 4, 6 and 8?
Why A: Sorted values 2, 4, 6, 8 have two middle values, 4 and 6, so the median is their average, 5, and 4 is only one of them.
Why B: Twenty is the sum of 2+4+6+8, not the median, and the median is the average of the two middle values, 4 and 6, giving 5.
Why C: With four values the median is the average of the two middle ones, so (4+6)/2 = 10/2 = 5.
Why D: Six is the third value and only one of the two middle values, and the median is (4+6)/2 = 5, not 6.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the mode?
A: The value that occurs most often
B: The smallest value in the data set
C: The average of all the values
D: The middle value of the data
Why A: The mode is the value that occurs most often in a data set, and a set can have one mode, several modes or none.
Why B: The smallest value is the minimum and has nothing to do with how often a value occurs, which is what the mode measures.
Why C: The average of all the values is the mean, which is a different measure of center from the mode.
Why D: The middle value of the data is the median, so this is a different measure from the mode, which counts frequency.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3 and 6?
Why A: Six appears once in 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6, while 3 appears three times, so 6 is not the most common value.
Why B: Thirty-seven tenths is not even a value in the list, and the mode must be a value that occurs, so 3.7 cannot be the mode.
Why C: Four appears once, while 3 appears three times, so 4 is not the most frequent value and cannot be the mode.
Why D: Three appears three times in the list, more often than any other value, so the mode is 3.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the range of a dataset?
A: The average of all of the values in the data set
B: The middle value when the data are put in order first
C: The most common value in the data set of numbers
D: The difference between the largest and smallest values
Why A: The average of all values is the mean, which measures center and not spread, so it is not the range.
Why B: The middle value in order is the median, a measure of center, while the range measures the full spread of the data.
Why C: The most common value is the mode, which is a different measure from the range, and it does not describe spread.
Why D: The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values, giving a simple measure of how far apart the extremes in the data are.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the range of 12, 7, 20, 15 and 9?
Why A: About 12.6 is the mean of the values (12+7+20+15+9 = 63, and 63/5 = 12.6), not the range, which is max minus min.
Why B: The largest value is 20 and the smallest is 7, so the range is 20 - 7 = 13.
Why C: Seven is the smallest value and not the range, which needs the smallest subtracted from the largest, 20 - 7 = 13.
Why D: Twenty is the largest value alone, and the range subtracts the smallest, 7, from it, giving 20 - 7 = 13.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which measure is least affected by an extreme outlier?
A: The sum
B: The mean
C: The median
D: The range
Why A: The sum includes every value, so one extreme outlier changes it greatly, which makes it very sensitive to outliers.
Why B: The mean uses every value, so a single extreme outlier pulls it toward the outlier, which makes it sensitive to extremes.
Why C: The median depends only on the middle position in sorted data, so an extreme outlier barely changes it, which makes it the least affected measure.
Why D: The range is the largest value minus the smallest, so an outlier directly changes it, and it is highly sensitive to extremes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is variance?
A: The average of squared differences from the mean
B: The middle value after the data are put in order
C: The sum of the values divided by their count
D: The largest value minus the smallest value
Why A: Variance is the average of the squared differences from the mean, which measures how spread out the values are in squared units.
Why B: The middle value after ordering is the median, a measure of center, so it does not describe variance, which measures spread.
Why C: The sum divided by the count is the mean, which is a measure of center, so it is a different measure from variance.
Why D: The largest minus the smallest value is the range, a simpler spread measure that uses only two values, whereas variance uses all values.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a quartile?
A: A type of chart that shows data as bars, lines or slices on a graph
B: One of three values that split ordered data into four equal parts
C: A type of mean found by adding the values and dividing by the count
D: A type of outlier that is far above or far below the rest of the data
Why A: A type of chart showing bars, lines or slices is a graph type, not a quartile, which is a value that divides ordered data.
Why B: Quartiles are the three values Q1, Q2 and Q3 that split ordered data into four equal parts, each holding about 25% of the data.
Why C: A type of mean found by adding and dividing describes an average, which is a different idea from quartiles that split the data into parts.
Why D: An outlier is a value far from the rest, and a quartile is a dividing point of the data, so these are different ideas.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
A: Max minus min
B: The mean
C: Q1 plus Q3
D: Q3 minus Q1
Why A: Max minus min is the range, which uses only the two extreme values, and the IQR uses the quartiles instead.
Why B: The mean is the average of all values, a measure of center, so it is not the IQR, which measures the spread of the middle half.
Why C: Adding Q1 and Q3 gives a sum with no meaning as a spread, whereas the IQR is found by subtracting Q1 from Q3.
Why D: The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, which gives the spread of the middle 50% of the data and resists the effect of outliers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a box plot show?
A: The median, quartiles and potential outliers of a dataset
B: The correlation between two variables across a dataset
C: The frequency of each value in a dataset as bars
D: The trend of a variable over time as a line
Why A: A box plot displays the median, the quartiles and potential outliers, giving a compact picture of the spread and center of the data.
Why B: Correlation is shown by a scatter plot. A box plot shows the median, quartiles and potential outliers.
Why C: Bars of value frequencies make a histogram. A box plot shows the median, quartiles and potential outliers.
Why D: A line over time is a line chart. A box plot shows the median, quartiles and potential outliers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a histogram?
A: A pie chart showing shares of a whole as slices of a circle
B: A line of best fit drawn through the points on a scatter plot
C: A bar chart showing the frequency of values in ranges (bins)
D: A scatter of two variables plotted against each other
Why A: A pie chart shows shares of a whole as slices, whereas a histogram shows how many values fall in each range of a numeric variable.
Why B: A line of best fit is drawn on a scatter plot to show a trend, which is a different tool from a histogram.
Why C: A histogram is a bar chart showing the frequency of values in ranges, called bins, which reveals the shape of the distribution.
Why D: A scatter of two variables plotted against each other is a scatter plot and shows a relationship, whereas a histogram shows one variable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a normal distribution, about what percent of data lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
Why A: By the empirical rule, about 68% of the data in a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean.
Why B: About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations of the mean, so this figure is for a wider interval than one deviation.
Why C: About 95% lies within two standard deviations, not one, so this figure belongs to a wider interval than the one asked about.
Why D: Fifty percent is the share on each side of the mean and not the share within one standard deviation, which is about 68%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a normal distribution, about what percent of data lie within two standard deviations of the mean?
Why A: About 68% lies within one standard deviation, not two, so this figure is too low for the interval asked about.
Why B: By the empirical rule, about 95% of the data in a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
Why C: Seventy-five percent is not a value from the empirical rule, which gives 68%, 95% and 99.7% for one, two and three deviations.
Why D: About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations, so this is the figure for three and not for two.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is skewness?
A: A measure of size for a set of data values
B: A measure of spread around the mean of data
C: A measure of center for a set of data values
D: A measure of the asymmetry of a distribution
Why A: Size is measured by count or by total, and skewness is a measure of the shape of a distribution, not its size.
Why B: Spread around the mean is measured by variance and standard deviation, while skewness describes how lopsided the distribution is.
Why C: Center is measured by the mean, median or mode, and skewness is a different measure that describes the shape of a distribution.
Why D: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution, showing whether it has a longer tail on the right or on the left.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A distribution has a long tail to the right. It is described as:
A: Uniform in shape overall
B: Symmetric in shape overall
C: Right (positively) skewed
D: Left skewed, long left tail
Why A: A uniform distribution has roughly equal frequency across values and no long tail, so it does not match a long right tail.
Why B: A symmetric distribution looks the same on both sides of the center, and a long right tail makes it lopsided, so it is not symmetric.
Why C: A long tail to the right is right skewed, also called positively skewed, with the mean usually pulled above the median.
Why D: A left skewed distribution has its long tail on the left, but this one has its long tail on the right, so it is not left skewed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What is the probability of drawing red?
Why A: There are 3 red marbles out of 3 + 7 = 10 total, so the probability of drawing red is 3/10, which equals 0.3.
Why B: The value 0.37 does not match any ratio here, because 3 red out of 10 marbles gives exactly 3/10 = 0.3, not 0.37.
Why C: The value 0.7 is the probability of drawing blue, since 7 of the 10 marbles are blue, but the question asks about red marbles.
Why D: A probability can never exceed 1, so 3 is impossible; the correct fraction is 3 red out of 10 marbles, which is 0.3.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the probability of rolling a 5 on a fair six-sided die?
Why A: The value 1/5 would apply to a five-sided die, but a fair six-sided die has six equally likely faces, so one face gives 1/6.
Why B: A fair six-sided die has six equally likely faces and only one of them shows a 5, so the probability is 1 out of 6.
Why C: The fraction 5/6 is the chance of rolling anything except a 5, which is the complement; the chance of rolling a 5 itself is 1/6.
Why D: The fraction 1/2 would mean three of the six faces show a 5, but only one face does, so the correct probability is 1/6.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a fair six-sided die?
Why A: The fraction 1/6 is the chance of one single face, but an even roll can be 2, 4 or 6, which is three faces, not one.
Why B: The fraction 2/3 would need four even faces, but a die has only three even faces: 2, 4 and 6, giving 3/6 = 1/2.
Why C: The even faces are 2, 4 and 6, which is 3 of the 6 equally likely faces, so the probability is 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2.
Why D: The fraction 1/3 would mean only two faces are even, but 2, 4 and 6 are all even, so there are three, giving 3/6 = 1/2.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean for two events to be independent?
A: The two events have the same probability of happening
B: They are the same event described in two different ways
C: One event must happen before the other can occur
D: One event's outcome does not affect the other's probability
Why A: Equal probability is a different idea; independent events can have different chances. Independence means one outcome does not change the other's probability.
Why B: Two independent events are different events, not one event described twice; they just do not influence each other's probabilities, so describing them as identical is wrong.
Why C: That describes dependence, where one outcome affects the other. Independent events do not change each other's probability.
Why D: Independent events have outcomes that do not change each other's probabilities, so P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B), as with two separate coin flips.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the probability of getting heads on two consecutive fair coin flips?
Why A: A probability cannot be greater than 1, so 2 is impossible; two heads in a row has chance 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4.
Why B: The flips are independent, so multiply the chances: 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4, meaning one of four equally likely outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT) is two heads.
Why C: A probability of 1 would mean two heads is certain, but each flip has only a 1/2 chance, so the combined chance is 1/4.
Why D: The value 1/2 is the chance of heads on a single flip; for two consecutive heads you multiply 1/2 times 1/2 to get 1/4.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the probability of rolling two 6s in two rolls of a fair die?
Why A: The fraction 2/6 adds the single-roll chances (1/6 + 1/6), but independent events must be multiplied, so the answer is 1/6 times 1/6 = 1/36.
Why B: The value 1/6 is the chance of one 6 on a single roll; getting a second 6 as well multiplies by another 1/6, giving 1/36.
Why C: The value 1/12 would come from 1/6 times 1/2, but the second roll also has a 1/6 chance of a 6, so the product is 1/36.
Why D: The two rolls are independent, so multiply the chances: 1/6 times 1/6 = 1/36, which matches 1 favorable outcome out of 36 possible pairs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are mutually exclusive events?
A: Events whose outcomes do not change each other's odds
B: Events that happen one right after the other
C: Events that cannot happen at the same time
D: Equally likely events in a single trial
Why A: That describes independent events, which can happen together. Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time.
Why B: Events in sequence can both occur in a trial. Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time.
Why C: Mutually exclusive events cannot both occur in one trial, such as rolling a 2 and a 5 on one die, so their joint probability is zero.
Why D: Equally likely events share the same probability, which is a different idea from mutual exclusivity; two equally likely events could still happen together, like heads on two coins.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the complement of an event?
A: All outcomes in which the event does not occur
B: The event itself as it occurs in the sample
C: A guess about the chance of the event in the trial
D: A different event that cannot happen with the first
Why A: The complement of an event is every outcome in the sample space where the event does not occur, and its probability equals 1 minus P(event).
Why B: The event itself is the set of outcomes where it occurs, which is the opposite of its complement, since the complement contains the outcomes outside the event.
Why C: A guess about the chance is only an estimate and not an outcome set; the complement is a defined set of outcomes in which the event fails.
Why D: An event that cannot occur with the first is mutually exclusive but need not cover everything else; the complement must include every remaining outcome, so exclusivity alone is not enough.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If the chance of rain is 0.35, what is the chance of no rain?
Why A: Probabilities cannot exceed 1, so 1.35 is impossible; the chance of no rain is 1 minus 0.35, which gives 0.65.
Why B: The value 0.35 is the chance of rain itself, not of its absence; the complement is 1 - 0.35 = 0.65.
Why C: The chance of no rain is the complement of rain, so subtract from 1: 1 - 0.35 = 0.65, meaning a 65 percent chance of staying dry.
Why D: The value 0.35% means 0.0035, which is far too small; the correct answer is 1 - 0.35 = 0.65, not a tiny percentage.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the law of large numbers?
A: As sample size grows, the sample average approaches the true average
B: Outliers dominate large samples, so the average moves from the true value
C: Small samples are best because they are easy to collect and to read
D: Averages never converge toward any value as more data are gathered
Why A: The law of large numbers says that as more observations are collected, the sample average gets closer to the true expected value, so large samples are more reliable.
Why B: Large samples do the opposite of letting outliers dominate, because any single odd value is diluted by many others and the average moves toward the true value.
Why C: Small samples are less reliable because chance can swing their averages widely; the law of large numbers says bigger samples converge on the true mean.
Why D: Averages do converge toward a value as more data are gathered, which is precisely what the law of large numbers states, so claiming they never converge is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is expected value?
A: A guaranteed value that the outcome will reach every time
B: The most likely value that a single trial could produce
C: The largest value that a single trial could ever produce
D: The long-run average outcome weighted by probabilities
Why A: Expected value is an average over many trials, not a guarantee; a single trial can land far from it, as a fair coin never pays half a head.
Why B: Expected value is not the most likely outcome of one trial; it is a probability-weighted average and may be a value that never actually occurs.
Why C: Expected value is not the maximum possible result; it sits among the possible values, weighting each outcome by its probability, so it is usually below the largest outcome.
Why D: Expected value is the sum of each outcome times its probability, which gives the average result you would see over many repeated trials in the long run.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and $0 otherwise. What is the expected value?
Why A: The value $8 is wrong because it ignores the probabilities; the expected value is 10 times 0.2 plus 0 times 0.8, which equals $2.
Why B: Multiply each payout by its probability and add: 10 times 0.2 plus 0 times 0.8 = 2 + 0 = $2, which is the long-run average per game.
Why C: The value $0.2 is the probability of winning, not a dollar amount; the expected value multiplies it by the $10 payout, giving 10 times 0.2 = $2.
Why D: The value $10 is the prize when winning, but you win only 20 percent of the time, so the average is 10 times 0.2 = $2.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a correlation of −0.9 indicate?
A: A strong negative relationship
B: A perfect positive relationship
C: No relationship at all there
D: A weak positive relationship
Why A: A correlation of -0.9 is close to -1, meaning that as one variable rises the other tends to fall strongly, which is a strong negative relationship.
Why B: A perfect positive relationship would have a correlation of +1; the negative sign on -0.9 means the variables move in opposite directions.
Why C: No relationship would give a correlation near 0; a value of -0.9 is far from zero, so a strong linear pattern is present.
Why D: A weak positive relationship would show a small positive value such as +0.2; -0.9 is both negative and large in size, so it is strong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a correlation near 0 indicate?
A: A strong positive linear link
B: A strong negative linear link
C: Little or no linear relationship
D: A perfect linear relationship
Why A: A strong positive linear link would have a correlation close to +1; a value near 0 means there is no such pattern in the data.
Why B: A strong negative linear link would have a correlation close to -1; a value near 0 is nowhere near that, so no such pattern exists.
Why C: A correlation near 0 means the points do not follow a straight-line trend, so there is little or no linear relationship between the variables.
Why D: A perfect linear relationship gives a correlation of exactly +1 or -1; a value near 0 is the opposite extreme, showing almost no linear link.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why does correlation not imply causation?
A: Correlation is measured wrongly when the variables are in different units
B: Causation is established once the correlation is above 0.5
C: The variable measured first in time is the cause of the other
D: A third factor or chance may explain why two variables move together
Why A: Correlation works across different units. It does not imply causation because a third factor or chance may explain why variables move together.
Why B: No correlation value establishes causation. A third factor or chance may explain why two variables move together.
Why C: Order in time does not prove cause. A third factor or chance may explain why two variables move together.
Why D: Two variables can move together because a hidden third factor drives both, or by chance, so a correlation alone cannot show that one causes the other.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer. What best explains this?
A: Drowning causes ice cream sales
B: A confounding variable, hot weather
C: Pure coincidence only, nothing more
D: Ice cream causes drowning deaths
Why A: Drowning does not cause ice cream sales; both numbers rise in summer, so the link is not one causing the other, and the hidden factor is the weather.
Why B: Hot summer weather drives more swimming, which raises drownings, and also raises ice cream buying, so weather is a confounding variable behind both patterns.
Why C: The rise in both is not pure coincidence, because a real shared cause exists in hot weather, which brings more swimmers and more ice cream buyers at once.
Why D: Eating ice cream does not cause drowning; the two simply rise together because warm summer weather increases both swimming and ice cream purchases, so this is a spurious link.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a confounding variable?
A: The outcome that a researcher measures at the end of an experiment on subjects
B: An outside factor that influences both the cause and effect, hiding the true relationship
C: The only variable in a study, which the researcher changes on purpose to see the results every time
D: The sample of people who are chosen to take part in a study of the topic at hand
Why A: The outcome measured at the end of an experiment is the dependent variable, not a confounder; a confounder is a separate outside factor that influences both cause and effect.
Why B: A confounding variable is an outside factor that affects both the supposed cause and the effect, which can create a false link or mask a real one.
Why C: The variable the researcher changes on purpose is the independent variable; a confounder is not controlled by the researcher and instead distorts the apparent relationship between variables.
Why D: The group chosen to take part is the sample; a confounding variable is not a group of people but a hidden factor that influences both cause and effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hypothesis test?
A: A way to collect data from a sample of people by using a short written survey
B: A chart that shows the results of a test or a survey in the form of bars or lines
C: A procedure for deciding whether sample data support a claim about a population
D: A database query that pulls a set of records from a table by using a filter key
Why A: Collecting data from a sample with a survey is data collection, not testing; a hypothesis test is the step that uses that sample data to judge a claim.
Why B: A chart displays results but does not decide anything; a hypothesis test is a statistical procedure that uses sample data to judge whether a claim about a population holds.
Why C: A hypothesis test is a procedure that weighs sample evidence to decide whether a claim about a population is supported or should be rejected.
Why D: A database query retrieves stored records and has nothing to do with statistics; a hypothesis test checks whether sample data support a claim about a population.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a null hypothesis?
A: A default claim of no effect or no difference
B: A proven fact the data have already confirmed
C: A claim of a big effect, hoped to be proven
D: A sample statistic such as the mean of the data
Why A: The null hypothesis is the default assumption of no effect or no difference, and a test asks whether the data give enough evidence to reject it.
Why B: The null is not a proven fact; it is only a starting assumption, and a test can reject it but never prove it true.
Why C: A claim of a big effect that the researcher hopes to prove is the alternative hypothesis, which is the opposite of the null's claim of no effect.
Why D: A sample statistic such as the mean describes the data you collected, whereas the null hypothesis is a claim about the population that the statistic is used to test.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A test has p = 0.02 and the significance level is 0.05. What is the conclusion?
A: The result is impossible
B: Collect no more data at all
C: Accept the null as proven
D: Reject the null hypothesis
Why A: A p-value of 0.02 does not make the result impossible; it only means the data would be fairly unlikely if the null were true, so the null is rejected.
Why B: A small p-value is a result to act on, not a reason to stop; we conclude from this test, and more data is not required.
Why C: Hypothesis tests never prove the null; since p = 0.02 is below 0.05 the data actually argue against the null, so it is rejected instead.
Why D: Because p = 0.02 is smaller than the significance level of 0.05, the result is statistically significant, so we reject the null hypothesis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a margin of error?
A: The range of uncertainty around a survey estimate
B: The mean of the sample data collected in a survey
C: The sample size, which is the number of people asked
D: A data entry mistake made by a clerk at a desk
Why A: A margin of error states how far a survey estimate may plausibly differ from the true population value, giving a range of uncertainty around the estimate, such as plus or minus 3 points.
Why B: The mean of the sample is the estimate itself, not its uncertainty; the margin of error is the range around that estimate within which the true value likely falls.
Why C: The number of people asked is the sample size, which affects the margin of error but is not the same thing; the margin is the range of uncertainty.
Why D: A data entry mistake is a recording error, while the margin of error is a statistical measure of sampling uncertainty that exists even when all the data are recorded correctly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is statistical significance?
A: The share of people in the group who were surveyed
B: Evidence that a result is unlikely to be due to chance alone
C: The result can be repeated by the same researcher
D: The effect is important in practice, as the change is large
Why A: That describes sampling coverage. Statistical significance is evidence that a result is unlikely to be due to chance.
Why B: A result is statistically significant when it would be unlikely to appear through random chance alone, typically when the p-value falls below a chosen level such as 0.05.
Why C: Repeatability is a separate idea. Statistical significance means a result is unlikely to be due to chance.
Why D: Practical importance is about the size of the effect, while statistical significance only says the result is unlikely to be chance; a tiny effect can be significant in a large sample.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Type I error?
A: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis here
B: A correct decision made by the analyst after a test
C: A data entry mistake made by a clerk at a desk
D: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive)
Why A: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a Type II error, a false negative, whereas a Type I error is rejecting a null that is actually true.
Why B: A correct decision is not an error at all; a Type I error occurs only when the analyst wrongly rejects a null hypothesis that is true.
Why C: A data entry mistake is a recording problem, not a statistical decision error; a Type I error specifically means rejecting a true null hypothesis.
Why D: A Type I error is a false positive: the null hypothesis is actually true, yet the test rejects it, and its probability is the significance level alpha.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Type II error?
A: Rejecting a true null hypothesis, a false positive result
B: A correct decision made by the analyst after the test is run
C: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative)
D: A data entry mistake made by a clerk when typing in the figures
Why A: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, a false positive; a Type II error is the opposite mistake of missing a real effect.
Why B: A correct decision is not an error; a Type II error occurs when the test fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false.
Why C: A Type II error is a false negative: the null hypothesis is false, yet the test fails to reject it, so a real effect goes undetected.
Why D: A data entry mistake is a clerical slip and not a hypothesis testing result; a Type II error means failing to reject a false null.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How can missing values be handled?
A: Ignoring them always and never filling in any gaps in the records of data every time
B: Replacing the gaps with random text taken from any other column of data
C: Deleting the entire dataset whenever any one value is missing from it
D: By removing records or filling them with estimates such as the mean or median
Why A: Ignoring missing values always is not a valid rule, since gaps can bias results or break calculations; analysts usually remove records or fill the gaps with sensible estimates.
Why B: Random text from another column would corrupt the data and mix up meanings; missing numeric values should be filled with sensible estimates such as the mean or median instead.
Why C: Deleting the entire dataset because one value is missing would waste all other useful information; analysts remove only affected records or fill gaps with estimates.
Why D: Common methods are dropping records with gaps or imputing estimates such as the mean or median, which keep the dataset usable while limiting bias from the missing values.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data normalization (scaling)?
A: Filling in missing values with the average of each column
B: Adjusting values to a common scale so features are comparable
C: Converting category labels into numbers for a model
D: Combining records from two tables into one data set
Why A: Filling gaps is imputation. Normalization adjusts values to a common scale so features are comparable.
Why B: Normalization rescales features onto a common range or scale, such as 0 to 1, so that no feature dominates just because its numbers are larger.
Why C: That is encoding. Normalization adjusts values to a common scale so features are comparable.
Why D: Combining tables is a join. Normalization adjusts values to a common scale so features are comparable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is one-hot encoding?
A: Replacing missing values in a column with the most common value
B: Assigning each category a single number in rank order, such as 1, 2, 3
C: Converting a categorical variable into binary columns, one per category
D: Deleting categories that appear rarely in the data and merging the rest
Why A: That is imputation. One-hot encoding turns a categorical variable into binary columns, one per category.
Why B: That is ordinal or label encoding, which uses one column of ranked numbers. One-hot encoding creates a binary column for each category.
Why C: One-hot encoding turns a categorical variable into binary columns, one per category, with a 1 marking the category present, so models can use it as numbers.
Why D: Deleting or merging rare categories is a grouping step; one-hot encoding keeps every category and gives each its own binary column.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows the relationship between two numerical variables?
A: Scatter plot
B: Bar chart
C: Word cloud
D: Pie chart
Why A: A scatter plot puts one numeric variable on each axis, so each point shows a pair and the pattern reveals how the two variables relate.
Why B: A bar chart compares values across categories using one numeric measure, so it does not show how two numeric variables move together.
Why C: A word cloud displays the frequency of words in text, not numeric variables, so it cannot show a relationship between two numerical quantities.
Why D: A pie chart shows parts of one whole as slices and uses a single measure, so it cannot display how two numeric variables relate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows change over time?
A: Line chart
B: Pie chart
C: Table of names
D: Scatter plot
Why A: A line chart connects points in time order, so rises and falls across days, months or years are easy to see, which suits change over time.
Why B: A pie chart shows how a whole splits into parts at one moment, so it cannot display how a value changes across time.
Why C: A table of names lists labels with no values plotted over time, so it cannot show trends or changes, and names alone carry no time pattern.
Why D: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, not a sequence of changes through time, though it could plot time on an axis; a line chart is the standard choice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows parts of a whole?
A: Histogram
B: Line chart
C: Scatter plot
D: Pie chart
Why A: A histogram shows how values are distributed in bins for one numeric variable, not how parts add up to a whole.
Why B: A line chart tracks how a value changes over time, so it does not display parts that make up a whole.
Why C: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, not how shares combine to form a whole.
Why D: A pie chart splits a circle into slices sized by share, so it shows how parts make up a whole, such as budget categories adding to 100 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best compares values across categories?
A: Line chart
B: Bar chart
C: Scatter plot
D: Heat map
Why A: A line chart is best for trends across time, not for comparing separate categories side by side.
Why B: A bar chart gives each category its own bar, so heights are easy to compare directly across categories such as products or regions.
Why C: A scatter plot shows how two numeric variables relate, not how a measure compares across separate categories.
Why D: A heat map uses color intensity across a grid, which suits dense matrices or patterns, whereas a bar chart makes direct comparisons across categories simpler and clearer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a heat map?
A: A text report that lists numbers in rows and columns
B: A list of names and addresses kept in a database
C: A visualization using color intensity to show values
D: A weather forecast only, with the temperature by region
Why A: A text report listing numbers in rows and columns is a table, whereas a heat map turns values into colors so patterns stand out visually.
Why B: A list of names and addresses is a contact record, not a visual; a heat map shades cells or areas by value to show intensity.
Why C: A heat map uses color intensity to represent values, so high and low areas stand out at a glance, whether in a grid or on a map.
Why D: Heat maps are not limited to weather; they are used for website clicks, correlations and many other data, so restricting them to temperatures is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why can truncating a bar chart's axis be misleading?
A: It exaggerates differences between bars
B: It has no effect on the way bars look
C: It improves the accuracy of the chart
D: It hides all differences between the bars
Why A: Starting the axis above zero makes small differences look big because bar lengths no longer reflect true proportions, so truncating exaggerates differences between bars.
Why B: Truncating the axis changes how long each bar appears, so it does affect how bars look; bar length should reflect the true size starting from zero.
Why C: Truncation does not improve accuracy; it distorts the proportions between bars, making small gaps look large and misleading the reader.
Why D: A truncated axis does the opposite of hiding differences; by cutting off the lower part of the scale it makes differences look bigger than they are.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a KPI?
A: A kind of chart used to show key figures such as sales and profit over a year
B: A database key used to link one table to another table in a relational design
C: A keyboard shortcut that lets a user perform an action with a few key presses
D: Key performance indicator, a measurable value showing progress toward a goal
Why A: A chart is a visual display, whereas a KPI is a measurable number tracked against a goal; a KPI can appear on a chart but is not itself one.
Why B: A database key links tables, which is a database concept, while a KPI is a measurable value that shows progress toward a business goal.
Why C: A keyboard shortcut triggers an action by key presses, which is a computing convenience, whereas a KPI is a metric used to track performance against objectives.
Why D: KPI stands for key performance indicator, a measurable value such as monthly sales that shows how well progress is going toward a goal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data storytelling?
A: Hiding data so that nobody can see the numbers behind a result
B: Deleting data that does not support the story an analyst wants to tell overall
C: Communicating insights with data, visuals and narrative to drive action
D: Writing fiction that tells an invented tale about a made up company
Why A: Hiding data means nobody sees the numbers, the opposite of storytelling, which exposes the data and explains what it means so people understand it.
Why B: Deleting data that does not support a story is cherry-picking and is dishonest, whereas data storytelling presents the real evidence clearly and honestly.
Why C: Data storytelling blends data, visuals and narrative to explain insights clearly, so that the audience understands them and is moved to take action.
Why D: Writing fiction about an invented company has no real data behind it; data storytelling communicates true findings from actual data using visuals and a clear narrative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the SQL clause WHERE do?
A: Joins tables on shared columns
B: Filters rows by a condition
C: Groups rows by a column
D: Sorts rows by a column value
Why A: Joining tables on shared columns is done by the JOIN clause, not by WHERE, which filters rows rather than combining tables.
Why B: The WHERE clause keeps only rows that satisfy a condition, such as price greater than 10, so it filters rows before results are returned.
Why C: Grouping rows by a column is the job of GROUP BY, whereas WHERE only filters individual rows by a condition.
Why D: Sorting rows by a column is done by ORDER BY, not WHERE, which filters rows instead of arranging them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the SQL clause GROUP BY do?
A: Filters rows that meet a given condition in a table
B: Adds columns to a table that hold new values for each row
C: Groups rows sharing values so aggregates can be computed
D: Deletes duplicates only from the table and groups no rows
Why A: Filtering rows that meet a condition is done by WHERE, whereas GROUP BY collects rows with shared values into groups for summarizing.
Why B: Adding columns is done by altering a table or by computed expressions in SELECT, and GROUP BY does not create new columns of values.
Why C: GROUP BY collects rows sharing the same value in a column into groups, so aggregate functions such as COUNT or SUM can be computed per group.
Why D: Removing duplicates is done with DISTINCT, and GROUP BY does group rows rather than remove them, so saying it groups no rows is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an SQL JOIN do?
A: Adds a new column to one table with a default value
B: Combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column
C: Backs up a table to a second server for use in an emergency
D: Counts the rows in a table and groups them by category
Why A: Adding a column is done with ALTER TABLE. A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables using a related column.
Why B: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables by matching values in a related column, such as a customer ID that appears in both tables.
Why C: Backing up a table to another server is a database administration task, whereas a JOIN is a query operation that merges rows from related tables.
Why D: Counting and grouping is done with COUNT and GROUP BY. A JOIN combines rows from tables based on a related column.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a primary key in a database?
A: A column that uniquely identifies each row
B: A password that guards access to a database
C: A chart that shows the rows of a table
D: A column that repeats values from row to row
Why A: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose values uniquely identify each row, so no two rows share the same key value.
Why B: A password guards access, which is a security feature, whereas a primary key is a column that makes each row uniquely identifiable in the table.
Why C: A chart displays data visually, while a primary key is a structural database feature that gives each row a unique identity.
Why D: A primary key must have unique values in every row, so a column that repeats values cannot serve as one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a foreign key?
A: A duplicate row that appears twice in the same table
B: A key from another country used to open a foreign branch overall
C: A password that protects a table from outside access
D: A column that references the primary key of another table
Why A: A duplicate row is a data quality problem and not a key; a foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table.
Why B: A foreign key is a database term for linking tables and has nothing to do with countries or branches abroad, despite the word foreign.
Why C: Passwords protect access, whereas a foreign key is a column whose values match a primary key in another table, creating a link between the two.
Why D: A foreign key is a column holding values that match the primary key in another table, which links the tables and maintains referential integrity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a pivot table?
A: A table of passwords that stores the secret logins of every user
B: A hardware table that holds computers and tools in a lab or shop
C: A summary table that reorganizes and aggregates data by categories
D: A table that rotates a screen so that the data is shown from another angle
Why A: A table of passwords is a security risk and unrelated to analysis; a pivot table summarizes and regroups data by categories.
Why B: A hardware table for tools and computers is furniture; a pivot table is a software feature in spreadsheets that summarizes and reorganizes data.
Why C: A pivot table reorganizes data and aggregates it, such as summing sales by region and month, so patterns can be seen quickly in a compact summary.
Why D: A pivot table does not rotate a screen; the name refers to turning rows and columns into summary views, so it is a data tool, not a display feature.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the spreadsheet function VLOOKUP do?
A: Draws charts from a range of cells and puts them on a separate sheet
B: Deletes duplicates from a column and keeps only the first copy of each value
C: Sorts data in a range from smallest to largest and puts it in order
D: Looks up a value in the first column and returns a value from another column
Why A: Drawing charts is done with chart tools, whereas VLOOKUP searches for a value in a table and returns related data from the same row.
Why B: Removing duplicates is a separate data tool; VLOOKUP does not delete anything and instead finds a matching value to return a related value from another column.
Why C: Sorting arranges data in a range in order, which is a different feature, while VLOOKUP searches for a key and returns a matching value from the row.
Why D: VLOOKUP searches the first column of a range for a value and returns a value from another column in the same row, such as a price for a product ID.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ETL?
A: Extract, transform, load, the process of moving and preparing data
B: Email, text, letter, the three common ways of sending a message
C: Encrypt, test, launch, the three steps in releasing new software overall
D: Edit, type, link, the three common steps in writing a document
Why A: ETL stands for extract, transform, load: data is pulled from sources, cleaned and reshaped, then loaded into a target such as a warehouse for analysis.
Why B: Email, text and letter do not form ETL; the acronym stands for extract, transform, load, which is a data pipeline process, not a messaging method.
Why C: Encrypt, test and launch do not spell ETL, which is a data engineering process that extracts, transforms and loads data, not a software release routine.
Why D: Edit, type and link describe document writing, while ETL means extract, transform, load, a standard process in data engineering for moving and preparing data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data mining?
A: Printing data on paper so that managers can read it
B: Discovering patterns and relationships in large datasets
C: Deleting data from a table once it has been used up
D: Digging for minerals deep in the ground with a drill in general
Why A: Printing data on paper is reporting, not mining; data mining analyzes large datasets to uncover hidden patterns and relationships automatically.
Why B: Data mining applies statistics and algorithms to large datasets to find patterns and relationships that are not obvious, such as which products are bought together.
Why C: Deleting data after use is data cleanup or retention management, whereas data mining analyzes existing data to find useful patterns.
Why D: Digging minerals is physical mining; data mining only borrows the name because analysts extract valuable patterns from large datasets, and nothing is excavated from the ground.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is A/B testing?
A: Grading students on tests and giving them scores for the term
B: Testing alphabets to see which letters are used most in a language
C: Testing only one version of something to see how well it works
D: Comparing two versions of something to see which performs better
Why A: Grading students gives scores for learning, whereas A/B testing compares two versions of a product, page or ad to see which one performs better.
Why B: A/B testing does not involve alphabets; the letters label two versions, A and B, and the test measures which version performs better with users.
Why C: Testing only one version gives nothing to compare against; A/B testing needs two versions shown to similar groups so the results can be compared.
Why D: A/B testing shows two versions to comparable groups and measures a result such as clicks or purchases to decide which version performs better.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store tests two ads and Ad B gets more clicks from a randomly split audience. What can it conclude?
A: Ad B likely performs better, subject to statistical significance
B: Nothing can be learned from the clicks that each ad received
C: Both are identical in their results, whatever the clicks show in general
D: Ad A is certainly better, since it was shown to more people
Why A: Ad B got more clicks from a randomly split audience, so it likely performs better, but a significance test must check that the gap is not due to chance.
Why B: The clicks are real evidence from a randomized test, so claiming nothing can be learned is wrong; a significance test can tell whether the difference is likely real.
Why C: The two ads got different click counts, so calling them identical ignores the data; whether the difference is real depends on statistical significance.
Why D: Ad A being certainly better contradicts the data, since Ad B received more clicks; also the audience was split randomly, so exposure to more people is not shown.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is churn?
A: A profit margin that shows earnings as a share of total sales overall
B: The rate at which customers stop doing business with a company
C: Making butter from cream by churning it in a barrel by hand
D: Customer growth over time as more people buy from a company
Why A: A profit margin shows earnings as a share of sales, whereas churn measures how many customers leave over a period, so it is a loss rate.
Why B: Churn is the rate at which customers stop buying from or subscribing to a company over a given period, such as 5 percent leaving each month.
Why C: Making butter is the dairy meaning of churning, but in business analytics churn means customers leaving, not cream turning into butter.
Why D: Customer growth over time describes gains, but churn measures losses, meaning the share of customers who leave during a period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a time series?
A: A database table that holds records in rows and columns
B: A list of random numbers made by a computer program
C: Data points recorded at successive points in time
D: A set of categories used to group data into bins
Why A: A table of rows and columns describes data layout in a database, whereas a time series is data recorded in order across successive points in time.
Why B: A list of random numbers has no time ordering, but a time series is defined by observations recorded at successive points in time.
Why C: A time series is a sequence of data points recorded at successive points in time, such as daily sales or monthly temperature, so order matters.
Why D: A set of categories used to group data into bins describes a histogram setup, not a time series, which has observations ordered across time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is seasonality in a time series?
A: A one-time spike in the data that happens only once
B: A repeating pattern at regular intervals such as yearly
C: A data error caused by a mistake in recording a value
D: A random change in the data that follows no regular pattern
Why A: A one-time spike is an outlier or event, whereas seasonality is a pattern that repeats at regular intervals, so it does not happen only once.
Why B: Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at regular, predictable intervals, such as higher retail sales every December, within a time series.
Why C: A recording error is a data quality issue, whereas seasonality is a real repeating pattern in the values at regular intervals.
Why D: Seasonality follows a regular repeating schedule, such as yearly or weekly, so describing it as random with no regular pattern is the opposite of true.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a trend in a time series?
A: A random jump in the data at one point
B: A repeating cycle that returns every year
C: A long-term upward or downward movement
D: A data error caused by a recording mistake
Why A: A random jump at one point is noise or an outlier, whereas a trend is a sustained movement in one direction over a long period.
Why B: A repeating cycle that returns every year is seasonality, while a trend is a long-term rise or fall that does not repeat on a schedule.
Why C: A trend is the long-term upward or downward direction of a time series, such as steadily rising prices over many years.
Why D: A recording mistake is a data error, whereas a trend is a real long-term direction in the data, not an error.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is artificial general intelligence (AGI)?
A: Hypothetical AI able to learn and perform any intellectual task a human can
B: AI for one task such as sorting mail or playing a game of chess at home
C: A type of calculator that adds and multiplies numbers on a small screen
D: A spreadsheet that holds numbers in rows and columns for use in a report in the end
Why A: AGI is hypothetical AI that could learn and carry out any intellectual task a human can, instead of being limited to one narrow job.
Why B: AI built for a single task, such as sorting mail or playing chess, is narrow AI, which is the opposite of general intelligence across many tasks.
Why C: A calculator adds and multiplies on request but does not learn or reason across tasks, so it has nothing to do with artificial general intelligence.
Why D: A spreadsheet stores numbers in rows and columns, but it does not learn or reason like a human, so it is not AGI.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is robotics?
A: Trading stocks only, buying and selling shares on an exchange as a rule
B: Writing poems and verses for readers in a magazine or a book
C: Cooking recipes for meals in a home kitchen or a restaurant
D: The design and use of machines that perform tasks, often with AI
Why A: Trading stocks is finance, not robotics; robotics concerns designing and using physical machines that perform tasks, often guided by AI.
Why B: Writing poems is literature, not robotics; robotics is the field that designs machines, often with AI, to carry out physical tasks.
Why C: Cooking recipes belong to the culinary world; robotics is about designing and using machines that perform tasks, though a robot might be built to cook.
Why D: Robotics covers the design, building and use of machines that carry out tasks, often with AI to perceive and decide, as in factory arms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a heuristic?
A: A database query that pulls a set of records from a table
B: A full search method that tests each possible answer to be sure
C: A rule stored in a database to keep field values valid
D: A practical shortcut that finds a good-enough solution quickly
Why A: A database query retrieves stored records and has nothing to do with problem solving by shortcuts, whereas a heuristic is a practical rule for finding good-enough answers.
Why B: Testing each possible answer is exhaustive search, which is slow. A heuristic is a practical shortcut that finds a good-enough solution quickly.
Why C: That is a validation constraint. A heuristic is a practical shortcut for finding a good-enough solution quickly.
Why D: A heuristic is a practical shortcut or rule of thumb that quickly finds a good-enough solution when a perfect one would be too slow.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a generative AI model?
A: A model that creates new content such as text, images or audio
B: A model that prints reports and sends them to a printer
C: A model that deletes files from a disk to free up room fast
D: A model that only sorts data into groups and cannot create anything
Why A: A generative AI model produces new content, such as text, images or audio, learned from patterns in its training data.
Why B: Printing reports is a basic output task, not generative AI; generative models create new content like text, images or audio from patterns they learned.
Why C: Deleting files frees space and is a system utility, not generative AI, which instead produces new content such as writing or images.
Why D: A model that only sorts data into groups is a classifier or clustering model, whereas generative models can create new text, images or audio.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a prompt in generative AI?
A: The model's output, which is the answer that it gives back
B: The model's weights, the numbers it has learned so far
C: The input instruction or question given to the model
D: The training data that was used to teach the model
Why A: The model's output is the response it returns, which is the opposite end of the process; the prompt is the input given to it.
Why B: Weights are the learned numbers inside the model, not what a user types; a prompt is the instruction or question given to the model.
Why C: A prompt is the input instruction, question or context you give a generative model, and it shapes the response the model produces.
Why D: Training data is used earlier to teach the model, whereas a prompt is what a user supplies at use time to request an output.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hallucination in AI?
A: A model update that changes the code and releases a new version
B: When a model produces confident but false or fabricated information
C: A correct answer that is supported by facts and by sources cited in general
D: A security feature that blocks hackers from entering the system
Why A: A model update changing the code is a release, not a hallucination; a hallucination is when a model generates confident but false or made-up information.
Why B: A hallucination occurs when a model states fabricated or incorrect information confidently, such as inventing a citation, so its output cannot be trusted without checking.
Why C: A correct answer backed by facts and sources is the opposite of a hallucination, which is false or fabricated content presented with confidence.
Why D: A security feature blocking hackers is protection, not a hallucination, which describes a model producing confident but false or invented information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An AI chatbot cites a book that does not exist. This is an example of:
A: Overfitting
B: Encryption
C: Hallucination
D: Normalization
Why A: Overfitting is when a model memorizes training data and fails on new data, which does not describe inventing a nonexistent source.
Why B: Encryption protects data by scrambling it and has no connection to a chatbot inventing a source that does not exist.
Why C: A chatbot citing a book that does not exist is a hallucination, since the model confidently generates fabricated information that sounds plausible but is false.
Why D: Normalization scales data to a common range and does not describe a chatbot inventing a fake source.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is prompt engineering?
A: Fixing code bugs by testing and rewriting the faulty lines
B: Crafting inputs to guide an AI model toward useful outputs
C: Building hardware such as chips and servers in a lab
D: Training from scratch on a huge set of data for many weeks
Why A: Fixing code bugs is debugging, whereas prompt engineering is the skill of designing inputs so an AI model produces useful results.
Why B: Prompt engineering crafts and refines the inputs given to a model, such as clear instructions and examples, so it produces more useful and accurate outputs.
Why C: Building chips and servers is hardware engineering, whereas prompt engineering works only with the text instructions given to an existing AI model.
Why D: Training from scratch on a huge dataset is model development, whereas prompt engineering works with an already trained model by improving the input it receives.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a token in an LLM?
A: A password that a user types to log in to an account safely each day
B: A database key that links a record in one table to a record in another in general
C: A coin that is used to pay for access to an online service or game
D: A chunk of text, such as a word or part of a word, that the model processes
Why A: A password used to log in is an authentication credential, whereas a token in an LLM is a piece of text that the model reads and writes.
Why B: A database key links records between tables, which is a data concept, whereas an LLM token is a small chunk of text the model processes.
Why C: A coin used to pay for service is a currency token; in a language model, a token is instead a piece of text, not a payment unit.
Why D: A token is a chunk of text, such as a whole word or part of a word, which is the basic unit that a language model reads and generates.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fine-tuning?
A: Further training a pre-trained model on specific data for a task
B: Deleting a model once it is old and replacing it with a new one overall
C: Tuning a musical instrument before a concert so its notes blend
D: Printing a model on paper so that people can read its code
