Why A: Fine-tuning continues training an already pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so that it performs better on that particular task.
Why B: Deleting an old model is retirement, not tuning; fine-tuning keeps the model and trains it further on specific data for a task.
Why C: Tuning an instrument is a musical activity; in machine learning, fine-tuning means adjusting a pre-trained model with additional task-specific data, not music.
Why D: Printing a model on paper does nothing to improve its performance; fine-tuning actually continues training the model on specific data for a task.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a pre-trained model?
A: A deleted model that was removed from the server and is gone
B: A hardware chip that is built into a computer for fast math
C: An untrained model that has not yet seen any data or examples as a rule
D: A model already trained on large data that can be reused or adapted
Why A: A deleted model has been removed, whereas a pre-trained model has finished training on large data and is available to reuse or adapt.
Why B: A hardware chip is a physical component, whereas a pre-trained model is software with learned parameters that has already been trained on large data.
Why C: An untrained model has not seen data, which is the opposite of pre-trained; a pre-trained model has already learned from large amounts of data.
Why D: A pre-trained model has already learned from large data, so it can be reused as is or adapted by fine-tuning, which saves time and cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
A: Compressing images to make files smaller so they load faster online overall
B: Combining a language model with retrieved documents to ground answers
C: Encrypting model weights so that only approved staff can read them
D: Training from scratch on a very large data set for many weeks
Why A: Compressing images shrinks file sizes and has no link to language models; RAG combines a model with retrieved documents to ground its answers.
Why B: RAG retrieves relevant documents and gives them to a language model along with the question, so answers are grounded in real sources instead of memory alone.
Why C: Encrypting model weights protects them from unapproved readers and is a security task, whereas RAG supplies retrieved documents to improve answers.
Why D: Training from scratch builds a new model over a long time, whereas RAG leaves the model as it is and adds retrieved documents when it answers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an AI agent?
A: A system that perceives its environment and takes actions to reach goals
B: A human travel agent who books flights and hotels for people on trips
C: A spreadsheet that holds numbers in rows and columns for use in a report
D: A hardware cable that links a computer to a screen or to a printer
Why A: An AI agent perceives its environment through inputs and takes actions to reach goals, such as a software system that completes tasks on a user's behalf.
Why B: A human travel agent is a person, not software; an AI agent is a system that senses its surroundings and acts to reach goals.
Why C: A spreadsheet only stores and calculates numbers when told to, and it neither perceives nor acts toward goals, so it is not an AI agent.
Why D: A hardware cable only carries signals between devices; it neither perceives nor decides, so it cannot be an AI agent that takes actions toward goals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is multimodal AI?
A: AI with one task, such as sorting mail or playing a game of chess
B: AI with only text, so that it cannot handle any images or sounds
C: AI that processes more than one type of data, such as text and images
D: AI with several monitors, so that it can show many screens at once overall
Why A: AI with one task, such as sorting mail or playing chess, is narrow AI, while multimodal AI handles more than one type of data.
Why B: An AI limited to text is unimodal; multimodal AI can handle several kinds of data such as images and sound as well as text.
Why C: Multimodal AI can process more than one type of data, such as text, images and audio, and can combine them to understand or generate content.
Why D: Multimodal does not refer to several monitors; mode here means a type of data, such as text or images, not a number of screens.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is regression in machine learning?
A: Predicting a category or class label
B: Grouping similar items without any labels
C: Predicting a continuous numerical value
D: Reducing features in a large data set
Why A: Predicting a category or class label is classification, whereas regression predicts a continuous number such as a price or temperature.
Why B: Grouping similar items without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task, whereas regression predicts a numerical value from labeled examples.
Why C: Regression predicts a continuous numerical value, such as house price or temperature, by learning the relationship between input features and a number.
Why D: Reducing features in a large data set is dimensionality reduction, which differs from regression, whose aim is to predict a continuous number.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model predicts tomorrow's temperature in degrees. This is:
A: Regression
B: Clustering
C: Reinforcement
D: Classification
Why A: Temperature in degrees is a continuous number, and predicting a continuous numerical value is regression, so this task is regression.
Why B: Clustering groups similar items without labels and does not predict a specific number such as a temperature in degrees.
Why C: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and actions, which does not fit a model that predicts a number such as temperature from data.
Why D: Classification predicts discrete categories such as sunny or rainy, but a temperature in degrees is a continuous number, so this task is regression.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model labels emails as spam or not spam. This is:
A: File compression
B: Regression
C: Clustering
D: Classification
Why A: File compression shrinks file sizes, which is not a machine learning task for labeling emails as spam or not spam.
Why B: Regression predicts a continuous number, but spam or not spam is a category, not a number, so this is not regression.

Question: What is an IDE?
A: A database that stores tables of records and lets users search them
B: A chart that shows values as bars, lines or slices on a graph
C: An internet device such as a router or a modem or a cable box
D: An integrated development environment for writing and testing code
Why A: A database that stores tables of records is a data store, while an IDE is the application where programmers write, run and debug their code in one place.
Why B: A chart showing values as bars, lines or slices is a data visualization, and it is not a tool for editing source code or testing programs.
Why C: A router, modem or cable box is networking hardware that connects devices to the internet, whereas an IDE is software used by developers to write and test code.
Why D: An IDE is an integrated development environment, a single program that combines a code editor, debugger and testing tools so developers can write and test code efficiently.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is AutoML?
A: Tools that automate steps of building machine learning models
B: A database that stores records in tables for use by firms
C: A car manual that lists parts, fuel types and repair steps
D: A manual spreadsheet where cells are filled in by hand daily overall
Why A: AutoML is a set of tools that automate steps of building machine learning models, such as choosing features, picking algorithms and tuning settings, which saves time and expert effort.
Why B: A database that stores records in tables is a data store that holds information, but AutoML is about automating model building rather than storing business records.
Why C: A car manual lists parts and repair steps for vehicles, which has no link to machine learning, since AutoML is software that helps build predictive models automatically.
Why D: A spreadsheet filled by hand is a manual process, which is the opposite of AutoML, because AutoML exists precisely to automate the work of building models.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hiring model trained on past data mostly from men tends to rank women lower. What is the cause?
A: The model has no data
B: Bias in the training data
C: The model is too accurate
D: The computer is too slow
Why A: The model having no data cannot be the cause, because it was trained on past hiring data that mostly came from men, so data existed but was skewed.
Why B: Bias in the training data is the cause: past hiring records mostly from men teach the model to favor male patterns, so it ranks women lower.
Why C: Being too accurate does not explain unfair rankings, because the problem is that the model accurately copies a skewed history, so the fault lies in the data, not accuracy.
Why D: A slow computer only affects how long training or scoring takes, and it cannot make a model systematically rank women lower than men in its results.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is explainable AI (XAI)?
A: AI that hides its logic from users so decisions look secret
B: AI without data, a system that has nothing to learn from
C: Methods that make AI decisions understandable to humans
D: AI that explains jokes and riddles to people at a party
Why A: AI that hides its logic is the black box problem, which is the opposite of explainable AI, whose whole goal is to make decisions open and understandable.
Why B: AI without data has nothing to learn from and could not make decisions at all, whereas explainable AI is about clarifying how a working model reaches its outputs.
Why C: Explainable AI refers to methods that make AI decisions understandable to humans, so people can see why a model gave a result and can trust or challenge it.
Why D: AI that explains jokes is just a language task for entertainment, while XAI is a field focused on making a model's own decision process transparent and reviewable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the black box problem in AI?
A: A security feature that locks files with a code or password
B: Flight recorders that store data from an aircraft in a crash in practice
C: It is hard to understand how some complex models reach decisions
D: A hardware box that holds a computer's parts in a case frame
Why A: A security feature that locks files with a code is encryption or password protection, which is unrelated to the black box problem, a matter of model transparency.
Why B: Flight recorders store aircraft data after a crash and are literally called black boxes, but that is aviation equipment and not the AI transparency issue asked about.
Why C: The black box problem is that it is hard to understand how some complex models, like deep neural networks, reach their decisions, which makes them difficult to audit or trust.
Why D: A hardware box holding a computer's parts is a case or chassis, which is about physical housing and has no connection to understanding AI decision making.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is GDPR?
A: A European Union law protecting personal data and privacy
B: A banking rule that sets the interest rate on loans to firms
C: A U.S. tax law that sets the rates of income tax for firms
D: A trade treaty that sets duties on goods sold between nations
Why A: GDPR is a European Union law that protects personal data and privacy, giving people rights over how organizations collect, store and use information about them.
Why B: A banking rule setting loan interest rates would be financial regulation, but GDPR deals with personal data protection and not with interest rates on loans.
Why C: A U.S. tax law setting income tax rates is not GDPR, which is a European data protection regulation and has nothing to do with taxation in the United States.
Why D: A trade treaty setting duties on goods is about tariffs and commerce, whereas GDPR is a privacy law governing how personal data is handled.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is CCPA?
A: A trade law that sets tariffs on goods that are imported from abroad
B: A bank rule that limits how much a customer may withdraw in a day
C: A federal tax that businesses pay on all of the profits they earn
D: A California law giving residents rights over their personal data
Why A: A trade law setting tariffs on imports concerns customs duties, while CCPA is a California privacy law about personal data, so tariffs are not its subject.
Why B: A bank rule limiting daily withdrawals is a financial policy, which has nothing to do with CCPA, a law that protects how businesses handle consumer personal data.
Why C: A federal tax on business profits is a revenue measure, but CCPA is a state law from California and it covers privacy rights, not taxes of any kind.
Why D: CCPA is a California law that gives residents rights over their personal data, including the rights to know what is collected, to delete it and to opt out of its sale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data minimization?
A: Keeping data forever, long after it has any use for the firm
B: Collecting only the data needed for a specific purpose
C: Collecting as much as possible in case it is useful later
D: Selling extra data to other firms that pay for the records
Why A: Keeping data forever, long after it has any use, is the opposite of minimization, because holding unneeded data raises privacy risk and breach exposure without any benefit.
Why B: Data minimization means collecting only the data needed for a specific purpose, which lowers privacy risk and exposure if a breach happens and respects the people involved.
Why C: Collecting as much as possible in case it is useful later is the opposite of minimization, since it gathers data with no stated purpose and adds needless risk.
Why D: Selling extra data to other firms is a monetization practice that spreads personal data further, so it goes against minimization, which aims to limit how much is held.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A video shows a public figure saying something they never said, created with AI. What is the main concern?
A: Lower storage costs for the whole firm
B: Misinformation and harm to reputation
C: Faster internet speeds for most users
D: Better camera quality and sharper video
Why A: Lower storage costs are not a concern with a fake video, since the real harm of a deepfake is deceiving viewers, not the price of keeping files.
Why B: The main concern is misinformation and harm to reputation, because a convincing fake video can make viewers believe a public figure said something false and damage their name.
Why C: Faster internet speeds have no link to a fabricated video, which is a content authenticity problem that can mislead people no matter how quickly it spreads online.
Why D: Better camera quality is irrelevant, since a deepfake is generated by AI rather than filmed, and the worry is that fake footage looks real enough to deceive.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is human oversight important in high-stakes AI decisions?
A: AI never errs and so humans need not check what it does
B: It slows all work for no reason, since people must check overall
C: Humans can catch errors, bias and unintended consequences
D: It removes accountability from people and from the firm
Why A: Claiming AI never errs is false, since models make mistakes and show bias, which is exactly why humans must check high-stakes decisions rather than skip review.
Why B: Saying oversight slows work for no reason ignores the benefit, because for high-stakes decisions the short delay is worth it to catch harmful mistakes before they cause damage.
Why C: Human oversight matters because humans can catch errors, bias and unintended consequences that a model misses, which is vital when decisions affect health, money, safety or rights.
Why D: Removing accountability from people is the opposite of the goal, since oversight keeps a named person responsible for the outcome instead of blaming a machine.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does fairness mean in AI?
A: Systems should treat individuals and groups equitably without unjust bias
B: Ignoring affected people when a system makes decisions about them
C: Always favoring majority groups over smaller groups in every decision
D: Treating everyone identically in all cases, whatever their needs or past overall
Why A: Fairness in AI means systems should treat individuals and groups equitably without unjust bias, so similar people get similar outcomes and no group is harmed without reason.
Why B: Ignoring affected people is a failure of fairness, since fair systems consider how decisions impact the people they touch and give them a voice and a way to appeal.
Why C: Always favoring majority groups is itself bias, because fairness requires that smaller groups are not disadvantaged, so putting one group first in every decision breaks the idea.
Why D: Treating everyone identically in all cases can still be unfair when people have different needs or histories, so fairness aims at equitable results, not identical treatment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is copyright concern in generative AI?
A: Models cannot create text, so they cannot copy anything from others
B: Only hardware is protected by copyright, and software is never covered in the end
C: Copyright does not apply to anything that is made by a machine or AI
D: Models may be trained on or reproduce copyrighted works without permission
Why A: Saying models cannot create text is false, because generative models write fluent text and can reproduce passages, which is exactly why copying from others is a concern.
Why B: Claiming only hardware is protected is wrong, since copyright covers software, writing, images and music, so training data and outputs can raise real legal questions.
Why C: Saying copyright does not apply to machine made work is too simple, because the concern is about whether protected works were used or copied, and the law is still unsettled.
Why D: The concern is that models may be trained on or reproduce copyrighted works without permission, which raises questions about owners' rights, payment and whether outputs copy protected material.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an AI ethics review board used for?
A: Evaluating AI projects for risks, bias and societal impact
B: Training models on large data sets for use in many tasks
C: Selling AI products to customers in stores and online shops
D: Cleaning data by removing errors and gaps from tables
Why A: An ethics review board evaluates AI projects for risks, bias and societal impact, so concerns can be found and fixed before a system is released to the public.
Why B: Training models on large data sets is the job of engineers and data scientists, while a review board checks whether a project is safe and fair.
Why C: Selling AI products to customers is a sales role, and an ethics board does not market anything, since its purpose is to judge risks and not to earn revenue.
Why D: Cleaning data by removing errors is routine data preparation work, whereas an ethics review board looks at the wider harm, fairness and social effect of an AI project.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is surveillance capitalism?
A: A charity that raises money for good causes and gives aid to people in need
B: A camera brand that makes lenses and cameras for sale in stores around the world
C: A security business that guards buildings and sites with cameras and staff
D: An economic model that profits from collecting and analyzing personal data
Why A: A charity raising money for good causes is a nonprofit, which is the opposite of surveillance capitalism, a profit driven model built around gathering personal data about users.
Why B: A camera brand making lenses sells hardware, but surveillance capitalism is an economic model, not a company that makes cameras, and it centers on data about people.
Why C: A security business guarding buildings with cameras sells protection services, whereas surveillance capitalism describes earning profit by collecting and analyzing people's personal data for prediction and advertising.
Why D: Surveillance capitalism is an economic model that profits from collecting and analyzing personal data, often to predict and influence behavior and to target advertising at people.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is facial recognition's main privacy risk?
A: It makes photos blurry and lowers their quality on screens
B: It improves lighting in rooms by adjusting lamps for people
C: Tracking and identifying people without their knowledge or consent
D: It reduces image size so that photos take up less room on disks overall
Why A: Making photos blurry affects image quality only, but the main privacy risk of facial recognition is that it can identify and track real people from their faces.
Why B: Improving the lighting in rooms is an unrelated function of lamps and sensors, and it does not describe how facial recognition puts personal privacy at risk.
Why C: The main privacy risk is tracking and identifying people without their knowledge or consent, since faces captured in public can be matched to names and followed over time.
Why D: Reducing image size is a compression task that saves disk space, which has no bearing on the privacy risk of being identified by a face matching system.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does it mean to audit an AI system?
A: Hide its results so the public cannot see how it makes decisions
B: Review its data, performance and outcomes for accuracy and fairness
C: Sell the system to another company that wants to run it for profit  quickly
D: Delete its code so that nobody can use or change the system again
Why A: Hiding results so the public cannot see how decisions are made is the opposite of auditing, which aims to bring transparency and let reviewers check the system's behavior.
Why B: To audit an AI system means to review its data, performance and outcomes for accuracy and fairness, checking that it works as intended and does not harm any group.
Why C: Selling the system to another company is a business deal and not an audit, since an audit examines how the system behaves instead of transferring who owns it.
Why D: Deleting its code so nobody can use it would destroy the system and any evidence, whereas an audit studies the system and leaves it intact so it can be improved.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is knowledge representation in AI?
A: Showing slides to an audience in a meeting or at a lecture
B: A hardware part that fits inside a computer case or box frame as a rule
C: How information is structured so a computer can use it to reason
D: A user interface that lets people click on buttons and menus
Why A: Showing slides to an audience is a way of presenting information to people, but knowledge representation is about structuring facts so a computer can store and reason about them.
Why B: A hardware part that fits inside a computer case is a physical component, while knowledge representation is a software concept about encoding facts and relationships for machines.
Why C: Knowledge representation is how information is structured so a computer can use it to reason, for example through rules, graphs or ontologies that encode facts and their links.
Why D: A user interface with buttons and menus is about how people interact with software, which is different from how an AI system structures knowledge for its own reasoning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an ontology in AI?
A: A formal description of concepts in a domain and their relationships
B: A branch of biology that studies plants and animals in the wild
C: A chart type used to show shares of a total as slices in a pie form
D: A database engine that stores tables and runs queries on large sets of data
Why A: An ontology in AI is a formal description of concepts in a domain and the relationships between them, which lets systems share a common vocabulary and reason about it.
Why B: Ontology in biology-sounding terms may confuse, but the AI meaning is not a study of plants and animals; it is a structured map of concepts and their links.
Why C: A chart showing shares of a total as slices is a pie chart, a visualization tool, whereas an ontology organizes concepts and relations to represent knowledge.
Why D: A database engine stores tables and runs queries, but an ontology is a conceptual model of a domain's terms and relationships rather than software for storing rows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is machine translation?
A: Typing speed measured in words per minute on a keyboard
B: Automatically converting text from one language to another
C: Moving machines from one site to another across a country overall
D: Fixing machines that break down in a factory or a plant
Why A: Typing speed in words per minute measures how fast a person types, which is a keyboard skill and has no connection to converting text between human languages.
Why B: Machine translation is the automatic conversion of text from one language to another by software, as when a tool turns an English sentence into Spanish within seconds.
Why C: Moving machines from one site to another is about logistics and relocation, so it is unrelated to language, and the word translation here refers to text, not transport.
Why D: Fixing machines that break down in a factory is maintenance work, whereas machine translation is a language technology that converts written or spoken words between languages automatically.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is reasoning in AI?
A: Printing rules on paper so that staff can read them
B: Memorizing data and repeating it back word for word later
C: Storing files on a disk or in the cloud for later use
D: Drawing logical conclusions from known facts and rules
Why A: Printing rules on paper only records them for staff to read, but reasoning in AI means a system applies rules to facts to reach new conclusions.
Why B: Memorizing data and repeating it back word for word is rote recall, which lacks inference, whereas reasoning draws new conclusions from known facts and rules.
Why C: Storing files on a disk or in the cloud is data storage, which keeps information but does not process it to infer anything, so it is not reasoning.
Why D: Reasoning in AI means drawing logical conclusions from known facts and rules, for example concluding that a bird can fly unless it is known to be a penguin.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an if-then rule?
A: The fan is blue and it sits on the desk
B: If temperature is above 80, turn on the fan
C: Fans are useful in hot rooms and offices
D: Temperature is 80 degrees in the room now
Why A: The fan is blue and it sits on the desk is a plain description of a fact, with no condition leading to an action, so it is not an if-then rule.
Why B: If temperature is above 80, turn on the fan is an if-then rule because it states a condition, temperature above 80, and the action that follows when it is true.
Why C: Fans are useful in hot rooms and offices is a general statement of opinion or fact, and it has no condition paired with a specific action, so it is no rule.
Why D: Temperature is 80 degrees in the room now only reports a current reading, giving a fact with no condition and no resulting action, so it cannot be an if-then rule.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is sensor fusion?
A: Combining data from multiple sensors for a more accurate picture
B: Melting sensors with heat so that they form one new part
C: Hiding sensors behind panels so that people cannot see them as a rule
D: Replacing sensors every year with newer ones from the maker
Why A: Sensor fusion means combining data from multiple sensors to get a more accurate picture, as when a self driving car blends camera, radar and lidar readings.
Why B: Melting sensors with heat to form one part would destroy them, and the term actually refers to merging their data, not physically joining the devices together.
Why C: Hiding sensors behind panels is an installation choice about appearance, and it does not describe sensor fusion, which is about merging readings from several sensors into one view.
Why D: Replacing sensors every year is a maintenance schedule, which does not combine any data, so it fails to describe the way sensor fusion improves accuracy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is lidar?
A: A microphone that records sound so a computer can turn it into text
B: A radio that sends out waves to carry a driver's voice between cars
C: A sensor that uses laser light to measure distance and build 3D maps
D: A thermometer that reads heat so a machine can sense room temperature
Why A: A microphone that records sound so a computer can turn it into text is speech input hardware, whereas lidar works with laser light, not sound waves.
Why B: A radio sending waves to carry a driver's voice between cars is communications gear, but lidar is a sensor measuring distance and not a voice link.
Why C: Lidar is a sensor that uses laser light to measure distance and build 3D maps, which is why self driving cars use it to see the shape of their surroundings.
Why D: A thermometer reads heat to sense temperature, but lidar measures distance with pulses of laser light and does not measure the warmth of a room.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is edge computing?
A: Computing in the cloud only, on remote servers far from the user and the source
B: Computing at the edge of a table, with parts joined by a hinge to the legs
C: Printing data on paper at the end of a long shift in the office each day
D: Processing data near where it is generated rather than in a distant data center
Why A: Computing in the cloud only, on remote servers far from the source, is the opposite of edge computing, which moves processing closer to where the data is created.
Why B: Computing at the edge of a table with a hinge is a silly literal reading, since edge computing is a networking idea and has nothing to do with furniture.
Why C: Printing data on paper at the end of a shift is a manual reporting task and does not describe processing data close to its source on a device.
Why D: Edge computing means processing data near where it is generated rather than in a distant data center, which cuts delay, saves bandwidth and helps with devices that need fast responses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A data set has the values 4, 8, 6, 5, 7. What is the mean?
Why A: 30 is the sum of the values, since 4 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 7 = 30, but the mean needs that sum divided by the 5 values.
Why B: 8 is the largest value in the set, which is the maximum, and it is not the mean because the mean is the total divided by the count.
Why C: The mean is the sum divided by the count: 4 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 7 = 30, and 30 divided by 5 values equals 6.
Why D: 5 is one of the values in the list, but it is not the mean, since the sum of 30 divided by 5 values gives 6, not 5.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the median of 3, 9, 4, 7, 5?
Why A: 5.6 is the mean, because 3 + 9 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 28 and 28 divided by 5 is 5.6, whereas the question asks for the median, the middle value.
Why B: Sorting gives 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle of those five values is 5, so the median is 5.
Why C: 9 is the largest value in the set, which makes it the maximum, and it sits at the end of the sorted list, not in the middle position.
Why D: 3 is the smallest value, the minimum, and it sits at the start of the sorted list 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, so it cannot be the median.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, 5?
Why A: 5 appears only twice in the list, while 3 appears three times, so 5 is not the most frequent value and cannot be the mode.
Why B: 7 appears just once in the list 2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, 5, so it is a rare value and certainly not the one that occurs most often.
Why C: 3.7 is not even a value in the list, and a mode must be a value that occurs, while the mean here is 28 divided by 7, which equals 4.
Why D: The mode is the value that appears most often, and 3 appears three times in the list, more than 5 which appears twice or any other value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the range of 12, 20, 15, 31, 18?
Why A: The range is the maximum minus the minimum, so 31 - 12 = 19, which measures how far apart the largest and smallest values are.
Why B: 31 is the largest value, the maximum, but the range subtracts the smallest value from it, giving 31 - 12 = 19 instead.
Why C: 12 is the smallest value, the minimum, and the range needs the difference between the largest and smallest, which is 31 - 12 = 19.
Why D: 96 is the sum of all five values, since 12 + 20 + 15 + 31 + 18 = 96, but the range is a difference, not a total.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A fair coin is flipped once. What is the probability of heads?
Why A: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes, heads and tails, so the probability of heads is 1 divided by 2, which equals 0.5.
Why B: A probability can never exceed 1, so a value of 2 is impossible, and it also does not match one favorable outcome out of two.
Why C: 0.25 is the chance of getting two heads in a row, since 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, but this question flips the coin only once.
Why D: A probability of 1 means certainty, but heads is not guaranteed on a fair coin, which gives heads only half of the time, so 0.5.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?
Why A: 3 is the count of red marbles, not a probability, because a probability must be between 0 and 1 and is found by dividing 3 by the total of 10.
Why B: 0.43 comes from comparing 3 red to 7 blue as 3 divided by 7, but the total is 10 marbles, so the chance is 3 divided by 10.
Why C: 0.7 is the probability of drawing a blue marble, since 7 out of 10 are blue, while the question asks about red, which is the other 3 of 10.
Why D: There are 3 red marbles out of 10 in total, so the probability of drawing red is 3 divided by 10, which equals 0.3.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
Why A: 1/12 would mean 3 favorable outcomes out of 36, but a sum of 7 has 6 ways: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1, giving 6/36.
Why B: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes sum to 7, namely 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1, so the probability is 6/36, which is 1/6.
Why C: 1/36 is the chance of one exact pair such as a 3 and a 4 in order, but a sum of 7 can come from 6 different pairs.
Why D: 7/36 wrongly treats the target sum of 7 as the number of ways to roll it, but the real count of ways is 6, so the answer is 6/36.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?
Why A: 0.9 is the sum of 0.5 and 0.4, but for independent events P(A and B) is found by multiplying the two probabilities, not by adding them.
Why B: 0.1 would be the gap between 0.5 and 0.4, but independent events combine by multiplication, and the product is 0.5 x 0.4, which is not 0.1.
Why C: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B), so 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.2, meaning both events happen together in about one case in five.
Why D: 0.45 is the average of 0.5 and 0.4, but averaging has no role in joint probability, which for independent events is the product 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.2.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a standard deviation of zero indicate?
A: The data has a very large spread overall
B: The data set is empty and has no values
C: All values in the data set are identical
D: The mean is zero so every value is also zero
Why A: A very large spread corresponds to a large standard deviation, so it is the opposite of zero, which means no spread at all among the values.
Why B: An empty data set has no values, so a standard deviation cannot even be computed, and a computed value of zero describes data that exists but does not vary.
Why C: A standard deviation of zero means all values in the data set are identical, because each value equals the mean and there is no distance from the center.
Why D: A zero standard deviation says nothing about the mean being zero; values such as 5, 5, 5 have a mean of 5 and still have no spread.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a correlation coefficient of -0.9 suggest?
A: A strong negative relationship between the two variables
B: No relationship at all between the two variables here
C: A strong positive relationship in which both tend to rise
D: That the first variable causes the second to fall in value
Why A: A correlation of -0.9 is close to -1, which suggests a strong negative relationship: as one variable rises, the other tends to fall, along a fairly tight line.
Why B: No relationship at all would give a correlation near 0, but -0.9 is far from zero, which shows a strong link between the two variables.
Why C: A strong positive relationship would give a coefficient near +1, but the negative sign on -0.9 means the variables move in opposite directions instead of rising together.
Why D: Correlation alone does not prove one variable causes the other to fall; it only describes how they move together, so a causal claim goes beyond what -0.9 shows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A survey of 400 people finds 120 prefer brand A. What is the sample proportion?
Why A: 0.12 would come from dividing 120 by 1,000, but the sample has 400 people, so the proportion is 120 divided by 400, which is 0.30.
Why B: 3.33 is 400 divided by 120, which flips the fraction; a proportion is the part over the whole, 120 divided by 400, and cannot exceed 1.
Why C: 0.70 is the share of people who do not prefer brand A, since 280 of 400 is 0.70, but the question asks about the 120 who do.
Why D: The sample proportion is the part divided by the whole, so 120 divided by 400 equals 0.30, meaning 30 percent of those surveyed prefer brand A.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a larger sample size usually do to a margin of error?
A: It has no effect on the margin of error
B: It makes the margin of error smaller
C: It makes the margin of error much larger
D: It makes the error margin equal to zero
Why A: Saying sample size has no effect is wrong, because the margin of error shrinks roughly with the square root of the sample size as more data adds precision.
Why B: A larger sample size usually makes the margin of error smaller, because estimates from more people vary less and sit closer to the true population value.
Why C: A larger sample does not make the margin of error much larger; it moves the other way, since more data reduces sampling variation and tightens the estimate.
Why D: A margin of error never drops to exactly zero for a sample, because only surveying the whole population removes sampling error, so bigger samples only shrink it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A p-value of 0.03 is found in a test with a significance level of 0.05. What is the conclusion?
A: Fail to reject the null
B: Accept the null as proven
C: The test is not valid here
D: Reject the null hypothesis
Why A: Failing to reject the null applies when the p-value is above the significance level, but here 0.03 is below 0.05, so the opposite conclusion follows.
Why B: Accepting the null as proven is never the right wording, because a test cannot prove the null true, and here p is below 0.05 so it is rejected.
Why C: Nothing suggests the test is invalid; a p-value of 0.03 is perfectly usable and simply falls below the 0.05 threshold, which leads to a decision to reject.
Why D: Since the p-value of 0.03 is less than the significance level of 0.05, the result is statistically significant and we reject the null hypothesis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which measure of center is least affected by extreme outliers?
A: The mean
B: The range
C: The median
D: The sum
Why A: The mean uses every value in its calculation, so one extreme outlier can pull it far from the center, which makes it very sensitive to outliers.
Why B: The range is the maximum minus the minimum, so an outlier directly changes it, and it is a measure of spread, not a measure of center.
Why C: The median is the middle value of the sorted data, so an extreme outlier at either end does not move it much, which makes it robust.
Why D: The sum adds all values, so one extreme outlier changes it a great deal, and a sum is also not a measure of center in the first place.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A data set is right-skewed. Which is usually true?
A: The mean is greater than the median
B: The mean is less than the median
C: The mode is greater than the mean
D: The median moves farther into the tail
Why A: In a right-skewed set the long tail of high values pulls the mean upward, so the mean is usually greater than the median, which sits closer to the bulk.
Why B: A mean below the median is the pattern for a left-skewed set, where a tail of low values drags the mean down, so it is wrong here.
Why C: In right-skewed data the mode sits near the peak on the low side, below the mean. The mean is greater than the median.
Why D: The mean is pulled farther toward the tail than the median, which resists extreme values. In right-skewed data the mean is greater than the median.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart is best for showing how a share of a whole is divided?
A: A line chart
B: A pie chart
C: A histogram
D: A scatter plot
Why A: A line chart shows how a value changes over an ordered sequence such as time, so it does not display how a whole is divided into shares.
Why B: A pie chart is a circle cut into slices sized by proportion, which makes it the best choice for showing how a share of a whole is divided.
Why C: A histogram shows how often values fall within ranges, or bins, of one numeric variable, which is a distribution and not a split of a whole.
Why D: A scatter plot places points to show the relationship between two numeric variables, so it is not suited to showing how parts share a whole.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart is best for showing a trend over time?
A: A pie chart
B: A name table
C: A single bar
D: A line chart
Why A: A pie chart shows how parts divide a whole at one moment, so it cannot show how a value moves across several time periods.
Why B: A name table lists labels and does not draw any trend, so it fails to make a change over time easy to see at a glance.
Why C: A single bar shows one value at one moment, so it gives no sequence of points and cannot display a trend over time.
Why D: A line chart connects points in time order, so rises and falls are easy to follow, which makes it the best chart for showing a trend over time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which chart best shows the relationship between two numeric variables?
A: A pie chart
B: A word cloud
C: A scatter plot
D: A bar chart
Why A: A pie chart shows how parts divide a whole, so it cannot display how two numeric variables relate to one another across many observations.
Why B: A word cloud sizes words by how often they appear in text, so it shows no numeric relationship between two variables at all.
Why C: A scatter plot puts one numeric variable on each axis and plots points, so patterns such as upward trends or clusters between the two variables become visible.
Why D: A bar chart compares values across categories, with one axis holding labels, so it is not designed to show how two numeric variables move together.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a histogram used for?
A: Showing a change in a value over a period of days
B: Showing how often values fall within ranges (bins)
C: Showing the link between two variables as points
D: Showing how a total is divided into parts or shares
Why A: Showing a change in value over a period of days is the job of a line chart, whereas a histogram groups values into ranges and counts them.
Why B: A histogram shows how often values fall within ranges, called bins, so you can see the shape of a distribution, such as its center, spread and skew.
Why C: Showing the link between two variables as points is a scatter plot, while a histogram describes only one variable and counts how many values land in each bin.
Why D: Showing how a total is divided into parts is the job of a pie chart, but a histogram instead displays the frequency of values within numeric intervals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0, making a small gap look huge. What is this?
A: A truncated axis that exaggerates differences
B: A confidence interval for each of the values
C: A fair chart that shows the true differences
D: A normalization step making all the bars equal
Why A: A truncated axis starts above zero, here at 90, which makes bars differ in visible height far more than the true values do and so exaggerates differences.
Why B: A confidence interval shows uncertainty around an estimate with error bars, and it has nothing to do with where the vertical axis of a bar chart begins.
Why C: Calling it a fair chart is wrong, since starting at 90 instead of 0 distorts bar lengths and makes a small gap look much larger than it truly is.
Why D: Normalization rescales data values onto a common range, but moving the axis start changes only the display and leaves the bars unequal, so it is a different thing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is one way to handle missing values?
A: Delete every column so that no missing values remain overall
B: Fill them using the mean or median, or remove the rows
C: Ignore them and treat each one as the number zero
D: Replace them with random words to fill the column
Why A: Deleting every column removes all the data, including the useful parts, so it does not handle missing values and would leave nothing to analyze.
Why B: Filling missing values with the mean or median keeps the rows, and removing the affected rows is another common option, so both are accepted ways to handle gaps.
Why C: Treating every missing value as zero can distort results, because zero is a real number that may differ greatly from the true value, so it is not a safe default.
Why D: Replacing missing values with random words would put text into a numeric column and corrupt the data, so it creates errors and does not repair the gaps.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does data cleaning involve?
A: Finding and fixing errors, gaps and duplicates
B: Moving the data to a new computer for safer storage
C: Deleting all of the data to start again from scratch
D: Making the charts brighter and more colorful
Why A: Data cleaning means finding and fixing errors, gaps and duplicates, so that later analysis rests on accurate and complete records that can be trusted for decisions.
Why B: Moving the data to a new computer is a storage or migration task, and it does not correct any mistakes, gaps or duplicates in the records themselves.
Why C: Deleting all the data to start again discards valuable information, whereas cleaning repairs specific problems and keeps the good data in place for analysis.
Why D: Making charts brighter and more colorful is a presentation choice made after analysis, and it does nothing to fix errors or gaps in the underlying data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a categorical variable?
A: A variable whose value is calculated by a formula
B: A variable that has the same value in every row
C: A variable that takes any numeric value in a range
D: A variable that places items into groups or labels
Why A: A variable calculated by a formula is a computed or derived variable, which says how its value is obtained, while a categorical variable describes the kind of value it holds.
Why B: A variable with the same value in every row is a constant, and it carries no information, while a categorical variable usually has several distinct groups.
Why C: A variable taking any numeric value in a range is continuous, such as height, which is different from a categorical variable that sorts items into groups.
Why D: A categorical variable places items into groups or labels, such as color, city or type of pet, instead of measuring them on a numeric scale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A survey about school lunches only asks students eating in the cafeteria. What is the problem?
A: The questions are too long, so results are unreliable
B: The survey is too large to analyze the answers
C: Sampling bias, because other students are left out
D: The mean is wrongly calculated as it uses few numbers
Why A: Long questions can hurt reliability, but the described flaw is that only cafeteria students were asked, which is who was surveyed, and not how the questions were worded.
Why B: A survey being too large is rarely a problem, and the real issue here is who was left out, not how many responses the survey collected.
Why C: Asking only students who eat in the cafeteria leaves out those who bring lunch or eat elsewhere, so the sample is not representative, which is sampling bias.
Why D: The mean may be calculated correctly; the flaw lies earlier, in who was chosen to answer, so even perfect arithmetic would describe only part of the student body.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a pivot table do?
A: Rotates a screen to show data at an angle
B: Summarizes data by grouping and totaling
C: Draws pictures of people in the table rows
D: Deletes duplicate files to free up disk room
Why A: Rotating a screen to show data at an angle is a display setting, while a pivot table is a spreadsheet feature that reorganizes and summarizes data.
Why B: A pivot table summarizes data by grouping and totaling, for example showing total sales by region or month, without changing the original data in the sheet.
Why C: Drawing pictures of people in the table rows is not a spreadsheet function, and the name pivot refers to turning rows into a grouped summary, not artwork.
Why D: Deleting duplicate files frees disk room, but a pivot table works inside a spreadsheet to group and total values, and it does not manage files on a disk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a spreadsheet, what does =SUM(B2:B6) do?
A: Counts how many cells in B2 to B6 hold text
B: Multiplies the values in B2 through B6
C: Adds the values in cells B2 through B6
D: Finds the largest value in B2 through B6
Why A: Counting cells that hold text uses a function such as COUNTA or COUNTIF, whereas SUM adds numbers together and does not count any cells.
Why B: Multiplying values in a range uses the PRODUCT function, but SUM adds them, so =SUM(B2:B6) does not multiply the values in B2 through B6.
Why C: =SUM(B2:B6) adds the values in cells B2 through B6, giving the total of those five cells in one result.
Why D: Finding the largest value uses the MAX function, while SUM adds the values together, so =SUM(B2:B6) returns a total and not a maximum.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a formula showing #DIV/0! most likely mean?
A: A cell is being divided by zero or an empty cell
B: The cell has too many digits for the column width
C: The workbook is protected by a user password
D: The formula refers to a sheet that has been renamed
Why A: #DIV/0! appears when a formula tries to divide by zero or by an empty cell, which is undefined in math, so the spreadsheet shows this error code.
Why B: Too many digits for a column width usually shows as ##### in the cell, which is a display issue and is different from the #DIV/0! error.
Why C: A protected workbook blocks editing or opening and asks for a password, but it does not produce a formula error, and #DIV/0! is about division.
Why D: A formula that refers to a missing or renamed sheet gives a #REF! error, which differs from #DIV/0!, the code that appears when you divide by zero.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an absolute cell reference ($A$1) do when a formula is copied?
A: It moves to the next cell down
B: It formats the cell as currency
C: It deletes that cell entirely
D: It stays fixed on that cell
Why A: Moving to the next cell down is what a relative reference does when copied down a column, while an absolute reference does not move at all.
Why B: Formatting a cell as currency is done with a number format, and the dollar signs in $A$1 lock the reference rather than change how the value looks.
Why C: An absolute reference only points to a cell, so copying a formula never deletes the cell it refers to, and the $ signs simply keep the address fixed.
Why D: The dollar signs in $A$1 lock both the column and the row, so when the formula is copied it stays fixed on that cell.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Heights are in centimeters and incomes in dollars. Why scale both before some analyses?
A: To make all values the same, so no variation is left
B: To change the data's meaning so results look better
C: So that features with large numbers do not dominate
D: To remove the need for data cleaning before analysis
Why A: Scaling does not make all values the same, since that would erase the variation that analysis needs, and it only puts features on comparable ranges.
Why B: Scaling does not change the meaning of the data, since it only rescales numbers, and it should never be done to make results look better.
Why C: Scaling puts features on similar ranges so that features with large numbers, like incomes in dollars, do not dominate ones with small numbers, like heights in centimeters.
Why D: Scaling does not replace cleaning, because errors, gaps and duplicates still need to be fixed, and scaling only adjusts the size of the numbers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does SELECT * FROM customers do?
A: Returns the number of rows in the customers table
B: Returns the customers who have placed an order
C: Creates a new table called customers with no columns
D: Returns all columns for all rows in the customers table
Why A: Counting rows needs SELECT COUNT(*). SELECT * returns all columns for all rows in the customers table.
Why B: Filtering by orders needs a WHERE clause or a join. SELECT * FROM customers returns all columns for all rows.
Why C: Creating a new table is done with CREATE TABLE, but SELECT reads from a table that already exists, and it never builds one with no columns.
Why D: SELECT * FROM customers returns all columns for all rows in the customers table, because the asterisk stands for every column and no WHERE clause filters the rows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the SQL function COUNT(*) return?
A: The number of rows
B: The max column value
C: The mean column value
D: The column value sum
Why A: COUNT(*) returns the number of rows in a table or result, since it counts every row whether or not individual columns hold values.
Why B: The maximum value of a column is returned by MAX, not COUNT, and COUNT(*) reports how many rows there are and not how big a value is.
Why C: The mean of a column is returned by the AVG function, but COUNT(*) only counts rows and does no averaging of any column values.
Why D: The sum of column values is returned by the SUM function, whereas COUNT(*) simply tallies rows and does not add up the numbers inside them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data quality?
A: How colorful and attractive a chart of the data looks
B: How accurate, complete, consistent and timely data is
C: How many people can access a data set at one time
D: How large a file is when the data is saved on a disk
Why A: How attractive a chart looks is about presentation and design, but data quality refers to qualities of the data itself, such as accuracy and completeness.
Why B: Data quality is how accurate, complete, consistent and timely data is, because data with these traits can be trusted when making decisions and building models.
Why C: How many people can access a data set describes availability or permissions, which is not a measure of whether the data itself is correct or complete.
Why D: File size on a disk tells how much space the data takes up, but a large file can still be full of errors, so size says nothing about quality.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does ETL stand for in data work?
A: Estimate, track, log costs
B: Enter, trace, label files
C: Edit, test, launch a site
D: Extract, transform, load
Why A: Estimate, track, log costs is not a data process, and ETL describes moving data through three set steps: extract, transform and load.
Why B: Enter, trace, label files does not match any data pipeline, and the letters ETL stand for extract, transform and load, not those actions.
Why C: Edit, test, launch a site describes web publishing, which is not what ETL means, since ETL is a pipeline that moves and reshapes data.
Why D: ETL stands for Extract, transform, load: data is pulled from sources, cleaned and reshaped, then loaded into a target such as a data warehouse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is CSV?
A: A plain-text file format where values are separated by commas
B: A secure format that encrypts data so only the owner can read it
C: A programming language used to write phone and tablet apps
D: A type of chart that shows how a total is divided into parts
Why A: CSV is a plain-text file format where values are separated by commas, so each line is a row and any spreadsheet or program can open it easily.
Why B: A secure format that encrypts data is something else; CSV stores plain readable text with no encryption, so anyone who opens the file can read it.
Why C: A programming language for phone apps has logic and syntax, but CSV is only a data format that holds values and cannot run code of any kind.
Why D: A chart showing a total divided into parts is a pie chart, which is a visual display, whereas CSV is a file format for storing rows of data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an API used for?
A: Counting inventory by hand each night with a pen and clipboard
B: Cleaning errors from a data set with no rules from the analyst
C: Letting programs request data or services from one another
D: Printing reports from a database with page numbers and headings
Why A: Counting inventory by hand is a manual task that needs no software interface, whereas an API lets one program talk to another and exchange data automatically.
Why B: Cleaning errors from a data set is data preparation work, which is not what an API does, since an API is an interface for requests between programs.
Why C: An API lets programs request data or services from one another, for example a weather app asking a server for a forecast using a defined set of rules.
Why D: Printing reports from a database is a reporting task, and an API is not a printing tool but a way for software systems to communicate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is version control useful for?
A: Blocking all users from changing a file so that it stays the same for years
B: Tracking changes to files and allowing earlier versions to be restored
C: Deleting all earlier versions so that only the newest file is kept
D: Making files larger so that they take up more space on the disk
Why A: Blocking all users from changing a file would defeat teamwork, whereas version control lets many people edit while the history of changes is recorded and can be reviewed.
Why B: Version control tracks changes to files and lets earlier versions be restored, so a team can see who changed what and roll back mistakes.
Why C: Deleting earlier versions so only the newest file remains is the opposite of version control, which keeps the full history so past states can be recovered.
Why D: Making files larger and using more disk space is not a goal, since version control stores changes efficiently and its purpose is history and recovery, not size.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Git do?
A: Stores large data sets in a cloud account
B: Checks grammar and fixes spelling mistakes
C: Translates code from one language to another
D: Tracks changes to code and files over time
Why A: Storing large data sets in a cloud account is cloud storage work, while Git is a tool for tracking changes in code and files over time.
Why B: Checking grammar and fixing spelling is done by a proofreading tool, and Git has no language features because it records changes to files, not writing quality.
Why C: Translating code from one language to another is done by a transpiler or converter, and Git does not rewrite code, since it just records its history.
Why D: Git tracks changes to code and files over time, so developers can see the history, work in parallel on branches and go back to earlier versions when needed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a no-code AI tool?
A: A tool that lets engineers deploy models to servers using written scripts
B: A tool that rewrites old programs into newer coding languages for users
C: A tool that lets users build simple AI solutions without writing programs
D: A tool that removes all errors from a program without any human review in practice
Why A: Script-based deployment requires programming. A no-code AI tool lets users build simple AI solutions without writing programs.
Why B: Code translation still produces code to maintain. A no-code AI tool lets users build simple AI solutions without writing programs.
Why C: A no-code AI tool lets users build simple AI solutions without writing programs, usually through drag and drop screens, so non programmers can create useful models.
Why D: No tool removes all errors from a program without human review, and no-code does not mean error free; it only means users do not write the code.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is robotic process automation (RPA)?
A: Software bots that perform repetitive rule-based tasks
B: Programs that learn from data to predict prices in a store
C: Physical robots that move paper around from desk to desk
D: Machines that build cars on an assembly line using welding
Why A: RPA uses software bots that perform repetitive, rule-based tasks, such as copying data between systems or filling forms, following fixed steps just as a person would.
Why B: Programs that learn from data to predict prices describe machine learning, whereas RPA bots follow fixed rules and do not learn or predict anything.
Why C: Despite the word robotic, RPA is not physical robots moving paper; the bots are software programs working on a computer screen and systems.
Why D: Machines that build cars with welding are industrial robots in manufacturing, while RPA refers to software that automates office tasks, not to hardware on a line.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a firewall?
A: A program that speeds up a network by compressing the files it sends
B: A security tool that controls traffic into and out of a network
C: A tool that stores backups of files on a remote server abroad
D: A wall that stops fires in buildings, made of brick or steel
Why A: A program that compresses files to speed up a network is a compression or optimization tool, while a firewall filters traffic to protect the network.
Why B: A firewall is a security tool that controls traffic into and out of a network by following rules, blocking connections that are unauthorized or look unsafe.
Why C: Storing backups on a remote server is a backup service, which protects against data loss but does not filter traffic as a firewall does.
Why D: A wall that stops fires in buildings is a physical safety barrier, and in computing the name is only an analogy for a network security barrier.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a software update used for?
A: Deleting all data stored in the software each year
B: Making the software slower to save battery power
C: Removing user accounts no longer in use at the firm
D: Fixing issues and improving security or features
Why A: Deleting all data stored in the software would destroy information, whereas a software update fixes issues and adds improvements while leaving the user's data in place.
Why B: Updates are not meant to make software slower to save battery power, since their purpose is to fix bugs, close security holes and add useful features.
Why C: Removing unused user accounts is an administrative cleanup, which is not the aim of a software update, a release that improves the program itself.
Why D: A software update fixes issues and improves security or features, which is why installing updates promptly protects against known vulnerabilities and brings improvements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A navigation app finds the shortest route between two cities. Which AI idea is this?
A: Generating new roads on the map to shorten each trip
B: Searching over possible paths to find the best one
C: Recognizing faces in photos along the route taken
D: Writing a poem about each town the driver passes
Why A: Generating new roads on the map would be creating content, but the app only uses the roads that exist and picks the shortest route between them.
Why B: Finding the shortest route is search: the app explores many possible paths through the road network and picks the best one, for example with an algorithm like A star.
Why C: Recognizing faces in photos is a computer vision task, which has no role in picking the quickest road between two cities on a map.
Why D: Writing a poem about each town is a text generation task, and it has nothing to do with computing the shortest path between two cities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A streaming service suggests a show because people with similar watch histories liked it. What technique is this?
A: Rule-based programming
B: Speech recognition tools
C: Collaborative filtering
D: Optical character reading
Why A: Rule-based programming follows fixed rules written by people, but this service recommends shows from the viewing habits of similar users, which is learned from data.
Why B: Speech recognition tools turn spoken words into text, which has no connection to suggesting shows based on what similar viewers liked.
Why C: Collaborative filtering recommends items because users with similar histories liked them, which matches the example of a show suggested from the watch histories of similar people.
Why D: Optical character reading converts images of printed text into digital text, so it plays no part in recommending shows from viewing habits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model labels emails as spam or not spam. What type of task is this?
A: Classification
B: Compression
C: Clustering
D: Regression
Why A: Sorting emails into spam or not spam means assigning each email to a category, which is classification, a supervised learning task with discrete labels.
Why B: Compression reduces the size of data for storage, and it does not assign emails to labelled groups, so it cannot describe a spam filter.
Why C: Clustering groups similar items without predefined labels, but here the labels spam and not spam are known in advance, so the task is classification.
Why D: Regression predicts a continuous number, such as a price, whereas a spam filter picks between two categories, so regression does not fit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model predicts the price of a house from its size and location. What type of task is this?
A: Reinforcement
B: Clustering
C: Classification
D: Regression
Why A: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and penalties from its actions, but predicting a house price from known examples is a supervised task.
Why B: Clustering groups similar items without labels, but here the model predicts a specific price value learned from past sales, so clustering does not fit.
Why C: Classification assigns items to categories, but a price is a continuous number rather than a category, so this is not a classification task.
Why D: Predicting a price from size and location means estimating a continuous number, which is regression, whereas classification would choose among labelled categories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store groups customers by buying habits without predefined categories. What technique is this?
A: Image reading
B: Clustering
C: Classification
D: Regression
Why A: Image reading handles pictures, but the store is grouping customers by buying habits, which involves numbers describing purchases and not images.
Why B: Grouping customers by similar buying habits without predefined categories is clustering, an unsupervised technique that finds natural groups by itself in the data.
Why C: Classification needs predefined labels to learn from, but here there are no set categories, so the groups must be discovered, which is clustering.
Why D: Regression predicts a numeric value, but the goal here is to form groups of similar customers, not to estimate a number such as spending.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a data set that is 99 percent negative and 1 percent positive, a model that always predicts negative has what accuracy?
A: 50 percent, as it guesses one class
B: 100 percent, as it never errs
C: 99 percent, which is misleading
D: 1 percent, since it predicts none
Why A: 50 percent would be the accuracy of a coin flip on balanced data, but this model gets all 99 negatives right out of 100, so its accuracy is far higher.
Why B: A model that always predicts negative misses every positive case, so it is wrong on 1 percent of examples and cannot reach 100 percent accuracy.
Why C: Always predicting negative is correct for 99 out of 100 cases, so accuracy is 99 percent, which is misleading because it finds none of the positives.
Why D: 1 percent is the share of positive cases, but the model predicts negative every time and is right on the 99 percent that are negative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is linear regression used to predict?
A: A continuous numerical value
B: A group of similar items
C: The next move of a player
D: A category such as spam or not
Why A: Linear regression predicts a continuous numerical value, such as a price or temperature, by fitting a straight line through the data points.
Why B: Finding a group of similar items is clustering, an unsupervised task, while linear regression predicts a number from input values.
Why C: Predicting the next move of a player is more like game playing or sequence modeling, and linear regression predicts numbers from features.
Why D: Choosing a category such as spam or not spam is classification, which uses methods like logistic regression, and not a numerical prediction from a line.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is informed consent for data collection?
A: People understand how their data will be used and agree to it
B: Data is collected from a third party who gave permission
C: Data is collected without telling anyone, then used for any purpose
D: Data is collected after a click without reading anything about it
Why A: Informed consent means people understand how their data will be used and agree to it, so their agreement is a real choice made with full knowledge.
Why B: Collecting data from a third party that gave permission lacks the consent of the people themselves, who may never have been told or asked.
Why C: Collecting data without telling anyone and using it for any purpose is the opposite of informed consent, because people had no knowledge and no choice.
Why D: A click without reading anything is not informed, because people did not learn how their data would be used, so their agreement is not meaningful consent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A video shows a public figure saying something they never said, created with AI. What is the main risk?
A: A faster internet connection for viewers
B: Better camera quality and sharper video
C: Lower cost of making news programs
D: Misinformation and harm to reputation
Why A: A faster internet connection is a benefit for viewers and not a risk, whereas the danger of a fake video is that people believe false claims.
Why B: Better camera quality is not a risk of AI made video, since the footage is generated rather than filmed, and the issue is deceiving viewers.
Why C: Lower cost of making news programs is an efficiency gain and not a harm, while the main risk of a deepfake is false information that damages people.
Why D: The main risk is misinformation and harm to reputation, because a realistic fake of a public figure can spread false claims that many viewers will believe.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copyright concern with AI training data?
A: Whether the model runs faster on one brand of hardware
B: Whether the data is stored in the cloud or on a disk
C: Whether protected works were used without permission
D: Whether the training computer is the correct size
Why A: Whether a model runs faster on one brand of hardware is a performance question, and it has no bearing on legal rights over the training material.
Why B: Whether data is stored in the cloud or on a disk is a storage choice, and it does not decide whether using the works was legally allowed.
Why C: The copyright concern is whether protected works were used without permission, since training on books, images or articles without a license may infringe the owners' rights.
Why D: Whether the training computer is the correct size is a technical detail about equipment, and it has no relation to the legal rights of the work's creators.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the best reason to audit an AI system regularly?
A: To make the system more costly, since audits add expense in the end
B: To find errors, bias or harmful outcomes that appear over time
C: To prove that the system is perfect and needs no changes
D: To replace the system with a new one every single month
Why A: Audits do add some cost, but making the system costlier is a side effect and not the reason to audit, which is to protect people and results.
Why B: Auditing regularly helps find errors, bias or harmful outcomes that appear over time, since data and conditions change and a system that once worked well can drift.
Why C: An audit cannot prove a system is perfect, and no AI system is, so regular audits exist to find issues that need changes and not to claim flawlessness.
Why D: Replacing the system every month is wasteful and is not the purpose of an audit, which reviews how the current system performs and decides whether it needs fixes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a strong password practice?
A: Writing passwords on a note stuck to the monitor so they are not lost overall
B: Using one simple password everywhere, changed only when a site asks
C: Using a long, unique password for each account with a password manager
D: Using the name of a pet and a birth year, easy for the user to recall
