Why A: Writing passwords on a note stuck to the monitor lets anyone passing by read and use them, so it is an insecure habit and not a strong practice.
Why B: Using one simple password everywhere means a single leak exposes every account, and changing it only when a site asks leaves it weak and reused.
Why C: A long, unique password for each account, kept in a password manager, resists guessing and limits damage if one site is breached, which makes it a strong practice.
Why D: A pet name and birth year are easy to remember but also easy for attackers to guess from social media, which makes the password weak and predictable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ransomware?
A: Malware that locks data until a ransom is paid
B: A tool that finds and removes viruses on computers
C: A program that speeds up a computer by deleting junk
D: A bank loan program for small firms short of cash
Why A: Ransomware is malware that locks data or systems until a ransom is paid, usually by encrypting files and demanding payment in return for a key.
Why B: A tool that finds and removes viruses is antivirus software, which defends against threats, whereas ransomware is the harmful program that holds data hostage.
Why C: A program that speeds up a computer by deleting junk is a cleanup utility, while ransomware is malicious software that demands money from its victim.
Why D: A bank loan program for firms short of cash is a finance product, and the word ransom in ransomware refers to a demand made by criminals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is malware?
A: Software that speeds up a computer by deleting its files
B: Software designed to harm or steal from a computer
C: Software that checks spelling and grammar in documents
D: Software that backs up files and stores them online
Why A: Software that speeds up a computer by deleting its files describes a cleaning utility at best, whereas malware is built to cause harm and not to help.
Why B: Malware is software designed to harm or steal from a computer, for example viruses, spyware and ransomware that damage systems or take data without consent.
Why C: Software that checks spelling and grammar is a useful writing tool, which is harmless and so the opposite of malware, a harmful program.
Why D: Software that backs up files and stores them online protects data, and it is a legitimate tool, whereas malware works against the user.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should an organization do first after learning of a data breach?
A: Hide the problem from customers to protect the firm's name
B: Blame the customers for weak passwords and take no action
C: Delete the evidence of the breach so nobody finds out
D: Contain the breach and notify affected people as required
Why A: Hiding the problem from customers delays their chance to protect themselves, and many laws require prompt notice, so concealment makes the damage and the penalties worse.
Why B: Blaming customers for weak passwords shifts responsibility and does nothing to stop the breach, so it fails the duty to act and to help those affected.
Why C: Deleting the evidence destroys the information needed to learn what happened and may break the law, so it blocks the investigation and makes recovery harder.
Why D: The right first steps are to contain the breach to stop further loss and notify affected people as required, so they can protect themselves quickly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is access control in a data system?
A: Letting everyone see all records so staff can find facts fast
B: Storing data on a remote server so nobody can reach it
C: Limiting who can view or change data based on their role
D: Counting how many times the data is read during a day
Why A: Letting everyone see all records lowers protection, because people who do not need the data can read or misuse it, which is the reverse of access control.
Why B: Storing data on a remote server so nobody can reach it makes the data useless, while access control still lets the right people use data safely.
Why C: Access control limits who can view or change data based on their role, so staff see only what their job needs and sensitive records stay protected.
Why D: Counting how many times data is read is logging or monitoring, which can help with audits but does not itself decide who is allowed in.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a data privacy notice for customers?
A: A message that tells customers their data will be sold to the highest bidder
B: A statement telling customers what data is collected and how it is used
C: A list of customers' credit card numbers kept by the firm in a file
D: A bill sent to customers for the cost of storing their data in a database
Why A: A message saying data will be sold to the highest bidder is not what a notice is for, since it must explain collection and use honestly to customers.
Why B: A data privacy notice is a statement telling customers what data is collected and how it is used, so they can make informed choices about sharing information.
Why C: A list of credit card numbers kept in a file would itself be a serious privacy failure, and a notice never publishes customers' private details.
Why D: A bill for the cost of storing data is a financial document, whereas a privacy notice explains data practices to customers and does not charge any fee.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why does the existence of AI regulation matter to businesses?
A: Rules apply to AI developers, but business users are exempt
B: Rules take effect once a harm has been reported to authorities
C: Rules ban firms from using AI for customer decisions
D: Rules can set limits on risky uses and require safeguards
Why A: Laws can reach firms that use AI, not just those that build it. Rules can set limits on risky uses and require safeguards.
Why B: Many rules require safeguards before and during use. Regulation sets limits on risky uses and requires safeguards, so businesses must plan ahead.
Why C: Regulation restricts risky uses but does not ban such uses outright. It sets limits on risky uses and requires safeguards.
Why D: Regulation matters because rules can set limits on risky uses and require safeguards, so businesses must plan for compliance and avoid fines, harm and lost trust.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model finds 40 true positives, 10 false positives and 20 false negatives. What is its precision?
A: 80 percent
B: 20 percent
C: 67 percent
D: 50 percent
Why A: Precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives: 40 / (40 + 10) = 40 / 50 = 0.8, so the precision is 80 percent.
Why B: 20 percent is the share of predicted positives that were wrong, 10 / 50, which is the false discovery rate, and it is not the precision of 40 / 50.
Why C: 67 percent comes from 40 / (40 + 20), which is the recall because it uses false negatives, whereas precision uses false positives in the denominator.
Why D: 50 percent does not match the counts; precision is 40 / (40 + 10) = 0.8, so a value of 50 percent would need as many false positives as true ones.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model finds 40 true positives, 10 false positives and 20 false negatives. What is its recall?
A: About 80 percent
B: About 50 percent
C: About 25 percent
D: About 67 percent
Why A: About 80 percent is the precision, 40 / (40 + 10), because it uses false positives, whereas recall divides by true positives plus false negatives.
Why B: About 50 percent does not follow from the counts, since recall is 40 / (40 + 20), which is well above one half and so cannot equal 50 percent.
Why C: About 25 percent is far too low, because recall is 40 divided by 60 actual positives, which is about two thirds, and not a quarter of them.
Why D: Recall is true positives divided by actual positives: 40 / (40 + 20) = 40 / 60, which is about 0.67, so roughly 67 percent of real positives were found.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the F1 score?
A: The time taken to train a model on data
B: The share of correct predictions overall
C: The harmonic mean of precision and recall
D: The simple sum of precision and recall
Why A: The time taken to train a model is a measure of training duration, while the F1 score measures prediction quality, combining precision and recall into one value.
Why B: The share of correct predictions overall is accuracy, a separate metric, and the F1 score focuses on positive predictions by balancing precision and recall.
Why C: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it is high only when both are high, giving one balanced figure for a classifier.
Why D: The simple sum of precision and recall would range up to 2 and ignores balance, whereas F1 uses a harmonic mean, which stays between 0 and 1.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model has precision 0.5 and recall 0.5. What is its F1 score?
Why A: 0.25 is the product of precision and recall, 0.5 x 0.5, but F1 is 2 x (0.5 x 0.5) / (0.5 + 0.5), which equals 0.5.
Why B: F1 = 2 x (precision x recall) / (precision + recall) = 2 x 0.25 / 1.0 = 0.5, so when both values are 0.5 the F1 score is also 0.5.
Why C: An F1 of 0.0 occurs only when precision or recall is zero, but here both equal 0.5, so the harmonic mean is 0.5 and not zero.
Why D: An F1 of 1.0 needs perfect precision and recall, and with both at 0.5 the harmonic mean cannot exceed that value, so it equals 0.5.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarize?
A: How well a classifier separates the classes across thresholds
B: How much memory a model needs while it runs on a computer
C: How many features a model uses to make each prediction
D: How long a model takes to train, as timed in hours by a clock
Why A: AUC summarizes how well a classifier separates the classes across all thresholds, with 1.0 meaning perfect separation and 0.5 meaning no better than chance.
Why B: Memory needed while running is a resource measure, and AUC says nothing about it, since it is computed from predicted scores and true labels.
Why C: The number of features a model uses is a design detail, whereas AUC summarizes how well the classifier ranks positives above negatives across thresholds.
Why D: Training time is measured with a clock, and AUC is a performance metric computed from predictions, so it says nothing about how long training took.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An AUC of 0.5 suggests that a classifier is:
A: No better than random guessing
B: Perfect at separating the classes
C: Faster than most other models
D: Always wrong about the classes
Why A: An AUC of 0.5 means the classifier ranks positives above negatives only half the time, which equals random guessing and shows no useful separation of the classes.
Why B: Perfect separation of the classes corresponds to an AUC of 1.0, so a value of 0.5 is far from perfect and sits at the chance level.
Why C: AUC measures how well classes are separated and not speed, so a value of 0.5 says nothing about the model being faster than other models.
Why D: Always being wrong would give an AUC near 0, which is informative since flipping its output would fix it, while 0.5 means no signal at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is k-fold cross-validation?
A: Training k separate models on different features and averaging their predictions into one final answer
B: Training a model k times on the same data without any change to the way the data is split between runs
C: Splitting data into k parts and training and testing k times, each time with a different part held out
D: Repeating the same training run k times with different random starting weights and keeping the best
Why A: That describes an ensemble of models. K-fold cross-validation splits data into k parts and trains and tests k times, holding out a different part each time.
Why B: Training k times on the same unchanged split would give the same result each time, but k-fold cross-validation changes the held-out part on every one of its runs.
Why C: K-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, then trains and tests k times, each time holding out a different part, to give a more reliable estimate.
Why D: Changing starting weights compares initializations, not data splits. K-fold cross-validation holds out a different part of the data in each of its k runs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff?
A: A balance between the price and the quality of data that a firm buys from vendors each year
B: A balance between training time and testing time, so that a model is neither too slow nor too fast to use
C: A balance between the speed of a model and the memory that it needs to run on a server
D: A balance between a model that is too simple and one that is too sensitive to the training data
Why A: A balance between price and quality of purchased data is a procurement matter, while the bias-variance tradeoff concerns model error from being too simple or too flexible.
Why B: A balance between training and testing time is about computing cost, and the bias-variance tradeoff is instead about prediction error caused by model complexity.
Why C: A balance between speed and memory is a matter of efficiency, whereas the bias-variance tradeoff describes how model simplicity and sensitivity to the data affect errors.
Why D: The bias-variance tradeoff balances a model that is too simple, with high bias, against one too sensitive to the training data, with high variance, to generalize well.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model with high variance usually:
A: Is too simple to learn patterns, so it misses the signal in the data
B: Fits the training data very closely but performs poorly on new data
C: Has no errors at all on the training data or the new data sets
D: Performs poorly on both training and new data because it is too simple
Why A: A model that is too simple to learn patterns has high bias and underfits, while high variance is the opposite problem of being too sensitive to the data.
Why B: High variance usually means the model fits the training data very closely, even its noise, but performs poorly on new data, which is overfitting.
Why C: Having no errors on both training and new data would be an ideal model, but high variance means errors on new data are clearly large.
Why D: Performing poorly on both training and new data because the model is too simple is underfitting caused by high bias, not by high variance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A model with high bias usually:
A: Is too simple and performs poorly on both training and new data
B: Fits the training data perfectly and fails on new data it has not seen
C: Has no errors at all on the training data or the new data we test
D: Learns noise in the training data and fits it too closely
Why A: High bias means the model is too simple to capture the real patterns, so it underfits and performs poorly on both the training data and new data.
Why B: Fitting the training data perfectly yet failing on unseen data is overfitting, which comes from high variance and not from high bias.
Why C: Having no errors on training or new data is the ideal case, whereas a high bias model makes clear errors on both because it is too simple.
Why D: Learning the noise in the training data and fitting it too closely is overfitting from high variance, which is the opposite of the underfitting caused by high bias.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is regularization?
A: A technique that speeds up training by using larger batches and more hardware
B: A technique that increases the model size by adding more layers and nodes
C: A technique that discourages overly complex models to reduce overfitting
D: A technique that adds noise to the data so the model learns faster than before
Why A: Using larger batches and more hardware speeds up training, but regularization is a different idea aimed at limiting model complexity so it generalizes better.
Why B: Increasing the model size with more layers and nodes makes a model more complex, which raises the risk of overfitting, while regularization works to limit complexity.
Why C: Regularization discourages overly complex models, usually by adding a penalty on large weights, which reduces overfitting so the model performs better on new data.
Why D: Adding noise to the data to speed learning is not what regularization means, which is a penalty on complexity and not a way to make learning faster.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is L1 regularization (lasso) known for?
A: Making all coefficients larger, so the model puts more weight on every feature
B: Pushing some coefficients to exactly zero, which performs feature selection
C: Doubling the learning rate on each pass through the training data set
D: Removing all training data from the model once the fit is done to save room
Why A: Making all coefficients larger is the reverse of what L1 does, because the L1 penalty pushes coefficients down, and it does not add weight to every feature.
Why B: L1 regularization, called lasso, pushes some coefficients to exactly zero, which removes those features and so performs feature selection as a side effect of fitting.
Why C: Doubling the learning rate is an optimizer setting that controls step size, and it has no connection to the penalty on coefficients that L1 adds.
Why D: Removing all training data from the model is not part of any regularization method, since L1 adds a penalty on coefficients and leaves the data in place.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is L2 regularization (ridge) known for?
A: Making the model deeper by adding many more layers between input and output
B: Setting all coefficients to one so every feature has the same weight
C: Deleting features at random from the table until the model is simple
D: Shrinking coefficients toward zero without usually making them exactly zero
Why A: Making the model deeper with many more layers raises its complexity, which is the reverse of regularization, and L2 is a penalty on large coefficients, not on structure.
Why B: Setting all coefficients to one would give every feature the same weight and ignore the data, whereas L2 only shrinks coefficients toward zero by a small amount.
Why C: Deleting features at random describes dropping inputs rather than ridge, whereas L2 keeps every feature and just makes its coefficient smaller through a penalty.
Why D: L2 regularization, called ridge, shrinks coefficients toward zero without usually making them exactly zero, so all features stay in the model but with smaller weights.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is dropout in neural networks?
A: Dropping rows with missing values from the data set before training overall
B: Removing the last layer of the network permanently after training
C: Stopping training when accuracy is perfect, so it learns no more
D: Randomly ignoring some neurons during training to reduce overfitting
Why A: Dropping rows with missing values is data cleaning done before training, and it has nothing to do with switching off neurons inside the network during learning.
Why B: Dropout does not delete the final layer for good; it only mutes random neurons temporarily during training, and the full network is used again when predicting.
Why C: Halting training when progress stalls is early stopping, a different regularization tool; dropout keeps training going while randomly silencing neurons, and it does not wait for perfect accuracy.
Why D: Dropout randomly ignores a share of neurons on each training step, which stops units from relying on each other and so reduces overfitting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an activation function in a neural network?
A: A function that measures training time for each pass over the whole data set in the end
B: A function that decides a neuron's output from its inputs, adding non-linearity
C: A function that splits the data into training and test sets before fitting
D: A function that loads the data from a file on disk into the program memory
Why A: Time spent per pass over the data is measured by a timer or profiler; an activation function acts on each neuron's values and has no role in measuring duration.
Why B: An activation function takes a neuron's weighted inputs and produces its output, and its non-linear shape lets stacked layers learn patterns that a plain linear model cannot.
Why C: Splitting data into training and test sets is a preprocessing step done before fitting; activation functions work inside the network on neuron values, not on whole data sets.
Why D: Loading data from disk into memory is an input and output task handled by data loaders; activation functions only transform neuron values during the forward pass.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the ReLU activation function do?
A: Outputs the square of the input for every value that it receives
B: Outputs a probability between 0 and 1 for any input, which is read as a chance
C: Outputs zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs
D: Outputs a random value between zero and one for each input it gets
Why A: ReLU does not square anything; squaring would make large inputs grow quickly, while ReLU simply passes positive values through unchanged and sets negative ones to zero.
Why B: Squashing any input into a probability between 0 and 1 describes the sigmoid function, whereas ReLU leaves positive values unbounded and does not produce probabilities.
Why C: ReLU returns max(0, x): a negative input such as -3 becomes 0, and a positive input such as 5 stays 5, which keeps computation cheap.
Why D: ReLU is fully deterministic; the same input always gives the same output, and no random number between zero and one is ever drawn by it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the sigmoid function output?
A: A value between 0 and 1
B: Zero for negative inputs
C: A value from -10 to 10 only
D: The input unchanged
Why A: The sigmoid function 1 / (1 + e^-x) squeezes every real input into the open range between 0 and 1, which is why it is used for probabilities.
Why B: Sigmoid does not output zero for negative inputs; a negative input such as -2 gives about 0.12, which is small but positive, so zero is wrong.
Why C: Sigmoid outputs never leave the range from 0 to 1, so a range of -10 to 10 is wrong; that range is not what the function produces.
Why D: Returning the input unchanged is the identity function, which is a straight line; sigmoid bends the input into an S shape that stays between 0 and 1.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a batch in neural network training?
A: A group of features used together as inputs to the model at once
B: A group of models that are trained and combined to make one prediction
C: A subset of the training data processed together in one update step
D: The full set of test data held back to check the final model
Why A: Features are the input columns that describe each example; a batch is a group of examples, not a group of features, so this describes input variables instead.
Why B: Training several models and combining their predictions is called an ensemble; a batch is only a slice of the data used in a single weight update.
Why C: A batch is a subset of the training examples fed through the network together, after which one update of the weights is computed from that group.
Why D: Test data held back for the final check is the test set; a batch comes from the training data and is used for learning, not for the final evaluation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If a data set has 1,000 examples and the batch size is 100, how many batches make up one epoch?
Why A: One epoch is one pass through all the data, so 1,000 examples divided by a batch size of 100 gives 10 batches, each with 100 examples.
Why B: 1,000 is the total number of examples, not the number of batches; with 100 examples per batch the count must be smaller, namely 1,000 / 100 = 10.
Why C: 0.1 would come from dividing 100 by 1,000, which flips the division; the number of batches is 1,000 / 100 = 10, and a count cannot be a fraction.
Why D: 100 is the size of each batch, not the number of batches; dividing the 1,000 examples by 100 per batch gives 10 batches in one epoch.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is early stopping?
A: Stopping data collection once enough rows have been gathered for use
B: Stopping the computer before training begins so the model never learns
C: Stopping the model from making predictions on the test data set
D: Halting training when performance on validation data stops improving
Why A: Stopping data collection when enough rows are gathered is a sampling decision made before modelling; early stopping concerns when to end the training loop itself.
Why B: Halting the computer before training starts would leave a model that has learned nothing; early stopping happens during training, after the model has begun to learn.
Why C: Early stopping does not block predictions on test data; the model still predicts on the test set, and the technique only decides when training should end.
Why D: Early stopping ends training once the validation score stops improving, which prevents the model from overfitting the training data as it keeps training for too long.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a recurrent neural network (RNN) handle well?
A: Images such as photos and scans in a grid
B: Sequential data such as text or time series
C: Data tables with fixed columns and no order
D: Geographic maps and spatial location data
Why A: Grid images suit convolutional networks. An RNN is built for sequential data such as text or time series.
Why B: An RNN carries a hidden state from step to step, so it can use earlier items in a sequence, which suits text, speech and time series.
Why C: Unordered tables suit trees or feed-forward networks. An RNN uses a hidden state across steps, which suits sequential data such as text or time series.
Why D: Spatial data is better handled by grid or graph models. An RNN suits sequential data such as text or time series.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the attention mechanism in transformers?
A: A way to shorten the data by cutting rows from the table, so that fewer records are left to process as a rule
B: A way for a model to weigh the importance of different parts of the input when producing each output
C: A way to pay attention to the user, by showing alerts and pop-up messages on the screen now
D: A way to store data on a disk, in files that are kept in folders on a computer or a server
Why A: Cutting rows from a table is data reduction, which has no link to attention; the attention mechanism works on the tokens inside the model, not on table records.
Why B: Attention lets the model assign weights to the parts of the input, so each output token can focus on the most relevant words, wherever they sit.
Why C: Showing alerts and pop-up messages is a user interface feature; the attention in transformers is a mathematical weighting inside the model and has nothing to do with users.
Why D: Storing data in files and folders is file system work; transformer attention is a calculation that scores how much each input token matters, not a storage method.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is tokenization in natural language processing?
A: Removing common words such as the and of from a text
B: Translating text from one language into another for readers
C: Splitting text into smaller units such as words or sub-words
D: Grouping documents by topic using their word patterns
Why A: That is stop-word removal. Tokenization splits text into smaller units such as words or sub-words.
Why B: Translating text from one language to another is machine translation, a task a model performs; tokenization is only the earlier step of cutting text into units.
Why C: Tokenization splits text into smaller units, called tokens, such as words, sub-words or characters, which are then mapped to numbers the model can use.
Why D: Grouping by topic is clustering or topic modeling. Tokenization splits text into smaller units such as words or sub-words.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a context window in a large language model?
A: The time a model takes to answer each user question
B: The window where the user types a question to it
C: The number of users who ask the model questions
D: The amount of text the model can consider at once
Why A: The time to answer a question is latency; the context window is about how much text the model can read at once, not about speed.
Why B: The place where a user types a question is the chat box or input field; the context window is a limit inside the model on the text it can use.
Why C: The number of users asking questions is a measure of traffic or load; the context window is a size limit on the text for a single request.
Why D: The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can take into account at one time, including both the prompt and its reply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)?
A: Training a model using human preferences as a reward signal
B: Training a model on labeled photos supplied by crowd workers
C: Training a model to copy the human body and how it moves overall
D: Training a model to win a game by playing against itself
Why A: RLHF collects human judgments on which outputs are better, trains a reward model from them, and uses that reward signal to tune the model toward preferred behavior.
Why B: Labeled examples describe supervised learning. RLHF uses human preferences between outputs as a reward signal.
Why C: Copying how the human body moves is robotics or motion imitation; RLHF uses human feedback on text outputs as a reward, and has no concern with bodies.
Why D: Self-play uses the game result as the reward, not human preferences. RLHF uses human preferences as a reward signal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is prompt injection?
A: An attack in which crafted input tricks an AI system into ignoring its instructions
B: A way to add data to a table in a database by using a form on the web page for users
C: A medical injection given by a nurse to protect a patient from disease at a clinic
D: A way to speed up a model by adding more chips and memory to the server hardware
Why A: Prompt injection is an attack where crafted text makes an AI system ignore its original instructions and do what the attacker wants instead, such as leaking data.
Why B: Adding rows to a database through a web form describes inserting records, and the similar sounding SQL injection attack, but it does not describe attacks on a language model's prompt.
Why C: A medical injection given by a nurse is a vaccination or treatment; the term here refers to a software security attack and has no medical meaning at all.
Why D: Adding chips and memory to servers is hardware scaling for speed; prompt injection is a security attack that manipulates the text given to a model.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a guardrail in an AI system?
A: A fence around the data center to keep out visitors
B: A way to make the model faster by using bigger chips
C: A rule or filter that limits harmful or off-topic outputs
D: A tool that stores data in a table for later use by staff
Why A: A fence around a data center is physical security; in AI a guardrail is a software rule or filter on model behavior, and it does not stop visitors.
Why B: Bigger chips would raise speed but not safety; a guardrail does not change how fast a model runs, only what the model is allowed to output.
Why C: A guardrail is a rule, filter or check that limits harmful, unsafe or off-topic outputs, keeping the AI system within its intended and safe behavior.
Why D: Storing data in a table is database work; a guardrail does not store anything for staff and instead restricts or screens what the AI says.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is zero-shot prompting?
A: Giving no instructions to the model about the task at all
B: Training a model from scratch on a new data set with labels
C: Giving a model many examples of the task in the prompt
D: Asking a model to do a task with no examples in the prompt
Why A: Zero-shot does not mean giving no instructions; the task is still described in the prompt, and what is missing is only worked examples of it.
Why B: Training from scratch on labeled data is ordinary supervised learning; zero-shot prompting uses an already trained model and changes nothing about its weights.
Why C: Giving many examples in the prompt is few-shot or many-shot prompting; zero-shot has zero examples, which is the exact reverse of what this option says.
Why D: Zero-shot prompting gives the model only the task description and no worked examples, relying on what it already learned during its training to answer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is few-shot prompting?
A: Asking the model a few times in a row to see if it repeats itself
B: Including a few examples in the prompt to show the model the task
C: Giving no examples in the prompt, only a plain description
D: Retraining the model on thousands of examples to learn the task
Why A: Asking the same question several times in a row is repeated sampling; few-shot refers to the number of examples placed in the prompt, not repeats of the question.
Why B: Few-shot prompting places a small number of worked examples in the prompt, which shows the model the pattern and format of the task without any retraining.
Why C: Giving no examples and only a plain description is zero-shot prompting; few-shot means that a handful of examples, often two to five, are included.
Why D: Retraining on thousands of examples is fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights; few-shot prompting leaves the weights alone and only adds examples to the prompt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
A: Chaining computers together in a network to share the work of a task
B: Asking a model to answer instantly, with no steps or reasoning shown
C: Linking many prompts in a row with no logic so the model writes more
D: Asking a model to reason step by step before giving its answer
Why A: Chaining computers into a network to share work is distributed computing; chain-of-thought is a prompting method about the model's own reasoning steps.
Why B: Asking for an instant answer with no reasoning shown is the opposite of chain-of-thought, which deliberately asks for the intermediate steps to be written out.
Why C: Chain-of-thought is not about linking many prompts with no logic; it asks one model to reason through steps, and random linking would not improve any answer.
Why D: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to work through the problem step by step before answering, which often improves results on math and logic questions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is temperature in a language model's settings?
A: The size of the model in terms of the number of its parameters
B: The speed of the internet link used by the model, in Mbps
C: A setting that controls how random or predictable the output is
D: The heat of the computer chips as the model runs on a server rack
Why A: The number of parameters measures model size, which is a separate property; temperature is a setting applied when the model chooses each next token.
Why B: Internet speed in Mbps is a network property; temperature in a language model has no link to bandwidth and only affects how the output is sampled.
Why C: Temperature controls randomness when sampling: a low value gives focused, predictable output, while a high value gives more varied and creative output.
Why D: The heat of chips is a hardware reading in degrees; the temperature setting in a language model is a sampling parameter and does not measure any physical heat.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vector database used for in AI applications?
A: Storing transactions so that totals stay accurate when updated
B: Storing embeddings so that similar items can be found quickly
C: Storing passwords for the accounts of a firm in a safe vault
D: Storing logs so errors can be traced after a crash
Why A: Transaction consistency is the job of a relational database. A vector database stores embeddings so similar items can be found quickly.
Why B: A vector database stores embeddings, which are lists of numbers capturing meaning, and quickly finds the nearest ones, supporting similarity search and retrieval for AI apps.
Why C: Storing passwords is the job of a secrets manager or a credential vault; a vector database is built for similarity search over embeddings, not for security.
Why D: Log storage supports debugging. A vector database stores embeddings so that similar items can be found quickly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is data labeling?
A: Adding tags or answers to raw data so that a model can learn from it
B: Encrypting data so that only approved users can read the files
C: Deleting old data from the tables so that the disk has more room
D: Removing the names of columns from a table so nobody else can read it
Why A: Data labeling attaches tags or correct answers to raw data, such as marking images as cat or dog, so that supervised models can learn from examples.
Why B: Encrypting data so only approved users can read it is a security step; data labeling adds meaning to data and does not hide anything from users.
Why C: Deleting old data to free disk space is data retention or cleanup; labeling adds information to data instead of removing any of it.
Why D: Removing column names from a table would make the data harder to use; labeling does the opposite by adding useful tags and answers to the data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is label quality important?
A: Errors in labels teach the model wrong patterns
B: Labels decide how fast the computer trains the model
C: Labels make the data much smaller on disk
D: Labels are just names for the columns of the data
Why A: Labels are the answers a model learns from, so mistakes in them teach it wrong patterns, which lowers accuracy and gives poor predictions on new data.
Why B: Labels do not set training speed. They are the targets a model learns from, so errors in them teach wrong patterns.
Why C: Labels add information to the data and do not shrink it; file size is unrelated to why label quality matters for what the model learns.
Why D: Labels are the target answers a model learns from, not column names. Errors in them teach the model wrong patterns.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is oversampling?
A: Collecting a new random sample of the whole data set to replace the old one
B: Sampling less data from the large class so that the set is smaller to handle
C: Adding more examples of a rare class, for example by duplicating or synthesizing them
D: Adding random noise to each feature value so the model cannot memorize the data
Why A: A fresh random sample keeps the same class imbalance. Oversampling adds more examples of the rare class, by duplicating or synthesizing them.
Why B: Taking less data from the large class is undersampling; oversampling goes the other way and increases the number of rare examples rather than shrinking the big class.
Why C: Oversampling increases the number of minority class examples, either by duplicating them or by creating synthetic ones, which helps balance an imbalanced data set.
Why D: Adding noise is a regularization idea and does not change class sizes. Oversampling adds examples of the rare class by duplicating or synthesizing them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is SMOTE?
A: A technique that scales features to a common range before training
B: A technique that creates synthetic examples of a minority class
C: A technique that deletes outliers so the points lie closer to the mean
D: A technique that compresses data files so that they use less disk space
Why A: Scaling features to a common range is normalization or standardization; SMOTE does not rescale anything and instead creates new examples of the minority class.
Why B: SMOTE creates synthetic minority class examples by interpolating between existing ones and their nearest neighbors, which helps balance classes without simply copying rows.
Why C: Deleting outliers to move points toward the mean is outlier removal; SMOTE adds new minority points and does not delete any existing ones.
Why D: Compressing data files is storage work; SMOTE is a class balancing technique and does not change how much disk space the data takes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is principal component analysis (PCA)?
A: A technique that labels data by hand, giving each row a tag that names its class
B: A technique that adds columns to a table by combining the values of existing ones
C: A technique that sorts rows of a table by the value in one chosen column each time overall
D: A technique that reduces dimensions by finding directions that capture the most variance
Why A: Labeling data by hand is annotation, which gives examples tags; PCA is an unsupervised technique and needs no labels at all to find its directions.
Why B: PCA does not add columns; it replaces many correlated columns with fewer new ones, whereas combining columns to add more is closer to feature engineering.
Why C: Sorting rows by one column is simple ordering and leaves the data's dimensions unchanged; PCA instead creates new axes that capture variation across the columns.
Why D: PCA finds new directions, called principal components, that capture the most variance in the data, so it can reduce the number of dimensions while keeping most information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In k-means clustering, what does k stand for?
A: The number of steps it takes
B: The number of clusters to find
C: The number of features used
D: The number of rows in the table
Why A: The number of steps is an iteration count; the letter k in k-means stands for how many clusters the algorithm should find, which is chosen in advance.
Why B: In k-means, k is the number of clusters; for example k = 3 asks the algorithm to split the points into three groups around three centers.
Why C: The number of features is the dimension of the data and is not k; k only sets how many groups the algorithm will form.
Why D: The number of rows is the sample size; k is chosen independently of it, and it counts the clusters, not the records in the table.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the elbow method used for?
A: Choosing a chart color that makes the data easy to read for the whole audience in the end
B: Choosing a learning rate that sets the size of each update step in training
C: Choosing a sensible number of clusters by looking at how error falls as k increases
D: Choosing a database system to store the records of the firm in tables and keys
Why A: Choosing a chart color is a design matter; the elbow method is about picking the number of clusters by plotting error against k.
Why B: The learning rate is tuned with search or schedules; the elbow method looks at error against the number of clusters, not at update step size.
Why C: The elbow method plots error against k and picks the point where the drop slows sharply, which marks a sensible number of clusters for k-means.
Why D: Choosing a database system is an engineering decision about storage; the elbow method is a clustering tool and has nothing to do with databases or keys.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In k-nearest neighbors with k = 3, how is a new point classified?
A: By the majority class among its 3 closest training points
B: By the average of all points in the training set data
C: By a random choice made by the computer at each step
D: By the class of the farthest point, as distant points weigh more
Why A: With k = 3, the algorithm finds the 3 training points closest to the new point and assigns the class that most of those 3 neighbors have.
Why B: Averaging all points in the training set ignores distance; kNN uses only the nearest few neighbors, and the vote is on classes, not an average of everything.
Why C: kNN is deterministic and uses distance to its neighbors; it does not choose randomly, so the same point gets the same class every time.
Why D: kNN looks at the closest points, not the farthest, because nearby points are the most similar; far points do not carry more weight, so this is backwards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hyperparameter search (tuning)?
A: Searching the internet for data to add to the training set to help
B: Searching for new features only, in the columns of the data set
C: Searching for errors in code and fixing the lines that fail
D: Trying different model settings to find those that perform best
Why A: Searching the internet for data is data collection; hyperparameter search tries different settings such as learning rate or depth on the model that already exists.
Why B: Searching only for new features is feature engineering; tuning hyperparameters changes model settings such as tree depth, and does not look for columns of data.
Why C: Finding errors in code is debugging; hyperparameter tuning looks for the best model settings and does not fix any lines of code that fail.
Why D: Hyperparameter tuning tries different model settings, such as learning rate or tree depth, and keeps the combination that scores best on validation data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a baseline model?
A: The most complex model that could be built
B: A simple model used as a point of comparison
C: The model with the highest cost of running it
D: A model that has not been trained, so it predicts
Why A: A baseline is meant to be simple, not complex; the most complex model would be a poor yardstick, since the point is an easy reference to beat.
Why B: A baseline is a simple model, such as always predicting the average, that gives a reference score to compare against, showing whether a fancier model adds value.
Why C: Cost of running is unrelated to being a baseline; what defines it is simplicity and its role as the benchmark for comparison, not high expense.
Why D: An untrained model produces meaningless output, so it is not a useful point of comparison; a baseline is a simple model that is actually fitted to the data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a naive Bayes classifier?
A: A classifier based on Bayes' theorem that assumes features are independent
B: A classifier that works only on images and cannot use numbers or text
C: A classifier that has no assumptions about how the features relate to each other
D: A classifier that uses deep layers of nodes to learn from large data sets
Why A: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem and naively assumes that features are independent of each other given the class, which keeps it fast and simple.
Why B: Naive Bayes works well on text and numbers, so saying it handles only images is wrong; it is often used for spam filtering on text.
Why C: Naive Bayes makes a strong assumption, namely that features are independent, so saying it has no assumptions is false; the word naive points to that assumption.
Why D: Deep layers of nodes describe neural networks; naive Bayes is a simple probabilistic model built on Bayes' theorem and uses no layers of nodes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a support vector machine (SVM)?
A: A model that groups customers without labels, to find similar shoppers in the data
B: A model that predicts a number from a line fitted through the points
C: A model that finds a boundary that separates classes with the widest margin
D: A model that stores data in a vector of numbers for use in a search
Why A: Grouping customers without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task; an SVM is a supervised model that needs labeled classes to find its boundary.
Why B: Predicting a number from a fitted line is linear regression; an SVM classifies by finding a boundary, though a variant can do regression.
Why C: An SVM finds the boundary, called a hyperplane, that separates classes with the widest possible margin, which tends to generalize well on new data.
Why D: Storing data as a vector for a search is an embedding index; an SVM is a classification model that learns a decision boundary from labeled examples.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is gradient boosting?
A: A method that increases the learning rate each round, so the model trains faster
B: A method that boosts the speed of a GPU by raising its clock rate and power use
C: A method that raises the prices of goods when demand for them goes up in a market every time
D: An ensemble method that builds trees one after another, each correcting earlier errors
Why A: Gradient boosting does not raise the learning rate each round; it adds new trees that fit the previous errors, and a rising rate would make training unstable.
Why B: Raising a GPU clock rate is overclocking, a hardware matter; gradient boosting is a machine learning method named for its way of fitting errors.
Why C: Raising prices when demand grows is economics; gradient boosting is a machine learning ensemble method and has nothing to do with prices or markets.
Why D: Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, with each new tree fitted to the errors of the earlier ones, so the ensemble improves step by step.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is bagging?
A: Training one model many times without change, using the same data each run
B: Training several models on random samples of the data and combining their results
C: Putting data in a bag, a container used to carry papers and files around town in this case
D: Deleting data from a table that has gone stale, to free up room on a server
Why A: Training one model many times on the same data gives identical results and no gain; bagging uses different random samples so the models differ and can be combined.
Why B: Bagging trains several models, each on a random sample of the data, then combines their predictions by voting or averaging, which lowers variance.
Why C: Putting data in a bag to carry papers is a literal reading of the word; bagging is short for bootstrap aggregating, a machine learning ensemble technique.
Why D: Deleting stale data to free room is data cleanup; bagging is an ensemble method that keeps data and trains models on random samples of it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the R-squared (R²) of a regression model?
A: The average error of the model on the test data, from the mistakes
B: The number of features used by the model to make predictions
C: The learning rate used by the optimizer for each update step
D: The share of variation in the outcome explained by the model
Why A: The average error on test data describes measures such as MAE or RMSE; R-squared is a proportion of variance explained, not an average mistake.
Why B: The number of features is the model's size or dimension and is not R-squared; R-squared reports how well the model explains the outcome.
Why C: The learning rate is an optimizer setting; R-squared is computed after fitting, to show how much of the outcome's variation the model accounts for.
Why D: R-squared is the share of the variation in the outcome that the model explains, running from 0 to 1, where higher means the model fits better.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A regression model has an R² of 0.85. What does this suggest?
A: About 85 percent of the variation in the outcome is explained by the model
B: The model predicts the outcome correctly in 85 percent of the test cases
C: The data has 85 rows, and each row has one column of values in it
D: The model's predictions miss the true value by 0.85 units on average
Why A: An R-squared of 0.85 means the model explains about 85 percent of the variation in the outcome, leaving about 15 percent unexplained by the model.
Why B: R-squared measures explained variation, not the share of correct predictions. A value of 0.85 means about 85 percent of the variation is explained.
Why C: The number of rows has nothing to do with R-squared; the value 0.85 is a proportion of variance explained, not a count of data rows.
Why D: R-squared is a proportion of variance explained, not an average error in units. A value of 0.85 means about 85 percent of the variation is explained.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is mean squared error (MSE)?
A: The largest error made by the model on any single case in the data set in this case
B: The average of the actual values in the data set, found by adding them
C: The average of the squared differences between predictions and actual values
D: The number of errors made by the model across all of the test cases
Why A: The largest error on any case is the maximum error; MSE averages the squared errors over all cases and so it is not a single worst mistake.
Why B: The average of the actual values is just the mean of the target; MSE instead averages the squared gaps between predictions and those actual values.
Why C: MSE takes the difference between each prediction and the actual value, squares it, and averages these squares, so larger errors are penalized more heavily.
Why D: The number of errors is a count, such as in a misclassification tally; MSE measures the size of errors by squaring and averaging them, not how many occur.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a regression y = 3 + 2x, what is the predicted y when x = 5?
Why A: 10 comes from 2 times 5 and forgets the intercept of 3; the full prediction is 3 + 2(5) = 3 + 10 = 13.
Why B: 25 comes from adding first and then multiplying, (3 + 2) x 5; the correct order of operations gives 3 + 2(5) = 13.
Why C: 8 comes from adding 3 and 5 and ignoring the slope of 2; substituting x = 5 into the equation gives 3 + 10 = 13.
Why D: Substituting x = 5 gives y = 3 + 2(5) = 3 + 10 = 13, so the predicted value is 13.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In the regression y = 3 + 2x, what does the 2 represent?
A: The change in y for each one-unit rise in x
B: The value of y when x is zero at start
C: The error between a point and the line
D: The number of data points in the sample overall
Why A: The slope, here 2, shows how much y changes when x rises by one unit, so each extra unit of x adds 2 to the predicted y.
Why B: The value of y when x is zero is the intercept, which is 3 here; the 2 is the slope instead and multiplies x.
Why C: The error between a point and the line is the residual; the coefficient 2 is a fixed part of the line's equation, not an error.
Why D: The number of data points in the sample is the sample size n; the 2 in the equation is the slope and says nothing about the count.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In the regression y = 3 + 2x, what does the 3 represent?
A: The number of rows in the data set
B: The change in y for each one-unit rise in x
C: The predicted value of y when x is zero
D: The error between a point and the line
Why A: The number of rows is the sample size and is not found in the equation; the 3 is the intercept, which is the starting value of y.
Why B: The change in y for each one-unit rise in x is the slope, which is 2 in this equation; the 3 is the intercept, not the slope.
Why C: The 3 is the intercept, the predicted value of y when x equals zero, since y = 3 + 2(0) = 3.
Why D: The error between a point and the line is a residual, which differs for each point; the 3 is a constant that does not vary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is multicollinearity?
A: When there are too few features in the data for the model to learn
B: When predictor variables are strongly correlated with each other
C: When the target is missing from many of the rows in the data
D: When data is too large to fit into the memory of the computer
Why A: Too few features is a different problem, called underfitting or missing information; multicollinearity needs several features that are strongly related to each other.
Why B: Multicollinearity means that predictor variables are strongly correlated with one another, which makes regression coefficients unstable and their individual effects hard to separate.
Why C: A target missing in many rows is a missing data problem; multicollinearity concerns relationships among the predictors, not gaps in the outcome column.
Why D: Data too large for memory is a scaling problem; multicollinearity is about strong correlation between predictor variables and not about how big the data is.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a residual in regression?
A: The sum of all values in the data set, added together in one total
B: The difference between an actual value and the predicted value
C: The number of predictors used in the regression model fitted to data
D: The slope of the line fitted through the points on the plot
Why A: The sum of all values in the data set is just a total; a residual is a difference for a single point between what was observed and predicted.
Why B: A residual equals the actual value minus the predicted value for a point, so it shows how far the fitted line misses that observation.
Why C: The number of predictors is the model's size; a residual is an error for one observation, so a count of predictors cannot be one.
Why D: The slope of the fitted line is a coefficient of the model; a residual is the vertical gap between a point and that line.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a learning curve?
A: A curve of the price of data over time as it is bought and sold
B: A curve showing how fast a person learns a new task over weeks
C: A curve showing company profits over a number of years in a report
D: A plot of model performance as training data or time increases
Why A: The price of data over time is a market curve; a learning curve in machine learning plots model performance against training data size or training time.
Why B: A curve of how fast a person learns is a human learning curve; in machine learning the term refers to a model's performance as training grows.
Why C: Company profits over the years is a financial chart; a machine learning learning curve is a plot of model scores against training size or time.
Why D: A learning curve plots model performance, such as error, against training set size or training time, which helps to diagnose underfitting and overfitting.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is semi-supervised learning?
A: Learning that a human supervises half the time, with the rest left to the machine
B: Learning from a large set of labeled data together with a small set of test data
C: Learning from a small amount of labeled data together with a large amount of unlabeled data
D: Learning by trial and error from rewards given after each action the model takes
Why A: Semi-supervised learning is about the mix of labeled and unlabeled data, not about a human supervising half the time while the machine works on the rest.
Why B: That describes ordinary supervised learning with a test set. Semi-supervised learning mixes a small labeled set with a large unlabeled pool.
Why C: Semi-supervised learning mixes a small set of labeled examples with a large pool of unlabeled data, which cuts the cost of labeling while still improving the model.
Why D: That is reinforcement learning. Semi-supervised learning combines a small amount of labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is self-supervised learning?
A: Learning from patterns in unlabeled data by creating its own training signals
B: Learning from a small set of human-labeled examples that a teacher prepared
C: Learning by grouping similar items together without predicting a target
D: Learning by copying the answers of a larger model after training is done
Why A: Self-supervised learning builds its own training signals from unlabeled data, for example by predicting a hidden word from its context, so no human labels are needed.
Why B: Human-labeled examples describe supervised learning. Self-supervised learning creates its own training signals from unlabeled data.
Why C: Grouping without targets is unsupervised clustering. Self-supervised learning builds its own prediction tasks from unlabeled data, such as guessing a hidden word.
Why D: Copying a larger model is distillation. Self-supervised learning creates its own training signals from patterns in unlabeled data.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Markov decision process used for?
A: Drawing charts from the rows of a table so that results can be shown to an audience
B: Cleaning data by removing duplicates and fixing errors in the rows of a table of records in the end
C: Encrypting files so that only approved users can read them, with a key held by the owner
D: Modeling decisions in situations where outcomes depend on the current state and the action
Why A: Drawing charts from table rows is data visualization; a Markov decision process is a mathematical framework for sequential decisions and has no link to charts.
Why B: Cleaning data by removing duplicates is data preparation; a Markov decision process models states, actions and rewards, and does not clean any records.
Why C: Encrypting files is a security task; a Markov decision process is a model for decisions over time and has no role in protecting files with keys.
Why D: A Markov decision process models decisions where the outcome depends on the current state and the action taken, and it forms the basis of reinforcement learning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In reinforcement learning, what is a reward?
A: A prize for the user who wins a game of chance
B: A signal telling the agent how good an action was
C: A tax paid by the agent to the state on its earnings
D: A bonus paid to the programmer when the run is done
Why A: A prize for a game winner is an everyday meaning of reward; in reinforcement learning a reward is a numeric signal the environment gives to the agent.
Why B: The reward is a numeric signal from the environment that tells the agent how good its last action was, so the agent learns to earn more over time.
Why C: A tax paid to the state is a financial idea with nothing to do with learning; a reward is feedback the agent receives, not a payment it makes.
Why D: A bonus paid to the programmer is a payroll matter; in reinforcement learning the reward goes to the learning agent as a signal, not to a person.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In reinforcement learning, what is the agent?
A: The learner that takes actions in an environment
B: The computer's operating system that runs the program
C: The dataset that the learner uses for training
D: The person who owns the data and the model
Why A: The agent is the learner or decision maker that observes the environment, takes actions, and receives rewards, which lets it improve its behavior over time.
Why B: The operating system runs the program but does not learn; the agent in reinforcement learning is the learner that chooses actions inside an environment.
Why C: The data set used for training is not the agent; the agent is the actor that learns by acting and receiving rewards, rather than a data collection.
Why D: The person who owns the data and model is the developer or owner; the agent is a software learner that acts in the environment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A disease affects 1 percent of people. A test is 90 percent accurate for those who have it and has a 5 percent false positive rate. Roughly what share of positive tests are true cases?
A: About 90 percent
B: About 50 percent
C: About 15 percent
D: About 1 percent
Why A: 90 percent is the test's sensitivity, how often sick people test positive; it ignores that healthy people are far more numerous, so most positives are false alarms.
Why B: About 50 percent would need roughly equal true and false positives; here per 100 people 0.9 true positives face about 4.95 false ones, so it is far lower.
Why C: Per 100 people, 1 is sick and tests positive with 0.9, while 99 are healthy and 5 percent, about 4.95, test positive; 0.9 / 5.85 is about 15 percent.
Why D: Positives are more common than the 1 percent base rate suggests; with 0.9 true and about 4.95 false positives per 100 people, the share is about 15 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Bayes' theorem allow you to do?
A: Sort data into order from the smallest to largest
B: Update the probability of an event given new evidence
C: Calculate the mean of any set of numbers or data
D: Predict the weather only, using satellite and ground data
Why A: Putting data in order from smallest to largest is sorting; Bayes' theorem is a rule about conditional probabilities and does not order any values.
Why B: Bayes' theorem lets you revise the probability of an event after seeing new evidence, by combining the prior probability with how likely the evidence is.
Why C: Calculating the mean is done by adding values and dividing by the count; Bayes' theorem concerns conditional probability and not averages of numbers.
Why D: Bayes' theorem applies to any event with conditional probabilities, including medical tests and spam, so limiting it to weather is wrong and far too narrow.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a z-score?
A: The number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean
B: The mean of a data set found by adding up all of the values overall
C: The probability of an event, found as favorable over total
D: The size of the sample that was drawn from the population
Why A: A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean, which makes values from different scales comparable on one standard scale.
Why B: The mean found by adding values and dividing is the average, a different statistic; a z-score uses the mean and spread to place one value.
Why C: Favorable outcomes over total outcomes is the classical definition of probability; a z-score is a standardized distance and not a probability.
Why D: The size of a sample is the count n; a z-score describes where one observation sits relative to the mean and the standard deviation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A test score is 85, the mean is 75 and the standard deviation is 5. What is the z-score?
Why A: 10 is the raw difference 85 - 75 and is not divided by the standard deviation; the z-score is 10 / 5 = 2.
Why B: 15 does not follow from the numbers; the z-score divides the difference of 10 by the standard deviation of 5, which gives 2.
Why C: The z-score is (value minus mean) divided by standard deviation, so (85 - 75) / 5 = 10 / 5 = 2 standard deviations above the mean.
Why D: 0.5 comes from dividing 5 by 10, which turns the division upside down; the correct calculation is 10 / 5 = 2.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the central limit theorem say?
A: All data are normally distributed, whatever the shape of the sample that is taken
B: The spread of the raw data shrinks to zero as the sample size grows
C: The sample median becomes equal to the sample mean once the sample is large
D: The distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows
Why A: The central limit theorem does not say that all data are normal; it says the distribution of sample means becomes approximately normal, whatever the shape of the data.
Why B: The raw data keep their spread; it is the standard error of the sample mean that shrinks. The theorem says sample means approach a normal distribution.
Why C: Mean and median stay different in skewed data however large the sample. The theorem concerns sample means approaching a normal distribution as sample size grows.
Why D: The central limit theorem says that as sample size grows, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution, whatever shape the population has.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the standard error of the mean?
A: The error made by a clerk in a data entry on a form sheet
B: The difference between two means found by subtracting averages overall
C: The range of the data, found as the largest minus the smallest
D: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean
Why A: A clerk's data entry error is a human mistake; the standard error of the mean is a statistic that describes how much sample means vary.
Why B: A difference between two means is found by subtraction and is a different quantity; the standard error describes the spread of a single mean across samples.
Why C: The range is the maximum minus the minimum; the standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n.
Why D: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean, showing how much sample means vary around the true mean.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A 95 percent confidence interval for a mean is 48 to 52. What is the best interpretation?
A: We are fairly confident the true mean lies between 48 and 52
B: The true mean is certainly 50 and there is no doubt about it
C: 95 percent of individual values lie between 48 and 52
D: The sample mean is 95 and the spread of the data is five units
Why A: A 95 percent confidence interval of 48 to 52 means we are fairly confident the true mean lies in that range, which is the usual practical reading.
Why B: The interval does not prove that the true mean is exactly 50; it only gives a plausible range, and certainty is never claimed by a confidence interval.
Why C: The interval is about the mean, not about individual values; individual values spread much wider, so 95 percent of them need not lie in that range.
Why D: The 95 percent is the confidence level, not the sample mean; the sample mean is the center of the interval, here 50, and spread is not five units.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a t-test used for?
A: Sorting data into order, from the smallest value up to the largest value in a set
B: Cleaning data by removing duplicate rows and filling in the gaps in the table of records
C: Comparing means, for example between two groups, when the population variance is unknown
D: Drawing charts from the rows of a table so that the results can be shown to a team
Why A: Sorting data from smallest to largest is ordering and uses no test statistic; a t-test compares means to decide whether a difference is likely to be real.
Why B: Cleaning data by removing duplicates is preparation done before analysis; a t-test is a hypothesis test and does not alter or clean the table.
Why C: A t-test compares means, for instance between two groups, and is used when the population variance is unknown, so the sample standard deviation stands in for it.
Why D: Drawing charts is visualization; a t-test is a statistical hypothesis test that produces a statistic and a p-value, not a chart of the rows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a chi-square test commonly used for?
A: Comparing the means of two groups, using each sample
B: Testing whether categorical variables are related
C: Finding the median of a sorted set of numbers
D: Predicting a number from the other values in a data set
Why A: Comparing the means of two groups is the job of a t-test; a chi-square test works with counts in categories and not with averages.
Why B: A chi-square test checks whether two categorical variables are related, by comparing observed counts in a table with the counts expected if they were independent.
Why C: Finding the median is a descriptive calculation on ordered numbers; a chi-square test is an inferential test for categorical data and does not compute medians.
Why D: Predicting a number from other values is regression; a chi-square test does not predict anything and only tests for association between categories.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ANOVA used for?
A: Comparing the means of three or more groups
B: Comparing only two means from two samples
C: Cleaning data by removing errors and gaps
D: Counting categories in a column of a table
Why A: ANOVA, or analysis of variance, compares the means of three or more groups at once, so it avoids running many separate t-tests that raise the error rate.
Why B: Comparing only two means is the typical use of a t-test; ANOVA is designed for three or more groups, so limiting it to two is wrong.
Why C: Cleaning data by removing errors is a preparation step; ANOVA is a statistical test that compares group means and does not modify the data.
Why D: Counting categories in a column is a frequency count; ANOVA tests for differences between group means and does not tally categories of any column.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is effect size?
A: The size of the sample, found by counting the number of rows in the data set overall
B: The number of tests run on the data set by the analyst during a single study
C: A measure of how large a difference or relationship is, not just whether it exists
D: The size of a file that holds the data, measured in megabytes on the disk
Why A: Counting rows gives the sample size, which is not effect size; effect size shows how big a difference or relationship is, whatever the number of rows.
Why B: The number of tests run is a count of analyses and has no link to effect size, which measures the magnitude of a result.
Why C: Effect size measures how large a difference or relationship is, and not only whether one exists, which p-values alone cannot tell you about practical importance.
Why D: The size of a file in megabytes is a storage measure; effect size is a statistical idea about the magnitude of a result.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why can a very small p-value still be unimportant in practice?
A: A p-value shows the probability that the null hypothesis is true
B: With a huge sample even tiny effects can be statistically significant
C: A small p-value is calculated from the size of the effect
D: Small samples tend to produce smaller p-values than large ones
Why A: A p-value is the chance of data this extreme if the null is true, not the chance the null is true, and it says nothing about effect size.
Why B: With a huge sample even a tiny difference can reach statistical significance, so a very small p-value can accompany an effect too small to matter in practice.
Why C: P-values depend on sample size and variability as well as effect size. With a huge sample even tiny effects can be statistically significant.
Why D: Small samples have less power, so they tend to give larger p-values. With a huge sample even tiny effects can reach significance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is p-hacking?
A: Cracking passwords by trying many guesses until one works on the account
B: Reporting all results honestly, including those not reaching significance
C: Cleaning data by removing errors, gaps and duplicates from the table of records
D: Trying many analyses until a significant result appears, then reporting it
Why A: Cracking passwords by guessing is a security attack; p-hacking is a research practice problem about misusing statistical analysis to reach significance.
