Why A: Letting everyone see all records violates privacy rules and the minimum necessary standard, so it is the opposite of access control.
Why B: Access control limits who can view or change records based on their role, so users see only the information they need for their duties.
Why C: Printing records for visitors would disclose private data to people without authorization; access control restricts exposure rather than expanding it.
Why D: Deleting passwords weekly would remove the way users prove identity and would weaken protection; access control relies on authentication and permissions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A billing clerk should not be able to read a patient's detailed clinical notes. Which principle does this show?
A: Public disclosure of data
B: Open access for all staff
C: Minimum necessary access
D: Unlimited sharing of records
Why A: Public disclosure of data would expose private details to everyone, which conflicts with a clerk being kept away from clinical notes.
Why B: Open access for all staff would let the clerk read clinical notes, which is the exact situation the restriction is meant to prevent.
Why C: Minimum necessary access means each person sees only the data needed for their job, so a billing clerk gets billing data but not detailed clinical notes.
Why D: Unlimited sharing of records would allow anyone to read any chart, which contradicts the limit placed on the clerk's access.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a wearable health device?
A: A device worn on the body that tracks health data such as heart rate
B: A hospital bed on wheels that is used to move patients between wards
C: A hospital gown that patients wear during a stay in a ward at night
D: A type of surgical tool used by the doctors in an operating room
Why A: A wearable health device is worn on the body and tracks health data such as heart rate, steps or sleep, often sending it to apps.
Why B: A wheeled hospital bed is furniture used to transport patients; it is not worn on the body and does not track personal health data.
Why C: A hospital gown is clothing worn during a stay; it has no sensors or data tracking, so it is not a wearable health device.
Why D: A surgical tool is held by clinicians during operations and is not worn by patients to track health data, so it is not a wearable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is remote patient monitoring?
A: Watching patients through hospital windows from the street
B: Monitoring doctors' computers to check how fast they type each day
C: Sending patients to the hospital daily for tests of their health
D: Using technology to track a patient's health data from home
Why A: Watching patients through windows from the street is not a medical practice and collects no health data, so it is not remote monitoring.
Why B: Monitoring doctors' typing speed tracks staff computer use, not a patient's health, so it does not describe remote patient monitoring.
Why C: Sending patients in daily for tests requires travel to the hospital, whereas remote monitoring collects data from the patient's home without visits.
Why D: Remote patient monitoring uses technology to track a patient's health data, such as blood pressure or glucose, from home so clinicians can respond early.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is health insurance?
A: A loan to pay hospital bills that must be repaid later
B: Coverage that pays part of the cost of medical care
C: A savings account for retirement that earns interest
D: A discount card for pharmacies that lowers drug prices
Why A: A loan must be repaid with interest, whereas insurance pools risk and pays part of covered medical costs when care is needed.
Why B: Health insurance is coverage that pays part of the cost of medical care in return for premiums, which protects members from very large bills.
Why C: A retirement savings account earns interest for later life and does not pay for medical care when illness or injury occurs.
Why D: A pharmacy discount card lowers drug prices only; it is not insurance, which covers a range of medical services and not only medicines.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a premium?
A: The amount paid regularly to keep an insurance policy active
B: The limit an insurer will pay for a person in a single year
C: The fee paid at each visit to a doctor by the patient at the desk
D: The amount paid for coverage before the policy year begins
Why A: A premium is the amount paid regularly, often monthly, to keep an insurance policy active, whether or not the member uses care.
Why B: The yearly limit an insurer will pay describes a benefit maximum or coverage cap, not the regular price paid to hold the policy.
Why C: The fee paid at each visit is a copayment, which is collected for a service, whereas a premium is paid regularly for coverage.
Why D: Paying before the policy year begins describes only the timing of a payment; a premium is the regular price for coverage, usually paid monthly during it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an out-of-pocket maximum?
A: The most an insurer pays for a person over a lifetime
B: The amount a member pays before the plan starts to pay
C: The most a member pays in a year for covered care
D: The fixed fee a member pays at each doctor visit
Why A: A lifetime payment limit is a different cap on the insurer, whereas an out-of-pocket maximum caps what the member pays each year.
Why B: That is the deductible. The out-of-pocket maximum is the most a member pays in a year for covered care.
Why C: The out-of-pocket maximum is the most a member pays in a year for covered care, after which the plan pays covered costs in full.
Why D: That is a copay. The out-of-pocket maximum is the yearly cap on what a member pays for covered care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a claim?
A: A request sent to an insurer for payment of services
B: A list of insurance rules that a member must follow
C: A medicine order sent to a pharmacy after a visit
D: A patient's complaint about a doctor sent for review
Why A: A claim is a request sent to an insurer asking for payment of services the provider gave to a patient, such as a visit or test.
Why B: A list of rules for members describes the policy terms or benefits handbook, not a request for payment sent by a provider.
Why C: A medicine order sent to a pharmacy is a prescription, which directs a drug to be dispensed and is not a billing request.
Why D: A complaint about a doctor is a grievance or a report to a review board, and has no role in requesting payment from an insurer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a CMS-1500 form used for?
A: Recording a patient's allergies in the chart at the start of a stay
B: Applying for a medical license from the state board of doctors
C: Admitting patients to a hospital, with a form the doctor signs at the bed
D: Billing insurers for services provided by physicians and suppliers
Why A: Recording allergies is a clinical task done in the chart, while the CMS-1500 is a claim form and holds no allergy history.
Why B: A medical license application goes to a state board and uses different forms, so it has nothing to do with the CMS-1500 billing form.
Why C: Admitting patients uses admission paperwork inside the hospital, whereas the CMS-1500 is sent to payers to request payment, not to admit anyone.
Why D: The CMS-1500 is the standard paper claim form used to bill insurers for services provided by physicians and other suppliers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is medical coding?
A: Writing computer software that runs the systems of a hospital or a clinic
B: Converting diagnoses and procedures into standard codes for billing and records
C: Designing hospital logos and signs for the walls and halls of the wards as a rule
D: Encrypting patient data so that only approved staff can read the files
Why A: Writing software is programming work, whereas medical coding turns clinical information into standard codes for billing and records, so this describes a different job.
Why B: Medical coding converts diagnoses and procedures into standard codes, which lets insurers process claims and lets organizations keep consistent records and statistics.
Why C: Designing logos and signs is graphic design and wayfinding; it has no connection to translating clinical documentation into standard billing codes.
Why D: Encrypting data is a security measure, whereas coding translates diagnoses and procedures into codes, so it does not describe medical coding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do ICD-10 codes represent?
A: Hospital room numbers
B: Procedures done by doctors
C: Diagnoses and conditions
D: Insurance plan names
Why A: Room numbers are facility labels; ICD-10 codes classify diseases and conditions, so they do not identify rooms in a hospital.
Why B: Procedures done by doctors are described by CPT codes in the United States, not by ICD-10, which classifies diagnoses.
Why C: ICD-10 codes represent diagnoses and conditions, giving each disease or health problem a standard code used for billing, research and records.
Why D: Insurance plan names are identified by plan and payer identifiers, not ICD-10, which is a classification of diseases and conditions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do CPT codes represent?
A: Procedures and services provided to patients
B: Employee ID numbers used by the payroll office
C: Prescription drug names and their doses
D: Diagnoses and conditions of the patients
Why A: CPT codes represent procedures and services provided to patients, such as office visits, tests and operations, so payers know what was done.
Why B: Employee ID numbers belong to payroll systems and have no link to the medical procedure codes that CPT defines.
Why C: Drug names and doses are identified by drug codes such as NDC and by prescriptions, whereas CPT codes describe services and procedures.
Why D: Diagnoses and conditions are coded with ICD-10, not CPT; CPT states what was done, while ICD-10 states why.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A claim lists a diagnosis code and a procedure code. What does the diagnosis code show?
A: Who performed the service
B: Why the service was needed
C: How much the service cost
D: Where the patient lives
Why A: The rendering provider is shown by a provider identifier on the claim, not by the diagnosis code, which gives the clinical reason.
Why B: A diagnosis code shows why the service was needed, which helps the insurer judge medical necessity for the procedure that was billed.
Why C: The cost of a service appears in the charge field on the claim, not in the diagnosis code, which describes a condition.
Why D: A patient's address is demographic data in a separate claim field; the diagnosis code says nothing about where the patient lives.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is medical necessity?
A: Services that a patient's family asks the doctor to provide for comfort
B: Services that are the most expensive on the price list of the hospital
C: Services that a hospital offers to attract more patients than its rivals
D: Services that are reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition
Why A: A request for comfort does not show clinical need. Medical necessity means services reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition.
Why B: Price has nothing to do with necessity; costly services are not automatically necessary, and necessity depends on clinical need and not on the fee.
Why C: Marketing appeal is not clinical need. Medical necessity means services reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition.
Why D: Medical necessity means services that are reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition, and payers usually cover only such services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is prior authorization?
A: A bill sent after surgery to the patient for the care that was given
B: A refund of premiums to the member at the end of a year of cover
C: Insurer approval required before certain services or drugs are provided
D: A patient's signature after treatment, which proves the care was received
Why A: A bill sent to a patient after surgery is a statement for payment, whereas prior authorization is approval obtained before the service is provided.
Why B: A refund of premiums at year end is a premium adjustment and does not involve approval before care, which defines prior authorization.
Why C: Prior authorization is insurer approval required before certain services or drugs are provided, and without it the insurer may refuse to pay.
Why D: A signature after treatment can show the care was received but cannot be prior authorization, which must come from the insurer before care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A procedure needs prior authorization but the office did not get it. What is the likely result?
A: The insurer pays double rates
B: The insurer may deny the claim
C: The claim is paid with no review
D: The patient gets a full refund
Why A: An insurer does not pay double for missing approval; skipping a required step makes payment less likely, not more generous.
Why B: Without the required prior authorization, the insurer may deny the claim, leaving the provider or the patient responsible for the cost of the procedure.
Why C: Claims that need prior authorization are checked for it, so being paid with no review is unlikely when the approval is missing.
Why D: A patient does not get a full refund because of missing approval; the problem raises the chance of denial and unpaid bills.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a referral?
A: A discount on services given to patients who pay in cash
B: A bill sent to a patient after a visit to a doctor's office overall
C: A medicine prescribed by the doctor after an examination
D: A recommendation from a primary provider to see a specialist
Why A: A discount for paying cash is a pricing arrangement and does not involve one provider directing a patient to another provider.
Why B: A bill sent after a visit is a statement of charges, whereas a referral directs a patient to another provider for care.
Why C: A prescribed medicine is a treatment order for a pharmacy, not a recommendation to see another provider, which is what a referral is.
Why D: A referral is a recommendation from a primary care provider that a patient see a specialist, and some plans require it for coverage.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an explanation of benefits (EOB)?
A: A statement from an insurer showing how a claim was processed
B: A list of hospital departments and the names of their managers
C: A bill demanding payment from a patient for care already given
D: A patient's medical history kept in a chart by the doctor
Why A: An EOB is a statement from an insurer showing how a claim was processed, including amounts billed, allowed, paid and owed by the patient.
Why B: A list of departments and managers is an organization chart or directory and says nothing about how an insurer handled a claim.
Why C: An EOB is not a bill; it explains the claim, and the provider sends the actual bill, so a demand for payment is a different document.
Why D: A medical history in a chart is a clinical record kept by the doctor, whereas an EOB is a payer document about claim payment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An EOB shows billed $500, allowed $320 and plan paid $256. What does the patient likely owe?
Why A: The figure 244 is the billed 500 minus the plan's 256, but 500 less 320 is a write-off the patient does not owe.
Why B: The full 500 is the billed charge; the patient owes only the part of the allowed 320 that the plan did not pay.
Why C: The patient owes the allowed amount less the plan payment: 320 minus 256 equals 64, which covers the deductible, copay or coinsurance share.
Why D: No step with the given figures produces 176; the patient owes allowed 320 minus plan paid 256, which equals 64 and not 176.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the allowed amount?
A: The total a provider chooses to bill, whatever the insurer pays
B: The maximum an insurer will recognize for a covered service
C: The insurer's monthly profit after all claims are paid
D: The patient's deductible for the year under the plan
Why A: The total a provider bills is the billed charge, which can be higher than what the insurer recognizes as the allowed amount.
Why B: The allowed amount is the maximum an insurer will recognize for a covered service, and the plan and patient payments are based on it.
Why C: Insurer profit is a financial result for the company and is unrelated to the contracted rate recognized for a single service.
Why D: A deductible is the amount a patient pays before coverage begins, which differs from the maximum fee an insurer recognizes for a service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is balance billing?
A: Billing an insurer twice for the same service that was given to the patient in one visit as a rule
B: Balancing a checkbook at the end of the month in the billing office of a hospital
C: Refunding a patient's premium when a plan is ended early by the insurer or the employer
D: Billing a patient for the difference between the provider's charge and the insurer's payment
Why A: Billing an insurer twice for one service is duplicate billing, which is an error or fraud, and it differs from billing a patient for a balance.
Why B: Balancing a checkbook is personal bookkeeping and has no link to a provider billing a patient for amounts the insurer did not pay.
Why C: A premium refund when a plan ends early is an insurance adjustment and has no relation to billing a patient for a charge difference.
Why D: Balance billing is billing a patient for the difference between the provider's charge and the insurer's payment, and it is limited for in-network providers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a denied claim?
A: A claim the insurer refuses to pay
B: A claim already paid in full to us
C: A claim awaiting all data entry
D: A claim cancelled by the insurer
Why A: A denied claim is one the insurer refuses to pay, often because of errors, missing information or a service that is not covered.
Why B: A claim already paid in full has been accepted and settled, so it is the opposite of a claim the insurer refused to pay.
Why C: A claim awaiting data entry has not yet been submitted or decided, so it has not been denied by the insurer.
Why D: A claim cancelled by the insurer is withdrawn or voided, which differs from a denial, where the insurer reviews the claim and refuses to pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a common reason for claim denial?
A: Correct codes and full documentation
B: A complete and accurate claim sheet
C: Missing or incorrect patient information
D: Timely filing within the deadline in the end
Why A: Correct codes and full documentation support payment, so they help claims get paid and are not a typical reason for denial.
Why B: A complete and accurate claim sheet meets payer requirements, so it makes approval more likely and is not a common cause of denial.
Why C: Missing or incorrect patient information, such as a wrong name, birth date or policy number, is a common reason for denial because the insurer cannot match the claim.
Why D: Filing within the deadline is correct practice that supports payment; it is filing late, after the deadline, that causes denials.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an appeal in billing?
A: A request to cancel a patient's insurance as premiums were unpaid
B: A request to raise premiums for all of the members of a plan
C: A formal request asking an insurer to reconsider a denied claim
D: A request to see a doctor on the same day as a booked visit
Why A: Canceling insurance for unpaid premiums is a termination by the insurer, not a request to reconsider a denied claim, which an appeal is.
Why B: Asking to raise premiums is a pricing matter for insurers and has no connection to contesting how a single claim was decided.
Why C: An appeal is a formal request asking an insurer to reconsider a denied claim, usually with supporting records, to get the decision reversed and payment made.
Why D: Asking for a same-day visit is a scheduling request with a clinic and has nothing to do with disputing an insurer's decision on a claim.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a clean claim?
A: A claim that has been laundered or cleaned by the billing office staff before it is sent
B: A claim with complete and correct information that can be processed without correction
C: A claim printed on white paper and sent by mail to the insurer after a hospital visit
D: A claim with no patient name and no codes on it at all, so it is sent back by mail
Why A: Cleaning or laundering a claim suggests altering it improperly; a clean claim is simply accurate and complete, with no tampering or special treatment by staff.
Why B: A clean claim has complete and correct information and can be processed without correction, so it is usually paid faster and with fewer denials.
Why C: The paper color and the mail method do not matter; a clean claim is defined by accurate and complete content, not by how it is sent.
Why D: A claim without a patient name or codes is incomplete and would be rejected, so it is the opposite of a clean claim.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the typical timeline concept of timely filing?
A: A deadline for hospitals to pay rent to the owner
B: A deadline for patients to schedule visits each year
C: A deadline for insurance cards to expire for members
D: A deadline for submitting a claim to an insurer
Why A: Rent payments between hospitals and owners are lease terms and have no relation to the deadline for sending a claim to an insurer.
Why B: Scheduling visits is an access matter for patients and does not set the time limit for providers to file claims with insurers.
Why C: Insurance card expiry relates to coverage dates, not to the deadline a provider has to submit claims, which is timely filing.
Why D: Timely filing is the deadline for submitting a claim to an insurer, and claims sent after it can be denied with no appeal on that basis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Medicare?
A: A federal health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older and some with disabilities
B: A federal health insurance program for low-income families, with costs shared by the states
C: A health insurance program for military service members and their families through the Defense Department
D: A program that pays for children's health care in families that earn too much for Medicaid
Why A: Medicare is a federal health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities, funded by federal sources.
Why B: That describes Medicaid. Medicare is a federal program mainly for people 65 and older and some with disabilities.
Why C: That is TRICARE. Medicare is a federal program mainly for people 65 and older and some with disabilities.
Why D: That describes CHIP. Medicare is a federal program mainly for people 65 and older and some with disabilities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Medicare Part A mostly cover?
A: Hospital inpatient care and some skilled nursing
B: Doctor visits and outpatient care, paid under Part B
C: Prescription drugs and the cost of medicine
D: Dental care only and routine eye exams for all
Why A: Medicare Part A mostly covers hospital inpatient care and some skilled nursing, hospice and home health, which is why it is called hospital insurance.
Why B: Doctor visits and outpatient care are covered by Part B, not Part A, so this describes the wrong part of Medicare.
Why C: Prescription drugs are covered by Part D, so this describes a different part of Medicare and not Part A.
Why D: Original Medicare does not cover routine dental care or eye exams, and Part A is about hospital stays, not dental or vision.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Medicare Part B mostly cover?
A: Vacation travel for those who need to rest and relax
B: Hospital inpatient stays and surgery done during them
C: Prescription drugs taken at home for any illness
D: Doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive services
Why A: Vacation travel for rest is not medical care and is not covered, since Part B pays for medically needed services and prevention.
Why B: Inpatient hospital stays and the surgery done during them are covered mostly by Part A, not Part B.
Why C: Prescription drugs taken at home are covered mainly by Part D, so Part B does not mostly cover them.
Why D: Part B mostly covers doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive services, and is often called medical insurance for care outside inpatient stays.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Medicaid?
A: A federal program that covers health costs mainly for adults 65 and older
B: A program run by the Defense Department that covers military families and retirees
C: A joint federal and state program that helps cover health costs for people with low income
D: A private insurance company that sells plans to people and firms for a monthly fee
Why A: That describes Medicare. Medicaid is a joint federal and state program that helps cover health costs for people with low income.
Why B: That is TRICARE. Medicaid is a joint federal and state program for people with low income.
Why C: Medicaid is a joint federal and state program that helps cover health costs for people with low income and certain other groups.
Why D: A private insurance company sells plans for a fee, whereas Medicaid is a government program funded by federal and state money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
A: Medicare is run by the states; Medicaid is run by the federal government
B: Medicare is mostly based on age or disability; Medicaid is based on income
C: They are the same program, run in the same way by each state and region
D: Medicare is for employees of large firms; Medicaid is for the self-employed
Why A: This reverses them. Medicare is federal and based on age or disability, while Medicaid is run by states with federal funding and based on income.
Why B: Medicare is mostly based on age or disability while Medicaid is based on income, which is the main difference between the two programs.
Why C: The programs are not the same: Medicare is federal and mainly for older adults, while Medicaid is run by states with federal funding.
Why D: Neither program depends on employer size. Medicare is mostly based on age or disability, and Medicaid is based on income.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is TRICARE?
A: A private dental plan sold by insurers to people and their families
B: A federal program for adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities
C: A joint federal and state program for people with low income
D: A health program for military service members, retirees and their families
Why A: A private dental plan is sold by insurers, whereas TRICARE is a government health program for the military community.
Why B: That is Medicare. TRICARE is a health program for military service members, retirees and their families.
Why C: That is Medicaid. TRICARE is a health program for military service members, retirees and their families.
Why D: TRICARE is a health program for military service members, retirees and their families, run through the Department of Defense.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is coordination of benefits?
A: Refunding all premiums to members when a claim is paid in full twice
B: Combining two patients' bills into one single total for the hospital
C: Determining which insurer pays first when a patient has more than one plan
D: Sending bills to the government only, whatever the patient's insurance may cover
Why A: Refunding premiums after a double payment is a billing correction and has no link to deciding which of several plans pays first.
Why B: Combining patients' bills into one total is a billing practice, not the process that decides the order of payment among insurers.
Why C: Coordination of benefits determines which insurer pays first when a patient has more than one plan, so payments do not exceed the cost of care.
Why D: Sending bills only to the government ignores private plans, whereas coordination of benefits sets payer order among all the plans a patient has.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A child is covered by both parents' plans. Which plan is usually primary?
A: The plan of the parent with the higher pay, whatever the birthdays
B: The plan of the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year
C: The plan chosen by the child when they come of age or later
D: The plan of the older parent in years of age or pay earned
Why A: Pay level does not decide which plan is primary; the birthday rule looks at which parent's birthday falls earlier in the calendar year.
Why B: Under the birthday rule, the plan of the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year is primary for a child covered by both plans.
Why C: The child does not choose; the order of payment is set by rules such as the birthday rule, not by the child's own preference.
Why D: The rule uses birthday within the year and not age or income, so the older or higher-paid parent's plan is not automatically primary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a self-pay (cash) patient?
A: A patient who pays for services directly without using insurance
B: A patient insured by Medicare or another public health plan
C: A patient who never pays a bill for the care given to them at all
D: A patient whose employer pays the whole bill directly to the hospital
Why A: A self-pay patient pays for services directly, without using insurance, and often receives a self-pay or cash rate from the provider.
Why B: A patient insured by Medicare is covered by a public plan and so does not pay directly without insurance, which self-pay means.
Why C: A patient who never pays is a bad debt or charity case, whereas a self-pay patient pays the provider directly for the care.
Why D: When an employer pays the bill directly, the patient is not paying out of pocket, which is what makes someone a self-pay patient.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a flexible spending account (FSA)?
A: An account funded with pre-tax pay to cover eligible health costs
B: A credit card for hospitals to pay their suppliers and their staff
C: An account for retirement savings funded with after-tax pay by a worker
D: A loan for medical bills from a bank, repaid with interest later
Why A: An FSA is an account funded with pre-tax pay that covers eligible health costs, lowering taxable income, and funds often must be used within the plan year.
Why B: A credit card for hospitals to pay suppliers is a business tool, whereas an FSA is an employee account for personal health costs.
Why C: Retirement savings accounts are for later life, and an FSA is funded with pre-tax pay for current health costs, not after-tax pay.
Why D: A loan must be repaid with interest, whereas an FSA is the employee's own pre-tax money set aside for eligible health expenses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a health savings account (HSA)?
A: A free insurance plan that the state gives to all adults who ask for it each year in the end
B: A tax-advantaged account for medical costs used with a high-deductible health plan
C: A loan from a hospital to pay for the cost of care over several years or more
D: A fund for building hospitals and clinics in rural areas of the state each year
Why A: An HSA is not a free state insurance plan; it is a personal savings account that the owner funds for medical costs.
Why B: An HSA is a tax-advantaged account for medical costs, used together with a high-deductible health plan, and the money stays with the owner.
Why C: A loan from a hospital must be repaid, whereas an HSA holds the owner's own money set aside for medical expenses.
Why D: A fund for building rural hospitals is public or charitable funding, whereas an HSA is an individual account for the owner's medical costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a key advantage of an HSA?
A: Unused money is forfeited when the plan year ends
B: It is an employer account that pays company business expenses
C: It lets you spend on non-medical items without a tax penalty
D: Contributions, growth and qualified withdrawals can be tax-advantaged
Why A: HSA funds belong to the owner and roll over from year to year, so there is no use-it-or-lose-it rule; that rule belongs to a flexible spending account.
Why B: An HSA is owned by the individual and pays that person's qualified medical costs. Employers may contribute, but the account does not cover company bills.
Why C: Withdrawals for non-medical items are taxed and usually penalized. Tax-free treatment applies only when the money goes to qualified medical expenses.
Why D: Contributions, growth and qualified withdrawals can all be tax-advantaged, which is a key HSA advantage, along with funds rolling over each year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does HIPAA stand for?
A: Health Information and Public Access Rules Act
B: Hospital Infection Prevention and Alert Act, 1996
C: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
D: Hospital Insurance Payment and Administration Act
Why A: That name is invented; HIPAA does not refer to public access rules, and its title centers on insurance portability and accountability.
Why B: HIPAA is not about hospital infection prevention; the 1996 law covers health insurance portability and accountability, including privacy and security of health data.
Why C: HIPAA stands for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a 1996 federal law that protects health information and allows coverage to carry over.
Why D: That name is wrong because HIPAA is not about hospital insurance payment; it concerns portability of coverage and accountability, including privacy and security.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is protected health information (PHI)?
A: General health tips on a website for the public to read at home
B: Individually identifiable health information held by covered entities
C: Public information about hospital prices and services posted on the site
D: Information about weather and climate for a region over many years
Why A: General health tips for the public are not tied to any individual, so they are not protected health information.
Why B: PHI is individually identifiable health information held by covered entities, such as names tied to diagnoses, treatment or payment, and HIPAA protects it.
Why C: Public price and service information does not identify any patient, so it is not protected health information.
Why D: Weather and climate data have no link to an individual's health, so they are not PHI.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Who must follow HIPAA rules?
A: Drug makers and medical device manufacturers
B: Auto and life insurance companies and their agents
C: Patients who ask for copies of their own records
D: Providers, health plans and their business associates
Why A: Manufacturers are not covered entities under HIPAA. The rules bind providers, health plans, clearinghouses and their business associates that handle protected health information.
Why B: Auto and life insurers are not health plans, so HIPAA does not apply to them. The rules cover healthcare providers, health plans and their business associates.
Why C: Patients are the people HIPAA protects, and they hold rights to their records. The duty to follow the rules falls on organizations that handle health information.
Why D: HIPAA applies to healthcare providers, health plans, clearinghouses and their business associates, since they create, receive or hold protected health information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A nurse looks up a famous patient's record out of curiosity. What is this?
A: Normal practice
B: A privacy improvement
C: A HIPAA violation
D: A required step
Why A: Looking up a record without a job need is not normal practice, because access is allowed only for treatment, payment or operations.
Why B: Snooping does nothing to improve privacy; it harms privacy, since the nurse had no care reason to see the record.
Why C: Looking up a patient's record out of curiosity, with no work reason, is a HIPAA violation because access must be limited to those with a need.
Why D: Nothing in care requires a nurse to open a famous patient's record out of curiosity, so it is not a required step.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the HIPAA Privacy Rule mainly about?
A: Who may use and share patients' health information
B: How many beds a hospital has and rooms in each ward
C: How much hospitals charge for care and drugs each year
D: How long nurses work on each shift in a hospital ward
Why A: The Privacy Rule mainly sets who may use and share patients' health information, and it gives patients rights over their own records.
Why B: Bed counts and ward rooms are facility planning matters, not what the Privacy Rule regulates, which concerns protecting health information.
Why C: Hospital charges are pricing issues outside the Privacy Rule, which governs how health information is used and disclosed.
Why D: Nurse shift length is a labor and staffing matter and is not regulated by the Privacy Rule, which governs use and disclosure of health information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the HIPAA Security Rule mainly about?
A: Staff uniform rules and dress codes for work in a hospital
B: Safeguards for electronic protected health information
C: Insurance cost limits and caps on the fees that are charged
D: Security guards in parking lots, who watch the cars of staff
Why A: Uniform and dress rules are workplace policy, whereas the Security Rule sets safeguards for electronic protected health information.
Why B: The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information, so electronic records stay confidential, intact and available.
Why C: Limits on insurance fees are cost regulation and not part of the Security Rule, which protects electronic health data.
Why D: Parking lot guards are a physical measure for vehicles, whereas the Security Rule protects electronic health information with safeguards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a permitted use of PHI without special authorization?
A: Selling patient lists to advertisers who pay for the names listed
B: Posting a patient's diagnosis on social media for friends to see
C: Sharing information for treatment, payment and healthcare operations
D: Telling a neighbor about a patient's condition, as they are friends overall
Why A: Selling patient lists to advertisers is a disclosure for marketing that requires authorization, so it is not allowed without special permission.
Why B: Posting a diagnosis on social media is an unauthorized disclosure that breaks HIPAA, because it serves no treatment, payment or operations purpose.
Why C: HIPAA permits use and sharing of PHI for treatment, payment and healthcare operations without special authorization, because these functions are needed to run care.
Why D: Telling a neighbor about a condition is an unauthorized disclosure, since friendship does not create a need to know or any permitted purpose.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is informed consent?
A: A patient's agreement to treatment after understanding the risks and benefits
B: A patient's signature on a blank form before any explanation is given
C: A relative agreeing to treatment for a capable adult patient
D: A doctor's recommendation of the best treatment for the patient
Why A: Informed consent is a patient's agreement to treatment after understanding the risks and benefits, so the choice is based on real knowledge.
Why B: A signature on a blank form without explanation shows no understanding of the treatment, so consent is not informed.
Why C: A capable adult must give consent personally after understanding the risks and benefits. A relative's agreement cannot replace the patient's own informed decision.
Why D: A recommendation is just advice. Informed consent needs the patient to understand the risks and benefits and then agree, so the doctor's opinion alone does not count.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient signs a consent form without anyone explaining the procedure. What is the problem?
A: The insurer must pay double for care
B: There is no problem with the consent
C: The consent is stronger than before
D: The consent may not be truly informed
Why A: The insurer's payment has no link to whether the patient understood the procedure, so double payment is not a consequence.
Why B: There is a problem because signing without explanation shows no understanding, so the consent may not be valid.
Why C: A signature without explanation makes consent weaker, not stronger, since the patient could not weigh the risks and benefits.
Why D: Without anyone explaining the procedure, the patient could not weigh its risks and benefits, so the consent may not be truly informed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an advance directive?
A: A bill sent in advance to a patient for the care that they may need later on in a year
B: A staff schedule that lists who works on which ward and on what days of the week
C: A legal document stating a person's wishes for care if they cannot speak for themselves
D: A hospital marketing plan to attract more patients to the wards and the clinics it runs
Why A: An advance bill for future care is a billing item and does not state a person's wishes for care, which an advance directive does.
Why B: A staff schedule lists work shifts for employees and has no relation to a patient's wishes about future medical care.
Why C: An advance directive is a legal document stating a person's wishes for care if they cannot speak for themselves, such as a living will.
Why D: A marketing plan aims to attract patients and has no role in recording a person's wishes about their own medical treatment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order?
A: An order to stop medicines and comfort care for a patient
B: An order to place a patient in intensive care after surgery
C: An order to discharge the patient from the hospital at once today
D: A medical order not to attempt CPR if a patient's heart or breathing stops
Why A: A DNR covers CPR only. The patient still receives medicines, comfort care and other treatment, so it does not end ordinary care.
Why B: A DNR is about whether to attempt CPR if the heart or breathing stops. It has nothing to do with where a patient is placed after surgery.
Why C: A DNR concerns resuscitation only and has no connection to discharge, so it does not order the patient to leave the hospital.
Why D: A DNR is a medical order not to attempt CPR if a patient's heart or breathing stops, based on the patient's wishes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Affordable Care Act (ACA)?
A: A law that bans private insurance and makes care a government service
B: A federal law that expanded access to health insurance and set standards
C: A law that makes Medicare available to people of all ages
D: A law that protects the privacy of patient health records
Why A: The ACA does not ban private insurance; it regulates it and adds subsidies and marketplaces, so private plans remain central.
Why B: The ACA is a federal law that expanded access to health insurance and set coverage standards, including rules on pre-existing conditions.
Why C: The ACA expanded coverage through marketplaces, subsidies and Medicaid expansion. It did not open Medicare to everyone, and Medicare still depends on age or disability.
Why D: Privacy of health records is the purpose of HIPAA. The ACA deals with insurance access and coverage standards, not record privacy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a protection under the ACA?
A: Insurers cannot deny coverage because of pre-existing conditions
B: Premiums must be zero for all members of a plan every year
C: Insurers can refuse anyone with a past illness, as the law allows
D: All care is free for everyone who has a plan in the state
Why A: Under the ACA, insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more because of pre-existing conditions, which protects people with past illness.
Why B: The ACA does not require zero premiums; members still pay premiums, though subsidies lower the cost for many people.
Why C: The ACA forbids refusing coverage for past illness, so saying insurers can refuse anyone with a past illness reverses the protection.
Why D: The ACA does not make all care free; members still pay deductibles, copays or coinsurance, though preventive services are covered without cost sharing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA)?
A: A law that protects the privacy of patient records held by hospitals and clinics
B: A law requiring emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients regardless of ability to pay
C: A law that gives workers unpaid leave to care for a newborn or a sick family member
D: A law that requires payment before care, so patients must show cash at the door of the hospital first
Why A: Record privacy is covered by HIPAA. EMTALA deals with emergency care, requiring hospitals to screen and stabilize patients regardless of their ability to pay.
Why B: EMTALA requires hospitals with emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients regardless of ability to pay, so no one is turned away because of cost.
Why C: Job-protected family leave comes from the FMLA. EMTALA instead requires emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients who arrive, whatever they can pay.
Why D: EMTALA forbids demanding payment before screening and stabilizing, so requiring cash at the door is the reverse of what the law says.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the FDA's role in healthcare?
A: Paying hospital bills for the patients who lack insurance
B: Running hospitals and clinics across the whole of the country
C: Regulating the safety of drugs, medical devices and food
D: Licensing nurses and doctors in every state and region now
Why A: The FDA does not pay hospital bills; Medicaid, Medicare and insurers pay, while the FDA regulates drugs, devices and food safety.
Why B: The FDA does not run hospitals or clinics; it is a regulator of products, not an operator of care facilities.
Why C: The FDA regulates the safety of drugs, medical devices and food, approving products and monitoring problems after they reach the market.
Why D: State boards license nurses and doctors, not the FDA, whose role is to regulate drugs, devices and food.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the role of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)?
A: Building hospitals and clinics in rural parts of the country
B: Selling private insurance policies to people and firms
C: Licensing all doctors in the country and checking records
D: Administering Medicare and overseeing Medicaid programs
Why A: CMS does not build hospitals; it runs payment and oversight programs, so building rural hospitals is not its main role.
Why B: CMS does not sell private insurance; private companies do that, while CMS is a federal agency that runs public programs.
Why C: State medical boards license doctors, not CMS, which instead sets rules and pays for services in Medicare and Medicaid.
Why D: CMS administers Medicare and oversees Medicaid programs, along with the Children's Health Insurance Program and quality and payment rules for providers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Joint Commission?
A: An independent organization that accredits healthcare organizations on quality and safety
B: A government agency that sets prices for hospital services across the nation each year
C: A company that makes medical devices such as scanners, beds and monitors for hospitals
D: A union of nurses that bargains with hospitals over pay, hours and the safety of its members
Why A: The Joint Commission is an independent organization that accredits healthcare organizations on quality and safety, using on-site surveys against set standards.
Why B: The Joint Commission is a private nonprofit and not a government agency, and it does not set prices for hospital services.
Why C: The Joint Commission does not make scanners, beds or monitors; it surveys and accredits organizations that use such equipment.
Why D: The Joint Commission is not a union of nurses and does not bargain over pay; its role is accreditation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a scope of practice?
A: The hours a clinic is open to see patients on each day of the working week
B: The procedures and actions a licensed professional is legally allowed to perform
C: The size of a hospital's campus and the number of its buildings and car parks in this case
D: The cost of a service as set out on the price list of the hospital or clinic
Why A: Clinic opening hours are an operational schedule and do not define what actions a licensed professional may legally perform.
Why B: Scope of practice is the set of procedures and actions a licensed professional is legally allowed to perform, set by state law and training.
Why C: Campus size and building count describe facilities and have nothing to do with the legal limits on what a professional may do.
Why D: Service cost is a pricing matter on a charge list, whereas scope of practice defines which actions a licensed professional may legally perform.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A medical assistant begins prescribing drugs. What is the problem?
A: It goes beyond the legal scope of practice
B: Normal practice for a medical assistant
C: A required step in the care of a patient
D: A privacy improvement, as fewer staff handle it
Why A: Prescribing is outside a medical assistant's scope of practice, since only licensed prescribers may do it, so the act is unlawful and unsafe.
Why B: Prescribing is not normal for a medical assistant, whose legal scope excludes it, so calling it normal practice is incorrect.
Why C: Care steps do not require an assistant to prescribe; prescribing belongs to licensed prescribers, so it is not a required step.
Why D: Prescribing by an assistant does nothing for privacy; the real problem is exceeding legal scope, which risks patient harm and liability.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is malpractice?
A: A routine medical check-up for a healthy adult now
B: A billing error without harm to the patient at the clinic
C: Professional negligence that causes harm to a patient
D: A patient's late payment of a bill to the clinic office
Why A: A routine check-up for a healthy adult is normal preventive care and involves no negligence or harm, so it is not malpractice.
Why B: A billing error without harm is an administrative mistake, and malpractice requires negligent professional conduct that causes harm to a patient.
Why C: Malpractice is professional negligence that causes harm to a patient, when care falls below the accepted standard and injury results.
Why D: A late payment is a financial matter on the patient's side and involves no negligence by a professional, so it is not malpractice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the False Claims Act concerned with?
A: Hospital parking fines charged to visitors and staff
B: Patients forgetting visits and costing the clinic
C: Staff uniform rules and dress codes for the hospital
D: Fraudulent billing of government health programs
Why A: Parking fines are local fees with no link to the False Claims Act, which deals with fraud against government programs.
Why B: Missed visits are an operational cost issue for a clinic, not fraud against the government, which is what the False Claims Act addresses.
Why C: Uniform rules are workplace policy and have no relation to the False Claims Act, which targets false billing of government funds.
Why D: The False Claims Act concerns fraudulent billing of government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid, and it lets whistleblowers sue on the government's behalf.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A clinic bills Medicare for services never provided. What is this?
A: A patient courtesy
B: A permitted practice
C: Healthcare fraud
D: A coding shortcut
Why A: Billing for services never given is not a courtesy to a patient; it is a false claim, which causes loss to the program.
Why B: Billing for services never provided is not permitted by any rule; it is a deliberate false statement to get payment.
Why C: Billing Medicare for services never provided is healthcare fraud, a false claim for payment that can bring fines, repayment and criminal charges.
Why D: A coding shortcut is a mistake in assigning codes, but billing for services never provided is knowing fraud, not a shortcut.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Stark Law about?
A: Setting visiting hours for the wards and the rules for visitors to follow
B: Requiring doctors to wear uniforms and name badges while they treat patients
C: Capping the cost of drugs that are sold by pharmacies to the public in a year overall
D: Limiting physician referrals to entities they have a financial relationship with
Why A: Visiting hours are hospital policy and are not governed by the Stark Law, which regulates physician financial relationships and referrals.
Why B: Uniform and badge requirements are workplace rules and have no connection to the Stark Law on referrals.
Why C: Drug price caps would be pricing regulation, whereas the Stark Law deals with physician referrals and financial ties.
Why D: The Stark Law limits physician referrals to entities with which they have a financial relationship, to stop referrals driven by profit instead of patient need.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Anti-Kickback Statute about?
A: Banning payments meant to induce referrals for federal healthcare program business
B: Banning all gifts of flowers, cards and small items to the staff of a hospital in practice
C: Capping insurance premiums that members pay each month to the insurer, by law
D: Setting minimum wages for the staff who work in the hospitals of each state
Why A: The Anti-Kickback Statute bans payments meant to induce referrals for federal healthcare program business, which protects patients and programs from decisions driven by money.
Why B: It does not ban all small gifts; it targets payments intended to induce referrals for federal program business, not tokens of thanks like cards.
Why C: Insurance premium caps are a separate type of regulation and do not form part of the Anti-Kickback Statute.
Why D: Minimum wage rules are labor law, and the Anti-Kickback Statute covers payments that induce referrals, not pay for hospital staff.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mandatory reporter?
A: A journalist who writes about hospitals for a newspaper or site
B: A person legally required to report suspected abuse or neglect
C: A person who reports weather on a news show every single day
D: A person who reports profits to the owners of a firm each year
Why A: A journalist reports news to the public and has no legal duty regarding abuse, so that is not a mandatory reporter.
Why B: A mandatory reporter is a person legally required to report suspected abuse or neglect, and clinicians like nurses are commonly in this group.
Why C: A weather reporter shares forecasts on a news show, so the word reporter here has nothing to do with legal duties.
Why D: Reporting profits to owners is business accounting and has no connection to the legal duty to report suspected abuse or neglect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A nurse suspects a child is being abused. What is the nurse's duty?
A: Wait a year before acting on the suspicion of abuse or harm
B: Ignore it unless the parent confirms it is true or says so first overall
C: Report the suspicion to the proper authorities as required by law
D: Discuss it with the child's neighbors first, to check the story
Why A: Waiting a year leaves a child at risk, and the law requires prompt reporting of suspected abuse, not delay.
Why B: Reporting duty does not depend on a parent's confirmation; the law requires reports on reasonable suspicion, and waiting for parents could endanger the child.
Why C: The nurse must report the suspicion to the proper authorities as required by law, because mandatory reporting laws apply to suspected abuse.
Why D: Discussing it with neighbors breaches confidentiality and can tip off the abuser; the duty is to inform the authorities, not to investigate informally.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is clear communication important in healthcare?
A: It helps staff avoid teamwork on the ward
B: It removes the need for records and charts
C: It makes appointments last longer for all
D: Mistakes in information can harm patients
Why A: Clear communication supports teamwork on the ward, so saying it helps staff avoid teamwork is the reverse of the truth.
Why B: Records and charts remain necessary for continuity and legal reasons, and clear communication does not remove the need for them.
Why C: Clear communication tends to make visits more efficient and understood, and it does not exist to lengthen appointments.
Why D: Clear communication matters because mistakes in information, such as wrong doses or missed allergies, can harm patients, so accuracy protects safety.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is active listening?
A: Looking at your phone during a talk, to reply to messages
B: Fully focusing on a speaker and responding thoughtfully
C: Interrupting to give advice before the speaker is done
D: Waiting for your turn to speak and not hearing the speaker
Why A: Looking at a phone during a talk shows inattention, so it is the opposite of active listening, which needs full focus.
Why B: Active listening means fully focusing on the speaker and responding thoughtfully, with attention, questions and feedback that show the message was understood.
Why C: Interrupting to give advice cuts the speaker off before the message is complete, which breaks active listening, where you hear it all first.
Why D: Waiting for a turn to speak without hearing the other person is passive and self-focused, so it lacks the attention active listening needs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is empathy in patient care?
A: Understanding and acknowledging a patient's feelings
B: Keeping conversations as short as possible with patients
C: Agreeing with every demand that a patient makes to staff
D: Ignoring a patient's concerns and moving on to the next
Why A: Empathy is understanding and acknowledging a patient's feelings, which builds trust and helps patients feel heard and supported during care.
Why B: Keeping talk short does not show understanding of feelings; empathy involves taking time to listen and respond to a patient's emotions.
Why C: Empathy does not mean agreeing to every demand; it acknowledges feelings while staff still apply clinical judgment and policy.
Why D: Ignoring concerns shows no understanding of a patient's feelings, which is the opposite of empathy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient is upset about a long wait. Which response shows good communication?
A: Ignore the patient until the name is called out aloud
B: Argue that the wait is not too long for the patient
C: Apologize, explain the delay and give an estimated time
D: Tell the patient to be patient and then walk away fast overall
Why A: Ignoring an upset patient adds to the frustration and shows disregard, so it is poor communication that makes the situation worse.
Why B: Arguing that the wait is not long dismisses the patient's feelings and is likely to escalate, so it is not good communication.
Why C: Apologizing, explaining the delay and giving an estimated time acknowledges the patient's feelings and offers information, which is good communication.
Why D: Telling the patient to be patient and walking away dismisses their concern and gives no information, so it fails as communication.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is health literacy?
A: A person's ability to understand and use health information to make decisions
B: A person's score on a spelling test taken in school each year of study
C: A person's ability to read medical journals only and follow clinic rules in most cases
D: A person's ability to memorize drug names and doses by heart quickly
Why A: Health literacy is a person's ability to understand and use health information to make decisions about their care, and low levels can lead to poor outcomes.
Why B: A spelling test measures a school skill and says nothing about understanding health information, which defines health literacy.
Why C: Health literacy is not limited to reading journals; it covers understanding and using health information in daily decisions, not clinic rules alone.
Why D: Memorizing drug names is a narrow skill; health literacy is the broader ability to understand and use health information to decide.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which approach best helps a patient with low health literacy understand instructions?
A: Use medical jargon quickly and skip any questions asked
B: Use plain language and ask the patient to repeat the plan back
C: Hand over a long document without explaining it, to read later
D: Skip the instructions and let the patient work it out alone
Why A: Jargon and skipped questions make instructions harder to follow, which especially hurts patients with low health literacy.
Why B: Plain language with a request to repeat the plan back makes instructions clear and confirms understanding, which helps patients with low health literacy.
Why C: A long document handed over without explanation is hard to use for patients with low health literacy, who need clear guidance.
Why D: Skipping instructions leaves the patient without needed guidance, which can cause harm, and it ignores the duty to help patients understand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the teach-back method?
A: Teaching staff to return equipment to the store room after each shift ends
B: Asking patients to teach the doctor medicine, so that the staff can learn from their stories
C: Teaching with a textbook only, with no practice or tests at all in class
D: Asking patients to explain information in their own words to confirm understanding
Why A: Returning equipment to the store room is a housekeeping task and has no relation to confirming a patient's understanding, which teach-back does.
Why B: Teach-back does not mean the patient teaches medicine to the doctor; the clinician checks how well they explained by hearing the patient's own words.
Why C: A textbook lesson without practice describes a classroom style and is not the teach-back method of confirming patient understanding.
Why D: Teach-back asks patients to explain information in their own words to confirm they understood, so the clinician can correct any gaps in understanding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are interpreters used in healthcare settings?
A: To avoid keeping records of the care that is given to patients
B: To shorten every visit by cutting talk with patients and staff alike
C: To help patients with limited English understand and be understood
D: To replace licensed clinicians so hospitals can hire fewer doctors
Why A: Interpreters do not replace record keeping; care is still documented, and their role is to support communication between patients and staff.
Why B: Interpreters do not exist to cut talk; they make real conversation possible, and cutting talk would harm understanding.
Why C: Interpreters help patients with limited English understand and be understood, so they can follow care instructions and give an accurate history.
Why D: Interpreters do not replace licensed clinicians; they carry language between clinicians and patients, and hospitals still need doctors to treat.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is generally better than using a patient's family member as an interpreter?
A: Using a stranger from the waiting room
B: Using a trained medical interpreter
C: Guessing what the patient means
D: Skipping interpretation entirely
Why A: A stranger from the waiting room is untrained and unvetted, and that raises risks of errors and privacy breaches, so it is no better.
Why B: A trained medical interpreter knows medical terms, stays accurate and keeps confidentiality, so this is better than relying on a family member.
Why C: Guessing what the patient means risks errors and misunderstanding, so it is worse than a family member and far worse than a trained interpreter.
Why D: Skipping interpretation leaves the patient unable to understand or be understood, so it is unsafe and does not improve on a family member.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is confidentiality?
A: Keeping patient information private and shared only with permission or need
B: Posting information on a staff bulletin board so that every worker can read it
C: Sharing information with anyone who asks, even if it is not needed
D: Discussing patients in public places such as lifts and halls at work
Why A: Confidentiality means keeping patient information private and sharing it only with permission or need, which protects trust and meets legal duties.
Why B: Posting information on a staff bulletin board lets every worker read it, whether or not they need it, which breaks confidentiality.
Why C: Sharing with anyone who asks, even without need, exposes private details and violates confidentiality rules and law.
Why D: Discussing patients in lifts and halls lets bystanders overhear private details, which violates confidentiality.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two staff members discuss a patient's diagnosis in a crowded elevator. What is the problem?
A: Nothing wrong, since elevators are private
B: They are speaking too quietly to be heard
C: The elevator is too slow to get to the floor
D: Others could overhear private information
Why A: Elevators are shared public spaces, so anyone riding along can hear a conversation, which makes discussing a diagnosis there a privacy problem and not a safe, private setting.
Why B: Speaking quietly would actually reduce the risk of being overheard, so volume is not the issue here; the real problem is that the topic itself is confidential patient information.
Why C: The speed of the elevator has nothing to do with patient confidentiality, so a slow ride is only an inconvenience and does not describe the actual problem with this conversation.
Why D: A crowded elevator means strangers, visitors and other patients can overhear the diagnosis, which breaches patient privacy and confidentiality rules, so sensitive details must only be discussed in private, secure places.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is professionalism in healthcare?
A: Behaving with respect, reliability and ethics while serving patients
B: Doing only the tasks you like and leaving the rest to other members of staff
C: Avoiding teamwork with the other staff on the ward or in the clinic
D: Arriving late often to shifts and meetings without any good reason
Why A: Professionalism means behaving with respect, reliability and ethics while serving patients, which builds trust, supports safe care and reflects well on the whole healthcare team and organization.
Why B: Picking only the tasks you like and leaving the rest to colleagues is unfair and unreliable, so it shows a lack of professionalism and harms both teamwork and patient care.
Why C: Avoiding teamwork damages communication and patient safety, because healthcare depends on coordinated effort, so refusing to cooperate with colleagues is the opposite of professional behavior in a clinic or ward.
Why D: Arriving late often without good reason shows unreliability and disrespect for patients and colleagues, so it is a sign of unprofessional behavior and not something that professionalism involves.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is teamwork in a healthcare setting?
A: Each person working in isolation from all of the others on the staff
B: Competing to avoid sharing information, so each worker keeps an edge
C: Staff from different roles working together toward patient care goals
D: Leaving all tasks to the manager while the staff look on without helping
Why A: Working in isolation defeats the purpose of teamwork, because it blocks sharing of information and coordination of care, which are exactly what a healthcare team needs to keep patients safe.
Why B: Competing and withholding information is the opposite of teamwork, since it puts personal advantage ahead of patient goals and can lead to mistakes and delays in care.
Why C: Teamwork means staff from different roles cooperate and share information toward common patient care goals, which improves safety, efficiency and outcomes compared with people acting alone.
Why D: Leaving all tasks to the manager while others look on is not teamwork, because teamwork needs shared effort and responsibility from every member of the group, not passive watching.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is SBAR used for?
A: A system for storing bars of soap and other items used by cleaners daily
B: A structured way to share situation, background, assessment and recommendation
C: A set of drug dosage tables kept by pharmacists for use on the wards daily
D: A schedule for billing and records that nurses fill in at the end of shifts in practice
Why A: SBAR has nothing to do with soap or cleaning supplies; it is a communication tool used by clinicians, and the letters stand for steps in sharing patient information, not objects.
Why B: SBAR is a structured communication method that organizes a message into situation, background, assessment and recommendation, so clinicians share clear and complete patient information quickly, especially in urgent calls and handoffs.
Why C: SBAR is not a set of dosage tables; drug doses are found in pharmacy references, while SBAR is a way of structuring spoken or written clinical communication between staff.
Why D: SBAR is not a billing or records schedule; it guides how information is communicated between caregivers, whereas billing uses codes and claims forms, so this option describes a different function altogether.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the S in SBAR stand for?
A: Staffing
B: Surgery
C: Schedule
D: Situation
Why A: Staffing is not what the S means; in SBAR the first letter stands for Situation, which describes what is happening with the patient right now, and not workforce levels.
Why B: Surgery is not the meaning of S in SBAR; the letter stands for Situation, the current problem, and the tool is not limited to surgical settings at all.
Why C: Schedule is incorrect because SBAR is a communication format, not a timetable; the S stands for Situation, which briefly states the current patient problem to the listener.
Why D: The S in SBAR stands for Situation, the first step in which the speaker states clearly who the patient is and what the current problem is before giving background.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a handoff (handover) in healthcare?
A: Passing a patient's belongings to a visitor at the end of the working day as a rule
B: Passing a bill to the insurance company for payment of the care given
C: Giving hospital keys to a janitor at the end of the evening shift there
D: Passing patient information and responsibility from one caregiver to another
Why A: Handing belongings to a visitor is a routine courtesy at most, not a handoff; in healthcare the term refers to transferring patient information and responsibility between caregivers at shift change.
Why B: Passing a bill to an insurer is claims submission, which is a billing task; a handoff is the clinical transfer of patient information and responsibility from one caregiver to another.
Why C: Giving keys to a janitor is an operational task unrelated to patient care; a handoff is about communicating patient status and transferring responsibility between caregivers so care continues safely.
Why D: A handoff is the transfer of patient information and responsibility from one caregiver to another, such as at shift change, and doing it clearly prevents errors and gaps in care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a leader in a healthcare team expected to do?
A: Avoid communicating with staff on the unit
B: Blame others for mistakes that occur on the ward
C: Guide the team, set direction and support staff
D: Make every decision alone without input from the team
Why A: Avoiding communication would leave the team without direction or feedback, so a leader who stays silent fails at the core duty of keeping staff informed and coordinated on the unit.
Why B: Blaming others for mistakes damages trust and discourages reporting, so it is poor leadership; a good leader helps the team learn from errors and fixes the underlying system problems.
Why C: A leader guides the team, sets direction and supports staff, which keeps everyone working toward shared patient care goals and helps people do their jobs well and feel valued.
Why D: Making every decision alone ignores the knowledge of team members and slows work, so it is not expected of a good leader, who invites input and shares responsibility.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is delegation?
A: Assigning tasks to others with the authority needed to complete them
B: Ignoring tasks until they pile up, then handing them all out at once
C: Firing staff who make mistakes, without any warning or review
D: Doing every task personally and refusing to hand any work to others
Why A: Delegation means assigning tasks to others along with the authority needed to complete them, so the work gets done properly while the delegator stays accountable for the outcome.
Why B: Ignoring tasks and then handing them all out at once is poor planning and not delegation, which requires thoughtful assignment of suitable tasks with clear authority and timing.
Why C: Firing staff for mistakes is a disciplinary action and has nothing to do with delegation, which is the assignment of tasks and authority to capable team members.
Why D: Doing every task personally and refusing to hand out work is the opposite of delegation, and it overloads the individual while leaving other staff skills unused.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which task should a nurse manager NOT delegate to an unlicensed assistant?
A: Restocking supplies in the storeroom and on the wards each day in this case
B: Performing a nursing assessment that requires professional judgment
C: Taking a patient's temperature, which any trained aide can do
D: Helping a patient walk down the hall after a short rest in bed
