Why A: Restocking supplies is a routine non-clinical task that needs no professional judgment, so it can safely be delegated to an unlicensed assistant and is therefore not the task to avoid delegating.
Why B: A nursing assessment requires professional judgment, clinical knowledge and licensure, so it cannot be delegated to an unlicensed assistant, who may only help with tasks that need no such judgment.
Why C: Taking a temperature is a routine, standardized task that trained aides can do, and the nurse then interprets the result, so it is acceptable to delegate and not the answer.
Why D: Helping a patient walk is an assisted activity of daily living that trained aides commonly perform under supervision, so it can be delegated and is not the task that must stay with a nurse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is conflict resolution?
A: Punishing everyone involved in the dispute equally and at once
B: Avoiding all disagreement by silence, so nobody raises an issue
C: Winning every argument by being loud and by talking over others
D: Working to settle disagreements in a fair and respectful way
Why A: Punishing everyone equally and at once ignores the facts and fairness; resolving conflict means understanding the dispute and settling it, not issuing blanket punishment that leaves the cause untouched.
Why B: Avoiding disagreement through silence only hides the problem, which tends to grow; conflict resolution means addressing the issue openly so that the people involved can reach a settlement.
Why C: Winning by being loud and talking over others silences the other side and damages relationships, so it is aggression and not resolution, which depends on listening and fairness.
Why D: Conflict resolution means working to settle disagreements in a fair and respectful way, so both sides are heard, the cause is addressed and the team can keep working well together.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two coworkers disagree about a task assignment. What is the best first step for a supervisor?
A: Listen to both sides and guide them to a fair solution
B: Ignore the conflict and hope that it ends by itself
C: Choose a side without listening to the other person
D: Move both to another unit so they no longer share a shift
Why A: The best first step is to listen to both sides and then guide them to a fair solution, which respects each person, clarifies the facts and keeps the team working together.
Why B: Ignoring the conflict and hoping it fades usually lets tension grow and hurts teamwork and patient care, so a supervisor should step in early and not wait passively.
Why C: Choosing a side without hearing the other person is unfair and biased, so it damages trust and leaves the real cause unresolved, which makes it a poor first step.
Why D: Moving both coworkers to other units avoids the problem without solving it and disrupts staffing, so it is an extreme step; the supervisor should first listen and mediate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is emotional intelligence?
A: The ability to memorize medical terms and drug names by heart
B: The ability to recognize and manage your own and others' emotions
C: The ability to type quickly on a computer keyboard at the desk
D: The ability to avoid emotions altogether, to make logical choices
Why A: Memorizing medical terms and drug names is knowledge recall, not emotional intelligence, which concerns understanding and handling feelings, both your own and those of the people around you.
Why B: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and those of others, which supports empathy, calm communication and good teamwork with patients and colleagues.
Why C: Typing quickly is a technical skill unrelated to emotions, so it does not describe emotional intelligence, which is about awareness and management of feelings in yourself and other people.
Why D: Avoiding emotions altogether is neither possible nor healthy; emotional intelligence means recognizing and managing emotions, not suppressing them, so this option describes the opposite of the concept.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is burnout?
A: A bonus for hard work paid to staff at the end of the year
B: A fire in the building that staff must put out using water
C: Exhaustion and reduced effectiveness from prolonged stress
D: A new job promotion given to a worker after years of good service
Why A: A bonus is a reward paid for good work and has no link to stress; burnout is instead a state of exhaustion that harms a worker's health and performance.
Why B: A fire in the building is a physical emergency and not burnout; burnout is a psychological and physical condition caused by long-term stress that makes workers feel exhausted and less effective.
Why C: Burnout is exhaustion and reduced effectiveness from prolonged stress, and it can lead to errors, absence and staff leaving, which is why managers watch for early warning signs.
Why D: A promotion is a career reward and has no relation to burnout, which is the exhaustion and reduced effectiveness that builds up when a worker faces stress for a long time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action best helps reduce staff burnout?
A: Increasing hours without support so staff finish work faster
B: Removing all breaks from the shift so staff can work longer
C: Ignoring staff concerns when they ask for help or for rest
D: Providing manageable workloads, support and recognition
Why A: Adding hours without support increases fatigue and stress, which makes burnout worse, so it cannot reduce staff burnout even if it seems to finish work faster for a short time.
Why B: Removing all breaks removes the rest that workers need to recover, which speeds exhaustion and errors, so it increases burnout and fails to reduce it in any way.
Why C: Ignoring concerns makes staff feel unheard and unsupported, which adds to stress and exhaustion, so it increases burnout and does not help reduce it for anyone.
Why D: Manageable workloads, support and recognition ease chronic stress and make staff feel valued, which directly reduces burnout and keeps employees healthier, more engaged and more effective in their work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is customer service in a healthcare office?
A: Ignoring phone calls to finish paperwork so staff can work in peace
B: Helping patients and visitors in a courteous and helpful way
C: Making patients wait without any explanation or an apology
D: Refusing to answer questions from patients and their families
Why A: Ignoring phone calls leaves patients unable to reach the office, which is poor service; good customer service means responding to people promptly, not avoiding them to finish paperwork in peace.
Why B: Customer service in a healthcare office means helping patients and visitors in a courteous and helpful way, which builds trust, reduces frustration and supports a positive experience of care.
Why C: Making patients wait with no explanation or apology is discourteous and shows poor service, whereas good service communicates delays kindly and respects the time and worries of the patient.
Why D: Refusing to answer questions leaves patients and families confused and anxious, so it is poor service; good customer service means answering questions politely or finding someone who can.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A caller asks about a family member's test results. What should the front desk staff member do?
A: Verify permission before sharing any information
B: Share results with anyone who sounds worried by phone
C: Post the results on a public board for anyone to read
D: Share the results with any caller who asks for them
Why A: The front desk should verify that the caller has permission before sharing anything, because health information is protected and may only be released to people the patient has authorized.
Why B: Sharing results with anyone who sounds worried ignores privacy law, since concern does not equal authorization; the patient must have given permission before information is released by phone.
Why C: Posting results on a public board exposes private health information to everyone and clearly violates patient confidentiality, so it is never acceptable in any office or clinic.
Why D: Giving results to any caller who asks risks releasing private information to unauthorized people, which breaks confidentiality rules, so identity and permission must be verified first.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is patient advocacy?
A: Promoting the hospital's products to patients and visitors
B: Limiting what patients may ask of the staff and doctors
C: Supporting and protecting patients' rights and interests
D: Making decisions without asking the patient for any consent
Why A: Promoting hospital products is marketing and serves the organization, whereas patient advocacy means supporting and protecting the rights and interests of the patient, so this option describes a different activity.
Why B: Limiting what patients may ask for works against them, but advocacy is about speaking up for patients and protecting their rights, not restricting their questions or requests to staff.
Why C: Patient advocacy means supporting and protecting patients' rights and interests, such as helping them understand options, voice concerns and receive safe, respectful care from the healthcare system.
Why D: Making decisions without patient consent violates patient rights, which is the opposite of advocacy; advocates make sure the patient is informed and takes part in decisions about their own care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the prefix 'hyper-' mean?
A: Above or excessive
B: Within or inside
C: Below or deficient
D: Around or surrounding
Why A: The prefix hyper- means above or excessive, as in hypertension, which is high blood pressure, so it signals that something is more than normal in amount or degree.
Why B: Within or inside is the meaning of intra-, not hyper-; hyper- signals above or excessive, so this option confuses two different prefixes that point in different directions.
Why C: Below or deficient is the meaning of hypo-, which is the opposite of hyper-; the prefix hyper- means above or excessive, as in hyperglycemia, so this option reverses it.
Why D: Around or surrounding is the meaning of peri-, as in pericardium, and not hyper-, which means above or excessive, so this option mixes up two unrelated medical prefixes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the prefix 'hypo-' mean?
A: Many or much of it
B: Above or excessive
C: Without or lacking
D: Below or deficient
Why A: Many or much is the meaning of poly-, as in polyuria, and not hypo-, which means below or deficient, so this option confuses two different medical prefixes.
Why B: Above or excessive is the meaning of hyper-, the opposite prefix; hypo- means below or deficient, as in hypoglycemia, which is low blood sugar, so this option reverses it.
Why C: Without or lacking is the meaning of a- or an-, as in anemia, and not hypo-, which means below or deficient, so the two ideas are similar but not the same.
Why D: The prefix hypo- means below or deficient, as in hypotension, which is low blood pressure, so it marks something that is under the normal amount or level.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-itis' mean?
A: Study of body
B: Pain or ache
C: Inflammation
D: Removing part
Why A: Study of is the meaning of the suffix -ology, as in cardiology, and not -itis, which refers to inflammation, so this option swaps the wrong suffix.
Why B: Pain or ache is the meaning of -algia, as in neuralgia, and not -itis, which means inflammation; pain may occur with inflammation, but the suffix itself does not name pain.
Why C: The suffix -itis means inflammation, as in arthritis, which is inflammation of the joints, so any term ending in -itis names a swollen or irritated condition of a body part.
Why D: Removal of parts is the idea behind -ectomy, as in appendectomy, and not -itis, which means inflammation, so this option confuses a surgical suffix with a disease suffix.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-ectomy' mean?
A: Tool for viewing
B: Surgical removal
C: Inflammation
D: Disease or illness
Why A: Tool for viewing is the meaning of -scope, as in endoscope, and not -ectomy, which means surgical removal, so this option names an instrument instead of a procedure.
Why B: The suffix -ectomy means surgical removal, as in appendectomy, the removal of the appendix, so it tells you that a body part is cut out during an operation.
Why C: Inflammation is the meaning of -itis, as in tonsillitis, and not -ectomy, which means surgical removal, so this option confuses a condition suffix with a procedure suffix.
Why D: Disease or illness is the meaning of -pathy, as in neuropathy, and not -ectomy, which describes surgical removal, so this option names a condition instead of a surgical action.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'cardi' refer to?
A: Heart
B: Kidney
C: Liver
D: Brain
Why A: The root cardi refers to the heart, as in cardiology, the study of the heart, and cardiac, meaning relating to the heart, so it appears in many heart terms.
Why B: Kidney is represented by the root nephr or ren, as in nephritis, and not cardi, which refers to the heart, so this option names the wrong organ.
Why C: Liver is represented by the root hepat, as in hepatitis, and not cardi, which refers to the heart, so this option confuses two different organ roots.
Why D: Brain is represented by the root encephal or cerebr, as in encephalitis, and not cardi, which refers to the heart, so this option names the wrong organ.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'hepat' refer to?
A: Lung
B: Bone
C: Stomach
D: Liver
Why A: Lung is represented by the roots pulmon or pneumon, as in pulmonary, and not hepat, which refers to the liver, so this option names the wrong organ.
Why B: Bone is represented by the root oste, as in osteoporosis, and not hepat, which refers to the liver, so this option confuses two unrelated body part roots.
Why C: Stomach is represented by the root gastr, as in gastritis, and not hepat, which refers to the liver, so this option names an organ from a different root.
Why D: The root hepat refers to the liver, as in hepatitis, which is inflammation of the liver, so terms built on hepat concern liver structure, disease or function.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the term 'tachycardia' mean?
A: A normal heart rate
B: Irregular breathing
C: A fast heart rate
D: A slow heart rate
Why A: A normal heart rate would be called normocardia or a normal rate; tachycardia names an abnormal rate, since tachy means fast, so this option describes the wrong heart condition.
Why B: Irregular breathing relates to the respiratory system, but tachycardia concerns the heart; tachy means fast and cardia refers to the heart, so breathing is not involved.
Why C: Tachycardia means a fast heart rate, built from tachy for fast and cardia for heart, and it usually refers to a resting rate above about 100 beats per minute.
Why D: A slow heart rate is bradycardia, the opposite condition; tachycardia comes from tachy meaning fast, so this option reverses the meaning of the word.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the term 'bradycardia' mean?
A: A fast heart rate
B: A slow heart rate
C: A heart operation
D: An inflamed heart
Why A: A fast heart rate is tachycardia, the opposite condition; bradycardia comes from brady meaning slow, so this option reverses the meaning of the word.
Why B: Bradycardia means a slow heart rate, built from brady for slow and cardia for heart, and it usually refers to a resting rate below about 60 beats per minute.
Why C: A heart operation would be named with a surgical suffix such as -tomy or -plasty; bradycardia describes rate, not surgery, since brady means slow and cardia means heart.
Why D: An inflamed heart is carditis, formed with the suffix -itis; bradycardia has no inflammation meaning, since brady means slow and cardia refers to the heart rate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'NPO' mean in a medical order?
A: Needs physician note
B: New patient order
C: Nothing by mouth
D: Normal pulse noted
Why A: Needs physician note is not what NPO stands for; the abbreviation comes from Latin and means nothing by mouth, an instruction used before surgery or tests.
Why B: New patient order is not the meaning of NPO, which is a restriction on eating and drinking; it comes from the Latin phrase for nothing by mouth.
Why C: NPO means nothing by mouth, from the Latin non per os, and it tells staff the patient must not eat or drink, often before surgery or certain tests.
Why D: Normal pulse noted is not what NPO stands for; the abbreviation relates to food and drink, meaning nothing by mouth, and not to vital signs such as a pulse reading.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'STAT' mean on an order?
A: Statistics
B: Next week
C: Daily
D: Right now
Why A: STAT comes from the Latin statim, meaning immediately. It tells staff the order is urgent and must be done right away, and it has nothing to do with data or statistics.
Why B: Next week is the opposite of what STAT conveys; the term signals urgency, so the order must be carried out at once and not delayed by days.
Why C: Daily would describe a routine schedule, but STAT means immediately. The term flags an urgent order that cannot wait for a regular cycle.
Why D: STAT means immediately, from the Latin statim, and it flags an order as urgent so staff carry it out right away without any delay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do vital signs usually include?
A: Temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure
B: Height, weight and shoe size, taken on admission overall
C: Name, address, age, phone number and next of kin
D: Allergies, history, diet and exercise habits
Why A: Vital signs usually include temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure, which are the basic measurements showing how well the body is functioning and are checked at most patient encounters.
Why B: Height, weight and shoe size are body measurements, and shoe size is not clinical at all; vital signs are temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure, so this list is wrong.
Why C: Name, address, age, phone number and next of kin are demographic details, not measurements of body function, so they are not vital signs even though they are recorded at registration.
Why D: Allergies, history, diet and exercise habits are part of a patient history, not measurements of body function, so none of these are vital signs, which are objective readings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A blood pressure reading is 120/80. What does the 80 represent?
A: Body temperature taken with a thermometer by the nurse
B: Diastolic pressure, when the heart rests between beats
C: Systolic pressure, when the heart beats and pushes out blood
D: Heart rate per minute as counted by a pulse monitor
Why A: Body temperature is measured in degrees, not in a pair like 120/80, so the 80 cannot be temperature; it is the second number of a blood pressure reading.
Why B: In 120/80 the lower number, 80, is the diastolic pressure, which is the pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats, so it shows the minimum pressure.
Why C: Systolic pressure is the top number, 120, which measures pressure when the heart beats and pushes blood out; the 80 is the lower number and represents diastolic pressure instead.
Why D: Heart rate is counted in beats per minute and reported as a single number such as 72, so the 80 in a blood pressure reading is not the pulse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patient chart?
A: A map of the hospital showing the halls and the wards
B: A list of staff schedules posted in the nurses' station in general
C: A bill for services sent to a patient by the hospital
D: A record of a patient's health history, treatment and notes
Why A: A map of the hospital is a floor plan or directory, not a chart; a patient chart is the record of a patient's health history, treatment and notes.
Why B: A staff schedule lists who works when and is kept apart from patient records; a patient chart is the record of an individual patient's health history, treatment and notes.
Why C: A bill for services is a financial document sent for payment, whereas a patient chart is the clinical record of a patient's health history, treatment and care notes.
Why D: A patient chart is a record of a patient's health history, treatment and notes, which lets caregivers share information, follow progress and keep care safe, continuous and legally documented.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A medical record entry has a mistake. What is the proper way to correct it?
A: Cross it out with a marker so it cannot be read
B: Use correction fluid to hide it so the record looks clean
C: Draw a single line through it, date and initial the correction
D: Write the correction over the mistake in the same space
Why A: Blacking out an entry hides the original and looks like tampering. A proper correction keeps the error legible with a single line, then adds a date and initials.
Why B: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which makes the record look altered and unreliable, so it is not acceptable; the original text must stay readable after a correction.
Why C: The proper method is to draw a single line through the error, then date and initial the correction, so the original stays readable and the change is traceable.
Why D: Writing over a mistake hides the original text and makes the change untraceable. The error should stay readable under a single line, with the correction dated and initialed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of appointment scheduling?
A: To increase wait times for the patients in the clinic
B: To organize patient visits efficiently and reduce waiting
C: To avoid seeing patients who call the office to ask for visits
D: To confuse staff and patients about the time of each visit
Why A: Increasing wait times is the opposite of the goal; scheduling exists to organize visits so patients are seen promptly and the clinic runs smoothly, not to lengthen waiting.
Why B: The purpose of scheduling is to organize patient visits efficiently and reduce waiting, so that patients are seen on time and clinic staff and rooms are used well.
Why C: Avoiding patients who call for visits would defeat the purpose of a clinic; scheduling serves patients by giving them appointments, not by turning away those who ask for care.
Why D: Confusing staff and patients about visit times would cause missed visits and delays; scheduling is meant to give clear, organized times, not to create uncertainty for anyone involved.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is double-booking in scheduling?
A: Scheduling two patients for the same time slot
B: Leaving open slots for urgent add-on visits
C: Booking a patient twice for two doctors on a day
D: Booking patients in the evening to extend clinic hours
Why A: Double-booking means scheduling two patients for the same time slot, which can cause overlaps, longer waits and rushed care unless the practice plans carefully for it.
Why B: Holding slots for urgent visits is a planning practice, not double-booking. Double-booking means two patients are given the same time slot.
Why C: Booking one patient twice with two doctors in a day is a multi-visit schedule, not double-booking, which specifically means two patients assigned to the same time slot.
Why D: Evening appointments simply extend availability. Double-booking is when two patients are assigned to the same time slot, whatever the hour.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a no-show?
A: A patient who is seen on time by the doctor today
B: A patient who misses an appointment without canceling
C: A patient who arrives early for a visit with the doctor
D: A patient who cancels days ahead, so the slot is reused
Why A: A patient seen on time did attend the visit, so that is not a no-show; a no-show is someone who misses the appointment without canceling in advance.
Why B: A no-show is a patient who misses an appointment without canceling, which leaves an empty slot that cannot be refilled and wastes clinic time and resources.
Why C: A patient who arrives early did attend, so the person is not a no-show; a no-show fails to come at all and gives no notice of canceling.
Why D: Canceling days ahead gives the clinic time to reuse the slot, so it is a cancellation and not a no-show, which means missing the visit with no cancellation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which practice helps reduce no-shows?
A: Removing the phone number from the records of patients
B: Never confirming appointments with patients before a visit
C: Scheduling without telling the patient the date or time
D: Sending appointment reminders by phone, text or email
Why A: Removing the phone number from records would prevent reminders and contact, which would increase no-shows, so it cannot reduce them; reaching patients is key to keeping appointments.
Why B: Never confirming appointments leaves patients likely to forget their visit, which raises no-shows; confirmation and reminders are proven ways of getting patients to attend as planned.
Why C: Scheduling without telling the patient the date or time guarantees confusion and missed visits, so it raises no-shows; patients must be told exactly when and where to come.
Why D: Sending reminders by phone, text or email helps patients remember their appointments and reschedule if needed, which lowers the number of missed visits and empty slots for the clinic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is triage?
A: Sorting patients by urgency of need
B: Sorting patients by age only here
C: Sorting patients by insurance type
D: Sorting patients by name or age
Why A: Triage is the process of sorting patients by urgency of need, so those with the most serious conditions are treated first and those who can safely wait are seen later.
Why B: Sorting by age only ignores how serious the condition is; triage ranks patients by urgency of need, so a stable older patient could correctly wait behind a critical younger one.
Why C: Sorting by insurance type is a billing concern and would be unfair and unsafe in care; triage ranks patients by clinical urgency and never by how they will pay.
Why D: Sorting by name or age has nothing to do with medical need; triage ranks patients by urgency of need, so alphabetical order could delay a patient with a serious problem.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which patient should be seen first in an emergency department triage?
A: A patient with a mild cold and a runny nose
B: A patient needing a routine prescription refill today
C: A patient with chest pain and trouble breathing
D: A patient with a minor scrape on the knee
Why A: A mild cold with a runny nose is not life-threatening and can safely wait, so this patient has low priority in triage compared with a patient in serious distress.
Why B: A routine prescription refill is not urgent and can be handled later or by other means, so this patient ranks low in triage behind patients with emergencies.
Why C: Chest pain with trouble breathing may signal a heart attack or another life-threatening problem, so this patient has the highest urgency and is seen first in emergency triage.
Why D: A minor scrape on the knee is a small injury that can safely wait, so this patient ranks low in triage compared with someone who has life-threatening symptoms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a referral authorization?
A: A discount on specialist fees given to some patients by plans
B: A letter of thanks to a patient for choosing the hospital for care overall
C: Approval needed before a patient sees a specialist under some plans
D: A tax form for providers filed each year with the state office
Why A: A discount on specialist fees is a pricing benefit and not a referral authorization, which is an approval from the plan that is needed before seeing a specialist.
Why B: A letter of thanks is a courtesy message with no insurance function; a referral authorization is approval from a plan that is needed before a patient sees a specialist.
Why C: A referral authorization is approval needed before a patient sees a specialist under some plans, and without it the plan may refuse to pay, leaving the patient with the bill.
Why D: A tax form is filed with government agencies for revenue purposes and has no link to patient care; a referral authorization is plan approval for seeing a specialist.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the front desk's role in patient check-in?
A: Prescribe medicine for the patients who arrive at the front desk
B: Diagnose the illness of each patient who comes in to the office
C: Perform surgery on patients who come in to the clinic each day
D: Verify identity and insurance and collect forms and payments
Why A: Prescribing medicine requires a licensed provider with prescriptive authority, so front desk staff cannot do it; their role is administrative tasks such as registration and verifying details.
Why B: Diagnosing illness requires clinical training and licensure that front desk staff do not have, so it is not their role; they handle administrative tasks during check-in.
Why C: Performing surgery requires a licensed surgeon and a sterile operating setting, so it is far outside the front desk role, which is administrative tasks such as registration and payments.
Why D: At check-in, the front desk verifies identity and insurance and collects forms and payments, which makes the visit run smoothly and ensures records and billing details are accurate from the start.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is it important to verify a patient's insurance at check-in?
A: To make the visit longer than it needs to be
B: To confirm coverage and avoid claim denials
C: To raise the price of the care for the patient
D: To avoid seeing the patient and send them away
Why A: Making the visit longer is not a goal of verification; checking insurance is done to confirm coverage and avoid claim denials, and it actually helps prevent later billing delays.
Why B: Verifying insurance at check-in confirms that coverage is active and that services are covered, which avoids claim denials and surprise bills for the patient and the practice later.
Why C: Raising the price of care is not a purpose of verification; the cost of services is set separately, and insurance checks confirm coverage and help avoid claim denials.
Why D: Verification is not meant to turn patients away; it confirms coverage and avoids claim denials so that the visit and the payment proceed correctly for both patient and provider.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a superbill?
A: A form listing services provided, used to bill insurance
B: A report of weather and temperature for each day of the week
C: A very large hospital bill sent to the insurer for payment
D: A tax return for hospitals filed with the government each year
Why A: A superbill is a form listing services provided, with diagnosis and procedure codes, which the practice uses to bill insurance and which a patient may submit for reimbursement.
Why B: A weather report has nothing to do with healthcare billing; a superbill is a form that lists services provided and is used to bill insurance for the care given.
Why C: A superbill is not a very large hospital bill; it is an itemized form of services and codes used to create an insurance claim, whatever the size of the charges.
Why D: A tax return is a government filing about income and has no link to care; a superbill is a form listing services provided that is used to bill insurance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'HIPAA-compliant' disposal of paper records involve?
A: Shredding or securely destroying documents containing patient information
B: Leaving them in a public bin for anyone to pick up and read later
C: Giving them to visitors to take home as a keepsake of their visit
D: Throwing them in the regular trash bins behind the clinic each week in general
Why A: HIPAA-compliant disposal means shredding or securely destroying documents containing patient information so that no one can read them, which protects patient privacy once the records are no longer needed.
Why B: Leaving records in a public bin lets anyone read private health information, which violates HIPAA; compliant disposal requires secure destruction so the contents can never be recovered by others.
Why C: Giving records to visitors as a keepsake exposes private data to people with no right to see it, which violates HIPAA; documents must be destroyed securely instead.
Why D: Regular trash bins let anyone retrieve discarded papers and read patient details, so this is not HIPAA compliant; documents with patient information must be shredded or otherwise securely destroyed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hospital's governing board responsible for?
A: Submitting insurance claims and collecting patient payments
B: Treating each patient directly, with members taking turns on wards
C: Setting policy and overseeing quality, finances and leadership
D: Managing the daily work schedules of nursing staff
Why A: Claims and collections are handled by the billing staff. The governing board works at a higher level, setting policy and overseeing quality, finances and leadership.
Why B: Treating patients directly is the work of licensed clinicians, not board members; the governing board has the role of setting policy and overseeing the hospital as a whole.
Why C: The governing board is responsible for setting policy and overseeing quality, finances and leadership, which means it holds the hospital accountable to its community and appoints senior executives.
Why D: Daily staff scheduling is a job for unit managers. The governing board sets policy and oversees quality, finances and leadership for the whole hospital.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient with a rash first sees a family doctor who then refers them to a dermatologist. Who is the dermatologist?
A: A board member
B: A billing clerk
C: A family nurse
D: A specialist
Why A: A board member sits on the hospital's governing body and sets policy, not treating patients; the dermatologist, to whom the family doctor referred the rash, is a physician specialist.
Why B: A billing clerk handles claims and payments and does not treat skin conditions; a dermatologist is a physician who specializes in skin, hair and nail disorders.
Why C: A family nurse works in primary care under a different role; a dermatologist is a physician who has trained in skin disorders, which makes this person a specialist.
Why D: A dermatologist is a specialist, meaning a physician trained in one area, here the skin, to whom a family doctor refers patients whose needs go beyond general primary care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an urgent care center?
A: A hospital unit for major surgery that needs a long stay in a bed on the ward
B: A walk-in clinic for non-life-threatening problems needing prompt care
C: A long-term care home for people who need help to live each day
D: A pharmacy only, where drugs are filled for patients on an order
Why A: Major surgery with a long bed stay describes a hospital inpatient unit, not urgent care, which offers prompt walk-in treatment for problems that are not life-threatening.
Why B: An urgent care center is a walk-in clinic for non-life-threatening problems needing prompt care, such as sprains or minor infections, with no appointment and shorter waits than an emergency department.
Why C: A long-term care home provides ongoing living assistance over months or years, while urgent care offers short walk-in visits for problems that need prompt attention but are not life-threatening.
Why D: A pharmacy fills prescriptions and does not diagnose or treat injuries; urgent care is a walk-in clinic where clinicians treat non-life-threatening problems that need prompt attention.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A person has a minor sprain on a Sunday. Which setting is usually most appropriate and cost-effective?
A: Urgent care
B: Hospice care
C: Trauma unit
D: Surgery room
Why A: Urgent care is usually most appropriate and cost-effective for a minor sprain on a Sunday, since it is open on weekends and costs less than an emergency department.
Why B: Hospice provides comfort care for people near the end of life, so it does not treat a sprain; the injury needs a walk-in setting like urgent care instead.
Why C: Intensive care treats critically ill patients with life support, which is far more intensive and costly than a minor sprain needs, so this setting is not appropriate.
Why D: An operating room is for surgery and is not a place for walk-in care of a minor sprain, which does not need an operation and is better treated elsewhere.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is long-term care?
A: A single short checkup at a clinic with one doctor visit
B: A quick vaccination given by a nurse at a clinic or a school
C: A billing service that sends claims to insurers for the clinic overall
D: Ongoing support for people who cannot fully care for themselves
Why A: A single short checkup is a one-time visit, whereas long-term care means continuing support over months or years for people who cannot fully care for themselves.
Why B: A quick vaccination is a brief preventive service, not long-term care, which refers to ongoing support given over a long period to people who cannot fully care for themselves.
Why C: A billing service submits claims and has nothing to do with the care itself; long-term care is ongoing support for people who cannot fully care for themselves.
Why D: Long-term care is ongoing support for people who cannot fully care for themselves, including help with daily activities and health needs, often provided in nursing homes or at home.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a major benefit of electronic health records?
A: They replace clinical judgment with automatic decisions
B: Providers can share accurate information quickly
C: They remove the need for privacy rules in a hospital
D: They remove the need for patients to sign consent forms
Why A: Electronic records support clinicians but do not replace their judgment. Their benefit is fast, accurate sharing of information between providers.
Why B: A major benefit of electronic health records is that providers can share accurate information quickly, which supports coordinated, timely and safer care across different clinicians and settings.
Why C: Electronic records still require privacy protection, and rules like HIPAA apply to them fully; digital storage actually raises the need for security, so it does not remove those rules.
Why D: Consent is still required whether records are paper or electronic. Electronic records mainly help providers share accurate information quickly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a budget in a healthcare setting?
A: A schedule of shifts for the nurses on each ward
B: A list of patients treated, with the dates of their visits
C: A plan estimating revenues and expenses for a period
D: A record of past mistakes made by the staff in care
Why A: A schedule of shifts is a staffing roster, not a budget; a budget is a plan that estimates the revenues and expenses of an organization for a defined period.
Why B: A list of patients and visit dates is a census or visit record and not a budget, which is a financial plan estimating revenues and expenses for a given period.
Why C: A budget is a plan estimating revenues and expenses for a period, which helps managers control spending, set priorities and see whether a unit can afford staff or equipment.
Why D: A record of past mistakes is an incident or quality log and not a budget, which is a forward-looking financial plan estimating revenues and expenses for a period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A clinic pays $8,000 rent and $5 supplies per visit. Total cost for 1,000 visits is:
Why A: Five thousand dollars covers only the per-visit supplies and ignores the fixed rent of $8,000, so the total is incomplete; supplies are 1,000 visits times $5, which is $5,000 only.
Why B: Eight thousand dollars counts only the fixed rent and leaves out the supply costs, which are 1,000 visits times $5, or $5,000, so the total is missing a major cost.
Why C: Forty thousand dollars is not obtainable from the data; multiplying $8,000 by 5 is meaningless here, since rent is fixed and the supplies of $5 per visit add up to only $5,000.
Why D: Total cost equals fixed rent plus variable supplies, so $8,000 plus 1,000 visits times $5, which is $5,000, gives $13,000 in total for the 1,000 visits.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is revenue cycle management?
A: Managing staff vacations and the leave dates for the year ahead
B: Managing hospital cafeteria menus and the food orders for kitchen staff
C: Managing the process from patient registration through final payment
D: Managing building repairs and the upkeep of the hospital grounds
Why A: Managing staff vacations is a human resources task; revenue cycle management follows money from patient registration through final payment, so this option describes an unrelated administrative process.
Why B: Managing cafeteria menus is a food service task and has no relation to income; revenue cycle management covers the process from patient registration through final payment for services.
Why C: Revenue cycle management is the management of the process from patient registration through final payment, including coding, billing and collections, so the organization is paid correctly and on time.
Why D: Managing building repairs is a facilities task; revenue cycle management follows each patient account from registration to final payment, so it has nothing to do with the upkeep of buildings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is capitation?
A: A payment based on hours worked by the staff of a hospital in a pay week
B: A payment of a fixed amount per patient per period regardless of services used
C: A payment from patients only, made at the desk before each visit begins
D: A payment for each service performed on a patient by the clinic or the hospital
Why A: A payment based on hours worked is hourly wages for staff; capitation is a fixed payment per patient per period that has no link to the hours anyone works.
Why B: Capitation is a payment of a fixed amount per patient per period regardless of services used, so the provider is paid the same sum whether the patient visits often or not at all.
Why C: Patient-only payments made at the desk describe out-of-pocket fees, not capitation, which is a fixed payment from a plan to a provider per patient for each period.
Why D: A payment for each service performed is fee-for-service, the opposite of capitation, which pays a fixed amount per patient per period regardless of how many services the patient uses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A group is paid $40 per member per month whether members visit or not. This is:
A: Capitation
B: A copayment
C: A deductible
D: Fee-for-visit
Why A: This is capitation, because the group receives a fixed $40 per member each month regardless of whether the members visit, which matches payment per patient per period regardless of the services used.
Why B: A copayment is a fixed amount a patient pays at the time of service, not a payment to a group per member per month regardless of visits, so this does not fit.
Why C: A deductible is the amount a patient pays before coverage begins, so it is not a monthly payment to a group for each member, whether or not members visit the clinic.
Why D: Fee-for-visit pays for each visit made, but this payment is made whether or not members visit, so it does not depend on visits and is not fee-for-visit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is credentialing?
A: Verifying a provider's qualifications, licenses and training
B: Ordering supplies for the wards and clinics of the hospital overall
C: Setting a provider's pay each year, based on patient visits
D: Scheduling shifts for the staff of the wards and clinics
Why A: Credentialing is verifying a provider's qualifications, licenses and training, which protects patients by ensuring that only properly qualified clinicians are allowed to treat them at the facility.
Why B: Ordering supplies is a purchasing task and not credentialing, which concerns checking a provider's qualifications, licenses and training before that provider can treat patients.
Why C: Setting pay by visits is a compensation matter and not credentialing, which concerns verifying a provider's qualifications, licenses and training rather than deciding how much the provider earns.
Why D: Scheduling shifts is a staffing task and not credentialing, which concerns verifying a provider's qualifications, licenses and training before the provider is granted privileges at the hospital.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hospital checks a new physician's license and training history before granting privileges. This is:
A: Discharge plan
B: Triage rules
C: Capitation
D: Credentialing
Why A: A discharge plan prepares a patient to leave the hospital and has nothing to do with checking a physician's license, which is the work of credentialing.
Why B: Triage rules sort patients by urgency in an emergency setting and do not involve checking a physician's license and training history, which is the work of credentialing.
Why C: Capitation is a payment method of a fixed amount per patient, and it does not involve checking a physician's license or training, which is what credentialing means.
Why D: Checking a new physician's license and training history before granting privileges is credentialing, which verifies qualifications so only properly trained and licensed providers treat patients at the hospital.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is turnover?
A: The number of patients treated in a single month
B: The rate at which employees leave and are replaced
C: The yearly profit made by the hospital after all costs
D: The speed at which beds are changed between patients
Why A: The number of patients treated in a month is patient volume and not turnover, which measures how fast employees leave and are replaced in the workforce.
Why B: Turnover is the rate at which employees leave and are replaced, and a high rate raises hiring and training costs and can harm continuity of care for patients.
Why C: Yearly profit after costs is net income, a financial measure, and not turnover, which measures how often employees leave and have to be replaced in an organization.
Why D: The speed at which beds are changed between patients is bed turnover, a different operational measure; staff turnover is the rate at which employees leave and are replaced.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A clinic loses many nurses each year. Which step best addresses turnover?
A: Increase workload so the remaining staff cover more
B: Remove all training for the nurses on staff
C: Improve workload, pay, support and recognition
D: Ignore staff feedback on workload and pay
Why A: Increasing workload on remaining staff adds stress and exhaustion, which pushes more nurses to leave, so it worsens turnover and does not address its causes.
Why B: Removing training leaves nurses less skilled and less valued, which reduces job satisfaction and tends to raise turnover, so it fails to address why nurses are leaving.
Why C: Improving workload, pay, support and recognition tackles the common reasons nurses leave, so staff are more satisfied and more likely to stay, which lowers turnover over time.
Why D: Ignoring feedback about workload and pay leaves the causes of dissatisfaction unsolved, which keeps nurses leaving and raises turnover, so it is not an effective step.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is continuing education for healthcare workers?
A: A billing audit of the claims sent to insurers
B: A one-time orientation given to new staff on day one
C: A vacation program for the staff of the hospital
D: Ongoing learning to maintain skills and licenses
Why A: A billing audit reviews claims and finances and does not help staff learn; continuing education means ongoing learning to maintain skills and licenses over a career.
Why B: A one-time orientation introduces new staff on their first day, but continuing education is ongoing learning that goes on throughout a career to maintain skills and licenses.
Why C: A vacation program is time off and not learning; continuing education is ongoing learning that helps healthcare workers maintain their skills and licenses throughout their careers.
Why D: Continuing education is ongoing learning to maintain skills and licenses, which keeps healthcare workers current with new practices and meets the requirements for renewing their professional credentials.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a nurse-to-patient ratio?
A: The size of a hospital in beds and rooms
B: The salary of a nurse in a full year of work
C: The number of patients assigned to each nurse
D: The cost of a nurse's uniform paid by staff
Why A: The size of a hospital in beds and rooms is its capacity; a nurse-to-patient ratio instead states the number of patients assigned to each nurse.
Why B: A nurse's salary is a pay figure and has nothing to do with a ratio of staff to patients, which tells how many patients each nurse looks after.
Why C: A nurse-to-patient ratio is the number of patients assigned to each nurse, and lower ratios generally allow more attention for each patient and support safer care.
Why D: The cost of a uniform is a small expense and unrelated to staffing levels; a nurse-to-patient ratio states how many patients each nurse is assigned to care for.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a strategic plan in healthcare?
A: A daily to-do list kept by a nurse for the ward staff
B: A long-range plan setting goals and how to reach them
C: A list of drug prices used by the hospital pharmacy
D: A single patient chart kept in the records office file
Why A: A daily to-do list covers short-term tasks for one shift, but a strategic plan is a long-range plan setting goals and how to reach them.
Why B: A strategic plan is a long-range plan setting goals and the steps to reach them, so the organization can direct resources and decisions toward its mission over several years.
Why C: A list of drug prices is a pharmacy price reference and not a strategic plan, which is a long-range plan setting organizational goals and how to reach them.
Why D: A single patient chart is a clinical record for one person, not a plan for the organization; a strategic plan is a long-range plan setting goals and how to reach them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hospital studies community needs and decides to expand cancer services. This is an example of:
A: Strategic planning based on community needs
B: Ignoring data when the plan is being made
C: Random spending on whatever comes up first
D: Closing services without any plan or review
Why A: Studying community needs and then expanding cancer services is strategic planning based on community needs, because the decision rests on data about local health problems and long-term goals.
Why B: The hospital studied community needs and used that information, so it did not ignore data; ignoring data would be the opposite of what this example shows.
Why C: Random spending on whatever comes first has no study behind it, but this hospital studied community needs first and then decided, which is deliberate planning and not random spending.
Why D: The hospital is expanding cancer services, not closing services, and it followed a study of community needs, so this example does not show closing services without a plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a community health needs assessment?
A: A tax form for hospitals filed with the state each year every time
B: A list of staff birthdays and anniversaries kept in HR
C: A review of the health problems and resources in a community
D: A listing of drug prices used by the hospital pharmacy
Why A: A tax form is filed with the state for revenue and compliance, while a community health needs assessment reviews the health problems and resources in a community to guide planning.
Why B: A list of staff birthdays is an internal human resources record and says nothing about community health, which a community health needs assessment reviews along with local resources.
Why C: A community health needs assessment is a review of the health problems and resources in a community, which a hospital uses to plan services that match what local people need.
Why D: A listing of drug prices is a pharmacy reference and does not study a community; a community health needs assessment reviews local health problems and resources to guide planning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are key performance indicators (KPIs)?
A: Measures used to track progress toward goals
B: Names of department heads and their staff
C: Dates of company parties and staff holidays
D: Costs of office supplies, such as paper and pens
Why A: Key performance indicators are measures used to track progress toward goals, such as wait times or patient satisfaction scores, which let managers see whether the organization is meeting its targets.
Why B: Names of department heads form an organizational listing and not a performance measure; key performance indicators are measures used to track progress toward goals over time.
Why C: Dates of company parties are social calendar items and not performance measures; key performance indicators are measures used to track progress toward goals, such as wait times or satisfaction.
Why D: Costs of office supplies are one budget item, not a set of measures of progress toward goals; key performance indicators track results such as wait times or patient satisfaction.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which patient benefits most from telehealth?
A: One needing emergency surgery in the next few minutes
B: One living far from a clinic who needs a routine follow-up
C: One who needs a broken bone set, as a physician must see it
D: One in cardiac arrest who needs urgent care at once
Why A: Emergency surgery in the next few minutes requires immediate in-person care in an operating room, so telehealth cannot help and this patient would not benefit from a remote visit.
Why B: A patient who lives far from a clinic and needs a routine follow-up benefits most from telehealth, which saves travel time and cost while still allowing a clinician to review progress.
Why C: A broken bone must be examined and set in person by a physician, so a video visit cannot provide the needed treatment and this patient would not benefit most.
Why D: A patient in cardiac arrest needs immediate hands-on resuscitation and emergency services, so a remote visit is useless and this patient cannot benefit from telehealth at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient's lab results from one hospital appear in another provider's system. This shows:
A: Capitation fees
B: Redundancy of data
C: Triage process
D: Interoperability
Why A: Capitation fees are a payment method and have nothing to do with sharing lab results between systems; the ability of systems to exchange data is called interoperability.
Why B: Redundancy of data means duplicate copies and is not the same as different systems exchanging and using data; here the lab results move between providers, which shows interoperability.
Why C: Triage is the sorting of patients by urgency and does not describe computer systems exchanging data; lab results appearing in another system show interoperability, not a triage process.
Why D: Lab results from one hospital appearing in another provider's system shows interoperability, the ability of different health information systems to exchange and use data, which supports coordinated care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which practice best protects patient data?
A: Email records to personal accounts at home or at work
B: Share logins among staff so that anyone can open any chart
C: Leave screens open in public areas so staff can reach records
D: Use unique passwords and limit access to those who need it
Why A: Emailing records to personal accounts moves private data outside secure systems and risks leaks, so it endangers patient data and is not a good protective practice in any workplace.
Why B: Sharing logins hides who accessed which chart and lets anyone open any record, which defeats access control and audit trails, so it does not protect patient data.
Why C: Leaving screens open in public areas lets passersby see private information, so it exposes patient data; screens should be locked or hidden whenever staff step away from them.
Why D: Unique passwords and limited access let only those who need it view records and allow accountable tracking of use, which best protects patient data from misuse or unauthorized viewing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copayment?
A: The insurer's payment to a provider for a service
B: The total monthly premium paid to the insurer
C: A fixed amount a patient pays for a covered service
D: The amount paid before coverage begins, which resets
Why A: The insurer's payment to a provider is a reimbursement, not a copayment, which is a fixed amount that the patient pays directly for a covered service.
Why B: The monthly premium is the regular payment to keep coverage active and is different from a copayment, which is a fixed amount a patient pays for a covered service.
Why C: A copayment is a fixed amount a patient pays for a covered service, such as $20 for a doctor visit, with the insurer paying the remaining allowed cost.
Why D: The amount paid before coverage begins, which resets, is a deductible and not a copayment, which is a set fee paid at each visit for covered services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient has met the deductible. A $1,000 bill has 20% coinsurance. What does the patient owe?
Why A: With the deductible met, 20% coinsurance on a $1,000 bill means the patient pays 0.20 times $1,000, which is $200, and the insurer pays the remaining $800.
Why B: Eight hundred dollars is the insurer's share, since it pays 80% of $1,000; the patient owes only the 20% coinsurance, which is $200, so this reverses the shares.
Why C: One thousand dollars would be the patient's full cost with no coverage, but the deductible is met and coinsurance is 20%, so the patient owes only $200.
Why D: Twenty dollars would be 2% of the bill and misplaces the decimal; 20% of $1,000 is 0.20 times 1,000, which equals $200, not $20.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an HMO?
A: A government hospital run by the state for people in need there as a rule
B: A health plan that usually requires using a network and referrals
C: A type of surgery done to treat a problem in the heart valve
D: A plan with no network of providers, so any doctor may be used
Why A: A government hospital run by the state is a public facility, not an HMO, which is a health plan that usually requires members to use a network and referrals.
Why B: An HMO is a health plan that usually requires using a network of providers and getting referrals to see specialists, which helps control costs through coordinated care.
Why C: A heart valve operation is a surgical procedure and has no link to insurance; an HMO is a health plan that usually requires using a network and referrals.
Why D: A plan with no network describes a free-choice arrangement, but an HMO usually restricts members to a network of providers and requires referrals, so this option reverses the idea.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a PPO?
A: A plan for pets that pays vet bills for dogs, cats and other small animals
B: A health plan offering more freedom to see out-of-network providers at higher cost
C: A plan with no premiums, so members pay nothing for their cover at any time
D: A plan that requires referrals for everything, and covers no care outside its network
Why A: A plan for pets would cover animal care and is unrelated to human health insurance; a PPO is a health plan that offers more freedom to see out-of-network providers at higher cost.
Why B: A PPO is a health plan that gives more freedom to see out-of-network providers at higher cost, usually without needing referrals, in exchange for higher premiums or out-of-pocket costs.
Why C: A plan with no premiums does not exist in a PPO, which charges premiums; its defining feature is freedom to see out-of-network providers at higher cost, not free coverage.
Why D: Requiring referrals and refusing care outside the network describes a strict HMO, which is the opposite of a PPO, since PPO members may see out-of-network providers at higher cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient wants to see specialists without referrals and accepts higher premiums. Which plan fits?
A: A PPO
B: Pet plan
C: An HMO
D: No cover
Why A: A PPO fits, because it lets members see specialists without referrals and use out-of-network providers, and in return members usually accept higher premiums than they would for an HMO.
Why B: A pet plan covers animals and is not a health plan for people, so it cannot cover a patient's specialist visits or meet this patient's needs.
Why C: An HMO usually requires referrals and a network, which is the opposite of what the patient wants; the patient wants specialist access without referrals, which a PPO provides.
Why D: Having no cover would give no insurance help with specialist costs, while the patient is willing to pay higher premiums for coverage, so a PPO fits better.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A claim is denied because of a coding error. What is the best next step?
A: Delete the record of the denied claim
B: Ignore the denial and drop the claim
C: Correct the error and resubmit or appeal
D: Bill the patient for the whole service
Why A: Deleting the record of a denied claim destroys financial documentation and loses the money owed, so it does nothing to fix the coding error that caused the denial.
Why B: Ignoring the denial and dropping the claim means the practice goes unpaid for care it gave, when the denial could be fixed and the claim paid.
Why C: The best next step is to correct the error and resubmit or appeal, because a fixed code lets the insurer process the claim and pay for the service.
Why D: Billing the patient for the whole service is unfair when the denial came from the practice's own coding error, and it may break the insurer contract, so the claim should be fixed first.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are ICD-10 codes used for?
A: Describing procedures
B: Describing room numbers
C: Describing prices only
D: Describing diagnoses
Why A: Describing procedures is the job of CPT codes, not ICD-10; ICD-10 codes describe diagnoses, meaning the diseases and conditions found in a patient, so this swaps the two systems.
Why B: Room numbers are location details inside the facility and have no connection to ICD-10, which is a coding system used for describing diagnoses of patients' illnesses and conditions.
Why C: Prices are not described by ICD-10 codes; they are set in charge lists, while ICD-10 codes describe diagnoses, so the word only does not fit the system.
Why D: ICD-10 codes describe diagnoses, meaning the diseases and conditions found in a patient, and they are used on claims to explain why a service was needed and to track health statistics.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are CPT codes used for?
A: Describing hospital locations and wards overall
B: Describing staff titles and their ranks
C: Describing medical procedures and services
D: Describing diagnoses and health issues
Why A: Hospital locations and wards are described by facility records and not by CPT codes, which are a system for describing medical procedures and services provided to patients.
Why B: Staff titles and ranks are human resources information, not something CPT codes describe; CPT codes describe medical procedures and services provided to patients and billed to insurers.
Why C: CPT codes describe medical procedures and services, such as an office visit or an X-ray, and they appear on claims so insurers know what care was provided.
Why D: Diagnoses and health issues are described by ICD-10 codes, not CPT codes, which describe the medical procedures and services performed, so this option swaps the two coding systems.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does HIPAA protect?
A: The privacy and security of patients' health information
B: The hours of clinics and the days they are open to all
C: The price of drugs sold in pharmacies to the public
D: The salary of staff who work in hospitals and in clinics
Why A: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of patients' health information, setting rules for how it may be used, shared and safeguarded by healthcare providers and their business partners.
Why B: Clinic hours and open days are a matter for each practice to decide, and HIPAA does not regulate them; it protects the privacy and security of patients' health information.
Why C: Drug prices in pharmacies are not set by HIPAA, which instead protects the privacy and security of patients' health information, so this option names a different issue.
Why D: Staff salaries are set by employers and wage laws, not by HIPAA, which protects the privacy and security of patients' health information held by healthcare providers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A receptionist discusses a patient's diagnosis with a friend. Which law is likely violated?
A: FLSA
B: OSHA
C: ADA
D: HIPAA
Why A: FLSA is the Fair Labor Standards Act, covering minimum wage and overtime, so it does not govern discussing patient diagnoses; that act concerns pay and not patient privacy.
Why B: OSHA sets workplace safety standards, such as protection from hazards, and does not govern the privacy of a diagnosis; sharing a patient's diagnosis is a privacy matter.
Why C: The ADA prohibits discrimination based on disability, and discussing a diagnosis with a friend is a privacy breach and not a disability discrimination issue, so it is not the likely violation.
Why D: Discussing a patient's diagnosis with a friend discloses protected health information without permission, which violates HIPAA, the law that protects the privacy and security of patient health information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is OSHA's role in healthcare?
A: Licensing doctors and nurses in each state
B: Setting and enforcing workplace safety standards
C: Setting hospital service prices nationally
D: Running insurance plans for the whole public overall
Why A: State boards license doctors and nurses; OSHA does not license anyone, because its role is setting and enforcing workplace safety standards, so this option names a different agency's duty.
Why B: OSHA's role is setting and enforcing workplace safety standards, including protection from bloodborne pathogens, sharps injuries and hazardous chemicals, so healthcare workers can do their jobs without avoidable harm.
Why C: OSHA does not set hospital prices; service prices come from hospitals, payers and negotiation, while OSHA's role is workplace safety standards, so this option confuses the purpose of the agency.
Why D: Running public insurance plans is the work of agencies like CMS, not OSHA, whose role in healthcare is setting and enforcing workplace safety standards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hospital trains staff on safe handling of sharps and bloodborne pathogens. Which agency's standards most directly drive this?
A: The FTC
B: The IRS
C: OSHA
D: The SEC
Why A: The FTC deals with consumer protection and competition in commerce, so it does not set standards for safe sharps handling; that work belongs to the workplace safety agency, OSHA.
Why B: The IRS administers taxes and does not write rules about sharps or bloodborne pathogens; those workplace safety standards come from OSHA, which also requires staff training.
Why C: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard requires training, protective equipment and safe sharps handling to protect workers, so its standards most directly drive this hospital training on sharps.
Why D: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor protection, so it sets no standards for sharps or bloodborne pathogens; those workplace safety standards come from OSHA.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Affordable Care Act known for?
A: Raising hospital prices by law, so that care costs more for all patients
B: Banning all insurance, so that patients pay for each service in cash alone overall
C: Eliminating Medicare and moving its members to private plans instead of it
D: Expanding health coverage and protections such as covering pre-existing conditions
Why A: The Affordable Care Act did not raise hospital prices by law; it is known for expanding coverage and protections, so this option states the opposite of its purpose.
Why B: The Act did not ban insurance; it expanded health coverage through marketplaces and subsidies, so paying for each service in cash alone is not what it created.
Why C: The Act did not eliminate Medicare, which continued as a public program for older adults; it is known for expanding coverage, so this option wrongly says members moved to private plans.
Why D: The Affordable Care Act is known for expanding health coverage and adding protections such as covering pre-existing conditions, so insurers cannot refuse people because of their prior health problems.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A nurse repeats back a verbal medication order to the physician to confirm it. This practice is called:
A: Coding of the claims
B: Read-back verification
C: Triage of patients
D: Capitation payments
Why A: Coding of claims turns diagnoses and procedures into billing codes and does not involve a nurse repeating an order; this practice is read-back verification, used to confirm verbal orders.
Why B: Repeating back a verbal medication order to the physician is read-back verification, which confirms that the order was heard correctly and prevents medication errors caused by mishearing.
Why C: Triage sorts patients by urgency and has no link to repeating an order; the nurse repeating an order back to confirm it is read-back verification.
Why D: Capitation is a fixed payment per patient and has nothing to do with confirming an order; the nurse repeating an order back to the physician is read-back verification.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cultural competence?
A: Respecting patients' diverse backgrounds, values and beliefs
B: Avoiding patients from other cultures to prevent a clash
C: Learning the medical terms used in each specialty
D: Following one standard script to keep care fair
Why A: Cultural competence is understanding and respecting patients' diverse backgrounds and beliefs, which helps staff communicate well, build trust and give care that fits each patient's values and needs.
Why B: Avoiding patients from other cultures is discriminatory and denies care; cultural competence means understanding and respecting diverse backgrounds, not avoiding people, so this option opposes the concept.
Why C: Medical vocabulary is useful, but it is not cultural competence. Cultural competence means understanding and respecting patients' diverse backgrounds and beliefs.
Why D: A single script ignores differences in language, beliefs and needs. Cultural competence adapts communication and care to fit each patient's background.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A patient speaks limited English. What should a provider do?
A: Use a qualified medical interpreter
B: Skip explaining the treatment fully
C: Speak louder and only in English
D: Use a child to interpret for them
Why A: A qualified medical interpreter translates accurately and keeps information confidential, so the patient understands the care and gives informed consent, which makes this the right step for limited English.
Why B: Skipping the full explanation denies the patient informed consent and risks harm, so it is wrong; a patient with limited English still needs a clear explanation, with an interpreter helping.
Why C: Speaking louder does not help a person who does not understand the words, and English alone leaves the barrier in place, so this fails; a qualified interpreter is needed.
Why D: Using a child to interpret is inappropriate because children may not know medical terms and should not hear private or upsetting information, so a qualified medical interpreter should be used.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is patient-centered care?
A: Care driven by staff convenience, with schedules set to suit workers
B: Care that respects and responds to patients' needs, values and preferences
C: Care organized around insurance coverage and claim approval rules
D: Care planned by the physician and explained after the fact
Why A: Care driven by staff convenience puts workers first and not the patient, so it is the opposite of patient-centered care, which is built around the needs of the patient.
Why B: Patient-centered care respects and responds to patients' needs, values and preferences, which involves patients in decisions and improves satisfaction, trust and outcomes compared with care that ignores their views.
Why C: Organizing care around coverage rules puts payers ahead of the patient. Patient-centered care responds to the patient's needs, values and preferences.
Why D: Explaining a plan after it is set leaves the patient out of the decision. Patient-centered care involves patients in choices as they are made.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patient grievance process?
A: A tax process for hospitals to file returns with the state
B: A hiring process for new staff who join the hospital each year
C: A way for patients to raise complaints and receive responses
D: A way to hide complaints from the board so the record looks clean
Why A: A tax process involves filing returns with the state and has no link to patient complaints; a patient grievance process lets patients raise complaints and receive responses.
Why B: A hiring process brings in new staff and has no link to patient complaints; a patient grievance process is a way for patients to raise complaints and receive responses.
Why C: A patient grievance process is a way for patients to raise complaints and receive responses, which helps the organization fix problems, protect patient rights and improve the quality of care.
Why D: Hiding complaints from the board defeats the purpose of a grievance process, which exists to let patients raise concerns and get responses, so problems can be corrected and not concealed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'appendectomy' mean?
A: Pain in the appendix and gut
B: Inflammation of the appendix
C: Study of the appendix organ here
D: Surgical removal of the appendix
