Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is HCPCS?
A: A staffing rule that sets how many workers each unit must have on every shift of the day
B: A drug approval that lets a company sell a new medicine to the public in the country
C: A code set used to bill for supplies, equipment and services, including Medicare items
D: A hospital rating that shows how patients scored its care and service in a national survey
Why A: A staffing rule on workers per shift is unrelated; HCPCS is a code set used for billing supplies, equipment and services.
Why B: A drug approval lets a company sell a medicine and comes from the FDA, whereas HCPCS is a billing code set.
Why C: HCPCS is a code set used to bill for supplies, equipment and services, including many Medicare items, so this option is correct.
Why D: A hospital rating from a patient survey is a quality score; HCPCS is a coding system used for billing, not a rating.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is upcoding?
A: Updating software on the computers that run a hospital
B: Billing for a more expensive service than was provided
C: Billing correctly for each service that was given
D: Billing for less than the service that was given
Why A: Updating software is an IT task, a pun on the word code; upcoding is a billing fraud practice, not a software update.
Why B: Upcoding means billing for a more expensive service than was actually provided, which is improper and can be fraud, so this is correct.
Why C: Billing correctly for each service given is proper coding, the opposite of upcoding, which inflates charges.
Why D: Billing for less than the service given is undercoding, the reverse of upcoding, which bills for a more expensive service than was provided.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is unbundling?
A: Billing separately for services that should be billed together at a single price
B: Combining services correctly into a single bill at a price set by the insurer
C: Reducing a bill by cutting the charges for the services given to a patient
D: Cancelling a claim after it was sent to the insurer for payment of the services as a rule
Why A: Unbundling means billing separately for services that should be billed together at a single price, which inflates payment and is improper, so this is correct.
Why B: Combining services correctly into one bill at the insurer's set price is proper bundled billing, the opposite of unbundling.
Why C: Reducing a bill by cutting charges is a discount or adjustment, not unbundling, which splits bundled services to charge more.
Why D: Cancelling a claim after sending is a claim void or withdrawal; unbundling is about splitting services that belong together on one bill.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the CMS-1500 form?
A: A tax form that a hospital files each year with the state office
B: An admission form that a patient signs on arrival at a ward desk
C: A consent form that a patient signs before a procedure is done
D: The standard claim form for physician and professional services
Why A: A tax form filed with the state is unrelated; the CMS-1500 is the standard claim form for physician and professional services.
Why B: An admission form signed on arrival records patient registration, whereas the CMS-1500 is a claim form sent to payers.
Why C: A consent form is signed before a procedure for permission; the CMS-1500 is a billing claim form used by professionals.
Why D: The CMS-1500 is the standard claim form for physician and professional services, so this option is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the UB-04 form used for?
A: Physician claims sent to insurers by doctors' offices
B: Institutional claims from hospitals and facilities
C: Patient intake forms filled in at the front desk
D: Tax filings made by hospitals to the revenue office
Why A: Physician claims go on the CMS-1500 form, not the UB-04, which is used by hospitals and facilities for institutional claims.
Why B: The UB-04 is used for institutional claims from hospitals and facilities, so this option is correct.
Why C: Patient intake forms are registration documents, whereas the UB-04 is a billing claim form for institutional providers.
Why D: Tax filings go to the revenue office; the UB-04 is a claim form used by hospitals to bill payers, not a tax document.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a claim denial?
A: An insurer's decision not to pay for a submitted claim
B: A refund paid to a patient after an insurer has paid in full
C: Full payment of a claim sent to an insurer by a provider
D: A partial payment of a claim made by an insurer to a clinic
Why A: A claim denial is an insurer's decision not to pay for a submitted claim, for reasons such as lack of coverage or errors, so this is correct.
Why B: A refund to a patient after full payment is an overpayment return, not a denial, which is a refusal to pay.
Why C: Full payment of a claim is the opposite of denial, since a denial means the insurer declines to pay at all.
Why D: Partial payment means the insurer pays some of the claim, whereas a denial is a refusal to pay any of it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a primary payer?
A: A pharmacy that fills drug orders in town
B: The last payer to settle a claim in turn
C: The insurer responsible for paying first
D: The patient only, who pays the whole bill
Why A: A pharmacy that fills orders is a provider of drugs, not a payer; the primary payer is the insurer responsible for paying first.
Why B: The last payer to settle is a secondary or later payer, while the primary payer pays first, so this reverses the order.
Why C: The primary payer is the insurer responsible for paying first when a patient has more than one source of coverage, so this is correct.
Why D: The patient alone paying the whole bill is self-pay, whereas the primary payer is an insurer that pays before others.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Medicare Part A generally cover?
A: Inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing and hospice
B: Prescription drugs taken by patients at home each day
C: Doctor visits and tests done in an outpatient clinic
D: Dental care and routine checkups for teeth and gums
Why A: Medicare Part A generally covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care and hospice, so this option is correct.
Why B: Prescription drugs taken at home are covered by Part D, not Part A, which covers inpatient and facility based care.
Why C: Doctor visits and outpatient tests are covered by Part B, not Part A, which covers inpatient and facility based care.
Why D: Dental care and routine checkups for teeth are generally not covered by Original Medicare Part A, which covers inpatient hospital care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Medicare Part B generally cover?
A: Long-term care in a nursing home for people who need help
B: Outpatient care, doctor services and preventive services
C: Prescription drugs taken by patients at home each day
D: Hospital stays that last for several nights in a ward
Why A: Long-term nursing home care is largely not covered by Medicare; Part B covers outpatient and preventive services instead.
Why B: Part B generally covers outpatient care, doctor services and preventive services, so this option is correct.
Why C: Prescription drugs taken at home are covered by Part D, not Part B, which covers outpatient and physician services.
Why D: Hospital stays lasting several nights are inpatient care covered by Part A, not Part B, which covers outpatient services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does Medicare Part D cover?
A: Inpatient hospital care
B: Dental exams
C: Outpatient doctor visits
D: Prescription drugs
Why A: Inpatient hospital care is covered by Part A. Part D is the prescription drug benefit, offered through private plans.
Why B: Original Medicare generally does not cover routine dental exams. Part D is the prescription drug benefit, offered through private plans.
Why C: Outpatient doctor visits fall under Part B. Part D is the prescription drug benefit, offered through private plans.
Why D: Medicare Part D covers prescription drugs, offered through private plans, so this option is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is Medicare Advantage (Part C)?
A: A tax credit given to hospitals that treat poor patients
B: A Medicaid program run by each state for people with low pay in general
C: An alternative to Original Medicare offered by private insurers
D: A hospital group that owns and runs clinics in one region
Why A: A tax credit for hospitals is unrelated; Medicare Advantage is an alternative to Original Medicare offered by private insurers.
Why B: A Medicaid program run by states for low-income people is Medicaid, not Medicare Advantage, which is a Medicare option.
Why C: Medicare Advantage, or Part C, is an alternative to Original Medicare offered by private insurers, so this option is correct.
Why D: A hospital group that runs clinics is a health system, not an insurance option; Medicare Advantage is offered by private insurers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is CHIP?
A: The Children's Health Insurance Program covering uninsured children in low-income families
B: A seniors program that pays for care for people who are over sixty-five years of age
C: A computer chip that stores a patient's records inside a device worn on the wrist
D: A drug program that pays for the cost of prescription medicine for adults of all ages overall
Why A: CHIP is the Children's Health Insurance Program covering uninsured children in low-income families, so this option is correct.
Why B: A program for people over sixty-five is Medicare, not CHIP, which is for children in low-income families.
Why C: A wrist computer chip is a literal reading of the acronym; CHIP is a government insurance program for children.
Why D: A drug program for adults of all ages is not CHIP, which covers children in low-income families who lack insurance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is workers' compensation billing?
A: Billing Medicare for care that was given to a patient in a hospital
B: No billing for the care that is given to a patient who has no cover
C: Billing the employer's insurer for treatment of work-related injuries
D: Billing the patient only, with no claim sent to any insurer for payment
Why A: Billing Medicare is for Medicare-covered patients; workers' compensation billing targets the employer's insurer for work-related injuries instead.
Why B: Providing no billing for uninsured patients describes charity care or self-pay; workers' compensation billing sends claims to the employer's insurer.
Why C: Workers' compensation billing sends charges to the employer's insurer for treatment of work-related injuries, so this option is correct.
Why D: Billing only the patient with no insurer claim is self-pay, whereas work injuries are billed to the employer's workers' compensation insurer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a co-insurance example?
A: The yearly deductible that a member pays before cover begins
B: A $25 flat fee per visit paid by the patient at the front desk
C: The monthly premium paid to the insurer to keep a plan active
D: Insurer pays 80% of an allowed charge and the patient pays 20%
Why A: A yearly deductible is an amount paid before coverage begins, not co-insurance, which is a percentage split of costs after that.
Why B: A flat fee per visit is a copayment, a fixed dollar amount, not co-insurance, which is a percentage of cost.
Why C: A monthly premium keeps the plan active and is not shared cost per service, which is what co-insurance is.
Why D: Co-insurance is a percentage split, such as the insurer paying 80% of an allowed charge and the patient 20%, so this is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The allowed amount is $1,000 and coinsurance is 20% after the deductible is met. What does the patient pay?
Why A: $1,000 is the whole allowed amount; with 20% coinsurance, the patient owes only 0.20 times $1,000, which is $200.
Why B: Coinsurance of 20% on an allowed amount of $1,000 means the patient pays 0.20 times $1,000, which equals $200.
Why C: $800 is the insurer's 80% share of the allowed amount, not the patient's; the patient pays the remaining 20%, which is $200.
Why D: $20 would be 20% of $100 or 2% of $1,000; 20% of $1,000 is $200, so $20 is too low.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A procedure is billed at $2,000 but the insurer's allowed amount is $1,200. What is the contractual adjustment?
Why A: $3,200 adds the billed and allowed amounts, which is meaningless; the contractual adjustment is the billed charge minus the allowed amount.
Why B: $2,000 is the billed charge itself, not the write-off; the adjustment is billed minus allowed, $2,000 minus $1,200.
Why C: The contractual adjustment equals billed charge minus allowed amount, so $2,000 minus $1,200 equals $800, which the provider writes off.
Why D: $1,200 is the allowed amount that the insurer and patient pay, not the amount written off; the adjustment is $2,000 minus $1,200, or $800.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the No Surprises Act?
A: A drug law that caps the price of prescription medicine for seniors
B: A federal law protecting patients from many unexpected out-of-network bills
C: A staffing law that limits how many hours nurses can work in a row
D: A federal tax law that sets how much hospitals owe on their yearly income  each year
Why A: Capping drug prices for seniors is a drug pricing law; the No Surprises Act protects patients from unexpected out-of-network bills.
Why B: The No Surprises Act is a federal law protecting patients from many unexpected out-of-network bills, so this option is correct.
Why C: Limiting nurse hours is a staffing law matter, unrelated to billing protections like those in the No Surprises Act.
Why D: A tax law setting hospital income obligations is unrelated; the No Surprises Act limits surprise out-of-network billing for patients.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is days in accounts receivable?
A: The average number of days it takes to collect payment after billing
B: The days patients stay in a hospital ward after surgery or illness overall
C: The days staff work in a pay period at the hospital or clinic site
D: The days that supplies last on the shelves of the ward storeroom
Why A: Days in accounts receivable is the average number of days it takes to collect payment after billing, so this is correct.
Why B: Days patients stay after surgery is length of stay, a clinical measure, while days in AR is a billing collection metric.
Why C: Days staff work in a pay period is a payroll matter, unrelated to how long it takes to collect payments after billing.
Why D: Days supplies last on shelves is an inventory measure, whereas days in accounts receivable measures the speed of collecting payments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a formulary?
A: A list of codes used by billers to send claims out overall
B: A list of doctors who work at a hospital or clinic
C: A list of staff who work on a ward during the week
D: A list of drugs covered by a health plan or facility
Why A: A list of codes for billers is a code set or chargemaster, while a formulary is a list of covered drugs.
Why B: A list of doctors at a hospital is a provider directory, not a formulary, which lists drugs covered by a plan or facility.
Why C: A list of staff on a ward is a roster, whereas a formulary is a list of drugs covered by a plan or facility.
Why D: A formulary is a list of drugs covered by a health plan or facility, so this definition is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a generic drug?
A: A cheaper drug with a weaker dose and fewer safety checks
B: A drug with the same active ingredient as a brand-name drug, often cheaper
C: An unapproved drug that has not been cleared for sale by any agency
D: A medication that is sold over the counter without a doctor's prescription
Why A: Generics must match the brand drug's active ingredient, strength and safety standards, and the FDA reviews them. Lower price does not mean lower quality.
Why B: A generic drug has the same active ingredient as a brand-name drug and is usually cheaper, so this option is correct.
Why C: Generic drugs are approved by the FDA, so calling them unapproved drugs not cleared by any agency is false.
Why D: Over-the-counter status describes how a drug is sold, not what a generic is. A generic shares the active ingredient of a brand-name drug and usually costs less.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is COBRA?
A: A law that gives every worker free health insurance for life after retirement
B: A federal drug program that pays for medicine for low-income families in each state
C: A law letting some workers keep employer health coverage temporarily after leaving a job
D: A law that lets employees pick any doctor they want and skip insurance forms at will as a rule
Why A: COBRA does not provide free insurance for life; it lets workers keep employer coverage temporarily, usually at their own cost.
Why B: A federal drug program for low-income families describes a Medicaid or assistance program, not COBRA, which concerns continuing employer coverage.
Why C: COBRA lets some workers keep employer health coverage temporarily after leaving a job, usually paying the full premium, so this is correct.
Why D: COBRA does not let employees pick any doctor or skip insurance forms; it continues group coverage for a limited time after job loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is HIPAA's Privacy Rule?
A: A rule on drug prices that sets what a pharmacy may charge the public each year in practice
B: A rule on staffing that sets how many nurses must be on each ward at night
C: A rule on billing codes that tells providers which numbers go on a claim form
D: A rule that protects individuals' medical records and personal health information
Why A: Drug price rules are not part of HIPAA; the Privacy Rule protects medical records and personal health information.
Why B: Nurse staffing levels are not set by HIPAA; the Privacy Rule protects the privacy of individuals' health information.
Why C: Billing codes belong to coding standards such as CPT and ICD-10, whereas the HIPAA Privacy Rule protects health information.
Why D: The HIPAA Privacy Rule protects individuals' medical records and personal health information, setting limits on use and disclosure, so this is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a covered entity under HIPAA?
A: A health plan, clearinghouse or provider that transmits health information electronically
B: Any business that has employees and handles customer information in some way or other
C: A patient who receives treatment and signs a consent form at a clinic or hospital
D: A bank or payment processor that handles money for medical offices and hospitals  across the country
Why A: A covered entity is a health plan, clearinghouse or provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with covered transactions, so this is correct.
Why B: Any business with employees is not automatically a covered entity; HIPAA applies to health plans, clearinghouses and certain providers.
Why C: A patient is the person whose information is protected, not a covered entity, which is an organization subject to HIPAA.
Why D: A bank handling payments is generally not a covered entity; covered entities are health plans, clearinghouses and providers who transmit electronic transactions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business associate?
A: A vendor that handles PHI on behalf of a covered entity
B: A bank customer who holds an account at a local bank
C: A patient who is treated at a hospital or a clinic in town
D: A coworker who shares an office or a ward with other staff
Why A: A business associate is a vendor that handles PHI on behalf of a covered entity, and it must follow HIPAA, so this is correct.
Why B: A bank customer is unrelated to HIPAA roles; a business associate is a vendor handling protected health information.
Why C: A patient is an individual receiving care, not a business associate, which is a vendor serving a covered entity.
Why D: A coworker sharing an office is a colleague, not a business associate, which refers to an outside vendor handling PHI.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A billing company processes claims containing PHI for a clinic. What must the clinic have?
A: A parking permit for staff
B: A marketing contract for ads
C: No written agreement at all
D: A business associate agreement
Why A: A parking permit has nothing to do with PHI; when a billing company processes PHI, the clinic must have a business associate agreement.
Why B: A marketing contract for ads does not cover protection of PHI; HIPAA requires a business associate agreement with the billing company.
Why C: Having no written agreement would violate HIPAA, which requires a written contract with any business associate handling PHI.
Why D: HIPAA requires a business associate agreement with a vendor, such as a billing company, that processes PHI for a covered entity, so this is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the HIPAA minimum necessary standard?
A: Sharing with the public any record that a patient has in the chart
B: Sharing nothing ever, so that not even the doctors may read the chart
C: Using or disclosing only the least PHI needed to accomplish a purpose
D: Sharing everything with any person who asks about a patient at any time
Why A: Sharing any record with the public violates the minimum necessary standard, which limits disclosure to the least PHI needed.
Why B: Sharing nothing ever is not the standard; clinicians may read charts to give care, and the rule just limits use to what is needed.
Why C: The minimum necessary standard means using or disclosing only the least PHI needed to accomplish a purpose, so this is correct.
Why D: Sharing everything with anyone who asks violates the standard, which restricts disclosure to the minimum amount needed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When may PHI be disclosed without patient authorization?
A: To the media, whenever a reporter calls the hospital to ask about a patient
B: For treatment, payment and healthcare operations, and as required by law
C: To any curious coworker who asks about a patient they happen to know
D: For marketing by default, whenever a firm wants to send ads to patients
Why A: Telling the media whenever a reporter calls would breach privacy; disclosure to media needs patient authorization.
Why B: PHI may be disclosed without authorization for treatment, payment and healthcare operations, and as required by law, so this option is correct.
Why C: A curious coworker has no need to know, so disclosing a patient's information to them without authorization is a violation.
Why D: Marketing generally requires patient authorization, so disclosing PHI for marketing by default is not allowed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A nurse looks up a celebrity's chart out of curiosity though not involved in the care. This is:
A: A HIPAA violation
B: Required by law
C: Acceptable use
D: Part of treatment
Why A: Looking up a chart without a job-related reason is snooping, which violates HIPAA's minimum necessary and permitted-use rules, so this is correct.
Why B: No law requires a nurse to view a chart of a patient she does not care for; the access is unauthorized.
Why C: Curiosity is not an acceptable reason; access must relate to treatment, payment or operations, so calling it acceptable is wrong.
Why D: Since the nurse is not involved in care, looking at the chart is not part of treatment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule?
A: A rule on hiring that tells hospitals how to recruit and screen workers for open posts
B: A rule on parking that tells visitors where to leave their cars when they come to a hospital
C: A rule on billing that tells providers how to send claims to insurers for each service
D: A rule requiring notice to affected individuals and HHS after a breach of unsecured PHI
Why A: Hiring and recruiting rules are employment matters, not part of the Breach Notification Rule, which requires notice after a breach.
Why B: Parking instructions for visitors have nothing to do with the Breach Notification Rule, which is about notifying people when PHI is breached.
Why C: Billing and claims submission rules are separate from the Breach Notification Rule, which covers notices after a breach of unsecured PHI.
Why D: The Breach Notification Rule requires notice to affected individuals and HHS after a breach of unsecured PHI, so this option is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order?
A: An order to resuscitate a patient in every case, whatever the wishes of the patient
B: A diet order that tells the kitchen which meals a patient may eat each day of a stay
C: An order stating that CPR should not be performed if the heart or breathing stops
D: A discharge order that tells a patient when and how to leave the hospital after care
Why A: An order to resuscitate in every case is a full code, which is the opposite of a DNR order.
Why B: A diet order tells the kitchen what meals a patient may eat, whereas a DNR order concerns CPR.
Why C: A DNR order states that CPR should not be performed if the heart or breathing stops, so this is correct.
Why D: A discharge order tells a patient when and how to leave the hospital, not about CPR, which a DNR order addresses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a healthcare proxy (power of attorney for healthcare)?
A: A billing agent who sends claims to insurers on behalf of a hospital
B: A person designated to make medical decisions for someone unable to do so
C: A pharmacist who fills the prescriptions that doctors write for patients as a rule
D: A staff member who greets visitors and checks them in at the front desk
Why A: A billing agent sends claims for a hospital, a business role, not a healthcare proxy who makes medical decisions for a patient.
Why B: A healthcare proxy is a person designated to make medical decisions for someone unable to do so, so this option is correct.
Why C: A pharmacist fills prescriptions, a clinical job, while a healthcare proxy decides care for a patient who cannot decide.
Why D: A receptionist greets and checks in visitors, an administrative job, not someone appointed to make a patient's medical decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the elements of negligence?
A: Intent, motive, plan and profit overall
B: Price, quality, speed and style
C: Duty, breach, causation and damages
D: Time, date, place and cost of care
Why A: Intent, motive, plan and profit are not elements of negligence, which does not require intent to harm.
Why B: Price, quality, speed and style are business attributes, not the legal elements of negligence.
Why C: The elements of negligence are duty, breach, causation and damages, all of which must be shown, so this is correct.
Why D: Time, date, place and cost of care are facts of a case, not legal elements needed to prove negligence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Stark Law?
A: A law on privacy that decides who may read the records kept for a patient at a hospital
B: A law on drug approval that tests new medicines before they reach the market in the country
C: A law on staffing that sets how many nurses must work on each hospital shift in every state
D: A law restricting physician referrals to entities in which they have a financial interest
Why A: A law on privacy of records is HIPAA, not the Stark Law, which restricts physician referrals with financial ties.
Why B: Drug approval laws fall under the FDA; the Stark Law restricts physician referrals to entities where they have a financial interest.
Why C: Nurse staffing laws are state level and unrelated, while the Stark Law restricts physician self-referrals.
Why D: The Stark Law restricts physician referrals for certain services to entities in which they have a financial interest, so this is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Anti-Kickback Statute?
A: A law prohibiting payments to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business
B: A law on coding that tells billers which numbers to use for services on a claim form
C: A law on staffing that sets how many nurses must work on each shift in a hospital ward
D: A law on privacy that controls who may read a patient's health record in the system
Why A: The Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits payments to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business, so this option is correct.
Why B: Coding instructions for billers are coding guidelines, not the Anti-Kickback Statute, which targets payments for referrals.
Why C: Nurse staffing rules are separate; the Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits payments to induce referrals of federal program business.
Why D: Privacy laws control access to records and are HIPAA, whereas the Anti-Kickback Statute bans payments for referrals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the False Claims Act?
A: A law on privacy that decides who may read the records kept for a patient
B: A law imposing liability on those who submit false claims to the government
C: A law on drug approval that tests new medicines before sale in the country overall
D: A law on staffing that sets how many nurses must work on each ward shift
Why A: A law on privacy of patient records is HIPAA, not the False Claims Act, which imposes liability for false claims.
Why B: The False Claims Act imposes liability on those who submit false claims to the government, with penalties and whistleblower provisions, so this is correct.
Why C: Drug approval laws belong to the FDA; the False Claims Act addresses fraud against government payers.
Why D: Staffing level laws are unrelated, since the False Claims Act addresses false claims for payment submitted to the government.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a compliance program?
A: A sales campaign that offers discounts to attract new customers during the holiday season
B: A hiring plan that explains how many workers a company will recruit in the next year
C: A system of policies and training to ensure an organization follows laws and ethics
D: A marketing plan that sets the message and media for a new product to be sold in shops
Why A: A sales campaign with discounts is marketing, not a compliance program, which ensures an organization follows laws and ethics.
Why B: A hiring plan on recruitment numbers is workforce planning, whereas a compliance program ensures adherence to laws and ethics.
Why C: A compliance program is a system of policies and training to ensure an organization follows laws and ethics, so this is correct.
Why D: A marketing plan for a product is promotional, not compliance, which is about following laws and ethical standards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Office of Inspector General (OIG)?
A: An insurer that pays claims for patients who have a health plan with the firm
B: A drug maker that develops and sells prescription medicine to pharmacies
C: A hospital group that owns and runs several clinics in one region of the country
D: A federal office that investigates fraud, waste and abuse in HHS programs
Why A: An insurer paying claims is a payer; the OIG is a federal office that investigates fraud, waste and abuse.
Why B: A drug maker develops medicines, a business role, while the OIG is a federal office overseeing HHS programs.
Why C: A hospital group running clinics is a health system, not the OIG, which investigates fraud, waste and abuse in HHS programs.
Why D: The Office of Inspector General is a federal office that investigates fraud, waste and abuse in HHS programs, so this is correct.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a pre-existing condition protection under the ACA?
A: Insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more due to health history
B: Insurers can deny coverage to any person who has a past illness or injury
C: It requires no insurance for any person who lives in a state there
D: It applies only to dental care and not to any other kind of care
Why A: ACA protection means insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more due to health history, so this option is correct.
Why B: The ACA bars denial for past illness or injury, so claiming insurers can deny coverage for pre-existing conditions is the opposite.
Why C: The ACA does not eliminate insurance for state residents; pre-existing condition protection is about coverage for people with health history.
Why D: The protection is not limited to dental care; it applies to health coverage generally, not only one kind of care.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the individual mandate under the ACA?
A: A requirement to buy drugs from a pharmacy in the town where the patient lives
B: A requirement to have coverage, with the tax penalty reduced to zero in 2019
C: A requirement to see a doctor each year for a full check-up of the body and mind
D: A requirement to work for a set number of hours each week in a job site
Why A: The individual mandate concerned holding health insurance coverage, not where a patient buys drugs, and the ACA set no rule tying prescriptions to a local pharmacy.
Why B: The ACA individual mandate required most people to hold health coverage or pay a tax penalty, and Congress reduced that penalty to zero beginning in 2019.
Why C: The mandate never required annual check-ups; preventive visits are a covered benefit patients may choose to use, while the mandate itself only concerned holding insurance coverage.
Why D: Work hour requirements belong to some Medicaid rules, not the individual mandate, which only required people to carry health insurance coverage or pay a penalty.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is certificate of need (CON)?
A: A state requirement that providers get approval before building or expanding facilities
B: A drug approval that lets a company sell a new medicine to the public in the country as a rule
C: A staff license that lets a person work as a nurse or as a doctor in a hospital
D: A patient permission slip that is signed before a procedure is done on a ward
Why A: Certificate of need is a state process requiring providers to win approval before building, expanding or buying major equipment, which aims to limit duplicated services and rising costs.
Why B: Approval to sell a new drug comes from the FDA through its drug review, which is a separate federal process and has nothing to do with certificate of need.
Why C: A nurse or doctor is licensed by a state board, which grants personal practice permission, whereas certificate of need applies to facilities and projects instead of individual workers.
Why D: A signed patient permission slip describes informed consent for a procedure, which is an individual patient matter and not the state facility approval known as certificate of need.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a state medical license?
A: A drug approval given to a new medicine by the FDA
B: A hospital permit that lets a building be used for care
C: A billing number that names a provider on a claim form
D: Official permission from a state to practice medicine
Why A: Drug approval for new medicines is granted by the FDA, which is a federal agency, while a state medical license is permission given to a physician to practice.
Why B: A hospital permit is a facility license for a building, but a state medical license is granted to an individual physician rather than to any building.
Why C: A billing number such as an NPI identifies a provider on claims, but it does not give legal permission to practice medicine, which a license does.
Why D: A state medical license is the official permission a state board grants a physician to practice medicine within that state, after meeting education, exam and character requirements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patient's right to access their medical records under HIPAA?
A: Patients cannot see their records, as the hospital owns them alone
B: Patients can generally inspect and obtain copies of their records
C: Only doctors can see them, and patients may never view them at all
D: Records belong to the public and anyone may ask to read them
Why A: HIPAA gives patients a right to see their records, so the claim that the hospital owns them and bars patients from viewing them is wrong.
Why B: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, patients generally have a right to inspect their records and obtain copies, with limited exceptions such as some psychotherapy notes.
Why C: HIPAA does not limit record access to doctors, because patients are given a right to inspect and get copies of their own records.
Why D: Medical records are protected health information under HIPAA, so they are not public property and strangers cannot demand to read them without proper authorization.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Patient Self-Determination Act?
A: A law on billing that tells hospitals how to charge patients and insurers for each service
B: A law on drug prices that limits what pharmacies can charge for medicine in the whole country
C: A law requiring facilities to inform patients of their decision rights and advance directives
D: A law on staffing that sets the number of nurses for each hospital ward in the country
Why A: Billing rules are set by other laws and payer contracts, while the Patient Self-Determination Act is about informing patients of their rights to accept or refuse treatment.
Why B: The Act has nothing to do with pharmacy drug price limits; it concerns patient rights, not what pharmacies charge for medicine across the country.
Why C: The Patient Self-Determination Act requires facilities that receive Medicare or Medicaid funds to tell patients about their rights to make decisions and to use advance directives.
Why D: Nurse staffing ratios are set by state laws or hospital policy, not by the Patient Self-Determination Act, which is about patient decision rights.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Controlled Substances Act?
A: A law on billing that tells hospitals how to charge patients for care
B: A law on hospital staffing that sets how many nurses work on each ward as a rule
C: A law on privacy that decides who may read a patient's record file
D: A law regulating manufacture and distribution of drugs with abuse potential
Why A: Billing rules come from other laws, whereas the Controlled Substances Act regulates the making, distribution and possession of drugs that have a potential for abuse.
Why B: Nurse staffing levels are not covered by the Controlled Substances Act, which deals with drug control and not with how many nurses work on a ward.
Why C: Patient record privacy is governed by HIPAA, not the Controlled Substances Act, which concerns drugs that carry abuse or dependence risks rather than who may read a record.
Why D: The Controlled Substances Act sets federal rules for manufacturing, distributing and dispensing drugs with abuse potential, sorting them into five schedules according to risk and medical use.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which drug schedule has the highest potential for abuse and no accepted medical use?
A: Schedule I
B: Schedule IV
C: Schedule V
D: Schedule III
Why A: Schedule I drugs have the highest abuse potential and no accepted medical use under federal law, with heroin and LSD as examples.
Why B: Schedule IV drugs have a low abuse potential and do have accepted medical uses, such as certain sleep and anxiety medicines, so they do not fit this description.
Why C: Schedule V drugs have the lowest abuse potential of the scheduled groups and accepted medical uses, such as some cough preparations, so they cannot be the highest risk.
Why D: Schedule III drugs have moderate abuse potential and accepted medical uses, such as some anabolic steroid products, so they do not match the highest risk with no medical use.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is mandatory reporting in healthcare?
A: Reporting to friends and family about the cases that a nurse sees at work
B: A legal duty to report certain situations such as suspected child abuse
C: Reporting to the media about the cases of patients seen at the hospital
D: Optional gossip about the cases that staff see on the wards each day
Why A: Telling friends and family about cases breaks patient privacy, and mandatory reporting means a legal duty to report to authorities, not to private contacts.
Why B: Mandatory reporting is a legal duty placed on certain professionals to report situations such as suspected child abuse, elder abuse or some diseases to the proper authorities.
Why C: Telling the media about patients violates confidentiality, whereas mandatory reporting sends specific legal information to designated agencies rather than to the press.
Why D: Gossip about cases is a privacy breach and never optional, while mandatory reporting is a legal requirement that sends specific concerns to proper authorities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is active listening important in healthcare?
A: It replaces documentation of the care that is given to patients
B: It avoids patient questions so that visits are over more quickly
C: It helps staff understand patient needs and prevents errors
D: It shortens visits at all costs, so more patients are seen
Why A: Documentation is still required for care given, and listening does not replace it; active listening helps staff understand what patients need and say.
Why B: Active listening invites patient questions and does not avoid them, so it does not work to end visits quickly but to improve understanding.
Why C: Active listening helps staff truly understand patient needs, concerns and instructions, which builds trust and prevents errors such as missed symptoms or misunderstood directions.
Why D: Active listening does not aim to shorten visits at any cost, since rushing causes missed information and errors that listening is meant to prevent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is empathy?
A: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
B: Ignoring emotions and focusing only on facts and on tasks
C: Giving orders to patients and to staff on the ward
D: Feeling sorry in pity for another person in need
Why A: Empathy is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings, which helps staff connect with patients and respond to their emotional needs.
Why B: Ignoring emotions to focus on tasks is the opposite of empathy, because empathy requires noticing and responding to how a person feels.
Why C: Giving orders is a form of directing others, not empathy, which means understanding and sharing feelings instead of commanding patients or staff.
Why D: Feeling pity is sympathy, which looks down on someone from a distance, whereas empathy means sharing and understanding the other person's feelings from their view.

Question: Which approach best helps a patient with low health literacy?
A: Giving a detailed pamphlet with technical terms
B: Speaking quickly to save time during each visit

D: Using plain language and the teach-back method
Why A: Technical pamphlets are hard for patients with low health literacy to follow. Plain language and teach-back confirm real understanding.
Why B: Speaking quickly gives a patient with low health literacy less time to take in information, so it hurts understanding even if it saves time.
Why C: Volume does not improve understanding of complex terms. Plain language and teach-back address low health literacy directly.
Why D: Plain language avoids jargon, and teach-back asks the patient to repeat instructions in their own words, which confirms real understanding for patients with low health literacy.

Question: What is cultural competence in healthcare?
A: Treating all patients identically, whatever their background, beliefs or language
B: Speaking one language only, and using it with all patients on the ward
C: Providing care that respects patients' cultural beliefs, values and languages
D: Ignoring culture and treating each patient in the same way each day there
Why A: Treating everyone identically ignores differences in belief and language, so it is not cultural competence, which adapts care to each patient's background.
Why B: Using only one language with every patient excludes those who speak another language, whereas cultural competence includes using interpreters and respecting language needs.
Why C: Cultural competence means giving care that respects patients' cultural beliefs, values and languages, so that care fits who they are and is understood.
Why D: Ignoring culture treats everyone the same way and misses beliefs that affect care, so it is the opposite of cultural competence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When should a qualified medical interpreter be used?

Why A: A longer visit does not solve a language barrier. A qualified interpreter is used when a patient has limited English proficiency.
Why B: A qualified medical interpreter should be used when a patient has limited English proficiency, so that instructions, consent and symptoms are conveyed accurately and completely.
Why C: Anxiety calls for reassurance and clear explanation, not an interpreter. Interpreters are used when a language barrier affects communication.
Why D: Relatives may mistranslate or omit details and can compromise privacy. Qualified interpreters give accurate, complete communication.

Question: What is SBAR?

Why B: SBAR is a structured communication tool standing for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation, used to pass clear and concise patient information between clinicians.
Why C: SBAR is not a drug name used for orders, since it is a communication format and has nothing to do with medications or prescriptions.
Why D: Billing codes such as CPT identify services for insurers, but SBAR is a communication format for handing patient information between clinicians, not a code.

Question: What is a chain of communication problem?

Why C: A phone cord is a physical device, not a communication problem, while a chain of communication problem concerns messages being changed as they pass between people.

Question: What is transformational leadership?
A: Rewarding staff with pay for meeting set targets and punishing misses
B: Letting the group vote on each decision with equal say
C: Inspiring followers with a vision to exceed expectations and drive change
D: Ignoring staff and leaving them to work without any lead or support
Why A: Reward and punishment for targets is transactional leadership. Transformational leaders inspire staff with a vision and encourage them to exceed expectations.
Why B: Group voting describes a democratic style. Transformational leaders inspire followers with a vision and drive change.
Why C: Transformational leadership inspires followers with a vision so they exceed expectations, and it drives change by motivating people instead of relying on orders and rules.
Why D: Ignoring staff and offering no support is laissez-faire neglect, while transformational leaders actively engage, motivate and develop their teams toward a vision.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is servant leadership?
A: Serving food to the patients and staff in a hospital cafeteria
B: Demanding obedience from staff and giving no reasons for any order
C: Avoiding responsibility for the work and the results of the team
D: Leading by prioritizing the needs and growth of team members
Why A: Serving food in a cafeteria is a job, not a leadership style, whereas servant leadership means leaders put the needs of their team first.
Why B: Demanding obedience without explaining orders is autocratic leadership, the opposite of servant leadership, which puts team needs and growth ahead of the leader's authority.
Why C: Avoiding responsibility is poor leadership, while servant leaders accept responsibility and work to support their team so that people can do their best work.
Why D: Servant leadership means leading by putting the needs and growth of team members first, so the leader serves the team and helps people develop and succeed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an autocratic leadership style?
A: The team votes on everything and the leader counts
B: No direction at all is given to the staff by the leader
C: The leader makes decisions alone with little input
D: Decisions by consensus of the whole team after talk
Why A: A team voting on everything describes democratic leadership, where the leader counts votes, whereas an autocratic leader decides alone without seeking much input from the group.
Why B: Giving no direction describes laissez-faire leadership, not autocratic, because an autocratic leader gives firm direction and issues orders.
Why C: An autocratic leadership style means the leader makes decisions alone with little or no input from the team, and expects staff to follow the instructions given.
Why D: Decisions made by consensus of the whole team describe participative or democratic leadership, which is the opposite of an autocratic leader deciding alone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a laissez-faire leadership style?
A: Leaders give team members freedom to make decisions with little direction
B: A leader who rewards good results and corrects mistakes with penalties
C: A leader who inspires staff with a shared vision of change
D: Voting on all choices, with each member of the team having a single vote
Why A: Laissez-faire leaders give team members freedom to make their own decisions with little direction, which suits skilled and self-motivated staff but can leave a team without guidance.
Why B: Rewards and penalties describe transactional leadership. A laissez-faire leader steps back and gives team members freedom with little direction.
Why C: Inspiring through a shared vision is transformational leadership. Laissez-faire means leaving decisions to the team with little direction.
Why D: Voting on all choices describes a democratic style, while laissez-faire leaders leave decisions to team members without formal votes and give little direction.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Two nurses disagree about shift coverage. What is the best first step for their manager?
A: Post the dispute publicly so nurses can take sides

D: Meet with both to listen and find a fair solution
Why A: Posting a dispute publicly invites side-taking and embarrasses staff, which makes the conflict worse instead of resolving it, so it is not a good first step.
Why B: Punishing both nurses without hearing either side is unfair and ignores the facts, so it could add resentment and does nothing to solve the coverage problem.
Why C: Ignoring a conflict rarely makes it disappear and may let it grow, so a manager should address it early rather than hoping it resolves itself.
Why D: The best first step is to meet with both nurses, listen to each view and work toward a fair solution, which handles the disagreement respectfully and constructively.

Question: What is a code of ethics in healthcare?

C: A billing code that names a service on a claim form

Why C: A billing code names a service on a claim for payment, so it concerns finances and not the moral principles that make up a code of ethics.
Why D: A dress code covers what staff wear, which is a workplace policy on appearance, whereas a code of ethics guides moral and professional conduct.

Question: What does beneficence mean in medical ethics?
A: Avoiding all treatment, so that no risk is run
B: Acting in the best interest of the patient
C: Saving costs for the hospital each year
D: Following orders only, with no thought of care
Why A: Avoiding all treatment to prevent risk would deny patients needed care, whereas beneficence means actively doing good, so it does not equal withholding care.
Why B: Beneficence means acting in the best interest of the patient, doing good and promoting well being, which is a core principle of medical ethics.
Why C: Saving hospital costs is a financial goal and may conflict with patient welfare, whereas beneficence concerns the patient's good rather than the hospital's savings.
Why D: Following orders without thinking about care ignores patient welfare, while beneficence requires thoughtful action that aims at the good of the patient.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does nonmaleficence mean?
A: Do all asked
B: Do most tasks
C: Do no harm
D: Do nothing
Why A: Doing everything asked would sometimes cause harm, so it is not the meaning of nonmaleficence, which sets a limit by forbidding harm to patients.
Why B: Doing most tasks has nothing to do with harm, so it does not capture the meaning of nonmaleficence, which concerns avoiding injury to patients.
Why C: Nonmaleficence means do no harm, so health workers must avoid actions that injure patients, and it is among the core principles of medical ethics.
Why D: Doing nothing can itself harm a patient who needs care, so nonmaleficence means avoiding harm and does not mean taking no action at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does patient autonomy mean?
A: Staff decide for patients about their care and treatment plans
B: The duty of staff to do no harm to the patient
C: The duty to treat patients fairly and share resources equitably
D: The patient's right to make informed decisions about their care
Why A: Staff deciding for patients describes paternalism, which is the opposite of autonomy, where patients choose after receiving information about their care and options.
Why B: Doing no harm is the principle of nonmaleficence. Autonomy is the patient's right to make informed decisions about care.
Why C: Fair treatment is the principle of justice. Autonomy is the patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care.
Why D: Patient autonomy is the right of the patient to make their own informed decisions about care, which is why consent and refusal must be respected.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does justice mean in medical ethics?
A: Fair distribution of healthcare resources and treatment
B: Courtroom punishment given by a judge after a trial in court
C: Treating only some people and leaving the rest without care
D: Giving more care to the wealthy than to patients who wait
Why A: Justice in medical ethics means the fair distribution of healthcare resources and treatment, so that patients are treated equitably and burdens and benefits are shared fairly.
Why B: Courtroom punishment is a legal idea, but justice in medical ethics is about fairness in distributing care and resources, not about trials or penalties.
Why C: Treating only some people and leaving others without care is unfair, so it is the opposite of the justice principle, which requires fairness for all.
Why D: Giving more care to the wealthy is unfair favoritism, whereas justice in medical ethics requires that resources be shared fairly, regardless of wealth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patient advocate?
A: A pharmacist who fills the prescriptions that doctors write for patients

C: A billing collector who contacts patients about the bills they still owe
D: Someone who helps patients understand their rights and resolve concerns
Why A: A pharmacist fills prescriptions, which is a dispensing role, whereas a patient advocate helps patients understand their rights and sort out problems with their care.
Why B: A security guard protects the building and people inside, so that role is safety and not helping patients with their rights, which is advocate work.
Why C: A billing collector pursues payment on unpaid accounts, which serves the hospital's finances, while a patient advocate supports patients in understanding rights and resolving concerns.
Why D: A patient advocate helps patients understand their rights, speak up and resolve concerns about their care, serving as a guide and voice inside the system.

Question: What does patient experience measure?

Why C: A billing code names a service on a claim, but HCAHPS is a patient survey, so it is not a code of any kind.

Question: What is root cause analysis?
A: Blaming an individual for the error and giving them a penalty
B: Dismissing an event as a one-off and taking no further action
C: A structured process to find underlying causes of an error or event
D: Planting trees on the grounds of the hospital for shade and calm in general
Why A: Blaming an individual and penalizing them ignores system problems, whereas root cause analysis searches for underlying system causes of an error rather than seeking someone to punish.
Why B: Dismissing an event as a one-off means no learning, but root cause analysis digs into why an event happened so it can be prevented.
Why C: Root cause analysis is a structured process for finding the underlying causes of an error or adverse event, so that fixes can prevent it from recurring.
Why D: Planting trees on hospital grounds is landscaping, so it has no link to the study of why errors or adverse events occur.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a just culture in healthcare?
A: Punishing all errors in the same way, whatever their cause or the intent of the staff overall
B: An environment balancing accountability with learning from errors without blaming unfairly
C: Ignoring errors that occur on the wards and taking no steps to learn from them at all
D: Hiding errors from the managers and from the patients so the record looks clean
Why A: Punishing every error alike ignores intent and cause, so it is not a just culture, which separates honest mistakes from reckless behavior and treats each fairly.
Why B: A just culture balances accountability with learning from errors, so staff report mistakes openly and are not blamed unfairly, while reckless behavior is still addressed.
Why C: Ignoring errors prevents learning and leaves risks in place, so it is not a just culture, which investigates errors to improve safety.
Why D: Hiding errors prevents learning and endangers patients, whereas a just culture encourages open reporting so that mistakes can be reviewed and corrected.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an incident report?
A: A lab result that shows the levels of chemicals in a patient's blood
B: A billing statement sent to a patient to show the charges for care
C: A document recording an unusual event involving a patient or staff
D: A staff review of the work done by a nurse over the past year there
Why A: A lab result reports chemical levels in blood, which is a clinical test report, not an incident report, which documents unusual events.
Why B: A billing statement shows charges for care and requests payment, so it is a financial document and not an incident report about an unusual event.
Why C: An incident report is a document recording an unusual event involving a patient or staff, such as a fall or medication error, so the facts can be reviewed.
Why D: A yearly review of a nurse's work is a performance evaluation, and it is not an incident report, which records a specific unusual event.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-ology' mean?
A: The study of

Question: What does the root 'oste' refer to?

Question: What does the root 'derm' refer to?
A: Eye

Question: What does the root 'gastr' refer to?
A: Liver
B: Lung
C: Stomach
D: Brain
Why A: Liver is named by the root hepat, as in hepatitis, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.
Why B: Lung is named by the root pulmon or pneumon, as in pulmonary, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.
Why C: The root gastr refers to the stomach, as in gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach, and gastroenterology, the study of the digestive tract.
Why D: Brain is named by the root cerebr or encephal, as in encephalitis, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.

Question: What does 'tachycardia' mean?
A: A normal heart rate today
B: An abnormally fast heart rate
C: No heartbeat at all in the heart
D: A slow heart rate below sixty
Why A: A normal heart rate is not tachycardia, because the root tachy means fast, so tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate instead of a normal one.
Why B: Tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate, usually above 100 beats per minute at rest, from tachy for fast and cardia for heart.
Why C: No heartbeat is called asystole or cardiac arrest, whereas tachycardia means a fast heart rate, so the heart is still beating.
Why D: A slow heart rate below sixty is bradycardia, from brady for slow, and so it is the opposite of tachycardia, which is fast.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'bradycardia' mean?
A: A normal heart rate today
B: No heartbeat at all in the heart
C: A fast heart rate above a hundred
D: An abnormally slow heart rate
Why A: A normal heart rate is not bradycardia, because brady means slow, so bradycardia refers to an abnormally slow heart rate instead of a normal one.
Why B: No heartbeat is asystole or cardiac arrest, whereas bradycardia means a slow heart rate, which means the heart is still beating.
Why C: A fast heart rate above a hundred is tachycardia, from tachy for fast, and it is the opposite of bradycardia, which is slow.
Why D: Bradycardia means an abnormally slow heart rate, usually under 60 beats per minute at rest, from brady for slow and cardia for heart.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'dyspnea' mean?
A: Difficult or labored breathing
B: Normal breathing at rest in adults

D: No breathing at all in the patient
Why A: Dyspnea means difficult or labored breathing, from dys for difficult or painful and pnea for breathing, and patients often describe it as shortness of breath.
Why B: Normal breathing is called eupnea, from eu for good, and not dyspnea, which refers to breathing that is difficult or labored.
Why C: Fast breathing is called tachypnea, from tachy for fast, and not dyspnea, which refers to difficult or labored breathing.
Why D: No breathing at all is called apnea, from a for without, and not dyspnea, which refers to difficult or labored breathing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'hematoma' mean?
A: A skin rash that appears on the arms and legs
B: A tumor of bone found by an X-ray scan

D: A heart murmur heard through a stethoscope
Why A: A skin rash is an eruption of the skin, whereas a hematoma is a collection of blood, from hemat for blood and oma for mass.

Why C: A hematoma is a collection of blood outside blood vessels, such as a bruise or a larger pool of blood under the skin or in tissue.
Why D: A heart murmur is a sound heard with a stethoscope, whereas a hematoma is a pool of blood in the tissue that forms after a vessel leaks.

Question: What does 'NPO' stand for on a patient order?
A: Nothing by mouth
B: Needs pain overview
C: Normal patient care
D: Nurse patient order
Why A: NPO stands for nil per os, a Latin phrase meaning nothing by mouth, an order given before surgery or tests so the stomach is empty.
Why B: Needs pain overview is not a real meaning of NPO, which is a Latin abbreviation, nil per os, meaning nothing by mouth.
Why C: Normal patient care is not what NPO stands for, since it comes from the Latin nil per os and means nothing by mouth.
Why D: Nurse patient order is an invented expansion, because NPO comes from the Latin nil per os, meaning that the patient may take nothing by mouth.

Question: What does 'STAT' mean in medical orders?
A: Sometime today
B: Statistics
C: Standard time
D: Immediately
Why A: Sometime today is far too loose for STAT, which comes from the Latin statim and means to act immediately, with no delay.
Why B: STAT does not mean statistics, since it comes from the Latin statim, meaning immediately, and it flags an order that must be done at once.
Why C: Standard time suggests ordinary routine timing, but STAT comes from statim and signals urgency, meaning the order must be carried out immediately.
Why D: STAT comes from the Latin statim and means immediately, so a STAT order must be carried out at once, usually in an emergency or urgent situation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'PRN' mean?
A: After surgery
B: Before meals
C: As needed
D: Every night

Why C: PRN comes from the Latin pro re nata and means as needed, so a PRN medication is given only when the patient requires it, such as for pain.

Question: What does 'BID' mean in prescriptions?
A: Four a day
B: Twice a day
C: Three a day
D: Once a day

Why C: Three a day is abbreviated TID, from ter in die, and not BID, which stands for bis in die, meaning twice a day.

Question: What does 'TID' mean in prescriptions?

Why C: Once a day is written QD or daily. TID comes from ter in die and means three times a day.

Question: The Joint Commission's 'Do Not Use' list includes which abbreviation?
A: BP, which is used for blood pressure readings
B: mg, the standard abbreviation for milligrams
C: U for units, which can be mistaken for 0 or 4
D: mL, which is used to show a volume in milliliters
Why A: BP is a standard abbreviation for blood pressure that is widely used and is not on the Do Not Use list, which names error-prone shorthand.

Why D: The abbreviation mL for milliliters is standard and accepted, and it is not on the Do Not Use list, which names only error-prone abbreviations.

Question: What are vital signs?
A: Billing codes that describe the services that a provider performed during a visit to a clinic overall
B: Patient names and dates of birth that are written on every page of the chart and on bills
C: Laboratory results that are collected from blood tests ordered by a doctor and sent home
D: Measurements of basic body functions such as temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure
Why A: Billing codes describe services for insurers, and they are not vital signs, which are measurements of the body's basic functions taken at each visit.
Why B: Names and birth dates identify the patient and are not vital signs, which are measurements of basic body function, such as pulse and temperature.
Why C: Laboratory results come from tests of blood and other specimens, and they are not vital signs, which are quick bedside measurements of basic body function.
Why D: Vital signs are measurements of basic body functions, namely temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure, and they give a quick picture of a patient's health.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a typical normal adult resting pulse range?
A: 120 to 160 beats a minute
B: 60 to 100 beats per minute
C: 20 to 40 beats a minute
D: 200 to 250 beats a minute
Why A: A pulse of 120 to 160 beats a minute is tachycardia in an adult at rest, so it is far above the normal range.
Why B: A normal adult resting pulse ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute, and below 60 is bradycardia while above 100 is tachycardia.
Why C: A pulse of 20 to 40 beats a minute is severe bradycardia, far below the normal adult resting range of 60 to 100.
Why D: A pulse of 200 to 250 beats a minute is dangerously fast and far above the normal adult resting range of 60 to 100.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a typical normal adult body temperature?
A: About 98.6°F (37°C)
B: About 88°F or less
C: About 108°F or more
D: About 78°F or less
Why A: A typical normal adult body temperature is about 98.6 degrees F, or 37 degrees C, though healthy people vary slightly around this figure.
Why B: A temperature of about 88 degrees F or less is severe hypothermia, which is a medical emergency and far below normal.
Why C: A temperature of about 108 degrees F or more is a life threatening hyperpyrexia, far above the normal body temperature of about 98.6 degrees F.
Why D: A temperature of about 78 degrees F or less is extreme hypothermia, far below the normal body temperature of about 98.6 degrees F.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a blood pressure reading of 120/80 represent?
A: Height over weight in feet and inches
B: Pulse over respiration at the bedside
C: Systolic over diastolic pressure in mm Hg
D: Age over weight in years and in pounds overall
Why A: Height and weight are body measurements, but a reading of 120/80 is blood pressure, so the number is not a height over weight ratio.
Why B: Pulse and respiration are other vital signs, but they are not written as a fraction; 120/80 is a blood pressure reading.
Why C: A blood pressure reading of 120/80 represents systolic pressure over diastolic pressure, measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg), the pressure when the heart beats and rests.
Why D: Age and weight are not written as a fraction in a reading, since 120/80 is a blood pressure measured in mm Hg, not age over weight.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the first step in the patient check-in process?
A: Sending the bill to the insurer or the patient
B: Verifying identity and insurance information
C: Ordering tests of the blood and other fluids
D: Discharging the patient after the treatment
Why A: Sending the bill comes after care is delivered, so it cannot be the first step at check-in, which starts with confirming who the patient is.
Why B: The first step in check-in is verifying the patient's identity and insurance information, which ensures the right chart is used and that billing is correct later.
Why C: Ordering tests of blood and other fluids happens during care, after check-in and the provider's assessment, so it cannot be the first step of check-in.
Why D: Discharging the patient happens at the end of the visit, so it cannot be the first step of the check-in process.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a patient's chief complaint?
A: To record staff concerns about the work and the hours on the ward
B: To record billing disputes between a patient and the insurer or the hospital
C: To record insurance details such as the plan, the member number and the group
D: To record the main reason the patient is seeking care in their own words
Why A: Staff concerns about work and hours are an employment matter and not recorded in a chief complaint, which captures the reason the patient came.
Why B: Billing disputes are handled by the business office and are not documented as a chief complaint, which records why the patient is seeking care.
Why C: Insurance details are registration data and not the chief complaint, which states the main reason the patient is seeking care.
Why D: The chief complaint records the main reason the patient is seeking care, ideally in the patient's own words, and it guides the rest of the visit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the SOAP note format?
A: Staff, Office, Admin and Policy headings
B: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
C: Sign, Order, Act, Pay for the care
D: Scan, Open, Add, Print for the chart
Why A: Staff, Office, Admin and Policy are not SOAP headings; SOAP is a clinical note format with sections for the patient's findings and plan.
Why B: SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan, a standard format for organizing clinical notes so that information is recorded in a consistent order.
Why C: Sign, Order, Act and Pay do not describe a clinical note; SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan.
Why D: Scan, Open, Add and Print describe office computer tasks and not a clinical note; SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a SOAP note, which section includes the patient's description of symptoms?
A: Subjective
B: Assessment
C: Objective
D: Plan only
Why A: The Subjective section records what the patient says, such as symptoms, history and complaints, in the patient's own description of how they feel.
Why B: The Assessment section holds the provider's diagnosis or impression after reviewing the findings, not the patient's own description of symptoms, which is the subjective part.
Why C: The Objective section holds measurable findings such as vital signs, exam results and labs, not the patient's own description of symptoms, which is subjective.
Why D: The Plan section lists the treatment and follow up steps, so it does not contain the patient's description of symptoms, which belongs in the Subjective section.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a SOAP note, which section includes lab results and vital signs?
A: Plan only
B: Subjective
C: Assessment
D: Objective
Why A: The Plan section lists treatment and follow up steps, so it does not hold lab results or vital signs, which are objective findings.
Why B: The Subjective section holds what the patient reports, so lab results and vital signs, which are measured data, do not belong there.
Why C: The Assessment section holds the provider's diagnosis or impression, so lab results and vital signs, which are measured data, are listed elsewhere.
Why D: The Objective section includes measurable data such as vital signs, physical exam findings and lab results, which are facts that can be observed or measured.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is appointment scheduling 'double booking'?
A: Booking a room twice for cleaning so it is ready
B: Booking two offices at the same time for the same doctor
C: Scheduling more than one patient in the same time slot
D: Booking staff only, with no patients put in the slots
Why A: Booking a room twice for cleaning is a facilities matter and not the scheduling term double booking, which concerns patients sharing a time slot.
Why B: Booking two offices for the same doctor is not double booking, which means placing more than one patient into the same appointment time slot.
Why C: Double booking means scheduling more than one patient in the same time slot, which is sometimes used to allow for no shows but can cause long waits.
Why D: Booking staff with no patients is not double booking, which describes more than one patient assigned to the same appointment time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a filing system that arranges records by last name called?
A: Alphabetic filing
B: Numeric filing
C: Geographic filing
D: Chronological filing
Why A: Alphabetic filing arranges records by last name, then first name, in alphabet order, so a record is found by looking up the patient's name.
Why B: Numeric filing arranges records by assigned numbers, not by name, so it is not the system that sorts by last name.
Why C: Geographic filing arranges records by location such as city or region, not by last name, so it does not match the description.
Why D: Chronological filing arranges records by date, not by last name, so it does not match a system that sorts by patient surname.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a numeric filing system?
A: Records filed by color of the folder
B: Records are filed by assigned numbers
C: Records filed by date of the visit
D: Records filed by name of the patient
Why A: Folder color is used in color coded systems and not in a numeric system, which arranges records by assigned numbers.
Why B: A numeric filing system files records by assigned numbers, such as a chart number given to each patient, and it needs an index to find a name.
Why C: Filing by date of visit is chronological filing, not numeric filing, which arranges records by assigned numbers.
