D: Prepares medicines for the patients on the wards as ordered by the doctors
Why A: Cleaning rooms and halls of the wards is the work of environmental services staff. A patient access representative works at registration, so cleaning after each shift is not part of the job.
Why B: Performing tests on blood and other samples is done by laboratory staff. A patient access representative handles registration and insurance, so running tests on patient samples is not a duty of the role.
Why C: A patient access representative registers patients, verifies their insurance and collects the information needed at admission, which sets up the account and records so care and billing can follow smoothly afterward.
Why D: Preparing medicines for the wards is done by pharmacists and pharmacy technicians. A patient access representative works on registration and insurance, and has no part in preparing or giving drugs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the Medicare Conditions of Participation?
A: Rules for staff uniforms that tell nurses and doctors what to wear on the wards
B: Rules for patients' diets that set the meals and foods served on the hospital wards as a rule
C: Rules for parking that tell visitors and staff where they may leave their cars
D: Federal health and safety standards that hospitals must meet to take part in Medicare
Why A: Staff uniform rules are an internal hospital policy matter. The Medicare Conditions of Participation are federal health and safety standards for hospitals, and do not simply tell nurses and doctors what to wear.
Why B: Patient diets are set by dietitians and physicians for each case. The Conditions of Participation are broad federal standards a hospital must meet for Medicare, not a rule set for what foods are served.
Why C: Parking rules are a local facility matter. The Medicare Conditions of Participation are federal health and safety requirements for hospitals, and they do not cover where visitors and staff leave their cars.
Why D: The Medicare Conditions of Participation are the federal health and safety standards hospitals must meet in order to take part in Medicare and be paid for care of Medicare patients.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are National Patient Safety Goals?
A: Goals for hospital profits that set the sums to be earned by each ward
B: Goals for visitor numbers that set how many people may come to each ward
C: Joint Commission requirements to prevent common patient safety problems
D: Goals for staff hiring that set how many people the hospital must recruit
Why A: Profit targets for wards are a financial management matter. National Patient Safety Goals come from the Joint Commission and aim to prevent safety problems, not to set earnings for any ward.
Why B: Visitor numbers per ward are set by hospital visiting policy. National Patient Safety Goals address patient safety problems such as identification errors and infections, so they do not limit how many people may visit.
Why C: National Patient Safety Goals are Joint Commission requirements designed to prevent common patient safety problems, such as patient misidentification, medication errors and infections, and accredited hospitals are expected to follow them.
Why D: Staff hiring numbers are a human resources decision. National Patient Safety Goals focus on preventing harm to patients, and do not tell a hospital how many people it must recruit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why must staff use two patient identifiers before giving medication?
A: To save time when a ward is busy and many patients are waiting
B: To make sure the right patient receives the right treatment
C: To collect data for sale to advertisers who want drug lists
D: To satisfy visitors who ask staff about the patients on the wards
Why A: Using two identifiers is not about saving time. It adds a small step on purpose, because patient safety matters more than speed, even when a ward is busy and many patients wait.
Why B: Using two identifiers, such as name and birth date, confirms the right patient receives the right treatment, which prevents medication errors and mix-ups between patients with similar names or conditions.
Why C: Data for sale to advertisers is not a purpose of identifiers and would violate patient privacy rules. The two identifiers exist to protect patients from wrong treatment, not to build lists.
Why D: Satisfying visitors is not the reason. Visitors have no role in the check, and patient information is private. The identifiers are used to protect patients from receiving the wrong drug or treatment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a hospital-acquired infection (HAI)?
A: An infection a patient develops during a hospital stay that was not present on admission
B: An infection in computers, such as a virus that spreads across the hospital network
C: An infection a patient has when arriving at the hospital, which is recorded on the day of admission
D: An infection spread among staff only, with no patients caught up in the outbreak
Why A: A hospital-acquired infection is one a patient develops during a hospital stay that was not present on admission, which is how it differs from infections the patient brought with them when they arrived.
Why B: Computer viruses are not infections of people. A hospital-acquired infection is a medical condition caught by a patient in the hospital, so a virus on the network is the wrong meaning.
Why C: An infection present on arrival is a community-acquired infection, recorded at admission. A hospital-acquired infection is one that was not there at admission, so this option describes the opposite case.
Why D: An infection limited to staff is an occupational illness. A hospital-acquired infection is defined by patients developing an infection during their stay, so excluding all patients makes this definition incorrect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the single most effective way to prevent infection spread in healthcare?
A: Shaking hands
B: Hand hygiene
C: Wearing jewelry
D: Closed doors
Why A: Shaking hands passes germs from one person to another on the skin, so it spreads infection rather than preventing it. Hand hygiene breaks the chain of transmission and is the best defense.
Why B: Hand hygiene, which means washing with soap and water or using an alcohol rub, removes or kills germs on the hands and is the single most effective way to stop infection spreading.
Why C: Wearing jewelry can trap germs under rings and bracelets and makes hands harder to clean well, so it increases infection risk. It does not prevent the spread of infection among patients.
Why D: Closed doors may limit airflow or noise, but they do not remove germs from hands, which are the main route of spread. Hand hygiene is far more effective at preventing infection.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
A: A blood donation event held at the hospital each year there
B: A fall in blood pressure after a loss of blood from an injury
C: A broken IV pump that stops the flow of fluids to the patient
D: A serious infection linked to a central venous catheter
Why A: A blood donation event is a drive that collects blood. CLABSI is an infection linked to a central line, so the name refers to infection, not to giving blood.
Why B: A fall in blood pressure after blood loss is called hypotension or shock. CLABSI stands for central line-associated bloodstream infection, which is a germ infection in the blood and not low pressure.
Why C: A broken IV pump is an equipment failure. CLABSI is an infection of the bloodstream tied to a central line, so a machine fault that stops fluids is not what the term means.
Why D: CLABSI is a serious bloodstream infection linked to a central venous catheter, a tube placed in a large vein, and hospitals work to prevent it with strict insertion and care procedures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a never event in healthcare?
A: A serious, preventable error such as surgery on the wrong body part
B: A meeting that gets canceled because too few staff are able to attend
C: A rare disease that has no known cure and few patients
D: A known side effect that appears even when proper care is given
Why A: A never event is a serious, largely preventable error that should never happen, such as surgery on the wrong body part, and it signals a major failure in safety systems and procedures.
Why B: A canceled meeting is an ordinary scheduling matter. A never event is a serious patient safety error that is largely preventable, not a meeting that fails because too few staff can attend.
Why C: A rare disease is a medical condition, not a care error. A never event is a serious, largely preventable error such as wrong-site surgery.
Why D: A known side effect can occur despite proper care, so it is not a preventable error. A never event is a serious error that should not happen.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a near miss?
A: A mistake that harmed a patient and was reported
B: A canceled visit that a patient did not attend at all
C: An error that was caught before reaching the patient
D: A late bill that was sent to the patient after due
Why A: A mistake that harmed a patient and was reported is an adverse event. A near miss is an error that did not reach the patient, so it cannot have caused harm.
Why B: A canceled visit that a patient skipped is a no-show. A near miss relates to safety errors that were caught in time, and has nothing to do with attendance at visits.
Why C: A near miss is an error or unsafe situation that was caught before it reached the patient, so no harm occurred, but it shows where a process could fail another time.
Why D: A late bill sent after the due date is an administrative problem. A near miss is a safety event caught before reaching a patient, so billing delays are not an example.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should near misses be reported?
A: To blame staff for each error that is reported
B: To raise costs for the hospital through added paperwork
C: To avoid training of staff on the wards and in the clinics
D: They reveal weaknesses so that harm can be prevented
Why A: Reporting is meant to improve systems, not to blame staff. Blame discourages reporting, so a culture of safety treats near misses as chances to learn rather than to punish people.
Why B: Reporting is not meant to raise hospital costs. Near miss reports help prevent harm and the costs of real errors, so the benefit outweighs the small amount of paperwork involved in reporting.
Why C: Reporting does not avoid training. Near misses often show where staff need more training or better processes, so the reports lead to more learning on wards and in clinics, not less.
Why D: Near misses reveal weaknesses in processes and systems, so the hospital can fix them and prevent harm before an error reaches a patient, which is the main reason they should be reported.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a culture of safety?
A: An environment where staff report problems freely and learn from them
B: A museum of safety tools that shows old gear used in early hospitals
C: A ban on reporting, so that staff never tell anyone about a problem or a risk
D: A rule to hide errors from the managers and from the patients and families
Why A: A culture of safety is an environment where staff report problems freely, without fear of blame, and learn from them so that care improves and patients are better protected from harm.
Why B: A museum of old gear is a display of history. A culture of safety is a set of shared values and habits in a workplace, not a place that shows early hospital tools.
Why C: A ban on reporting is the opposite of a culture of safety. Such a culture encourages staff to speak up about problems and risks so that they can be fixed.
Why D: Hiding errors from managers, patients and families is the opposite of a safety culture. Openness and honest reporting are needed so that errors can be understood, corrected and prevented in future.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a medication reconciliation process?
A: To bill insurers for the drugs that were given to patients on the ward
B: To order new drugs for the pharmacy shelves when stocks run low each month
C: To compare a patient's medication lists at transitions to avoid errors
D: To count pills for sale in shops, by staff who work in a pharmacy
Why A: Billing insurers for drugs given is a finance task. Medication reconciliation is a safety process that compares medication lists, so it has no purpose related to charging insurers for drugs.
Why B: Ordering drugs for the pharmacy shelves is inventory work. Medication reconciliation compares what a patient is taking across care settings to avoid mistakes, and does not restock the pharmacy when stock runs low.
Why C: Medication reconciliation compares a patient's medication lists at transitions of care, such as admission, transfer and discharge, to find omissions, duplicates and conflicts so that medication errors can be avoided.
Why D: Counting pills for sale in shops is a retail pharmacy task. Medication reconciliation is a patient safety process that checks a patient's medication lists, not a way to count stock for sale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the 'five rights' of medication administration?
A: Right color, shape, size, smell and taste
B: Right patient, drug, dose, route and time
C: Right doctor, nurse, aide, clerk and guard
D: Right price, brand, store, bag and receipt
Why A: Color, shape, size, smell and taste are traits of a pill, and they are not the five rights. Checking appearance alone does not confirm the right patient, drug, dose, route and time.
Why B: The five rights of medication administration are the right patient, right drug, right dose, right route and right time, and checking all five before giving a drug helps prevent medication errors.
Why C: Doctor, nurse, aide, clerk and guard are job roles in the hospital. The five rights check the details of a medication order, not the people who work in the building.
Why D: Price, brand, store, bag and receipt are shopping details. The five rights of medication administration are the right patient, drug, dose, route and time, which protect patients from errors, not buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the role of an institutional review board (IRB)?
A: To review staff schedules and the shifts worked by the nurses on each ward
B: To review hospital menus and the meals served to patients on the wards each day
C: To review parking for staff and visitors, including the number of spaces
D: To review research involving people to protect participants' rights and welfare
Why A: Staff schedules and nurses' shifts are managed by nursing administration. An institutional review board reviews research involving people, so it does not review work schedules of any ward.
Why B: Hospital menus are the concern of dietary services. An IRB protects people who take part in research, so reviewing meals served to patients is not its role.
Why C: Parking is a facilities matter. An IRB exists to protect research participants, so reviewing the number of parking spaces for staff and visitors has nothing to do with its purpose.
Why D: An institutional review board reviews research involving people in order to protect participants' rights and welfare, checking that risks are reasonable, consent is informed and the study is ethical.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the minimum necessary standard under HIPAA?
A: Using or sharing only the least amount of PHI needed for a purpose
B: Keeping patient records for the minimum number of years the law requires
C: Removing names from PHI before it is shared with researchers
D: Giving patients a copy of their records within a set time
Why A: The minimum necessary standard under HIPAA means using or sharing only the least amount of protected health information needed for a given purpose, which limits exposure of private patient data.
Why B: Record retention is a separate rule. The minimum necessary standard limits how much PHI is used or shared for a given purpose.
Why C: Removing identifiers is de-identification, a different HIPAA provision. The minimum necessary standard limits PHI use and disclosure to what a purpose needs.
Why D: Patient access to records is a separate HIPAA right. The minimum necessary standard limits how much PHI is used or shared.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business associate agreement (BAA)?
A: A contract to rent space for a clinic in a building owned by another firm in practice
B: A contract requiring a vendor that handles PHI to protect it as HIPAA requires
C: A contract to hire staff for the wards and clinics for a term of one year
D: A contract to sell a business to a buyer who will take over all its sites
Why A: Renting clinic space is a lease. A business associate agreement concerns vendors that handle protected health information, so a contract about renting a building does not match the term.
Why B: A business associate agreement is a contract that requires a vendor handling PHI for a covered entity to protect it as HIPAA requires, with safeguards and limits on use and disclosure.
Why C: Hiring staff for the wards is an employment contract. A BAA binds an outside vendor that handles protected health information, so a one year staffing contract is not what the term means.
Why D: Selling a business to a buyer is a sale agreement. A business associate agreement is about protecting patient information held by vendors, so it does not transfer ownership of a business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which drug schedule includes drugs with no accepted medical use and high abuse potential?
A: Schedule IV
B: Schedule V
C: Schedule I
D: Schedule III
Why A: Schedule IV drugs have a low potential for abuse and an accepted medical use. Drugs with no accepted medical use and high abuse potential are in Schedule I, not this one.
Why B: Schedule V drugs have the lowest abuse potential among controlled drugs and accepted medical uses. The schedule with no accepted use and high abuse potential is Schedule I instead.
Why C: Schedule I holds drugs with no accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse, such as heroin, so it is the most restricted of the controlled substance schedules and the correct answer.
Why D: Schedule III drugs have an accepted medical use and moderate to low potential for abuse. The category with no accepted medical use and high abuse potential is Schedule I.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the DEA do in healthcare?
A: Inspects food served in the cafeteria of a hospital site
B: Licenses nurses who pass an exam and meet state standards as a rule
C: Sets insurance rates charged to members of a health plan
D: Enforces controlled-substance laws and registers prescribers
Why A: Inspecting cafeteria food is done by health departments and food safety inspectors. The DEA enforces controlled substance laws, so food inspection is not part of its work in healthcare.
Why B: Licensing nurses is done by state boards of nursing after an exam. The DEA is a federal agency for controlled substances and does not license nurses in general.
Why C: Setting insurance rates is done by insurers and state regulators. The DEA deals with controlled substances, so it has no role in the rates charged to members of a health plan.
Why D: The DEA, or Drug Enforcement Administration, enforces controlled-substance laws and registers prescribers who can write prescriptions for controlled drugs, which links it directly to healthcare practice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the FDA regulate?
A: Hospital billing and the claims sent to insurers
B: The safety and effectiveness of drugs, devices and food
C: Nurse staffing levels for each ward in the hospital
D: Insurance premiums charged to members of a health plan overall
Why A: Billing and claims sent to insurers are handled by payers and by agencies such as CMS. The FDA regulates drugs, devices and food, so it does not oversee hospital billing.
Why B: The FDA regulates the safety and effectiveness of drugs, medical devices and food, approving products before they reach the public and monitoring problems after, so this option correctly describes its role.
Why C: Nurse staffing levels are set by hospital policy and some state rules. The FDA regulates drugs, devices and food, and does not decide how many nurses work on each ward.
Why D: Insurance premiums are regulated by state insurance departments and by health plan rules. The FDA regulates the safety of drugs, devices and food, and has no role in premium prices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the role of state medical boards?
A: Billing insurers for the care given
B: Setting drug prices for pharmacies
C: Licensing and disciplining physicians
D: Building hospitals in the whole state
Why A: Billing insurers is done by providers and billing offices. State medical boards license and discipline physicians, so they do not handle claims for the care given.
Why B: Setting drug prices is not the job of state medical boards. They license and discipline physicians, while prices result from manufacturers, insurers and the market.
Why C: State medical boards license physicians to practice in the state and discipline those who break standards, which protects the public by keeping unfit or unsafe doctors from treating patients.
Why D: Building hospitals is done by owners, developers and health systems. State medical boards focus on licensing and disciplining physicians, so construction across a state is not their function.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the National Practitioner Data Bank?
A: A federal database that tracks malpractice payments and certain adverse actions against practitioners
B: A data bank of recipes that cooks and chefs use to plan meals for large hospital kitchens daily in the end
C: A blood bank that stores units of blood for use in operations and in emergencies at a hospital
D: A bank for money where hospitals keep their funds and take out loans to pay for new buildings
Why A: The National Practitioner Data Bank is a federal database that tracks malpractice payments and certain adverse actions against practitioners, so hospitals and boards can review a clinician's history before granting privileges.
Why B: A recipe database for kitchens is not a healthcare data bank. The National Practitioner Data Bank is a federal database about practitioners, malpractice payments and adverse actions, not food planning.
Why C: A blood bank stores blood for transfusions. The National Practitioner Data Bank stores information about practitioners and malpractice, not blood, even though both use the word bank in the name.
Why D: A bank that keeps money and lends funds is a financial institution. The National Practitioner Data Bank holds information on practitioners and adverse actions, not hospital funds or loans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Good Samaritan law?
A: A law on hospital beds that sets how many each ward may hold in a given year
B: A law that punishes helpers who give care to a stranger in an emergency
C: A law on charity taxes that sets what hospitals must pay on gifts they receive
D: A law that protects people who give reasonable emergency help from liability
Why A: Hospital bed limits are set by licensing and capacity rules. A Good Samaritan law protects people who give emergency help, so it does not set how many beds a ward may hold.
Why B: A Good Samaritan law does the opposite of punishing helpers. It protects people who give reasonable emergency help from liability, so that bystanders are not discouraged from aiding a stranger.
Why C: Charity taxes are a tax law matter. A Good Samaritan law concerns liability protection for emergency helpers, and does not set what hospitals pay on gifts they receive.
Why D: A Good Samaritan law protects people who give reasonable emergency help from liability, which encourages bystanders and off-duty professionals to assist at an emergency without fear of being sued if things go wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is vicarious liability?
A: An employer's responsibility for the acts of employees done within their work
B: A patient's liability for care that was given to them, to be paid in full
C: An employee's liability for the employer's debts, which the worker must pay from pay
D: A liability for lost items such as coats and keys left behind by patients
Why A: Vicarious liability is an employer's responsibility for the acts of employees done within the scope of their work, so a hospital can be held liable for a nurse's negligence on duty.
Why B: A patient's duty to pay for care is a financial obligation. Vicarious liability concerns an employer being responsible for what employees do at work, not what a patient owes.
Why C: An employee paying an employer's debts is not vicarious liability. The doctrine runs the other way, with the employer answering for employees' acts done within the scope of their work.
Why D: Lost items such as coats and keys fall under bailment or property loss. Vicarious liability is about responsibility for the acts of others, not a duty for belongings left behind.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a statute of limitations in a malpractice case?
A: A limit on damages only, set by the court there
B: A limit on staff numbers in each ward of a hospital
C: The time limit within which a claim must be filed
D: A limit on the patients a doctor may treat in a week
Why A: A limit on damages only is a damages cap. A statute of limitations sets a deadline for filing a claim, not a ceiling on what the court may award.
Why B: A limit on staff numbers per ward is a staffing rule. A statute of limitations in a malpractice case is about time, not about how many people work in a ward.
Why C: A statute of limitations is the time limit within which a malpractice claim must be filed, and after it passes the claim is generally barred, however strong the case might have been.
Why D: Limiting the patients a doctor treats in a week is a workload rule. A statute of limitations is a filing deadline, and has nothing to do with how many patients are seen.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between a patient's capacity and competence?
A: Capacity is legal, while competence is a medical judgment made by the doctor at the bedside
B: Capacity is the clinical ability to make a specific decision; competence is a legal finding
C: Capacity applies to minors, while competence applies to adult patients
D: Capacity refers to the clinician's skill, while competence refers to the patient's wishes
Why A: This reverses the terms. Capacity is the clinical ability to make a specific decision, judged by clinicians, while competence is a legal determination made by a court, so the option mislabels both.
Why B: Capacity is the clinical ability to make a specific decision at a given time, assessed by clinicians, while competence is a legal determination made by a court, so the two are related but different.
Why C: Both terms apply to adults. Capacity is the clinical ability to make a specific decision, while competence is a legal determination by a court.
Why D: Both terms describe the patient's ability to decide, not staff skill or wishes. Capacity is clinical and decision-specific, while competence is a legal determination.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If a patient lacks capacity and has no advance directive, who usually makes decisions?
A: A legally authorized surrogate, often a family member
B: A stranger who happens to be near the patient at the time
C: The insurer that pays the claims for the care given
D: The nearest hospital employee on duty at the time
Why A: When a patient lacks capacity and has no advance directive, a legally authorized surrogate, often a family member, usually makes decisions based on the patient's known wishes or best interests.
Why B: A stranger nearby has no legal authority to decide for the patient. Decisions go to a legally authorized surrogate such as a family member, chosen under the law and not by chance.
Why C: An insurer pays claims and has no authority to make treatment decisions for the patient. A legally authorized surrogate, often a family member, decides when the patient lacks capacity.
Why D: The nearest hospital employee on duty has no legal authority to consent for the patient. A legally authorized surrogate, often a family member, is the usual decision maker in this case.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a living will?
A: A will that gives away property to heirs after the death of the person who made it
B: A will for living things such as plants and pets that need care when the owner is away
C: A document stating a person's wishes about treatment if they cannot speak for themselves
D: A will written after death by the heirs of a person to share out the estate that is left
Why A: A will that gives property to heirs after death is a last will and testament. A living will is about medical treatment wishes while the person is alive but unable to speak for themselves.
Why B: Plants and pets need care, but a living will has nothing to do with living things in that sense. It records the person's own wishes about medical treatment if they cannot speak for themselves.
Why C: A living will is a document stating a person's wishes about medical treatment if they can no longer speak for themselves, such as whether to use life support, which guides doctors and family.
Why D: Heirs cannot write a will after a person dies, and sharing out an estate is handled by a last will. A living will records the person's treatment wishes while still alive.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a POLST form?
A: A form for parking that lets staff and visitors reserve spaces near the entrance
B: A form for hiring that lists the skills and the pay of a new member of staff
C: A form for billing that lists the charges for services given to a patient
D: A medical order that records a seriously ill patient's treatment wishes
Why A: Parking forms are a facilities matter. POLST stands for Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment and is a medical order, so a form to reserve spaces near the entrance is wrong.
Why B: A hiring form lists skills and pay and belongs to human resources. A POLST form is a medical order about life-sustaining treatment, so it has nothing to do with new staff.
Why C: A billing form lists charges for services. A POLST form is a medical order about treatment wishes, so it is a clinical document rather than a record of charges to a patient.
Why D: A POLST form is a medical order that records a seriously ill patient's treatment wishes, such as resuscitation or breathing support, so other clinicians and emergency staff can honor them across settings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the prefix 'brady-' mean?
A: Fast
B: Slow
C: Large
D: Small
Why A: Fast is the meaning of tachy-, as in tachycardia, a fast heart rate. Brady- is the opposite prefix and means slow, as in bradycardia, so this option reverses the two.
Why B: Brady- means slow, as in bradycardia, a slow heart rate. The prefix is used in terms that describe a reduced speed or rate, which is the opposite of fast.
Why C: Large is the meaning of macro- or mega-, as in megacolon. Brady- means slow, so large does not match the prefix used in bradycardia.
Why D: Small is the meaning of micro-, as in microscope. Brady- means slow, as in bradycardia, so small does not match the prefix in the question.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the prefix 'tachy-' mean?
A: Fast
B: Across
C: Slow
D: Below
Why A: Tachy- means fast, as in tachycardia, which is a fast heart rate. The prefix describes an increased speed or rate, and this is the standard meaning in medical terminology.
Why B: Across is the meaning of trans- or dia-, as in transfusion. Tachy- means fast, so across is the wrong meaning for the prefix in tachycardia.
Why C: Slow is the meaning of brady-, as in bradycardia. Tachy- is its opposite and means fast, so this option gives the meaning of the other prefix.
Why D: Below is the meaning of sub- or hypo-, as in subcutaneous or hypodermic. Tachy- means fast, so below is not the meaning of this prefix.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-emia' mean?
A: Inflammation of a body part
B: A condition of the blood
C: Removal of a body part
D: Pain in a body part or nerve
Why A: Inflammation of a body part is the suffix -itis, as in arthritis. The suffix -emia refers to a condition of the blood, as in anemia, so this option gives the wrong suffix.
Why B: The suffix -emia means a condition of the blood, as in anemia or leukemia, where the word ending tells that the term refers to something found in the blood.
Why C: Removal of a body part is the suffix -ectomy, as in appendectomy. The suffix -emia refers to a blood condition, so removal does not match this ending.
Why D: Pain in a body part or nerve is the suffix -algia or -dynia, as in neuralgia. The suffix -emia refers to the blood, so pain does not fit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-algia' mean?
A: Removal
B: Swelling
C: Pain
D: Study of
Why A: Removal is the meaning of -ectomy, as in appendectomy. The suffix -algia means pain, as in neuralgia, so this option gives the meaning of a different surgical suffix.
Why B: Swelling is related to terms like edema. The suffix -algia means pain, as in neuralgia, so swelling does not match this ending in medical terms.
Why C: The suffix -algia means pain, as in neuralgia, which is nerve pain, and myalgia, which is muscle pain, so the ending marks a painful condition in a body part.
Why D: Study of is the meaning of -ology, as in cardiology. The suffix -algia means pain, so a study or science does not match this ending.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-plasty' mean?
A: Surgical removal of a body part
B: Cutting into a vein or artery
C: Viewing the inside of the body
D: Surgical repair or reconstruction
Why A: Surgical removal of a body part is the suffix -ectomy, as in appendectomy. The suffix -plasty means surgical repair or reconstruction, so removal is the wrong meaning here.
Why B: Cutting into a vein or artery is not a suffix meaning. The suffix -plasty means surgical repair or reconstruction, and cutting into a body part would be -otomy.
Why C: Viewing the inside of the body is the suffix -scopy, as in endoscopy. The suffix -plasty means surgical repair or reconstruction, so viewing is not its meaning.
Why D: The suffix -plasty means surgical repair or reconstruction, as in rhinoplasty, which reshapes the nose, so the ending signals that a body part is being rebuilt or reshaped by a surgeon.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-scopy' mean?
A: Visual examination with an instrument
B: Inflammation of a joint or a body part
C: Surgical repair of a body part now
D: Surgical removal of a part of the body
Why A: The suffix -scopy means visual examination with an instrument, as in endoscopy or colonoscopy, where a scope lets the clinician see inside the body without a large incision.
Why B: Inflammation of a joint or a body part is the suffix -itis, as in arthritis. The suffix -scopy means visual examination with an instrument, so inflammation does not match this ending.
Why C: Surgical repair of a body part is the suffix -plasty, as in rhinoplasty. The suffix -scopy means looking with an instrument, so repair is the wrong meaning for this ending.
Why D: Surgical removal of a part is the suffix -ectomy, as in appendectomy. The suffix -scopy means visual examination with an instrument, so removal does not fit this ending.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the suffix '-otomy' mean?
A: Removal of a part
B: Study of cells
C: A cutting into
D: Repair of a part
Why A: Removal of a part is the suffix -ectomy, as in appendectomy. The suffix -otomy means a cutting into, so this option gives the meaning of a different surgical suffix.
Why B: Study of cells is cytology, from the root cyto- and the suffix -ology. The suffix -otomy means a cutting into, so study of cells does not match this ending.
Why C: The suffix -otomy means a cutting into a body part, as in tracheotomy, where an opening is cut into the windpipe, and the part is not removed or repaired.
Why D: Repair of a part is the suffix -plasty, as in rhinoplasty. The suffix -otomy means a cutting into, so repair is not the meaning of this ending.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'pulmon' refer to?
A: Liver
B: Lung
C: Heart
D: Kidney
Why A: Liver is hepat-, as in hepatitis. The root pulmon refers to the lung, as in pulmonary, so the liver is the wrong organ for this root.
Why B: The root pulmon refers to the lung, as in pulmonary, which describes things related to the lungs, such as a pulmonary embolism or pulmonary function tests.
Why C: Heart is cardi-, as in cardiology. The root pulmon refers to the lung, as in pulmonary, so the heart is the wrong organ for this root.
Why D: Kidney is ren- or nephr-, as in renal or nephritis. The root pulmon refers to the lung, as in pulmonary, so the kidney is the wrong organ here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'hem' or 'hemat' refer to?
A: Skin
B: Bone
C: Liver
D: Blood
Why A: Skin is derm- or dermat-, as in dermatitis. The roots hem and hemat refer to blood, as in hematology, so skin is the wrong body part.
Why B: Bone is oste-, as in osteoporosis. The roots hem and hemat refer to blood, as in hematology, so bone does not match these roots.
Why C: Liver is hepat-, as in hepatitis. The roots hem and hemat refer to blood, as in hematology, so liver is not the meaning of these roots.
Why D: The roots hem and hemat refer to blood, as in hematology, the study of blood, and hemorrhage, which is bleeding, so these roots mark terms about blood.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'my' refer to?
A: Nerve
B: Muscle
C: Skin
D: Bone
Why A: Nerve is neur- or neuro-, as in neurology. The root my refers to muscle, as in myalgia, so nerve is the wrong tissue for this root.
Why B: The root my refers to muscle, as in myalgia, which is muscle pain, and myocardium, the heart muscle, so this root marks terms about muscle tissue.
Why C: Skin is derm- or dermat-, as in dermatitis. The root my refers to muscle, as in myalgia, so skin is the wrong meaning for this root.
Why D: Bone is oste-, as in osteoporosis. The root my refers to muscle, as in myalgia, so bone does not match this root in medical terms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'arthr' refer to?
A: Joint
B: Muscle
C: Bone
D: Skin
Why A: The root arthr refers to a joint, as in arthritis, which is inflammation of a joint, and arthroscopy, which is a look inside a joint with a scope.
Why B: Muscle is my- or myo-, as in myalgia. The root arthr refers to a joint, as in arthritis, so muscle is the wrong tissue for this root.
Why C: Bone is oste-, as in osteoporosis. The root arthr refers to a joint, as in arthritis, where bones meet, so bone is not the meaning of this root.
Why D: Skin is derm- or dermat-, as in dermatitis. The root arthr refers to a joint, as in arthritis, so skin is the wrong body part here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'ophthalm' refer to?
A: Ear
B: Nose
C: Skin
D: Eye
Why A: Ear is ot- or aur-, as in otitis. The root ophthalm refers to the eye, as in ophthalmology, so the ear is the wrong organ for this root.
Why B: Nose is rhin-, as in rhinoplasty. The root ophthalm refers to the eye, as in ophthalmology, so the nose is not the meaning of this root.
Why C: Skin is derm- or dermat-, as in dermatitis. The root ophthalm refers to the eye, as in ophthalmology, so skin is the wrong body part here.
Why D: The root ophthalm refers to the eye, as in ophthalmology, the study of the eye and its diseases, and ophthalmoscope, an instrument used to look into the eye.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'ot' refer to?
A: Eye
B: Throat
C: Ear
D: Nose
Why A: Eye is ophthalm- or opt-, as in ophthalmology. The root ot refers to the ear, as in otitis, so the eye is the wrong organ for this root.
Why B: Throat is pharyng- or laryng-, as in pharyngitis. The root ot refers to the ear, as in otitis media, so throat is not the meaning of this root.
Why C: The root ot refers to the ear, as in otitis, an inflammation of the ear, and otology, the study of the ear, so this root marks terms about hearing and the ear.
Why D: Nose is rhin-, as in rhinitis. The root ot refers to the ear, as in otitis, so the nose is the wrong organ for this root.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the root 'rhin' refer to?
A: Ear
B: Nose
C: Eye
D: Mouth
Why A: Ear is ot- or aur-, as in otitis. The root rhin refers to the nose, as in rhinitis or rhinoplasty, so the ear is the wrong organ for this root.
Why B: The root rhin refers to the nose, as in rhinitis, which is inflammation of the nasal lining, and rhinoplasty, which is surgical reshaping of the nose.
Why C: Eye is ophthalm- or opt-, as in ophthalmology. The root rhin refers to the nose, as in rhinitis, so the eye is not the meaning of this root.
Why D: Mouth is or- or stomat-, as in oral or stomatitis. The root rhin refers to the nose, as in rhinitis, so the mouth is the wrong part here.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the abbreviation 'QID' mean in a prescription?
A: Four times a day
B: Once a day
C: Twice a day
D: Three times a day
Why A: QID stands for quater in die, which means four times a day. It is used on prescriptions to tell the patient how often to take a dose, so this option is correct.
Why B: Once a day is written QD or daily. QID means four times a day, so a once daily dose would be far too small.
Why C: Twice a day is written BID. QID means four times a day, so this gives half the doses the abbreviation calls for.
Why D: Three times a day is written as TID. QID means four times a day, so a TID dose gives one fewer dose a day than QID requires.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the abbreviation 'AC' mean in a medication order?
A: As needed
B: After meals
C: Before meals
D: At bedtime
Why A: As needed is PRN. The abbreviation AC means before meals, from the Latin ante cibum, so as needed is the wrong meaning for AC in a medication order.
Why B: After meals is PC, from post cibum. The abbreviation AC means before meals, from ante cibum, so this option gives the opposite timing to what AC says.
Why C: AC stands for ante cibum, which means before meals, so a drug marked AC is taken before eating, such as thirty minutes ahead, in order to work properly.
Why D: At bedtime is HS. The abbreviation AC means before meals, so a drug given at bedtime would be given at the wrong time if it is ordered AC.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the abbreviation 'PC' mean in a medication order?
A: At bedtime
B: As needed
C: Before meals
D: After meals
Why A: At bedtime is HS, from hora somni. The abbreviation PC means after meals, from post cibum, so bedtime is the wrong meaning for PC in a medication order.
Why B: As needed is PRN. The abbreviation PC means after meals, from post cibum, so as needed does not match PC on a medication order.
Why C: Before meals is AC, from ante cibum. The abbreviation PC means after meals, from post cibum, so this option gives the opposite of what PC says.
Why D: PC stands for post cibum, which means after meals, so a medication marked PC is taken after eating, often to lessen stomach upset or to match how food affects the drug.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the abbreviation 'HS' mean in a medication order?
A: Before meals
B: At bedtime
C: After meals
D: Every hour
Why A: Before meals is AC, from ante cibum. The abbreviation HS means at bedtime, from hora somni, so before meals is the wrong meaning for HS on an order.
Why B: HS stands for hora somni, which means at bedtime, so a drug marked HS is given at the hour of sleep, such as a sleep aid or a drug best taken before resting.
Why C: After meals is PC, from post cibum. The abbreviation HS means at bedtime, so this option gives the meaning of a different abbreviation on a medication order.
Why D: Every hour is written as q1h or QH. The abbreviation HS means at bedtime, so an hourly schedule would be a far shorter interval than HS orders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'PO' mean in a medication order?
A: By mouth
B: Into the eye
C: By injection
D: Under tongue
Why A: PO stands for per os, which means by mouth, so a drug marked PO is swallowed as a tablet, capsule or liquid and taken by the oral route.
Why B: Into the eye is an ophthalmic route, shown as OU, OD or OS for the eyes. PO means by mouth, so a drug into the eye would be a wrong route.
Why C: By injection is a parenteral route such as IM, IV or SC. PO means by mouth, so an injection is the wrong route for a drug ordered PO.
Why D: Under the tongue is the sublingual route, written SL. PO means by mouth, to be swallowed, so a drug ordered PO is not meant to dissolve under the tongue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'IV' mean?
A: By mouth, to be swallowed
B: Intramuscular, into muscle
C: Intravenous, into a vein
D: Under the skin of a patient
Why A: By mouth, to be swallowed, is PO, from per os. IV means intravenous, into a vein, so a drug given by mouth is a different route from IV.
Why B: Intramuscular, into muscle, is IM. IV means intravenous, into a vein, so this option gives the meaning of a different abbreviation for another injection route.
Why C: IV stands for intravenous, which means into a vein, so a drug or fluid given IV enters the bloodstream directly and acts quickly.
Why D: Under the skin is subcutaneous, written SC or SQ. IV means intravenous, into a vein, so a drug given under the skin uses a different route than IV.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'IM' mean?
A: By mouth, to be swallowed
B: Under the tongue, to dissolve
C: Intravenous, into a vein
D: Intramuscular, into a muscle
Why A: By mouth, to be swallowed, is PO. IM means intramuscular, into a muscle, so a drug given by mouth is a different route from the injection that IM describes.
Why B: Under the tongue, to dissolve, is the sublingual route, written SL. IM means intramuscular, into a muscle, so this option gives the meaning of another route.
Why C: Intravenous, into a vein, is IV. IM means intramuscular, into a muscle, so a drug given into a vein is the wrong route for IM.
Why D: IM stands for intramuscular, which means into a muscle, so a drug marked IM is given by injection deep into muscle tissue, where it is absorbed at a steady pace.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'CBC' stand for?
A: Chronic bone condition
B: Central brain center
C: Cardiac blood circuit
D: Complete blood count
Why A: Chronic bone condition is not what CBC stands for. A CBC is a blood test, so a term naming a bone problem does not match the lab abbreviation.
Why B: Central brain center is not a medical term used for CBC. The abbreviation CBC stands for complete blood count, a common blood test, and not an organ of the brain.
Why C: Cardiac blood circuit is not the meaning of CBC. The abbreviation stands for complete blood count, a lab test of blood cells, and not a path of blood through the heart.
Why D: CBC stands for complete blood count, a common lab test that measures red cells, white cells and platelets in a blood sample to check health and find conditions such as infection or anemia.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'ECG' or 'EKG' record?
A: The electrical activity of the heart
B: Muscle strength of the patient's arm
C: Lung capacity of a patient at rest
D: Brain waves of a patient when asleep
Why A: An ECG or EKG records the electrical activity of the heart, shown as a tracing, which helps clinicians find rhythm problems, heart attacks and other heart conditions.
Why B: Muscle strength of the arm is not recorded by an ECG. Strength is tested by physical examination, while an ECG records electrical activity of the heart rather than a limb.
Why C: Lung capacity at rest is measured by spirometry or pulmonary function tests. An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, so it does not measure breathing volume.
Why D: Brain waves during sleep are recorded by an EEG. An ECG or EKG records the electrical activity of the heart, so it does not show brain waves.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'EEG' record?
A: The electrical activity of the heart
B: The electrical activity of the muscles
C: The electrical activity of the brain
D: The electrical activity of the lungs
Why A: The electrical activity of the heart is recorded by an ECG or EKG. An EEG records the brain, so this option gives the test for the wrong organ.
Why B: The electrical activity of muscles is recorded by an EMG, or electromyogram. An EEG records the brain, so muscle activity is not what this test shows.
Why C: An EEG, or electroencephalogram, records the electrical activity of the brain, shown as waves on a tracing, and it helps diagnose seizures, sleep problems and other brain conditions.
Why D: The lungs are tested with pulmonary function tests and imaging, not electrical recordings. An EEG records the electrical activity of the brain, so lung activity is not its subject.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'MRI' stand for?
A: Muscle repair injection
B: Magnetic resonance imaging
C: Major risk inventory list
D: Medical records index file
Why A: Muscle repair injection is not a real expansion of MRI. MRI is an imaging scan and does not repair muscle or involve any injection to treat it.
Why B: MRI stands for magnetic resonance imaging, a scan that uses strong magnets and radio waves to make detailed pictures of soft tissues, organs and joints without using radiation.
Why C: Major risk inventory list is not a medical term. MRI stands for magnetic resonance imaging, a type of scan, and not a list of risks kept by an organization.
Why D: Medical records index file is a made up phrase. MRI means magnetic resonance imaging, a scan that takes pictures inside the body, and it is not a records system.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'CT' stand for in imaging?
A: Cardiac test result
B: Computed tomography
C: Clinical trial of drugs
D: Chest tube drain
Why A: Cardiac test result is not what CT stands for in imaging. CT means computed tomography, a scan, and the letters do not name a test result of the heart.
Why B: CT stands for computed tomography, an imaging method that uses X-rays and a computer to make cross-sectional pictures of the body, which show organs, bones and other tissues in detail.
Why C: Clinical trial of drugs is a research study, not an imaging term. In imaging, CT means computed tomography, a scan, so this option gives an unrelated phrase from research.
Why D: Chest tube drain is a treatment device and not an imaging term. In imaging, CT stands for computed tomography, a scan that makes cross-sectional pictures of the body.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a chief complaint?
A: The main reason a patient seeks care, in the patient's words
B: A complaint about billing made by a patient to the office
C: A complaint by a manager about a member of staff at work
D: A complaint about the hospital made by a patient to a manager
Why A: A chief complaint is the main reason a patient seeks care, recorded in the patient's own words, such as chest pain for two days, and it guides the rest of the visit.
Why B: A complaint about billing is a patient grievance sent to the billing office. A chief complaint is the main reason for the visit recorded at the start of an encounter.
Why C: A complaint by a manager about staff is a personnel issue handled by human resources. A chief complaint is the patient's main reason for seeking care, so this option is unrelated.
Why D: A complaint about the hospital made to a manager is a grievance. A chief complaint is the main reason the patient seeks care, recorded in the patient's own words.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a SOAP note, what does the 'A' stand for?
A: Allergy
B: Admission
C: Assessment
D: Action
Why A: Allergy is recorded in the history, but it is not what the A in SOAP stands for. SOAP means subjective, objective, assessment and plan, so A is assessment.
Why B: Admission is a stage of a hospital stay, not a part of a SOAP note. The A in SOAP stands for assessment, the clinician's diagnosis or impression after reviewing the findings.
Why C: In a SOAP note, the A stands for assessment, which is the clinician's evaluation or diagnosis based on the subjective and objective information gathered in the visit.
Why D: Action is not a part of the SOAP format. SOAP stands for subjective, objective, assessment and plan, so the A is assessment, and the steps to take belong to the plan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a SOAP note, what does the 'P' stand for?
A: Payment
B: Patient
C: Pulse
D: Plan
Why A: Payment is not part of the SOAP note. SOAP stands for subjective, objective, assessment and plan, so the P is plan, and billing details are recorded elsewhere in the chart.
Why B: Patient is not what the P stands for. The SOAP note is already about a patient, and the P means plan, the steps for treatment and follow up.
Why C: Pulse is a vital sign recorded under the objective part of the note. In SOAP, the P stands for plan, so pulse is not the meaning of the letter.
Why D: In a SOAP note, the P stands for plan, which lists the treatment, tests, medications and follow up the clinician intends, based on the assessment of the patient's condition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a release of information (ROI) form?
A: To release a bill to the insurer or the patient after a visit to them
B: To release a patient from the hospital once the doctor has signed the order overall
C: To authorize sharing a patient's records with a named person or organization
D: To release staff from work early when the wards are quiet at night hours
Why A: Releasing a bill is a billing task. A release of information form authorizes sharing a patient's records, so it is not used to send a bill to an insurer.
Why B: Discharging a patient from the hospital is done by a physician's order. An ROI form authorizes sharing records and does not release a patient from care at the hospital.
Why C: A release of information form authorizes the sharing of a patient's records with a named person or organization, which respects privacy law by requiring the patient's permission before disclosure.
Why D: Releasing staff from work early is a scheduling decision by managers. A release of information form concerns patient records, and has nothing to do with the hours that staff work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a master patient index (MPI)?
A: A list of drugs kept by the pharmacy for each ward in the hospital site
B: A list of staff kept by the office for each ward in the hospital campus
C: A list of beds kept by the ward for each room in the hospital building site in the end
D: A database that links each patient to a unique identifier across a health system
Why A: A list of drugs kept by the pharmacy is a formulary or inventory. A master patient index links each patient to a unique identifier, so it is not a drug list.
Why B: A list of staff kept by the office is a staff directory. A master patient index is a database of patients and their identifiers, so it is not a list of employees.
Why C: A list of beds is a bed census or room inventory. A master patient index is a database of patients, so a list of beds in a building is the wrong thing.
Why D: A master patient index is a database that links each patient to a unique identifier across a health system, so records for the same person can be found and matched correctly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What problem can a duplicate medical record cause?
A: Incomplete information that could harm a patient
B: Lower costs only, with no effect on care quality
C: Faster care for all patients seen in the clinic
D: Better privacy for the records of each patient
Why A: A duplicate record splits a patient's information across two charts, so a clinician may miss allergies, medications or history, and incomplete information could harm the patient, which is why duplicates are a safety problem.
Why B: A duplicate record does not only lower costs. It adds cost through rework and risks harm to patients, so claiming no effect on care quality is incorrect.
Why C: Duplicate records slow care rather than speed it. Staff must search and reconcile several charts, and missing information can delay or harm treatment, so faster care for patients is not the result.
Why D: Duplicate records do not improve privacy. They can lead to information being sent to the wrong place or being missed, and they make it harder to protect the records of each patient.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a patient registration form?
A: To collect donations only, from patients who give to a fund
B: To collect demographic, contact and insurance information
C: To advertise the clinic to people who live in the town
D: To list staff birthdays and the dates of work anniversaries
Why A: Collecting donations is not the purpose of a registration form. It gathers the information needed to identify and treat the patient and to bill, and donations are handled by other channels.
Why B: A patient registration form collects demographic, contact and insurance information, which identifies the patient, allows the office to reach them and supports billing and claims for the visit.
Why C: Advertising the clinic is a marketing task. A registration form collects information from the patient for the record, not a message sent to people who live in the town.
Why D: Staff birthdays and anniversaries are human resources information. A patient registration form is completed by patients and collects demographic, contact and insurance details, not facts about employees.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a co-pay collection best practice at check-in?
A: Ignore it until the bill is due
B: Wait six months to bill the patient
C: Collect it at the time of service
D: Collect it by mail only, later on
Why A: Ignoring a co-pay until the bill is due is poor practice, because it delays payment and makes collection harder. The best practice is to collect it at the time of service.
Why B: Waiting six months to bill the patient delays revenue and makes collection less likely. A co-pay should be collected at check-in, at the time of service, as the best practice.
Why C: Collecting the co-pay at the time of service is the best practice, because the patient is present, the amount is known and the office avoids later billing costs and unpaid balances.
Why D: Collecting only by mail later delays payment and adds billing costs and the risk of nonpayment. The best practice is to collect the co-pay at the time of service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a wait-time statistic measure?
A: How long staff wait for breaks
B: How long a drug takes to work
C: How long an operation lasts there
D: How long patients wait to be seen
Why A: How long staff wait for breaks is a staffing matter. A wait-time statistic measures how long patients wait to be seen, so staff break times are not what it tracks.
Why B: How long a drug takes to work is a pharmacology measure. A wait-time statistic measures how long patients wait to be seen, so drug action time is not part of it.
Why C: How long an operation lasts is a surgical duration measure. A wait-time statistic measures how long patients wait to be seen, not the length of a procedure.
Why D: A wait-time statistic measures how long patients wait to be seen, from arrival or appointment time until care begins, and it helps a clinic judge access and patient satisfaction.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an appointment reminder reduce?
A: No-shows
B: Staff pay
C: Coverage
D: Safety
Why A: Appointment reminders reduce no-shows, the visits that patients miss without notice, by prompting patients by phone, text or mail, which fills the schedule better and improves access to care.
Why B: Reminders do not reduce staff pay. They are a scheduling tool that lowers missed visits, and pay is set by employment terms, so this option has no link to what reminders do.
Why C: Reminders do not reduce insurance coverage. Coverage is set by the health plan, and reminders only prompt patients to attend visits, so the two are unrelated.
Why D: Reminders do not reduce safety. They help patients keep appointments and receive care on time, which supports safe care, so the idea that they reduce safety is the reverse of their effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a walk-in appointment?
A: A visit on foot by the patient
B: A visit with no scheduled time
C: A visit by phone call
D: A visit booked weeks in advance
Why A: A visit on foot describes how a patient arrives, not the type of appointment. A walk-in appointment is defined by having no scheduled time, not by how the patient travels.
Why B: A walk-in appointment is a visit without a scheduled time, where the patient arrives and is seen as the clinic can fit them in, rather than at a time booked ahead.
Why C: A phone call is a telephone visit. A walk-in appointment is an in-person visit with no scheduled time.
Why D: A visit booked in advance is a scheduled appointment, the opposite of a walk-in, where the patient arrives without a set time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is wave scheduling?
A: Booking one patient at a time at fixed intervals throughout the day
B: Booking several patients at the start of each hour and seeing them in order of arrival
C: Booking one patient a day and no more, whatever the length of the visit needed
D: Booking patients by urgency so that the sickest are seen before the rest
Why A: One patient per fixed interval is standard scheduling. Wave scheduling books several patients at the start of each hour and sees them in order of arrival.
Why B: Wave scheduling books several patients at the start of each hour and sees them in order of arrival, which allows for late arrivals and no-shows and keeps the provider busy throughout the hour.
Why C: Booking one patient a day is far too slow for a clinic and is not wave scheduling. Wave scheduling books several patients at the start of each hour, so it is the opposite.
Why D: Seeing the sickest first is triage. Wave scheduling books several patients at the start of each hour and sees them in order of arrival.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is open-access (same-day) scheduling?
A: Keeping slots open so patients can be seen the day they call
B: Booking visits several weeks ahead to keep the calendar full
C: Leaving the office doors open so patients walk in at any hour
D: Limiting visits to patients with a referral from another doctor
Why A: Open-access scheduling keeps slots open so patients can be seen the day they call, which reduces waiting and no-shows, and gives patients quick access to care when they need it.
Why B: Booking far ahead is traditional scheduling. Open access holds slots so patients can be seen the day they call.
Why C: Leaving the doors open for walk-ins at any hour is not what open access means. It is a scheduling method that holds appointment slots for same-day calls, and not an unlimited walk-in policy.
Why D: Open access does not require a referral. It keeps slots free so patients who call can be seen the same day.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the best way to handle a patient who arrives 30 minutes late?
A: Scold them in front of the other patients in the room there
B: Refuse to speak to them and ask them to leave the office now
C: Follow clinic policy: see them if possible or reschedule politely
D: Ignore them and carry on with the work of the front desk staff every time
Why A: Scolding a patient in front of others is unprofessional and harms trust. A late patient should be treated with courtesy while the clinic follows its own policy on late arrivals.
Why B: Refusing to speak to the patient and asking them to leave is rude and ignores clinic policy. The staff should follow policy, either seeing the patient if possible or rescheduling politely.
Why C: The best way is to follow clinic policy, seeing the patient if the schedule allows or rescheduling politely, which keeps the office fair to others and treats the late patient with respect.
Why D: Ignoring the patient is unprofessional and leaves them unsure about their care. Staff should greet them and follow clinic policy, either seeing them if possible or rescheduling in a polite way.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is scarcity?
A: A tax placed on rare goods and on gems
B: A shortage of money in one family or home
C: Having more goods than anyone can use
D: Limited resources to meet unlimited wants
Why A: A tax on rare goods and gems is a luxury tax or tariff. Scarcity is the basic problem of limited resources to meet unlimited wants, and not a tax on any item.
Why B: A shortage of money in one family is a personal budget problem. Scarcity is the economic problem that all resources are limited compared with unlimited wants, and it applies to every society.
Why C: Having more goods than anyone can use is a surplus, which is the opposite of scarcity. Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with the wants people have.
Why D: Scarcity means limited resources to meet unlimited wants, so people and societies must make choices about how to use what they have, which is the central problem of economics.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a need?
A: Something you like but can live without for a while
B: Something required to live, such as food and shelter
C: Something advertised on television and in print
D: Something that costs a lot of money to buy new
Why A: Something you like but can live without is a want. A need is something required to live, such as food and shelter, so this option describes a want instead.
Why B: A need is something required to live, such as food and shelter, which people cannot go without, and this separates needs from wants, which people can live without for a long time.
Why C: Something advertised on television is just a product that is marketed. Advertising does not make something a need, since a need is something required to live, such as food and shelter.
Why D: Something that costs a lot of money may be a luxury, not a need. A need is something required to live, such as food and shelter, whatever its price might be.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a want?
A: Something required for health, such as food and shelter
B: Something the law requires you to buy each year now
C: Something you desire that is not essential for survival
D: Something that cannot be bought with money at all
Why A: Something required for health, such as food and shelter, is a need. A want is something you desire but is not essential for survival, so this describes the opposite.
Why B: Something the law requires you to buy each year is an obligation, such as insurance in some places. A want is something desired that is not essential for survival.
Why C: A want is something you desire that is not essential for survival, such as a game or a new phone, so people can live without it while still wishing to have it.
Why D: Many wants can be bought with money, such as toys and entertainment. A want is something desired but not essential for survival, so saying it can never be bought is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is opportunity cost?
A: The value of the next best choice you give up
B: The cost of making a product in a factory
C: The price you pay at the store, with the tax added
D: The tax added at checkout on a purchase here
Why A: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best choice you give up when you make a decision, so every choice has a cost measured by the best alternative left behind.
Why B: The cost of making a product in a factory is a production cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, not the money spent making goods.
Why C: The price at the store with tax is the money cost of an item. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best choice you give up, which may not be a money price.
Why D: The tax added at checkout is a sales tax. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best choice you give up, so a tax on a purchase is a different idea.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Jamal can spend Saturday working for $60 or going to a free concert. What is his opportunity cost of going?
A: Nothing, as the concert is free
B: The cost of the concert ticket
C: The $60 he could have earned
D: The cost of a snack he buys
Why A: The concert is free, but going still has a cost. Jamal gives up the chance to earn $60, so his opportunity cost is the $60 and not nothing.
Why B: There is no ticket cost, because the concert is free. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, which here is $60 in wages, not a ticket price.
Why C: Jamal's opportunity cost of going to the concert is the $60 he could have earned by working, because that is the value of the next best alternative that he gives up.
Why D: A snack is an extra expense, not the next best choice he gives up by going. His opportunity cost is the $60 he could have earned working on Saturday instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are goods?
A: Physical products that people buy, such as shoes
B: Ideas that cannot be sold or traded at all
C: Money earned from a job each week or month
D: Work done for someone else, such as a haircut overall
Why A: Goods are physical products that people buy, such as shoes, food and cars, which can be touched and owned, and this separates them from services, which are work done for others.
Why B: Ideas that cannot be sold or traded are not goods in economics. Goods are physical products that people buy, such as shoes, and they are things that can be bought and sold.
Why C: Money earned from a job is income, not a good. Goods are physical products that people buy, such as shoes, and income is what people use to buy them.
Why D: Work done for someone else, such as a haircut, is a service. Goods are physical products that people buy, such as shoes, so this option describes the other category.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are services?
A: Products that can be touched and held by buyers
B: Natural resources like land and water bodies
C: Machines used in a factory to make goods
D: Work performed for others, such as a haircut
Why A: Products that can be touched and held are goods. Services are work performed for others, such as a haircut, so this option describes goods and gives the wrong category.
Why B: Natural resources like land and water are factors of production. Services are work performed for others, such as a haircut, so this option describes a different idea in economics.
Why C: Machines used in a factory are capital, a factor of production. Services are work performed for others, such as a haircut, so machines are not the meaning of services.
Why D: Services are work performed for others, such as a haircut, a medical exam or a repair, where the buyer receives the benefit of labor and not a physical product to keep.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a service?
A: A loaf of bread from a shop
B: A dentist cleaning your teeth
C: A new bicycle from a store
D: A pair of running shoes bought
Why A: A loaf of bread is a physical product that can be held, so it is a good. A service is work done for others, so bread is not an example.
Why B: A dentist cleaning your teeth is a service, because it is work done for you by another person and gives you a benefit but not a physical product to take away.
Why C: A new bicycle is a physical product bought from a store, so it is a good. A service is work done for others, so a bicycle is not an example.
Why D: A pair of running shoes is a physical product that can be held and owned, so it is a good. A service is work done for others, so shoes are not an example.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the four factors of production?
A: Banks, stores, farms and factories in town
B: Supply, demand, cost and revenue of firms
C: Land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
D: Price, profit, product and place of sale
Why A: Banks, stores, farms and factories are kinds of businesses and places. The four factors of production are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, which are the inputs businesses use, not the businesses themselves.
Why B: Supply, demand, cost and revenue are market concepts, not inputs to production. The four factors of production are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, which firms use to make goods and services.
Why C: The four factors of production are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, the resources that are combined to make goods and services, and each one plays a distinct part in production.
Why D: Price, profit, product and place of sale are marketing and business terms. The four factors of production are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, which are the inputs for making goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is labor as a factor of production?
A: Tools and machines used in production at a plant
B: The physical and mental work people contribute
C: The risk of starting a business for profit
D: Natural resources like water and soil in a region
Why A: Tools and machines used in production are capital, not labor. Labor is the physical and mental work people contribute to producing goods and services.
Why B: Labor as a factor of production is the physical and mental work people contribute to producing goods and services, such as a factory worker lifting parts or a designer planning a product.
Why C: The risk of starting a business is taken by an entrepreneur. Labor is the physical and mental work that people contribute, and it is a separate factor of production.
Why D: Natural resources like water and soil are land, which is a different factor of production. Labor is the physical and mental work that people contribute to making goods and services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is capital as a factor of production?
A: Land and natural resources, such as forests and rivers
B: The money in your wallet or in a bank account
C: The work that people do to earn a wage each day
D: Tools, machines and buildings used to make goods
Why A: Land and natural resources, such as forests and rivers, are the factor called land. Capital is made up of tools, machines and buildings used to make goods, so this option describes land.
