Why B: Money in a wallet or bank is financial capital in everyday speech, but it is not a factor of production. Capital in economics means tools, machines and buildings used to make goods.
Why C: The work people do to earn a wage is labor, a different factor of production. Capital in economics is made of tools, machines and buildings used to make goods and services.
Why D: Capital as a factor of production means the tools, machines and buildings used to make goods, which are made by people and help workers produce more than they could by hand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an entrepreneur do?
A: Starts a business and takes on its risks
B: Lends money to the government for its needs
C: Works for a fixed wage at a factory each week
D: Collects taxes for the government each year
Why A: An entrepreneur starts a business and takes on its risks, organizing land, labor and capital in the hope of a profit, and also accepts that the venture may lose money.
Why B: Lending money to the government is done by buyers of government bonds. An entrepreneur starts a business and takes on its risks, so lending for government needs is a different role.
Why C: Working for a fixed wage at a factory is the role of a worker, who supplies labor. An entrepreneur starts a business and takes on its risks, so a fixed wage does not fit.
Why D: Collecting taxes for the government is done by tax agencies. An entrepreneur starts a business and takes on its risks, so collecting taxes is not what the role means.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is demand?
A: How much of a product sellers will offer at each price they set
B: The number of stores in a town or a city that sell goods to buyers overall
C: How much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at a price
D: The price a store sets for a good or service and all its sales
Why A: How much of a product sellers will offer at each price is supply, not demand. Demand is how much buyers are willing and able to buy at a price.
Why B: The number of stores selling goods is a count of sellers in a market. Demand is how much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at a price.
Why C: Demand is how much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price, and both willingness and ability to pay are needed for real demand.
Why D: The price a store sets for a good is a price chosen by the seller. Demand describes how much buyers are willing and able to buy at a price, not the price set by a seller.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is supply?
A: How much of a product sellers are willing to offer at a price
B: The profit earned on each item, the price minus the cost
C: The cost of materials used to make a good for sale there
D: How much buyers want to buy at a given price today in a shop overall
Why A: Supply is how much of a product sellers are willing to offer at a price, and it usually rises when the price rises because selling more becomes more profitable for them.
Why B: The profit earned on each item, the price minus the cost, is profit per unit. Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer at a price, so profit is not its definition.
Why C: The cost of materials used to make a good is a production cost. Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer at a price, so a cost of materials does not define supply.
Why D: How much buyers want to buy at a given price is demand, not supply. Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer at a price, so this option describes the buyers' side.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the law of demand say?
A: As price rises, sellers must produce less
B: As price rises, buyers usually buy less
C: Price never affects buying by people
D: As price rises, buyers usually buy more
Why A: As price rises, sellers produce more, not less, which is the law of supply. The law of demand concerns buyers and says that a higher price usually leads to buying less.
Why B: The law of demand says that as price rises, buyers usually buy less, because a higher price makes a good cost more compared with other things the buyers could choose.
Why C: Price does affect buying, so the claim that it never does is wrong. The law of demand says that as price rises, buyers usually buy less of a good.
Why D: As price rises, buyers usually buy less, not more. Buying more at a higher price would reverse the law of demand, which is an inverse link between price and quantity bought.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the law of supply say?
A: Sellers ignore price completely when they sell
B: As price rises, sellers usually offer less
C: Buyers decide what sellers must then make
D: As price rises, sellers usually offer more
Why A: Sellers do respond to price, so ignoring it completely is wrong. The law of supply says that as price rises, sellers usually offer more of a good for sale.
Why B: As price rises, sellers usually offer more, not less, because higher prices bring higher profits. Offering less at a higher price would reverse the law of supply.
Why C: The law of supply is about how sellers respond to price, not about buyers deciding what sellers make. It says that as price rises, sellers usually offer more.
Why D: The law of supply says that as price rises, sellers usually offer more of a good, because a higher price makes selling more profitable, which is a direct link between price and quantity supplied.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is equilibrium price?
A: The lowest price allowed by law for goods sold in a shop or store
B: The price set by a store manager for goods on the shelves daily
C: The price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded
D: The highest price a seller can charge before buyers stop buying it every time
Why A: The lowest price allowed by law is a price floor, such as a minimum wage. The equilibrium price is where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.
Why B: A price set by a store manager is a chosen price and may not clear the market. The equilibrium price is where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.
Why C: The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, so there is no surplus or shortage and the market clears at that price.
Why D: The highest price a seller can charge before buyers stop buying is not the equilibrium price. Equilibrium is where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, with no leftover goods or unmet demand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store has more shirts than customers want at the current price. What is this called?
A: A monopoly
B: A surplus
C: A shortage
D: A balance
Why A: A monopoly is a market with a single seller. A store with more shirts than customers want at the current price has a surplus, so monopoly is the wrong term.
Why B: A surplus occurs when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded at the current price, as with a store that has more shirts than customers want to buy.
Why C: A shortage is the opposite case, where customers want more than is available. More shirts than customers want at the current price is a surplus, so shortage is wrong.
Why D: A balance would mean the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, which is equilibrium. Here the store has more shirts than customers want, so there is a surplus.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Customers want more concert tickets than are available at the current price. What is this called?
A: A shortage
B: A tariff
C: Equilibrium
D: A surplus
Why A: A shortage occurs when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied at the current price, as when customers want more concert tickets than are available.
Why B: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Customers wanting more tickets than are available at the current price is a shortage, so a tariff is the wrong term.
Why C: Equilibrium is when the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded. Here customers want more tickets than exist at the current price, so the market is not in equilibrium.
Why D: A surplus is when the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded. Here customers want more tickets than are available, which is the opposite, so it is a shortage.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inflation?
A: A rise in the price of one item only
B: A rise in the number of workers
C: A general fall in prices over time
D: A general rise in prices over time
Why A: A rise in the price of one item only is a change in a relative price. Inflation is a general rise in prices across the economy over time.
Why B: A rise in the number of workers is employment or labor force growth. Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, so the number of workers is unrelated.
Why C: A general fall in prices over time is deflation, the opposite of inflation. Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, so this option reverses the meaning.
Why D: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, which means each unit of money buys less than before, so the cost of living goes up across the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is unemployment?
A: Being without a job while actively looking for work
B: Choosing not to look for work, to stay at home now
C: Having a job that you enjoy and find rewarding
D: Working fewer hours by choice in any given week
Why A: This describes a person who has a job and is working, so it is the opposite of unemployment, which means having no job at all.
Why B: This describes someone who chooses not to look for work, and such people are outside the labor force and are not counted as unemployed in official measures.
Why C: This describes a person who is employed and happy in the job, so it cannot be unemployment, which by definition means being without any paid job.
Why D: This describes a person who works part time by choice, so they still hold a job and are employed, which means they are not unemployed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does GDP measure?
A: The number of people in a country, as in a census
B: The value of goods and services produced in a country
C: The money held by the government in its accounts
D: The prices of common goods in a country, in a year overall
Why A: This is a population count, which a census records, whereas GDP measures the value of output rather than how many people live in a country.
Why B: GDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period, so it measures output and not money or population.
Why C: This describes government cash balances or reserves, which are a budget matter, while GDP measures the value of what the whole economy produces over a period.
Why D: This describes a price level, which a price index tracks, whereas GDP adds up the value of goods and services produced and not their average prices.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a recession?
A: A period with no prices charged on goods in shops anywhere
B: A period of fast growth in output and jobs for firms there
C: A period of declining economic activity lasting several months
D: A one-day stock rise that is followed by a fall the next week overall
Why A: A period in which no prices are charged is not a recession, since a recession is a fall in output and jobs and prices still exist.
Why B: Fast growth in output and jobs describes an economic expansion or boom, which is the opposite of a recession, where output and employment fall.
Why C: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity, shown by falling output, income and jobs, and it typically lasts for several months or longer.
Why D: A single day of stock gains followed by a later fall is ordinary market volatility, not a recession, which needs months of falling economic activity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business?
A: A group that raises donations to fund a charitable or public cause
B: A club whose members meet to share a hobby for fun
C: A government office that issues rules and licenses to firms
D: An organization that provides goods or services to earn a profit
Why A: A group that raises donations for a cause is a nonprofit or charity. A business provides goods or services to earn a profit.
Why B: A hobby club does not sell goods or services to earn a profit. A business provides goods or services to customers for money.
Why C: A government office that issues rules and licenses is a regulator, not a business, because it does not sell goods or services to earn a profit.
Why D: A business is an organization that provides goods or services to customers in exchange for money, with the aim of earning a profit for its owners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is profit?
A: The money borrowed from a bank to start
B: The money left after paying all costs
C: All money received from sales to buyers
D: The money spent on supplies each month
Why A: Money borrowed from a bank is a loan, which a business must repay with interest, so it is a source of funds and not profit.
Why B: Profit is what remains of a business's money after it has paid all of its costs, so it is revenue minus total costs.
Why C: All money received from sales is revenue, which is the starting amount before costs are subtracted, so it is bigger than profit and is not the same thing.
Why D: Money spent on supplies each month is only one cost, so it is an expense, and profit is what remains after all such costs are paid.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop earns $5,000 and spends $3,800. What is its profit?
Why A: $3,800 is the amount the shop spends, which is its cost, and profit is revenue minus cost, so this figure ignores the $5,000 earned.
Why B: $5,000 is the shop's revenue, but profit means what is left after costs, so $3,800 of expenses must still be subtracted from it.
Why C: $8,800 comes from adding $5,000 and $3,800, but profit is found by subtracting costs from revenue and not by adding them together.
Why D: Profit equals revenue minus costs, so $5,000 minus $3,800 gives $1,200, which is what the shop keeps after paying all its expenses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is revenue?
A: The money a business receives from selling goods or services
B: The cost of making goods in a factory or a plant each year
C: The money left after expenses, which an owner keeps in total
D: The money owed to suppliers for goods bought on credit
Why A: Revenue is the total money a business receives from selling its goods or services, before any costs are taken out, so this is the right definition.
Why B: The cost of making goods is an expense, and revenue is the money coming in from sales instead of the money spent on production.
Why C: Money left after expenses is profit, not revenue, because revenue is counted before any costs are subtracted from what customers paid.
Why D: Money owed to suppliers for goods bought on credit is a liability or accounts payable, and it is money going out and not revenue coming in.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an expense?
A: Money earned from customers for sales
B: Money invested by the owner of a firm
C: A cost a business pays to operate
D: Money saved for later use by a firm
Why A: Money earned from customers for sales is revenue, which is income coming into the business, while an expense is a cost that the business pays out.
Why B: Money invested by an owner is capital put into the firm, which is not an expense, since an expense is a cost paid to keep operating.
Why C: An expense is a cost that a business pays in order to operate, such as rent, wages, utilities and supplies, and it reduces the profit earned.
Why D: Money saved for later use is a reserve or savings, which the firm keeps, whereas an expense is money actually paid out to run the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do businesses need to make a profit?
A: To remove all competition from a market
B: To pay costs, grow and reward owners
C: To stop paying taxes to the state
D: To avoid serving customers each day
Why A: Making a profit does not remove competition, and trying to eliminate all rivals is not the purpose of profit, which instead supports the firm itself.
Why B: Profit lets a business pay its costs, fund growth and expansion, and reward its owners for the risk taken, so it needs profit to survive.
Why C: Businesses still pay taxes on their profits, so profit does not let them stop paying taxes, and tax avoidance is not why firms seek profit.
Why D: Businesses earn profit by serving customers, so they cannot avoid serving them, and profit does not remove the need to serve buyers every day.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a customer?
A: A person who owns the business and runs it
B: A person who works for the business and is paid
C: A person who supplies materials to a business
D: A person or business that buys goods or services
Why A: A person who owns and runs the business is the owner, not the customer, since a customer is someone who buys the goods or services offered.
Why B: A person who works for the business and is paid is an employee, whereas a customer is the buyer who pays the business for what it sells.
Why C: A person who supplies materials to a business is a supplier, who sells to the firm, whereas a customer buys from the firm instead.
Why D: A customer is a person or business that buys goods or services from a seller, so this matches the standard meaning of the word customer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a supplier?
A: A business that provides goods or materials to another business
B: A customer who buys goods from a business each week there
C: A competitor in the same market, who sells similar goods
D: An employee who sells products to customers in a store daily in general
Why A: A supplier is a business that provides goods or materials to another business so that it can make or sell its own products, which fits this definition.
Why B: A customer who buys goods from the business each week is the buyer, which is the opposite side of the sale compared with a supplier.
Why C: A competitor sells similar goods in the same market and rivals the business, whereas a supplier sells goods to the business and works with it.
Why D: An employee who sells products to customers works for the business and is paid wages, so this describes a salesperson and is not a supplier.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is competition?
A: Cooperation between firms to fix prices in a market
B: Selling products at no cost to buyers in a market
C: Rivalry between businesses selling similar products
D: A business having no rivals in its market area
Why A: Cooperation between firms to fix prices is collusion, which is usually illegal, and it is the opposite of competition, where firms rival each other.
Why B: Selling at no cost to buyers is giving goods away, and competition is rivalry among firms that sell for a price, so this does not define it.
Why C: Competition is the rivalry between businesses that sell similar products and try to win the same customers by price, quality or service.
Why D: A business with no rivals in its market is a monopoly, which is the absence of competition, so this describes the opposite of competition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How does competition usually help customers?
A: It can bring lower prices and better quality
B: It removes safety rules, so firms can cut costs
C: It reduces choices for buyers in a market
D: It raises prices on all goods in most shops
Why A: Competition makes firms compete for buyers, which can bring lower prices and better quality, and customers benefit because they can pick the best deal.
Why B: Competition does not remove safety rules, which still apply to all firms, and customers are not helped when firms cut costs by ignoring safety.
Why C: Competition tends to increase the choices available to buyers because more firms offer products, so a reduction in choice is the opposite effect.
Why D: Competition usually pushes prices down as firms try to win buyers, so claiming that it raises prices on all goods is the reverse of the effect.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a consumer?
A: A person who produces goods for sale
B: A person who uses goods and services
C: A person who sets trade rules for firms
D: A person who owns a factory or a plant
Why A: A person who produces goods for sale is a producer, while a consumer is a person on the other side of the market who uses them.
Why B: A consumer is a person who uses goods and services, usually after buying them, so this correctly names the person at the end of the chain.
Why C: A person who sets trade rules for firms is a regulator or lawmaker, whereas a consumer is simply the one who uses what is produced.
Why D: A person who owns a factory is an owner or producer, not a consumer, because a consumer is defined by using goods and services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a producer?
A: A person who only buys goods and never sells any at all
B: A person who advertises goods using posters and radio spots
C: A person or business that makes goods or provides services
D: A person who sets laws for the country and its firms
Why A: A person who only buys goods and never sells any is a consumer, which is the opposite of a producer, who makes goods or supplies services.
Why B: A person who advertises goods is working in marketing or promotion, which is one activity of selling, and does not itself define what a producer is.
Why C: A producer is a person or business that makes goods or provides services for others to use, so this matches the standard definition.
Why D: A person who sets laws for the country is a lawmaker or government official, whereas a producer is a maker of goods or services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is productivity?
A: The profit a business makes each year
B: The price of a finished product in a shop
C: The number of stores a firm owns in a region
D: The amount produced for the resources used
Why A: Profit is revenue minus costs, which measures money earned, whereas productivity measures how much output is made from the inputs, so it is different from yearly profit.
Why B: The price of a finished product is what buyers pay, which is a market value, and productivity instead compares output with the resources used.
Why C: The number of stores a firm owns measures its size or reach, not productivity, which compares how much is produced against the resources used.
Why D: Productivity is the amount produced for the resources used, such as output per worker or per hour, so more output from the same inputs means higher productivity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an economic system?
A: A collection of factories in a city that make goods there overall
B: A list of taxes a country charges to its firms and people
C: A set of banking rules that firms must follow each year
D: The way a society decides what, how and for whom to produce
Why A: A collection of factories is only part of the productive capacity of a place, and an economic system is the whole method a society uses to organize production.
Why B: A list of taxes is a tax code, which is only one tool of government, whereas an economic system decides what, how and for whom to produce.
Why C: A set of banking rules is financial regulation, which covers only banks and money, while an economic system sets up how all of the goods are produced.
Why D: An economic system is the way a society answers what, how and for whom to produce, using its limited resources, so this is the standard definition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a market economy, who mainly decides what to produce?
A: A central government plan that sets output of industries
B: Consumers and businesses through buying and selling
C: Tradition and custom passed down over many years
D: A foreign government that sets rules for the market
Why A: A central government plan setting output describes a command economy, not a market economy, where prices and demand direct what is produced instead.
Why B: In a market economy, consumers and businesses decide what to produce through buying and selling, as demand and prices signal what people want.
Why C: Tradition and custom guiding production describes a traditional economy, not a market economy, where choices follow buyers and sellers instead of past habits.
Why D: A foreign government setting market rules is not how a market economy works, since its own buyers and sellers decide what is produced through trade.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a command economy, who makes most decisions?
A: The central government
B: Competing businesses
C: Individual buyers alone
D: Local families by custom
Why A: In a command economy the central government makes most decisions about what to produce, how to produce it and who gets it.
Why B: Competing businesses making their own choices describes a market economy, whereas in a command economy the state plans and controls production.
Why C: Individual buyers alone deciding is a market feature, and a command economy puts the major choices in the hands of the government, not the buyers.
Why D: Local families following custom describes a traditional economy, while a command economy relies on central government planning for most decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a traditional economy?
A: An economy that depends mainly on exports and trade with other countries
B: An economy that mixes private business with some government control
C: An economy guided by customs and habits passed down through generations
D: An economy planned by the government and its officials each year
Why A: Heavy trade describes how an economy sells abroad, not how choices are made. A traditional economy follows customs passed down through generations.
Why B: Mixing private business and government control is a mixed economy. A traditional economy follows customs and habits passed down through generations.
Why C: A traditional economy is guided by customs and habits passed down through generations, so what to make and how to make it follow long standing practice.
Why D: An economy planned by the government and officials describes a command economy, while a traditional economy follows inherited customs and not state plans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mixed economy?
A: An economy with no private businesses, where the state owns all shops
B: An economy that only trades by barter, with no use of money
C: An economy with no government role in any part of the market
D: An economy that combines private choice with government involvement
Why A: An economy with no private businesses where the state owns all shops is a command economy, since a mixed economy keeps private firms in place.
Why B: An economy that trades only by barter is a simple traditional one, whereas a mixed economy uses money and combines private and government roles.
Why C: An economy with no government role in the market is a pure market economy, but a mixed economy includes real government involvement alongside private business.
Why D: A mixed economy combines private choice and markets with government involvement, such as regulation and public services, which makes this the correct definition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is capitalism?
A: A system where goods are shared equally among all people by custom
B: A system where private owners control businesses and resources
C: A system where the government owns all property and all firms
D: A system without markets, prices or any trade between people
Why A: Goods shared equally among all people by custom describes a communal or traditional arrangement, whereas capitalism rests on private ownership and market exchange.
Why B: Capitalism is a system where private owners control businesses and resources and operate them to earn profit, so this matches the usual definition.
Why C: A system where the government owns all property and firms describes socialism or communism, which is the opposite of capitalism and its private ownership.
Why D: A system without markets, prices or trade is not capitalism, which depends on markets and prices to coordinate the exchanges among people.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is private property?
A: Property that a person may use but cannot sell or give away
B: Property owned by the whole community, such as a park or library open overall
C: Property owned by individuals or businesses rather than the government
D: Property that is rented from a landlord for a limited time
Why A: Private property can be sold, rented or passed on by its owner. The right to transfer it is part of what makes it private.
Why B: Property owned by the whole community, such as a park, is public property, which is the opposite of the private property owned by individuals.
Why C: Private property is owned by individuals or businesses, not by the government, and its owners can use it, sell it or pass it on.
Why D: Rented property belongs to the landlord, not the renter. Private property is owned by an individual or business, which controls its use.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the role of profit in a market economy?
A: It rewards risk-taking and guides what businesses produce
B: It is illegal to earn in any market in the country
C: It discourages all production by firms in the market
D: It is set by the government for every firm, with a cap overall
Why A: Profit rewards risk taking and guides what businesses produce, because firms make more of goods that earn money, so it works as a signal and reward.
Why B: Profit is not illegal to earn in a market economy, where it is the normal reward for businesses that serve customers well, and the claim is false.
Why C: Profit encourages production and does not discourage it, since firms produce goods in order to earn profit from selling them to buyers.
Why D: Profit is not set by the government for each firm with a cap, because in a market economy firms earn whatever the market allows.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is free enterprise?
A: The freedom to start and run a business with limited government control
B: A policy of letting goods cross borders without tariffs or quotas
C: A system where workers jointly own and manage the business
D: A system where the government sets production goals for firms
Why A: Free enterprise is the freedom to start and run a business with limited government control, so people choose what to sell and keep their profit.
Why B: Letting goods cross borders freely is free trade. Free enterprise is the freedom to start and run a business with limited government control.
Why C: Joint worker ownership describes a cooperative. Free enterprise is the freedom to start and run a business with limited government control.
Why D: Government production goals are a feature of a command economy. Free enterprise leaves business choices to owners with limited government control.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of the government's role in a mixed economy?
A: Deciding what each factory will produce
B: Assigning workers to jobs based on a central plan
C: Taking over firms that earn large profits
D: Setting safety standards and providing public services
Why A: Deciding factory output is central planning in a command economy. A mixed economy leaves most production choices to private firms.
Why B: Assigning jobs by central plan is a command economy feature. A mixed economy leaves most job choices to workers and firms.
Why C: Seizing profitable firms is not a typical role in a mixed economy, where private firms keep their profits and the state sets standards.
Why D: Setting safety standards and providing public services are typical government roles in a mixed economy, where the state supports private business without running everything.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a fixed cost?
A: A cost that rises and falls with the level of output
B: A cost that stays the same no matter how much is produced
C: A cost paid once by a customer at the time of sale there
D: A cost the firm cannot predict until the end of the year
Why A: A cost that moves with output is a variable cost, such as materials. A fixed cost, such as rent, stays the same as production changes.
Why B: A fixed cost stays the same no matter how much is produced, such as rent or insurance, because it does not rise or fall with output.
Why C: A cost paid once by a customer at the time of sale is a price or a payment to the seller and not a cost the business bears as fixed.
Why D: Fixed costs are known in advance, such as rent or insurance. They do not change with the amount produced.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a variable cost?
A: A cost that never exists in any firm at all
B: A cost paid to the government once a year
C: A cost that changes with the amount produced
D: A cost that stays the same in each month
Why A: A cost that never exists in any firm is not a real cost type, whereas variable costs appear in nearly every business that makes or sells goods.
Why B: A cost paid to the government once a year describes a tax or fee, which is not defined by how it changes with output as a variable cost does.
Why C: A variable cost changes with the amount produced, such as materials or packaging, so producing more raises it and producing less lowers it.
Why D: A cost that stays the same in each month is a fixed cost, such as rent, and this is the opposite of a variable cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a fixed cost for a pizza shop?
A: Order boxes
B: Dough costs
C: Monthly rent
D: Cheese costs
Why A: Order boxes are used for each pizza that is sold, so the cost rises with the number of orders and makes it a variable cost.
Why B: Dough is used up with every pizza made, so the amount spent rises and falls with output, which makes it a variable cost and not a fixed cost.
Why C: Monthly rent is the same amount whether the shop makes ten pizzas or a thousand, so it does not change with output and is a fixed cost.
Why D: Cheese is used on each pizza, so the amount bought changes with the number of pizzas made, which makes it a variable cost, not a fixed one.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a variable cost for a pizza shop?
A: Cheese used on each pizza
B: Monthly rent for the shop
C: Loan payment on the oven
D: Yearly insurance for the shop
Why A: Cheese is used on each pizza, so more pizzas mean more cheese bought and a higher cost, which makes it a variable cost that changes with output.
Why B: Monthly rent is a fixed amount paid whether the shop sells many pizzas or none, so it does not vary with output and is a fixed cost.
Why C: A loan payment on the oven is a set amount each period regardless of pizzas sold, so it is a fixed cost and not a variable one.
Why D: Yearly insurance for the shop is a set charge that does not change when more pizzas are made, so it is a fixed cost, not variable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is total cost calculated?
A: Revenue minus the profit made
B: Fixed costs plus variable costs
C: Fixed costs minus variable costs
D: Price times the quantity sold
Why A: Revenue minus profit gives the costs that were paid, which is a way to find costs after the fact, and it is not the standard formula for total cost.
Why B: Total cost is fixed costs plus variable costs, because a firm must pay both the costs that stay steady and those that change with output.
Why C: Subtracting variable costs from fixed costs gives a meaningless difference, since total cost needs both parts added together to show everything the firm pays.
Why D: Price times quantity sold is the formula for revenue, which is money coming in, so it does not give total cost, which is money going out.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop has fixed costs of $500 and variable costs of $3 per item. What is the total cost of 200 items?
Why A: $503 adds the $500 fixed cost to only $3, which treats the variable cost as a single item, while the $3 is charged on each of the 200 items.
Why B: $600 is only the variable part, because 200 times $3 equals $600, but the $500 of fixed costs must be added to reach the total cost.
Why C: $1,500 comes from multiplying $500 by 3, which wrongly applies the $3 to the fixed cost, while variable cost is $3 times 200 items.
Why D: Variable cost is $3 times 200 items, which is $600, and adding the $500 fixed cost gives a total cost of $1,100.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is revenue calculated?
A: Price times quantity sold
B: Quantity divided by price
C: Cost plus profit earned
D: Price minus cost per item
Why A: Revenue is price times the quantity sold, so selling more units or at a higher price brings in more money from customers.
Why B: Dividing quantity by price does not give money earned, and the units come out wrong, because revenue is the product of price and quantity sold.
Why C: Cost plus profit earned is a way to reach the same amount in an accounting identity, but it is not how revenue is calculated from price and sales.
Why D: Price minus cost per item gives the profit on one item, not revenue, which is the whole amount received from all items sold at the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bakery sells 150 muffins at $2.50 each. What is its revenue?
Why A: $152.50 comes from adding 150 and 2.50, but revenue needs multiplication of the number of muffins sold by the price of each muffin.
Why B: Revenue is quantity times price, so 150 muffins at $2.50 each gives 150 times 2.50, which equals $375.
Why C: $60 comes from dividing 150 by 2.50, but revenue is found by multiplying quantity and price, not by dividing one by the other.
Why D: $3,750 is ten times too large, and it comes from a decimal slip, since 150 times $2.50 equals $375, not $3,750.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is profit calculated?
A: Fixed plus variable cost
B: Price times quantity
C: Revenue minus total cost
D: Revenue plus total cost
Why A: Fixed plus variable cost gives total cost, which is the money going out, so it is not profit, which is what remains after costs are paid.
Why B: Price times quantity gives revenue, the money received from sales, and profit requires subtracting the total cost from that revenue.
Why C: Profit is revenue minus total cost, so it is the money a business keeps after paying every cost it incurred in making its sales.
Why D: Adding revenue and total cost would give a larger number that has no meaning as profit, which needs total cost to be subtracted from revenue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business has revenue of $9,000 and total costs of $7,200. What is its profit?
Why A: $7,200 is the total cost of the business, not its profit, because profit means revenue minus costs, and $9,000 of revenue must be considered.
Why B: $16,200 comes from adding $9,000 and $7,200, but profit is found by subtracting costs from revenue, not by adding them together.
Why C: $9,000 is the revenue, which is the money received before paying costs, and profit is smaller because $7,200 of costs must be subtracted.
Why D: Profit is revenue minus total costs, so $9,000 minus $7,200 equals $1,800, which is what the business keeps after paying its costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a loss?
A: When costs are greater than revenue
B: When costs equal revenue exactly
C: When a business has no customers
D: When revenue is greater than costs
Why A: A loss occurs when costs are greater than revenue, so the business spends more than it earns and ends up with negative profit.
Why B: When costs equal revenue exactly, the business neither gains nor loses, which is the break even point, so this is not a loss.
Why C: Having no customers may lead to a loss, but a loss is defined by costs exceeding revenue, and a firm with customers can still lose.
Why D: When revenue is greater than costs, the business earns a profit, which is the opposite of a loss, so this cannot be the definition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is break-even?
A: When profit is at its highest
B: When a business has no revenue
C: When a business has no costs
D: When revenue equals total costs
Why A: Highest profit is the best outcome for a firm, while break even is a point where profit is exactly zero, so the two are quite different.
Why B: A business with no revenue earns nothing and has a loss if it has any costs, so this is not break even, which needs revenue to cover costs.
Why C: A business with no costs would keep all of its revenue as profit, so that is not break even, where revenue only covers total costs.
Why D: Break even is the point where revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss, which makes this the correct answer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is markup?
A: A tax added at checkout on a purchase in a shop
B: The amount added to a product's cost to set its price
C: A discount given to customers, taken off the list price
D: A fee for shipping goods to a buyer's home address
Why A: A tax added at checkout is a sales tax, which the government collects, whereas markup is an amount a seller adds to the cost to set a price.
Why B: Markup is the amount added to a product's cost to set its selling price, which covers other expenses and provides profit for the seller.
Why C: A discount taken off the list price is a markdown, which lowers the price, so it is the opposite of a markup that raises the price.
Why D: A fee for shipping goods is a delivery charge and is separate from markup, which is added to the product's cost to determine the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store buys a toy for $8 and adds a $4 markup. What is the selling price?
Why A: $2 is not the price, because the selling price is the $8 cost plus the $4 markup, and this figure matches neither of those numbers.
Why B: $32 comes from multiplying $8 by $4, but markup is added to the cost and not multiplied by it, so $8 plus $4 is the price.
Why C: Selling price equals cost plus markup, so $8 plus $4 gives $12, which is the price the store charges for the toy.
Why D: $4 is only the markup, and the selling price must include the $8 the store paid for the toy, so the price is $8 plus $4.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sole proprietorship?
A: A business owned by many shareholders
B: A business owned by two partners only
C: A business owned by the government
D: A business owned and run by one person
Why A: A business owned by many shareholders is a corporation, not a sole proprietorship, which has only one owner who runs the business personally.
Why B: A business owned by two partners only is a partnership with two owners, whereas a sole proprietorship has just a single owner.
Why C: A business owned by the government is a public enterprise, but a sole proprietorship is privately owned by one person.
Why D: A sole proprietorship is a business owned and run by one person, who keeps the profits and is responsible for the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an advantage of a sole proprietorship?
A: It can raise unlimited money easily
B: It continues forever after the owner
C: It is easy and inexpensive to start
D: The owner has no debt responsibility
Why A: A sole proprietorship cannot easily raise unlimited money, since it relies mainly on the owner's savings and loans, so this is a disadvantage and not an advantage.
Why B: A sole proprietorship usually ends when the owner dies or quits, so it does not continue forever, which is a trait of a corporation.
Why C: A sole proprietorship is easy and inexpensive to start, with few legal steps and low costs, which is why many small businesses begin this way.
Why D: The owner of a sole proprietorship is personally responsible for the debts of the business, so having no debt responsibility is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is unlimited liability?
A: The business pays no taxes on any profit it makes each year
B: The owner is personally responsible for all business debts
C: The owner has no responsibility for debts of the business
D: The business cannot borrow money from any bank or lender
Why A: Paying no taxes on profit is not what liability means, because liability concerns responsibility for debts, and owners usually must still pay tax on income.
Why B: Unlimited liability means the owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so personal assets such as savings or a home may be used.
Why C: Having no responsibility for the debts of the business describes limited liability, which is the opposite of unlimited liability for the owner.
Why D: Unlimited liability does not stop a business from borrowing, because the term describes who must repay debts and not whether a lender will lend.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a partnership?
A: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and duties
B: A business owned by one person who runs it alone and keeps all profit
C: A business owned by shareholders who elect directors to run it for them
D: A business run by a city and funded by its taxes and fees paid
Why A: A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share profits, duties and often the risks, which matches this definition.
Why B: A business owned and run by one person who keeps all the profit is a sole proprietorship, since a partnership has two or more owners.
Why C: A business owned by shareholders who elect directors describes a corporation, whereas partners usually manage a partnership directly and share its profits.
Why D: A business run by a city and funded by taxes is a public enterprise, not a partnership, which is owned by private partners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a corporation?
A: A business that is a legal entity separate from its owners
B: A business run by the government and funded by taxes
C: A business owned and run by one person, who is liable for debts
D: A business with no owners and no one in charge of it
Why A: A corporation is a business that is a legal entity separate from its owners, so it can own property, enter contracts and be sued.
Why B: A business run by the government and funded by taxes is a public enterprise, not a corporation, which is usually owned by private shareholders.
Why C: A business owned and run by one person with personal liability for debts is a sole proprietorship, whereas a corporation is legally separate from its owners.
Why D: A business with no owners and no one in charge does not exist, because a corporation has shareholders who own it and directors who lead it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a shareholder?
A: A person who buys the product of a firm each week
B: A person who works in a corporation for wages
C: A person who owns shares of stock in a corporation
D: A person who lends goods to a corporation for a fee
Why A: A person who buys the product of a firm is a customer, while a shareholder owns a part of the corporation itself.
Why B: A person who works in a corporation for wages is an employee, who is paid for work, not a shareholder, who holds ownership.
Why C: A shareholder is a person who owns shares of stock in a corporation, which makes the holder a part owner of the company.
Why D: A person who lends goods to a corporation for a fee is a lessor or lender, and a shareholder owns shares instead of lending to the firm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is limited liability?
A: Owners pay no taxes on the money that the firm earns each year in any state overall
B: Owners are not personally responsible for business debts beyond their investment
C: Owners cannot sell their shares to anyone else for any price at all ever
D: Owners are fully responsible for all debts, including those of other owners
Why A: Paying no taxes on earnings is not limited liability, which concerns debts and legal responsibility, and owners of limited liability firms still pay tax.
Why B: Limited liability means owners are not personally responsible for business debts beyond what they invested, so their personal assets are protected from the firm's creditors.
Why C: Limited liability does not stop owners from selling their shares, and shares of many companies can be sold, so this claim is false.
Why D: Owners being fully responsible for all debts, including those of other owners, describes unlimited liability, which is the opposite of limited liability.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a limited liability company (LLC)?
A: A company with only limited customers who may buy from it yearly
B: A company owned by the state and run by public officials
C: A company that cannot earn profit from the goods it sells
D: A business form that protects owners from personal liability
Why A: A company with limited customers is not what LLC means, because the word limited refers to the owners' liability and not to how many buyers there are.
Why B: A company owned by the state and run by public officials is a public enterprise, but an LLC is a private business form for owners.
Why C: An LLC can earn profit from its sales like any business, so the claim that it cannot earn profit is false and ignores its purpose.
Why D: An LLC is a business form that protects owners from personal liability for business debts while allowing simpler management and taxation than a corporation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a franchise?
A: A business that uses another company's brand and system for a fee
B: A business owned by a city and run for the public good there
C: A permit from the city that allows a firm to open
D: A business owned and run by several partners who share profits
Why A: A franchise is a business that uses another company's brand and operating system for a fee, so the owner gets a known name and support.
Why B: A business owned by a city and run for the public good is a public enterprise, and a franchise is run privately under another firm's brand.
Why C: A permit is a license from the government. A franchise is a business that uses another company's brand and system for a fee.
Why D: Several partners sharing profits describes a partnership. A franchise uses another company's brand and system for a fee.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business plan?
A: A contract with a customer that sets the price and terms of a sale made
B: A list of a business's employees, with their titles, pay rates and start dates
C: A record of past sales that shows what was sold in each month of the year
D: A written document describing a business's goals and how it will reach them
Why A: A contract with a customer that sets the price and terms of a sale is a sales agreement, and a business plan describes the firm's goals.
Why B: A list of employees with titles and pay rates is a payroll or staff record, and it does not describe the business's goals or strategy.
Why C: A record of past sales is a sales report, which looks back at what happened, whereas a business plan looks ahead at goals and methods.
Why D: A business plan is a written document describing a business's goals and how it will reach them, covering its market, money and operations.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a business plan usually include?
A: Employee payroll records and tax forms
B: Receipts and invoices from past customers
C: Goals, market, finances and marketing plans
D: Customer complaints and product returns
Why A: Payroll and tax forms belong to operating records, not a plan. A business plan includes goals, market, finances and marketing plans.
Why B: A new business has no past invoices. A business plan includes goals, market, finances and marketing plans.
Why C: A business plan usually includes goals, the target market, financial plans and marketing plans, which show how the business will operate and earn money.
Why D: Complaints and returns come from operating experience. A business plan sets out goals, market, finances and marketing plans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might a bank ask for a business plan before giving a loan?
A: To set the owner's salary for the first full year of work
B: To judge whether the business is likely to repay the loan
C: To avoid lending any money to a new business owner
D: To make the owner share secrets with the public and rivals
Why A: A bank does not use a business plan to set the owner's salary, since it wants to see whether the loan will be repaid.
Why B: A bank asks for a business plan to judge whether the business is likely to succeed and repay the loan, which lowers its lending risk.
Why C: A bank lends money to earn interest, so it asks for a plan to decide which loans are safe, not to avoid lending to new owners.
Why D: A business plan is not meant to make the owner share secrets with the public and rivals, since a bank keeps such information private.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is start-up capital?
A: Profit earned in the first year of trade
B: The money needed to start a business
C: The salary of the owner each year
D: The tax paid by a new business each year
Why A: Profit earned in the first year of trade is income that comes after the business has started, whereas start up capital is needed before opening.
Why B: Start up capital is the money needed to start a business, covering equipment, stock, rent deposits and other costs before sales begin.
Why C: The owner's salary is a regular wage or draw for work and is separate from start up capital, which pays for launching the business.
Why D: A tax paid by a new business each year is an ongoing expense and not start up capital, which is the money to begin trading.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a common source of start-up money?
A: Personal savings
B: Customer refunds
C: Refunds from firms
D: Future profits
Why A: Personal savings are a common source of start up money, since owners often put their own money into a new business to get it going.
Why B: Customer refunds are money returned to buyers, so they take money out of a business and are not a source of start up money.
Why C: Refunds from firms are returns of money for goods already bought, so they are not a planned source of start up money for a new business.
Why D: Future profits do not yet exist when a business is starting, so they cannot fund it, whereas savings and loans are available at the start.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a loan?
A: Money given as a gift that need not be repaid ever
B: Money earned from a job and paid at the end of a month
C: Money borrowed that must be repaid, usually with interest
D: Money kept in a safe at the home of the owner of a firm overall
Why A: Money given as a gift that need not be repaid is a gift or grant, whereas a loan is money borrowed that must be repaid.
Why B: Money earned from a job and paid at month end is a wage or salary, which a worker earns, and it is not money borrowed.
Why C: A loan is money borrowed that must be repaid, usually with interest, so the borrower pays back more than the amount originally received.
Why D: Money kept in a safe at the home of the owner is cash savings, which the owner already holds, and it is not borrowed money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an investor?
A: A person who sells supplies to shops and to restaurants
B: A person who works for wages in a shop or an office daily
C: A person who only buys products from stores and uses them at home
D: A person who puts money into a business hoping to earn a return
Why A: A person who sells supplies to shops and restaurants is a supplier or wholesaler, whereas an investor puts money into a business hoping for a return.
Why B: A person who works for wages in a shop or an office is an employee, who sells time and labor, not an investor, who supplies money.
Why C: A person who only buys products from stores and uses them is a consumer, while an investor puts money into a business to earn more.
Why D: An investor is a person who puts money into a business hoping to earn a return, such as profit, dividends or growth in value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a business license?
A: Permission from the government to operate a business
B: A guarantee of profit issued by the state to owners
C: A list of customers kept by the owner of the firm daily
D: A tax refund form sent to the owner each year end
Why A: A business license is permission from the government to operate a business, and it shows that the owner has met local legal requirements.
Why B: A guarantee of profit issued by the state does not exist, because no license assures profit, and a license only gives permission to operate.
Why C: A list of customers kept by the owner is a customer record, whereas a license is an official permit granted by the government.
Why D: A tax refund form sent to the owner is a tax document, which has nothing to do with a license that gives permission to operate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Before opening a shop, which step is most important?
A: Setting prices at random for all goods
B: Researching customers and competition
C: Choosing a color for the logo only
D: Opening without any plan or any funds
Why A: Setting prices at random is a poor step that can cause losses, because prices should cover costs and match what customers will pay.
Why B: Researching customers and competition shows whether demand exists and what rivals offer, so it is the most important step before opening a shop.
Why C: Choosing a color for the logo only is a small detail that does not tell the owner whether the shop will attract customers or earn money.
Why D: Opening without any plan or funds is likely to fail, since a shop needs planning and money to pay for stock, rent and wages.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a service business?
A: A business that gives away products to people for free all day
B: A business that sells only physical goods, such as tools and clothes
C: A business that makes machines and tools for use in factories
D: A business that sells work or expertise instead of physical products
Why A: A business that gives away products for free earns nothing, and a service business sells work or expertise to customers in return for payment.
Why B: A business that sells only physical goods is a product or retail business, whereas a service business sells work or expertise and not physical items.
Why C: A business that makes machines and tools is a manufacturer, which produces physical goods, and a service business sells work rather than making goods.
Why D: A service business sells work or expertise instead of physical products, as with a barber, a lawyer or a repair shop, which matches this definition.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a manufacturing business?
A: A business that resells goods bought from other firms
B: A business that lends money to buyers and firms
C: A business that makes products from raw materials
D: A business that offers advice to clients and firms
Why A: A business that resells goods bought from other firms is a retailer or wholesaler, whereas a manufacturer makes the goods itself from raw materials.
Why B: A business that lends money to buyers and firms is a financial business such as a bank, not a manufacturer, which produces goods.
Why C: A manufacturing business makes products from raw materials, such as a factory turning steel into cars or wheat into flour, which fits this definition.
Why D: A business that offers advice to clients and firms is a consulting service, not a manufacturer, because it makes no physical products from raw materials.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a retail business?
A: A business that sells goods directly to consumers
B: A business that makes goods in a factory or a mill
C: A business that grows crops on a farm or an orchard
D: A business that sells goods only to other businesses
Why A: A retail business sells goods directly to consumers, such as a shop or an online store, so it is the last step before the buyer.
Why B: A business that makes goods in a factory or mill is a manufacturer, not a retailer, since retailers sell finished goods to consumers.
Why C: A business that grows crops on a farm is in agriculture, which is a primary activity, and it is not a retailer, who sells goods.
Why D: A business that sells goods only to other businesses is a wholesaler, not a retailer, since retailers sell directly to consumers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a wholesaler?
A: A business that offers advice to firms for a fee each year
B: A business that buys goods in bulk and sells them to retailers
C: A business that sells goods to the public from a store or site
D: A business that makes goods in a plant for sale to others
Why A: A business that offers advice to firms for a fee is a consultant, which is a service, while a wholesaler sells goods in bulk.
Why B: A wholesaler buys goods in bulk, usually from makers, and sells them to retailers, so it is the link in the middle of the supply chain.
Why C: A business that sells goods to the public from a store or site is a retailer, not a wholesaler, who sells to other businesses.
Why D: A business that makes goods in a plant is a manufacturer, whereas a wholesaler does not make goods but buys and resells them in bulk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the channel of distribution?
A: The way a company advertises its goods to buyers
B: The list of a store's prices, in a catalog
C: A television channel that shows ads and news
D: The path goods take from producer to consumer
Why A: The way a company advertises goods to buyers describes promotion, which is one of the four Ps, and it is not the path goods follow.
Why B: A list of a store's prices in a catalog is a price list, which shows costs, and it does not describe how goods reach consumers.
Why C: A television channel that shows ads is a media outlet, and the word channel in this term refers to a route for goods, not a broadcast.
Why D: The channel of distribution is the path goods take from producer to consumer, which may include wholesalers and retailers along the way.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is marketing?
A: Hiring new workers and training them to do the tasks of the firm
B: Keeping financial records of the money that comes in and goes out daily overall
C: Activities that identify customer needs and promote products to meet them
D: Making products in a factory, using machines and the workers there
Why A: Hiring and training workers is human resources, which is a separate business function, and marketing instead identifies customer needs and promotes products.
Why B: Keeping financial records is accounting, which tracks money, and marketing is about understanding customers and promoting products to them.
Why C: Marketing is the set of activities that identify customer needs and promote products to meet them, including research, pricing, promotion and distribution.
Why D: Making products with machines and workers is production or operations, and marketing instead focuses on customers, promotion and getting goods to buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the four Ps of marketing?
A: Product, price, place and promotion
B: Plan, perform, prove and publish ads
C: People, profit, plan and paper work
D: Pay, purchase, produce and pack goods
Why A: The four Ps of marketing are product, price, place and promotion, which together describe what is sold, its cost, where it is sold and how it is advertised.
Why B: Plan, perform, prove and publish ads is not a recognized marketing model, and it leaves out the product, price and place that the four Ps cover.
Why C: People, profit, plan and paper work is not the marketing mix, since the four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.
Why D: Pay, purchase, produce and pack goods lists business tasks and is not the standard marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is promotion?
A: Choosing where to sell a product, such as in a shop or mall
B: Setting the price of a product for the buyers of it
C: Communication that informs and persuades customers to buy
D: Designing the product for its buyers and for users
Why A: Choosing where to sell a product, such as in a shop or a mall, is place, not promotion, which is about communicating with buyers.
Why B: Setting the price of a product is the price element of the marketing mix, and promotion instead covers communication that informs and persuades customers.
Why C: Promotion is communication that informs and persuades customers to buy, using tools such as advertising, sales offers and public relations.
Why D: Designing the product for its buyers is the product element of the marketing mix, whereas promotion is how the firm communicates about it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is accounting?
A: Hiring and training staff for the finance department
B: Making advertisements for goods to be sold in stores
C: Shipping goods to stores and to buyers by road or rail as a rule
D: Recording, summarizing and reporting a business's finances
Why A: Hiring and training staff is human resources, a separate function, whereas accounting deals with the money records and reports of a business.
Why B: Making advertisements is part of marketing and promotion, which is a separate function, and accounting is about recording and reporting finances.
Why C: Shipping goods by road or rail is logistics or distribution, which moves products, and it does not describe the accounting of money.
Why D: Accounting is the recording, summarizing and reporting of a business's finances, so owners and others can see how the business is doing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is human resources?
A: The function that records sales and keeps the books of a firm
B: The business function that hires, trains and supports employees
C: The function that makes products, using the machines and workers
D: The function that sets prices for goods sold by a firm each year
Why A: Recording sales and keeping the books is accounting, which is a separate function, and human resources instead handles the employees of the business.
Why B: Human resources is the business function that hires, trains and supports employees, so it manages the people who work for the firm.
Why C: Making products with machines and workers is operations or production, and human resources focuses on the people, not on making goods.
Why D: Setting prices for goods is part of marketing, whereas human resources handles hiring, training and supporting the employees of the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is operations?
A: The activity of tracking money in and out
B: The activity of advertising goods to buyers
C: The activity of hiring staff for a firm each year
D: The activities that produce goods or services
Why A: Tracking money in and out is accounting or finance, which is a different function, and operations deals with producing goods or services.
Why B: Advertising goods to buyers is marketing and promotion, which is a separate function, and operations instead covers how products are made.
Why C: Hiring staff is the work of human resources, a separate function, whereas operations covers the work that produces the goods or services.
Why D: Operations covers the activities that produce goods or services, such as making products, running service delivery and managing quality and supplies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is e-commerce?
A: Trading goods by barter instead of using any money
B: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet
C: Buying and selling goods through a catalog and phone orders
D: Selling goods at outdoor markets and trade fairs
Why A: Trading goods by barter does not use the internet, and e-commerce is defined by buying and selling online, not by exchanging goods without money.
Why B: E-commerce is the buying and selling of goods and services over the internet, such as online shops, so it fits this definition.
Why C: Catalog and phone orders are traditional mail order. E-commerce is buying and selling over the internet.
Why D: Markets and trade fairs are in-person selling. E-commerce is buying and selling over the internet.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which business activity helps a company learn what customers want?
A: Market research
B: Equipment repair
C: Payroll processing
D: Tax filing work
Why A: Market research gathers information about customers, their needs and their preferences, so a company learns what customers want before it makes or sells products.
Why B: Equipment repair keeps machines working, which supports production, but it tells a company nothing about what customers want to buy.
Why C: Payroll processing pays employees their wages, which is an internal task, and it does not help a company learn what customers want.
Why D: Tax filing work reports income to the government and has no link to finding out what customers want from the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is customer service?
A: The tax on a sale of goods to a customer in a store there
B: The design of a store, including its layout and its shelves every time
C: Help a business gives customers before, during and after a sale
D: The price of a product as shown on the tag in a store there
Why A: The tax on a sale of goods is a sales tax collected for the government, and it is not help given to customers.
Why B: The design of a store is its layout or merchandising, which may affect shopping, but customer service means help given to customers.
Why C: Customer service is the help a business gives customers before, during and after a sale, such as answering questions, fixing problems and handling returns.
Why D: The price of a product on the tag is part of pricing, and customer service is the help a business provides to buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an import?
A: A good sold to another country by a local firm
B: A tax on foreign goods sold in a country
C: A good or service bought from another country
D: A ban on trade with other countries for a year
Why A: A good sold to another country by a local firm is an export, which leaves the country, and an import comes in from abroad.
Why B: A tax on foreign goods is a tariff, which is a charge on imports, and the import itself is the good or service bought.
Why C: An import is a good or service bought from another country, so it enters the buyer's country from a foreign seller.
Why D: A ban on trade with other countries is an embargo, which blocks trade, and an import is a good or service that is bought abroad.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an export?
A: A tax on goods sold to buyers in a shop
B: A good or service sold to another country
C: A good bought from another country by a firm
D: A limit on goods that can be sold abroad
Why A: A tax on goods sold to buyers in a shop is a sales tax, which is unrelated to trade between countries, whereas an export is a sale abroad.
Why B: An export is a good or service sold to another country, so it leaves the seller's country and brings in money from foreign buyers.
Why C: A good bought from another country by a firm is an import, which comes into the country, and an export goes out.
Why D: A limit on goods that can be sold abroad is an export quota, which is a government rule, not the export itself.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a career?
A: A series of jobs and experiences over a person's working life
B: A tax on earnings paid by a worker each year to the state
C: A hobby done for fun in the free time of a person daily
D: A single day of work done by a person at a job site each week
Why A: A career is a series of jobs and experiences over a person's working life, which usually builds skills and leads toward long term goals.
Why B: A tax on earnings is an income tax, which is paid by workers to the state, and it is not a career.
Why C: A hobby done for fun is leisure and is not a career, which is a path of work that a person follows over many years.
Why D: A single day of work at a job site is just one workday, whereas a career is a series of jobs over a working life.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a career goal?
A: A job description that lists duties for a worker role
B: A salary the employer sets for a worker each year
C: A list of tasks done each day, signed by the supervisor overall
D: A specific target you want to reach in your working life
Why A: A job description lists duties for a worker role, and it is set by the employer, whereas a career goal is something a person wants to reach.
Why B: A salary the employer sets is pay for a job and is not a career goal, which is a target a person wants to achieve.
Why C: A list of tasks done each day is a work log or schedule, and it does not describe a target a person aims to reach.
Why D: A career goal is a specific target you want to reach in your working life, such as a role, a skill level or a type of work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an interest inventory used for?
A: Measuring how fast you type on a keyboard
B: Counting items in a warehouse by hand each year
C: Listing a company's products and their prices
D: Identifying careers that match what you enjoy
Why A: Measuring typing speed is done with a typing test, and an interest inventory does not test skill but explores what a person enjoys.
Why B: Counting items in a warehouse is a stock check, which has nothing to do with a career tool such as an interest inventory.
Why C: Listing a company's products and prices is a price list or catalog, and an interest inventory instead explores a person's likes and career fit.
Why D: An interest inventory identifies careers that match what you enjoy, since it asks about your likes and then suggests jobs that fit them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a skill?
A: An ability to do something well, often through training or practice
B: A feeling about a job that a person has at work on each day
C: A payment for work that is made by an employer each month end as a rule
D: A job title that is printed on the card of a worker at work
Why A: A skill is an ability to do something well, often built through training or practice, such as typing, cooking or speaking clearly to people.
Why B: A feeling about a job is an attitude or a mood, which is not a skill, because a skill is an ability that can be learned.
Why C: A payment for work from an employer is a wage or salary, and it is money earned and not an ability a person has.
