B: A person who buys the right to run a business under another company's brand
C: A bank that lends to the brand and holds its loans for years or more
D: A customer of the brand who buys its goods in a store each week or month
Why A: The company that owns the brand and licenses it is the franchisor, and the franchisee is the other party, who buys the right to run an outlet.
Why B: A franchisee buys the right to run a business under another company's brand, paying fees and following its rules in return for its name and system.
Why C: A bank that lends to the brand is a lender, which may finance firms but does not buy the right to run an outlet, so it is not a franchisee.
Why D: A customer who buys goods each week is a consumer of the brand, and does not run an outlet or hold rights, so this is not a franchisee.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an advantage of buying a franchise?
A: Freedom to change the brand, menu and prices at will
B: Lower start-up cost than an independent shop
C: Ownership of the brand and its trademarks
D: A proven business system and brand recognition
Why A: Freedom to change the brand, menu and prices at will is not allowed in a franchise, because the franchisor sets rules for all outlets to stay consistent.
Why B: Franchises often cost more to start because of fees. The advantage is a proven system and brand recognition.
Why C: The franchisor owns the brand and trademarks. The franchisee gets a proven system and brand recognition.
Why D: A franchise gives a proven business system and brand recognition, so the owner starts with customers and methods that already work, which lowers some risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a patent?
A: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
B: A license to open a store, issued by the city overall
C: A right to a book that you wrote and sell
D: A right to a brand name and to its logo mark
Why A: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to an invention for a set time, which stops others from making or selling it without permission.
Why B: A license to open a store is a business permit from the city, which allows a shop to operate and does not protect an invention.
Why C: A right to a book that you wrote is a copyright, which protects creative works, while a patent protects inventions.
Why D: A right to a brand name and logo is a trademark, which identifies a company's goods, whereas a patent protects an invention.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a trademark?
A: A tax on a brand name and its logo each year
B: A right to an invention granted for twenty years
C: A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand
D: A right to a song that you wrote and sing aloud
Why A: A tax on a brand name is not what a trademark is, because a trademark is a form of legal protection and not a payment.
Why B: A right to an invention for twenty years describes a patent, which protects inventions, whereas a trademark protects names and symbols.
Why C: A trademark is a word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and keeps others from using a confusingly similar mark for their goods.
Why D: A right to a song you wrote is a copyright, which protects creative works, whereas a trademark protects brand identifiers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a copyright?
A: Protection for trade secrets such as recipes
B: Legal protection for original creative works
C: Protection for brand names and logo marks
D: Protection for inventions and new devices
Why A: Protection for trade secrets such as recipes comes from keeping the information private and from trade secret law, which is a different protection from copyright.
Why B: Copyright is legal protection for original creative works such as books, music and art, giving the creator control over how they are copied and used.
Why C: Protection for brand names and logo marks is a trademark, which identifies a company's goods, whereas copyright covers creative works.
Why D: Protection for inventions and new devices is a patent, which covers how something works, whereas copyright protects creative expression like writing and music.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student writes an original song. Which protection fits it?
A: Trademark
B: Patent
C: License
D: Copyright
Why A: A trademark protects brand names and logos, which identifies a seller's goods, so it does not fit an original song written by a student.
Why B: A patent protects an invention or new device, whereas a song is a creative work and so a patent is the wrong protection for it.
Why C: A license is permission to use something, such as a work or a right, and does not itself protect a song the student wrote.
Why D: An original song is a creative work, and copyright gives its author legal protection and control over copying and performance of it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is insurance for a business?
A: A loan for new equipment from a bank or lender for a firm
B: A tax on property owned by a firm in a town each year
C: A discount from suppliers given to a business that buys in bulk
D: Protection against financial loss in exchange for a premium
Why A: A loan for new equipment is financing from a lender that must be repaid, which is different from insurance that covers losses for a fee.
Why B: A tax on property is a charge set by a local government, whereas insurance is a private agreement that pays out for covered losses.
Why C: A discount for buying in bulk is a supplier pricing term, which lowers cost per unit and does not protect a firm against loss.
Why D: Insurance protects a business against financial loss, and in exchange the owner pays a premium, so the insurer covers certain damages if they occur.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a premium?
A: The amount paid for an insurance policy
B: The amount you pay before coverage starts
C: The profit of the insurer on each policy
D: The money paid out after a loss occurs
Why A: A premium is the amount paid for an insurance policy, usually monthly or yearly, in return for coverage against a loss.
Why B: The amount you pay before coverage starts is the deductible, which is a different part of an insurance policy from the premium.
Why C: The insurer's profit on a policy is what remains after claims and costs, whereas the premium is what the customer pays to get coverage.
Why D: The money paid out after a loss is a claim payment or benefit, which goes to the policy holder, so it is not the premium.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should a new business owner buy insurance?
A: To guarantee profit for the business in every year of trade
B: To stop needing a business plan when seeking funds from banks and others
C: To protect against costly losses from events like fire or lawsuits
D: To avoid all taxes that apply to the business each year it pays
Why A: Insurance cannot guarantee profit, because it only covers certain losses, and a firm can still lose money from poor sales or high costs.
Why B: Insurance does not replace a business plan, which banks and investors usually still want when deciding whether to give funds.
Why C: Insurance helps protect an owner against costly losses from events like fire or lawsuits, which could otherwise force the business to close.
Why D: Insurance does not remove taxes, because a business must still pay the taxes the law requires whether it holds insurance or not.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a producer of raw materials?
A: A store that sells finished goods to customers in town
B: A business that grows or extracts basic materials
C: A firm that advises customers on how to buy goods
D: A bank that lends money to firms and to people
Why A: A store that sells finished goods to customers is a retailer, which sits later in the chain than a producer of raw materials.
Why B: A producer of raw materials grows or extracts basic materials, such as farm crops, timber or minerals, which other firms then use to make goods.
Why C: A firm that advises customers is a consulting or service business, which gives advice and does not grow or extract basic materials.
Why D: A bank lends money and provides financial services, which does not involve growing or extracting basic materials, so it is not a raw material producer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a financial service?
A: A service that repairs cars and trucks for their owners
B: A service that cuts hair for men, women and children
C: A service involving money, such as banking or insurance
D: A service that cleans offices each night for firms it serves
Why A: Repairing cars and trucks is an automotive service that fixes vehicles, which does not mainly involve handling money, so it is not a financial service.
Why B: Cutting hair is a personal care service, which has to do with grooming people and not with managing money.
Why C: A financial service involves money, such as banking, loans or insurance, helping people and firms save, borrow, invest and protect against loss.
Why D: Cleaning offices is a maintenance service that keeps buildings tidy, and it does not involve managing money, so it is not a financial service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a bank?
A: A company that prints newspapers and magazines for sale
B: A store that sells only coins and stamps to collectors
C: A government tax office that collects taxes from firms
D: An institution that takes deposits and makes loans
Why A: A company that prints newspapers is a publisher or printer, whose work is producing media and not taking deposits or lending money.
Why B: A store that sells coins and stamps to collectors is a specialty shop for hobbyists and does not take deposits or make loans like a bank.
Why C: A tax office collects taxes for the government, whereas a bank is a business that holds customers' money and lends it out.
Why D: A bank is an institution that takes deposits from savers and makes loans to borrowers, earning money from the interest it charges.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is advertising?
A: Paid messages that promote a product to an audience
B: Making the product in a plant for sale to buyers
C: Delivering the product to buyers by road or by rail
D: Setting the price of a product to cover its costs
Why A: Advertising is paid messages that promote a product to an audience, aiming to inform people and persuade them to buy.
Why B: Making a product in a plant is production or manufacturing, which creates the goods and does not promote them to buyers.
Why C: Delivering products by road or rail is distribution or shipping, which moves goods to buyers and does not promote them.
Why D: Setting the price of a product to cover its costs is pricing, which is another part of marketing but not the same as advertising.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company wants to reach teenagers. Which advertising choice fits best?
A: Printed flyers in an office
B: Short videos on social media
C: Radio ads at three at night
D: Ads in a retirement newsletter
Why A: Printed flyers in an office would mostly reach adults at work, and so they would miss teenagers, who spend their time in school and online.
Why B: Short videos on social media are where many teenagers spend time, so ads there reach the target audience in a place and style they use.
Why C: Radio ads at three at night would reach very few listeners, and teenagers are usually asleep then, so they would be missed.
Why D: Ads in a retirement newsletter would reach older readers, who are not the teenage audience, so this places the message in front of the wrong people.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a target market?
A: The business's competitors, who sell similar goods
B: Every person in the world, whoever they are
C: The group of customers a business aims to serve
D: The business's employees and their families
Why A: The business's competitors are other firms selling similar goods, and they are rivals and not the customers the business wants to serve.
Why B: Aiming at every person in the world is unrealistic, since a target market is a specific group, so this option is too broad.
Why C: A target market is the group of customers a business aims to serve, chosen by traits like age, interests or needs.
Why D: Employees and their families are the firm's workforce, and they are not the customer group that the business chooses to serve.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is market research?
A: Making products in a factory for the shops in town
B: Printing flyers to hand out in the street and in malls
C: Filing taxes with the state each year by the firm
D: Gathering information about customers and competitors
Why A: Making products in a factory is manufacturing, which produces goods and does not gather information about the market.
Why B: Printing flyers to hand out is a form of advertising that promotes products, and it does not gather information.
Why C: Filing taxes with the state is a legal and accounting duty, and it does not collect information about customers or competitors.
Why D: Market research is gathering information about customers and competitors, so a business can decide what to sell, to whom and at what price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a survey?
A: A legal contract signed by two firms that trade goods
B: A set of questions asked to collect opinions or information
C: A record of sales kept by the firm for each month there
D: A list of company products with their prices, shown to buyers
Why A: A legal contract signed by two firms is an agreement between parties and not a tool for collecting opinions, so it is not a survey.
Why B: A survey is a set of questions asked to collect opinions or information from people, which businesses use to learn what customers want.
Why C: A record of sales kept by the firm is a sales report, which tracks what was sold and does not gather opinions through questions.
Why D: A list of products with prices shown to buyers is a catalog or price list, and it does not ask people questions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is inventory?
A: Goods a business holds for sale or for making products
B: Employees assigned to a task, as listed on the schedule
C: Profit earned in a year by the firm and its owners there
D: Money owed to a business by customers who bought goods
Why A: Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale or for making products, such as stock on shelves or materials waiting in a storeroom.
Why B: Employees assigned to a task are a staffing roster, which is about people and their time and not about goods held by the business.
Why C: Profit earned in a year is income, which is a financial result and not the physical goods that a business holds.
Why D: Money owed to a business by customers is accounts receivable, which is a financial asset and not the goods a firm holds for sale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store orders too much of a seasonal item. What is the likely problem?
A: More customers than the store needs
B: Lower storage costs for the store
C: Unsold stock that ties up money
D: Higher profit for sure on all items
Why A: Having more customers than needed is not a problem caused by overordering, since ordering too much leaves extra goods and does not bring extra shoppers.
Why B: Ordering too much raises storage costs and does not lower them, since more stock takes more space and care.
Why C: Overordering a seasonal item leaves unsold stock after the season ends, which ties up the store's money in goods that cannot be sold at full price.
Why D: Extra stock does not guarantee profit, since unsold goods may need to be discounted or thrown away, so higher profit for sure is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is shipping?
A: Moving goods from one place to another
B: Advertising goods to buyers online
C: Making goods in a plant from raw materials
D: Counting goods in the stockroom daily
Why A: Shipping is moving goods from one place to another, such as from a factory to a warehouse or from a seller to a buyer.
Why B: Advertising goods to buyers online is a promotion activity, which spreads awareness and does not physically move products.
Why C: Making goods in a plant from raw materials is manufacturing, which creates the products and does not move them to buyers.
Why D: Counting goods in the stockroom is inventory control, which tracks stock on hand and does not move it between places.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vendor?
A: A buyer of goods and services
B: A seller of goods or services
C: A manager of a store or shop
D: A worker who repairs machines
Why A: A buyer of goods and services is a customer or consumer, and this is the opposite side of a vendor, who sells.
Why B: A vendor is a seller of goods or services, such as a supplier who sells products to a store or to the public.
Why C: A manager of a store runs daily operations and supervises staff, which is a different role from a vendor who sells goods.
Why D: A worker who repairs machines is a technician, whose job is maintenance, and this is not the same as a seller of goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is technology's role in business?
A: Replacing all employees with machines, so that no people are paid
B: Removing the need for customers by making products that sell by magic overall
C: Guaranteeing profit for every firm that buys a computer or a phone
D: Helping businesses work faster, reach customers and manage information
Why A: Replacing all employees is not technology's role, since firms still need people, so the idea that no people are paid is an exaggeration.
Why B: Technology does not remove the need for customers, and products do not sell by magic, since every business still depends on buyers.
Why C: Buying a computer or phone cannot guarantee profit, because results depend on how the tool is used, so this claim is false.
Why D: Technology helps businesses work faster, reach more customers and manage information, through tools like software, websites and databases that save time and effort.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a business using technology to improve service?
A: A shop ending its website and keeping paper order lists
B: A restaurant removing its phone so people must come in
C: A store letting customers order and pay on a mobile app
D: A bank refusing to update its old paper-based systems
Why A: Dropping the website and using paper lists removes technology and slows orders, so this lowers service instead of improving it.
Why B: Removing the phone makes it harder for customers to reach the restaurant, so this lowers service quality and uses no technology to improve it.
Why C: A mobile ordering and payment app uses technology to make buying faster and easier for customers, which is a clear way of improving service.
Why D: Refusing to update old paper systems avoids technology and keeps service slow, so it is the opposite of using technology to improve service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is global business?
A: Business that operates or trades across countries
B: Business that sells to other businesses
C: Business that trades within a single country's borders
D: Business that is run mostly from the owner's home
Why A: Global business operates or trades across countries, such as firms that import, export or run offices and factories in several nations.
Why B: Selling to other businesses is B2B and can be local. Global business operates or trades across countries.
Why C: Trade within one country is domestic business. Global business operates or trades across countries.
Why D: Where the owner works does not make a business global. Global business trades across countries.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a tariff?
A: A discount on imports
B: A tax on imported goods
C: A tax on exports alone
D: A ban on trade in goods
Why A: A discount on imports would make foreign goods cheaper, whereas a tariff adds a tax that makes imported goods cost more.
Why B: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, which raises their price and is often used to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.
Why C: A tax on exports alone describes an export duty, which is different, since a tariff applies to goods coming into a country.
Why D: A ban on trade in goods is an embargo or import ban, which stops trade completely, whereas a tariff only taxes the goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a job?
A: A volunteer role with no pay at all
B: A hobby done for fun at home daily
C: A lifelong series of work experiences
D: Work you do regularly to earn pay
Why A: A volunteer role with no pay at all is unpaid work, and a job is work you do to earn pay, so this does not fit.
Why B: A hobby done for fun at home is a leisure activity done without pay, and so it differs from a job that earns income.
Why C: A lifelong series of work experiences is a career, which spans many positions, whereas a job is a single position.
Why D: A job is work you do regularly to earn pay, usually for an employer, which separates it from volunteering or a hobby.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between a job and a career?
A: A career is unpaid, while a job is paid by the firm each month
B: A job is one position; a career is a long-term path of work
C: A job lasts for life, while a career lasts just a day
D: They mean exactly the same thing in all cases of use
Why A: A career is not unpaid, because it consists of paid work over a lifetime, so this reverses the true difference between the two.
Why B: A job is one position, whereas a career is a long term path of work that can include many jobs, often in a related field.
Why C: A job does not last for life and a career does not last a day, so this has the two terms reversed.
Why D: The terms do not mean the same, since a job is one position and a career covers a long path, so saying they are identical is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a values-based career choice?
A: Choosing work that fits what matters most to you
B: Choosing the job with the shortest title on the list
C: Choosing the first job offered to you in town
D: Choosing a job at random from a list of jobs
Why A: A values based career choice means choosing work that fits what matters most to you, such as helping others, security or creativity, which supports lasting satisfaction.
Why B: Picking the job with the shortest title ignores what you care about, and title length is a meaningless basis for a career choice.
Why C: Taking the first job offered is a choice of convenience, which may not reflect what matters to you, so it is not values based.
Why D: Choosing at random ignores your values altogether, and it is the opposite of a deliberate choice built on what matters to you.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why is it useful to know your strengths?
A: It lets you skip interviews when applying for jobs
B: It removes the need to learn new skills at work
C: You can choose careers where those strengths matter
D: It shows you the exact salary you will earn
Why A: Strengths do not remove interviews. Knowing them helps you choose careers where those strengths matter.
Why B: Knowing your strengths does not remove the need to learn new skills at work, since careers keep changing and require ongoing learning.
Why C: Knowing your strengths helps you choose careers where those strengths matter, so you are more likely to do well and enjoy the work.
Why D: Strengths do not set pay. Knowing them helps you pick careers where those strengths matter.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an aptitude?
A: A salary level paid by a firm to staff
B: A required degree that a worker must hold
C: A job title printed on a business card
D: A natural ability or talent for something
Why A: A salary level is the pay a firm offers for a role, which is set by the employer and is not a natural talent.
Why B: A required degree is an education credential that a role may demand, and it is learned, not a natural ability.
Why C: A job title printed on a business card is a label for a position, and it says nothing about a person's natural ability.
Why D: An aptitude is a natural ability or talent for something, which can point you toward careers where you may learn quickly and do well.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an occupation outlook?
A: A salary history listing the pay of your past jobs
B: A forecast of how many jobs will be available in a field
C: A list of past jobs and the dates that you held them
D: A view from a window at work, showing the street below overall
Why A: A salary history lists the pay of your past jobs and looks backward, whereas an outlook looks ahead at future job availability.
Why B: An occupation outlook is a forecast of how many jobs will be available in a field, helping people decide which careers may offer good openings.
Why C: A list of past jobs and the dates you held them is a work history on a resume, which looks backward and does not forecast demand.
Why D: A view from a window at work is a literal sight and not a career term, so it has no connection to forecasting job openings.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Where can you find reliable information on job growth and pay?
A: An advertisement for a job or a firm in a paper or a magazine
B: A rumor from a classmate who heard it from a friend of theirs
C: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook
D: An anonymous social media post that claims to know the pay of jobs
Why A: An advertisement is written to sell a product or fill a job, so it may be biased and does not give reliable data on job growth and pay.
Why B: A rumor from a classmate is secondhand and unchecked, so it is unreliable for judging job growth or pay compared with official data.
Why C: The Occupational Outlook Handbook from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics gives researched data on job growth, pay and training, so it is a reliable source.
Why D: An anonymous social media post cannot be verified and may be wrong, so it is a weak source for facts about pay and job growth.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mentor?
A: A person who hires employees for a firm or a shop each year
B: A person who sells products to buyers in a store each day
C: A person who repairs equipment in a factory, using tools and parts
D: An experienced person who guides someone with less experience
Why A: A person who hires employees is a recruiter or hiring manager, who decides who joins the firm, and that role is different from a mentor.
Why B: A person who sells products to buyers is a salesperson, who works in commerce and does not necessarily guide someone's growth.
Why C: A person who repairs equipment is a technician, whose job is maintenance, and this role does not involve guiding someone with less experience.
Why D: A mentor is an experienced person who guides someone with less experience, giving advice, feedback and support to help them grow in their career.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a portfolio in career planning?
A: A collection of your work samples and achievements
B: A list of stocks you own in a firm or in a fund overall
C: A record of your spending kept in a book or app
D: A bag for carrying papers to work, with pockets
Why A: A portfolio in career planning is a collection of your work samples and achievements, which you can show employers as proof of your skills.
Why B: A list of stocks you own is an investment portfolio, which is a financial meaning of the word and not the career planning meaning.
Why C: A record of your spending is a budget or expense log, which tracks money and does not show an employer samples of your work.
Why D: A bag for carrying papers to work is a briefcase, and although it shares the word with portfolio, it does not show your work or achievements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are extracurricular activities?
A: Classes that count toward a high school diploma
B: Exams taken at school at the end of each term or year
C: Grades earned on report cards each term
D: Activities outside class, such as clubs and sports
Why A: Classes toward a diploma are part of the regular curriculum. Extracurricular activities take place outside regular classes.
Why B: Exams are tests given at school as part of regular classes and grading, so they are academic requirements and not optional activities such as clubs or sports teams outside class.
Why C: Grades are results of coursework. Extracurricular activities are optional clubs and sports outside regular classes.
Why D: Extracurricular activities are optional programs such as clubs, sports and student groups that take place outside regular classes, which lets students build skills and interests beyond the standard curriculum and grades.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How do clubs like FBLA help with career planning?
A: They avoid all competition between members and schools
B: They build skills, leadership and contacts in business
C: They replace the need for school and for classes
D: They guarantee a job after graduation with a member company
Why A: FBLA actually runs competitive events between members and chapters, so saying it avoids all competition is false, and competing is one of the main ways members build business skills.
Why B: FBLA is a student business organization, and members build business skills, leadership experience and professional contacts that help when they plan a career and apply for jobs after school.
Why C: A club cannot replace school or classes, since members still attend them; FBLA adds experience to schooling and does not stand in for the education that careers require.
Why D: No club can guarantee a job after graduation, because employers make their own hiring choices; FBLA only improves a member's skills and contacts, which raises the chances of getting hired.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Where can you look for job openings?
A: A job that pays the most money in a large company
B: A job at the top of a company with a big staff
C: Job boards, company websites and personal contacts
D: Nowhere, since jobs are secret and filled without notice
Why A: This describes a kind of job a person might want, not a place to look, so it tells you nothing about where job openings are actually posted or advertised to applicants.
Why B: A job at the top of a company with a large staff is a type of position, not a source of listings, so it does not say where to find openings.
Why C: Job boards, company websites and personal contacts are the main places where openings are posted or heard about, so using all three gives a job seeker the widest chance of finding real openings.
Why D: Jobs are publicly advertised on boards, company sites and through contacts, and many openings are never secret, so claiming that no one can find them is false and discourages a real search.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should a resume include?
A: Contact details, education, skills and experience
B: Your friends' names and their phone numbers
C: Your passwords and your bank account numbers in general
D: Your favorite foods and your favorite shows
Why A: A resume summarizes who you are for an employer, so it lists contact details, education, skills and work experience, which together let the reader judge whether you fit the job quickly.
Why B: Friends' names and phone numbers do not belong on a resume, because an employer wants your own qualifications; only chosen references with permission may be listed on a separate page.
Why C: Passwords and bank account numbers are private and must never appear on a resume, since sharing them could lead to fraud or identity theft and they say nothing about job qualifications.
Why D: Favorite foods and shows are personal interests that do not show job qualifications, so they waste space on a resume that should focus on education, skills and experience relevant to the work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student has no work experience. What can they include on a resume?
A: A list of games played, with scores and teams
B: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills
C: Your social media photos and follower counts
D: Jobs held by your parents or relatives
Why A: A list of games played with scores and teams does not show workplace skills, so it adds little value; relevant school activities, volunteering and skills give a stronger picture of what a student offers.
Why B: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills show responsibility, teamwork and ability, so they fill a resume well for a student who has not held a paid job yet.
Why C: Social media content does not show workplace skills. School activities, volunteering and relevant skills do.
Why D: Relatives' jobs say nothing about your own skills. Use your school activities, volunteering and relevant skills.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should you tailor your resume to a job?
A: To avoid proofreading your own work later
B: To hide your experience from employers
C: To make it longer than a single page
D: To show you match what the employer needs
Why A: Tailoring a resume takes extra effort and does not remove the need to proofread; careful checking is still required, so this reason gets the purpose of tailoring backward.
Why B: Hiding experience would hurt your chances, because tailoring means highlighting the experience that matches the job, so employers see more relevant strengths and not fewer of them.
Why C: Length is not the goal, and most resumes for entry-level jobs should fit on one page, so tailoring focuses on relevance and does not try to stretch the document.
Why D: Tailoring highlights the skills and experience the employer asks for in the posting, which shows you match what the employer needs and makes your application stand out from the others received.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does proofreading mean?
A: Sending a document by email to a client
B: Writing a draft quickly in one sitting
C: Carefully checking writing for mistakes
D: Printing a document on paper for use
Why A: Sending a document by email is just delivering it and involves no review of the writing, so this describes transmission and not the careful checking that proofreading means.
Why B: Writing a quick draft in one sitting is drafting, which comes before proofreading; proofreading happens later, once the writing exists and needs checking for errors before it goes out.
Why C: Proofreading means carefully reading finished writing to find and fix mistakes in spelling, grammar and punctuation, which keeps a resume or letter looking professional and free of errors before sending.
Why D: Printing a document puts it on paper and does not check the content, so a printed resume can still hold mistakes that only careful proofreading would catch and correct beforehand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a professional email address for job applications?
A: One that uses your name
B: A funny nickname or slang
C: A joke phrase from a game
D: A random string of symbols
Why A: An address built from your own name looks professional and is easy for an employer to recognize, remember and match to the name on your resume and application materials.
Why B: A funny nickname or slang in an address looks unprofessional, and employers may judge the applicant as not serious, so it should be saved for personal use and not job applications.
Why C: A joke phrase from a game looks careless to an employer reading a job application, and it does not identify you by name, which makes it a poor choice.
Why D: A random string of symbols is hard to read, type and remember, and it does not identify you, so employers may mistype it or doubt that you are professional.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A hiring manager finds a rude public post on your social media. What may happen?
A: Nothing happens because employers never check social media
B: The employer will give you a bonus for being so honest in public
C: It will make you stand out in a positive way to the employer
D: The employer may doubt your judgment and reject your application
Why A: Nothing happens because employers never check social media is false, since many hiring managers review public profiles and may rethink an applicant after seeing a rude post.
Why B: An employer will not pay a bonus for being so honest online, since a rude public post reflects poor judgment and is more likely to cost you the job.
Why C: A rude public post will not help you stand out positively, since employers look for good judgment and respect, and a negative post usually hurts an application and harms your reputation.
Why D: Hiring managers often review public profiles, and a rude post can make them doubt your judgment and professionalism, so you may lose the job offer even if your resume is strong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should you bring to an interview?
A: A friend to answer the questions for you
B: Your lunch to eat during the interview
C: Extra copies of your resume and references
D: Nothing at all, since nothing is needed
Why A: A friend answering for you shows you cannot speak for yourself, and interviewers want to hear from the candidate directly, so bringing a friend to answer questions would hurt your chances.
Why B: Eating your own lunch during an interview is unprofessional and distracting, so food should not be brought into the room, and it does nothing to show your qualifications.
Why C: Extra copies of your resume and references let the interviewers read about your background and contact your references, which shows you are prepared and organized for the meeting at hand.
Why D: Arriving with nothing at all is poor preparation, because you would have no resume copies or reference list to give the interviewer and would look unready for the position.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the STAR method for interview answers?
A: Situation, Task, Action, Result
B: Skills, Training, Aims, Rewards
C: Salary, Title, Hours, Benefits
D: Speak, Think, Answer, Relax
Why A: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action and Result, which gives a clear structure for telling a story about a past experience and showing the skills the employer wants to see.
Why B: Skills, Training, Aims and Rewards is not what STAR stands for, and it gives no structure for telling a story about a past experience during an interview answer.
Why C: Salary, Title, Hours and Benefits are job offer details to discuss, not the meaning of STAR, which is a way of organizing answers about your past experience.
Why D: Speak, Think, Answer and Relax is invented advice and not the STAR method; STAR uses Situation, Task, Action and Result to structure a story about what you did.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An interviewer asks about a time you solved a problem. Which approach fits the STAR method?
A: Recite your whole work history from the first job onward
B: Describe the situation, your task, what you did and the result
C: Say you have never had a problem and change the subject
D: Blame a former coworker and avoid describing your own role
Why A: Reciting your whole work history does not answer a question about one problem, and it ignores STAR, which asks for a focused story with a situation, task, action and result.
Why B: STAR means describing the situation, your task, the action you took and the result, which turns a question about solving a problem into a clear and complete example for the interviewer.
Why C: Saying you never had a problem and changing the subject avoids the question, and it gives the interviewer no example of your skills, which is exactly what STAR is meant to supply.
Why D: Blaming a former coworker leaves out your own task and action and shows poor attitude, so it fails STAR, which asks you to describe what you did and the result.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a follow-up email after an interview?
A: A thank-you message that reminds the employer of your interest
B: A complaint to the employer about the interview questions
C: A request that the employer forward your resume to others
D: A long list of your hobbies and interests outside of work
Why A: A follow-up email thanks the interviewer and reminds the employer of your interest and fit, which keeps you in mind while the hiring decision is still being made.
Why B: A complaint about the interview questions would make you look negative and hurt your chances, and a follow-up email is meant to thank the employer and show interest.
Why C: Asking the employer to forward your resume to others is not the purpose of a follow-up email, which thanks the interviewer and restates your interest in the position.
Why D: A long list of hobbies adds clutter and is not what a follow-up email contains, since the message should thank the interviewer and remind the employer why you suit the job.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a probationary period?
A: A paid vacation that new workers receive in their first month
B: A period when workers cannot be fired for any reason at all
C: The final week of employment after a worker gives notice
D: An early time in a new job when performance is closely reviewed
Why A: A paid vacation in the first month is not what a probationary period is, which is a trial time when a new hire's performance is closely watched and reviewed by managers.
Why B: A rule that workers cannot be fired for any reason is the opposite of probation, because a probationary period lets the employer end employment more easily if the new hire performs poorly.
Why C: The final week before leaving a job is a notice period, not probation, which comes at the start of employment and tests whether the new employee suits the job.
Why D: A probationary period is an early time in a new job when the employer closely reviews performance, and it decides whether the worker is kept on after the trial ends.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a work permit for minors?
A: A license that lets an adult drive a car on public roads
B: An official document that allows a minor to work legally
C: A pass that gets a worker into a company event for free
D: A form employers use to report a worker's yearly wages
Why A: A driving license lets an adult drive on public roads and has nothing to do with legal employment of young workers, so it cannot be what a work permit is.
Why B: A work permit is an official document that lets a minor work legally, so employers can check that the young worker's age, hours and duties follow child labor rules.
Why C: A pass that gets a worker into a company event is only a ticket for entry and does not give a minor legal permission to hold a paid job.
Why D: A form that reports yearly wages is a W-2, which employers issue after work is done; it is not the permit that allows a minor to start working legally.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why must employers follow child labor laws?
A: To cut the pay of young workers
B: To stop teens from ever working
C: To protect young workers from harm
D: To help firms avoid paying any taxes
Why A: Child labor laws do not exist to cut young workers' pay; they set minimum ages, limit hours and protect teens, and cutting wages would run against that purpose of the laws.
Why B: Child labor laws do not ban all teen jobs, since teens may work within limits on hours and tasks; the laws regulate work and do not forbid it completely.
Why C: Employers must follow child labor laws because the laws protect young workers from harm, setting limits on hours, hazardous tasks and school conflicts so teens stay safe, healthy and in school.
Why D: Child labor laws do not help firms avoid taxes; they protect minors, and employers who ignore them face fines, penalties or legal action from the government.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a W-4 form?
A: A form reporting yearly wages
B: A form for applying to a job
C: A form to request a day off
D: A form for tax withholding
Why A: Yearly wages reported to the worker and the government appear on the W-2, not the W-4, which only tells an employer how much tax to hold back from pay.
Why B: A job application is a separate form that applicants fill out to be considered for hiring, whereas the W-4 is completed after being hired to set tax withholding.
Why C: Asking for a day off is done with a leave request, not a W-4, which is a tax form given to new employees at the start of a job.
Why D: The W-4 tells an employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck, which is why new employees complete it when they start a job and sometimes update it later.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a W-2 form?
A: A form telling the employer how much tax to withhold each pay
B: A form that a worker fills out to apply for a job opening
C: A yearly form from an employer reporting wages and taxes withheld
D: A form that proves a minor may legally take a job at a firm
Why A: Telling employers how much tax to withhold is the job of the W-4, which a worker completes when starting a job; the W-2 reports what happened after the year ends.
Why B: Applying for a job uses an application form or resume, not the W-2, which a worker only receives after earning wages from an employer during a tax year.
Why C: The W-2 is a yearly form from an employer reporting a worker's wages and the taxes withheld, which the worker needs to file a tax return each year.
Why D: Proof that a minor may work legally is a work permit, not a W-2; the W-2 reports earnings and taxes after the worker has been paid for the year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the factors of production?
A: Supply, demand, price and quantity of goods
B: Land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
C: Buyers, sellers, banks and brokers in a market
D: Taxes, tariffs, quotas and subsidies on trade
Why A: Supply, demand, price and quantity describe how markets work and do not name the inputs used to make goods and services, so they cannot be the factors of production.
Why B: The factors of production are land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, the four inputs an economy combines to make goods and services, so this list names exactly what the question asks.
Why C: Buyers, sellers, banks and brokers are participants in a market and not the inputs used to produce goods, so they are not the factors of production.
Why D: Taxes, tariffs, quotas and subsidies are government policies on trade, and none of them is an input used to make goods, so they are not factors of production.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A factory building and its machines are examples of which factor?
A: Capital
B: Land
C: Labor
D: Profit
Why A: A factory building and its machines are man-made goods used to produce other goods, which economists call capital, so capital is the factor these items represent.
Why B: Land means natural resources such as soil, water and minerals, and a factory with its machines is man-made, so it is not land.
Why C: Labor is the work done by people, and buildings and machines are not people, so a factory and its equipment cannot count as labor in this sense.
Why D: Profit is the money left after costs, not a factor of production, so it cannot describe a building and machines used to make goods and services.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The price of concert tickets rises and more tickets are offered for sale. Which law is shown?
A: The law of demand: higher prices lower the amount bought
B: The law of diminishing returns in a factory's output
C: The law of supply: higher prices bring more goods offered
D: The law of comparative advantage in international trade
Why A: The law of demand says buyers purchase less as price rises, but this question describes sellers offering more at a higher price, so demand does not fit.
Why B: Diminishing returns describes how extra inputs add less output in a factory, which has nothing to do with sellers offering more tickets when the price goes up.
Why C: The law of supply says that when price rises, sellers offer more for sale, which matches concert tickets getting costlier while more of them are offered for sale.
Why D: Comparative advantage explains why countries trade based on lower opportunity costs, and it does not describe sellers offering more tickets when prices rise, so it does not apply.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The price of coffee rises sharply. What happens to demand for tea, a substitute?
A: It rises, as buyers switch from costly coffee to tea
B: It stays the same, as tea and coffee are unrelated
C: It falls, because tea and coffee are used together
D: It drops to zero because all buyers stop drinking tea
Why A: When coffee gets much costlier, buyers switch to tea as a substitute, so demand for tea rises; that shift shows how substitutes respond when a related price goes up.
Why B: Tea and coffee are substitutes, so a price jump in one does affect the other; saying demand stays the same ignores that buyers move toward the cheaper drink.
Why C: Demand for tea would fall only if tea and coffee were complements, but they are substitutes, so buyers who leave coffee will buy tea and raise its demand.
Why D: Demand for tea would not drop to zero, because many people still enjoy tea and some will buy more of it when coffee becomes too costly for them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a market economy?
A: An economy where the government decides everything about what is made and who gets it
B: An economy where custom and tradition decide what is made and who gets it
C: An economy with no trade at all, where each home makes only what it uses
D: An economy where individuals and businesses make most decisions through markets
Why A: Having the government decide everything describes a command economy, not a market economy, where individuals and businesses decide and the market, not the state, answers what is produced and who gets it.
Why B: Custom and tradition deciding what is made describes a traditional economy, not a market economy, where individuals and businesses make most decisions through markets, prices and competition.
Why C: An economy with no trade at all, where each home makes only what it uses, is a subsistence economy and not a market economy that depends on exchange.
Why D: In a market economy, individuals and businesses make most decisions through markets, using prices and competition to decide what is produced and who receives it, with limited government involvement.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A village where farmers grow what their parents grew and trade by custom has which system?
A: A market economy driven by prices and competition
B: A traditional economy based on custom and habit
C: A command economy planned by the government
D: A mixed economy with equal state and private roles
Why A: A market economy relies on prices and competition rather than custom, so it does not match a village where farmers follow what their parents grew and trade by long-standing habit.
Why B: A village where farmers grow what their parents grew and trade by custom has a traditional economy, where habit and inherited roles decide what is made, how and for whom.
Why C: A command economy uses central planning by the government, but the village in the question follows custom and not state orders, so command does not describe it.
Why D: A mixed economy blends state and private decisions, whereas the village follows custom and heritage alone, with neither markets nor the state doing much to direct production.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the profit motive?
A: The desire to earn money that drives businesses to produce
B: A law that sets the highest prices firms may charge
C: A tax that the state charges on the earnings of firms
D: The general rise in prices of goods over a long time
Why A: The profit motive is the desire to earn money, which drives businesses to produce goods and services that buyers want and to lower their costs to keep more profit.
Why B: A law that sets the highest price firms may charge is a price ceiling, which limits profit and is not the desire to earn money that drives production.
Why C: A tax on earnings is a government charge that takes part of profit away, and it is not the desire for profit that motivates a business owner.
Why D: A general rise in prices over time is inflation, which is a measure of price change and not the desire to earn money that drives firms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A group sells baked goods and uses all the proceeds for a local shelter. This is most like:
A: A franchise
B: A retail chain
C: A nonprofit
D: A monopoly
Why A: A franchise is a business that licenses a brand to owners who operate for profit, so it does not fit a group that gives all proceeds to a shelter.
Why B: A retail chain is a for-profit set of stores that keeps profit for its owners, so it is unlike a group sending all proceeds to a shelter.
Why C: A nonprofit works for a public purpose and uses its income for that cause instead of paying owners, which matches a group that spends all bake sale proceeds on a shelter.
Why D: A monopoly is a single seller with no competitors who often charges high prices for profit, which is the opposite of a group donating all its proceeds.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the three main types of business activities?
A: Reading, writing and mathematics
B: Production, marketing and finance
C: Planning, taxing and borrowing
D: Eating, sleeping and relaxing daily
Why A: Reading, writing and mathematics are school subjects and do not describe the activities a business carries out, so this list cannot name the three main types of business activities.
Why B: The three main activities of a business are production, marketing and finance: making goods and services, selling them to customers, and managing money so the firm can operate and grow.
Why C: Planning, taxing and borrowing mix general management tasks and a government action, so they are not the standard three activities that every business carries out to operate.
Why D: Eating, sleeping and relaxing are personal daily habits and not business activities, so they cannot be the three main activities that a business carries out.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a service business?
A: A bakery that sells bread and cakes
B: A farm that grows wheat for sale
C: A factory that builds cars daily
D: A salon that cuts and styles hair
Why A: A bakery sells bread and cakes, which are physical goods it bakes and sells, so it is a product business and not a service business.
Why B: A farm that grows wheat for sale produces a physical good, wheat, so it is a producer of goods and not a service business.
Why C: A factory that builds cars makes a physical good from raw materials, so it is a manufacturer and not a service business that sells work or expertise.
Why D: A salon that cuts and styles hair sells work performed for customers and not a physical product, which is what makes it a service business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a merchandising business?
A: A firm that makes goods in a factory
B: A firm that sells only skilled services
C: A firm that gives away goods for free
D: A firm that buys goods to resell them
Why A: A firm that makes goods from raw materials in a factory is a manufacturer, which creates products and does not simply resell finished goods like a merchandising business.
Why B: A firm that sells only skilled services is a service business, since it offers work for others, and it does not buy finished goods to resell.
Why C: A firm that gives away goods for free would have no sales income, so it cannot be a merchandising business, which earns money by reselling goods.
Why D: A merchandising business buys finished goods from suppliers and resells them to customers at a higher price, which is how stores earn their profit without manufacturing the items.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which trait is most important for an entrepreneur?
A: Willingness to take calculated risks
B: Fear of every change in the market
C: Refusal to ever learn from mistakes
D: Waiting for others to make all decisions
Why A: Entrepreneurs start and run new ventures, so they must be willing to take calculated risks, weighing possible gains and losses before acting, and this trait is the most important to success.
Why B: Fear of every change would stop an entrepreneur from adapting to the market, so it is a weakness and not the most important trait.
Why C: Refusing to learn from mistakes keeps a business from improving, so it is a poor trait, whereas entrepreneurs need to adjust after setbacks to survive.
Why D: Waiting for others to make all decisions is the opposite of entrepreneurship, which needs someone to take charge, decide and accept the risk of new ventures.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop earns $12,000 and has $9,500 in expenses. What is its profit?
Why A: Adding expenses to revenue gives $21,500 ($12,000 + $9,500), but profit is found by subtracting expenses from revenue, so this uses the wrong operation.
Why B: Profit equals revenue minus expenses, so $12,000 - $9,500 = $2,500, which is the amount the shop earns after paying all its costs.
Why C: The amount of $9,500 is only the shop's expenses and ignores the $12,000 it earned, so it reports costs and not profit.
Why D: The amount of $12,000 is revenue before any costs are paid, so it ignores the $9,500 of expenses that must be subtracted to find profit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Fixed costs are $1,000 and each unit sells for $10 with $6 variable cost. What is the break-even quantity?
A: 167 units
B: 1,000 units
C: 250 units
D: 100 units
Why A: The result of 167 units comes from $1,000 divided by $6, which uses the variable cost and ignores that each sale contributes the $4 difference between price and variable cost.
Why B: The amount of 1,000 units simply repeats the fixed cost figure in dollars, and break-even quantity needs $1,000 divided by the $4 contribution per unit.
Why C: Each unit contributes $10 - $6 = $4 toward fixed costs, so break-even is $1,000 / $4 = 250 units, the point where total revenue equals total costs.
Why D: The figure of 100 units comes from $1,000 divided by $10, which uses the price alone and ignores that $6 of every sale goes to variable costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Sales $50,000, COGS $30,000, operating expenses $12,000. What is the net profit before taxes?
Why A: Adding all three figures gives $92,000 ($50,000 + $30,000 + $12,000), but costs must be subtracted from sales, so this adds when it should subtract.
Why B: Net profit before taxes is sales minus COGS minus operating expenses, so $50,000 - $30,000 - $12,000 = $8,000, which is what remains after paying both the product cost and running costs.
Why C: The amount of $18,000 does not come from the required subtraction; it only subtracts $12,000 from $30,000 of COGS, which mixes up the roles of sales and costs.
Why D: The amount of $20,000 is gross profit ($50,000 - $30,000), which leaves out the $12,000 of operating expenses that must also be subtracted to reach net profit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a markup?
A: An amount added to the cost price
B: A fall in price caused by a sale
C: A swap of money between two banks
D: A tax charged on goods at sale
Why A: A markup is an amount added to the cost of an item to set its selling price, so the seller covers expenses and earns a profit.
Why B: A fall in price during a sale is a markdown, which is the opposite of a markup because it lowers the price instead of adding to cost.
Why C: A swap of money between two banks is an interbank transfer and has nothing to do with how a store sets prices above its cost.
Why D: A tax charged on goods at sale is a sales tax paid to the government and not an amount the seller adds to cost to set a price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An item costs $20 and the store adds a 50% markup. What is the selling price?
Why A: The figure of $70 adds the 50 from the percentage as dollars to the $20 cost, but a 50% markup is half of the cost, not $50.
Why B: The figure of $10 is only the markup amount (50% of $20), and the selling price must add that markup to the $20 cost.
Why C: A 50% markup on $20 is $10, and adding it to the cost gives $20 + $10 = $30, the selling price of the item.
Why D: The figure of $40 doubles the cost, which would be a 100% markup, but a 50% markup adds only half the $20 cost, giving $30.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which form protects an owner's personal assets from business debts?
A: A sole proprietorship run by one person
B: A general partnership with shared debts
C: A joint business with unlimited liability
D: A limited liability company or corporation
Why A: A sole proprietorship has one owner who is personally responsible for business debts, so personal assets are not protected, and it fails the requirement in this question.
Why B: A general partnership shares debts among partners, and each partner can be personally liable for them, so personal assets remain at risk and it does not protect owners.
Why C: A joint business with unlimited liability leaves owners personally responsible for what the firm owes, so it is the opposite of a form that protects personal assets.
Why D: A limited liability company or corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners are generally not personally responsible for business debts, which protects their personal assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which section of a business plan explains how the company will attract customers?
A: The financial plan, which lists costs and income forecasts
B: The operations plan, which describes how work gets done
C: The company description, which gives its history and goals
D: The marketing plan, which describes promotion and sales
Why A: The financial plan covers costs, income forecasts and funding, and it does not explain how the company will attract customers, which is the work of the marketing plan.
Why B: The operations plan describes how the company will do its daily work, with locations, equipment and suppliers, and it does not explain how to attract customers.
Why C: The company description gives the history, goals and structure of the business, and it does not set out how the company will attract customers.
Why D: The marketing plan explains how the company will attract customers through promotion, pricing, products and distribution, so it is the business plan section that answers this question.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a license?
A: A tax on the profit a business earns
B: A loan to help a new business start
C: Legal permission to run a business
D: A written plan for a new business
Why A: Legal permission to run a business is a license, not a tax on the profit a business earns; a profit tax is paid after income is earned.
Why B: A loan is borrowed money that a firm must repay, and it is not the legal permission that a license gives to run a business.
Why C: A license is legal permission from a government to run a business or trade, which shows the firm meets the rules set for its field or location.
Why D: A written plan for a new business is a business plan, which describes goals and finances, and it does not give government permission to operate as a license does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company decides where and how customers can buy its product. Which P is this?
A: Place
B: Price
C: Product
D: Promotion
Why A: Place is the P that covers where and how customers can buy a product, including stores, online sales and the distribution channels that get goods to them.
Why B: Price covers the amount customers pay for the product and not where or how they buy it, so it does not fit this description.
Why C: Product covers what is sold, including its features and quality, not the locations and channels used to deliver it, so it fails the question.
Why D: Promotion covers advertising and other ways of informing buyers about a product, and it does not decide where or how customers can buy it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is production?
A: Advertising goods to buyers
B: Making goods and services
C: Selling goods to shoppers
D: Recording sales for the books
Why A: Advertising goods to buyers is promotion, a marketing activity, and it does not make the goods themselves, which is what production means.
Why B: Production is making goods and services, which turns resources into products people can buy, and it is a main activity of a business alongside marketing and finance.
Why C: Selling goods to shoppers is a marketing activity that follows production, since goods must be made before they are sold, so this describes sales and not production.
Why D: Recording sales for the books is an accounting task within finance and not the making of goods and services that production means.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does human resources do?
A: Designs ads and plans promotions for products
B: Keeps the books and prepares financial reports
C: Hires, trains and supports a firm's employees
D: Ships goods to customers and receives stock
Why A: Designing ads and planning promotions is marketing work, not human resources, which deals with staff, so this option names the wrong department for the question.
Why B: Keeping the books and preparing reports is accounting work, which handles money records and not employees, so it does not describe human resources.
Why C: Human resources hires, trains and supports a firm's employees, which includes recruiting, handling pay and benefits, and keeping workers productive and satisfied in their jobs.
Why D: Shipping goods to customers and receiving stock is logistics work for a warehouse and not the people management that human resources does.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which department would handle writing job descriptions and interviewing candidates?
A: Marketing team
B: Human resources
C: Shipping team
D: Accounting team
Why A: The marketing team promotes and advertises products and does not hire staff or write job descriptions, so it is the wrong department for these tasks.
Why B: Human resources handles recruiting, so it writes job descriptions and interviews candidates, which makes it the department responsible for finding and hiring new employees.
Why C: The shipping team moves goods in and out of the warehouse and has no role in writing job descriptions or interviewing job candidates.
Why D: The accounting team tracks money, pays bills and prepares financial reports, and it does not write job descriptions or interview people who apply for jobs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a transferable skill?
A: A skill that only works for one employer
B: A skill that is lost when you change jobs
C: A skill that has no use outside of school
D: A skill that is useful in many different jobs
Why A: A skill that works for only one employer is the opposite of transferable, since a transferable skill can be used in many different jobs and settings.
Why B: A skill lost when changing jobs is not transferable; a transferable skill stays with the worker and can be applied in new positions and fields.
Why C: A skill with no use outside school is not transferable, since a transferable skill is helpful across many jobs and workplaces and not only in one setting.
Why D: A transferable skill is useful in many different jobs, like communication or teamwork, so it helps a worker change roles or fields and remain valuable to employers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a transferable skill?
A: Communication, which is useful in almost any job you hold
B: Operating the one machine used only at one factory
C: Knowing the layout of one particular office building
D: Memorizing the menu prices at one particular store
Why A: Communication is useful in almost any job, which makes it transferable, since a worker can carry it to a new employer, field or position without having to learn it again.
Why B: Running the one machine used only at one factory is a skill tied to that workplace, so it cannot be moved easily to other jobs and is not transferable.
Why C: Knowing the layout of one office building helps only in that place and is lost when you change jobs, so it is not a transferable skill.
Why D: Memorizing menu prices at one store applies only to that employer, so the knowledge cannot be used in another job, which means it is not transferable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is networking?
A: Selling goods for cash at a shop to buyers
B: Building contacts that can help your career
C: Paying taxes to the government each year in full
D: Avoiding meeting anyone in your field of work
Why A: Selling goods for cash at a shop is retail selling, a form of commerce, and it does not describe building relationships with people who can help your career.
Why B: Networking means building contacts with people who can help your career, such as sharing job leads, advice and introductions, so it helps in the search for work and growth.
Why C: Paying taxes to the government is a civic duty and a financial task, and it has nothing to do with meeting people to build career contacts.
Why D: Avoiding meeting people in your field would defeat networking, which depends on making connections, so this action is the opposite of what networking means.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What belongs on a résumé?
A: A list of your favorite songs, foods and television shows
B: Your passwords and your bank account numbers for the firm
C: Your contact details, education, skills and work experience
D: The names and phone numbers of all of your close friends
Why A: A list of favorite songs, foods and television shows is personal trivia that does not show job qualifications, so it does not belong on a resume.
Why B: Passwords and bank account numbers are private details that must stay off a resume, since they could enable fraud and tell an employer nothing about your fit.
Why C: A resume lists your contact details, education, skills and work experience, which gives an employer what it needs to judge whether you are qualified for the job.
Why D: The names and phone numbers of close friends do not belong on a resume, since employers want your own qualifications, and any references should be chosen and listed with permission.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is the best way to end a job interview?
A: Leave quickly without saying anything to anyone
B: Complain about your last employer one more time
C: Say that you are unsure you want the position
D: Thank the interviewer and restate your interest
Why A: Leaving quickly without a word is rude and leaves a poor final impression, and it fails to thank the interviewer or restate your interest in the job.
Why B: Complaining about a past employer at the close of an interview looks unprofessional and leaves a negative last impression, so it is a poor way to finish.
Why C: Saying you are unsure you want the position at the end leaves doubt about your interest and can cost you the job.
Why D: Thanking the interviewer and restating your interest ends the meeting on a positive and professional note, and it leaves the employer remembering your enthusiasm for the position.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Before listing someone as a reference, you should:
A: Ask for their permission and confirm their contact details
B: To remove competition from the market and set prices high
C: Pick someone who has never met you or seen your work
D: Write their praise yourself and sign it in their name
Why A: Asking for permission and confirming contact details makes sure the person agrees to speak for you and is ready for a call, which protects your reputation with employers.
Why B: Assuming they will agree and listing them without asking may surprise the reference, who could be unprepared or unwilling, and it risks a poor recommendation for you.
Why C: Picking someone who has never met you or seen your work cannot give a useful reference, since a reference must speak from real knowledge of your abilities.
Why D: Writing their praise yourself and signing their name is dishonest, and employers can contact the person directly, so it would damage your credibility.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is professionalism?
A: Arriving late and leaving early whenever you feel like it each day
B: Ignoring coworkers and being rude to customers every day at work
C: Dressing in expensive clothes and showing off your wealth to others
D: Behaving in a respectful, responsible and ethical way at work each day
Why A: Arriving late and leaving early are unprofessional habits that hurt a worker's reputation and the team, so they are the opposite of professionalism, not its meaning.
Why B: Ignoring coworkers and being rude to customers is unprofessional behavior that harms teamwork and the business, so it is the opposite of professionalism and not what it means.
Why C: Dressing in expensive clothes and showing off wealth is not professionalism, which is about conduct such as respect and responsibility and not about money or fashion.
Why D: Professionalism means behaving in a respectful, responsible and ethical way at work, including being on time, communicating well and treating coworkers and customers courteously every day.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a job description?
A: A schedule showing the hours a worker was on duty
B: A written list of the duties and skills for a job
C: A letter telling a worker that the job has ended
D: A written review of how well a worker did last year
Why A: A schedule showing the hours a worker was on duty is a time record or timesheet, not a job description, which lists the duties and skills the job needs.
Why B: A job description is a written list of the duties, skills and requirements for a job, so applicants know what the work involves and what the employer expects.
Why C: A letter telling a worker that the job has ended is a termination notice and not a job description, which describes duties for a position.
Why D: A written review of how well a worker did last year is a performance evaluation, not a job description, which lists duties and requirements before or during the job.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Where can you find the required skills for a job you want?
A: A friend's opinion of the job
B: A guess based on its title only
C: The job posting or description
D: The company's logo and slogan
Why A: A friend's opinion of the job is secondhand and may be wrong or out of date, so it is not a dependable way to learn the required skills.
Why B: A guess based on the title alone ignores the details an employer lists, so it can leave out skills the job really requires.
