Why C: The job posting or description lists the duties and required skills set by the employer, so reading it is the most direct way to learn what the job needs.
Why D: A company logo and slogan are branding tools that tell you nothing about the skills a particular job requires, so they cannot answer the question.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store has $90,000 in revenue and $72,000 in expenses. What is its profit?
Why A: Profit is revenue minus expenses, so $90,000 - $72,000 = $18,000, which is what the store keeps after paying all of its costs.
Why B: The amount of $90,000 is the store's revenue before costs, so it ignores the $72,000 of expenses that must be subtracted to find profit.
Why C: The amount of $72,000 is only the expenses, which are costs and not profit, so it leaves out the revenue the store earned.
Why D: The figure of $162,000 adds revenue and expenses ($90,000 + $72,000), but profit requires subtracting expenses from revenue, so this uses the wrong operation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a good?
A: Work performed for a client for a fee
B: A physical item that people can touch
C: A promise to repay a loan with interest
D: An idea or skill sold as a service
Why A: Work performed for a client for a fee is a service, which is intangible, and so it is not a good, which is a physical item.
Why B: A good is a physical item that people can touch, like a book or a bicycle, so it is tangible, unlike an intangible service.
Why C: A promise to repay a loan with interest is a debt agreement and not a good, because it is not a physical item that people buy and use.
Why D: An idea or skill sold as a service is intangible and cannot be touched, whereas a good is a physical item, so this describes a service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a service?
A: A tangible item that a customer can touch and hold
B: A physical product made in a factory for sale to buyers
C: A raw material such as wood or iron ore from land
D: Work done for a customer for pay, such as cutting hair
Why A: A tangible item that a customer can touch and hold is a good, so this describes the opposite of a service, which is intangible work done for others.
Why B: A physical product made in a factory is a good that buyers can own, so it is not a service, which is work done for someone else.
Why C: A raw material taken from land, like wood or ore, is a physical resource used to make goods and is not a service.
Why D: A service is work done for a customer for pay, such as cutting hair, and the customer receives the benefit of the work instead of a physical item.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a service?
A: A bicycle sold new in a shop to a customer
B: A laptop computer made in a factory and boxed
C: A haircut given at a salon by a hair stylist
D: A pair of shoes made in a factory for retail
Why A: A bicycle sold in a shop is a physical good that a customer takes home, so it is a product and not a service.
Why B: A laptop made in a factory is a physical good that a buyer can own and use, so it is a product and not a service.
Why C: A haircut is work done for a customer for a fee, and it leaves no physical item behind, which is why it is a service and not a good.
Why D: A pair of shoes made in a factory is a physical good that a buyer carries home, so it is a product and not a service.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of the production factor 'labor'?
A: A worker who sews clothes at a factory
B: A factory building owned by the firm
C: Timber and ore taken from the earth
D: Money that the owner invests in the firm
Why A: A worker who sews clothes at a factory supplies human effort to production, and human work is what the production factor labor means, which makes this the right example.
Why B: A factory building owned by the firm is a man-made item used to produce goods, which makes it capital and not labor, since labor means human effort.
Why C: Timber and ore taken from the earth are natural resources, which makes them land in economics and not labor, since labor refers to people's work.
Why D: The money an owner invests in the firm is financial capital and not human work, so it is not an example of the production factor labor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of the production factor 'capital'?
A: Employees who are paid wages to do the daily work of the firm
B: A delivery truck and tools that the company uses to make goods
C: Timber, ore and fertile soil taken from the earth for products
D: The owner who takes the risk of starting a new business firm
Why A: Employees paid wages to do daily work supply labor, which is human effort, and so they are not capital, which means man-made goods used to make other goods.
Why B: A delivery truck and tools that a company uses to make goods are man-made items used in production, which is what capital means, so this is the correct example.
Why C: Timber, ore and fertile soil taken from the earth are natural resources, which economists call land, so they are not capital, which is man-made.
Why D: The owner who takes risks to start a new business is the entrepreneur, a separate factor of production, and so this is not an example of capital.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of the production factor 'land'?
A: Workers who are paid wages for their daily tasks and effort
B: Machines and tools that the firm owns to make its goods
C: Timber, minerals, fertile soil and water taken from nature
D: The person who takes the risk and starts a new business
Why A: Workers paid wages for daily tasks supply labor, which is human effort, so they are not land, which refers to natural resources in economics.
Why B: Machines and tools that the firm owns are man-made goods used to produce other goods, which makes them capital and not land, which is natural.
Why C: Timber, minerals, fertile soil and water taken from nature are natural resources, which economists call land, so this is the correct example of the factor.
Why D: The person who takes risks and starts a new business is the entrepreneur, a separate factor of production, so this is not an example of land.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a retailer?
A: A business that makes goods from raw materials in a factory
B: A business that buys goods in bulk and sells to shops
C: A business that moves goods between cities for a fee
D: A business that sells goods directly to final consumers
Why A: A business that makes goods from raw materials in a factory is a manufacturer, which produces goods, and it does not mainly sell finished goods to final consumers.
Why B: A business that buys goods in bulk and sells to shops is a wholesaler, and a retailer sells to the final consumer.
Why C: A business that moves goods between cities for a fee is a transport or shipping company, so it does not sell goods to final consumers.
Why D: A retailer is a business that sells goods directly to final consumers, such as a grocery store or clothing shop, and it earns money from the markup it adds.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a supply chain?
A: The path goods take to customers
B: A required procedure for staff
C: Good customer service for buyers
D: A schedule of staff pay and hours
Why A: The path goods take from producers to customers is the supply chain, which includes making, storing, moving and selling products, so this is the correct meaning.
Why B: A required procedure for staff is a company policy or rule, not a supply chain, which describes how goods move from producers to buyers.
Why C: Good customer service for buyers is a quality of how a firm treats shoppers, and it does not describe how goods move from producers to customers.
Why D: A schedule of staff pay and hours is a payroll or work plan, so it has nothing to do with how goods move from producers to customers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a stakeholder in a business?
A: A financial statement that lists the assets and debts of the firm
B: Anyone affected by the business, such as employees, customers or the community
C: A written contract that sets prices between a firm and a supplier
D: A yearly report that shows the sales and costs of the firm
Why A: A financial statement is a document, not a person or group. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business.
Why B: A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business, such as employees, customers or the community, because each group has an interest in how the business acts and performs.
Why C: A contract is a document, not a person or group. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business.
Why D: A report is a document, not a person or group. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a mission statement?
A: A forecast of sales and costs for next year
B: The money kept in a bank account of the firm
C: A list of all employees and their pay rates
D: A statement of the firm's purpose and goals
Why A: A forecast of sales and costs for next year is a financial projection used for planning, and it does not state why a firm exists or what it aims to do.
Why B: The money kept in a firm's bank account is its cash balance, which is a financial figure and not a statement of the firm's purpose and goals.
Why C: A list of employees and their pay rates is a payroll record, and it says nothing about the firm's purpose, values or goals.
Why D: A mission statement is a short statement of a firm's purpose and goals that tells employees and customers why the business exists and what it hopes to achieve.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How does competition benefit consumers?
A: It gives lower prices
B: It reduces choice
C: It raises all prices
D: It lowers the quality
Why A: Competition pushes sellers to cut prices to win buyers, so consumers benefit from lower prices, better quality and more choice than they would get from a single seller with no rivals.
Why B: Competition does the opposite of reducing choice, because firms compete by offering different goods; a single seller would limit choice, whereas many sellers expand it for buyers.
Why C: Competition tends to lower prices, since firms that charge too much lose customers to rivals, so claiming that it raises all prices contradicts how competitive markets work.
Why D: Firms face pressure to improve quality in order to win and keep customers, so competition raises quality and does not lower it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a risk faced by a new business?
A: A loyal base of repeat customers
B: A law that forbids any new firms
C: Failing to attract enough customers
D: A strong brand name known by buyers
Why A: Loyal customers are a benefit. A new business risks failing to attract enough customers.
Why B: A law that forbids new firms is not a risk that a new business faces, since new firms can legally start in a market economy.
Why C: Failing to attract enough customers is a real risk for a new business, because without sales it cannot cover costs and may close, which is why market research matters.
Why D: A known brand helps sales and is not a risk. New firms risk failing to attract enough customers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is ethics in business?
A: Rules for how a firm keeps its accounts
B: Moral principles that guide how a firm acts
C: A plan for how a firm sets its sales prices
D: A way to forecast sales for the next year
Why A: Rules for how a firm keeps its accounts describe accounting standards and do not address right and wrong behavior, which is what ethics in business covers.
Why B: Ethics in business means moral principles that guide how a firm acts, including honesty, fairness and respect for customers, workers and the community when it makes decisions.
Why C: A plan for how a firm sets its sales prices is a pricing strategy and does not concern moral principles, so it is not ethics.
Why D: A way to forecast sales for next year is a planning technique and has no connection to the moral principles that ethics in business covers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is globalization?
A: A tax placed on imported goods to protect home industries
B: The movement of people from farms to cities
C: The growing connection of global economies and cultures
D: The shift of production from factories to online services
Why A: A tax on imports is a tariff, a protectionist tool. Globalization is the growing connection of economies and cultures through trade.
Why B: People moving to cities is urbanization. Globalization is the growing connection of economies and cultures worldwide.
Why C: Globalization is the growing connection of economies and cultures worldwide through trade, investment and communication, so goods, money and ideas move easily between countries.
Why D: That shift is a change in industry mix. Globalization is the growing worldwide connection of economies through trade.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the marketing mix (4 Ps)?
A: People, process, plant and profit
B: Price, profit, people and planning
C: Production, pay, people and plant
D: Product, price, place and promotion
Why A: People, process, plant and profit are not the four Ps of marketing, so this list does not name the marketing mix.
Why B: Price, profit, people and planning mix business terms but are not the four Ps of the marketing mix, so this list does not match the set.
Why C: Production, pay, people and plant are general business terms and are not the four Ps, so they do not name the marketing mix.
Why D: The marketing mix, or four Ps, is product, price, place and promotion, the four tools a business combines to market its goods and services to customers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'place' in the marketing mix refer to?
A: How and where products are distributed to customers
B: The cost of the product to the customer in dollars
C: How a product is advertised to the public daily
D: The features, design and quality of the product
Why A: Place covers how and where products are distributed to customers, such as stores, websites and delivery channels, so this is the definition of place in the marketing mix.
Why B: The cost of the product to the customer is price, a different P in the marketing mix, so it does not describe place.
Why C: How a product is advertised to the public is promotion, a different P in the mix, so it does not describe place.
Why D: The features, design and quality of the product make up the product P, which is not the same as place, which is about distribution.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does 'promotion' in the marketing mix include?
A: The price charged to customers
B: The places where the product is sold
C: Ads and offers that draw in buyers
D: The design and quality of the item
Why A: The price charged to customers is the price P of the marketing mix, so it is not promotion, which is about informing and persuading buyers.
Why B: The places where the product is sold are the place P of the marketing mix, so they are not what promotion includes.
Why C: Promotion includes ads and offers that draw in buyers, such as advertising, publicity, sales offers and personal selling, which tell people about a product and persuade them to buy.
Why D: The design and quality of the item belong to the product P of the marketing mix and not to promotion, which communicates with buyers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is market segmentation?
A: Treating all buyers as one group
B: Dividing buyers into target groups
C: Closing a market to new sellers
D: Setting one price for all buyers
Why A: Treating all buyers as one group ignores differences between them, which is the opposite of segmentation, because segmentation divides a market into smaller groups with shared needs.
Why B: Market segmentation divides buyers into target groups that share needs or traits, so a business can tailor its products and marketing to each group more effectively.
Why C: Closing a market to new sellers is a barrier to entry and does not divide buyers into groups, so it is not segmentation.
Why D: Setting one price for all buyers is a pricing choice that treats the market the same, so it is not dividing buyers into groups.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is publicity?
A: Unpaid media coverage of a business or product
B: A tax on profits paid by firms to the state
C: A business's own plan for its sales and costs
D: Money given to firms by the state to help growth
Why A: Publicity is unpaid media coverage of a business or product, such as a news story, which is why it can be so credible and costs the firm nothing in ad fees.
Why B: A tax on profits paid to the state is a corporate income tax and is not media coverage, so it does not describe publicity.
Why C: A business's own plan for its sales and costs is a budget or forecast, not publicity, which is attention from the media that the firm does not pay for.
Why D: Money given to firms by the state is a subsidy or a grant and is not media coverage, so it is not publicity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is personal selling?
A: A paid advert on television
B: Free news coverage of a firm
C: A coupon that gives a discount
D: Selling to buyers in person
Why A: A paid advert on television is advertising, a form of promotion, and it is not personal selling, which involves direct contact between a seller and a buyer.
Why B: Free news coverage of a firm is publicity, which the firm does not pay for, and it is not personal selling, which is direct contact.
Why C: A coupon that gives a discount is a sales promotion and not personal selling, which involves a salesperson talking directly with a customer in person.
Why D: Personal selling is selling to buyers in person or by direct conversation, where a salesperson explains the product and answers questions, which helps persuade the customer to buy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sales promotion?
A: A paid ad placed in a newspaper or magazine
B: Free news coverage of the firm and its goods
C: A visit by a salesperson to a buyer's home
D: A short-term offer such as a coupon or discount
Why A: A paid ad placed in a newspaper or magazine is advertising, not a sales promotion, which is a short-term offer meant to boost sales quickly.
Why B: Free news coverage of a firm and its goods is publicity and not a sales promotion, which is a short-term incentive offered to buyers.
Why C: A visit by a salesperson to a buyer's home is personal selling and not a sales promotion, which uses short-term offers to bring in sales.
Why D: A sales promotion is a short-term offer, such as a coupon or discount, that encourages buyers to purchase right away and often boosts sales for a limited time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is human resources management?
A: Planning ads and setting prices for goods
B: Assets minus liabilities of a firm
C: Hiring, training and supporting staff
D: Buying and storing goods for sale
Why A: Planning ads and setting prices are marketing tasks, so this describes marketing and not human resources management, which deals with a firm's staff.
Why B: Assets minus liabilities of a firm is owner's equity, which is a financial figure, so it does not define human resources management.
Why C: Human resources management means hiring, training and supporting staff, so a firm has a skilled, motivated team, and it is the standard definition of the function.
Why D: Buying and storing goods for sale is purchasing and inventory management and not the management of the firm's staff.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is finance in business?
A: Managing a firm's money and its funding
B: Hiring and training a firm's workers
C: Moving goods from the factory to stores
D: Designing ads and planning promotions
Why A: Managing a firm's money and its funding is what finance in business means, covering budgeting, borrowing, investing and record keeping so the firm can pay its bills and grow.
Why B: Hiring and training a firm's workers is human resources work and not finance, which deals with money and funding.
Why C: Moving goods from the factory to stores is distribution, a part of the supply chain, and it does not describe managing a firm's money.
Why D: Designing ads and planning promotions is marketing work and not finance, which manages a firm's money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a purchase order?
A: A bill that a seller sends to a buyer asking for payment
B: A record given to a customer to show that payment was made
C: A list of the items a firm has in its storeroom or stock
D: A document that a buyer sends to a seller to order goods
Why A: A bill sent by a seller asking for payment is an invoice, which comes after goods are ordered, so it is not a purchase order.
Why B: A record given to a customer to show that payment was made is a receipt, so it is not a purchase order, which is used to place an order.
Why C: A list of the items a firm has in its storeroom is an inventory record and not an order, so it is not a purchase order.
Why D: A purchase order is a document a buyer sends to a seller to order goods, stating the items, quantities and agreed prices, which gives both sides a record of the deal.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an invoice?
A: A record of past sales over years
B: A bill sent to a buyer for goods
C: A request to buy goods from a seller
D: A tax return filed every year
Why A: A record of past sales over years is a sales history report and not a bill, so it does not describe an invoice.
Why B: An invoice is a bill sent to a buyer for goods or services supplied, listing the items, amounts and payment terms, so the buyer knows what is owed.
Why C: A request to buy goods from a seller is a purchase order, which comes before an invoice, so it does not describe an invoice.
Why D: A tax return filed every year reports income to the government, and it is not a bill sent to a customer, so it is not an invoice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a receipt?
A: Proof that a customer paid for goods or services
B: A request sent by a buyer to a supplier for goods
C: A bill sent to a customer asking for payment
D: A list of all the goods held in the stockroom
Why A: Proof that a customer paid for goods or services is a receipt, which gives the buyer a record of the sale and the amount paid.
Why B: A request sent to a supplier to buy goods is a purchase order, which is made before payment and is not proof of payment, so it is not a receipt.
Why C: A bill sent to a customer asking for payment is an invoice and comes before payment, so it is not a receipt, which confirms payment was made.
Why D: A list of goods held in the stockroom is an inventory record and not proof of payment, so it does not describe a receipt.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a quality control?
A: A fee for shipping goods to a buyer
B: Setting the retail prices of goods
C: Checking products against set standards
D: A tax on a sale of goods in a shop
Why A: A fee for shipping goods to a buyer is a delivery charge and not a check on product standards, so it is not quality control.
Why B: Setting the retail prices of goods is a pricing task and not a check on whether products meet standards, so it is not quality control.
Why C: Quality control means checking products against set standards before they reach customers, so defects are found and fixed, which protects the firm's reputation and customer satisfaction.
Why D: A tax on a sale of goods in a shop is a sales tax and not a check on product standards, so it is not quality control.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is shipping and receiving?
A: Advertising products to customers through mail, online ads and promotions
B: Recording daily sales and expenses in the company's financial books
C: Hiring and training the staff who work in the warehouse and the store
D: Sending out goods to customers and accepting goods from suppliers
Why A: Advertising products through mail, online ads and promotions is marketing and has nothing to do with moving goods in and out of the warehouse.
Why B: Recording daily sales and expenses in the company's books is accounting work and not the physical handling of goods, so it is not shipping and receiving.
Why C: Hiring and training warehouse and store staff is a human resources function and does not describe handling goods, so it is not shipping and receiving.
Why D: Shipping and receiving is the department that sends goods out to customers and accepts deliveries from suppliers, checking them against orders so inventory records stay accurate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a general partnership?
A: Owned by one person with no partners
B: Owners share profits, control and debts
C: It must share profits with shareholders
D: Owners are shielded from all business debts
Why A: A business owned by one person with no partners is a sole proprietorship, so it is not a general partnership, which has two or more owners.
Why B: In a general partnership owners share profits, control and debts, since each partner can act for the firm and is personally liable, which defines the form.
Why C: A general partnership does not share profits with shareholders, since it has partners and not shareholders, which is a feature of a corporation instead.
Why D: Partners in a general partnership are not shielded from business debts, because each has unlimited personal liability, so this describes a limited liability form and not a general partnership.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a limited partnership?
A: Every partner manages it and has unlimited liability for debts
B: It is owned by shareholders who vote for a board of directors
C: General partners manage it while limited partners only invest money
D: A single owner keeps all profits and owes all business debts
Why A: A form where every partner manages and has unlimited liability is a general partnership, not a limited partnership, which also has partners who only invest.
Why B: A firm owned by shareholders who vote for a board of directors is a corporation, not a limited partnership, which is owned by partners.
Why C: General partners manage a limited partnership while limited partners only invest money and have limited liability, which defines the form and separates management from passive investment.
Why D: A firm where one owner keeps all profits and owes all debts is a sole proprietorship, not a limited partnership, which has two kinds of partners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is double taxation in a C corporation?
A: Sales are taxed once at purchase and again when resold
B: Owners are taxed on profits and again on any loans they take
C: The firm pays tax to two different states on each sale it makes
D: Profits are taxed at the firm and again on shareholder dividends
Why A: That describes taxes on sales. Double taxation in a C corporation means profits are taxed at the firm and again as shareholder dividends.
Why B: Loans are not taxed as income. Double taxation means profits are taxed at the firm and again on dividends.
Why C: Two states taxing the firm on one sale is a multistate tax issue and not double taxation, which refers to taxing profits at two levels.
Why D: Double taxation means a C corporation's profits are taxed at the firm level and again when paid to shareholders as dividends, so the same money is taxed twice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an S corporation?
A: Income passes to the owners' tax returns
B: A corporation that faces double taxation
C: It is the cheapest form to start up
D: The owners pay no tax on firm profits ever
Why A: An S corporation passes income to owners' tax returns, which avoids the corporate level tax and so avoids the double taxation that a C corporation faces.
Why B: A corporation with double taxation describes a C corporation, not an S corporation, which avoids taxing profit at the corporate level and passes it to owners.
Why C: An S corporation is not the cheapest form to start, since it requires legal filings and must meet requirements, so cost is not what defines it.
Why D: Owners of an S corporation do pay taxes on profit, since it passes through to their personal returns, so the claim that they pay no taxes is false.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are articles of incorporation?
A: The yearly tax form that a corporation files with the nation
B: A legal document filed with the state to form a corporation
C: The internal rules for how a corporation holds its meetings
D: A record listing each shareholder and the shares each one owns
Why A: The yearly tax form that a corporation files is a tax return and not the document that creates the corporation, so it is not the articles of incorporation.
Why B: Articles of incorporation are the legal document filed with the state to form a corporation, stating its name, purpose and shares, which makes the business a separate legal entity.
Why C: The internal rules for how a corporation holds meetings are the bylaws, which come after incorporation, and they are not the articles of incorporation.
Why D: A record listing each shareholder and the shares each one owns is a stock ledger and not the articles of incorporation filed with the state.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a board of directors?
A: The managers who handle the daily work of the firm
B: A group of lenders who provide the firm with its loans
C: A team of auditors who check the firm's books each year
D: A group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation
Why A: The managers who handle daily work of the firm are the officers or management team, and a board of directors instead oversees them.
Why B: A group of lenders who provide a firm with loans are creditors and not a board of directors, which is elected by shareholders.
Why C: A team of auditors who check the books is an audit team and not the board, which is elected by shareholders.
Why D: A board of directors is a group elected by shareholders to oversee a corporation, setting major policies and hiring top executives, so it represents the owners' interests in the firm.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a franchisor?
A: The buyer who pays fees and runs an outlet under the brand
B: A bank that lends money to the brand and holds its loans
C: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others
D: A customer who buys goods in the store every week or so
Why A: The buyer who pays fees and runs an outlet under the brand is the franchisee, not the franchisor, who owns the brand and sells the right to use it.
Why B: A bank that lends money to the brand is a lender and not the franchisor, which is the brand owner that licenses its name and system.
Why C: The franchisor is the company that owns the brand and licenses it to others who run outlets, receiving fees and royalties in return for use of its name and methods.
Why D: A customer who buys goods in the store is a consumer and not the franchisor, which is the company that owns the brand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a royalty in franchising?
A: A fee the franchisee pays the franchisor, often a share of sales
B: A one-time purchase price paid for the first set of equipment
C: The wages paid by the franchisee to the outlet's staff members
D: A tax paid by the franchisee to the government on its sales
Why A: A fee the franchisee pays the franchisor, often a share of sales, is a royalty, which pays for continued use of the brand name and business system.
Why B: A one-time price paid for the first set of equipment is a startup cost, and a royalty is a continuing payment to the franchisor.
Why C: The wages paid to the outlet's staff are labor costs paid by the franchisee and are not a royalty, which the franchisee pays to the franchisor.
Why D: A tax paid by the franchisee to the government is a business tax, whereas a royalty is paid to the franchisor for use of the brand.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an executive summary in a business plan?
A: A detailed list of the firm's costs and the prices of its goods
B: A study of the competitors, customers and market for the product
C: A short overview of the whole business plan placed at its start
D: A chart of the staff who will work in the firm and their duties
Why A: A detailed list of the firm's costs and the prices of its goods belongs in the financial or marketing sections, not the short opening overview that an executive summary gives.
Why B: A study of the competitors, customers and market is the market analysis section of a business plan, so it is not the executive summary.
Why C: An executive summary is a short overview of the whole business plan placed at its start, so busy readers such as lenders can grasp the main points quickly.
Why D: A chart of the staff who will work in the firm and their duties belongs in the organization section and is not the executive summary.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the market analysis section of a business plan describe?
A: The firm's costs, profits and cash forecasts
B: The customers and rivals in its target market
C: A guaranteed profit for the owner each year
D: Who will run the firm and their experience
Why A: The firm's costs, profits and cash forecasts belong in the financial section of a business plan and not the market analysis, which studies customers and rivals.
Why B: The market analysis section describes the customers and rivals in the target market, including its size and trends, so readers can see that demand exists for the product.
Why C: A guaranteed profit for the owner each year cannot be promised, and a market analysis section describes customers and competitors and does not promise any profit.
Why D: Who will run the firm and their experience belong in the management section of a business plan and not in the market analysis section.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What do financial projections in a business plan show?
A: A description of the products that the firm will sell
B: A summary of the market and its customers
C: A plan for the firm's advertising and promotions
D: Forecasts of sales, costs, profit and cash flow
Why A: A description of the products to be sold belongs in the company or product section of a plan, and it does not show forecasts of money.
Why B: A summary of the market and its customers belongs in the market analysis section and not among the financial projections, which show forecast numbers.
Why C: A plan for the firm's ads and promotions belongs in the marketing section and is not a financial projection, which shows forecast numbers for money.
Why D: Financial projections show forecasts of sales, costs, profit and cash flow, so lenders and investors can judge whether the business will be profitable and able to repay its funding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is equity financing?
A: Raising money by selling a share of the firm
B: Borrowing money that is repaid with interest
C: Paying bills late to hold on to cash longer
D: Charging customers in advance for goods ordered
Why A: Raising money by selling a share of the firm is equity financing, since investors receive ownership in return for their funds, and they do not need to be repaid like a loan.
Why B: Borrowing money that is repaid with interest is debt financing and not equity financing, because lenders do not receive ownership in the firm.
Why C: Paying bills late to hold on to cash longer is a cash management tactic and not a way of raising funds from investors, so it is not equity financing.
Why D: Charging customers in advance for goods ordered is a way to collect cash from sales and is not equity financing, which involves selling ownership.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is debt financing?
A: Selling shares of ownership to investors
B: Getting a grant that need not be repaid
C: Borrowing money to be repaid with interest
D: Saving owner profits to pay for new equipment
Why A: Selling shares of ownership to investors is equity financing and not debt financing, because debt does not give lenders any ownership.
Why B: A gift or grant that need not be repaid is not debt, since debt financing means borrowing money that must be repaid.
Why C: Debt financing means borrowing money to be repaid with interest, such as a bank loan, so the owner keeps full ownership of the business.
Why D: Saving owner profits to pay for new equipment uses internal funds and is not borrowing, so it is not debt financing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is venture capital?
A: A loan from a local bank that the firm repays each month with interest
B: Investment from firms that fund high-growth startups in exchange for ownership
C: A sum of money paid by a customer in advance for goods and services ordered
D: A grant of money from the government that never has to be repaid by the firm
Why A: A loan from a local bank repaid monthly with interest is debt financing and not venture capital, which comes from investors who take an ownership share.
Why B: Venture capital is investment from firms that fund high-growth startups in exchange for ownership, so the investors share in the business's risk and also in its rewards if it succeeds.
Why C: A sum of money paid by a customer in advance for goods and services is a deposit or prepayment, and it is not venture capital funding.
Why D: A grant of money from the government that never has to be repaid is a public grant and not venture capital, which buys an ownership stake.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is crowdfunding?
A: A loan for new equipment from a bank or lender for a firm
B: A tax on property that a firm owns in a town every year
C: A discount from suppliers given to a business that buys in bulk
D: Raising small amounts of money from many people, usually online
Why A: A loan for new equipment from a bank is debt financing from a single lender and not a collection of small gifts from the public.
Why B: A tax on property that a firm owns in a town every year is a property tax and is not a way of raising money from supporters.
Why C: A discount from suppliers given to a business that buys in bulk lowers costs and does not raise money from many people, so it is not crowdfunding.
Why D: Crowdfunding raises small amounts of money from many people, usually online, which lets a business or project gather funds from supporters without a single large investor or bank loan.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an EIN?
A: An Employer Identification Number the IRS issues to identify a business for taxes
B: A license number the state gives to people who are allowed to drive vehicles
C: A Social Security number the nation issues to each worker for pay and taxes
D: A permit the city issues to a store allowing it to open for trade in town
Why A: An EIN is an Employer Identification Number that the IRS issues to identify a business for tax purposes, much like a Social Security number but for a company.
Why B: A license number the state gives to people allowed to drive vehicles is a driver's license number, which has nothing to do with identifying a business to the IRS.
Why C: A Social Security number issued to each worker for pay identifies a person and not a business, whereas an EIN identifies the business for tax purposes.
Why D: A permit the city issues to a store allowing it to open is a business license, which the city issues, whereas the IRS issues an EIN.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a trade secret?
A: A public record of the firm's sales that anyone may read
B: A patent that the state grants for twenty years of use to the holder
C: Confidential business information that gives a competitive edge
D: A legally registered brand name and logo that identify the firm
Why A: A public record of sales that anyone may read is the opposite of a secret, so it cannot be a trade secret, which a firm keeps private.
Why B: A patent that the state grants for twenty years is a legal protection that is publicly filed, so it is not a trade secret, which stays confidential.
Why C: A trade secret is confidential business information, such as a recipe or formula, that gives a firm a competitive edge as long as it stays secret.
Why D: A legally registered brand name and logo is a trademark, which is public and protects identity, so it is not a trade secret.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is liability insurance for a business?
A: Coverage that pays claims if the business causes harm
B: A loan that lets the business buy new equipment now
C: A plan that sets the prices of the goods it sells
D: A tax paid by the business on its yearly profits
Why A: Coverage that pays claims if the business causes harm is liability insurance, which protects a firm from paying large legal costs when someone is injured or loses property.
Why B: A loan that lets the business buy new equipment is debt financing and not insurance, because it does not cover claims against the business.
Why C: A plan that sets the prices of the goods it sells is a pricing strategy, not liability insurance, which covers claims against the firm.
Why D: A tax paid by the business on its yearly profits is an income tax, which is not insurance, since it covers no claims against the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cash flow?
A: The total profit a business keeps in a full year
B: The movement of money into and out of a business
C: The value of all the goods held in the stockroom
D: The amount that owners have invested in the business
Why A: The total profit a business keeps in a full year is net income, which is a measure of earnings and not the movement of money in and out.
Why B: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business, and it shows whether the firm has enough cash to pay its bills and keep running.
Why C: The value of goods held in the stockroom is inventory, which is a stock of items and is not the movement of money in and out.
Why D: The amount that owners have invested in the business is owner's equity, which is a balance and not the movement of money in and out.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business receives $20,000 and pays out $26,000 in a month. What is its net cash flow?
Why A: A positive $6,000 would mean more money came in than went out, but the business received $20,000 and paid out $26,000, so the flow is negative.
Why B: The amount of $26,000 is only the money paid out and ignores the $20,000 received, so it is not the net cash flow.
Why C: The amount of $46,000 adds the cash received to the cash paid out ($20,000 + $26,000), but net cash flow subtracts outflows from inflows, so this uses the wrong operation.
Why D: Net cash flow equals cash received minus cash paid out, so $20,000 - $26,000 = -$6,000, a negative value meaning more cash left the business than came in this month.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a balance sheet?
A: A report of yearly sales, costs and the profit earned
B: A plan showing how a firm will market its product
C: A list of the firm's employees and their pay rates
D: A report of assets, liabilities and owner's equity
Why A: This describes an income statement, which covers sales, costs and profit over a period; a balance sheet instead shows assets, liabilities and equity at one date.
Why B: A marketing plan sets out how a firm will promote and sell its product, but it is not a financial statement, so it cannot be a balance sheet.
Why C: A list of employees and pay rates is a payroll record kept for staff, not a financial statement of what the firm owns and owes.
Why D: A balance sheet lists what the firm owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner's equity left over, all at a single date.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the accounting equation?
A: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
B: Profit = Assets + Liabilities
C: Equity = Assets + Liabilities
D: Assets = Revenue minus Expenses
Why A: The accounting equation says everything a firm owns is financed by creditors or the owner, so Assets equal Liabilities plus Owner's Equity, and the sheet balances.
Why B: Profit comes from revenue minus expenses, not from adding assets and liabilities, so this mixes a balance sheet idea with an income statement idea.
Why C: Adding liabilities to assets gives a meaningless total; equity is what is left after liabilities are subtracted from assets, so this has the signs wrong.
Why D: Revenue minus expenses gives profit, which belongs on the income statement; assets are matched against liabilities and equity, not against revenue and expenses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business has assets of $50,000 and liabilities of $20,000. What is owner's equity?
Why A: $50,000 is the total assets, not the owner's equity; the $20,000 owed to creditors must be subtracted before the owner's share is known.
Why B: $20,000 is the liabilities figure itself, which is what the firm owes, not what is left for the owner after paying those debts.
Why C: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities, so $50,000 minus $20,000 leaves $30,000 as the owner's share of the business.
Why D: $70,000 comes from adding liabilities to assets ($50,000 + $20,000), but debts must be subtracted, so this overstates the owner's equity badly.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an income statement?
A: A report of assets, debts and equity at one date
B: Revenues and expenses that show profit or loss
C: A list of staff and their pay rates by job role
D: A schedule of loan payments owed to the bank
Why A: This describes a balance sheet, a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at one date, whereas an income statement covers a period of time.
Why B: An income statement lists revenues and expenses for a period and shows the resulting profit or loss, which is why it is called the profit and loss report.
Why C: A list of staff and pay rates is a payroll record; it does not show revenues, expenses or the profit the business earned.
Why D: A loan payment schedule tracks debt repayments to a bank, which is only one small item and not the full revenue and expense report.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop has sales of $60,000 and cost of goods sold of $36,000. What is gross profit?
Why A: $36,000 is the cost of goods sold itself; gross profit is what remains after subtracting that cost from the $60,000 of sales.
Why B: $60,000 is the sales figure before any cost is taken out, so it is revenue, not the gross profit left over.
Why C: Gross profit equals sales minus cost of goods sold, so $60,000 minus $36,000 leaves $24,000 earned on the goods before other expenses.
Why D: $96,000 comes from adding sales and cost ($60,000 + $36,000), but the cost has to be subtracted, so the answer is wrongly inflated.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A retailer buys an item for $40 and adds a markup of $25. What is the selling price?
Why A: Selling price equals cost plus markup, so $40 plus $25 gives $65, the price that covers the item's cost and adds the planned markup.
Why B: $40 is only what the retailer paid for the item; with no markup added, the shop would earn nothing on the sale.
Why C: $15 comes from subtracting the cost from the markup ($40 minus $25), but the markup is added to the cost, so this is wrong.
Why D: $1,000 comes from multiplying $40 by $25, but a markup is added to the cost rather than multiplied, so the arithmetic is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A retailer buys an item for $50 and marks it up 40% of cost. What is the selling price?
Why A: $50 is just the cost; a 40% markup adds $20 more, so selling at cost would leave the retailer with no profit.
Why B: $90 treats the 40% as $40 and adds it to $50, but 40% of $50 is only $20, so this overstates the price.
Why C: $20 is the markup amount alone (40% of $50), not the selling price, which must also include the $50 cost.
Why D: Forty percent of the $50 cost is $20, and adding it to the cost gives a selling price of $70.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a markdown?
A: An amount added to cost to set a selling price
B: A reduction in the selling price of an item
C: A fee charged by a bank for making a loan
D: A tax paid to the state on each sale made
Why A: This describes a markup, which raises the price above cost; a markdown goes the other way and lowers the price already set.
Why B: A markdown is a reduction from the original selling price, often used for sales or clearing old stock, so this is the right definition.
Why C: A fee charged for a loan is bank interest or a service charge, which has nothing to do with changing the price of a product.
Why D: A tax on each sale is a sales tax and is set by the state; a markdown is a price cut made by the seller.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A $80 jacket is marked down 25%. What is the sale price?
Why A: $100 comes from adding 25% of $80 ($20) to the price, which would be a markup, but a markdown lowers the price instead.
Why B: A 25% markdown takes $20 off ($80 x 0.25), and $80 minus $20 leaves a sale price of $60.
Why C: $20 is the amount of the discount, not the new price; the sale price is what remains after taking it off $80.
Why D: $55 treats the 25% as $25 and subtracts it from $80, but 25% of $80 is $20, so the price should be $60.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Rent for a bakery is $2,000 a month regardless of loaves baked. This is a:
A: Net profit
B: Variable
C: Fixed cost
D: Revenues
Why A: Profit is revenue minus costs, and rent is one of those costs, so rent cannot be profit.
Why B: A variable cost changes with output, but rent stays at $2,000 whether the bakery bakes many loaves or none, so it is not variable.
Why C: Rent stays the same at $2,000 a month no matter how many loaves are baked, which is the definition of a fixed cost.
Why D: Revenue is money earned from sales, while rent is money paid out, so rent is a cost and cannot be revenue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Flour used by a bakery rises as more loaves are baked. This is a:
A: Variable
B: Revenues
C: Fixed cost
D: Net profit
Why A: Flour is used up more as more loaves are baked, so its total cost rises with output, which makes it a variable cost.
Why B: Revenue is money coming in from sales, but flour is an input the bakery pays for, so it is a cost, not revenue.
Why C: A fixed cost stays the same at any output, but flour use rises with each extra loaf, so flour is not fixed.
Why D: Profit is what remains after costs are subtracted from revenue, so flour, which is one of those costs, is not profit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is total cost?
A: Revenue divided by units sold
B: Total cost divided by units made
C: Revenue minus all expenses
D: Fixed cost plus variable cost
Why A: Revenue divided by units is the average price. Total cost is fixed costs plus variable costs.
Why B: That gives average cost per unit. Total cost is fixed costs plus variable costs.
Why C: Revenue minus expenses gives profit, not cost, so this describes the firm's earnings and not what it spent in total.
Why D: Total cost is fixed costs plus variable costs, covering everything the firm pays whether or not output changes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A cafe has fixed costs of $3,000 and variable costs of $2 per cup. It sells 1,500 cups. What is total cost?
Why A: $7,500 is $3,000 plus $5 per cup, but the variable cost is $2 per cup, so the right sum is $3,000 plus $3,000.
Why B: $4,500 adds the 1,500 cups to the $3,000 fixed cost, but variable cost is $2 per cup, so 1,500 x $2 = $3,000 must be added.
Why C: $3,000 is the fixed cost only; it leaves out the variable cost of 1,500 cups at $2 each, which adds another $3,000.
Why D: Variable cost is 1,500 x $2 = $3,000, and adding the $3,000 fixed cost gives a total cost of $6,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Total cost is $6,000 for 1,500 cups. What is the average cost per cup?
Why A: $6 would be right only for 1,000 cups ($6,000 / 1,000); the question gives 1,500 cups, so the division is wrong.
Why B: Average cost per cup is total cost divided by cups, so $6,000 / 1,500 = $4 per cup.
Why C: $9,000 comes from multiplying $6,000 by 1.5, but average cost needs division by the 1,500 cups, not multiplication.
Why D: $2 is far too low; $2 x 1,500 cups is only $3,000, which would be half of the stated $6,000 total cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A cafe sells cups at $5 with total cost per cup of $4. What is profit per cup?
Why A: Profit per cup equals price minus cost per cup, so $5 minus $4 leaves $1 earned on each cup sold.
Why B: $9 comes from adding the price and the cost ($5 + $4), but profit needs the cost subtracted from the price.
Why C: $4 is the cost of each cup, not the profit; profit is what remains of the $5 price after that cost.
Why D: $20 comes from multiplying $5 by $4, but profit per unit is found by subtracting cost from price, not multiplying them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A product sells for $15 and costs $9 in variable costs. Fixed costs are $1,800. How many units must be sold to break even?
A: 1,800 units
B: 120 units
C: 300 units
D: 200 units
Why A: 1,800 units would only be right if each unit earned $1; here each unit contributes $6, so far fewer sales are needed.
Why B: 120 units comes from dividing $1,800 by the $15 price, but break-even must divide by the $6 contribution margin.
Why C: Each unit contributes $15 minus $9 = $6 toward fixed costs, so break-even is $1,800 / $6 = 300 units.
Why D: 200 units comes from dividing $1,800 by the $9 variable cost, but the divisor should be the $6 contribution margin.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is contribution margin per unit?
A: Selling price plus fixed cost per unit
B: Fixed cost divided by the units sold
C: Selling price minus variable cost per unit
D: Total revenue minus total cost
Why A: Adding fixed cost per unit to the price is not a margin; contribution margin subtracts variable cost from the selling price, so this has the wrong inputs.
Why B: Fixed cost divided by units sold is fixed cost per unit, which says nothing about how much each sale contributes after variable costs.
Why C: Contribution margin per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit, the amount each sale adds toward covering fixed costs.
Why D: Total revenue minus total cost is the overall profit for all units, not the per-unit amount left after variable costs are paid.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the law of diminishing returns?
A: Output rises faster as more inputs are used
B: Extra inputs add less and less extra output
C: Costs fall as a firm produces more units
D: Prices fall when more of a good is supplied
Why A: Faster rising output is increasing returns. Diminishing returns means extra inputs add less and less extra output.
Why B: The law of diminishing returns says that after some point each added unit of input brings a smaller gain in output.
Why C: Falling average costs describe economies of scale. Diminishing returns means extra inputs add less extra output.
Why D: Price falling with supply is a market effect. Diminishing returns is about smaller output gains from added inputs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are economies of scale?
A: Lower average cost as output grows
B: Higher average cost as output grows
C: A fixed price set for all goods
D: Selling fewer goods at higher prices
Why A: Economies of scale means average cost per unit falls as a firm grows its output, because fixed costs are spread over more units.
Why B: Higher average cost with growth describes diseconomies of scale, the opposite of the idea, where a firm becomes too big to run well.
Why C: Economies of scale concerns average cost falling as output grows, not a fixed price set for all goods by anyone.
Why D: Selling fewer goods would raise the average cost per unit because fixed costs are spread over fewer sales, which is the opposite.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is marginal cost?
A: The total cost of producing all units made
B: The cost per unit averaged over all units
C: The fixed cost that stays the same at any output
D: The extra cost of producing one more unit
Why A: The total cost of all units made is total cost, not marginal cost, which looks only at the added cost of one more unit.
Why B: Cost per unit averaged over all units is average cost; marginal cost looks only at the one additional unit being added.
Why C: Fixed cost stays the same at any output, so the extra cost of one more unit would not include it.
Why D: Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit, found as the change in total cost from adding that unit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is marginal revenue?
A: Extra revenue from selling one more unit
B: Extra cost of producing one more unit
C: Total revenue minus total cost
D: Revenue per unit averaged over all sales
Why A: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue earned from selling one more unit, found as the change in total revenue.
Why B: The extra cost of one more unit is marginal cost, which is compared with marginal revenue but is a different measure.
Why C: Total revenue minus total cost is profit, a total for all units, not the extra revenue from one added unit.
Why D: Revenue per unit averaged over all sales is average revenue, which differs from the extra revenue earned on one more unit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: When should a firm increase output according to marginal analysis?
A: When marginal cost is above marginal revenue
B: Only when fixed costs fall to zero for the firm
C: While marginal revenue is above marginal cost
D: Whenever total cost is lower than last year
Why A: If marginal cost is above marginal revenue, each added unit loses money, so a firm following marginal analysis should cut output.
Why B: Fixed costs do not change with output, so they are ignored by marginal analysis; the decision turns on marginal revenue and marginal cost.
Why C: A firm should raise output while each extra unit brings in more revenue than it costs, meaning marginal revenue is above marginal cost.
Why D: Lower total cost than last year is a comparison across time, not the marginal test of added revenue against added cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a direct cost?
A: A cost such as rent that stays fixed at any output
B: A cost traceable to a product, like raw materials
C: A shared overhead like office lighting for products
D: A tax charged on the final sale price of goods
Why A: Rent that stays fixed at any output is a fixed cost, which is often indirect; a direct cost is traced to a particular product.
Why B: A direct cost can be traced straight to a specific product, as raw materials can, which makes this the correct definition.
Why C: A shared overhead such as office lighting cannot be traced to one product, so it is an indirect cost, not a direct one.
Why D: A tax on the final sale price is not a cost traceable to producing a product, so it is not a direct cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is depreciation?
A: The increase in an asset's value over time
B: The cash a firm owes to its main suppliers
C: A tax on the yearly profit that a firm makes
D: The drop in an asset's value from use or age
Why A: Depreciation is a decrease, not an increase; a rise in an asset's value would be appreciation, so this is the opposite.
Why B: Cash owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability, not the loss of value of an asset over time.
Why C: A tax on profit is an expense paid to the government and is unrelated to an asset losing value through use or age.
Why D: Depreciation spreads the falling value of an asset, such as a machine or truck, over its useful life due to wear or age.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is return on investment (ROI)?
A: A measure of cost relative to sales revenue
B: A measure of profit relative to the investment
C: The total amount an owner puts into a business
D: The tax paid on income from investments
Why A: Cost relative to sales revenue is not ROI; return on investment compares the profit earned with the money put into the venture.
Why B: ROI measures profit relative to the amount invested, usually shown as a percentage, so it tells an owner how well the money worked.
Why C: The total an owner puts in is the investment, which is only the bottom of the ROI fraction and not the ratio itself.
Why D: Tax on investment income is a cost to the investor, not a measure of how much profit an investment earned.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An owner invests $10,000 and earns $1,500 profit. What is the ROI?
Why A: 6.7% comes from inverting the fraction, as $10,000 / $1,500 is about 6.67; ROI divides profit by investment, giving $1,500 / $10,000.
Why B: $11,500 adds the profit to the investment ($10,000 + $1,500), a dollar total, whereas ROI is a percentage ratio of profit to investment.
Why C: 150% moves the decimal wrongly; $1,500 / $10,000 = 0.15, which is 15%, not 150%.
Why D: ROI equals profit divided by investment, so $1,500 / $10,000 = 0.15, or 15%, the return earned on the owner's money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a profit margin?
A: Total cost divided by units produced
B: Fixed cost as a share of total cost
C: Net profit as a percentage of sales
D: Sales revenue as a percentage of total cost
Why A: Total cost divided by units produced is average cost per unit, not a margin, which compares profit with sales revenue.
Why B: Fixed cost as a share of total cost shows the cost structure, but it says nothing about how much profit each sale earns.
Why C: A profit margin is net profit as a percentage of sales, showing how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit.
Why D: Revenue as a percentage of cost compares sales with spending and has the ratio upside down; a margin divides profit by revenue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business has sales of $200,000 and net profit of $16,000. What is its profit margin?
Why A: Profit margin is net profit divided by sales, so $16,000 / $200,000 = 0.08, or 8%, the profit kept from each sales dollar.
Why B: 12.5% is $200,000 / $16,000 = 12.5, which inverts the fraction; the profit should be the top number and the sales the bottom.
Why C: 0.8% puts the decimal one place too far to the left; $16,000 / $200,000 is 0.08, which is 8%, not 0.8%.
Why D: 80% misplaces the decimal in the other direction; $16,000 is a small share of $200,000, so the margin is 8%, not 80%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the basic economic questions every society must answer?
A: What to produce, how to produce and for whom
B: Where to build roads, schools and parks only
C: Who to tax, who to hire and who to fire
D: Which currency to use and which bank to trust
Why A: Every society has scarce resources, so it must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, the three basic questions.
Why B: Where to build roads, schools and parks is just a planning detail; it is not the basic set of three questions about production.
Why C: Who to tax, hire and fire are management and government decisions, not the basic questions of what, how and for whom to produce.
Why D: Which currency or bank to use is a money matter; the basic questions concern what, how and for whom to produce.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a command economy?
A: An economy where private firms make every decision
B: An economy run by custom, habit and tradition alone
C: An economy with no trade between other countries
D: An economy where the state makes major decisions
Why A: An economy where private firms make every decision is a market economy, the opposite of a command economy run by government.
Why B: An economy run by custom and tradition alone is a traditional economy, not a command economy, where government makes the big decisions.
Why C: An economy with no trade between countries is called a closed economy, which describes trade, not who makes economic decisions.
Why D: In a command economy the government makes major decisions about what is produced, how and for whom, instead of markets deciding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is socialism?
A: A system where the market alone sets all prices
B: A system of private ownership of all firms
C: A system where the state owns key industries
D: A system run by tradition and custom
Why A: A system where the market alone sets all prices is a market economy or capitalism, not socialism, which gives the state a large role.
Why B: Private ownership of all firms describes capitalism; socialism rests on public or collective ownership of important industries.
Why C: Socialism is a system in which the state or community owns key industries and resources, in place of private owners.
Why D: A system run by tradition and custom is a traditional economy, not socialism, which relies on public ownership and planning.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is consumer sovereignty?
A: Government decides what firms must produce
B: Consumer buying choices decide what firms produce
C: Prices are fixed by law for all goods
D: Firms decide what to make without regard to buyers
Why A: Government deciding what firms must produce describes a command economy; consumer sovereignty gives that power to buyers.
Why B: Consumer sovereignty means buyers' choices decide what firms produce, since firms that fail to satisfy shoppers lose sales and profit.
Why C: Prices fixed by law for all goods describes price controls, not consumer sovereignty, where shoppers' choices guide what is made.
Why D: Firms ignoring buyers is the reverse of consumer sovereignty, where producers must respond to what consumers choose to buy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the law of demand?
A: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
B: Price has no effect on the quantity bought
C: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
D: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
Why A: Quantity demanded does not rise as price rises; this is the opposite of the law of demand, where higher prices cut buying.
Why B: Price has a clear effect on how much is bought, which is exactly what the law of demand describes.
Why C: The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price means buyers purchase a smaller quantity, so demand slopes downward.
Why D: As price falls, quantity supplied rises is not the law of demand; supply and demand are different, and sellers respond to prices differently.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the law of supply?
A: Supply is unaffected by price changes
B: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
C: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
D: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
Why A: Supply responds to price, so claiming it is unaffected is incorrect; the law of supply says it rises with price.
Why B: Quantity supplied falls as price rises would reverse the law; higher prices give sellers more incentive to produce, not less.
Why C: Quantity demanded falling as price rises is the law of demand, which describes buyers, not the law of supply for sellers.
Why D: The law of supply says that, other things equal, a higher price leads producers to offer a larger quantity for sale.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens when price is above equilibrium?
A: A surplus occurs
B: Demand rises
C: Equilibrium occurs
D: A shortage occurs
Why A: At a price above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus occurs.
Why B: A price above equilibrium makes buyers want less, not more, so demand does not rise; the result is a surplus.
Why C: Equilibrium is the price where supply meets demand, and a price above it is by definition not equilibrium.
Why D: A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium and buyers want more than sellers offer; a high price does the reverse.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens when price is below equilibrium?
A: A surplus occurs
B: A shortage occurs
C: Prices fall further
D: Equilibrium occurs
Why A: A surplus happens when the price is above equilibrium; a price below it leaves buyers wanting more than sellers offer.
Why B: When the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers supply, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage occurs.
Why C: Prices would tend to rise, not fall, when there is a shortage, so saying that they fall further is backwards.
Why D: Equilibrium is the price where the market clears, and a price below it is by definition not at equilibrium.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a price ceiling?
A: A legal minimum price
B: A legal maximum price
C: A tax on imported goods
D: A subsidy paid to producers
Why A: A legal minimum price is a price floor, not a ceiling; a ceiling sets the highest price that sellers may charge.
Why B: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price set by government, which sellers cannot charge above, as in rent control.
Why C: A tax on imported goods is a tariff, a trade measure that is unrelated to a legal limit on price.
Why D: A subsidy is money paid to producers to lower costs, not a legal limit on how high a price may go.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a price floor?
A: A tax on imported goods
B: A price set by the seller
C: A legal maximum on price
D: A legal minimum on price
Why A: A tax on imported goods is a tariff and does not set a lowest legal price for any product.
Why B: A price set by the seller alone is not a government rule, whereas a price floor is a legal limit set by authorities.
Why C: A legal maximum price is a price ceiling, which is the opposite of a floor that stops prices from falling below a set level.
Why D: A price floor is a legal minimum price that cannot be charged below, such as a minimum wage set by the government.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is GDP?
A: The value of goods and services made in a country
B: The total tax collected by a government in a year
C: The total money a government owes to its lenders
D: The total value of goods a country imports each year
Why A: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period, usually a year.
Why B: Tax revenue collected by a government is only one small item in a nation's finances and does not measure total production.
Why C: Money owed to lenders is national debt, which measures what the government owes, not the value of goods and services produced.
Why D: The value of imported goods counts trade only and leaves out most of what a country produces, so it is not GDP.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fiscal policy?
A: Central bank control of rates and the money supply
B: A firm's yearly plan for hiring and pay of staff
C: Government taxes and spending to guide the economy
D: Rules limiting how much a country may import
Why A: Central bank control of interest rates and the money supply is monetary policy, not fiscal policy, which belongs to the government.
Why B: A firm's plan for hiring and pay is a business decision, not a national policy tool for managing the whole economy.
Why C: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxes and spending to influence growth, jobs and prices in the economy.
Why D: Rules that limit imports are trade policy, which affects foreign trade, not the taxing and spending of fiscal policy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is monetary policy?
A: Government taxes and spending decisions
B: Central bank control of money and rates
C: Rules that limit imports of foreign goods
D: A family's plan for saving money monthly
Why A: Government taxes and spending choices are fiscal policy; monetary policy is run by the central bank, not by the government's budget.
Why B: Monetary policy is the central bank's control of the money supply and interest rates to steer inflation and growth.
Why C: Rules that limit imports are trade policy and have nothing to do with the supply of money or interest rates.
Why D: A family's plan for saving money is household budgeting, which works at home and does not set money supply for the nation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the Federal Reserve?
A: The central bank of the United States
B: The agency that collects federal income taxes
C: A commercial bank that lends to firms for profit
D: A stock exchange where shares are traded
Why A: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, which sets monetary policy and oversees banks across the country.
Why B: The agency that collects federal income taxes is the Internal Revenue Service, a different body from the Federal Reserve.
Why C: The Fed is not a commercial bank that lends to firms for profit; it is the central bank that serves banks and the government.
Why D: A stock exchange is a market where shares are traded, while the Federal Reserve runs monetary policy and supervises banks.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a quota?
A: A tax charged on imports
B: A legal ceiling on price
C: A subsidy paid to firms
D: A cap on units imported
Why A: A tax on imports is a tariff, which raises the price of foreign goods but does not cap how many may enter.
Why B: A price ceiling limits how high a price may be set, which is a price control and not a limit on imports.
Why C: A subsidy is money paid by government to producers, so it helps sellers and does not cap the quantity imported.
Why D: A quota sets a maximum quantity of a good that may be imported in a period, limiting supply from foreign producers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a trade deficit?
A: When there is no trade between countries
B: When exports and imports are equal in value
C: When a country imports more than it exports
D: When exports exceed imports in a country
Why A: When there is no trade, imports and exports are both zero, so this is not a deficit, which needs imports above exports.
Why B: When trade is balanced, exports equal imports, so no deficit exists; a deficit requires imports to be larger.
Why C: A trade deficit occurs when a country buys more from abroad than it sells abroad, so imports are larger than exports.
