Why D: Exports exceeding imports means the country sells more than it buys, which is a trade surplus and not a deficit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is comparative advantage?
A: A lower opportunity cost for a good
B: Having the most natural resources
C: Selling the most units of the good
D: Making each good at the lowest price
Why A: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than others do, so trade lets each side specialize and gain.
Why B: Having the most resources is absolute strength; comparative advantage depends on the lowest opportunity cost, not on resource size.
Why C: Selling the most describes sales volume; comparative advantage is about giving up less of other goods when producing something.
Why D: Making everything cheapest is absolute advantage, and a country cannot hold comparative advantage in every good at once.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an exchange rate?
A: A fee charged by banks
B: Price of foreign money
C: A tax on cash holdings
D: A rate paid on loans
Why A: A bank fee is a charge for a service and has nothing to do with the price of one currency in another.
Why B: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many dollars buy one euro.
Why C: A tax on money is not an exchange rate; the rate is a market price for swapping one currency for another.
Why D: A loan rate is interest charged on borrowing, which differs from the rate at which currencies are swapped.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a career pathway?
A: A form to apply for a job
B: A table of salary levels
C: Steps toward a career goal
D: A hallway in the workplace
Why A: A job application is a form sent to apply for a job, not a planned sequence of steps toward a career.
Why B: A salary table lists pay levels for jobs, which does not describe the education and experience needed to reach a career goal.
Why C: A career pathway is a planned sequence of education, training and experience that leads toward a chosen career goal.
Why D: A hallway is a physical passage in a building and has nothing to do with a plan for building a career.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are soft skills?
A: Math formulas and calculations
B: Machine operation and tool repair
C: Technical skills with computers
D: Communication and teamwork skills
Why A: Math formulas are technical knowledge that can be taught and measured, so they are hard skills, not soft skills.
Why B: Machine operation is a technical ability learned through training, which makes it a hard skill and not a soft skill.
Why C: Technical computer skills are measurable and can be taught directly, so they count as hard skills, not people skills.
Why D: Soft skills are interpersonal traits like communication, teamwork and adaptability that help workers succeed with others in any job.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are hard skills?
A: Friendliness and warmth
B: Teachable technical skills
C: Personality traits at work
D: Teamwork and cooperation
Why A: Friendliness is a personal trait that is hard to measure or test, so it is a soft skill, not a hard skill.
Why B: Hard skills are teachable, measurable abilities such as coding or accounting that can be tested and listed on a resume.
Why C: Personality traits are part of who a person is and are not taught in a course, so they are soft skills.
Why D: Teamwork is an interpersonal skill used with others and is hard to measure, so it is classed as a soft skill.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should a thank-you note after an interview do?
A: Express thanks and restate interest
B: Criticize the interviewer's methods
C: Demand that the firm give you a job
D: Skip sending it to the interviewer
Why A: A thank-you note after an interview expresses appreciation for the interviewer's time and reaffirms your interest in the job.
Why B: Criticizing the interview would give a poor impression and could cost you the job; a thank-you note should be polite and positive.
Why C: Demanding a job is rude and pushy; a thank-you note is a courteous message and is not a place for demands.
Why D: Skipping the note throws away a chance to stand out, because a short thank-you shows good manners and keeps you in mind.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is networking in career development?
A: Connecting computer networks
B: Filing papers in the office
C: Building contacts for new jobs
D: Buying office supplies in bulk
Why A: Connecting computers is computer networking, a technology activity, whereas career networking is about meeting and building contacts.
Why B: Filing papers is office work and does nothing to build the relationships that can lead to job openings.
Why C: Career networking means building professional relationships that can lead to job leads, advice, references and other opportunities.
Why D: Buying supplies is a purchasing task and is unrelated to meeting people who can help your career.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a professional reference?
A: A job title that is printed on a business card or resume
B: A salary figure that an employer offers to a new hire
C: A book list that shows what an applicant has read this year
D: A person who can vouch for your skills and character
Why A: A job title on a business card names a role you hold; a reference is a person who speaks for you.
Why B: A salary figure offered by an employer is a pay offer, not a person who can vouch for your skills.
Why C: A book list is a record of reading and does not help an employer judge your work or character.
Why D: A professional reference is a person, such as a past boss or teacher, who can vouch for your skills and character.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a portfolio?
A: A savings bank account
B: A wallet for holding cash
C: A list of company stocks
D: A set of your best work
Why A: A bank account holds money and does not show an employer what work you can do.
Why B: A wallet carries cash and cards; it is not a record of your work samples.
Why C: A stock list shows investments, which have nothing to do with demonstrating your skills to an employer.
Why D: A portfolio is a collection of work samples, such as writing or designs, that shows an employer what you can do.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a personal brand?
A: A product logo that a company prints on its packaging and in its ads
B: A tax label that is added to a product when it is sold overseas
C: How you present yourself and what you are known for professionally
D: A store name that appears on the sign above a shop's front door
Why A: A product logo identifies a company's goods on packaging and ads; a personal brand is about a person, not a product.
Why B: A tax label added to goods sold abroad concerns trade rules and has no link to how a person presents themselves.
Why C: A personal brand is how you present yourself and what you are known for, including your skills, values and reputation at work.
Why D: A store name on a sign identifies a shop and has nothing to do with how a person is seen professionally.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a work ethic?
A: A habit of blaming others whenever a project does not go well
B: A set of values centered on hard work, reliability and responsibility
C: A habit of doing only the minimum that a manager will accept
D: A habit of avoiding tasks whenever someone else is willing to do them
Why A: Blaming others when a project fails shows a lack of responsibility, which is the opposite of a strong work ethic.
Why B: A work ethic is a set of values built around hard work, reliability and responsibility, which employers prize in any role.
Why C: Doing only the minimum a manager accepts shows low effort, not the dedication and diligence a work ethic describes.
Why D: Avoiding tasks when others will do them shows a lack of responsibility, which is the reverse of a good work ethic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of a job application?
A: To show your qualifications
B: To accept a job offer letter
C: To request a loan from a bank
D: To pay income taxes on time
Why A: A job application gives employers information about your qualifications, such as education, experience and skills, so they can decide on an interview.
Why B: You accept a job through an offer and reply, not through the application, which only asks to be considered.
Why C: A loan is requested with a loan application, which is a separate document from one used to apply for a job.
Why D: Taxes are paid through tax forms and filings, which are not what a job application is meant for.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does W-4 determine?
A: Your yearly vacation days
B: Your official job title
C: Your hourly wage at work
D: Your federal tax withheld
Why A: Vacation days are set by company policy or an employment agreement, not by the W-4 tax form.
Why B: Your job title is set by the employer when you are hired and does not come from the W-4.
Why C: Your hourly wage is agreed with the employer at hiring; the W-4 only affects how much tax is withheld.
Why D: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck, based on your filing details.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an I-9 form used for?
A: Verifying eligibility to work
B: Reporting taxes to the state
C: Reporting hourly wages earned
D: Choosing employee benefits
Why A: The I-9 form lets an employer verify a new employee's identity and eligibility to work in the United States, using approved documents.
Why B: Reporting taxes is done with tax forms like the W-4 and W-2, not with the I-9, which checks work eligibility.
Why C: Wages are reported on forms like the W-2 and not on the I-9, which concerns identity and work authorization.
Why D: Choosing benefits is done in enrollment forms from the employer; the I-9 has no role in picking insurance or retirement plans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is gross pay?
A: Savings put aside for later use
B: Tax owed to the government today
C: Total earnings before deductions
D: Take-home pay, after deductions
Why A: Savings is money set aside from earnings and is not the same as what a worker earned before deductions.
Why B: Tax owed is just one deduction from pay; gross pay is the total earnings before any deductions are made.
Why C: Gross pay is total earnings before taxes and other deductions are taken out, so it is the full amount a worker earned.
Why D: Take-home pay is net pay, the amount left after deductions; gross pay is the larger figure before those are removed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is net pay?
A: Tax withheld from your paycheck
B: Pay left after all deductions
C: Total pay before any deductions
D: A bonus paid by the employer
Why A: Tax withheld is only one deduction taken from earnings, not the amount of pay that remains afterward.
Why B: Net pay is the pay remaining after taxes and other deductions are taken from gross pay, also called take-home pay.
Why C: Total earnings before taxes and deductions are gross pay, which is larger than net pay because deductions are not yet removed.
Why D: A bonus is extra pay on top of regular earnings, and it is not the amount left after deductions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A worker's gross pay is $1,500 and deductions are $330. What is net pay?
Why A: $330 is the amount of deductions only, not what the worker takes home after they are removed from $1,500.
Why B: Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions, so $1,500 minus $330 leaves $1,170 as the worker's take-home pay.
Why C: $1,830 adds the deductions to gross pay ($1,500 + $330), but deductions are taken away, so net pay must be lower.
Why D: $1,500 is the gross pay before any deductions, so it ignores the $330 that comes out of the paycheck.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a salary?
A: Fixed pay for a year
B: Pay per sale closed
C: A tip from a customer
D: Pay per hour worked
Why A: A salary is a fixed regular payment for work, usually stated as an annual amount and paid in equal installments.
Why B: Pay per sale is a commission, which varies with sales, whereas a salary stays fixed from one pay period to the next.
Why C: A tip is a gift of money from a customer for service, not a regular payment from an employer.
Why D: Pay per hour is a wage, which depends on hours worked, while a salary is a fixed amount set for the year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a wage?
A: A bonus paid at year end by firm
B: Sales percentage earned by staff
C: Pay based on the hours you worked
D: Fixed annual pay in monthly parts
Why A: A bonus is extra pay on top of regular earnings, not the basic rate based on hours worked.
Why B: A sales percentage is a commission, which depends on how much the worker sells and not on hours.
Why C: A wage is pay based on the hours worked, so a worker earns an hourly rate multiplied by the hours on the job.
Why D: Annual fixed pay in equal amounts is a salary, which does not change with hours, so it is not a wage.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Dana earns $14 per hour and works 35 hours. What is her gross weekly pay?
Why A: $49 adds the hourly rate and the hours ($14 + $35), but earnings come from multiplying the rate by the hours.
Why B: $4,900 puts the decimal two places too far; $14 x 35 hours is $490, not $4,900.
Why C: $2.50 comes from dividing hours by rate ($35 / $14), but gross pay is found by multiplying them.
Why D: Gross weekly pay equals the hourly rate times the hours worked, so $14 x 35 = $490 before any deductions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the best way to prepare for a job interview?
A: Research the firm
B: Skip the research
C: Arrive late for it
D: Wing it on the day
Why A: Researching the company and practicing answers shows interest and helps you give clear, confident replies to likely questions.
Why B: Skipping research leaves you unable to speak about the employer or the job, which hurts your chances in the interview.
Why C: Arriving late gives a poor first impression and suggests you are unreliable, so it is not preparation of any kind.
Why D: Winging it leaves you unready for common questions and shows little effort, whereas preparing ahead builds confidence.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an appropriate way to dress for most business interviews?
A: Casual beachwear
B: Neat business dress
C: Whatever is comfy
D: Pajamas to sleep in
Why A: Beachwear is far too casual for a business interview and suggests you do not take the job seriously.
Why B: Neat, professional attire shows respect for the employer and the interview, and it helps you make a good first impression.
Why C: Dressing only for comfort could leave you too casual or untidy, and that gives a poor impression to an employer.
Why D: Pajamas are for sleeping and are never suitable for an interview, which calls for neat, professional clothing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a good question to ask an interviewer?
A: How little can I do in this job?
B: How soon can I take my first vacation?
C: Can I leave early on a regular day?
D: What does success look like here?
Why A: Asking how little you can do shows a poor work ethic and would likely end the interviewer's interest in you.
Why B: Asking about a vacation before you have an offer suggests you care more about time off than the job itself.
Why C: Asking to leave early signals that you are unreliable and wish to work less, which hurts your chances.
Why D: Asking what success looks like shows you want to do well and helps you learn what the employer expects from the role.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How should you answer 'Tell me about yourself' in an interview?
A: Say nothing until they ask a question
B: Share personal secrets about your family
C: Give a brief summary relevant to the job
D: Read your resume aloud, word for word
Why A: Saying nothing wastes the chance to introduce yourself and shows poor communication skills, which an interviewer will notice at once.
Why B: Personal secrets about family and friends are not relevant to the job and are unprofessional to share in an interview.
Why C: A brief professional summary tied to the job highlights your skills and experience in a way that is relevant to the interviewer.
Why D: Reading your resume aloud repeats what the interviewer can already see and does not add anything new about you.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the STAR method for answering interview questions?
A: Start, Talk, Ask, Respond
B: Skill, Training, Award, Reference
C: Situation, Task, Action, Result
D: Sell, Trade, Acquire, Retain
Why A: STAR does not stand for Start, Talk, Ask, Respond; those words do not describe the steps of a structured answer.
Why B: Skill, Training, Award, Reference is not the STAR method; those words do not outline a story about a past experience.
Why C: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result, a way to answer by describing what happened, your role, what you did and the outcome.
Why D: Sell, Trade, Acquire, Retain is not the STAR method; it lists sales terms and says nothing about answering questions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should a resume's contact information include?
A: Name, phone and a professional email
B: Your password for your email account
C: Your birth date and your birthplace
D: Your Social Security number and address
Why A: Contact information should include your name, phone number and a professional email so an employer can reach you easily.
Why B: A password is private and must never appear on a resume, since sharing it could put your accounts at risk.
Why C: A birth date is not needed on a resume and can lead to age bias, so it is left off.
Why D: A Social Security number and parents' names are private and risky to share, and they do not belong on a resume.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a resume keyword?
A: A font style that makes the page look neat and easy to read
B: A margin setting that keeps the text from running off the page
C: A password that lets an employer open the application on a website
D: A term from the job posting that matches your skills
Why A: A font style is about appearance and is not a keyword; a keyword is a term from the job posting.
Why B: A margin setting is about layout and has nothing to do with matching the wording of the job posting.
Why C: A password for an employer's site is private login information and is not a resume keyword.
Why D: A resume keyword is a term from the job posting that matches your skills, helping applicant tracking systems and recruiters find you.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the best length for most entry-level resumes?
A: Five pages
B: One page
C: Ten pages
D: Half a line
Why A: Five pages is far too long for an entry-level candidate with little experience, and employers will not read that much.
Why B: Most entry-level resumes should be one page, which is enough to show the education and skills of a beginner clearly.
Why C: Ten pages is far beyond what any hiring manager would read, especially for a candidate early in a career.
Why D: Half a line cannot hold contact details, education and skills, so it gives the employer far too little information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which should be listed first on a resume for a recent graduate with little experience?
A: Education
B: Interests
C: Pay history
D: References
Why A: Education is the strongest item for a recent graduate with little experience, so it is listed first on the resume.
Why B: Hobbies are of minor interest to employers and, for a recent graduate, should come after education and skills.
Why C: Salary history should not appear on a resume at all, so it would never be listed first.
Why D: References are usually given on a separate sheet, if at all, and do not lead a graduate's resume.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How should you handle a gap in employment during an interview?
A: Blame your former boss
B: Be honest and positive
C: Lie about why you left
D: Refuse to answer them
Why A: Blaming others makes you look unprofessional and unwilling to take responsibility, which an interviewer will count against you.
Why B: Being honest and focusing on what you learned or did, such as courses or volunteering, shows maturity and keeps trust.
Why C: Lying about a gap can be found out and can cost you the job, so honesty is the safer course.
Why D: Refusing to answer looks evasive and leaves the interviewer to imagine the worst, instead of hearing a clear explanation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a job fair?
A: A tax filing event
B: A county farm fair
C: An employer meet-up
D: A funfair with rides
Why A: A tax event is a government function with no link to employers meeting people who are looking for work.
Why B: A county fair is a local festival with rides and exhibits, not an event where employers meet job seekers.
Why C: A job fair is an event where several employers meet job seekers to share openings and take applications.
Why D: A funfair is for entertainment, with rides and games, and has no role in hiring or job searching.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should you do before sharing someone as a reference?
A: Tell them after you have applied
B: Pay them a fee for their help
C: Nothing, just list their name
D: Ask for their permission first
Why A: Telling them after the application is sent means they may be caught off guard by a call, so you must ask first.
Why B: Paying a reference is improper and could cast doubt on their honesty; a reference gives their view freely.
Why C: Doing nothing risks surprising the person with a call and they may give a poor or unprepared answer.
Why D: Asking for permission is polite and makes sure the person is willing to give you a good reference when called.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is salary negotiation?
A: Skipping all talk of pay with the employer
B: Refusing to take any job that is offered
C: Demanding a high salary with no research
D: Discussing pay and benefits before hiring
Why A: Skipping pay talk means you may accept less than you could, so it is not negotiation at all.
Why B: Refusing to work is not a negotiation; it ends the discussion rather than seeking agreement on pay.
Why C: Demanding a high salary without research ignores what others pay, which is unrealistic and unlikely to succeed in a real negotiation.
Why D: Salary negotiation is discussing pay and benefits with an employer before accepting a job, so both sides agree on terms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should you do when you decide to leave a job?
A: Insult the boss as you walk out the door
B: Give proper notice and leave on good terms
C: Quit without notice and leave right away
D: Take company property as a souvenir to keep
Why A: Insulting the boss damages relationships and your reputation, which can hurt future references and job chances.
Why B: Giving proper notice and leaving on good terms protects your reputation and keeps the employer as a possible reference.
Why C: Quitting without notice leaves the employer in a bind and can harm your reputation and a future reference.
Why D: Taking company property is theft, which could lead to legal trouble and ruin your professional reputation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a typical notice period when resigning?
A: A fortnight
B: A full year
C: Not required
D: A few hours
Why A: Two weeks is the usual notice period, giving the employer time to cover your duties or find a replacement.
Why B: Two years is far longer than any normal notice period and would be unreasonable to ask of a worker.
Why C: Saying none is ever required is incorrect, since giving notice is the professional norm and may be required by contract.
Why D: Two hours is too short for an employer to plan for your leaving and counts as quitting without proper notice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a professional email address?
A: A phrase of slang words
B: A joke nickname or pun
C: One using your real name
D: An address made of emoji
Why A: A slang phrase looks unprofessional to employers and does not help them take your application seriously.
Why B: A joke nickname may amuse friends but makes a poor impression on an employer reading your resume.
Why C: A professional email address is based on your name rather than a nickname, which looks serious and is easy for employers to recognize.
Why D: An emoji address is not professional and may not even work in email, so employers would not take it seriously.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is LinkedIn mainly used for?
A: Streaming music, movies and videos online
B: Professional networking and job searching
C: Online gaming with friends and others
D: Sharing vacation photos with friends
Why A: Streaming music is done on audio services, not on LinkedIn, which is built for professional connections and careers.
Why B: LinkedIn is mainly used for professional networking and job searching, letting users share their work history and meet employers.
Why C: Online gaming is done on game platforms, which are separate from LinkedIn, a site for careers and contacts.
Why D: Sharing vacation photos is what personal social media is for; LinkedIn is mainly for professional contacts and job searching.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should you proofread your resume?
A: Employers ignore errors in a resume
B: It is unnecessary for most job seekers
C: Errors can create a poor impression
D: Errors make a resume look much better
Why A: Employers do notice errors and may reject careless applicants, so claiming they ignore mistakes is false.
Why B: Proofreading is necessary, because skipping it can leave mistakes that make you look careless to an employer.
Why C: Errors can create a poor impression of your care and attention, so proofreading before you send protects your chances.
Why D: Errors do not improve a resume; they make it look sloppy and can lead to rejection.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop sells 200 mugs at $8 each and its total costs are $1,200. What is its profit?
A: $400, found by subtracting the $1,200 cost from the $1,600 revenue
B: $1,200, which is the total cost of running the shop for the period
C: $2,800, found by adding the revenue to the costs of the business
D: $1,600, which is the total revenue before the costs are subtracted
Why A: Revenue is 200 x $8 = $1,600, and subtracting the $1,200 total costs leaves a profit of $400.
Why B: $1,200 is the total cost of running the shop, not the profit; profit is the revenue minus that amount, which is $400.
Why C: $2,800 adds revenue to costs ($1,600 + $1,200), but costs must be subtracted from revenue to find profit.
Why D: $1,600 is the total revenue of 200 mugs at $8, which is the figure before the $1,200 of costs is taken away.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bakery's fixed costs are $500 a month and each loaf costs $1 to make and sells for $3. How many loaves must it sell to break even?
A: 500 loaves, found by dividing the fixed costs by the cost of a loaf
B: 167 loaves, found by dividing the fixed costs by the price of a loaf
C: 1,500 loaves, found by multiplying fixed costs by the price of a loaf
D: 250 loaves, found by dividing the fixed costs by the profit per loaf
Why A: 500 loaves divides fixed costs by the $1 cost, but each loaf earns $2 toward fixed costs, so fewer are needed.
Why B: 167 loaves divides $500 by the $3 price, but break-even must use the $2 contribution per loaf, not the price.
Why C: 1,500 loaves multiplies the fixed costs by the price, but break-even is found by dividing, using the contribution of $2.
Why D: Each loaf contributes $3 minus $1 = $2 toward fixed costs, so the break-even is $500 / $2 = 250 loaves.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these is a variable cost for a lawn-care company?
A: The salary of the manager who runs the company all year round
B: The monthly lease payment on the office where the company works
C: Fuel used to run the mowers on the jobs the company completes
D: The yearly insurance premium paid on the company's trucks
Why A: A manager's salary is paid all year whatever the number of lawns cut, so it is a fixed cost, not variable.
Why B: The monthly office lease stays the same however many lawns are mowed, so it is a fixed cost.
Why C: Fuel rises and falls with the amount of mowing done, so it is a variable cost for the lawn-care company.
Why D: Yearly insurance on trucks and equipment is a set amount no matter how much work is done, so it is fixed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these is a fixed cost for a restaurant?
A: The monthly rent paid on the building the restaurant operates from
B: The cost of the ingredients used in the meals the kitchen prepares
C: The cost of the takeout boxes used for orders customers take home
D: The extra hourly wages of part-time staff hired for a busy weekend
Why A: Monthly rent stays the same however many meals are served, which is what makes it a fixed cost.
Why B: Ingredients used in each meal rise with the number of meals served, so they are a variable cost.
Why C: Takeout boxes are used up in proportion to the number of takeout orders, so their cost is variable.
Why D: Extra wages for a busy weekend are added only when trade is heavy, so they change with output and are variable.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company's revenue is $90,000 and its expenses are $95,000. What does this show?
A: A profit of $5,000, because the larger figure shows the profit
B: Break-even, because the revenue and expenses are close in amount
C: A profit of $185,000, found by adding the revenue and the expenses
D: A loss of $5,000, because expenses are greater than the revenue
Why A: Profit needs revenue above expenses, but $90,000 is less than $95,000, so the larger figure is the expenses and the result is a loss.
Why B: Break-even needs revenue to equal expenses exactly, and $90,000 does not equal $95,000, so there is a shortfall.
Why C: Adding revenue and expenses to get $185,000 is meaningless; profit comes from subtracting expenses from revenue.
Why D: Revenue minus expenses is $90,000 - $95,000 = -$5,000, so expenses are higher and the company has a loss of $5,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store buys a jacket for $40 and marks it up 50 percent. What is the selling price?
A: $50, which adds ten dollars to the cost, a quarter of the price
B: $60, since the markup is $20, which is added to the $40 cost
C: $20, which is the markup amount rather than the selling price
D: $90, which adds fifty dollars to the cost, not half the cost
Why A: $50 adds only $10, which is 25% of $40, but a 50% markup adds $20 to the cost.
Why B: Fifty percent of $40 is $20, and adding it to the $40 cost gives a selling price of $60.
Why C: $20 is the markup amount only; the selling price must include the original $40 cost as well.
Why D: $90 adds fifty dollars to the cost, but 50 percent of $40 is $20, so the price is $60.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business has revenue of $50,000 and net profit of $5,000. What is its profit margin?
A: 1 percent, found by moving the decimal point one place too far
B: 10 percent, found by dividing the net profit by the revenue
C: 90 percent, found by dividing the expenses by the total revenue
D: 45 percent, found by halving the 90 percent expense share
Why A: 1 percent puts the decimal point too far; $5,000 / $50,000 = 0.10, which is 10 percent.
Why B: Profit margin is net profit divided by revenue, so $5,000 / $50,000 = 0.10, or 10 percent.
Why C: 90 percent is expenses divided by revenue ($45,000 / $50,000), which is the cost share and not the profit share.
Why D: 45 percent has no basis here; halving the 90 percent expense share is not a margin, and $5,000 / $50,000 gives 10 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If a business raises its price and sells fewer units, what must it check?
A: Whether the firm's advertising costs have gone down
B: Whether the new price is higher than competitors
C: How many new stores competitors plan to open
D: Whether total revenue and profit rose or fell
Why A: Advertising costs are secondary. The business must check whether total revenue and profit rose or fell.
Why B: Comparing with competitors does not show profit. The firm should check whether total revenue and profit rose or fell.
Why C: Competitors' plans do not reveal the firm's own results. The firm should check whether revenue and profit rose or fell.
Why D: Revenue is price times units, so a business must check whether the higher price outweighs the lost sales and whether profit rose or fell.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the break-even point show?
A: The sales level where total revenue equals total costs, leaving profit at zero
B: The sales level at which the business must close as it can no longer pay staff
C: The sales level at which the profit of the business is at its highest in a year
D: The sales level at which the business has no customers and earns no revenue
Why A: Break-even is the sales level where total revenue equals total costs, so the business neither makes a profit nor suffers a loss.
Why B: The business does not have to close at break-even, since revenue already covers its costs, including staff wages.
Why C: Profit is not at its highest at break-even; profit there is zero, and it grows only as sales rise beyond that point.
Why D: At break-even the business has customers and earns revenue; it simply earns exactly enough to cover its costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do businesses track their costs closely?
A: To give the owner a reason to stop selling goods that customers want to buy
B: To avoid paying any tax on the profit that the business earns in each year
C: To set prices that cover costs and still earn a fair profit for the owner
D: To make the business look larger to banks than it actually is in sales
Why A: Tracking costs helps owners find which goods to promote and does not give a reason to stop selling goods customers want.
Why B: Costs are tracked to price correctly, not to dodge taxes; trying to avoid all tax on profit would be illegal.
Why C: Tracking costs lets a business set prices that cover its costs and still leave a profit, which keeps it running.
Why D: Making a business look larger to banks is misleading; costs are tracked to run the firm well, not to deceive lenders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm's total cost rises from $10,000 to $12,000 when output rises from 1,000 to 1,500 units. What is the extra cost per added unit?
A: $8, found by dividing the new total cost by the new units made
B: $4, found by dividing the $2,000 extra cost by the 500 added units
C: $10, found by dividing the original cost by the original units made
D: $2, found by dividing the extra cost by the original units made
Why A: $8 divides the new total cost by the units at the end ($12,000 / 1,500), which is average cost, not extra cost.
Why B: Extra cost is the change in cost over the change in output: $2,000 / 500 units = $4 per added unit.
Why C: $10 divides the original cost by the starting units ($10,000 / 1,000), which gives the earlier average cost, not marginal.
Why D: $2 divides the extra cost by the 1,000 original units; the divisor must be the 500 added units, which gives $4.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which action would most likely raise a company's profit?
A: Raising its costs while keeping the same prices and the same sales
B: Lowering its prices below its cost of making each unit of its goods
C: Spending money on a product that customers show no interest in buying
D: Cutting costs without lowering the quality of its goods or services
Why A: Higher costs with the same prices and sales cut the gap between revenue and costs, which lowers profit.
Why B: Pricing below cost means each sale loses money, so profit falls rather than rises.
Why C: Money spent on a product nobody wants adds cost without adding revenue, so profit falls.
Why D: Cutting costs without lowering quality keeps revenue the same while expenses shrink, so profit rises.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A freelancer earns $3,000 in a month and spends $1,800 on costs. What is the profit?
A: $4,800, found by adding the earnings and the costs for the month
B: $1,800, which is the amount spent on costs, not the profit
C: $1,200, found by subtracting the $1,800 costs from the $3,000
D: $3,000, which is the earnings figure before the costs are subtracted
Why A: $4,800 adds the earnings to the costs, but profit is earnings minus costs, so costs must be subtracted.
Why B: $1,800 is the amount spent on costs and not what is left over; the profit is $3,000 minus $1,800.
Why C: Profit is earnings minus costs, so $3,000 minus $1,800 leaves $1,200 for the freelancer that month.
Why D: $3,000 is the earnings before costs were taken out; subtracting the $1,800 of costs leaves a profit of $1,200.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a loss leader?
A: A product sold at a low price to attract more customers
B: A product with the highest profit of the goods the store sells
C: A product sold at a high price because it is rare
D: A product that is recalled because of a safety problem
Why A: A loss leader is a product sold at a low price, even at a loss, to attract customers who then buy other goods.
Why B: A loss leader is not the highest-profit product; it is priced low to draw shoppers, so its own profit is small or negative.
Why C: A rare, high priced product is the opposite. A loss leader is sold at a low price to attract customers.
Why D: A recalled product is withdrawn from sale. A loss leader is advertised at a low price to draw customers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of an opportunity cost for a business owner?
A: The tax that the business paid on its profits at the end of the financial year
B: The wages paid to the staff for the hours they worked in the shop that week
C: The price paid for the supplies used up in making goods during the month
D: The income given up by using a building for a shop instead of renting it out
Why A: Tax paid on profits is an actual payment of money, an explicit cost, not the value of a choice given up.
Why B: Wages paid to staff are an explicit cost already paid out of the firm's funds, not an income given up.
Why C: The price paid for supplies is an out-of-pocket expense, not the value of the next best use of resources.
Why D: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, here the rent income lost by using the building as a shop.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might a business lower a price on an item that is not selling?
A: To attract more buyers and clear the unsold stock
B: To raise the margin earned on each unit
C: To discourage competitors from stocking the item
D: To show customers the item's quality has dropped
Why A: Lowering a price on an item that isn't selling attracts buyers and clears stock, freeing space and cash for other goods.
Why B: A lower price shrinks the margin on each unit. The aim is to attract buyers and clear stock.
Why C: Price cuts target buyers, not competitors. The aim is to attract buyers and clear stock.
Why D: Lowering a price does not show that quality has fallen; stores cut prices mainly to move unsold goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A student can work for $90 or study for an exam. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
A: Nothing, because studying is free and the student pays no money
B: The $90 the student gives up by not working during the study time
C: The price of the textbook that the student already owns and uses
D: The grade the student will get on the exam if the studying goes well
Why A: Studying has a cost even without cash paid, because the student gives up the $90 that working would have earned.
Why B: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, so studying costs the student the $90 forgone from working.
Why C: A textbook the student already owns is a sunk cost, not the value of the alternative forgone by studying.
Why D: The grade is a benefit of studying, not what is given up; opportunity cost is the $90 not earned.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to the price of a good when demand rises and supply stays the same?
A: The price falls to zero because buyers have more power than sellers do
B: The price stays the same because supply has not changed in the market
C: The price tends to rise because more buyers compete for the same goods
D: The price tends to fall because more buyers bring more goods for sale
Why A: Prices do not fall to zero when demand rises; more buyers competing for the same supply push prices up.
Why B: Price does not stay the same, because rising demand against unchanged supply creates a shortage that bids prices up.
Why C: With supply unchanged, higher demand creates a shortage at the old price, so competing buyers push the price up.
Why D: More buyers do not create a larger supply; supply is unchanged, so higher demand tends to raise the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to the price of a good when supply rises and demand stays the same?
A: The price stays the same because demand did not change in the market
B: The price rises to a record because sellers have more power than buyers
C: The price tends to rise because there is now more of the good for sale
D: The price tends to fall because more of the good is offered for sale
Why A: The price does not stay fixed here, because a rise in supply alone shifts the supply curve right and moves the market to a new, lower price.
Why B: Sellers gaining more goods to sell does not give them pricing power; extra supply against unchanged demand pushes sellers to compete, so the price falls rather than rising.
Why C: A larger amount for sale pushes the price down, not up, because buyers are no more eager than before and sellers must cut prices to clear the extra goods.
Why D: When supply rises and demand stays the same, the supply curve shifts right, creating a surplus at the old price, so competition among sellers pushes the equilibrium price lower.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a surplus in a market?
A: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers cannot find goods
B: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so sellers have unsold goods
C: A situation in which the price of a good is exactly equal to its cost of production
D: A situation in which the government buys all of the goods that are offered for sale
Why A: This describes a shortage, not a surplus; a surplus is the reverse, where quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, leaving sellers rather than buyers without a match.
Why B: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a given price, leaving unsold goods on the shelves, which usually pushes the price down toward equilibrium.
Why C: A price equal to the cost of production says nothing about quantities, so it is not a surplus; a surplus is defined by supply exceeding demand at a price.
Why D: Government purchases of all goods offered is a policy such as price support, not the definition of a surplus; a surplus is simply supply exceeding demand at a price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a shortage in a market?
A: A situation in which a firm has more cash than it needs to pay its bills on time
B: A situation in which the government sets a limit on the price of a good for a year
C: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers cannot find the goods
D: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so sellers have goods left over
Why A: Having extra cash is a business finance situation and has nothing to do with quantities in a market; a shortage means buyers want more than sellers offer.
Why B: A government limit on price is a price ceiling, which can cause a shortage but is not the definition of one; a shortage is demand exceeding supply at a price.
Why C: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at a given price, so some buyers cannot get the good, which tends to push the price upward.
Why D: This describes a surplus, where sellers have leftover goods; a shortage is the opposite, with buyers wanting more than the quantity supplied at that price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a complementary good?
A: A good used together with another, such as a printer and printer ink
B: A good that has no value to customers and is not sold at any price
C: A good that is given away free to customers who buy a more expensive item
D: A good used in place of another when the price of the first rises
Why A: A complementary good is used together with another good, such as printers and ink, so when demand for one rises, demand for the other usually rises too.
Why B: A good with no value that is never sold is not a complement; complements have real value because they are consumed together with another product that buyers want.
Why C: A free gift with a purchase is a promotion, not a complement; complements are separate goods normally bought and used together, such as bread and butter.
Why D: That describes a substitute, which can be used in place of another good when its price rises; complements are used together rather than swapped for each other.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a normal good?
A: A good that has no price because the government provides it to everybody for free
B: A good that is bought by every consumer in exactly the same amount each year
C: A good whose demand falls as consumers' incomes rise as they buy better goods
D: A good whose demand rises as consumers' incomes rise, such as restaurant meals
Why A: A good with no price supplied free by government is a public provision; normal goods are ordinary market goods defined by how demand responds to rising income.
Why B: Identical yearly purchases by every consumer is not how normal goods work; their demand varies, rising when consumer incomes rise, so amounts bought are not fixed.
Why C: A good whose demand falls as income rises is an inferior good, the opposite of a normal good, because buyers switch to better alternatives when they can afford them.
Why D: A normal good is one whose demand rises as consumer incomes rise, because people with more income buy more of it, such as restaurant meals or new clothing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an oligopoly?
A: A market with thousands of small sellers that offer the same product
B: A market with one seller and no close substitutes for the good it sells
C: A market dominated by a few large sellers that can influence the price
D: A market in which the government sets the price of every good that is sold
Why A: Thousands of small sellers offering identical products describes perfect competition, not an oligopoly, which has only a few large firms controlling most of the market.
Why B: One seller with no close substitutes is a monopoly; an oligopoly has a few sellers, so several firms share the market and watch one another.
Why C: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers, such as airlines or car makers, where each firm reacts to the pricing choices of its rivals.
Why D: Government setting every price describes a command economy, not a market structure; an oligopoly is about the number of sellers, which is a few large firms.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the unemployment rate measure?
A: The share of workers who work part time and would like to work more hours
B: The share of the labor force that is jobless and looking for work
C: The share of workers who earn the minimum wage out of all those who have a job
D: The share of all people in the country who have no job, including children and retirees
Why A: That describes underemployment, where part-time workers want more hours; the unemployment rate counts only people with no job who are actively searching, divided by the labor force.
Why B: The unemployment rate is the number of jobless people looking for work divided by the labor force, which includes both employed and unemployed people who are able and seeking jobs.
Why C: Minimum wage earners all have jobs, so they are employed and not counted as unemployed; the rate concerns jobless people actively searching for work, not low wages.
Why D: The rate divides by the labor force, not by the whole population, so children and retirees who are not seeking work are excluded from both parts of the calculation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the circular flow model?
A: A model showing how money, goods and resources move between households and firms
B: A model showing how prices rise in a spiral over time as wages and costs push each other up
C: A model showing how a bank moves money between its branches in the same state
D: A model showing the path that a delivery truck takes around a city each day
Why A: The circular flow model shows how money, goods and resources move between households and firms, with households supplying labor and buying products while firms pay wages and sell output.
Why B: A wage and price spiral is inflation, which is a different idea; the circular flow model shows exchanges between households and firms, not prices rising over time.
Why C: Moving money between branches of one bank is a banking operation, not an economic model; the circular flow follows exchanges among households, firms and markets in the whole economy.
Why D: A delivery truck route is a logistics matter, not economics; the circular flow model tracks money, goods and resources moving between households and firms, not a physical driving path.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a subsidy?
A: A fine the government charges to a business that breaks the rules of the market
B: A tax the government charges on goods that are brought into the country from abroad
C: A fee the government charges for a license to run a business in the state
D: A payment from the government to support a producer or activity
Why A: A fine charged to rule breakers is a penalty paid to the government; a subsidy flows the other way, as a payment from the government to producers.
Why B: A charge on imports is a tariff, which collects money from importers; a subsidy is money paid out by government to support producers or an activity, not collected.
Why C: A license fee is money paid to the government for permission to operate; a subsidy reverses this flow because the government pays money to the producer instead.
Why D: A subsidy is a payment from the government to support a producer or activity, which lowers production costs and can raise output, such as farm support payments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes a command economy?
A: Individuals and firms make most decisions through markets, guided by prices and profit
B: Customs and habits passed down through generations decide who does what work
C: The government makes most decisions about production and prices
D: Private firms make all decisions while the government has no role of any kind
Why A: Decisions guided by markets, prices and profit describe a market economy; in a command economy the government, not private firms and consumers, decides what is produced.
Why B: Customs and habits passed down through generations describe a traditional economy; a command economy is run by government planners who set production targets and prices.
Why C: In a command economy the government makes most decisions about production and prices, using central planning instead of market forces to decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Why D: A system where private firms decide everything and government has no role is pure laissez-faire; a command economy is the opposite, with the state controlling most decisions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes a traditional economy?
A: Customs and habits passed down through generations guide decisions
B: The government makes most decisions about production and prices for the whole economy
C: Firms and the government share decisions in a mix of markets and public rules
D: Prices and profit guide the decisions of firms and consumers in free markets
Why A: A traditional economy is guided by customs and habits passed down through generations, with roles such as farming or hunting inherited, so decisions follow established practice rather than markets or plans.
Why B: Government decisions about production and prices describe a command economy; a traditional economy relies on custom and inherited roles instead of any central planning authority.
Why C: Sharing decisions between firms and the government describes a mixed economy; a traditional economy depends on long-standing customs rather than markets or public rules.
Why D: Prices and profit guiding free markets describes a market economy; in a traditional economy, customs and habits, not price signals, determine who produces what.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which describes a mixed economy?
A: All decisions are made by private firms and the state has no part in the economy
B: Private choice combined with government involvement in some key industries
C: Customs and habits decide outcomes and there are no markets or government rules
D: The government owns all firms and decides prices and output in the economy
Why A: Private firms deciding everything with no state role describes a pure market economy; a mixed economy combines private choice with a meaningful amount of government involvement.
Why B: A mixed economy combines private choice with government involvement, as in most modern countries where firms and consumers use markets while the state regulates, taxes and provides some services.
Why C: Customs deciding all outcomes with no markets describes a traditional economy; a mixed economy blends market choices with government rules, so it does include markets.
Why D: A government owning all firms and setting every price is a command economy; a mixed economy leaves much production to private firms alongside some state action.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is private property in a market economy?
A: The right of the government to seize any asset at will without paying the owners
B: The rule that only wealthy families may own land and the machines that make goods
C: The right of individuals and firms to own and use resources for their own profit
D: The rule that all land and factories belong to the community and not to people
Why A: Private property rights protect owners from arbitrary seizure; a government seizing assets at will without payment would destroy those rights, so it is the opposite of private property.
Why B: Private property is open to all individuals and firms, not restricted to wealthy families; limiting ownership to the rich is not part of how market economies define it.
Why C: Private property is the right of individuals and firms to own and use resources, which gives them incentives to work, invest and take care of what they own.
Why D: Community ownership of all land and factories describes collective or socialist ownership; private property in a market economy means individuals and firms hold ownership, not the whole community.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a key advantage of a market economy?
A: Wealth is shared equally among citizens by the state
B: Competition and prices spur efficiency and growth
C: A central office decides what firms produce
D: Basic goods are provided at no charge
Why A: Equal sharing by the state is a command or socialist feature. Markets reward effort and skill with different incomes.
Why B: A key advantage of a market economy is that prices and competition encourage efficiency and innovation, since firms that cut costs or improve products earn profit and win customers.
Why C: Central decisions are a command economy feature. In a market economy prices and competition guide production.
Why D: Goods at no charge are not typical of a market. Prices and competition encourage efficiency and innovation.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a key disadvantage of a market economy?
A: The government sets the price of every good, so firms have no freedom to compete
B: All firms are owned by the state and so there is no profit motive for the workers
C: Customs decide who does each job, which limits the choices people can make in life
D: Income inequality and a weak supply of public goods such as roads and city schools
Why A: Government price setting belongs to a command economy; in a market economy firms are free to compete, so this is not a disadvantage of markets.
Why B: State ownership of all firms describes a command economy; in market economies firms are privately owned and profit motivates workers and owners, so this is not a market weakness.
Why C: Customs deciding who does each job describes a traditional economy; market economies let people choose careers, so this is not a disadvantage of markets.
Why D: A key disadvantage of a market economy is income inequality and little provision of public goods, since profit-seeking firms undersupply goods such as roads and defense that cannot be sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a key disadvantage of a command economy?
A: Planners may misjudge what people want, leading to shortages and waste
B: Prices change so quickly that firms cannot plan and consumers cannot decide what to buy
C: Private firms earn too much profit and use it to take over the whole of the economy
D: Customs prevent any change in methods, so progress is very slow across the generations
Why A: A key disadvantage of a command economy is that planners may misjudge what people want, causing shortages of some goods and waste of others, because no price signals guide them.
Why B: Rapidly changing prices that confuse firms are a feature of unstable market economies; in command economies the government sets prices, so they usually do not change quickly.
Why C: Private firms earning large profits belongs to market economies; in a command economy the state owns most firms, so private profit is not the main problem.
Why D: Customs preventing change describes a traditional economy; a command economy is run by planners who direct production, so the slow progress is not caused by custom.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is privatization?
A: Transferring a government-owned business to private owners by a share sale
B: A person keeping a personal diary that no one else is permitted to read
C: A firm making its financial records secret from the public and from regulators
D: The government taking over a private firm and running it as a public agency
Why A: Privatization is transferring a government-owned business to private owners, such as selling a state airline to investors, which shifts decisions and profits from the public sector to private hands.
Why B: Keeping a personal diary private is about personal privacy and has no connection to business ownership; privatization concerns who owns an enterprise, not who may read a diary.
Why C: A firm keeping financial records secret is about confidentiality, not ownership; privatization specifically means selling or handing state-run businesses over to private owners.
Why D: The government taking over a private firm is nationalization, which is the opposite of privatization; privatization moves ownership from the public sector to private owners.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is nationalization?
A: A firm selling its goods in every region of the country at one national price
B: A firm moving its factories to a foreign country to take advantage of lower pay
C: The government taking ownership of a private industry, often paying its owners
D: Transferring a government-owned business to private owners by a public sale
Why A: Selling at one national price is a pricing policy and does not change who owns the firm; nationalization concerns the government taking over ownership.
Why B: Moving factories abroad for cheaper wages is offshoring, a location decision made by the firm; nationalization instead means the government takes ownership of a private industry.
Why C: Nationalization is the government taking ownership of a private industry, such as a state takeover of railways or utilities, putting those assets under public control.
Why D: A public sale of a government-owned business to private owners is privatization, which is the reverse of nationalization, where government takes over private companies.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do governments regulate businesses?
A: To stop new firms from entering a market that already has large companies
B: To raise the prices of all goods so that people buy fewer things from shops
C: To make sure every business earns the same profit in each year of operation
D: To protect consumers, workers and the environment from harm and unfair acts
Why A: Regulation does not aim to block all new firms; competition law actually tries to keep markets open, so stopping entry would harm consumers and is not the purpose.
Why B: Governments do not regulate in order to raise all prices; regulations such as safety and competition rules aim to protect people, and higher prices would hurt consumers.
Why C: Guaranteeing equal profit for every business is not a goal of regulation; profits vary with efficiency and demand, while regulation targets safety, fairness and harm to others.
Why D: Governments regulate businesses to protect consumers, workers and the environment, through rules on product safety, wages and working conditions, and pollution that firms might ignore if left alone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a financial business?
A: A business that sells groceries to the public from supermarkets in a town
B: A business that handles money, such as a bank or an insurance company
C: A business that grows wheat and corn on a farm and sells it to mills
D: A business that makes cars and trucks in a plant and sells them to dealers
Why A: Selling groceries in supermarkets is retail, a commerce business, not a financial one; financial businesses handle money, credit, savings or insurance rather than goods.
Why B: A financial business handles money, such as a bank that takes deposits and lends, or an insurer that pools risk, rather than making or selling physical goods.
Why C: Growing wheat and corn is agriculture, a primary industry producing raw products; it is not a financial business, which deals in money services.
Why D: Making cars and trucks is manufacturing, a secondary industry that turns materials into goods; financial businesses instead provide services such as banking, lending and insurance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is outsourcing?
A: Selling goods to customers abroad by opening a branch in a foreign country
B: Doing all work inside the firm with its own employees and its own equipment
C: Moving a factory to another city at home to cut the firm's cost of rent
D: Hiring another company to perform tasks or services for the hiring firm
Why A: Opening a foreign branch to sell abroad is exporting or expansion, and the firm still does its own work; outsourcing means hiring another company to do tasks.
Why B: Doing all work inside the firm with its own staff and equipment is the opposite of outsourcing, which hands tasks to an outside company.
Why C: Moving a factory to another city is relocation, still done by the firm itself; outsourcing means paying another company to perform a task or service.
Why D: Outsourcing is hiring another company to perform tasks or services, such as payroll, customer support or manufacturing, so the firm can focus on its core work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a supplier do?
A: Competes with the firm for the same customers in the same market and region
B: Lends the firm money for a fixed period and charges interest on the loan
C: Provides goods or materials to another business on agreed terms and prices
D: Buys finished goods from stores and sells them to customers at a profit
Why A: A firm competing for the same customers is a competitor, not a supplier; suppliers help a business by providing inputs rather than fighting for its buyers.
Why B: Lending money and charging interest is the role of a lender, such as a bank; a supplier provides goods or materials, not loans.
Why C: A supplier provides goods or materials to another business, such as a flour mill selling flour to a bakery, so the buyer has inputs to make its products.
Why D: Buying finished goods from stores and reselling them describes a middleman or reseller; a supplier sends goods or materials to businesses so they can operate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main purpose of a business?
A: To provide goods or services that meet needs and earn a profit
B: To reduce the number of customers so that the owner has less work to do each day
C: To give away goods and services to the public at no cost to any person who asks
D: To avoid paying taxes by spending all income on the costs of running the firm
Why A: The main purpose of a business is to provide goods or services that meet needs and earn a profit, which rewards owners and lets the firm keep operating.
Why B: Reducing customers to lower the owner's workload defeats a business, which needs customers to earn revenue; its purpose is serving customers, not avoiding work.
Why C: Giving away goods at no cost would bring no revenue and cause losses, so it is a charity activity, not the main purpose of a business.
Why D: Spending all income to avoid taxes would leave no profit and is not a legitimate purpose; businesses aim to earn a profit and still pay taxes owed.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Where might an entrepreneur get start-up funds?
A: Profits earned in its first year
B: Savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding
C: Selling shares on a public stock exchange
D: Government tax refunds from earlier years
Why A: Profits come after a business operates, so they cannot fund the start. Start-up funds come from savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding.
Why B: Entrepreneurs can raise start-up funds from several sources, including personal savings, bank loans, investors and crowdfunding, which is why this broad answer is correct.
Why C: A start-up cannot usually list on a stock exchange. Typical sources are savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding.
Why D: Tax refunds are not a reliable start-up source. Entrepreneurs use savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an entrepreneur?
A: A person who starts and runs a business and takes on the risk of losing capital
B: A person who works for a fixed wage in a store and has no say in how it is run
C: A person who buys goods from a business for his own use and does not resell them
D: A person who lends money to a business and receives interest in return each year
Why A: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on its risk, hoping to earn profit but also facing the chance of losing the money invested.
Why B: A fixed-wage store worker with no say in running the business is an employee, not an entrepreneur, who starts the enterprise and bears the risk.
Why C: A person buying goods for personal use and not reselling them is a consumer, not an entrepreneur, who produces or sells goods to earn profit.
Why D: Someone who lends money and receives interest is an investor or lender; an entrepreneur starts and runs the business and takes the risk of its success or failure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is a risk that entrepreneurs face?
A: Receiving a steady paycheck from an employer each week
B: Having the freedom to set your own working hours
C: No competition, as new businesses have the market to themselves
D: Losing the money they invested if the business fails badly
Why A: A steady paycheck is typical of employment. Entrepreneurs risk losing the money they invested if the business fails.
Why B: Setting your own hours is a benefit, not a risk. The real risk is losing the money invested if the business fails.
Why C: Having no competition for years is an advantage, not a risk, and rarely happens; competitors usually appear, and the risk comes from losses instead.
Why D: A real risk entrepreneurs face is losing the money they invested if the business fails, since savings and loans can be lost when sales fall short of costs.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sole proprietor's main tax feature?
A: The business pays corporate tax and the owner pays tax on dividends
B: The business is taxed at a lower corporate rate than individuals
C: Business income is reported on the owner's own personal tax return
D: The owner is taxed on salary but not on retained profit
Why A: Paying corporate tax and then tax again on dividends describes a C corporation with double taxation; a sole proprietorship does not have a separate taxable business entity.
Why B: A sole proprietorship has no separate corporate tax. Income is reported on the owner's personal tax return.
Why C: A sole proprietor reports business income on the owner's personal tax return, because the business and the owner are legally the same person, so profit is taxed as personal income.
Why D: The owner is taxed on all business profit, whether withdrawn or kept. It is reported on the personal return.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an apprenticeship?
A: A loan for starting a business, paid back over a number of years with interest
B: Paid on-the-job training combined with classroom learning for a skilled trade
C: A permanent management role in a company, with a fixed salary and a company car
D: A short course taken in a classroom with no work experience and no pay
Why A: A loan for starting a business is a form of financing, not training; an apprenticeship is paid on-the-job training with classroom learning for a skilled trade.
Why B: An apprenticeship combines paid on-the-job training with classroom learning, letting workers earn wages while building skills for a trade such as electrician or plumber.
Why C: A permanent management role with a company car is a job, not training; apprenticeships are temporary learning programs that prepare workers for skilled occupations.
Why D: An apprenticeship includes real work experience and pay, so a classroom-only course with no experience and no pay does not describe it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is networking in career planning?
A: Setting up computers in an office so staff can share files and printers
B: Building contacts who can share job leads and advice about a career path
C: Applying for many jobs at once without speaking to anyone at the firms
D: Waiting for employers to call after sending a single application by mail
Why A: Setting up office computers is computer networking, which connects machines; networking in career planning means building human contacts who share job leads and advice.
Why B: Networking in career planning means building contacts who can share job leads and advice, which helps people hear about openings and learn about careers they might want.
Why C: Applying for many jobs without speaking to anyone is the opposite of networking, which depends on conversations and relationships with people in your field.
Why D: Waiting for employers after one application is passive and involves no contacts; networking is the active process of building relationships that lead to job information.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might someone choose a job with lower pay but stronger benefits?
A: Benefits like insurance and retirement matches add real value
B: Benefits reduce the hours that the employee must work each week
C: Benefits are taxed at a higher rate than regular wages
D: Benefits raise the base salary on the pay stub
Why A: Benefits like health insurance and retirement matches add real value beyond salary, so a job with lower pay but stronger benefits can be worth more overall.
Why B: Benefits do not reduce hours worked; they are compensation such as insurance or retirement contributions, so this does not explain why someone would accept lower pay.
Why C: Benefits such as insurance are often untaxed or lightly taxed. They add value beyond salary, which can justify lower pay.
Why D: Benefits are separate from base salary. They add value such as insurance and retirement matches, which can justify lower pay.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a performance review?
A: A plan for a company party which the managers organize each year
B: A list of the reasons why an employee should be given a higher salary
C: A periodic evaluation of an employee's work and goals by a manager
D: A review of a product by a customer who has bought it and tried it
Why A: A company party plan is a social event and has nothing to do with judging work; a performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee.
Why B: A list of reasons for a raise is a request or argument by the employee; a performance review is an evaluation of the employee's work by the employer.
Why C: A performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee's work, where a manager assesses results, gives feedback and sets goals, often influencing raises and promotions.
Why D: A customer's review of a product evaluates the product, not an employee; a performance review is conducted by an employer to assess an employee's work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a résumé?
A: A form that employers fill out to describe the duties of an open job
B: A list of the company's products with prices, sent to possible customers
C: A letter that thanks an interviewer for the time he gave to a candidate
D: A summary of your education, skills and work experience for employers
Why A: A form describing a job's duties is a job description written by employers; a résumé is written by the applicant about their own background.
Why B: A list of products and prices is a catalog or price list for customers; a résumé presents the applicant's education, skills and work experience to employers.
Why C: A letter thanking an interviewer is a thank-you note sent after an interview; a résumé is a summary of the applicant's qualifications sent when applying.
Why D: A résumé is a summary of your education, skills and work experience, which employers use to decide whether to interview you for a job.
