Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the main purpose of a cover letter?
A: To introduce yourself and explain why you are a good fit for the job posted
B: To ask the employer for a higher salary than the one that the company posted
C: To list all jobs you have held, with dates, pay and the names of bosses
D: To complain about the way in which the company treats its present employees
Why A: A cover letter introduces you and shows your fit for the job, explaining why your background suits the role and the employer, and encouraging them to read your résumé.
Why B: Asking for higher pay in a cover letter is inappropriate; salary is discussed later, and the letter should show why you fit the job instead.
Why C: Listing every job with dates, pay and bosses is what a résumé or application does; a cover letter is a short introduction that highlights fit, not a full history.
Why D: Complaining about the company's treatment of its employees would damage your chances; a cover letter should be positive and show how you fit the job.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What should a student with no work experience include on a résumé?
A: Nothing, since employers do not hire people without any work history
B: Invented job titles and made-up skills to make the application impressive
C: A list of games played, with scores and the teams the student has played for
D: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills, plus any awards earned
Why A: Employers do hire people without work histories, such as students, who can show other strengths; including nothing at all would waste the chance to impress.
Why B: Inventing job titles and skills is dishonest and may cost you the job if discovered; a résumé must be truthful, so fabrication is never acceptable.
Why C: A list of games and scores shows little about job skills; employers want relevant evidence of responsibility and ability, not a record of games played.
Why D: A student with no work experience should include school activities, volunteering and relevant skills, since these show responsibility, teamwork and abilities employers value.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a good next step after an interview?
A: Post complaints about the company online if there is no reply
B: Wait silently for a year in case the employer decides to call you
C: Send a thank-you message to the interviewer within a day or two
D: Call the interviewer hourly until you get an answer about the job
Why A: Posting complaints online after a day is unprofessional and could harm your reputation; employers need time to decide, so patience is the better course.
Why B: Waiting silently for a year shows no interest and lets the employer forget you; sending a prompt thank-you message is the better follow-up.
Why C: Sending a thank-you message soon after an interview is a good next step, since it shows courtesy, repeats your interest and keeps your name in front of the employer.
Why D: Calling the interviewer every hour is harassment and would annoy the employer, hurting your chances; a single polite thank-you message is appropriate.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a behavioral interview question?
A: A question asking what you would do in an imaginary case that has not happened
B: A question asking about how you handled a past situation
C: A question that asks only for your name and the date of your birth
D: A question about your plans for the weekend and your favorite sports
Why A: A question about what you would do in an imaginary case is a hypothetical or situational question, not a behavioral one, which asks about real past events.
Why B: A behavioral interview question asks how you handled a past situation, such as a time you resolved a conflict, since past behavior helps predict future performance.
Why C: Asking only for name and birth date is a basic personal detail question, and birth date may be inappropriate; behavioral questions explore past actions at work.
Why D: Questions about weekend plans and sports are small talk and not behavioral questions, which investigate how you acted in earlier work or school situations.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which interview behavior is most professional?
A: Making eye contact and listening carefully to what the interviewer says
B: Arriving ten minutes late and apologizing if the interviewer asks about it
C: Checking your phone repeatedly while the interviewer is speaking to you
D: Interrupting the interviewer so that you can make your own points faster
Why A: Making eye contact and listening carefully shows respect, interest and good communication, which are professional behaviors that help an interviewer judge you favorably.
Why B: Arriving ten minutes late and apologizing only if asked shows poor punctuality and carelessness; professional candidates arrive early and do not wait to be questioned about lateness.
Why C: Checking your phone while the interviewer speaks is disrespectful and shows lack of interest, so it harms your impression instead of showing professionalism.
Why D: Interrupting the interviewer is rude and suggests poor listening; professional candidates wait until the interviewer finishes before speaking and make their points at the right time.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which question is generally illegal for an interviewer to ask?
A: Whether you can work the hours the job needs, including weekends
B: Whether you plan to have children or to start a family soon
C: Why you want this job and what skills you would bring to it
D: What your career goals are for the next five years in this field
Why A: Asking whether you can work the hours the job requires is legal because it concerns the ability to do the essential duties, so it is allowed.
Why B: Asking whether you plan to have children is generally illegal because it relates to family status and sex, which anti-discrimination laws protect from hiring decisions.
Why C: Asking why you want the job and what skills you bring is a normal and legal question, since it relates directly to your qualifications.
Why D: Asking about career goals for the next five years is a common, legal question that focuses on your plans and ambition, not a protected characteristic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do employers conduct background checks?
A: To lower employee pay by finding faults in the history of applicants
B: To find reasons for refusing to hire workers who apply to the firm
C: To verify information and reduce risks when hiring staff for firms
D: To discover which applicants have the most friends on social media
Why A: Background checks are not used to lower pay; they verify facts about applicants, and finding faults to cut salaries is not their purpose.
Why B: Employers run checks to confirm facts and manage risk, not to look for excuses to reject everyone who applies; that purpose is unfair and untrue.
Why C: Employers conduct background checks to verify information and reduce hiring risks, such as confirming past jobs, education and records relevant to the position.
Why D: Counting friends on social media is not a goal of background checks, which confirm facts like employment, education and criminal history that bear on job risk.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the best response to praise at work?
A: Brag about it to everyone in the office to show your worth to the firm
B: Ignore the praise and walk away without saying a word to the person
C: Say that the praise is not deserved and that the team did the work
D: Say thank you and share credit with the others who helped on the task
Why A: Bragging about praise to everyone is arrogant and annoys coworkers; a professional response is to be gracious and acknowledge others who helped.
Why B: Ignoring praise and walking away is rude and ungracious; the professional response is to thank the person for noticing your work.
Why C: Saying the praise is undeserved and the team did all the work denies your real contribution and is a false modesty; it is better to thank them.
Why D: The best response to praise is to say thank you and share credit with others who helped, showing gratitude, humility and good teamwork.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A freeze destroys much of the orange crop. What is the most likely effect on the price of orange juice?
A: The price falls because supply increases when oranges become scarce
B: The price falls because demand for juice drops when a freeze occurs
C: The price stays the same because demand for juice is not affected
D: The price rises because the supply of oranges and juice decreases
Why A: A freeze that destroys oranges reduces supply rather than increasing it, because fewer oranges reach the market, so the price does not fall for that reason.
Why B: The freeze affects how much fruit is produced, not what consumers want, so demand for juice does not drop and does not cause a lower price.
Why C: Supply falls because the crop is destroyed, so the supply curve shifts left; with demand unchanged, the price changes, and it does not stay the same.
Why D: The freeze destroys oranges, so supply decreases and the supply curve shifts left; with demand unchanged, buyers compete for fewer oranges and the price of juice rises.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A new study shows that a certain snack is healthy and many people begin buying it. What happens to its demand curve?
A: It shifts to the right as more people want to buy
B: It stays in place because only price changes demand
C: It becomes vertical so nobody can buy the snack
D: It shifts left because fewer people want the snack
Why A: A health study makes more people want the snack at every price, so the demand curve shifts to the right, which is an increase in demand.
Why B: Price changes cause movement along the curve, but tastes and information shift the whole curve; the health news changes tastes, so the curve does shift.
Why C: A demand curve does not become vertical because people begin buying more; vertical would mean quantity never responds to price, and buyers still can purchase the snack.
Why D: A leftward shift means fewer people want the snack, but the study led more people to buy it, so demand increases and shifts right.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A new machine lets a factory make twice as many shoes with the same workers. What happens to the supply of shoes?
A: Supply vanishes as shoes get too cheap to make
B: Supply increases as each worker's output rises
C: Supply stays the same as workers are the same
D: Supply falls since the firm needs fewer workers
Why A: Supply does not vanish when shoes become cheaper to make; lower costs encourage production, so the quantity supplied rises rather than falling to nothing.
Why B: A machine that doubles output with the same workers lowers the cost per pair, so the factory supplies more shoes at every price, and the supply curve shifts right.
Why C: The same workers can now produce twice as much, so technology matters more than the number of workers; supply does change by increasing, not staying the same.
Why D: The machine increases productivity, so the factory makes more shoes, not fewer; needing fewer workers lowers cost, which raises supply rather than decreasing it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Consumer incomes rise and demand for restaurant meals increases. Restaurant meals are a:
A: Capital good
B: Inferior good
C: Normal good
D: Public good
Why A: A capital good is a tool or machine used to produce other goods, and restaurant meals are consumed by households, so they are not capital goods.
Why B: An inferior good loses demand when incomes rise, but demand for restaurant meals increased as incomes rose, so they are not inferior goods.
Why C: A normal good is one whose demand rises as consumer incomes rise, and restaurant meals fit because higher incomes lead people to eat out more often.
Why D: A public good, such as national defense, is nonrival and nonexcludable; restaurant meals are sold to paying customers, so they are private goods, not public goods.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: As incomes rise, people buy less instant noodles and more fresh food. Instant noodles are an example of a(n):
A: A luxury good for the wealthy
B: Normal good as demand rises
C: A public good, shared by many
D: Inferior good, demand falls
Why A: A luxury good is a normal good whose demand rises strongly with income; instant noodles fall in demand when income rises, so they are not luxuries.
Why B: A normal good has demand that rises with income, but people buy fewer noodles as their income rises, so this option contradicts the facts given.
Why C: A public good is available to everyone without being sold to individuals, like street lighting; instant noodles are sold in stores, so they are not public goods.
Why D: Instant noodles are an inferior good because demand falls as incomes rise, with people switching to fresh food they prefer once they can afford it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is price elasticity of demand?
A: How quickly prices rise each year across the whole economy
B: How strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change
C: How much a good costs to make in a factory or on a farm
D: How much a firm earns when it sells goods at a fixed price
Why A: Rising prices across the economy measured by an index describes inflation, not elasticity, which measures how much buyers change quantity in response to one good's price change.
Why B: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price, so a large response means demand is elastic and a small one means inelastic.
Why C: Production cost in a factory concerns the supply side, while elasticity of demand describes how buyers react to a change in price, not what making a good costs.
Why D: Earnings at a fixed price describe revenue, but elasticity is about how quantity demanded changes when price changes, so a fixed price excludes the key idea.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which good tends to have inelastic demand?
A: Insulin for a person with severe diabetes
B: A brand of potato chips with many substitutes
C: A luxury cruise on a large ocean liner
D: A particular movie ticket at a cinema chain
Why A: Insulin for a diabetic has inelastic demand because it is a necessity with no substitutes, so people keep buying nearly the same quantity even if the price rises sharply.
Why B: A brand of chips with many close substitutes has elastic demand, since buyers switch to other brands when its price rises, so it is not inelastic.
Why C: A luxury cruise is a discretionary purchase that people can delay or skip when prices rise, so demand is elastic and not inelastic.
Why D: A particular movie ticket has many substitutes such as streaming or other entertainment, and it is not a necessity, so demand is fairly elastic, not inelastic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which good tends to have elastic demand?
A: Gasoline for a commuter with no options
B: Prescription drugs for chronic illness
C: A brand of soda with many alternatives
D: Table salt sold at a grocery store
Why A: A commuter with no alternative must keep buying gasoline even when prices rise, so quantity demanded barely changes and demand is inelastic, not elastic.
Why B: Medicine for a chronic illness is a necessity with no easy substitute, so patients keep buying despite price increases and demand is inelastic, not elastic.
Why C: A specific soda brand with many alternatives has elastic demand, because when its price rises buyers readily switch to other drinks, and quantity demanded falls sharply.
Why D: Table salt is cheap, a necessity and has few substitutes, so buyers hardly change quantity when its price rises, making demand inelastic rather than elastic.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store raises the price of a product with elastic demand. What happens to total revenue?
A: It falls as sales drop
B: It remains unchanged
C: It becomes zero dollars
D: It rises with the price
Why A: With elastic demand, a price rise cuts quantity demanded by a larger percentage than the price increase, so total revenue (price times quantity) falls.
Why B: Revenue does not stay the same in all cases; it depends on elasticity, and with elastic demand the lost sales outweigh the higher price, so revenue falls.
Why C: Revenue becomes zero only if nobody buys at all; with elastic demand, quantity falls by a large amount but not to zero, so revenue falls but stays positive.
Why D: A higher price raises revenue only when demand is inelastic; with elastic demand the drop in quantity is proportionally larger, so total revenue falls despite the higher price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store raises the price of a product with inelastic demand. What happens to total revenue?
A: It drops to nothing
B: It stays unchanged
C: It falls as sales dip
D: It rises with price
Why A: Revenue does not become zero, because buyers with inelastic demand keep purchasing most of the quantity even at a higher price, so sales continue.
Why B: Revenue changes in this case, because inelastic demand means quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so the result is not the same as before.
Why C: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so the lost sales do not outweigh the higher price and revenue does not fall.
Why D: With inelastic demand, quantity sold falls proportionally less than price rises, so price times quantity increases and total revenue rises after the price increase.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The government sets a maximum price on rent that is below the market price. What is a likely result?
A: A rise in quality of each unit
B: A shortage of rental housing
C: No change in the rental market
D: A surplus of rental housing
Why A: A price ceiling below the market price does not improve quality; sellers earn less and often reduce maintenance, so quality tends to fall rather than rise.
Why B: A maximum rent below equilibrium makes the quantity of housing demanded exceed the quantity supplied, producing a shortage of rental housing with more renters than available units.
Why C: A binding price ceiling changes the market by creating a gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied, so saying there is no change is wrong.
Why D: A surplus needs quantity supplied above quantity demanded, but a low maximum rent raises demand and lowers supply, so the result is a shortage, not a surplus.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The government sets a minimum price above the market price for a crop. What is a likely result?
A: A shortage of the crop
B: A fall in crop prices
C: A surplus of the crop
D: No effect on prices
Why A: A shortage requires demand above supply; a minimum price above equilibrium reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied, so it creates a surplus, not a shortage.
Why B: A minimum price above the market price keeps the price higher, not lower, so it cannot cause the price of the crop to fall.
Why C: A price floor above the market price raises quantity supplied and lowers quantity demanded, so more crop is produced than buyers want, creating a surplus.
Why D: A binding price floor interferes with the market, changing the quantities supplied and demanded, so it has an effect, namely a surplus of the crop.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a price ceiling?
A: A rent control law that caps monthly rent
B: A subsidy paid to farmers to cut their costs
C: A tax on tobacco products sold in shops
D: A minimum wage law set for hourly workers
Why A: A rent control law that caps monthly rent is a price ceiling, because it sets a legal maximum price that landlords may charge for housing.
Why B: A farm subsidy is a payment to producers to lower their costs, not a legal limit on price, so it is not a price ceiling.
Why C: A tax on tobacco raises costs and prices, but it is not a legal limit on what sellers may charge, so it is not a price ceiling.
Why D: A minimum wage law sets a lowest legal price for labor, which makes it a price floor, not a ceiling that caps a maximum price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of a price floor?
A: A rent control law
B: A minimum wage law
C: A cap on gasoline prices
D: A price limit on medicine
Why A: Rent control caps the price landlords can charge, which is a maximum price and therefore a price ceiling, not a floor.
Why B: A minimum wage law sets the lowest legal price for labor, so it is a price floor that prevents wages from falling below a set level.
Why C: A cap on gasoline prices limits how high the price can go, which is a price ceiling, not a floor that stops prices falling.
Why D: A price limit on medicine sets a maximum amount sellers may charge, so it is a price ceiling, not a price floor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the three types of unemployment commonly described?
A: Frictional, financial and fiscal unemployment
B: Seasonal, social and structural unemployment
C: Cyclical, circular and civil unemployment
D: Frictional, structural and cyclical forms
Why A: Financial and fiscal are not types of unemployment; the three commonly described types are frictional, structural and cyclical, each with its own cause.
Why B: Seasonal unemployment is a recognized type, but social is not a type of unemployment, so this set of three does not match the common classification.
Why C: Cyclical is a real type, but circular and civil are not types of unemployment, so this list is wrong.
Why D: The three types commonly described are frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch) and cyclical (caused by weak economic activity), which together explain most unemployment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A graduate is between jobs while searching for a better fit. What type of unemployment is this?
A: Structural
B: Seasonal
C: Frictional
D: Cyclical
Why A: Structural unemployment comes from skills no longer matching jobs, but a graduate between jobs is simply searching for a better fit, which is frictional.
Why B: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable yearly patterns such as holiday or farm work, but this graduate is searching for a better match, not facing a season.
Why C: Frictional unemployment occurs when workers are between jobs or searching for a better fit, as with a graduate who is looking for the right position.
Why D: Cyclical unemployment arises from a weak economy and general job losses, but the graduate is only searching for a better fit, which is frictional.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Factory workers lose jobs because their skills no longer match available jobs. What type of unemployment is this?
A: Cyclical
B: Structural
C: Seasonal
D: Frictional
Why A: Cyclical unemployment comes from a downturn in the economy, but these workers lost jobs because their skills no longer match available jobs, which is structural.
Why B: Structural unemployment occurs when workers' skills no longer match available jobs, often after technology or industry changes, as happened to these factory workers.
Why C: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable times of year, but nothing in the scenario links the job losses to a season; it concerns a skills mismatch instead.
Why D: Frictional unemployment is brief searching between jobs, but these workers lack skills the market needs, which makes their unemployment structural.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Workers lose jobs because the economy has slowed. What type of unemployment is this?
A: Frictional
B: Structural
C: Seasonal
D: Cyclical
Why A: Frictional unemployment is temporary job searching, but job losses from a general economic slowdown are cyclical in nature.
Why B: Structural unemployment results from a skills mismatch or industry change, but job losses from a general economic slowdown are cyclical.
Why C: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable times of year, but a slowing economy is not a seasonal pattern, so this scenario describes cyclical unemployment.
Why D: Cyclical unemployment occurs when the economy slows and firms cut jobs because demand for goods falls, which matches workers losing jobs during a downturn.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Ski instructors are out of work in summer. What type of unemployment is this?
A: Structural
B: Cyclical
C: Seasonal
D: Frictional
Why A: Structural unemployment arises from skills mismatch or industry change, but ski instructors idle in summer are out of work because of the time of year.
Why B: Cyclical unemployment follows the business cycle and economic downturns, but ski instructors lose work each summer regardless of how the economy is performing.
Why C: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work depends on the time of year, and ski instructors have little to do in summer when there is no snow.
Why D: Frictional unemployment is brief searching between jobs, but ski instructors are out of work because the season ends, not because they are looking for a better match.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the labor force?
A: People employed or actively seeking paid work
B: All the people who live in the whole country
C: People who hold jobs in factories and offices
D: People aged 16 or older who live in the country
Why A: The labor force is made up of people who are employed or actively seeking work, so it includes both employed and unemployed people who want to work.
Why B: The labor force does not include everyone in the country; children, retirees, students and others not seeking work are excluded from this group.
Why C: The labor force includes all kinds of jobs and people seeking work. It is the employed plus those actively seeking work.
Why D: Age and residence alone do not define the labor force. It counts people who are employed or actively seeking work.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A country has 200 million people in the labor force and 10 million are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A: 5 percent, by dividing 10 by 200 million
B: 210 percent, found by adding the numbers
C: 20 percent, found by dividing 200 by 10
D: 10 percent, found by using 10 as percent
Why A: The unemployment rate is unemployed divided by labor force, so 10 million divided by 200 million equals 0.05, or 5 percent.
Why B: Adding 200 and 10 gives 210, but a rate is a share found by dividing, and no unemployment rate can be above 100 percent here.
Why C: Dividing the labor force by the unemployed gives 200 divided by 10, which equals 20, but the formula is unemployed divided by labor force.
Why D: Treating 10 million as 10 percent ignores the labor force of 200 million; the correct division is 10 divided by 200, which is 5 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure?
A: The total value of goods made in a nation
B: The average interest rate charged on loans
C: Changes in the prices of a basket of goods
D: The number of jobs available in the economy
Why A: Total value of goods produced in a year is GDP, not CPI; the CPI tracks consumer prices for a typical basket of goods.
Why B: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money and is not what the CPI measures; the CPI tracks changes in the prices of goods.
Why C: The Consumer Price Index measures changes in the prices of a basket of goods and services bought by typical households, and is used to calculate inflation.
Why D: The number of jobs is an employment statistic; the Consumer Price Index measures how prices for a basket of goods and services change.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Prices rose from an index of 200 to 210 over a year. What was the inflation rate?
A: 2 percent, found by moving a decimal
B: 10 percent, found by using the change
C: 210 percent, using the new index
D: 5 percent, change over the old index
Why A: Moving the decimal does not give an inflation rate; the rate is the change in the index divided by the old index, 10 divided by 200, equal to 5 percent.
Why B: Using the change of 10 as a percent ignores the starting level of 200; the inflation rate is 10 divided by 200, which equals 5 percent.
Why C: Using the new index of 210 as a percent confuses a level with a rate of change; the rate is the increase relative to the old index.
Why D: Inflation is the percentage change in the index: 210 minus 200 equals 10, and 10 divided by 200 equals 0.05, which is 5 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is deflation?
A: A rise in wages across the economy
B: A general fall in prices over time
C: A broad rise in the level of prices
D: A fall in total output of the economy
Why A: A rise in wages is not deflation, which refers to the general price level; wages can rise while prices stay stable or even fall.
Why B: Deflation is a general fall in prices over time, which raises the purchasing power of money but can discourage spending and hurt business profits.
Why C: A general rise in prices that makes each dollar buy less is inflation, which is the opposite of deflation, where prices fall.
Why D: A fall in output describes a recession or contraction; deflation is about the general price level falling, not about the amount of production.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is stagflation?
A: A sharp fall in the stock market that hurts investors
B: High inflation together with high unemployment and slow growth
C: Low inflation with low unemployment and fast growth in output
D: Rapid growth together with falling prices and low unemployment
Why A: A stock market fall is a financial event, not stagflation, which is a combination of high inflation, high unemployment and slow growth in the economy.
Why B: Stagflation is high inflation together with high unemployment and slow growth, a rare combination, as seen in the 1970s oil shock years.
Why C: Low inflation, low unemployment and fast growth describes a healthy economy, the opposite of stagflation, which pairs rising prices with weak output and high joblessness.
Why D: Rapid growth with falling prices is the opposite of stagflation, which combines slow growth, high unemployment and rising prices, so this does not fit.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a depression?
A: A fall in one product's price in a local market
B: A short slowdown that lasts for a few weeks
C: A time of rapid growth in output and incomes
D: A severe, lasting downturn in economic activity
Why A: A price fall for one product in one local market is a minor event; a depression is a severe, prolonged downturn across the whole economy.
Why B: A short slowdown of a few weeks is too brief to count; a depression is a severe downturn lasting years, much deeper than a normal recession.
Why C: A time of rapid growth is an economic boom, the opposite of a depression, which involves falling output and widespread unemployment.
Why D: A depression is a severe and prolonged downturn in economic activity, with falling output, high unemployment and lost income lasting years, like the 1930s Great Depression.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does GDP stand for?
A: Government debt payment
B: General domestic prices
C: Gross domestic product
D: Gross dollar profit
Why A: Government debt payment is not what the initials stand for; GDP is gross domestic product, a measure of total output in a country.
Why B: General domestic prices does not match the initials; GDP stands for gross domestic product, which measures the value of goods and services produced.
Why C: GDP stands for gross domestic product, the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
Why D: Gross dollar profit is not a real economic term; GDP means gross domestic product, which measures output rather than profit in dollars.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is counted in GDP?
A: A new car produced and sold in this year
B: Money given between friends, with no sale
C: A purchase of shares on a stock exchange
D: A used car resold this year by a dealer
Why A: A new car produced and sold this year is a final good made in the current period, so its value is counted in that year's GDP.
Why B: Gifts between friends are transfers with no production or market sale, so they add nothing to the output measured by GDP.
Why C: A stock purchase is a transfer of ownership of a financial asset, not production of a new good or service, so GDP excludes it.
Why D: A used car resold this year was produced in an earlier year, so counting it again would be double counting; only new production is included.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why are intermediate goods left out of GDP?
A: They have no value to buyers
B: They are illegal to trade now
C: They come from other countries
D: To avoid counting value twice
Why A: Intermediate goods do have value; they are left out because their value is already included in the final good, not because they are worthless.
Why B: Intermediate goods are legal products used in making other goods, such as steel for cars, so illegality is not the reason they are excluded.
Why C: Intermediate goods are made at home as well as abroad, so being produced only in other countries cannot be why GDP leaves them out.
Why D: Intermediate goods are left out to avoid counting the same value twice, since their value is already included in the price of the final good.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are the four components of GDP in the expenditure approach?
A: Land, labor, capital and enterprise, the inputs to goods
B: Consumption, investment, government spending, net exports
C: Savings, taxes, debt, credit and the rate of interest
D: Wages, rent, interest and profit, the four factor incomes
Why A: Land, labor, capital and enterprise are the factors of production, inputs used to make goods, not the spending components of GDP.
Why B: The four expenditure components are consumption, investment, government spending and net exports, which together add up to the total spending on the economy's output.
Why C: Savings, taxes, debt and credit are financial concepts, not the spending categories that make up GDP in the expenditure approach.
Why D: Wages, rent, interest and profit are the income approach categories of GDP, not the four spending components of the expenditure approach.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In GDP, consumption is $700 billion, investment $200 billion, government spending $300 billion and net exports -$50 billion. What is GDP?
A: $1,150 billion, the sum of four parts
B: $1,200 billion, by adding net exports
C: $700 billion, which is consumption
D: $1,250 billion, ignoring net exports
Why A: GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, so 700 plus 200 plus 300 plus negative 50 equals 1,150 billion dollars.
Why B: Adding net exports would give 1,200 only if net exports were positive 50; here they are negative 50, so they must be subtracted, giving 1,150.
Why C: Consumption alone is only one part of GDP; investment of 200 and government spending of 300 must be added, and net exports of negative 50 subtracted.
Why D: Ignoring net exports gives 700 plus 200 plus 300, which equals 1,200, not 1,250; net exports of negative 50 must be included, leaving 1,150.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is real GDP?
A: GDP before any adjustment for inflation
B: GDP of a rich country, in dollars
C: GDP adjusted for inflation each year
D: GDP counted in a foreign currency
Why A: GDP not adjusted for inflation is nominal GDP, which is measured at current prices; real GDP removes the effect of price changes.
Why B: Real GDP has nothing to do with whether a country is rich; it is a measure of output after adjusting for changes in prices.
Why C: Real GDP is GDP adjusted for inflation, using constant prices, so it shows true changes in output rather than increases caused only by higher prices.
Why D: Converting GDP to a foreign currency is an exchange rate matter, not an inflation adjustment, so it does not define real GDP.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Nominal GDP rises 6 percent and prices rise 2 percent. About how much did real GDP grow?
A: About 3 percent, by dividing
B: About 12 percent, by multiplying
C: About 4 percent, by subtracting
D: About 8 percent, found by adding
Why A: Dividing 6 by 2 gives 3, but real growth is found by subtracting the price increase from nominal growth, which gives 6 minus 2 equals 4.
Why B: Multiplying 6 by 2 gives 12, but real growth subtracts inflation from nominal growth; the correct figure is 6 minus 2 equals 4 percent.
Why C: Real GDP growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation, so 6 percent minus 2 percent equals about 4 percent, after removing the effect of higher prices.
Why D: Adding 6 and 2 gives 8, but inflation is removed from nominal growth, not added; the correct calculation is 6 minus 2, equal to 4 percent.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is GDP per capita?
A: GDP multiplied by the total population
B: GDP divided by the population size
C: GDP minus the taxes that are paid
D: GDP of just one sector of the economy
Why A: Multiplying GDP by population gives a meaningless huge number; GDP per capita is found by dividing GDP by the population to get output per person.
Why B: GDP per capita is GDP divided by the population, which shows average output per person and is used to compare living standards across countries.
Why C: Subtracting taxes from GDP gives something like disposable income, not a per-person measure; per capita means divided by the number of people.
Why D: GDP of one sector is a sector's output, not a per-person average; per capita requires dividing the whole economy's GDP by its population.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: During a recession, the government cuts taxes and raises spending. What is this?
A: Expansionary money policy
B: Trade policy for imports
C: Tightening fiscal policy
D: Expansionary fiscal plan
Why A: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and money supply, while cutting taxes and raising spending are done by government, which is fiscal policy.
Why B: Trade policy concerns tariffs, quotas and trade agreements, not taxes and government spending, so it does not describe the response to a recession.
Why C: Contractionary fiscal policy raises taxes or cuts spending to slow the economy, the opposite of cutting taxes and raising spending during a recession.
Why D: Cutting taxes and raising government spending to boost demand during a recession is expansionary fiscal policy, because it increases spending and output in the economy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The Fed lowers interest rates to encourage borrowing. What is this?
A: Expansionary money policy
B: Tightening money policy
C: Expansionary fiscal policy
D: Trade policy for imports
Why A: Lowering interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending is expansionary monetary policy, since the central bank acts to stimulate economic activity.
Why B: Contractionary monetary policy would raise interest rates to discourage borrowing, the opposite of the Fed lowering rates to encourage it.
Why C: Fiscal policy involves government taxes and spending decisions, while the Fed changing interest rates is monetary policy, so this is not fiscal.
Why D: Trade policy covers tariffs and trade agreements, not interest rates, so lowering rates to encourage borrowing is not a trade policy.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How does the Fed typically respond to high inflation?
A: It prints extra money freely
B: It raises the interest rate
C: It bans prices from rising
D: It lowers interest rates
Why A: Printing more money without limit would raise inflation further, not lower it, so it is not how the Fed responds to high inflation.
Why B: The Fed typically raises interest rates in response to high inflation, which makes borrowing costlier, slows spending and reduces upward pressure on prices.
Why C: Banning price increases is a price control the Fed has no authority to impose, and it would cause shortages, so it is not a typical response.
Why D: Lowering interest rates makes borrowing cheaper and boosts spending, which would add to inflation, so the Fed does the opposite when inflation is high.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a budget deficit?
A: When government spending exceeds its revenue
B: A budget in which spending matches revenue
C: The total owed by government from past deficits
D: When government revenue exceeds its spending
Why A: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds its revenue in a year, so the government must borrow to cover the gap between what it spends and collects.
Why B: A balanced budget means spending equals revenue, so there is no gap and no deficit, which is the opposite of what is being asked.
Why C: The total owed from earlier deficits is the national debt, which accumulates over time, while a deficit is the shortfall in a single year.
Why D: Revenue exceeding spending is a budget surplus, not a deficit, since the government takes in more than it spends that year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the national debt?
A: The yearly shortfall in a budget
B: The government spending in a year
C: The cash held in the treasury
D: The total sum the government owes
Why A: The yearly shortfall is the budget deficit, a flow measured over one year, whereas the national debt is the accumulated total owed.
Why B: The amount spent in one year is government spending, not debt; the national debt is what accumulates from borrowing over many years.
Why C: Money in the treasury is government cash holdings, an asset, whereas the national debt is a liability showing what the government owes lenders.
Why D: The national debt is the total amount the government owes, built up from past borrowing to cover deficits, and includes bonds held by investors and others.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Country A can make cloth at a lower opportunity cost than Country B, while B has a lower opportunity cost for wheat. What should each do?
A: Neither should trade but each should rely on itself
B: Each should make both goods for its own people
C: A should make cloth and B wheat, then they trade
D: A should make wheat and B cloth, then they trade
Why A: If neither country trades, both lose the gains from specialization; comparative advantage shows each can be better off by specializing and trading.
Why B: Making both goods ignores comparative advantage; each country gains by concentrating on the good with the lower opportunity cost and trading for the other.
Why C: Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost is lower, so A makes cloth and B makes wheat, then they trade, giving both more of both goods.
Why D: This reverses the correct assignment, because A has the lower opportunity cost in cloth, not wheat, so A should make cloth and B should make wheat.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is absolute advantage?
A: The ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost
B: The ability to avoid taxes on imports and exports
C: The ability to produce more using the same inputs
D: The ability to charge higher prices than rivals
Why A: Producing at a lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, which compares how much each country can produce with the same resources.
Why B: Avoiding taxes is a legal or accounting matter and says nothing about production; absolute advantage compares the output possible with the same resources.
Why C: Absolute advantage is the ability to produce more of a good with the same resources than another producer can, so output per unit of input is higher.
Why D: Charging higher prices is a market behavior, not a production ability; absolute advantage concerns producing more with the same resources.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If the dollar strengthens against the euro, what happens to American exports to Europe?
A: They stop, as buyers leave the market
B: They get more expensive for Europeans
C: They become cheaper for Europeans
D: They are unaffected by the change
Why A: American exports do not stop when the dollar strengthens; they continue but become pricier for Europeans, so quantity sold may fall, not drop to nothing.
Why B: A stronger dollar buys more euros, so Europeans must pay more euros for the same American goods, making exports more expensive for them.
Why C: The reasoning is backwards, because a stronger dollar means Europeans need more euros to buy dollars, so American goods become more expensive for Europeans, not cheaper.
Why D: Exchange rates change the foreign price of American goods, so exports are affected; a stronger dollar makes them costlier for Europeans.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If $1 buys 0.90 euros, how many euros can you get for $200?
A: 180 euros, 200 times the rate
B: 222 euros, by dividing by 0.90
C: 200 euros, ignoring the rate
D: 20 euros, moving the decimal
Why A: Multiplying 200 dollars by 0.90 euros per dollar gives 180 euros, which is the amount you receive when converting at that rate.
Why B: Dividing 200 by 0.90 gives about 222, but each dollar buys 0.90 euros, so you multiply 200 by 0.90 to get 180.
Why C: Ignoring the rate would give 200 euros, but one dollar buys only 0.90 euros, so 200 dollars buys 180 euros, not 200.
Why D: Moving the decimal gives 20, which is not based on the exchange rate; multiply 200 by 0.90 to get 180 euros.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a free trade agreement?
A: A ban on trade between nations
B: A law that sets prices for goods
C: A tax placed on imported goods
D: A deal to reduce trade barriers
Why A: A ban on trade is the opposite of free trade; a free trade agreement removes or reduces barriers so goods can cross borders more easily.
Why B: A rule that sets prices is a price control, which is unrelated to trade agreements that lower barriers between countries.
Why C: A tax on imports is a tariff, which is a trade barrier; a free trade agreement reduces such tariffs instead of imposing them.
Why D: A free trade agreement is an agreement among countries to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers, so goods and services move more freely between them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is protectionism?
A: Policies that limit imports to protect local firms
B: Policies that protect the environment and wildlife
C: Policies that remove trade barriers between nations
D: Policies that protect consumers from fraud and scams
Why A: Protectionism is a set of policies, such as tariffs and quotas, that restrict imports to shield domestic industries from foreign competition.
Why B: Protecting the environment is environmental policy, which is unrelated to trade policy; protectionism concerns restricting imports to help domestic industries.
Why C: Removing all barriers to trade is free trade, the opposite of protectionism, which adds barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
Why D: Rules against false advertising are consumer protection laws, which are not trade policy; protectionism specifically restricts imports to protect domestic producers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a monopsony?
A: A market with just two sellers
B: Many buyers and many sellers
C: A market with a single buyer
D: A market with a single seller
Why A: A market with two sellers is a duopoly, a form of oligopoly; monopsony is about buyers, not sellers, so this option does not fit.
Why B: Many buyers and sellers describes a competitive market; monopsony has only one buyer, which gives that buyer power over prices.
Why C: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, such as one employer in a small town buying labor, which gives it power to set low wages.
Why D: A single seller is a monopoly; a monopsony is the reverse, with one buyer facing many sellers.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is perfect competition?
A: A market in which the state sets the prices of all goods
B: A market with one seller and many barriers to entry
C: A market with a few large sellers who watch rival prices
D: A market with many sellers of same goods and easy entry
Why A: Price controls only are government interventions, not a market structure; perfect competition is defined by many sellers, identical products and easy entry.
Why B: A market with one seller is a monopoly, which is the opposite extreme from perfect competition, where many sellers compete.
Why C: A few large sellers watching rivals' prices describes an oligopoly; perfect competition has many small sellers who cannot influence the price.
Why D: Perfect competition has many sellers of identical products and easy entry, so no single firm can influence price and all sellers accept the market price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is monopolistic competition?
A: A market with identical products and no pricing power
B: A market with many sellers of differentiated goods
C: A market with one seller and many entry barriers
D: A market with two sellers and high entry barriers
Why A: Identical products where no seller can differ in price describes perfect competition; monopolistic competition features differentiated products, which let firms charge somewhat different prices.
Why B: Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering differentiated products, such as restaurants or clothing brands, which gives each firm a limited ability to set its own price.
Why C: A market with one seller is a monopoly, not monopolistic competition, which has many sellers.
Why D: A market with two sellers is a duopoly, not monopolistic competition, which has many sellers with differentiated products.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a negative externality?
A: A benefit received by other people
B: A cost imposed on others, like smog
C: A tax paid by firms to the state
D: A fall in profit for a firm in a year
Why A: A benefit received by others is a positive externality, the opposite of a negative externality, which imposes costs on people outside the transaction.
Why B: A negative externality is a cost imposed on others who are not part of a transaction, such as pollution from a factory harming nearby residents.
Why C: A tax paid by firms is a government charge, not a spillover effect; negative externalities are costs that fall on third parties.
Why D: A loss in profit is a cost to the firm itself, whereas a negative externality is a cost imposed on outsiders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a positive externality?
A: A subsidy paid by the government
B: A profit earned by a firm in sales
C: A benefit for people outside a deal
D: A cost imposed on people outside it
Why A: A subsidy is a government payment, sometimes used to encourage positive externalities, but it is not the externality itself, which is a benefit to third parties.
Why B: A profit is a gain to the firm, not a spillover to outsiders, while a positive externality is a benefit received by people outside the transaction.
Why C: A positive externality is a benefit received by people not part of a transaction, such as a vaccine's protection of others who did not pay for it.
Why D: A cost imposed on others is a negative externality, the opposite of a positive externality, which gives benefits to outsiders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might a government tax a product that causes pollution?
A: To increase pollution and raise state revenue
B: To help the polluter earn a much bigger profit
C: To lower prices and boost output of the good
D: To make producers pay for harm and cut output
Why A: Taxing pollution aims to reduce it, not increase it; raising tax revenue is a side effect and does not describe the reason.
Why B: A pollution tax charges polluters for the harm they cause, so it hurts rather than helps them and is intended to reduce pollution.
Why C: A pollution tax raises the cost of production, which tends to raise prices rather than lower them, so lowering prices is not its aim.
Why D: A pollution tax makes producers pay for the harm they cause and reduces output, so the cost of the externality is built into the price.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the free rider problem?
A: People benefit from a good without paying for it
B: People pay more than their fair share for a good
C: People ride for free on a public bus system
D: People refuse to buy a good sold at high prices
Why A: The free rider problem occurs when people benefit from a good without paying for it, which makes it hard for markets to supply public goods.
Why B: Paying more than a fair share is the opposite of free riding, which involves paying nothing or less than your share while still benefiting.
Why C: Free riding is an economic concept about avoiding payment for benefits, not about riding a bus; the term is not literal.
Why D: Refusing to buy a good is a decision not to consume, whereas free riders do consume the benefits while avoiding payment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a sunk cost?
A: A cost paid to repair ships that sink at sea
B: A cost that is already paid and not recoverable
C: A cost expected to arise in the next year or two
D: A cost avoided by changing plans, as it is unpaid
Why A: A cost of ships is a play on the word sunk and is not an economic definition; sunk costs are costs already paid.
Why B: A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so it should not influence future decisions.
Why C: A cost expected next year is a future cost, which can still be changed; a sunk cost is one already incurred.
Why D: A cost that can be avoided is a future or avoidable cost; a sunk cost has already been paid, so it cannot be avoided.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company spent $50,000 on a design and now learns the product will lose money. What should it do about the $50,000?
A: Keep spending since the $50,000 cannot be recovered
B: Double the spending to try to win the money back
C: Ignore the future and focus on the past outlay
D: Treat it as sunk and weigh future costs and gains
Why A: Continuing to spend because of money already invested commits the sunk cost fallacy, since the 50,000 dollars is gone whatever happens next.
Why B: Doubling the spending adds more losses to a product that will lose money, and ignores that the earlier 50,000 dollars is already gone.
Why C: Ignoring the future is wrong, since decisions should depend on future costs and revenues; only the past, sunk spending should be ignored.
Why D: The 50,000 dollars is a sunk cost that cannot be recovered, so the company should base its decision on future costs and revenues, which show the product loses money.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is marginal analysis?
A: Comparing an action's extra benefit and extra cost
B: Comparing the past results with the present ones
C: Comparing total costs and ignoring the added benefit
D: Comparing two firms that sell to the same market
Why A: Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit of an action with its extra cost, and a person should act when marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Why B: Comparing past and present is a trend comparison, not marginal analysis, which looks at the additional benefit and cost of one more unit.
Why C: Comparing total costs only leaves out the extra benefit, so it is not marginal analysis, which weighs additional benefit against additional cost.
Why D: Comparing two firms is a competitor comparison and is unrelated to marginal analysis, which compares extra benefits and extra costs of an action.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Making a seventh slice of pizza gives you less satisfaction than the sixth. What does this illustrate?
A: Constant utility from each extra slice
B: Increasing marginal utility per slice
C: Diminishing marginal utility per slice
D: Perfect competition among pizza shops
Why A: Constant utility would mean each slice gives the same satisfaction, but the seventh slice gives less than the sixth, so utility is not constant.
Why B: Increasing marginal utility would mean each extra slice gives more satisfaction than the last, but the seventh gives less, so the pattern is the reverse.
Why C: Diminishing marginal utility means each additional unit gives less satisfaction than the one before, which matches the seventh slice of pizza being less enjoyable than the sixth.
Why D: Perfect competition is a market structure and has nothing to do with the satisfaction a person gets from eating slices of pizza.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is utility in economics?
A: The price paid for electricity
B: The benefit received from a good
C: A public water service company
D: The yearly profit earned by a firm
Why A: The cost of electricity is a price paid for power, not an economic definition of utility, which refers to satisfaction from consuming goods.
Why B: Utility in economics is the satisfaction or benefit a person gets from consuming a good or service, which helps explain why consumers choose what they buy.
Why C: A public service company is a utility company in everyday speech, but in economics utility means satisfaction, not a type of firm.
Why D: The profit of a firm is revenue minus costs, while utility measures the satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A bakery sells cakes for $20 each. Variable cost is $8 per cake and fixed costs are $1,200. How many cakes must it sell to break even?
A: 100 cakes, found by dividing $1,200 by $12
B: 150 cakes, dividing the fixed costs by $8
C: 1,200 cakes, found by using fixed costs
D: 60 cakes, found by dividing fixed cost by $20
Why A: Each cake gives a contribution of 20 minus 8, which is 12 dollars, so break-even is 1,200 divided by 12, which equals 100 cakes.
Why B: Dividing fixed costs by variable cost gives 1,200 divided by 8, which equals 150, but break-even requires dividing by the 12 dollar contribution per cake.
Why C: Using fixed costs of 1,200 as a number of units confuses dollars with cakes; break-even is 1,200 divided by the 12 dollar contribution, which is 100 cakes.
Why D: Dividing fixed costs by price gives 1,200 divided by 20, which equals 60, but each cake covers variable cost, so contribution of 12 is used, giving 100.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A cafe sells 400 cups a month at $4 each. Costs total $1,300. What is the monthly profit?
A: $2,900, by adding
B: $1,300, total cost
C: $1,600, the revenue
D: $300, net of costs
Why A: Adding revenue and costs gives 1,600 plus 1,300, which is 2,900, but profit is revenue minus costs, so the correct figure is 300 dollars.
Why B: Costs of 1,300 are not profit; profit is revenue minus costs, and revenue of 1,600 minus 1,300 leaves 300 dollars.
Why C: Revenue of 400 cups times 4 dollars is 1,600, but profit subtracts the 1,300 costs, leaving 300 dollars rather than 1,600.
Why D: Revenue is 400 times 4, which equals 1,600 dollars; subtracting costs of 1,300 gives a monthly profit of 300 dollars.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A product's selling price is $25 and variable cost is $10. What is the contribution margin per unit?
A: $10, variable cost
B: $35, found by adding
C: $15, price less cost
D: $2.50, from dividing
Why A: The variable cost of 10 dollars is what each unit costs to make, whereas contribution margin is price minus variable cost, which is 25 minus 10, equal to 15.
Why B: Adding price and variable cost gives 35, but contribution margin subtracts variable cost from the selling price, so it is 25 minus 10 equals 15 dollars.
Why C: Contribution margin per unit is selling price minus variable cost, so 25 minus 10 equals 15 dollars, which is available to cover fixed costs and profit.
Why D: Dividing 25 by 10 gives 2.50, which is a ratio and not a dollar margin; contribution margin is found by subtracting, giving 15 dollars.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A product sells for $40 and costs $28 to make. What percent of the selling price is the profit per unit?
A: 12 percent, using the dollar profit
B: 30 percent, profit divided by price
C: 70 percent, which is the cost share
D: 43 percent, found by dividing by cost
Why A: The $12 profit is a dollar amount, not a percent; dividing by the $40 selling price gives 30 percent, so 12 percent is wrong.
Why B: Profit is $40 minus $28, which is $12, and $12 divided by the $40 selling price equals 0.30, so profit is 30 percent of the price.
Why C: Seventy percent is the cost share, since $28 divided by $40 is 0.70, but the question asks for profit share, which is the remaining 30 percent.
Why D: Dividing $12 profit by the $28 cost gives about 43 percent, which is the markup on cost; the question asks about the selling price, so the divisor must be $40.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm's total revenue is $80,000 and total costs are $65,000. What is the profit margin?
A: About 81 percent, which is the cost share
B: About 23 percent, dividing profit by cost
C: About 1.9 percent, moving the decimal
D: About 18.75 percent, profit over sales
Why A: Costs divided by revenue is $65,000 over $80,000, about 81 percent, which is the cost share; profit margin is the profit share, so this is wrong.
Why B: Profit is $15,000, and dividing by costs of $65,000 gives about 23 percent, which is the markup on cost; margin uses revenue of $80,000 as the divisor instead.
Why C: About 1.9 percent comes from misplacing the decimal point; $15,000 divided by $80,000 is 0.1875, which is 18.75 percent, not 1.9 percent.
Why D: Profit is $80,000 minus $65,000, or $15,000, and $15,000 divided by $80,000 equals 0.1875, so the profit margin is 18.75 percent of revenue.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store marks up an item 25 percent of cost. The item costs $60. What is the selling price?
A: $85, found by adding 25
B: $15, which is the markup
C: $75, cost plus a markup
D: $60, ignoring the markup
Why A: Adding 25 dollars to the cost mixes a percent with dollars; a 25 percent markup on $60 is $15, so the price is $75, not $85.
Why B: Fifteen dollars is only the markup amount, which is 25 percent of $60; the selling price must add this markup back to the $60 cost.
Why C: Markup is 25 percent of $60, which is $15, and adding it to the $60 cost gives a selling price of $75.
Why D: Sixty dollars is just the cost; with a 25 percent markup of $15 added, the item must sell for $75, so ignoring the markup is wrong.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An item sells for $90 after a 25 percent markup on cost. What was the cost?
A: $72, found by dividing by 1.25
B: $112.50, found by adding 25 percent
C: $65, by subtracting 25 dollars
D: $67.50, taking 25 percent off
Why A: Selling price equals cost times 1.25, so cost is $90 divided by 1.25, which equals $72; check that $72 plus 25 percent ($18) gives $90.
Why B: Adding 25 percent to the $90 price gives $112.50, but the markup applies to cost, not price; the cost must be smaller than $90, not larger.
Why C: Subtracting 25 dollars treats the markup as a flat dollar amount; the markup is 25 percent of cost, so dividing $90 by 1.25 gives $72, not $65.
Why D: Taking 25 percent off $90 gives $67.50, but the markup was a percent of cost, not of price; $67.50 times 1.25 is only $84.38, not $90.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A retailer sells a TV for $500 that cost $400. What is the markup as a percent of cost?
A: 25 percent, markup divided by the cost
B: 80 percent, which is the cost share
C: 20 percent, markup divided by price
D: 100 percent, found by dividing by $100
Why A: Markup is $500 minus $400, which is $100, and $100 divided by the $400 cost equals 0.25, so the markup on cost is 25 percent.
Why B: Eighty percent is the cost share of the price, since $400 divided by $500 is 0.80; the markup percent divides the $100 markup by cost instead.
Why C: Dividing the $100 markup by the $500 selling price gives 20 percent, which is the margin on price; the question asks for markup on cost, so use $400.
Why D: One hundred percent would mean the markup equals the cost; the markup is $100 and cost is $400, so the ratio is 25 percent, not 100.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shirt priced at $40 is on sale at 30 percent off. What is the sale price?
A: $12, the discount alone
B: $52, found by adding 12
C: $28, after the discount
D: $10, found by taking 30
Why A: Twelve dollars is the discount amount, 30 percent of $40, not the sale price; the sale price subtracts the discount from $40 to give $28.
Why B: Fifty-two dollars adds the discount instead of subtracting it; a sale lowers the price, so $40 minus $12 gives $28, which is below the original price.
Why C: Thirty percent of $40 is $12, and $40 minus $12 equals $28, so the sale price is $28.
Why D: Subtracting 30 dollars treats the percent as a dollar amount; the discount is 30 percent of $40, which is $12, so the sale price is $28, not $10.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A store sells a $60 item at 25 percent off and then takes an additional 10 percent off the sale price. What is the final price?
A: $45, after just 25 percent off
B: $40.50, after both discounts
C: $50, found by taking 10 off
D: $39, by taking 35 percent off
Why A: Forty-five dollars is the price after only the first 25 percent discount; the extra 10 percent off the sale price must still be taken from $45.
Why B: Twenty-five percent off $60 leaves $45, and a further 10 percent off $45 is $4.50 less, so the final price is $40.50.
Why C: Fifty dollars takes a flat 10 dollars off the original price; the discounts are percents applied in turn, giving $45 and then $40.50, not $50.
Why D: Taking 35 percent off $60 gives $39, but the 10 percent applies to the already reduced $45 price, not the original, so discounts do not simply add.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?
A: They are the same figure in the income report
B: Net profit comes before gross profit in reports
C: Gross profit includes taxes and other expenses
D: Gross is sales less COGS; net also less costs
Why A: Gross and net profit are different measures; gross profit subtracts only cost of goods sold, while net profit also subtracts operating expenses and taxes, so they are not the same.
Why B: Net profit is calculated after gross profit, because it starts from gross profit and then subtracts further expenses and taxes, so net cannot come before gross.
Why C: Taxes are subtracted only when moving from gross profit to net profit; gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, with no taxes involved.
Why D: Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, and net profit goes further by also subtracting operating expenses and taxes, which is exactly the difference between them.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A shop has sales of $90,000, cost of goods sold of $54,000 and operating expenses of $20,000. What is the net operating profit?
A: $16,000, net of costs
B: $54,000, which is COGS
C: $36,000, gross profit
D: $164,000, from adding
Why A: Gross profit is $90,000 minus $54,000, which is $36,000, and subtracting $20,000 of operating expenses leaves a net operating profit of $16,000.
Why B: Fifty-four thousand dollars is the cost of goods sold, one input to the calculation, not the result; net operating profit also uses sales and operating expenses.
Why C: Thirty-six thousand dollars is gross profit, sales less cost of goods sold; net operating profit also subtracts the $20,000 of operating expenses, leaving $16,000.
Why D: Adding all three figures gives $164,000, but profit is found by subtracting costs from sales, so $90,000 minus $54,000 minus $20,000 equals $16,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is cost of goods sold (COGS)?
A: The price charged to customers for the goods sold
B: All expenses of the firm, both direct and indirect
C: The profit made on the goods after taxes are paid
D: The direct cost of making or buying the goods sold
Why A: That describes the selling price or sales revenue, which is what customers pay; cost of goods sold is what the firm itself pays to make or buy the goods.
Why B: All expenses of the firm would include rent, wages and other operating costs; cost of goods sold covers only the direct cost of the goods sold.
Why C: The profit on the goods is sales minus cost of goods sold, so profit is the result of using COGS, not what COGS itself means.
Why D: Cost of goods sold is the direct cost of producing or buying the goods that a firm sells, such as materials and direct labor or purchase cost.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is operating expense?
A: The profit made by the business in a year
B: The selling price of a product in a shop
C: Costs of running the firm, such as rent
D: The cost of the raw materials for goods
Why A: Profit is what remains after subtracting expenses from revenue, so it is a result and not a cost; operating expense is a cost of running the business.
Why B: The price of a product is what customers pay and counts as revenue; operating expense is a cost the business pays to keep running.
Why C: Operating expenses are the costs of running the business beyond the cost of goods, such as rent and wages, which are not tied directly to producing items.
Why D: Raw materials are part of the cost of goods sold, not operating expense; operating expense is broader overhead such as rent, wages and utilities.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm sells 1,000 units. Total fixed cost is $5,000 and variable cost per unit is $3. What is the average total cost per unit?
B: $8 a unit
Why A: Five dollars is the fixed cost per unit, $5,000 divided by 1,000. Adding the $3 variable cost per unit gives an average total cost of $8.
Why B: Fixed cost per unit is $5,000 divided by 1,000, or $5, and adding the $3 variable cost per unit gives an average total cost of $8.
Why C: Eight thousand dollars is the total cost, $5,000 plus $3 times 1,000 units; average cost per unit divides it by 1,000 units to get $8.
Why D: Three dollars is the variable cost per unit. Adding the fixed cost per unit of $5 gives an average total cost of $8.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What happens to average fixed cost per unit as output rises?
A: It turns to 0
B: It goes lower
C: It climbs up
D: It stays flat
Why A: Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output, which shrinks as output grows but never reaches zero because total fixed cost stays positive.
Why B: Total fixed cost stays constant, so dividing it by a larger output gives a smaller amount per unit; for example, $5,000 over 1,000 units is $5, but over 2,000 units it is $2.50.
Why C: Average fixed cost does not rise with output; the same fixed total is spread over more units, so each unit carries less of it and the average falls.
Why D: Fixed cost per unit changes with output because the unchanging total is divided by more units; it is the total, not the per-unit amount, that stays the same.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a cost-plus pricing method?
A: Setting a price by the value customers see
B: Setting a price at zero to give goods away
C: Setting a price by adding markup to its cost
D: Setting a price from rivals' prices, not cost
Why A: Setting a price by customer value is value-based pricing, which looks at what buyers will pay; cost-plus pricing starts from the cost of making the item.
Why B: A price of zero would give away the product and cover no costs; cost-plus pricing sets a price above cost so that a profit is earned.
Why C: Cost-plus pricing takes the unit cost and adds a markup, such as 25 percent of cost, to set the selling price so that costs are covered with profit.
Why D: Pricing by rivals alone is competitor-based pricing; cost-plus pricing specifically starts from the cost of making the goods and adds a markup to it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is break-even revenue?
A: The sales level where total revenue equals total costs
B: Sales that give the highest profit after costs are paid
C: The sales level of a firm that has just gone bankrupt
D: The total sales made during a single day of trading
Why A: Break-even revenue is the sales level where total revenue equals total costs, so the firm makes neither a profit nor a loss at that point.
Why B: Maximum profit is a different goal; at break-even, revenue only just covers costs, so profit is exactly zero and not at its highest.
Why C: A bankrupt firm cannot pay its debts, which is a legal state; break-even is a sales level where revenue equals total costs, and a firm may reach it.
Why D: Break-even is not tied to one day; it is a sales level, in units or dollars, at which total revenue equals total costs over any chosen period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a margin of safety?
A: The yearly profit that a firm earns after tax
B: The number of staff that a firm needs to hire
C: The price set by the maker and shown on a product
D: How far sales can fall before a firm breaks even
Why A: Profit is revenue minus costs; margin of safety measures the gap between actual sales and break-even sales, which says how far sales can fall before losses begin.
Why B: Staff numbers have no link to margin of safety; the measure compares actual sales with break-even sales to show how much sales can drop before a loss.
Why C: A price set by the maker and printed on packaging is a recommended retail price; margin of safety compares sales with break-even and says nothing about price tags.
Why D: Margin of safety is how far sales can fall before the firm hits break-even, found as actual sales minus break-even sales, and it shows the cushion against losses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Break-even sales are 400 units and actual sales are 500 units. What is the margin of safety in units?
A: 900 units, found by adding
B: 200 units, from halving
C: 400 units, the break-even
D: 100 units, 500 less 400
Why A: Adding 400 and 500 gives 900, but margin of safety is the difference between actual and break-even sales, so 500 minus 400 equals 100 units.
Why B: Halving does not apply here; margin of safety subtracts break-even sales from actual sales, so 500 minus 400 is 100 units, not 200.
Why C: Four hundred units is the break-even point itself; the margin of safety is the extra sales above it, which is 500 minus 400, or 100 units.
Why D: Margin of safety equals actual sales minus break-even sales, so 500 minus 400 gives 100 units, meaning sales could fall by 100 units before the firm makes a loss.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A firm's revenue is $120,000 and its costs are $100,000. If costs rise 10 percent and revenue is unchanged, what is the new profit?
A: $10,000, after the rise
B: $12,000, from revenue
C: $20,000, the old profit
