Why D: Paying only 40 hours gives 40 x 12 = $480, but she also worked 4 overtime hours that earn 4 x 18 = $72 more, so the total is higher.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a payroll deduction?
A: A bonus for good work
B: A raise in hourly pay
C: A gift from the boss
D: Amount taken from pay
Why A: A bonus is extra money added to pay, so it increases earnings, whereas a payroll deduction is an amount subtracted from gross pay before the worker is paid.
Why B: A raise increases a worker's pay rate, so it adds to earnings, while a payroll deduction takes money out of gross pay, making these opposite in effect.
Why C: A gift is something given without payment, and it is not a systematic subtraction from a paycheck, so it does not describe what a payroll deduction is.
Why D: A payroll deduction is an amount subtracted from gross pay, such as income tax, Social Security or insurance premiums, which leaves the smaller net pay that the worker actually receives.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a pay stub?
A: A record of pay, hours and tax
B: A bank statement of deposits
C: A tax form for the whole year
D: A job application to a new firm
Why A: A pay stub is a statement from the employer showing gross pay, hours worked, deductions and net pay for one pay period, which lets workers verify what they were paid.
Why B: A bank statement lists account deposits and withdrawals from the bank, not the employer's breakdown of hours, pay and deductions for a pay period, so it is a different document.
Why C: A tax form for the year, such as a W-2, summarizes annual earnings and taxes, whereas a pay stub covers a single pay period with hours and deductions.
Why D: A job application is what a person submits to apply for work before being hired, so it has no information about pay, hours or deductions from a paycheck.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should workers review each pay stub?
A: To impress the boss and get a promotion this year
B: To check hours, pay and deductions for errors
C: To pay more tax than the law requires of them
D: To skip records since the employer has a copy
Why A: Impressing the boss is not the purpose of checking a pay stub, which exists to protect the worker's own money by catching mistakes in what was paid.
Why B: Reviewing each pay stub lets workers check hours, pay rate and deductions for errors, so mistakes such as missing overtime or wrong withholding can be found and corrected quickly.
Why C: Reviewing a stub does not make anyone pay more tax, because taxes are set by law and withholding, and checking only confirms the amounts are correct.
Why D: Workers should keep records of earnings and compare them with stubs, and relying on the employer's copy would leave them unable to prove errors, so avoiding records is poor advice.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an elevator pitch for a job seeker?
A: A job application form with a cover letter and references
B: A speech given inside an elevator to a hiring manager
C: A short summary of you and what you offer, in 30 seconds
D: A long report presented to investors over several hours
Why A: A job application is a written form submitted to an employer, whereas an elevator pitch is a brief spoken introduction of yourself, so these are different tools.
Why B: An elevator pitch is not limited to elevators, because it can be used at networking events or fairs, and the name refers to its brevity, not its location.
Why C: An elevator pitch is a short summary of who you are and what you offer, delivered in about 30 seconds so that a listener quickly understands your value as a candidate.
Why D: A long report to investors over several hours is the opposite of an elevator pitch, which must be brief, personal and focused on a job seeker's strengths.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a career counselor do?
A: Hires staff for a firm after reading resumes
B: Pays wages to the staff of a firm each month
C: Sets taxes for firms and workers in the state
D: Helps people explore careers and plan a path
Why A: Hiring employees is the job of an employer or recruiter, while a career counselor works with people to explore careers, so this describes a different role.
Why B: Paying wages is the duty of an employer or payroll department, and a career counselor does not pay anyone, because the job is to advise people on careers.
Why C: Setting taxes is done by governments and legislatures, and it has nothing to do with the advising work of a career counselor, who guides people on career choices.
Why D: A career counselor helps people explore careers, match their interests and abilities to jobs, and plan the education and job steps needed to reach their career goals.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an applicant tracking system (ATS)?
A: A tool that trains staff for new roles in the firm
B: Software employers use to collect and screen applicants
C: A tool that tracks staff hours and attendance on the site
D: A tool that pays wages to workers by bank transfer
Why A: Training staff is done through training programs and instructors, not through an ATS, which is software that handles applications and not employee development.
Why B: An applicant tracking system is software that employers use to collect, organize and screen job applications, often filtering resumes by keywords before a human recruiter reads them.
Why C: Tracking employee hours and attendance is the work of a timekeeping or payroll system, while an ATS tracks job applicants during hiring, before they are employees.
Why D: Paying wages is a payroll function, and an ATS is a hiring tool that manages applicants, so it does not issue pay to anyone.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why might a resume include keywords from the job posting?
A: To make the resume longer so it fills the page
B: To hide experience from the employer reading it
C: To pass automated screening and show a match
D: To confuse the employer with unrelated words
Why A: Making a resume longer to fill the page is a poor reason, because employers prefer concise resumes, and keywords are chosen for relevance and not for length.
Why B: Keywords are meant to show your experience clearly and not hide it, so using them does the opposite of concealing what you have done.
Why C: Including keywords from the posting helps a resume pass automated screening software and shows a recruiter that your skills match what the employer asked for in the job.
Why D: The aim of keywords is to communicate clearly with the employer and show a match, so trying to confuse the employer would hurt the application instead of helping it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An interviewer asks about a weakness. What is a good approach?
A: Name a real weakness and explain how you improve
B: Name a weakness that makes you unfit for the job
C: Say you have no weaknesses that matter at work
D: Refuse to answer the question and change topics
Why A: A good approach is to name a real weakness and explain how you are improving, which shows honesty, self-awareness and a willingness to grow, qualities employers value.
Why B: Naming a weakness that makes you unfit for the job is honest but self-defeating, because it gives the interviewer a reason to reject you, and a better answer shows improvement.
Why C: Saying you have no weaknesses sounds unrealistic and lacks self-awareness, so interviewers may doubt your honesty, which makes this a weak answer.
Why D: Refusing to answer looks evasive and unprepared, and it gives the interviewer nothing to evaluate, so it is a poor way to handle a common question.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a typical notice period when resigning from a job?
A: Two years
B: Two minutes
C: None ever
D: Two weeks
Why A: Two years is far too long for a notice period, because standard practice is a short notice of a couple of weeks, so it does not match what employers expect.
Why B: Two minutes is not a real notice period, since it gives the employer no time to plan, and a professional resignation gives much more warning than that.
Why C: Giving no notice ever is not standard, because professional practice is to give notice so the employer can plan, and leaving abruptly can harm your reputation and references.
Why D: Two weeks is the typical notice period when resigning, giving the employer time to arrange a replacement and hand over duties while keeping a good professional reputation and references.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An interviewer asks, 'Why do you want to work here?' Which answer is best?
A: I don't know why I would want to work here now
B: Show you know the firm and how your skills fit
C: I have no other options so I apply to any firm
D: I need money to pay my bills and my rent today
Why A: Saying I do not know shows no interest or preparation, so it fails to give the interviewer any reason to think you want this particular job.
Why B: The best answer shows you know the company and explains how your skills fit, which proves you did your research and links what you offer to what they need.
Why C: Saying you have no other options and will apply anywhere makes you sound desperate and uninterested in this company, so it gives the interviewer no reason to hire you.
Why D: Saying I need money may be true, but it shows no interest in the company or the role, and so it does not persuade the interviewer to hire you.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas
